- `light/142.html:16`: <article class="prose light-prose"><p>Before sunrise, Carrow smelled like horses. Not only horses. Wet stone. Cold ash. Yesterday's beer outside a tavern that had closed recently enough for two men to still be arguing beside it. Bread somewhere I could not see. River damp under everything. But mostly horses.</p><p>I arrived at the theatre with my bag over one shoulder and discovered that I was late. I was not late. The sky was black. Teren had said before sunrise. This was before sunrise. The problem was that theatre people apparently interpreted departure times the way they interpreted scripts. The alley was already full.</p><p>One wagon stood backed almost to the theatre doors, canvas rolled over its top rails. Another waited crooked behind it with a horse that looked personally offended by the hour. Scenery leaned against both walls. A painted window rested upside down on a crate marked COSTUMES, and somebody had put three swords into a basket with a cabbage. I stopped. The cabbage was real.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>The soot-shirt worker looked up from a coil of rope.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>I pointed. He followed my finger.</p><p>"Oh."</p><p>He took the cabbage out.</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>He put it on a chair. That was not better.</p><p>"Gregory!"</p><p>Teren appeared in the theatre doorway carrying a lamp in one hand and a boot in the other.</p><p>"Why do you have one boot?"</p><p>"Not mine."</p><p>"Whose?"</p><p>He looked at it.</p><p>"No idea."</p><p>He threw it into the wagon. A woman inside shouted, "Fuck you."</p><p>"Found your boot."</p><p>"I was wearing the other one."</p><p>"Then you're halfway done."</p><p>Teren disappeared again. I stood in the alley with my bag. This was the organization I had joined. No. Not joined. Traveling with. Important distinction. The servant actor was sitting on the rear edge of the first wagon drinking something from a tin cup. He had a blanket around his shoulders and looked much less cheerful than usual.</p><p>"You came," he said.</p><p>"I said I would."</p><p>"People say things."</p><p>"What are you drinking?"</p><p>"Regret."</p><p>"Is it hot?"</p><p>"Not anymore."</p><p>He moved his cup and made space beside him. I did not sit.</p><p>"Where are the crutches going?"</p><p>He pointed toward the wagon rail. I inspected it. Someone had already tied a broom there.</p><p>"That is where you said."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"There is a broom."</p><p>"We'll move the broom."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>He looked at me over the cup.</p><p>"Gregory."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"The broom will survive."</p><p>I set my bag down. The extra cord was in the top section because I had planned properly. I found it immediately. That felt good. Then I spent several minutes trying to determine the best way to secure two crutches to a wagon that was still being loaded by people who did not respect fixed geometry. Every time I chose a position, someone needed the rail.</p><p>"That's scenery."</p><p>"I can see that."</p><p>"Then move."</p><p>"I am attaching mobility equipment."</p><p>The soot-shirt worker had one end of the painted tower on his shoulder.</p><p>"You can attach it after the tower."</p><p>"The tower blocks the rail."</p><p>"Only until we unload it."</p><p>"That is tomorrow."</p><p>"Exactly."</p><p>I stared at him. He stared back. The tower won. I moved. A second actor I knew mostly as a guard carried a crate past us.</p><p>"Put them inside."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>He jerked his head toward the wagon. I looked. The inside contained three people, four costume trunks, rolled fabric, a basket of kitchen things, two spears, one painted moon, and the cabbage. The cabbage had returned.</p><p>"No."</p><p>The guard shrugged.</p><p>"Then walk."</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>"Morning."</p><p>He kept going. The recurring woman arrived from the street carrying two bags and a long wrapped bundle. Her hair was tied up badly. She looked awake in the technical sense only. She saw me.</p><p>"You're here."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>"You told me there were shopkeepers in other towns."</p><p>She stared for a second. Then remembered.</p><p>"Oh."</p><p>She handed me one of her bags. I nearly dropped it.</p><p>"What is in this?"</p><p>"Shoes."</p><p>"How many feet do you have?"</p><p>"Depends on the show."</p><p>She walked into the theatre with the other bag. I looked at the one she had left me. It was heavier than my travel bag. The servant actor sipped his regret.</p><p>"Princess."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"Do you?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>I carried the shoe bag three awkward steps and put it beside the wagon. That counted as loading. Useful. The theatre emptied itself by degrees. Not neatly. Nothing came out in the order I would have chosen. A small table emerged before the legs that belonged to it. Costumes came before the trunk meant to hold them. A rolled backdrop was carried into the alley, returned inside because it was the wrong one, then brought out again because apparently the wrong one was coming too.</p><p>I stopped trying to understand the whole operation. That helped.</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>I turned. Teren stood beside the second wagon with a paper in his hand. Not Gregory. Greg. I waited. He looked at the paper.</p><p>"You're in this one."</p><p>"Which?"</p><p>"Second wagon."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"First is full."</p><p>"It was full twenty minutes ago."</p><p>"Now it is more full."</p><p>"Where do I sit?"</p><p>He pointed. There was no seat.</p><p>"There."</p><p>"That is a crate."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"What is in it?"</p><p>"Curtain weights."</p><p>"How heavy?"</p><p>"Enough."</p><p>"I am not sitting on curtain weights for three hours."</p><p>Teren looked into the wagon.</p><p>"Move the weights."</p><p>"To where?"</p><p>He looked around. I waited. Teren pointed at the first wagon. The servant actor shouted, "No." Teren pointed at the alley. The soot-shirt worker shouted, "No." Teren looked at me.</p><p>"You see the problem."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"That does not solve it."</p><p>"No."</p><p>He walked away. I hated theatre. A little later, the curtain weights went under the rear bench, the rear bench moved forward, two costume trunks traded wagons, the painted moon went flat beneath a stack of fabric, and the crate became a seat after all. Not the curtain-weight crate. A different crate. This one contained cups. I sat carefully. It held. Good.</p><p>My crutches were finally tied along the inner rail beside me, handles forward, cuffs wrapped in a scrap of cloth so the wood would not knock against the wagon every time we hit a rut. I had used one cord. The soot-shirt worker had watched me finish, tugged the knot once, and added a second knot above mine.</p><p>"What was wrong with mine?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"Then why?"</p><p>He had already walked away. I left both knots. The sky had begun turning from black to gray by the time the horses moved. There was no announcement. No speech. No count. Someone shouted that a lantern was still inside. Someone else shouted that it could stay there. The first wagon rolled forward anyway. Our driver swore. The horse moved.</p><p>The wagon lurched hard enough that I caught the rail with both hands. A cup inside my crate rattled. Then another. Then all of them. We rolled out of the alley. That was departure. I looked back once. The theatre doors were still open.</p><p>Teren stood in them with the lamp, shouting at someone I could not see. For one alarming moment I thought we had left him. Then he ran after the wagon carrying the unidentified boot. He climbed onto the back of the first wagon while it was moving. Nobody reacted. Carrow passed slowly around us. Shuttered shops. Dark upper windows. A baker carrying a tray through a side door. A woman sweeping yesterday out of a doorway.</p><p>The streets I knew looked narrower from the wagon because I was not choosing where to put my feet or crutches. I was simply being carried through them with cups under my ass. The city gate appeared. We went through. No one stopped us. Then Carrow was behind us. I turned forward. The road was terrible. Not immediately. For perhaps fifty yards it was acceptable. Then the paving ended. The wagon dropped into a rut. Every cup beneath me jumped. I jumped with them.</p><p>"Oh."</p><p>The guard actor sitting across from me opened one eye.</p><p>"First wagon trip?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>He closed his eye.</p><p>"This one."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>He smiled without opening his eyes. I adjusted my position. My left side did not like the crate edge. I shifted. My right foot needed somewhere to brace, but every useful surface already belonged to luggage or another person's boots. The recurring woman sat near the front with her back against a costume trunk, knees drawn up beneath a blanket. She had somehow acquired the cabbage. She was eating it. Raw. I watched. She noticed.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"You're staring."</p><p>"I was determining whether it was a prop."</p><p>She took another bite.</p><p>"It is now."</p><p>The cabbage had a bite missing from one side. I looked away. The road shook us east. For the first hour, nobody was interesting. This surprised me. Theatre people were extremely interesting inside a theatre. On the road they slept. The guard actor slept with his head against the side rail and woke every time it struck him. The recurring woman slept with the cabbage in her lap. A thin older man I had seen playing fathers and magistrates put his hat over his face and disappeared completely.</p><p>The driver did not sleep. Good. I tried to read page twelve. Impossible. The words moved. I knew they were not moving. That did not help. I got through four lines before the wagon struck a stone and the script hit me in the mouth. I folded it. The clerk could wait. The countryside east of Carrow was flatter than I remembered.</p><p>Fields spread beyond low walls and hedges, wet with morning. Smoke rose from farmhouses in thin gray lines. We passed a boy driving goats the opposite direction. He stared at the painted tower sticking above the first wagon. One goat stared too. The boy waved. Someone in the first wagon waved back with a severed wooden hand. The boy stopped waving. I laughed. The recurring woman opened one eye.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>She closed it. A mile later the servant actor climbed from the first wagon to ours. While both were moving. I watched him step onto the rear rail, catch the side of our wagon, and swing across the gap.</p><p>"No."</p><p>He landed beside the driver.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You cannot do that."</p><p>"I just did."</p><p>"That does not make it safe."</p><p>"It makes it possible."</p><p>"That is not the same thing."</p><p>He climbed over a trunk and sat on the floor near my crate.</p><p>"Move your foot."</p><p>"I only have one available."</p><p>"That one."</p><p>I moved it. He stretched his legs into the space.</p><p>"Why are you here?"</p><p>"King snores."</p><p>"The guard snores."</p><p>The guard opened his eyes.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You do."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You were."</p><p>"I was breathing."</p><p>"With your throat closed."</p><p>The guard shut his eyes again. The servant actor leaned his head against the crate. For a while we rode in silence. Then, without moving, he said, "Your sword was better late." I looked at him.</p><p>"At the market hall?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"You stopped trying."</p><p>"I did not."</p><p>He opened one eye.</p><p>"You did."</p><p>"I was still performing."</p><p>"Not what I said."</p><p>I waited. He closed his eye again.</p><p>"That is not useful criticism."</p><p>"Wasn't criticism."</p><p>"What was it?"</p><p>"Observation."</p><p>"Hessa does that."</p><p>"Who?"</p><p>"Never mind."</p><p>The wagon hit another rut. His head knocked against the crate. He swore. I smiled.</p><p>"Do you always travel like this?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"What changes?"</p><p>"Worse roads."</p><p>"That is not what I meant."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>He sat up and rubbed the back of his head.</p><p>"Sometimes we have three wagons. Sometimes one. Sometimes horses. Once a boat."</p><p>"A boat?"</p><p>"Bad."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Actors."</p><p>"That explains nothing."</p><p>"It explains the boat."</p><p>The recurring woman spoke without opening her eyes.</p><p>"He vomited on the king."</p><p>The servant actor pointed at her.</p><p>"Different king."</p><p>She smiled beneath the blanket. I looked between them.</p><p>"How many kings have there been?"</p><p>"Too many," she said.</p><p>"Four," he said.</p><p>"Six."</p><p>"Those two don't count."</p><p>"They wore crowns."</p><p>"One was a child."</p><p>"Still king."</p><p>The older man beneath the hat said, "Seven." Everyone looked at him. He did not move the hat. The servant actor frowned.</p><p>"Who was seven?"</p><p>"Pel."</p><p>"Pel wasn't king."</p><p>"Winter show."</p><p>"Oh."</p><p>The servant actor leaned back.</p><p>"Seven."</p><p>The hat remained over the older man's face. I looked at the road. This was apparently history. Not important history. Better. By the second hour my hands were fine. My shoulders were not. Neither was my ass. The crate had developed corners it had not possessed when we left. I shifted again. The recurring woman noticed.</p><p>"You can take the floor."</p><p>"I am not sitting on the floor."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Getting up."</p><p>She looked at the space beside her. Then at my crutches. Then back at me.</p><p>"Right."</p><p>No apology. No pity. She moved one of the shoe bags and pushed a folded blanket toward me with her foot.</p><p>"For the crate."</p><p>I took it.</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>"Don't make it strange."</p><p>"I said thank you."</p><p>"Exactly."</p><p>I put the blanket beneath me. Better. Much. I did not tell her how much. She knew. The sun came up properly. The fields turned gold-green. Mist stayed low in the ditches. Birds moved ahead of the wagon and then settled behind us again, irritated by the interruption.</p><p>At some point I realized I had not thought about mana since leaving Carrow. Then I had. Annoying. I looked at the road instead. The first stop appeared as a cluster of buildings around a crossroads, with a stable, a well, and an inn whose sign had lost enough paint that the animal on it might have been a fox or a burning dog. The first wagon pulled in. Ours followed. When we stopped, everyone became alive at once. Blankets came off. Bodies unfolded.</p><p>The guard actor climbed over me before I could object. The recurring woman stood on the wagon bed and stretched until her back cracked. The servant actor jumped down. I reached for my crutches. The knots were still tight. Both of them. Good. I untied the first. The second had pulled hard under vibration and would not loosen. I worked at it. Nothing. The soot-shirt worker appeared beside the wagon.</p><p>"Problem?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>He watched me pull at the knot.</p><p>"Problem."</p><p>"It tightened."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You tied it."</p><p>"I improved it."</p><p>"You trapped my crutch."</p><p>He climbed onto the wheel hub, reached over the rail, and pulled one short end I had not noticed. The knot fell open. I stared. He handed me the crutch.</p><p>"What was that?"</p><p>"Slipped hitch."</p><p>"Show me."</p><p>"Later."</p><p>He jumped down. I looked at the cord. Then at him.</p><p>"Later when?"</p><p>"Not now."</p><p>He walked toward the stable. The servant actor passed carrying two cups.</p><p>"Welcome to theatre."</p><p>"That was rope."</p><p>"Everything is theatre if Teren hasn't paid you."</p><p>I got down from the wagon. Right foot. Crutches. Weight. My body objected to becoming vertical. Not pain. Stiffness. A deep complaint through my back and shoulders, plus the unpleasant certainty that the crate had permanently altered the shape of me. I stood still. The recurring woman landed beside me.</p><p>"You alive?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>She walked toward the inn with the cabbage. I took one step. Then another. My body remembered walking. Mostly. Three hours. We had another three or four after this. I looked at the wagons. At the road east. At the cup crate. The servant actor came back and handed me one of the cups.</p><p>"What is it?"</p><p>"Regret."</p><p>I drank. Tea. Cold. Terrible. I drank again. The first wagon horse sneezed. Somewhere inside the inn, Teren was already arguing about food. I smiled into the cup. The road was awful. I was glad I had come.</p></article>

- `light/125.html:16`: <article class="prose light-prose"><p>Hessa had two threads. I disliked this immediately. They hung from the same wooden frame. Dark. Thin. One over the glazed tile beside the place my right forearm would go. The other farther away.</p><p>Not much farther. Enough. The gray cloth was folded on the side table. The copper was already out. Hessa was writing. I sat. She kept writing. I looked at the threads.</p><p>“Hands first,” Hessa said.</p><p>“I was observing.”</p><p>“Observe after I have your baseline.”</p><p>She finished the line.</p><p>“How are your hands?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>“Right calf?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>“Residual limb?”</p><p>“Baseline.”</p><p>“Phantom?”</p><p>“Ordinary.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Fingers?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Any urge to curl them?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Wrist?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>She held out her hand. I gave her mine. Right. She checked grip, thumb, fingers, wrist. Then left. Then residual limb.</p><p>Then the ordinary questions again in slightly different words because Hessa enjoyed catching lies I was not telling.</p><p>“Yesterday?”</p><p>“Theatre.”</p><p>“No magic?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Day before?”</p><p>“Lyssa.”</p><p>“No magic?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You understand that theatre using magic is not you using magic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good. I asked because your face did something.”</p><p>“There was a window.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I did not touch it.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>She went back to the table. I stared at the two threads.</p><p>“Why two?”</p><p>“Because one annoyed me.”</p><p>“That is not a scientific reason.”</p><p>“It is an excellent medical reason.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“The first test told me less about external effect than I wanted.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It told me more about your control than I expected.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That does not make the external result better.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You are saying that too quickly.”</p><p>“I still know.”</p><p>She pointed at the farther thread.</p><p>“This one is not for you.”</p><p>“Then why is it there?”</p><p>“For me.”</p><p>“That is irritating.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She rolled my right sleeve above the elbow. The charcoal mark today was not the same. Still wrist-side. Slightly higher. A short line. Not the circle. Not the old line. New enough. I noticed.</p><p>Hessa tapped the new mark.</p><p>“Use today's line.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She drew a second charcoal line on the glazed tile. One beneath each resting thread. The near thread hung approximately where the first had. The far one hung perhaps four inches beyond it. Both moved slightly while she worked.</p><p>One turned. Stopped. The other shifted sideways. Stopped. Hessa waited. I waited. She opened the door. Both moved. She closed it. Waited. She crossed the room heavily. The far thread trembled. Near one moved less.</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>“Table vibration,” I said.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You walked near the far leg.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“On purpose?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She opened the window a finger width. Both threads shifted. Near first. Far second. She closed it.</p><p>“Air.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She stood beside the apparatus without touching it. The near thread drifted slightly toward her sleeve. Then away.</p><p>“Heat.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Static.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Why are we doing this again?”</p><p>“Because I am not asking the same question.”</p><p>I looked at the two threads.</p><p>“You are comparing them.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is the same question with a control.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It is literally a control.”</p><p>Her mouth moved. Almost smile. Dangerous.</p><p>“What is the question?” I asked.</p><p>“Whether the thread closest to the altered region behaves differently from a second thread exposed to as much of the same room as I can manage.”</p><p>“That is a control.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I said that.”</p><p>“You said it was the same question.”</p><p>“It is related.”</p><p>“Everything is related if you talk long enough.”</p><p>I considered the horse. Did not say it. Good. Hessa put the copper in position.</p><p>“Rules.”</p><p>“Minimal draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Right forearm only.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Small localized alteration at the marked region.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Maintain underlying draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If instructed, REACH from existing altered region only, smallest extension toward the near thread.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No release.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No push.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No Barrier.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No hand, wrist, finger movement.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No increase in internal alteration.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop if it feels like force.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop if it broadens.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop when you say stop.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Far thread is not a target.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No attempt to influence both.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No attempt to compensate for room movement.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I paused.</p><p>“That last one was not in the first test.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Because now there are two.”</p><p>“Because now you know enough to be dangerous in a boring way.”</p><p>“That is rude.”</p><p>“That is medicine.”</p><p>She had me breathe normally for several minutes. I watched. Near thread moved. Far thread moved. Sometimes together. Sometimes not. Once both shifted left almost simultaneously. Once the near thread moved toward my empty chair before I sat.</p><p>Useful. Annoying. Hessa wrote everything.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat. Right forearm beside the near thread. Three quarters of an inch. Approximately. I did not measure. Hessa would kill me.</p><p>“Do not stare at the thread.”</p><p>“Where should I look?”</p><p>“My hand.”</p><p>She held two fingers above the copper.</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>“For you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I breathed. Ordinary. Phantom left heel present. No relevance. Right hand loose. No thumb. No fingers.</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I did. Minimal. Still strange. Less strange than months ago. More dangerous than it felt. Copper answered. Not strongly. Enough that Hessa watched it. Underlying draw stable.</p><p>“Shape.”</p><p>Small. Right forearm. Charcoal line. The altered response appeared. Localized. Slightly broader than the mark on the upper side. I reported it.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. No motor. No thumb. No left change. Hessa watched.</p><p>“How certain?”</p><p>“High.”</p><p>“Not maximum?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She waited. Long enough that I started wondering whether this was the entire test.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“REACH.”</p><p>Smallest extension. Toward the near thread. Not force. Not push. Not more. Different. The near edge became more distinct. As before. The alteration felt asymmetric. Toward the thread.</p><p>“Near edge sharper,” I said.</p><p>“Continue same amount.”</p><p>Same amount was impossible. I attempted not to change what I was doing. Copper shifted. Hessa's eyes moved. Not to me. Past me. Probably thread. I did not look.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>“RETURN.”</p><p>Immediately. I reduced the altered response. Near edge softened. Center dimmed. No elbow shift. No urge. No wrist. Underlying draw remained.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released. Ordinary arm. Hessa touched my wrist.</p><p>“Open.”</p><p>I opened.</p><p>“Close.”</p><p>Closed.</p><p>“Thumb.”</p><p>Moved.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Fine. Then she let me look. Near thread rested slightly right of its charcoal line. Far thread rested slightly left of its line.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“You tell me.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“You were not watching.”</p><p>“That was intentional.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So tell me.”</p><p>She checked my forearm again before answering.</p><p>“During baseline, both moved repeatedly.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“During your draw, both moved once.”</p><p>“Together?”</p><p>“Near first. Far followed.”</p><p>“Air.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“During shape?”</p><p>“Neither enough to record.”</p><p>“REACH?”</p><p>“The near thread moved toward your arm.”</p><p>My chest did something. Small. I hated that she saw it.</p><p>“The far thread?”</p><p>“Did not move at that moment.”</p><p>I stared. Hessa raised one finger.</p><p>“Keep it bounded.”</p><p>“What happened next?”</p><p>“While you maintained the same instruction, the near thread stopped. Then the far thread moved left.”</p><p>“Near?”</p><p>“Stayed.”</p><p>“So differential.”</p><p>“One differential observation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then keep it at one.”</p><p>I looked at the near thread. It did not move. Hessa continued.</p><p>“Controls are not magic truth machines. Continue.</p></article>

Today I removed the refinement question and asked for one continuous reduction.”</p><p>“All are reduction.”</p><p>“All involve reduction.”</p><p>“That is what I said.”</p><p>“No. You said they are the same count.”</p><p>“I said three.”</p><p>“You are trying to make a score.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>“I did not bring columns.”</p><p>“I am proud of you.”</p><p>“That sounded insulting.”</p><p>“It was mostly sincere.”</p><p>Mostly.</p><p>I looked at the fading charcoal line.</p><p>“So what did today answer?”</p><p>“That you can repeat the broad action under a slightly changed target without the two specific unwanted responses we saw before.”</p><p>“Broad action.”</p><p>“Deliberately reduce a small shaped alteration while keeping an underlying draw active.”</p><p>“That sounds less broad.”</p><p>“It is broad compared with precise control.”</p><p>“What would precise control be?”</p><p>“Not today&#x27;s question.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Does today increase confidence?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Does it change external effect?”</p><p>“It changes my confidence in considering it.”</p><p>My attention sharpened.</p><p>“That is almost clearance.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Scheduling?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then what changed?”</p><p>She looked at me for long enough that I regretted asking in that tone.</p><p>Then she answered anyway.</p><p>“I am less concerned that the moment you deliberately alter a draw, your only options are continue, lose the draw, or recruit some other pattern.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>That was more than I expected.</p><p>She continued.</p><p>“I have now seen you reduce an alteration while the draw remains. More than once. Under instructions that were not identical. Today you did it without the elbowward shift, without the finger urge, and without trying to repair the remaining edge separately.”</p><p>“So the next question is external.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She stared back.</p><p>“You enjoy this.”</p><p>“I enjoy accuracy.”</p><p>“You enjoy accuracy when it hurts me.”</p><p>“That is still accuracy.”</p><p>“What is the next question?”</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>“You know.”</p><p>“I have possibilities.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because then you will spend the next two days practicing a test you are not allowed to practice.”</p><p>“I cannot practice without mana.”</p><p>“You can rehearse decisions.”</p><p>That was offensive because it was true.</p><p>“I would only think about it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is not practicing.”</p><p>She gave me the same look Pessa had given me yesterday when I suggested choosing the route she was less likely to block.</p><p>Apparently my face was becoming a liability across professions.</p><p>I changed direction.</p><p>“How many living days?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“One?”</p><p>“One full day. No magic.”</p><p>“Then return?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Morning?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That sounds almost like momentum.”</p><p>“It sounds like a schedule.”</p><p>“What symptoms change it?”</p><p>“Any thumb tingling. Any finger-curl urge. Any involuntary movement. New weakness. Cold. Numbness. Pain. Anything in the left-side phantom pattern that is distinctly unusual for you. Anything you think is probably nothing but are tempted not to tell me.”</p><p>“That last category is too broad.”</p><p>“It is tailored.”</p><p>I sighed.</p><p>“One day.”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“That is shorter than last time.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Because today was cleaner?”</p><p>“In part.”</p><p>“What is the other part?”</p><p>“You tolerated the previous interval without delayed symptom.”</p><p>“That sounds like progress.”</p><p>“It is information.”</p><p>“You have an allergy to the word progress.”</p><p>“I have an allergy to you using it as permission.”</p><p>“I can progress without permission.”</p><p>“Not in here.”</p><p>That was fair enough to be irritating.</p><p>I rubbed my thumb against the crutch grip, then realized I was checking it.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Hessa noticed.</p><p>“Symptom?”</p><p>“No. Checking.”</p><p>“Stop checking.”</p><p>“That seems medically irresponsible.”</p><p>“Checking once because something feels wrong is useful. Checking every thirty seconds because you want certainty creates noise.”</p><p>I lowered my hand.</p><p>“You cannot possibly know I check every thirty seconds.”</p><p>“I know you.”</p><p>“That is not measurement.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She seemed completely comfortable with this.</p><p>“And then?”</p><p>“Assessment.”</p><p>“Not external effect.”</p><p>“I did not say that.”</p><p>I went still.</p><p>Hessa&#x27;s expression changed immediately.</p><p>Not alarm.</p><p>Annoyance.</p><p>“Do not do that.”</p><p>“Do what?”</p><p>“Turn an omitted answer into permission.”</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“You absolutely did.”</p><p>“I observed that you did not exclude it.”</p><p>“That is not clearance.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“This is humiliating.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I hated that word.</p><p>“External-effect testing is not cleared.”</p><p>“Or scheduled.”</p><p>“Or scheduled.”</p><p>“Casting?”</p><p>“Not cleared.”</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“Not cleared.”</p><p>“Left shaping?”</p><p>“Excluded.”</p><p>“Independent draw?”</p><p>“Not allowed.”</p><p>“Independent shaping?”</p><p>“Not allowed.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Now you may be pleased.”</p><p>“I was already pleased.”</p><p>“That was the problem.”</p><p>She wiped the charcoal from my arm.</p><p>I watched the black line smear, then disappear under the damp cloth.</p><p>“Can I ask one question?”</p><p>“You have asked approximately forty.”</p><p>“One more.”</p><p>“You will ask it regardless.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>She put the cloth down.</p><p>“What would make you decide not to test external effect?”</p><p>Her expression changed.</p><p>Small.</p><p>More serious.</p><p>“Several things.”</p><p>“Such as?”</p><p>“A delayed symptom.”</p><p>“Obvious.”</p><p>“A repeat control failure that looks meaningfully different from ordinary inconsistency.”</p><p>“Meaningfully how?”</p><p>“I will decide.”</p><p>I disliked that.</p><p>“Motor recruitment again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Broad familiar pattern?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Loss of ability to release?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That one landed differently.</p><p>I had not lost release.</p><p>Not once.</p><p>Still.</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>“If I decide we do not yet understand enough about what you are doing to make an external question worth the added uncertainty.”</p><p>“External effect is added uncertainty.”</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>“But isn&#x27;t that the point?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“The point is to ask a question we can interpret.”</p><p>That was annoyingly good.</p><p>“If something happens externally but we don&#x27;t know what internal change caused it, we learn less.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If nothing happens externally, we may also learn less.”</p><p>“Depending on the test.”</p><p>“So you need internal control good enough that external failure or success means something.”</p><p>Hessa&#x27;s mouth tightened.</p><p>I had gone too far.</p><p>Not wrong.</p><p>Too far.</p><p>“Approximately,” she said.</p><p>I wanted the rest.</p><p>I wanted the apparatus.</p><p>I wanted the exact threshold.</p><p>I wanted to know whether tomorrow&#x27;s living day was the last ordinary day before something new.</p><p>No.</p><p>That was not available.</p><p>I put my sleeve down.</p><p>Hessa watched me do it.</p><p>“You can go.”</p><p>“That was abrupt.”</p><p>“The appointment is over.”</p><p>“I am accustomed to more resistance.”</p><p>“To leaving?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That explains much.”</p><p>I stood.</p><p>Crutches.</p><p>Right hand normal on the grip.</p><p>Left.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>No dizziness.</p><p>No symptom.</p><p>At the door I stopped.</p><p>Hessa sighed before I turned.</p><p>“I have not asked yet.”</p><p>“You stopped walking.”</p><p>“That is not a question.”</p><p>“It is with you.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“What should I do today?”</p><p>She stared.</p><p>Then pointed toward the door.</p><p>“Live.”</p><p>“That instruction remains poorly specified.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>Outside, Carrow was offensively normal.</p><p>A cart had lost part of a load of onions near the corner.</p><p>Three people were collecting them while a fourth argued about whose fault it was.</p><p>A dog had acquired one onion and seemed disappointed.</p><p>I stood there longer than necessary.</p><p>One living day.</p><p>Then Hessa.</p><p>Maybe external effect.</p><p>Not scheduled.</p><p>Not cleared.</p><p>Maybe another control test.</p><p>Maybe draw only.</p><p>Maybe nothing.</p><p>I could build a decision tree.</p><p>I did not have the notebook open.</p><p>That was the only thing preventing it.</p><p>I started toward the Guild.</p><p>Not theatre.</p><p>Not because I had decided against theatre.</p><p>It was morning.</p><p>Rehearsal, if they were rehearsing, would be later.</p><p>Pessa might be working.</p><p>Lyssa might be working.</p><p>Jorren was certainly doing something he would refuse to explain properly.</p><p>The Guild would contain work I could accept or decline.</p><p>Food.</p><p>People.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Options.</p><p>My right forearm felt ordinary beneath the sleeve.</p><p>That was becoming an achievement I did not know how to value.</p><p>At the Guild entrance, I paused.</p><p>A posting board had three new slips.</p><p>Someone I knew only by face was arguing with a clerk about a route.</p><p>Two people came out carrying packs.</p><p>The day was already happening.</p><p>Tomorrow had a rule.</p><p>Today did not.</p><p>I went inside.</p><p>For once, that was enough.<br/></p></article>
- `light/385.html:502`: <p>Mana felt normal.</p>
- `light/207.html:730`: <p>I had not moved anything with mana.</p>
- `light/179.html:201`: <p>The mana came cleanly.</p>
- `light/179.html:258`: <p>The mana was already there.</p>
- `light/179.html:295`: <p>The mana held.</p>
- `light/179.html:341`: <p>Not mana.</p>
- `light/179.html:360`: <p>The mana went.</p>
- `light/278.html:146`: <p>The versions I remembered could make crossing the seam harder for air and water. Some later or better work had additional resistance to heat, smell, or mana leakage, but I did not know whether that came from the clasp, the collar, preparation of the vessel, or all three.</p>
- `light/133.html:16`: <article class="prose light-prose"><p>Hessa had removed the charcoal. Again. I liked that. Which probably meant I had developed opinions about blank forearms. Not ideal.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat. Morning baseline was boring. Excellent. Hands normal. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the vague way it usually was when I thought about it and less present when I did not.</p><p>No thumb. No fingers trying to participate. No unusual cold. No pain. Hessa checked anyway. She always checked anyway. Then she put the folded white towel beneath my right forearm. Copper sat farther up the table.</p><p>Not near enough to be interesting. I looked around. No threads. Still.</p><p>“Disappointed?” Hessa asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You looked.”</p><p>“I have eyes.”</p><p>“Tragic.”</p><p>I rested my arm. The outer forearm was unmarked. No charcoal target. No line. No point. Nothing to accidentally obey. Good. Hessa sat across from me with her notes. She had rewritten something. I could tell because one strip of paper had been pasted over another.</p><p>“What did you change?”</p><p>“My wording.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I wrote that you directed the edge wristward.”</p><p>“That is what happened.”</p><p>“That is what you reported.”</p><p>I looked at her. She looked back.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I hate your notes.”</p><p>“They are not for your emotional comfort.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>She put the pen down.</p><p>“Last time I told you the direction before shaping.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You reported a small asymmetry toward your wrist.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Today I want the same sequence with one change.”</p><p>“Elbowward.”</p><p>She stared at me.</p><p>“That was my guess.”</p><p>“Stop guessing.”</p><p>“You said one change.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“And opposite direction is the cleanest.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>I smiled. She did not.</p><p>“Your confidence is unattractive.”</p><p>“That seems unrelated.”</p><p>“It isn't.”</p><p>I stopped smiling. Mostly. Hessa touched two fingers lightly to the table near my elbow. Not my arm. Just direction.</p><p>“Elbowward.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not toward my fingers.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“You are indicating with your fingers.”</p><p>“I am indicating a direction. If I move my hand, the direction does not move with it.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“You understand?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“Toward my elbow. Not toward your hand.”</p><p>She moved her hand away. Good. No target. No destination. Only direction. That was cleaner. Probably. Hessa watched me.</p><p>“One draw.”</p><p>“One shape.”</p><p>“One directional instruction.”</p><p>“One RETURN.”</p><p>“One release.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No external question.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do not make the effect larger just to make it easier to report.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Report what happens.”</p><p>I breathed. Not special breathing. Just enough to stop talking.</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I reached. Carefully. The draw came more easily than it had weeks ago. That did not mean easy. It meant familiar. A narrow opening. A small pull. Mana. Contained. No broad flood. No rush into the left.</p><p>No fingers. No thumb. No urge to move my hand. I held. Hessa watched my face more than my arm.</p><p>“Stable?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. The temptation was to prepare for the next instruction. I noticed that. Then I noticed that noticing it was also preparation. Annoying.</p><p>“Shape.”</p><p>Neutral region. Outer right forearm. Small. Localized. Not direction yet. That mattered. I let the familiar alteration form. Not a point. Not a patch exactly. An area with an edge I could feel more clearly than I could describe.</p><p>The center changed first. Then the boundary became legible. Not visible. Mine. Internal.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Localized.”</p><p>“Size?”</p><p>“Small.”</p><p>“That is not size.”</p><p>“About the same as last time.”</p><p>“Comparison is not size.”</p><p>I almost opened my eyes. They were already open. I had been staring at the wall.</p><p>“Two fingers across. Maybe less.”</p><p>“Shape?”</p><p>“Uneven oval.”</p><p>“Already directional?”</p><p>I waited. Checked. Not pushed. Checked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Certain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>She wrote. I hated that too.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. The edge stayed. No broadening. No elbow pull. No wrist pull. Nothing external. Copper remained copper. Wonderful object. Hessa waited long enough that I started wondering whether she had forgotten the next instruction.</p><p>She had not.</p><p>“Smallest directional change toward your elbow.”</p><p>I did not move. That was the first thing. No hand. No wrist. No fingers. No shoulder. Inside. Elbowward. The previous wristward attempt wanted to become relevant. I tried not to use it. Impossible.</p><p>Memory existed. Fine. I did not reverse it. There was nothing to reverse. This was a new shape. Elbowward. For several breaths nothing happened. Or nothing I could distinguish happened. I felt the center.</p><p>The wrist-side edge. The elbow-side edge. The elbow-side edge seemed softer than the wrist side. Wrong. Maybe. I waited. Hessa said nothing. I wanted to fix it. That was dangerous wording. Not fix. Observe.</p><p>Then the elbow-side boundary sharpened. A little. I thought. The wrist side stayed where it was. The center stayed. Elbow side clearer. Not farther. Clearer. Maybe.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Elbow-side edge changed.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Sharper.”</p><p>“Extension?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Other edges?”</p><p>“Wrist side same.”</p><p>“Center?”</p><p>“Same.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Motor?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Force?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Broadening?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Left?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. The sharpened edge remained. Or my expectation of it remained. That was the problem. I knew what I was supposed to find. Hessa knew what I was supposed to find. The arm did not come with a second observer.</p><p>“Still?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Same?”</p><p>“I think.”</p><p>“Think or know?”</p><p>“Think.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“RETURN.”</p><p>I reduced. The elbow-side distinction softened first. Then the rest. The localized alteration diminished without sliding. No familiar broad response. No hand urge. No thumb. No fingers. No wrist. No elbow movement. Underlying draw stayed.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Reduced.”</p><p>“Gone?”</p><p>I checked.</p><p>“Maybe a little center.”</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. It faded.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Gone.”</p><p>“Draw?”</p><p>“Still.”</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released. The draw closed. Nothing chased it. Nothing jumped left. Nothing moved outside me. Hessa waited. Then checked my hand. Forearm. Wrist. Thumb. Asked about fingers. Asked about phantom foot. Asked about the left.</p><p>All boring. Excellent. She sat back. I looked at the copper. It had contributed nothing. Also excellent.</p><p>“Well?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“That is not an answer.”</p><p>“It is my answer to the answer you want.”</p><p>“What answer do I want?”</p><p>“That you can direct it.”</p><p>“I would accept that.”</p><p>“You would enjoy it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is why I am saying no.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>“So what happened?”</p><p>“You reported a small asymmetry toward the instructed elbow side under a direction-first condition with no prepared destination.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is the second time your report has favored the instructed side.”</p><p>“Opposite sides.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So.”</p><p>“So my confidence increases.”</p><p>I waited. She did not continue.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“More than last time.”</p><p>“That is not a number.”</p><p>“I did that intentionally.”</p><p>“Can I direct it?”</p><p>“I am not writing that.”</p><p>“Can I probably direct it?”</p><p>“I am not writing that either.”</p><p>“What are you writing?”</p><p>She turned the page enough that I could read the line. REPORTED ASYMMETRY FOLLOWED OPPOSITE INSTRUCTED DIRECTION UNDER OTHERWISE SIMILAR DIRECTION-FIRST CONDITION.</p><p>Below it:</p><p>NO INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION. I read it twice.</p><p>“That is obnoxious.”</p><p>“It is accurate.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is usually why you dislike things.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at my arm. Nothing visible. Nothing externally measurable. Two reports. Two directions. Same problem. But not the same problem as before. That mattered. I wanted to do it again. Of course.</p><p>“Next time wrist again?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I have not decided.”</p><p>“We could alternate.”</p><p>“We could do many stupid things in orderly patterns.”</p><p>“That is unfair.”</p><p>“It is extremely fair.”</p><p>She closed the notes.</p><p>“One full no-magic day.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I am fine.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That argument should eventually help me.”</p><p>“It does.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“You get one day instead of several.”</p><p>Annoying. Fair.</p><p>“Then next assessment?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Direction?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I narrowed my eyes. She noticed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Everyone says maybe now.”</p><p>“Perhaps you are contagious.”</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>Hessa stood. Assessment over. I rolled my sleeve down. My forearm felt normal. My whole body felt normal. That should have been satisfying. It was. Also I wanted a third direction. There were not many useful directions on a forearm.</p><p>Wrist. Elbow. Up. Down. Inward. Outward. That was already too much thinking. Hessa waited until I finished my sleeve.</p><p>“Tomorrow is not an unrecorded assessment.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“Tomorrow is not an unrecorded assessment.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I got my crutches.</p><p>At the door she said:</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>I turned.</p><p>“If you go to the theatre, do not decide that acting counts as neurological training.”</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“The herb seller.”</p><p>“Oh, fuck all of you.”</p><p>Hessa smiled. Barely. I left. The bread seller was outside. I crossed the street before he could speak. He shouted anyway.</p><p>“LANDLORD.”</p><p>I kept going.</p><p>“MESSENGER.”</p><p>Better. I raised one crutch without turning. Probably rude. He laughed. I had no magic tomorrow. I had Hessa again after that. And I had two opposite directional reports that were not proof. Good.</p><p>I could live with that. For one day. Probably. I turned toward the theatre without deciding to. That was becoming a lie I told myself. Fine. I decided. The theatre doors were open. I heard voices before I reached them.</p><p>Not rehearsal voices. Argument voices. Better. Inside, the soot-shirt worker was standing onstage with a sword. Not a real sword. A prop. Long. Silver-painted. Ridiculous crossguard.</p><p>A red stone in the pommel large enough to purchase a small house if it had been real. The servant actor stood three paces away with both hands spread.</p><p>“It sounds stupid.”</p><p>“It is a sword,” the soot-shirt worker said.</p><p>“It is a legendary sword.”</p><p>“It is wood.”</p><p>“Onstage it is legendary.”</p><p>The recurring woman sat on the edge of the stage. Teren stood below with pages. Nobody noticed me for several seconds. I liked that. The servant actor pointed at the sword.</p><p>“It cannot sound like Teren.”</p><p>Teren looked offended.</p><p>“I do not sound like that.”</p><p>“You do.”</p><p>“I absolutely do not.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker saw me. Her face changed. Danger.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I said it immediately. She held the sword out.</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The recurring woman turned.</p><p>“Landlord.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Teren looked at his pages. Then at me. Then at the sword. I should have left. I did not.</p><p>“What?” I asked.</p><p>The servant actor grinned.</p><p>“The sword talks.”</p><p>I looked at the prop. Of course it did.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>Everyone answered at once.</p><p>I caught:</p><p>“curse”</p><p>“king”</p><p>“third act”</p><p>“because it's funny”</p><p>and from Teren:</p><p>“Page forty-two.”</p><p>He held out the pages. I did not take them.</p><p>“What happened to whoever talks for it?”</p><p>“Nothing,” Teren said.</p><p>“He is standing right there,” the recurring woman said.</p><p>The servant actor pointed at himself.</p><p>“I hate doing both.”</p><p>“You have three lines,” Teren said.</p><p>“I hate all three.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker extended the sword another inch toward me.</p><p>“Voice it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I am not a sword.”</p><p>The recurring woman smiled.</p><p>“You were a person.”</p><p>“That was broader.”</p><p>The servant actor laughed.</p><p>Teren said:</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“Read the lines.”</p><p>“From here?”</p><p>“From wherever.”</p><p>That was suspiciously permissive. I took the pages. Page forty-two. Three sword lines. Not many.</p><p>The first was:</p><p>YOU HAVE DRAWN ME, LITTLE KING. TRY NOT TO EMBARRASS US BOTH. I read it silently. Then again. The line was stupid. I liked it. No. The servant actor climbed onto the stage. He took the sword from the worker.</p><p>Held it in front of him.</p><p>“Start before.”</p><p>Teren pointed. The recurring woman stood. Another actor moved into place. Apparently we were doing this. I stayed below the stage. Seated would have been smarter. There was a chair. I took it. Good.</p><p>Teren started them. The servant actor crossed. The recurring woman said something about the sealed tomb. The servant actor drew the sword. Held it up. Everyone looked at me. I looked at the line.</p><p>“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”</p><p>Silence. The servant actor lowered the sword.</p><p>“That is Greg.”</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>“The sword cannot be Greg.”</p><p>“Then use someone else.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker said:</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I looked at her. She shrugged. Apparently everyone had learned Teren's word. The servant actor reset. They started again. Sword came out. I tried lower.</p><p>“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”</p><p>The recurring woman made a face.</p><p>“Now it is Greg pretending to be old.”</p><p>“I am old.”</p><p>Everyone looked at me. Fuck.</p><p>“Older.”</p><p>The servant actor laughed. Teren did not. He was listening.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Third time. I stared at the sword. Wood. Silver paint. Ridiculous red stone. Legendary. Supposedly. What did legendary sound like? Wrong question. What did this sword want? Also probably wrong. I had three lines.</p><p>The first insulted a king. Not loudly. Not angrily. It expected to be obeyed. I hated that I knew the difference.</p><p>“Again,” I said.</p><p>Teren looked at me.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>The actors reset. The servant actor drew the sword. I waited half a beat longer than before. Not much. Enough that everyone was looking at the blade.</p><p>Then I said:</p><p>“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”</p><p>Different. The servant actor smiled. Not as himself. As the idiot king. The recurring woman looked at the sword. Not me. That was interesting. Teren tapped the page.</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>I had forgotten there were more lines. Of course.</p><p>The king said:</p><p>“You know me?”</p><p>Sword:</p><p>“I knew better kings.”</p><p>I said it. Too fast.</p><p>Teren:</p><p>“Again from sword.”</p><p>“I knew better kings.”</p><p>The servant actor flinched. Small. Funny. The recurring woman laughed. Not audience laugh. Actor laugh. She covered it badly. The servant actor pointed the sword toward me.</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>“That is not in the play.”</p><p>“It should be.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker said:</p><p>“Keep it.”</p><p>Teren said:</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Everyone argued. I looked down at the third line. The sword apparently had opinions about doors. Of course. I wanted to read it. That was the problem. Not a large problem. A very small one.</p><p>Three lines. Wooden sword. No magic. No role. No casting. Nothing. I looked at Teren.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>He smiled.</p><p>“Page forty-one.”</p><p>That was more than three lines. I opened to forty-one. The sword had been talking before it was drawn. From inside the scabbard. Ridiculous. Excellent. There were seven more lines before page forty-two. One complained about darkness.</p><p>One told the king his grip was embarrassing. One refused to answer a question because the king had asked it badly. I looked at Teren.</p><p>“Who wrote this?”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“It is rude.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Constantly.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The servant actor said:</p><p>“You like it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You moved your chair.”</p><p>I looked down. I had. The recurring woman leaned toward the sword.</p><p>“Ask it something.”</p><p>“That is not how scripts work,” Teren said.</p><p>She ignored him.</p><p>“Oh, great blade, should Gregory be allowed near a stage?”</p><p>I looked at the sword. Then at her. Then back at the line in front of me. There was no answer for that. Good. I lowered my voice slightly.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The servant actor folded over laughing. The recurring woman pointed at me.</p><p>“That one stays.”</p><p>Teren said:</p><p>“It absolutely does not.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker said:</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I was starting to understand how nothing ever got finished here. I moved the chair closer. Not onto the stage. Just closer. Tomorrow was no magic. Fine. Apparently I was a sword.</p></article>
- `light/397.html:178`: <p>"Mana load?"</p>
- `light/288.html:135`: <p>No mana.</p>
- `light/476.html:537`: <p>**ARTIFACT TEST ASSIST / CONTROLLED SHOP / STRONG MANA REQUIRED**</p>
- `light/275.html:175`: <p>I had used no mana.</p>
- `light/275.html:176`: <p>I was not going to use mana.</p>
- `light/129.html:16`: <article class="prose light-prose"><p>The threads were gone. I noticed before I sat down. The frame was gone too. No tile. No copper beside it. No white sleeve. No gray sleeve. Hessa had a cup of tea. This was worse.</p><p>“You stopped.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“You stopped the thread test.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat. She checked my hands first. Palms normal. No tenderness from yesterday. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the usual impossible way, mostly heel this morning. Thumb fine. Fingers fine.</p><p>Wrist fine. Grip. Again. Fine. Hessa wrote. I waited. She drank tea.</p><p>“You stopped.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There. I did not like how quickly she said it.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I reviewed the three attempts.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“The apparatus is not giving me enough interpretable signal to justify spending more of your safe attempts on it right now.”</p><p>I stared at the empty table.</p><p>“One failed replication.”</p><p>“One failed replication after two ambiguous attempts.”</p><p>“The second was better than ambiguous.”</p><p>“It was more interesting.”</p><p>“That is not the same word.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“The near thread moved toward me during REACH while the far thread didn&#x27;t.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is a differential observation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then the next test should repeat it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because we did.”</p><p>“Once.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is not enough.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then repeat again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I hated this. Hessa put down her cup.</p><p>“What answer are you trying to get?”</p><p>“Whether I moved it.”</p><p>“Can this apparatus tell us?”</p><p>“Eventually.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Then why stop?”</p><p>“Because your attempts are not free.”</p><p>“I am fine.”</p><p>“You are fine after the attempts we have done.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That does not make the next ten free.”</p><p>“I said one.”</p><p>“You will say one after that.”</p><p>“Only if it is useful.”</p><p>“You currently think another thread attempt is useful.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“I don&#x27;t.”</p><p>There it was. Jurisdiction. Annoying. Clean. I looked at the empty table again.</p><p>“So what did the three tests establish?”</p><p>“That thread moves.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“You asked.”</p><p>She ignored me.</p><p>“First, they established that suspended thread in this room is sensitive to more things than we can cheaply isolate.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Air movement. Heat. vibration. twist. static. position. breathing. room traffic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Second, they established that two threads exposed to much of the same room can still behave differently without your magic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Third, we observed one movement during REACH that was interesting enough to repeat.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“We repeated it.”</p><p>“It didn&#x27;t happen.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“That does not disprove it.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>I stopped. She waited. That was the problem. She was not saying impossible. She was saying not enough. Harder to argue with.</p><p>“Fourth,” she said, “the reliable part of all three external attempts was not external.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Your control.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You established the small alteration where instructed. You maintained the underlying draw. You attempted a directional change without broadening into the older response. You did not recruit your hand. You did not chase sensation when the apparatus did something interesting. You RETURNed when told.”</p><p>“Mostly.”</p><p>“What does mostly mean?”</p><p>“I argued afterward.”</p><p>“Afterward is allowed.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Your internal sequence is becoming more repeatable than the external observation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So that is what we test today.”</p><p>I looked at the empty space where the frame had been.</p><p>“Did you throw it away?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Where is it?”</p><p>“Cabinet.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because if I leave it out, you will spend the entire assessment looking at it.”</p><p>“I am looking at where it was.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That proves nothing.”</p><p>“It proves I know you.”</p><p>I did not answer. She pulled the three old pages from beneath a newer sheet. I recognized the white and gray labels in the margins.</p><p>“You kept the notes.”</p><p>“Obviously.”</p><p>“Show me.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you will argue with my abbreviations.”</p><p>“I can read.”</p><p>“That has not protected me before.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She turned the first page toward herself, not me.</p><p>“Attempt one. Single thread. Baseline movement. One movement toward arm during bounded external question, another later movement with multiple room confounds. No attribution.”</p><p>“Two movements.”</p><p>“I said one during the bounded question.”</p><p>“The other was still during maintained draw.”</p><p>“Which is why it is written down.”</p><p>Second page.</p><p>“Attempt two. Paired threads. Baseline differential behavior demonstrated before draw. During REACH, closer thread moved toward arm while farther did not at that same moment. Later farther moved independently.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Attempt three. Same general setup. During shape, closer moved away, farther moved shortly after. During REACH, no recorded movement from either.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She stacked the pages.</p><p>“If I only owned the second page, I would repeat.”</p><p>“You did.”</p><p>“If I owned the first two, I would repeat.”</p><p>“You did.”</p><p>“If I own all three, I have to ask whether a fourth attempt is the best use of your current tolerance.”</p><p>“And you decided no.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What would make you return to it?”</p><p>“Better reason.”</p><p>“That is vague.”</p><p>“A stronger external signal from some other bounded question. Better control. More mature shaping. A reason to think the thread&#x27;s sensitivity is useful instead of merely noisy.”</p><p>“Or time.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“So not abandoned.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>That helped more than it should have. I did not want the thread. I wanted the possibility to remain alive. It did. Annoyingly. I looked around.</p><p>“No apparatus.”</p><p>“Your arm is the apparatus.”</p><p>“That sounds medically threatening.”</p><p>“It should.”</p><p>She brought out the copper. Relief was embarrassing. Not because copper did anything important. Because it belonged to the sequence I knew. Hessa noticed.</p><p>“You expected it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You always use copper.”</p><p>“Not always.”</p><p>“Recently.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What does that tell you?”</p><p>“That you are predictable.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“No, that was an insult.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>She set it down well away from the old thread position. I watched her choose the place.</p><p>“Is that placement part of the test?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why there?”</p><p>“Because my tea is here.”</p><p>I looked at the tea. Reasonable constraints continued ruining elegant interpretation.</p><p>“What question?”</p><p>“Whether you can produce the same bounded directional change and RETURN at a different right-forearm target without an external object to pull your attention.”</p><p>“That is less interesting.”</p><p>“To you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Why remove the target?”</p><p>“Because I want to know whether REACH is currently an instruction you can execute internally, or whether the thread is part of what makes the response happen.”</p><p>I sat straighter. That was better. Not thread. Still a question.</p><p>“What direction?”</p><p>“Not toward the old thread position.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you have practiced that direction three times.”</p><p>“Two.”</p><p>“Three external attempts.”</p><p>“The first geometry differed.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She marked my forearm. Charcoal. Small target closer to the upper outer side than the recent wrist-near work. Not elbowward. Not the familiar broad direction. Different. I looked.</p><p>“Outward?”</p><p>“Toward that mark.”</p><p>“There is no object.”</p><p>“The mark is an object.”</p><p>“External object.”</p><p>“No suspended target.”</p><p>“You know what I mean.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can I look at it?”</p><p>“Before draw. Not during.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I want your report, not you steering with your eyes.”</p><p>“That is not how mana works.”</p><p>“Good. Then it should not matter.”</p><p>I disliked that answer. She checked position. Right forearm supported. Hand relaxed. Fingers visible. Copper was present after all. On the other side of the table. Not part of a thread apparatus. Just copper.</p><p>Familiar. Hessa placed two fingers above the new charcoal mark.</p><p>“Question is small.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One shape.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One directional instruction.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One RETURN.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If the response broadens, changes direction, recruits hand or wrist, produces thumb or finger symptoms, produces unusual left response, pain, cold, numbness, weakness, or anything you cannot describe, you stop.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No external effect question.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No spell.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No Barrier.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No proving anything.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“That one was unnecessary.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I did. Minimal. Copper answered. Right forearm. Stable. No hand. No thumb. No left.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“Shape.”</p><p>Localized. The altered region came slower than last time. Not much slower. Enough to notice. I said so.</p><p>“Continue only if stable.”</p><p>I waited. It settled. Small. Near the charcoal mark but not on it.</p><p>“Location?”</p><p>I described it. Hessa touched the skin outside the region. No change.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>Held. Then she moved her fingers. Not toward the mark. Away. Two inches farther up and outward. I looked at her.</p><p>“That is not the mark.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You said toward the mark.”</p><p>“I changed the instruction.”</p><p>“That seems bad.”</p><p>“Can you follow it?”</p><p>Maybe. That was different. Not REACH toward something. REACH from the altered region toward a direction Hessa indicated in space over my arm. No thread. No fixed destination. Just direction.</p><p>“Smallest extension,” she said. “Toward my fingers. No force. Maintain draw.”</p><p>I did. Or tried. The near edge sharpened. Wrong edge. Toward the charcoal mark. I stopped.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“It went toward the mark.”</p><p>“Did you intend that?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Stop directional instruction. Hold.”</p><p>Held. Interesting. Bad. Interesting. She moved her fingers away.</p><p>“RETURN.”</p><p>I returned. The alteration reduced. Underlying draw remained. No hand. No thumb. No broadening.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>Held.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>Released. Hessa checked everything. Again. Fine. I looked at the charcoal mark.</p><p>“You tricked me.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You established a target and then changed it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That was intentional.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So you were testing whether I was following the instruction or the prepared target.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is a trick.”</p><p>“It is a test.”</p><p>“You could have told me.”</p><p>“That would change the test.”</p><p>I hated that she was right. Mostly.</p><p>“What did I do?”</p><p>“You shaped near the prepared target.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“When I redirected the directional instruction, your first altered edge sharpened toward the prepared target instead of toward my indicated direction.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So I failed.”</p><p>“You did not execute the changed direction as instructed.”</p><p>“That is failure.”</p><p>“For that question, yes.”</p><p>Clean. Again. I appreciated it. Also hated it.</p><p>“Did the altered region move at all?”</p><p>“The edge changed.”</p><p>“Toward the prepared mark.”</p><p>“By your report.”</p><p>“You did not feel it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Copper?”</p><p>“Changed with draw and shape. Nothing I would distinguish during the directional instruction.”</p><p>“So no independent confirmation.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Could I have simply reported what I expected?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“That is a problem.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You believe me?”</p><p>“I believe you are trying to report accurately.”</p><p>“That is not the same.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. More problems. I had missed having enough problems.</p><p>“Can you touch the edge while I do it?”</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Contact changes sensation.”</p><p>“Could still be useful.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then next time.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You hate commitments.”</p><p>“I make them when I have enough information.”</p><p>“That is a lie. You committed to no magic tomorrow very quickly.”</p><p>“That decision has excellent evidence.”</p><p>I laughed despite myself. She wrote something.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You wrote because I laughed.”</p><p>“I wrote because your hand stayed relaxed while you laughed.”</p><p>I looked at my right hand. Still open on the support.</p><p>“That matters?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You just did it.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Made everything information.”</p><p>“Everything is information.”</p><p>“That is convenient.”</p><p>“Only if I don&#x27;t care what it says.”</p><p>I recognized that. She knew I recognized it. Neither of us mentioned the last time.</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“I don&#x27;t know yet.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“It may mean the prepared target strongly organizes what you are doing.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It may mean changing directional instruction after shaping is harder than beginning with the intended direction.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It may mean you anticipated the old sequence.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It may mean my instruction was poor.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“One attempt.”</p><p>“I am fine.”</p><p>“One attempt.”</p><p>“But this is internal.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And it failed.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So repeat.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because failure is data before it is an invitation.”</p><p>That sentence was offensive. I leaned back.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“No magic.”</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How many days?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“Then assessment?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What are you going to test?”</p><p>“I don&#x27;t know.”</p><p>“You absolutely know.”</p><p>“I have questions.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She picked up her tea. Cold now, probably.</p><p>“Today I learned something I did not know.”</p><p>“That I follow charcoal instead of fingers.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“That sounds stupid.”</p><p>“It sounds like learning.”</p><p>“I knew the charcoal was the target.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>I stopped. She drank. I thought about it. I had built the shape around the mark before she changed the instruction. Of course the response favored it. Maybe. Or I had simply failed to redirect.</p><p>Or REACH was not direction at all and I had been interpreting noise. Or the thread had mattered. Or Hessa&#x27;s fingers were a terrible target. Many possibilities. I started listing them. Hessa held up a hand.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I have four.”</p><p>“Keep them.”</p><p>“I can tell you.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You do not know mine.”</p><p>“I know enough.”</p><p>“That is arrogant.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Fair. I looked at my forearm. Charcoal still there. Nothing else.</p><p>“Are we farther from external effect than we were?”</p><p>“That is not how I would describe it.”</p><p>“How would you?”</p><p>“We stopped spending attempts on a poor measurement.”</p><p>“That is farther.”</p><p>“It is different.”</p><p>“It feels farther.”</p><p>She considered that.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Good. At least she allowed that. I expected the feeling to disappear once named. It did not. Three days ago I had been staring at a thread that might have moved because of me.</p><p>Today Hessa had put the thread in a cabinet and made me fail to follow two fingers. Objectively, that felt like retreat. Also objectively, my arm had done something small on command and then stopped when told.</p><p>Again. The second fact was less exciting. It was also the one Hessa trusted. I knew which one I preferred. That did not change which one she trusted. I rubbed neither arm. Kept hands still.</p><p>Not because instructed. Habit.</p><p>“Am I getting better?”</p><p>“At the parts we can currently observe reliably.”</p><p>“That is a Hessa answer.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Which parts?”</p><p>“Minimal draw. Localized shaping. maintaining draw while altering. RETURN. avoiding the older broad response. avoiding motor recruitment.”</p><p>“Directional control?”</p><p>“Unclear.”</p><p>“External?”</p><p>“Unestablished.”</p><p>“Casting?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I sighed. She smiled. Actually smiled. Small. Cruel woman.</p><p>“Go live tomorrow.”</p><p>“I lived yesterday.”</p><p>“You were a messenger.”</p><p>I froze. Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“How do you know that?”</p><p>“Teren&#x27;s sister buys herbs from the woman downstairs.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“She mentioned the theatre had acquired a tall messenger on crutches who forgot his letter.”</p><p>I closed my eyes. No. Absolutely not.</p><p>“That was rehearsal.”</p><p>“I assumed.”</p><p>“I was not acquired.”</p><p>“I assumed.”</p><p>“I am not a messenger.”</p><p>“You were yesterday.”</p><p>“For thirty minutes.”</p><p>“That seems sufficient.”</p><p>“This city is too small.”</p><p>“Carrow is not small.”</p><p>“Then people need to stop talking.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stood. She pointed at my forearm.</p><p>“Wash the charcoal off later.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No magic tomorrow.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No practicing directional attention.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“You know exactly what it means.”</p><p>“I cannot stop looking at things.”</p><p>“You can stop sitting at a table trying to recreate today&#x27;s task without mana.”</p><p>“That would not be magic.”</p><p>“It would be rehearsal.”</p><p>I stared. She raised an eyebrow. I refused to give her that.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I left. Outside, the morning had become bright. Not warm. Bright. I walked three streets before realizing I was heading toward the theatre. I stopped. Hessa tomorrow was no magic. Theatre was allowed. That was not why I had turned.</p><p>Probably. I looked west. Then east. Then at the street ahead. No test. No conclusion. No thread. My right forearm felt completely ordinary. I went to buy lunch.</p><p>At the bread stall, the seller said:</p><p>“Messenger.”</p><p>I nearly left Carrow.</p></article>
- `light/114.html:16`: <article class="prose light-prose"><p>I told Hessa about the fire because she asked why my green shirt smelled like smoke.</p><p>I was not wearing the green shirt.</p><p>This was unfair.</p><p>“You smelled it yesterday?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then how do you know?”</p><p>“Keeper told Nerin. down.”</p><p>“You think I moved because I was aiming visually.”</p><p>“I think movement was one thing that happened.”</p><p>“Not necessarily cause.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“You're training
