table.</p><p>No curved one.</p><p>A shallow ceramic dish sat beside it.</p><p>Empty.</p><p>I looked at the dish.</p><p>“What is that?”</p><p>“A dish.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“What is it for?”</p><p>“Nothing yet.”</p><p>I hated nothing yet.</p><p>It had become a whole category of threat.</p><p>Hessa sat across from me.</p><p>“Today's test is one attempt.”</p><p>I stopped joking.</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Even if nothing happens?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Even if I fail immediately?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Even if I succeed?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That last one mattered.</p><p>I nodded.</p><p>“Instruction?”</p><p>“Minimal draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Hold stable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then make one deliberate alteration toward the marked point.”</p><p>“Into the hand?”</p><p>“Toward the marked point.”</p><p>“How localized?”</p><p>“Smaller than the whole hand.”</p><p>“That is generous.”</p><p>“It is deliberately less precise than the thumb instruction.”</p><p>I thought about that.</p><p>“You changed difficulty.”</p><p>“I changed the question.”</p><p>“Which is?”</p><p>“Whether you can make a deliberate unfamiliar alteration toward a new intact-side target without immediately falling into the same broader pattern we saw before.”</p><p>There.</p><p>Clean.</p><p>Not whether I could make perfect finger magic.</p><p>Not whether Barrier was broken.</p><p>Not whether my left leg had magical ghosts.</p><p>One question.</p><p>“Why less precise?”</p><p>“Because if you fail a harder task twice in two different ways, I learn less than you think.”</p><p>“That sounds wrong.”</p><p>“It isn't.”</p><p>“It feels wrong.”</p><p>“That is allowed.”</p><p>“What counts as failure?”</p><p>“I am not giving you a score.”</p><p>“What counts as success?”</p><p>“I am not giving you a score.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She pointed at my hand.</p><p>“You attempt exactly one deliberate change toward that point. I observe. You report. Then we stop.”</p><p>“Can I stop first?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If I feel Barrier?”</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“If the wrist rotates?”</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“If the thumb tingles?”</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“If anything hurts?”</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“If I think something is wrong?”</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“If I become spiritually offended by the dot?”</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>Unfair.</p><p>I breathed.</p><p>Not mana.</p><p>Just breathing.</p><p>I wanted this too much.</p><p>That was obvious.</p><p>My heart was faster.</p><p>Right hand warm against the towel.</p><p>Black dot near little-finger knuckle.</p><p>I had never trained a spell around that location.</p><p>As far as I remembered.</p><p>Memory was not perfect.</p><p>But no immediate pattern came with it.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Hessa lifted the copper strip.</p><p>“Ready?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I drew.</p><p>Mana arrived.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Familiar enough now that the arrival itself no longer felt like crossing a cliff every time.</p><p>Still supervised.</p><p>Still bounded.</p><p>Chest.</p><p>Shoulders.</p><p>Arms.</p><p>Right side.</p><p>Left thigh.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Nothing unusual below.</p><p>Ordinary phantom foot.</p><p>Right hand quiet.</p><p>“Stable?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do not look at the mark.”</p><p>I almost looked.</p><p>Did not.</p><p>“Now. One alteration. Toward the mark. Small.”</p><p>I reached.</p><p>Not with the hand.</p><p>That distinction was suddenly difficult.</p><p>The first instinct was movement.</p><p>Not Barrier exactly.</p><p>Something more general.</p><p>Move hand toward target.</p><p>Body solves physical instruction physically.</p><p>I held still.</p><p>Mana was not a liquid.</p><p>Except when it was useful to think of it like one.</p><p>Not useful now.</p><p>I tried again.</p><p>Not more draw.</p><p>Not more force.</p><p>Just change where the existing small amount felt gathered.</p><p>Toward the outside edge of the hand.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Then something.</p><p>A pressure?</p><p>No.</p><p>Attention?</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>Mana shifted.</p><p>Tiny.</p><p>Not to the dot.</p><p>Near it.</p><p>Or I thought near it.</p><p>The back of my hand felt denser in a patch perhaps two fingers wide.</p><p>No wrist rotation.</p><p>No forearm tightening.</p><p>No palm spread.</p><p>No Barrier.</p><p>My pulse jumped.</p><p>I stopped before excitement changed anything.</p><p>“Release,” Hessa said.</p><p>I released.</p><p>Gone.</p><p>My hand remained still.</p><p>The black dot remained offensively ordinary.</p><p>I looked at Hessa.</p><p>She was looking at the copper.</p><p>Then my hand.</p><p>Then me.</p><p>“Well?”</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Draw stable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I attempted to alter toward the marked point.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“First attempt produced nothing I could distinguish.”</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>“I stopped myself from physically moving the hand.”</p><p>Her eyes changed slightly.</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>“Second mental attempt.”</p><p>“Do not call it mental.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You made a magical attempt while holding your hand still. That is enough.”</p><p>“Fine. Second attempt within the same shaping attempt.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I felt a small localized change on the outer back of the hand.”</p><p>“How small?”</p><p>“Approximately two fingers wide.”</p><p>“Centered where?”</p><p>I looked.</p><p>Now allowed.</p><p>The black dot.</p><p>I touched nothing.</p><p>“Maybe half an inch inward from the mark.”</p><p>“Maybe?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Palm?”</p><p>“Nothing broad.”</p><p>“Wrist?”</p><p>“No rotation. No urge.”</p><p>“Forearm?”</p><p>“No engagement I noticed.”</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Tingling?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Heat?”</p><p>“Normal hand warmth.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Numbness?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Below-knee sensation?”</p><p>“Ordinary phantom foot only.”</p><p>She put the copper down.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I waited harder.</p><p>“You are enjoying this,” I said.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You could say one sentence.”</p><p>“I am writing several.”</p><p>“Out loud.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She finished.</p><p>Then looked at me.</p><p>“I observed a localized change.”</p><p>My entire body went still.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Outer right hand.”</p><p>“How localized?”</p><p>“More localized than the prior palm-and-wrist redistribution.”</p><p>“Did it move toward the mark?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How close?”</p><p>“I am not measuring distance that precisely.”</p><p>“But yes.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Copper?”</p><p>“Responded.”</p><p>“To the alteration?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Wrist?”</p><p>“Stayed still.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Forearm?”</p><p>“No obvious engagement.”</p><p>“Barrier pattern?”</p><p>“I did not observe the same familiar setup.”</p><p>There.</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>She raised a finger.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I am not doing anything.”</p><p>“You are turning this into a conclusion.”</p><p>“I made the intended change.”</p><p>“You made a change toward the intended area.”</p><p>“That is success.”</p><p>“It is one successful-looking response to one narrow instruction.”</p><p>“That is a very long way to say success.”</p><p>“It is exactly as long as necessary.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>Could not help it.</p><p>Hessa did not stop me.</p><p>That was suspicious.</p><p>“I did it.”</p><p>“You did something closer to what I asked.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>“Good. Language remains intact.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>Bad chair.</p><p>Best chair in Carrow.</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>No.</p><p>Still terrible.</p><p>“What does it mean?”</p><p>“One unfamiliar intact-side target did not immediately produce the same broad hand-and-wrist pattern.”</p><p>“Old Barrier pattern not inevitable.”</p><p>“Not established as inevitable.”</p><p>“That is what I said.”</p><p>“No. You made it stronger.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“One attempt does not tell us whether the prior pattern was Barrier, whether it was automatic, whether it appears only with some instructions, whether today's change would repeat, or whether you can do anything more useful than make a small patch of your hand magically different for a moment.”</p><p>“It was magically different.”</p><p>“Subjectively and by my observation, yes.”</p><p>“And copper.”</p><p>“And copper.”</p><p>I grinned again.</p><p>She sighed.</p><p>“Your standards are very low today.”</p><p>“My standards have adapted to circumstance.”</p><p>“That sounds dangerous.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>She took my right hand.</p><p>Examined.</p><p>Thumb.</p><p>Back of hand.</p><p>Wrist.</p><p>Grip.</p><p>Fingers.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Then she unfolded the towel and shook it once.</p><p>A little charcoal dust fell.</p><p>“That is the dish.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>The ceramic dish.</p><p>She put the used charcoal nub into it.</p><p>“That is what it was for?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You let me speculate.”</p><p>“You speculated without permission.”</p><p>“That is how speculation works.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>Cruel woman.</p><p>“What now?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“No waiting?”</p><p>“Waiting.”</p><p>“Here?”</p><p>“For a few minutes.”</p><p>“Then?”</p><p>“Then you leave.”</p><p>“No second target?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“No repeat?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Because one attempt.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Even though it went well.”</p><p>“Especially because you are excited.”</p><p>“That is not medical.”</p><p>“It is operational.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>I looked at the mark on my hand.</p><p>“Can I wash this off?”</p><p>“After we finish observing.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because washing involves using the hand.”</p><p>“I have used the hand before.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>We waited.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>No pain.</p><p>No weakness.</p><p>No cold.</p><p>No strange patch.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>The child from the other day was not in the outer room.</p><p>Someone else was.</p><p>Low voice.</p><p>Nerin moving things.</p><p>Street noise.</p><p>Carrow continued.</p><p>I looked at the wall crack.</p><p>Still there.</p><p>Probably not growing.</p><p>Not my problem.</p><p>Hessa said, “Move fingers.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>“Grip.”</p><p>Normal.</p><p>“Wrist.”</p><p>Normal.</p><p>“Stand.”</p><p>Both crutches.</p><p>Right hand to grip.</p><p>Up.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>“Walk.”</p><p>Door.</p><p>Back.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I sat.</p><p>“You're done.”</p><p>“That was fast.”</p><p>“It was not.”</p><p>“It felt fast.”</p><p>“You spent most of it arguing.”</p><p>“That does not count.”</p><p>“It counts to me.”</p><p>I looked at my hand again.</p><p>“Can I tell people I shaped successfully?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She stared back.</p><p>“What can I say?”</p><p>“You completed one supervised attempt in which you made a small localized alteration toward the target without reproducing the same broad pattern from the first attempt.”</p><p>“That is unusable in conversation.”</p><p>“Then say less.”</p><p>“I shaped.”</p><p>“You altered.”</p><p>“We are back here.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did I shape mana?”</p><p>Hessa considered.</p><p>This time longer than I expected.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The word hit harder than it should have.</p><p>She immediately continued.</p><p>“Once, in a small supervised test, without a spell.”</p><p>Still.</p><p>Yes.</p><p>I swallowed.</p><p>Not dramatic.</p><p>Just body.</p><p>Nineteen.</p><p>Magic had mattered before I died.</p><p>Magic mattered now.</p><p>Different body.</p><p>Same appetite.</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Say it again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cruel.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So shaping clearance?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Obviously.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Can I draw independently?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Can I practice the hand target?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Can I mentally rehearse it?”</p><p>“Do not deliberately rehearse the magical sequence.”</p><p>“Can I think about what happened?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Generous.”</p><p>“Write it in prose.”</p><p>“No table.”</p><p>“No table.”</p><p>“Could I make one later?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You cannot prohibit future tables forever.”</p><p>“I can try.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>Then the harder question arrived.</p><p>“Does this change what you think about casting?”</p><p>Hessa leaned against the table.</p><p>“A little.”</p><p>My chest tightened.</p><p>Not magic.</p><p>“What direction?”</p><p>“It makes me somewhat more confident that deliberate shaping may still be possible without every attempt immediately falling into an old trained pattern.”</p><p>“May still be possible.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is terrible optimism.”</p><p>“It is the amount I have.”</p><p>“Does it make you think I can cast?”</p><p>“It gives me one more reason not to conclude that you cannot.”</p><p>That was careful enough to hurt.</p><p>Also enough.</p><p>“Still don't know.”</p><p>“Still don't know.”</p><p>I nodded.</p><p>“What next?”</p><p>“Tomorrow no magic.”</p><p>I groaned.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you shaped today.”</p><p>“Successfully.”</p><p>“Do not make me regret the word.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“No recurrence of tingling so far. I want another ordinary day.”</p><p>“Then?”</p><p>“Come back the following day.”</p><p>“For another target?”</p><p>“Assessment.”</p><p>“Possible target?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“You survived the word before.”</p><p>“Barely.”</p><p>“What about Pessa?”</p><p>“Ask Pessa if you want movement work and your body remains at baseline.”</p><p>“Any objection because of shaping?”</p><p>“Not medically from what I see now. If hand symptoms return, tell me and use judgment before loading it heavily.”</p><p>“Use judgment again.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You are degrading.”</p><p>“I am adapting to circumstance.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>My own sentence.</p><p>Theft.</p><p>“I hate you.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Professionally.”</p><p>“Still no.”</p><p>I stood.</p><p>At the door I stopped.</p><p>“Right hand only still?”</p><p>“For shaping tests?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“For now.”</p><p>“Left remains not yet.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Because you don't want the missing-side question.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>Not fear.</p><p>Not hidden knowledge.</p><p>Just scope.</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Can you wash the dot off?”</p><p>“There's a basin.”</p><p>I went to it.</p><p>Water.</p><p>Soap.</p><p>Charcoal faded.</p><p>I noticed the hand moving.</p><p>Did not turn it into a test.</p><p>Mostly.</p><p>When I came back, Hessa was writing.</p><p>“Gone.”</p><p>“I can see.”</p><p>“Any significance?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>I left.</p><p>Outside, I wanted to tell someone.</p><p>Immediately.</p><p>This was not a subtle desire.</p><p>Jorren first.</p><p>No.</p><p>He would say I succeeded at hand failure.</p><p>Alden would ask twenty questions and then try to invent an audience.</p><p>Lyssa.</p><p>That thought arrived differently.</p><p>Not because she would understand the magical mechanics better.</p><p>She would not.</p><p>Because I wanted her to know.</p><p>Simple.</p><p>I started toward where she worked.</p><p>Then stopped.</p><p>Independent schedules.</p><p>She might be busy.</p><p>That did not mean I could not go.</p><p>It meant I could not expect availability.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>I went.</p><p>She was busy.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>I saw her through the open front of the shop speaking to a customer and holding up two lengths of ribbon.</p><p>One dark.</p><p>One pale.</p><p>Her natural hair made a soft dark shape around her head, and she stood taller than the customer beside her.</p><p>She saw me.</p><p>One glance.</p><p>Then back to the customer.</p><p>No rescue.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I waited outside.</p><p>Not directly in the doorway.</p><p>Learned civilization.</p><p>Five minutes.</p><p>Maybe ten.</p><p>I did not time it.</p><p>Eventually the customer left with the pale ribbon.</p><p>Lyssa came out.</p><p>“You're lurking.”</p><p>“I am waiting.”</p><p>“Suspiciously.”</p><p>“I shaped mana.”</p><p>Her face changed.</p><p>Not huge.</p><p>Real.</p><p>“You what?”</p><p>“Small.”</p><p>“What does small mean?”</p><p>“Hand.”</p><p>She looked at my right hand.</p><p>Everyone did this.</p><p>I held it up.</p><p>“Nothing visible.”</p><p>“Did it hurt?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Are you allowed?”</p><p>“Yes. One attempt. Supervised.”</p><p>“Hessa?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did she look angry?”</p><p>“Her normal face.”</p><p>“That bad.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>Lyssa smiled.</p><p>Then looked at me more carefully.</p><p>“You're happy.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was all.</p><p>No explanation.</p><p>No recovery speech.</p><p>No question about whether this meant I was fixed.</p><p>She stepped closer and kissed my cheek.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Jorren had said the same word.</p><p>Completely different.</p><p>I smiled like an idiot.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>I told her the short version.</p><p>Not Hessa's version.</p><p>“I had to move a tiny amount toward a charcoal mark on my hand. First time I tried shaping, it went wrong and started doing something that felt like Barrier. Today it went where I wanted. Mostly.”</p><p>“Mostly?”</p><p>“Close enough for Hessa to use the word shaped.”</p><p>“That sounds serious.”</p><p>“It is extremely serious.”</p><p>“Can you do magic now?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She laughed.</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>“I can do one useless tiny thing once under supervision.”</p><p>“Very impressive.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“I believe you.”</p><p>She did.</p><p>That was dangerous.</p><p>“What are you doing?”</p><p>“Working.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>“I have another customer coming.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Soon.”</p><p>“Specific.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Everyone hated precision now.</p><p>“Food later?”</p><p>She considered.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I groaned.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“That word.”</p><p>“What word?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>Cruel.</p><p>“I'll be at the Guild.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Good reason.”</p><p>“Maybe Jorren.”</p><p>“Tell him I said your hand is heroic.”</p><p>“I will not.”</p><p>“Coward.”</p><p>She went back inside.</p><p>I stayed there another second.</p><p>Not because there was more.</p><p>Because I was happy.</p><p>Then I went.</p><p>At the Guild, Jorren was there.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>He had the dark-handled food knife out.</p><p>Not threatening anyone.</p><p>Cutting an apple with ceremonial seriousness.</p><p>I sat.</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I shaped.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He stopped cutting.</p><p>“That sounds like cheating.”</p><p>“Hessa changed target.”</p><p>“What target?”</p><p>“Back of hand.”</p><p>“Did you fail it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He looked disappointed.</p><p>“Sorry.”</p><p>“You succeeded?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>There it was again.</p><p>He cut another apple slice.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>“That is all?”</p><p>“What do you want?”</p><p>“I don't know. Awe.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Questions?”</p><p>“Did it hurt?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Can you cast?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then good.”</p><p>He handed me apple.</p><p>I took it.</p><p>That was enough.</p><p>Later, my thumb did not tingle.</p><p>Neither did the marked patch.</p><p>Nothing strange happened.</p><p>This was almost disappointing.</p><p>I wrote the report upstairs:</p><p>One supervised shaping attempt. New intact-side target on outer back of right hand. Small localized alteration toward target. No broad palm/wrist pattern. No obvious Barrier-like setup. No pain, tingling, weakness, cold, numbness, or external release. No unusual below-knee sensation.</p><p>Then I added:</p><p>Hessa used the word shaped.</p><p>I looked at it.</p><p>That was not a symptom.</p><p>It stayed.</p><p>For once, the conclusion was allowed to be small and still be a conclusion.</p><p>I had shaped mana.</p><p>Once.</p><p>Nothing more.</p><p>Nothing less.<br/></p></article>
- `chapters/035.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 28: The Friend — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 28</div><h1>THE FRIEND</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The drink was worse after the third swallow. That seemed backwards. Jorren watched me discover this.</p><p>“You keep checking it.”</p><p>“I am verifying.”</p><p>“It’s beer.”</p><p>“It is pretending to be.”</p><p>“That’s most beer.”</p><p>I drank again. Still bad. The drink shop had no sign. Or had once had one and lost it. Six tables fit inside if everyone agreed not to breathe deeply. Three more sat outside under a patched awning. The floor sloped toward the street. The cups did not match.</p><p>A woman behind the counter poured from two barrels and insulted customers according to a system I could not identify. Jorren knew her.</p><p>“Another?” she asked.</p><p>He looked at me. I had consumed perhaps half a cup. My body felt warmer. Young body. Lower tolerance than memory. Important.</p><p>“No,” I said.</p><p>Jorren said, “One.” The woman poured him another. Not me. Good. She took his empty.</p><p>“You paying tonight?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That’s new.”</p><p>“I paid last time.”</p><p>“You paid half.”</p><p>“Other half was moral support.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“You his creditor?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Debtor,” Jorren said.</p><p>I turned.</p><p>“Temporary.”</p><p>She nodded as if that clarified everything.</p><p>“Vale?”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Jorren grinned.</p><p>The woman said, “Everybody owes Vale.”</p><p>“I do not think that is true.”</p><p>“Everybody interesting.”</p><p>That was worse. She went back inside.</p><p>“What’s her name?” I asked.</p><p>Jorren stared.</p><p>“You’ve been here ten minutes.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And now you ask.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I want to know.”</p><p>He considered.</p><p>“Mara.”</p><p>I froze. Memory arrived before permission. A letter. Chapter one. No. Not chapter. Morning. Cheap room. A name on paper. Mara. Someone who might have broken my nose. Or maybe not. I looked toward the counter. This Mara was perhaps thirty-five.</p><p>Too old to be the same Mara from nineteen-year-old correspondence unless my earlier memory was wrong. Possible. Likely. Different Mara. Jorren saw my face change.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You did the thing.”</p><p>“What thing?”</p><p>“Went somewhere.”</p><p>“I am here.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I looked at Mara. She was yelling at a man who had tried to put his boots on a chair. Not my Mara. Probably. Maybe my Mara had also yelled at chairs. </p><p>Memory did not help. I let it go. Mostly. </p><p>Jorren said, “You know her?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why stare?”</p><p>“Name.”</p><p>He waited. I waited. He drank. That was all. Good. He did not ask what the name meant. Not every curiosity required collection. The street in front of us had shifted from workday to evening without announcing it. Carts moved slower. Shop doors closed. Apprentices appeared in groups. A dog slept beneath a bench while three people stepped around it without complaint.</p><p>Two men at the next table argued over whether a local fighter had cheated in a prize bout. A woman in blue work trousers arrived carrying a basket of laundry.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Evening Beer Shop" decoding="async" height="189" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/035/v45_c35_evening-beer-shop.png" width="497"/></figure><p>Jorren moved his cup before she set the basket on our table. She sat.</p><p>“You’re in my chair.”</p><p>He looked at the chair beneath him.</p><p>“I was here.”</p><p>“You’re in my chair.”</p><p>“There are six chairs.”</p><p>“That one.”</p><p>Jorren sighed and moved. She took his seat. I watched. No argument. Interesting. She looked at me.</p><p>“New?” Nessa asked.</p><p>“No,” Jorren said.</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>She looked between us.</p><p>“Useful,” Nessa said.</p><p>“Greg,” Jorren said. “This is Nessa.”</p><p>“Nessa?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Nothing. Good.</p><p>“Nessa, Greg.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Old man.”</p><p>I looked at Jorren. He looked pleased.</p><p>“You told her.”</p><p>“He tells everyone,” Nessa said.</p><p>“I do not fight like an old man.”</p><p>“You complain like one.”</p><p>“We have just met.”</p><p>“You said beer was pretending.”</p><p>I looked at Jorren.</p><p>“How much do you talk?”</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>Nessa opened the laundry basket. It contained no laundry. Bread. Two wrapped parcels. Three apples. A small jar. Jorren reached. She slapped his hand.</p><p>“Pay.”</p><p>“I bought the last round.”</p><p>“Not from me.”</p><p>He put two copper on the table. She gave him bread and one parcel. I stared.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Food,” she said.</p><p>“You sell food out of a laundry basket.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why laundry?” I asked.</p><p>“So watch doesn’t tax me as a street seller,” Nessa said.</p><p>Jorren said, “That’s not why.” </p><p>Nessa looked at him.</p><p>“It helps,” Nessa said.</p><p>“What’s the real reason?” I asked.</p><p>She held up the basket.</p><p>“My sister does laundry,” Nessa said.</p><p>“Ah.”</p><p>That explained almost nothing. I liked it.</p><p>“What’s in the parcel?”</p><p>“Chicken.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Two.”</p><p>“Two copper?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good chicken?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Honest.”</p><p>I bought one. It was not good chicken. It was warm. That made up for some of it. Nessa sold the other parcel to a dockworker at the next table, then took one apple for herself.</p><p>“You work with him?” she asked.</p><p>She meant Jorren.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Sometimes,” Jorren said.</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“We spar.”</p><p>“That’s not work.”</p><p>“It feels like work when he starts talking.”</p><p>I ate. The chicken had too much salt. My body did not care. Hunger had apparently been waiting under the beer. Nineteen did that. Need arrived suddenly. Eat now. Sleep now. Move now. Old Greg had been better at ignoring body signals. Or his body had been quieter. Different. Nessa looked at the wrapped regulator under my arm.</p><p>“You carry that everywhere?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>“Regulator.”</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Low flow.”</p><p>“Of?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>Nessa tucked the coins deeper into the laundry basket. No follow-up. I had expected one. Interesting. Then she asked Jorren, “You working gate tomorrow?”</p><p>“Morning.”</p><p>“North?”</p><p>“Dock.”</p><p>“Tell Pellin his mother came by.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because she did.”</p><p>“What does she want?”</p><p>“She did not tell me.”</p><p>Jorren nodded. Existing people. Existing errands. No relation to me. Restful again. I drank more beer. Mistake. Not large. Enough. Warmth moved from stomach to face. My shoulders loosened. The street got louder without actually changing volume. I knew this state. Had known it. Later body had required more. Much more. Young Greg had probably been good at becoming drunk cheaply. Efficient.</p><p>I smiled. Jorren saw.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You look happy.”</p><p>That accusation was strange enough that I stopped.</p><p>“I am eating bad chicken.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And bad beer.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And carrying an unfinished regulator.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“My sword is at a smith.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I owe Antonius money.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Your point?”</p><p>“I don’t have one.”</p><p>That was worse. No point. I took another bite. Nessa looked at Jorren.</p><p>“He always like this?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You’ve known me how long?”</p><p>“Long enough.”</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>He thought.</p><p>“A while.”</p><p>“That is not a number.”</p><p>“See?”</p><p>Nessa nodded. I disliked them. A man came out of the shop carrying a small wooden board with five carved pegs. He put it on our table.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Jorren said that immediately.</p><p>The man said, “One copper.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Half.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Nessa said, “Play.” </p><p>Jorren looked at her.</p><p>“You play.”</p><p>“I have food.”</p><p>She shook the basket. The man looked at me.</p><p>“Know Five Roads?”</p><p>Memory. Yes. Maybe. Board game. Five pegs. Roads between carved points. Simple movement. Or gambling variant? I looked at the board.</p><p>“I know something called Five Roads.”</p><p>“Same thing?”</p><p>“Probably not.”</p><p>Jorren groaned.</p><p>“Do not teach him.”</p><p>The man sat opposite me.</p><p>“Half copper.”</p><p>I had half copper. Physically? No. Copper coins did not split cleanly. The shop had marks. Credit against drinks. Of course.</p><p>“I’ll play.”</p><p>Jorren put both hands over his face. The rules took thirty seconds. I had played it before. Not exactly. Future variant had two extra junctions and a blocking rule that did not exist yet. Important.</p><p>I lost the first game because I used the later blocking assumption. The man smiled.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Jorren said, “No.” </p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“You are not involved.”</p><p>“I know what your face does.”</p><p>“My face is playing.”</p><p>“Your face is building a war.”</p><p>Nessa laughed. Second game. I won. Not because I knew the future. Because the man favored the left crossing after losing center. Third game. He changed. Good. I lost. Fourth. Won. Fifth. Nessa put her apple core on the board.</p><p>“Stop,” Nessa said.</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Why?” I asked.</p><p>“You’re not talking anymore,” Nessa said.</p><p>“That is usually considered improvement.”</p><p>Jorren said, “He does that.”</p><p>“Does what?”</p><p>“Falls into things.”</p><p>I looked at the board. Five roads. Tiny system. Bounded. Legible. Wonderful. I wanted another. Very much. Not for money. For the shape. The man waited. I could see three adjustments already. He had started baiting my center response. I wanted to see whether he knew I knew. One more. That phrase had history. Cards. Gambling. One more hand. One more person.</p><p>One more test. I looked at Jorren. He was not correcting me. He was drinking. Nessa was packing the remaining bread. The man had his hand on the first peg. I said, “One more.” </p><p>Jorren laughed.</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>We played. I lost. Badly. The man had been waiting for the exact line I wanted to test. I stared at the board. Then laughed. Not politely. Actually laughed. He grinned.</p><p>“There.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You think too much.”</p><p>“That is not why I lost.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No. I lost because you trained a false response over four games and punished the fifth.”</p><p>He blinked. Jorren groaned. </p><p>Nessa said, “You could have just lost.”</p><p>“I did just lose.”</p><p>“No. You’re making losing paperwork.”</p><p>The man collected the half-copper mark. I nearly asked for another game. Did not. Progress? Maybe. Mostly I was hungry again. Nessa had one bread heel left. I bought it. She looked at the coins in my hand.</p><p>“You paid twice.”</p><p>I had. Beer. Young body. Bad arithmetic. She gave one copper back. I stared at it.</p><p>“That is mine.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You could have kept it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why didn’t you?”</p><p>She looked confused.</p><p>“Because it’s yours.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/035/Ch035_Fast-Coverage-003-A22.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 35." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>No system. No lesson. Fine. I ate bread. By the time the lamps were lit, the table had changed people twice. Nessa left with the empty basket. She had somewhere to be.</p><p>“Sister will murder me,” she said.</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Basket.”</p><p>“That seems excessive.”</p><p>“Then you haven’t met her.”</p><p>She left. The Five Roads man disappeared.</p><p>Mara brought Jorren water without being asked.</p><p>Jorren put two fingers around the cup but did not lift it.</p><p>She said, “You work tomorrow.”</p><p>He drank it.</p><p>Again. Existing life. Jorren had routines here. People knew his schedule. People knew which chair Nessa claimed. Mara knew when to stop pouring him beer. I had entered it. Not created it.</p><p>That felt different from following him to a tavern the first time. Maybe because I had stopped trying to understand what every piece meant. Mostly.</p><p>“What are you doing tomorrow?” I asked.</p><p>“Dock gate.”</p><p>“After?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>“On?”</p><p>“Work.”</p><p>“That is circular.”</p><p>“It’s tomorrow.”</p><p>I nodded. My head felt pleasantly slow. That was dangerous. Also nice. I remembered being drunk at nineteen. Not a specific night. A category. Warm face. Fast laughter. Poor decisions. Walking farther than necessary because someone else was going that way. Kissing people whose names later became uncertain. Getting punched. Punching back. Losing buttons. Waking thirsty. Old Greg had compressed all of that into immaturity.</p><p>Some of it was. A lot. Still. There had been pleasure in being stupid before the consequences were expensive enough to have departments. I looked at my hands. No liver spots. No scars from half the things I remembered. Beer cup between them. </p><p>Jorren said, “You’re doing it.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Leaving.”</p><p>“I am here.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I tried to explain. Did not. Instead I said, “I used to drink more.” </p><p>Jorren looked at the half-finished second cup I had somehow acquired.</p><p>“When?”</p><p>Danger. Not much. I smiled.</p><p>“Younger.”</p><p>“You are nineteen.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>He stared. Then laughed. Good. Deflected. Maybe too strange. Fine. Mara came by.</p><p>“Closing soon.”</p><p>Jorren looked at the street.</p><p>“It’s early.”</p><p>“It’s late for you.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You owe me.”</p><p>He checked his pocket. Nothing. I looked at him. He looked at me.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Two copper.”</p><p>He said, “I have money.”</p><p>“Then show it.”</p><p>He searched again. One copper. A button. A small nail. No second copper. I put down one. Jorren pointed.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You paid for my first drink.”</p><p>“Someone else’s.”</p><p>“Still.”</p><p>“I owe you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then subtract it.”</p><p>“From what?”</p><p>“Whatever.”</p><p>“That is not accounting.”</p><p>Mara took the copper.</p><p>“Resolved.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“No ledger?”</p><p>She walked away. Hostile systems everywhere. Jorren stood. Too fast. He swayed. Not badly. I laughed. He shoved my shoulder. My nineteen-year-old body shoved back before old judgment finished deciding whether this was socially appropriate. Jorren shoved harder. I stepped. Caught his wrist. Not combat. Play. He turned. I turned with him. For half a second the street became practice yard. Weight.</p><p>Balance. Hip. Then my ribs objected. I let go.</p><p>“Fuck.”</p><p>Jorren immediately stopped.</p><p>“You good?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You made a noise.”</p><p>“Ribs.”</p><p>“Darrowmere?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He nodded. No lecture. No apology. Just recalibration. We started walking.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>I asked after half a block.</p><p>“Home.”</p><p>“Yours?”</p><p>“Mine.”</p><p>“Why am I coming?”</p><p>“You followed me.”</p><p>I looked behind. The drink shop was already half a block back. He was right. I had simply walked with him.</p><p>“I need my room.”</p><p>“Then turn.”</p><p>I did not. Not immediately. The night air felt good. My body wanted movement after sitting. Young legs. Slight beer. No sword at hip. That absence felt wrong. Also light. We walked three more streets.</p><p>Jorren pointed out a baker who cheated on morning rolls by making them too small. I asked how he knew. He said because he bought them. That was evidence. A woman dumped wash water from a second-floor window and missed us by luck or skill. Jorren shouted up. She shouted back. Apparently they knew each other. I did not ask her name.</p><p>At the next corner he stopped.</p><p>“This is me.”</p><p>The building had four narrow floors and a front door painted green badly.</p><p>“You live here?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Alone?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“People.”</p><p>Reasonable.</p><p>A male voice from an upstairs window shouted, “Jorren, you owe me four copper.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He looked at the window.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The voice said, “Five now.”</p><p>“Fuck off, Tam.”</p><p>A laugh. Friend. Roommate. Coworker. Brother? Not my problem. Jorren opened the door.</p><p>“You coming up?”</p><p>I almost said why. Caught it. For what purpose? Bad question. I looked at the stairs. Then at the regulator under my arm. Then at my room three streets away.</p><p>“Not tonight.”</p><p>Jorren nodded. No disappointment.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>He went inside. That was all. I stood outside the green door for a moment. The upstairs voice said something about piss. Jorren shouted back. Ordinary. I walked home. My body was more drunk than my mind considered justified.</p><p>This offended me until I remembered the body got a vote. At my room I set the regulator on the desk. Removed my boots. Missed the chair with one. Sat on the bed. The mirror showed a young man with flushed cheeks and messy hair. Not impressive. Alive. I looked away before it became a theme. Water. Drink water. Old experience useful.</p><p>I drank two cups. Then a third. The second life had been built around advantage so far. Money sooner. Magic sooner. People sooner. Avoid mistakes. Compress years. Tonight had produced nothing. I had lost half a copper at Five Roads. Bought bad chicken. Paid Jorren’s beer. Learned Mara’s name. Met Nessa. Walked three extra streets.</p><p>My ribs hurt because I had shoved a friend like an idiot. Nothing advanced. I lay back. That should have bothered me. It did not. Not enough. Morning punished me. Not dramatically. My head did not split. No vomiting. No divine judgment. Dry mouth. Heavy eyes. Stiff ribs. And hunger violent enough to qualify as political. I sat up.</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>Nineteen. Again. Recovery was better. Tolerance was worse. Tradeoffs. I checked my channels. Quiet. No heat. No pressure. Good. LIMITED CASTING tag still there. Less good. The regulator waited. My sword did not. That was the first practical problem. Second: food. Third: Hessa. Was I scheduled? I searched notes. Yes. Late morning. Good. Sword first. Food before sword. No. Food first. Strongly.</p><p>I dressed. Outside, the city was offensively functional. Bread smell. Carts. Children going somewhere at speed. Workers already annoyed. I bought two rolls from a stall. Too small. I stopped. Baker. Jorren’s baker? No. Different street. I laughed alone. The seller looked at me.</p><p>“Problem?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I ate both. At the smith, the woman was already working. My sword lay on the counter. Edge clean. Chip reduced. Not erased. Good. She saw me.</p><p>“Two copper paid.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She handed it over. I checked balance. Same. Edge. Better.</p><p>“Could have taken more out.”</p><p>“Why didn’t you?”</p><p>“Would change the line.”</p><p>Good. Competence. I admired it. Did not ask what else she could become. Progress. Maybe.</p><p>“What’s your name?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Dara.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Alden talks?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Too much.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I sheathed the sword.</p><p>“Wrist?”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>That was all. I left before I could turn her into a question. Hessa’s practice room had someone else in it. Good. A man perhaps twenty-five stood over a shallow bowl trying to keep three metal beads suspended in a thin mana field. One bead dropped. Then another. </p><p>He swore. </p><p>Hessa said, “Again.” </p><p>I waited outside. Not because she told me. Because there was a lesson happening.</p><p>That felt obvious. Five minutes later the man came out sweating. He saw my tag.</p><p>“Restricted?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Lucky.”</p><p>I looked at him. He kept walking. I entered. Hessa pointed at the mat.</p><p>“You drank.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“You smell like old beer.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>Not magical perception. Excellent.</p><p>“Not much.”</p><p>“Doesn’t matter.”</p><p>“I drank water.”</p><p>“Congratulations.”</p><p>She checked my eyes. Pulse. Hands. Then the tag.</p><p>“Headache?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>“Meaning?”</p><p>“Dry. Mild. Not channel.”</p><p>“You know the difference?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She accepted that. Good.</p><p>“Cast?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Wanted to?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Didn’t?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She looked at me. That was apparently notable. I became defensive.</p><p>“I follow instructions.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She had me produce a tiny Barrier. Coin-sized. Two breaths. Release. Clean. Again. Three breaths. Clean. Stop. I stopped. No pressure. She checked my palm. Then removed the LIMITED CASTING tag. I stared.</p><p>“Done?”</p><p>“No repeated pressure work today.”</p><p>“That sounds limited.”</p><p>“It is less limited.”</p><p>“New tag?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then how will strangers control me?”</p><p>“They won’t.”</p><p>Dangerous.</p><p>“What can I do?”</p><p>“Small casting. Normal beginner volume. Stop on symptoms. No deliberate limit testing.”</p><p>“That last one persists?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“For how long?”</p><p>“Until you become less stupid.”</p><p>“So permanent.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I smiled. She did not. But almost. Maybe.</p><p>“Barrier work tomorrow?”</p><p>“If you remain symptom-free.”</p><p>There. Magic returning. Slowly. Real. My chest lifted. Hessa saw. Of course.</p><p>“Do not celebrate by casting in the street.”</p><p>“I wasn’t going to.”</p><p>“You were.”</p><p>“I was going to consider it.”</p><p>“That is the first half.”</p><p>Fair. Outside, I touched the bare wrist where the tag had been. No dramatic freedom. Just skin. I wanted to cast. Very much. Instead I took the regulator from my bag. Mechanical test. Arlo had given me something to do. Could test with water. No mana. I headed toward a public pump. Halfway there, someone called my name. Alden. He was across the street with Berren.</p><p>Berren limped slightly. Boot thicker on one side. Alive alive. Alden raised a hand. Berren raised two fingers. I could cross. Ask about Darrowmere. Drainage ditch. Fire. Creature turns. Or I could test the regulator. Or go back to Antonius. Or find Jorren after dock shift. Too many. Good. Normal. I crossed the street. Not because Berren was historically important. Not because Alden needed improvement.</p><p>Because they were there.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="034.html">← Chapter 27</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="036.html">Chapter 29 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

- `chapters/370.html:327`: <p>Mana did not care about my feelings.</p>

- `chapters/172.html:639`: <p>Hessa knew what happened when I drew mana and failed to make anything<br>
- `chapters/074.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 59: The Consultant — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 59</div><h1>THE CONSULTANT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p><strong>Lerris arrived with wood before breakfast.</strong> This was offensive. Not the wood. The hour. He leaned three lengths of smooth ash against the kitchen wall and immediately made the staircase unusable. I stared. He stared back.</p><p>“You weren't going up.”</p><p>“Still.”</p><p>“You can object after tea.”</p><p>“I haven't had tea.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>Terrible man. The keeper handed him tea. Not me. Worse. I crutched to the table. My right shoulder complained from yesterday's knife drills. Not badly. Enough to remind me that sitting still with Alden had somehow involved muscles. Lerris had already marked three post positions along the open side of the stairs. I looked. Then looked away. Carpenter. His work. Good.</p><p>“How long blocked?”</p><p>“Part of morning.”</p><p>“I need Guild.”</p><p>“Front door remains functional.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then why ask?”</p><p>“I didn't.”</p><p>He smiled. I hated tradesmen who enjoyed themselves. The rail was ordinary ash. No ornament. Rounded enough for a hand. Lerris had brought the posts cut long and would fit them on site. Dela's material. My labor. Three copper each side of the arrangement. Simple. I ate bread and cheese while he worked. Saw. Chisel. Measure. Fit.</p><p>The noise made the storage room impossible, so I stayed in the kitchen. This was mildly annoying and unexpectedly pleasant. Someone else was changing the stairs. I did not supervise. Mostly. At one point Lerris set a post against the stringer and sighted upward. I saw the angle.</p><p>“That's not vertical,” I said.</p><p>“No,” Lerris said.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Stair isn't,” he said.</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>I shut up. Good.</p><p>Ten minutes later:</p><p>“Are the fasteners long enough?”</p><p>He stopped. Looked at me.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Into stringer?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much bite?”</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>Useless unit. I opened my mouth. Closed it. He resumed. This was work. Not my work. The keeper saw me.</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then what?”</p><p>“Restraint.”</p><p>She laughed. Rude.</p><p>*</p><p>The Guild cart arrived at second bell. Not Mira's boy. A different driver. I had arranged it yesterday before leaving. Progress. I carried nothing. Also progress. Calendar stayed home. Notebook stayed home. Medical instructions stayed in belt pouch because those were supposed to. Crutches went in first. I got in. No drama. At Guild, the contract board had six new postings. I saw them.</p><p>Did not stop. That felt almost suspiciously healthy. No. I had a wound check. Priorities existed before amputation too. Sera's room smelled like boiled cloth. She unwrapped the limb. Less swelling again. The skin around the incision looked calmer. Still ugly. Less frightening.</p><p>Maybe I was getting used to it. I did not know whether that was good.</p><p>“Margin?”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Drainage?”</p><p>“Almost none.”</p><p>“Heat?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Revision?”</p><p>“No current reason.”</p><p>There. No current reason. Good. She pressed. One place sharp. Another dull. The end of the limb had begun to feel less like one giant injury and more like several different sensations occupying the same area. Pressure. Pull. Itch. Ache. Numb patch. Sharp spot. Phantom toes. Phantom heel. Phantom ankle turned inward today. None of them agreed.</p><p>“How were stairs?”</p><p>“Seven.”</p><p>“I know. I was there.”</p><p>“Then why ask?”</p><p>“I asked how.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Swelling after?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Resolved?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Rail installation?”</p><p>“Started.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Everyone.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>She rewrapped.</p><p>“Seven again?”</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You went out two nights ago, worked the day before that, did seven yesterday, then knife drills.”</p><p>“How do you know knife drills?”</p><p>“Alden.”</p><p>“Why are all my friends informants?”</p><p>“He asked if seated hand work was likely to damage your leg.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>“He also described it badly.”</p><p>“That sounds right.”</p><p>“Today you rest the stair work.”</p><p>“I came all the way here.”</p><p>“For wound care.”</p><p>“I could do five.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Three.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>Fine. My right thigh was sore anyway. She had noticed. Annoying.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“If swelling remains down.”</p><p>Bad unit. Fine. I left.</p><p>*</p><p>Edrin was in the main hall. I saw her before she saw me. Dark coat. Guild papers under one arm. Talking to a clerk. Normal. For half a second I thought about turning around. Not because I disliked her. Because I knew what she owned. Sinkstone. Varo. The three batches.</p><p>The question that had sat untouched while my leg became a medical event. My brain woke so fast it was embarrassing. Edrin finished with the clerk. Turned. Saw me. Her eyes went to the crutches. Then back to my face.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Edrin.”</p><p>“You're out.”</p><p>“Apparently.”</p><p>“How are you?”</p><p>“Missing something.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Bad joke?”</p><p>“Medium.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She did not ask to see the wound. Excellent.</p><p>“You have a minute?”</p><p>There.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She looked toward a side room.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“I am excellent at that now.”</p><p>“Still medium.”</p><p>We took a small interview room off the hall. Chair. Table. No stairs. I noticed. Of course. Edrin put the papers down. Not the seized samples. Papers.</p><p>“Varo.”</p><p>There. My hands tightened on crutch grips. Wrapped. No pain.</p><p>“What did they say?”</p><p>“I spoke to Master Varo and two workers separately.”</p><p>“Master Varo is a person?”</p><p>“Varo Chemical is his shop.”</p><p>Good. New fact. Small.</p><p>“Name?”</p><p>“Jalen Varo.”</p><p>I stored it.</p><p>“Did they treat the seized stock?” I asked.</p><p>“No evidence they did,” Edrin said.</p><p>Not no. No evidence. Good.</p><p>“Silas Marris?”</p><p>“Varo recognizes the company as freight and purchasing intermediaries. Says they've bought common reagents before. Nothing unusual enough that he remembered until I showed records.”</p><p>“What reagents?”</p><p>“Lime wash. Brine salts. Two mineral binders. Ordinary processing materials.”</p><p>“Could any produce the profiles?”</p><p>“Not alone.”</p><p>“Together?”</p><p>Edrin gave me a look.</p><p>“I asked.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Varo says the three seized profiles are not what he would expect from one treatment applied to inconsistent kestrin.”</p><p>That matched.</p><p>“Because internal variance too narrow?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did he test?”</p><p>“He examined my notes. I did not give him seized material.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I don't hand evidence to every chemist I interview.”</p><p>Correct.</p><p>“Could he reproduce?”</p><p>“He thinks he could reproduce one profile approximately if given time, stock, and enough rejected pieces.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“Strong immediate suppression, some residual.”</p><p>Batch two.</p><p>“Approximate.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not narrow?”</p><p>“He specifically refused to promise the narrowness.”</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>“How would he get narrow?”</p><p>“He gave me four answers,” Edrin said.</p><p>I leaned forward. Residual limb pulled. Ignored.</p><p>“One: start with unusually uniform raw stone,” she continued.</p><p>Dorrin sorting. Possible.</p><p>“Two: test individual pieces and reject aggressively.”</p><p>Bale. Slow. Expensive.</p><p>“Three: process pieces separately and adjust treatment based on response.”</p><p>Very expensive.</p><p>“Four: process a larger lot, test, then sort finished pieces into behavior bands.”</p><p>There. Not manufacturing consistency. Selecting it after.</p><p>“Could look like process control.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Without being process control.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Did he think that likely?”</p><p>“He thinks some combination is more likely than a single clever treatment.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>Edrin paused. There was.</p><p>“Varo asked why anyone would pay for it.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What did you say?”</p><p>“That is one of my questions.”</p><p>“His answer?”</p><p>“He said suppression stone is cheap because most uses tolerate variation. If you need exact behavior, there are better materials.”</p><p>“More expensive.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So making cheap kestrin exact only makes sense if cheap matters or kestrin matters.”</p><p>“Or if someone needs enough volume that better material becomes expensive.”</p><p>Volume.</p><p>“How much seized?”</p><p>“Enough to matter. Not enough to answer.”</p><p>“Shipment sizes?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>Her investigation. I sat back.</p><p>“Did Varo know anyone doing this?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Could he name shops capable?”</p><p>“Several could do parts. None he would accuse based on this.”</p><p>“Did he?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. No convenient producer.</p><p>“Silas Marris records?”</p><p>“Still being traced.”</p><p>“Origin?”</p><p>“Declared origin changes by shipment.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“That sounds bad.”</p><p>“It sounds like a trading company.”</p><p>Right. Freight intermediaries. Multiple origins normal.</p><p>“Any one region recurring?”</p><p>“Not enough to say.”</p><p>“Darrowmere?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Immediate. Good.</p><p>“Any reason to connect?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Excellent. I liked Edrin.</p><p>“Why tell me now?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Because you asked good questions before.”</p><p>There. Not needed. Valued. Different.</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“And because you are sitting here.”</p><p>“Could have sent note.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did you need me?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. It hurt less than expected. Maybe because she had brought the information anyway.</p><p>“What do you want from me?”</p><p>“Nothing today.”</p><p>Terrible.</p><p>“Then why room?”</p><p>“Because if I told you in the hall, you would ask twenty questions while blocking traffic.”</p><p>Fair. I looked at her papers.</p><p>“Can I see notes?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because they include names and purchasing records you do not need.”</p><p>“Can I see the four mechanisms?”</p><p>“I just told you.”</p><p>“Exact wording?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Edrin.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. Boundaries remained. My brain ran anyway. Uniform raw. Reject aggressively. Piece-specific treatment. Post-process sorting. Could combine. Cheap kestrin exactness. Why? Volume. Compatibility. Specific residual profile. Repeat exposure. Three profiles maybe three specifications. Or one producer testing variants. Or different producers.</p><p>Or one customer with multiple use cases. Or seized batches unrelated beyond company. Stop.</p><p>“Were the three batches shipped together?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I had asked before stopping. Fine.</p><p>“How far apart?” I asked.</p><p>“I am not giving you shipment records,” Edrin said.</p><p>“Days? Months?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She almost smiled.</p><p>“Anything from Varo that surprised you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>“He was less impressed by the chemistry than by the sorting problem.”</p><p>There.</p><p>“Meaning?”</p><p>“He said making kestrin suppress mana is easy. Making many pieces behave nearly alike is mostly a measurement problem.”</p><p>Oh. That landed. Testing. Measurement. Reference. Bale's brass line and mana bead. Edrin's piece-level tests.</p><p>“How fast can you measure?”</p><p>“Currently? Not fast enough for bulk commercial sorting.”</p><p>“Could someone have a faster test?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Holl.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I stopped. Holl had invited faster cheap test work. Different context. No Silas Marris link. Do not manufacture.</p><p>“Varo?”</p><p>“He uses chemical proxies for some treatment steps, not final magical response.”</p><p>“So someone could control process variables tightly without testing final behavior.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Or test final behavior with a method we don't know.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Or start uniform.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Or all.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Fuck. The question had not narrowed. No. It had. The hard part was measurement or selection, not suppression chemistry. Maybe. According to Varo. Professional opinion. Not truth.</p><p>“What do you think?”</p><p>I asked. Edrin looked at me for a moment.</p><p>“I think somebody cares about repeatability enough to spend money on it.”</p><p>“That we knew.”</p><p>“We suspected.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“I think Varo makes a single secret treatment less likely.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/074/Ch074_Fast-Coverage-003-A10.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 74." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“I think the production chain may involve more hands than we assumed.”</p><p>“Raw sorting, treatment, testing, resorting.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“Silas Marris could be only freight.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“Or purchasing.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“Or customer.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“This is terrible.”</p><p>“It is investigation.”</p><p>I smiled. There it was. Interest. Pure. For maybe five minutes I had forgotten the crutches against the table. Then I shifted to stand. My body reminded me. Right foot. Hands. Crutches. Edrin watched. Not pity. Assessment.</p><p>“You going somewhere?”</p><p>“Varo.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Immediate. I laughed.</p><p>“I was joking.”</p><p>“You were not.”</p><p>“Partly.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I could hire a cart.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She waited. I wanted to go. Not because she needed me. Because the problem existed. Varo had a shop. People. Processes. Equipment. I could ask. Observe. Maybe see what he meant by measurement problem. Edrin owned contact.</p><p>She had explicitly told me before not to manufacture access. That had not changed because I lost a leg. Physical capability was not even the first barrier. Permission was. Annoying. Good.</p><p>“Can I talk to Holl about faster testing?”</p><p>Edrin considered.</p><p>“Holl already invited you to work on faster cheap testing in his own context.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You may talk to Holl about Holl's work.”</p><p>“Not seized stock.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Not Silas Marris.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Not Varo.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Can I ask general questions about throughput?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There. Permission. Bounded. My brain immediately planned route. No. Not today. Sera said no stair work, not no Holl. Different. But I was tired. Also rail installation. Also no need.</p><p>“Tomorrow maybe.”</p><p>Edrin looked almost surprised.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I hated that she noticed.</p><p>“Do not make a face.”</p><p>“I didn't.”</p><p>“Everyone does.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She gathered papers.</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Your leg.”</p><p>I looked down.</p><p>“What about it?”</p><p>“Does magic feel different?”</p><p>There. First direct magic question from Edrin after loss. I thought.</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Channels quiet.”</p><p>“Hessa?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Body reference?”</p><p>I looked at her. Interesting. Dangerous.</p><p>“Phantom foot exists.”</p><p>“I meant in spell architecture.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>Good answer. True. Edrin nodded.</p><p>“Don't test because I asked.”</p><p>“I wasn't.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“I wasn't today.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>She left. I sat another minute. The room felt too small. Not because storage. Because Varo existed somewhere in Carrow and I could not simply go there. No. Could not simply go there had always been true. I had obeyed before the accident. Important. The crutches made the limitation visible, not new. Still irritating. I stood. Slow. Went home.</p><p>*</p><p>Lerris had installed two posts. The rail itself was not attached. The staircase looked worse.</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>He was kneeling at the third post.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Now I have neither rail nor clear stairs.”</p><p>“You still weren't climbing.”</p><p>“Principle.”</p><p>“Go away.”</p><p>I did. The storage room smelled faintly of cut ash. My damaged left boot sat beside the folded table. I looked at it. Then at my right boot. Then away. Not today. I wanted to write Varo notes. Notebook upstairs. Wrong notebook again. Current notebook was on crate. Fine.</p><p>I wrote:</p><p>VARO:<br/>SUPPRESSION EASY.<br/>CONSISTENCY HARD.<br/>POSSIBLE: UNIFORM RAW / REJECT / ADJUST PIECES / SORT AFTER.<br/>MEASUREMENT PROBLEM?<br/>WHY PAY?</p><p>Then:</p><p>PEL MARRIS MAY ONLY BE FREIGHT.</p><p>Crossed out MAY ONLY.</p><p>Wrote:</p><p>ROLE UNKNOWN.</p><p>Better.</p><p>Then:</p><p>HOLL: GENERAL THROUGHPUT ONLY. DO NOT MENTION SEIZED STOCK.</p><p>Good. Boundary written. I stared at the page. My old instinct wanted arrows. Producer. Processor. Tester. Trader. Customer. Three batches. Three profiles. Could draw. No. Not because forbidden. Because Lerris started hammering and I could not think. I went to kitchen.</p><p>“Can you stop?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Five minutes?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“This is intellectual work.”</p><p>“This is a staircase.”</p><p>He hammered. I laughed. Fine.</p><p>*</p><p>Arlo arrived while Lerris was still working. Not for me. He had come to borrow a clamp from Lerris. Of course they knew each other. Carrow had approximately twelve people. Arlo saw me.</p><p>“Contact test worked.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Lampblack.”</p><p>I forgot Varo immediately.</p><p>“Show.”</p><p>“No regulator.”</p><p>“Then explain.”</p><p>He did. Thin lampblack on mount face. Clamp. Release. Uneven transfer. Outer edge contacting first. Changing clamp order changed how body seated against face. There.</p><p>“Warp?”</p><p>“Maybe mount. Maybe body. Vessa is checking straightedge.”</p><p>“Hot?”</p><p>“Cold first. Hot tomorrow.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Arlo nodded.</p><p>“Your idea helped.”</p><p>There. I felt pleased.</p><p>Then he added:</p><p>“Vessa says don't become unbearable.”</p><p>“Too late.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/074/Ch074_Fast-Coverage-006-01.jpg" alt="A loose sketch-style story scene from Chapter 74." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>He borrowed clamp. Left. No invitation. No job. Fine. Lerris looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Face.”</p><p>Fuck everyone.</p><p>*</p><p>By late afternoon, the rail was attached through the first nine steps. Not complete. Lerris stopped.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Wood needs final fit at landing tomorrow.”</p><p>“You said two days.”</p><p>“This is day one.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then.”</p><p>Terrible. I put one hand on the new rail from the floor. Smooth. Solid. Pulled. No movement. Lerris watched.</p><p>“Don't test my work like that.”</p><p>“That was barely a test.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>Good line. I released.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“Finish.”</p><p>“Then can I use it?”</p><p>“Ask your healer.”</p><p>Everyone owned something. Fine. I paid him one copper of my three labor now, two on completion. His terms. Reasonable.</p><p>*</p><p>Before dinner, Sevren appeared in the doorway with rain on one shoulder and no obvious reason to be there.</p><p>“South route?”</p><p>“Done.”</p><p>“That was fast.”</p><p>“It was yesterday.”</p><p>Right. Time.</p><p>“Where are you going?”</p><p>“Octavia.”</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“She has a package.”</p><p>“Romantic.”</p><p>“It's cloth.”</p><p>“Very romantic.”</p><p>He looked at the half-finished rail.</p><p>“That's new.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can you use it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then terrible rail.”</p><p>“Unfinished.”</p><p>“Excuses.”</p><p>He came in. Saw my notebook open.</p><p>“Work?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Sinkstone.”</p><p>He waited.</p><p>“Rocks.”</p><p>“Ah.”</p><p>He had no interest. This was refreshing.</p><p>“Edrin talked to Varo.”</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>“Chemical shop.”</p><p>“Good?”</p><p>“Interesting.”</p><p>“Are you going there?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Really?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Not my investigation.”</p><p>“Since when has that stopped you?”</p><p>“Frequently.”</p><p>He thought.</p><p>“Has it?”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>He laughed. Then he noticed the damaged boot.</p><p>“That yours?”</p><p>“Was.”</p><p>He picked it up before I could object. Turned it over.</p><p>“Tam can use this.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good leather here.”</p><p>He pressed the upper near heel. I watched. Nothing happened. It remained leather.</p><p>“Take it to him?”</p><p>“Not now.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>Sevren put it back exactly where it had been.</p><p>“Okay.”</p><p>No question. Good. He sat on the crate.</p><p>“Cards?”</p><p>“You have package.”</p><p>“Ten minutes.”</p><p>We played one hand. I won. Finally.</p><p>“Cheater,” he said.</p><p>“I learned from you.”</p><p>He left for Octavia's delivery. The sinkstone problem remained open on the notebook. The boot remained beside the table. The rail remained incomplete. Three unfinished things. I did not touch any of them for several minutes. At dinner I tried explaining Varo to the keeper. Mistake.</p><p>“So rocks?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Different rocks?”</p><p>“Same kind, processed.”</p><p>“Bad?”</p><p>“Not necessarily.”</p><p>“Illegal?”</p><p>“Unknown.”</p><p>“Stolen?”</p><p>“Seized.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Investigation.”</p><p>“By you?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why do you care?”</p><p>I stopped. Because future? No. Because unusual consistency. Because measurement. Because someone did something difficult. Because I liked problems.</p><p>“Interesting.”</p><p>She nodded. That answer required no justification. Good.</p><p>“Rail interesting?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“More than rocks?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She laughed. I ate stew.</p><p>*</p><p>At night the hammering was gone. The house sounded wrong without it. I looked at the half-finished rail. Nine steps. Not usable yet. Could maybe practice first five? No. Lerris said incomplete. Sera said rest stairs today. Two owners. Enough. I stayed downstairs. This was less difficult than yesterday. Not easy. Less. I opened the notebook again.</p><p>WHO IS PRODUCING CONSISTENT SINKSTONE / HOW?</p><p>Old question. Still good.</p><p>Under it I added:</p><p>MAYBE WRONG UNIT.<br/>WHO SORTS / MEASURES / SPECIFIES?</p><p>There. That felt useful. Maybe too useful. I stared. The producer might not be one person. Could be chain. Raw seller. Treater. Tester. Trader. Customer. Who sets tolerance? Customer maybe. Who rejects? Processor maybe. Who measures? Unknown. The hard part might be the test. Holl. No. General only. I closed notebook. Boundary. Good.</p><p>Then I looked at the rail again. Someone had changed a staircase because I asked. Edrin had brought me information because she thought I saw things differently. Arlo had used an idea because it happened to help.</p><p>None of those made me necessary. I did not need to decide whether that was good. My phantom heel pressed into the floor. I lifted my actual thigh slightly. The phantom heel stayed. Wrong. Fine.</p><p>Tomorrow Lerris would finish the rail. Tomorrow I might talk to Holl. Maybe. No promise. No chase. I turned out the lamp. Upstairs remained upstairs. Varo remained elsewhere. For once, elsewhere could stay elsewhere overnight.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="072.html">← Chapter 58</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="075.html">Chapter 60 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/251.html:16`: <p>Right shoulder stiff from sleeping badly, not injured. Hands fine. Right leg fine. Residual limb fine. No headache. No mana-related anything.</p>
- `chapters/356.html:27`: <p>Old life had included several kinds of mana-heavy fog that bent sound.</p>
- `chapters/356.html:86`: <p>It carried existing sound along mana gradients and returned it late, bent, or displaced.</p>
- `chapters/356.html:459`: <p>Upstairs, I wrote nothing about mana density.</p>
- `chapters/330.html:57`: <p>Still did not channel mana into it.</p>
- `chapters/008.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 8: The Collector — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 8</div><h1>THE COLLECTOR</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Rusk handed me a list. I smiled. He took it back.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Don't do that."</p><p>"Do what?"</p><p>"Look happy."</p><p>"I am allowed to enjoy my work."</p><p>"Not this work." </p><p>I reached for the list. </p><p>He held it above my hand. Rusk was taller than me by perhaps an inch.</p><p>At nineteen. Future Greg would have found that irrelevant. Present Greg found it irritating.</p><p>"Antonius finally put me on collections."</p><p>"Rent."</p><p>"Debt."</p><p>"Rent."</p><p>"Money owed after an agreed date is debt." </p><p>Rusk considered this.</p><p>"You're going to make today long."</p><p>"Almost certainly," I said.</p><p>Rusk gave me the list.</p><p>Three names. Three addresses. Amounts. No explanation. I read them once. Then again. The second name bothered me. Merren. Not the given name. Surname. Merren. I knew that name. Maybe. I stopped walking.
