Because then forgetting someone meant nothing simple. And remembering Antonius meant something I did not yet understand. I walked three streets before realizing Rusk was still beside me.</p><p>"Why are you following me?"</p><p>"I'm going this way."</p><p>"Oh." </p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>"You really do disappear."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"In your head."</p><p>"I was thinking."</p><p>"You stopped avoiding carts." </p><p>I looked behind us. A carter had apparently sworn at me. I had not heard him.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Face" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/008/v28_c08_s01_the-face.png"/></figure><p>"Reasonable." </p><p>Rusk shook his head. At the next corner he turned away.</p><p>"Merren pays in two days," I called. </p><p>He raised a hand.</p><p>"If she doesn't?"</p><p>"She will." </p><p>He stopped.</p><p>Looked back. I corrected myself.</p><p>"Probably." </p><p>Rusk smiled.</p><p>Progress. I went to Hessa. Late. Again. She looked at me.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You have the face."</p><p>Everyone. Everyone knew the fucking face.</p><p>"What face?"</p><p>"The one where your body is here and you are somewhere else."</p><p>That stopped me. Rusk had just said almost the same thing. I looked down at my hands. Dust in the creases from the warehouse. Ink on one finger from Selka's agreement. A shallow sword blister reopening near my thumb. Three different lives on one hand.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Three Lives One Hand" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/008/v28_c08_s03_three-lives-one-hand.png"/></figure><p>"Greg," Hessa said.</p><p>I looked up. </p><p>Hessa pointed to the mat.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Here" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/008/v28_c08_s02_here.png"/></figure><p>"Here."</p><p>One word. Constraint. I stepped onto the mat. Breathed. For the next hour, I was only the student. That was easier. Afterward I went home instead of gambling. That was harder. I sat on the bed. The room was still cheap. My sword leaned against the wall. My notes covered the table.</p><p>SHALE.</p><p>TERE.</p><p>MANA.</p><p>WARRIOR.</p><p>DEBT.</p><p>ANTONIUS.</p><p>MERRREN.</p><p>I stared. Then crossed out the extra R.</p><p>MERREN.</p><p>Better.</p><p>Under it I wrote:</p><p>WHY DO I KNOW THIS NAME?</p><p>No answer. Under ANTONIUS I wrote:</p><p>WHY DO I REMEMBER HIM?</p><p>That one bothered me more. I almost started listing possibilities. Political leverage. Financial network. War financing. Guild influence. Criminal organization. Merchant coalition. Something with Konia? Maybe. My pen hovered. Then I remembered Ors. Open field. Branches.</p><p>No.</p><p>I drew a box around tomorrow.</p><p>ANTONIUS.</p><p>One constraint. See what happens. I put the pen down. Five minutes later I picked it back up and wrote:</p><p>MERRREN TEXTILES?</p><p>I stared.</p><p>"Fuck."</p><p>Crossed out the extra R again. Then went to bed.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="007.html">← Chapter 7</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="009.html">Chapter 9 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/473.html:237`: <p>Apparently some parts survived reincarnation better than mana.</p>
- `chapters/141.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 110: The Packer — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 110</div><h1>THE PACKER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Page twelve had seventeen lines. This was an unreasonable number of lines for a page Teren had handed me less than a day before leaving Carrow. I read them once at the theatre. Then again while someone dragged a painted tree past my chair and struck the doorframe hard enough to remove a branch. Nobody stopped. The tree continued outside with one fewer branch. I looked at the script. The role was a clerk. Of course it was.</p><p>Not a useful clerk. A comic clerk who had lost a document and spent most of the scene insisting the document had never existed. I understood the profession immediately.</p><p>"Do I need to learn all of this?"</p><p>Teren was tying pages into separate packets with red string.</p><p>"Page twelve."</p><p>"There are seventeen lines on page twelve."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Why only page twelve?"</p><p>"Because if we do the third show, that scene is changing."</p><p>"Into what?"</p><p>"I don't know."</p><p>"You handed me lines for a scene you know is changing."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"That seems inefficient."</p><p>Teren pulled the knot tight with his teeth.</p><p>"Learn page twelve."</p><p>I took the packet home. By late afternoon I had packed three times. The first packing was practical. The second was because the first packing had been wrong. The third was because I had removed half the things from the second packing and could no longer remember why I had included them. Travel had been easier when other people decided what I carried. That was not a good argument for other people deciding things. I put the bag on the bed. Two shirts. One spare pair of trousers. Underclothes.</p><p>Cloth for the residual limb. Extra wrapping. Small repair kit. Soap. Cup. Food for the morning. Money. Script. Hessa's drawing. No. The drawing came out. I looked at it. Wrist-side boundary dark. Upper edge less certain. Broken lower line. It was information.</p><p>It was also exactly the kind of information I would look at in a wagon until I convinced myself the bumps in the road had revealed something about mana. I put it in the drawer. Then I took it out. Hessa had told me to take it. That did not mean she had told me to carry it east. I put it back in the drawer. Closed the drawer. Opened it. The drawing remained there. Good. I closed it again.</p><p>The room was warm. Evening light came through the window and caught the dust over the bed. Somewhere downstairs, someone was cooking onions in too much fat. The smell climbed through the floorboards and made the bread on my table seem inadequate. I looked at the bag. Crutches. Those were difficult to forget.</p><p>I added a second length of cord for tying them to the wagon rail. Then a third. No. Two. I removed one. There was a knock.</p><p>"Come in."</p><p>The door opened. Lyssa looked at the bag on the bed. Then at the folded shirt in my hands.</p><p>"You're packing."</p><p>"No."</p><p>She closed the door behind her.</p><p>"What are you doing?"</p><p>"Determining what to bring."</p><p>"That is packing."</p><p>"I haven't finished."</p><p>"That is still packing."</p><p>She carried a small paper parcel and a bottle. Her hair was pulled back loosely, though several curls had escaped around her face. She had changed clothes since the morning, simpler and softer, and the black-patched work bag was gone. I looked at the parcel.</p><p>"What is that?"</p><p>"Food."</p><p>"I have food."</p><p>She looked at the piece of bread on my table.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"That is bread."</p><p>"That is sadness with a crust."</p><p>"It was cheap."</p><p>"I can tell."</p><p>She put the parcel beside it. I opened it. Cheese. Two small meat pies. Dried fruit. Something wrapped separately in waxed paper. I opened that too. Sweet cake. I looked at her.</p><p>"This is too much."</p><p>"Then leave some."</p><p>"I won't."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>She sat on the edge of the bed, which made the bag tilt toward her.</p><p>"What are you bringing?"</p><p>I showed her. She picked up one shirt.</p><p>"This one?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"It has a hole."</p><p>"It is small."</p><p>She put it on the floor.</p><p>"Lyssa."</p><p>"You have another."</p><p>"I have two others."</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/141/Ch141_Forward-Coverage-004-01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 141." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>"Then why are you taking the one with a hole?"</p><p>"Because travel damages clothing."</p><p>"So you brought damaged clothing in preparation."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>She stared at me.</p><p>"That makes sense."</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>"I hate it."</p><p>She put the shirt back in the bag. I sat beside her. The mattress dipped. My left leg ended where it ended, and the empty space beyond it was no longer strange enough to notice every time. Lyssa noticed other things. She picked up the extra wrapping cloth.</p><p>"Enough?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"For six days?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"What if it gets wet?"</p><p>I looked at her. She smiled.</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>"You need more."</p><p>"I can buy cloth."</p><p>"In the town?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You've never been there."</p><p>"There will be cloth."</p><p>"Theatre has chairs. Town has cloth."</p><p>"Exactly."</p><p>"This is how civilizations collapse."</p><p>I added another piece. Not because she was right. Because there was room. She watched me do it and said nothing. I disliked successful silence.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"You're pleased."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You are."</p><p>"I brought you food. I'm miserable."</p><p>I laughed. She leaned back on her hands. For a while we packed without making it important. She rolled the spare trousers tighter than I had. I objected, then kept them that way. I found a loose stitch on the bag strap and repaired it while she ate half of one meat pie despite claiming they were for me.</p><p>"You are stealing my travel food."</p><p>"I bought it."</p><p>"You transferred ownership."</p><p>"No contract."</p><p>"Verbal."</p><p>"No witness."</p><p>"I am a witness."</p><p>"Interested party."</p><p>I pointed the needle at her.</p><p>"You've spent too much time around me."</p><p>"Five days will fix it."</p><p>"Maybe six."</p><p>"Even better."</p><p>I tied off the stitch. The room became quieter as the street outside changed from work to evening. Wheels were less frequent. Voices carried farther. Somebody below laughed loudly, then shushed themselves for reasons that were not apparent. Lyssa took the clerk pages from the table.</p><p>"What is this?"</p><p>"Third show."</p><p>"You said there were two."</p><p>"There are two."</p><p>She looked at the pages.</p><p>"This says three."</p><p>"There may be three."</p><p>"You're leaving before sunrise for a trip that may be five or six days to perform two or three shows in a building you've never seen."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"And you know seventeen lines."</p><p>"On page twelve."</p><p>She flipped the page.</p><p>"There are more after twelve."</p><p>"I was instructed not to learn those."</p><p>"That seems dangerous."</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>She handed it back.</p><p>"Do the voice."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"What voice?"</p><p>"I don't know yet."</p><p>"You have a voice."</p><p>"I have several."</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>"I knew it."</p><p>"That woman was wrong."</p><p>"Do the clerk."</p><p>"I haven't built him."</p><p>"Built?"</p><p>"Voice. Pace. How he answers."</p><p>"You could just talk."</p><p>"That would be me."</p><p>"You're playing a clerk."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Have you considered that clerks can sound like people?"</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>"That is radical."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>I picked up the page. The scene began with another character demanding a permit. The clerk denied that permits were issued in that office. The other character produced a permit issued by that office. The clerk explained that this proved the permit had already been issued and therefore there was no need to issue one. I liked him. That was concerning. I read the first line in a narrow, fussy voice. Lyssa's face changed.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Don't."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"You sound like a dying bird."</p><p>"He is bureaucratic."</p><p>"He is sick."</p><p>I tried lower.</p><p>"Now he sounds old."</p><p>"He could be old."</p><p>"Is he?"</p><p>"I don't know."</p><p>"Then why are you making him old?"</p><p>I lowered the page.</p><p>"You are interfering with my process."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>I read it in my normal voice. Lyssa listened.</p><p>"Again."</p><p>I did.</p><p>"Slower."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because he knows the other person has to wait for him."</p><p>I looked at the page. Oh. I read it again. Not slow exactly. Unhurried. The permit seeker had urgency. The clerk did not. The line changed. Lyssa pointed.</p><p>"That."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"You didn't."</p><p>"I was about to."</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/141/Ch141_Forward-Coverage-004-02.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 141." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>"You were a dying bird."</p><p>"That was exploratory."</p><p>She laughed. I read the next exchange. By the fourth line I stopped performing the clerk and started answering as if the permit seeker were wasting my time. That worked better. Annoyingly. Lyssa stretched out across the bed on her stomach, chin on her hands, while I went through the page. She interrupted whenever I sounded false. She did not use that word. Her words were worse.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Too much."</p><p>"Why are you doing that?"</p><p>"Normal person."</p><p>"That one."</p><p>"Again."</p><p>Once she said nothing. I stopped.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Continue."</p><p>"You reacted."</p><p>"I breathed."</p><p>"You breathed differently."</p><p>She rolled onto her back.</p><p>"You are impossible."</p><p>"Was it good?"</p><p>"It sounded like you believed him."</p><p>"Believed what?"</p><p>"That the missing document is someone else's problem."</p><p>I looked at the line. Yes. That was the clerk. Not fussy. Not old. Protected. He lived inside a system where inconvenience moved downhill and he had arranged to be uphill. I read the next line. Lyssa closed her eyes.</p><p>"Better."</p><p>I kept going. At the end of page twelve she sat up.</p><p>"Again?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>"No?"</p><p>"You know it enough to ruin it if you keep going."</p><p>I stared.</p><p>"That is what Teren said."</p><p>"I am smarter than Teren."</p><p>"You don't know Teren."</p><p>"I don't need to."</p><p>Fair. I put the pages down. The bag was packed. Mostly. There were still decisions available if I wanted them. Another shirt. More food. Different cord. A small knife. The drawing. I did not touch the drawer. Lyssa stood. For a moment I thought she was leaving. Instead she took my crutches and moved them away from the bed.</p><p>"What are you doing?"</p><p>"Making room."</p><p>"For what?"</p><p>She looked at me. Oh.</p><p>"That was a stupid question."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>She came back and stood between my knees. I put my hands on her hips. She touched the side of my face. Neither of us said anything useful. Then she kissed me. The first kiss was easy. The second was not. I pulled her closer. She shifted one knee onto the bed beside me, careful of my left side without looking at it, and kissed me until I stopped thinking about page twelve. That took less time than expected. When we separated, she rested her forehead against mine.</p><p>"Before sunrise?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"That's disgusting."</p><p>"It is."</p><p>"You'll be terrible."</p><p>"I am good in the morning."</p><p>"No one is good before sunrise."</p><p>"Farmers."</p><p>"Miserable."</p><p>"Bakers."</p><p>"Miserable with bread."</p><p>I smiled. She kissed the corner of my mouth.</p><p>"Come back."</p><p>The words were quiet. Not dramatic. Not a demand. I felt them anyway.</p><p>"It's five days."</p><p>"Maybe six."</p><p>"Six."</p><p>"Gregory."</p><p>"I'll come back."</p><p>She nodded. Then immediately reached past me and pulled the bag closer.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You forgot socks."</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>"I did not."</p><p>She opened the bag. I had forgotten socks.</p><p>"Fuck."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>I got up. Lyssa sat in the warm hollow I left on the mattress while I crossed to the drawer. The socks were in the second drawer. The drawing was in the first. I opened the second. Took three pairs. Closed it. Lyssa watched me.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>I put the socks in the bag. She did not ask what was in the other drawer. Good. I tied the bag shut. Then untied it because the sweet cake was still on the table. Lyssa laughed.</p><p>"Shut up."</p><p>"I didn't say anything."</p><p>I packed the cake. Retied the bag. This time I left it closed. Tomorrow before sunrise I would get into a wagon with actors, scenery, bad wheels, too many scripts, and no reliable answer about where I would sleep. I was looking forward to it. That seemed unwise. I went back to Lyssa. There was still an evening left.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="140.html">← Chapter 109</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="142.html">Chapter 111 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/112.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 89: The Audience — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 89</div><h1>THE AUDIENCE</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Lyssa finished with the customer before she looked at me.</p><p>Not because she had not seen me.</p><p>Because she was working.</p><p>I approved.</p><p>Privately.</p><p>She tied the last bit of wrapping, took payment, said something I could not hear, and only then came outside.</p><p>“You&#x27;re smiling.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You are.”</p><p>“Hessa let me shape.”</p><p>Lyssa stopped.</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Are you allowed to be doing magic today?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That was fast.”</p><p>“Thank you for asking the important question first.”</p><p>“Did it hurt?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“What did you do?”</p><p>I explained.</p><p>Badly.</p><p>Because explaining mana shaping to someone who did not shape mana required either metaphors or lying.</p><p>I chose metaphors.</p><p>“So,” Lyssa said, “she told you to stop doing the thing without stopping the other thing.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And you sort of did.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And your wrist moved.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And now you&#x27;re happy.”</p><p>“Reasonably.”</p><p>She laughed.</p><p>I hated that word now.</p><p>“Tomorrow no magic.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That is not the correct response.”</p><p>“It is if I want you for tomorrow.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“For what?”</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>“Are you busy?”</p><p>I considered my schedule.</p><p>No Hessa.</p><p>No required work.</p><p>Pessa not promised.</p><p>No Sevren route.</p><p>No appointment.</p><p>“I can become busy.”</p><p>“Don&#x27;t.”</p><p>“What are we doing?”</p><p>“I&#x27;m not telling you.”</p><p>“That is manipulative.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Expensive?”</p><p>“Not very.”</p><p>“Food?”</p><p>“Eventually.”</p><p>“Dangerous?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Relevant question.”</p><p>“Not intentionally.”</p><p>That answer would age poorly.</p><p>The next evening I wore the dark green shirt.</p><p>Obviously.</p><p>I also spent too long deciding whether the blue shirt might look better because wearing the green one every time Lyssa saw me risked making it look like I owned one acceptable shirt.</p><p>I owned at least two.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>The gray-white one did not count.</p><p>I chose green.</p><p>Vanity was a form of evidence.</p><p>The keeper watched me come downstairs.</p><p>“Date?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She looked at the shirt.</p><p>“Date.”</p><p>I left.</p><p>Lyssa met me near the Guild.</p><p>She had changed after work.</p><p>I noticed.</p><p>I did not catalogue.</p><p>Growth.</p><p>She looked me over.</p><p>“Green.”</p><p>“You said you liked it.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“That influenced the decision.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>She kissed my cheek.</p><p>Good start.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>She pointed west.</p><p>We walked.</p><p>Not fast.</p><p>Lyssa had learned my current speed without turning it into ceremony.</p><p>That was nice.</p><p>She also did not walk artificially slowly.</p><p>She moved, stopped at stalls, doubled back once because she wanted sugared nuts, and generally behaved like the city belonged to both of us at different speeds.</p><p>I bought the nuts.</p><p>She ate most of them.</p><p>The building appeared after a turn between a chandlery and a narrow brick shop.</p><p>Three stories.</p><p>Old stone first floor.</p><p>Timber above.</p><p>Wide doors.</p><p>Painted sign.</p><p>People entering.</p><p>I looked at Lyssa.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You are not inspecting the building.”</p><p>“I haven&#x27;t said anything.”</p><p>“You looked at the upper windows.”</p><p>“They&#x27;re narrow.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>Theatre.</p><p>I had seen performances.</p><p>Small ones.</p><p>Street performers.</p><p>Guild celebrations.</p><p>Bad music in taverns.</p><p>This was different.</p><p>Tickets.</p><p>Ushers.</p><p>Printed playbill.</p><p>Actual seating.</p><p>A stage.</p><p>Lyssa had bought the cheaper seats, which I approved because I was not paying for architectural prestige.</p><p>Our seats were on the aisle.</p><p>That mattered physically.</p><p>She had thought about it.</p><p>She did not mention that she had thought about it.</p><p>Also good.</p><p>I sat.</p><p>Crutches angled where they would not trip anyone.</p><p>Residual limb comfortable enough.</p><p>Right foot planted.</p><p>Lyssa beside me.</p><p>People filled the room.</p><p>A lot of people.</p><p>More than I liked being responsible for.</p><p>Fortunately I was responsible for none.</p><p>“What is it?” I asked.</p><p>“You didn&#x27;t read the bill?”</p><p>“I was evaluating the exits.”</p><p>“You promised.”</p><p>“I promised not to inspect the building.”</p><p>“That is the building.”</p><p>“Exits are safety.”</p><p>She took the playbill from me.</p><p>“You are impossible.”</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>“A comedy.”</p><p>“About?”</p><p>“You&#x27;ll see.”</p><p>“I dislike preventable uncertainty.”</p><p>“You love preventable uncertainty.”</p><p>That was slander.</p><p>The lamps lowered.</p><p>Conversation softened.</p><p>Curtain.</p><p>I forgot the exits.</p><p>Not immediately.</p><p>But eventually.</p><p>The play was stupid.</p><p>This was not criticism.</p><p>A merchant had disguised himself as his own dead uncle to avoid paying a debt.</p><p>His daughter knew.</p><p>His wife did not.</p><p>A magistrate was sleeping with someone he should not have been sleeping with.</p><p>A servant understood everything and was paid by everyone to understand nothing.</p><p>It was excellent.</p><p>The merchant&#x27;s dead-uncle voice was terrible.</p><p>Intentionally.</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>Lyssa looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You looked.”</p><p>“You laughed.”</p><p>“It was funny.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then why are you looking at me?”</p><p>“Because you look surprised.”</p><p>“I am not surprised.”</p><p>The dead uncle tripped over his own cane.</p><p>I laughed harder.</p><p>Fuck.</p><p>At some point I stopped thinking about how the scenery changed.</p><p>Then I noticed how the scenery changed and became angry at myself.</p><p>Two people moved a wall while everyone watched an actor argue with a hat.</p><p>The wall was gone before the hat lost.</p><p>Good.</p><p>There was a musical bit.</p><p>I disliked it.</p><p>Then liked the end.</p><p>Intermission came.</p><p>I needed to stand.</p><p>Not because of pain.</p><p>Because sitting that long had made everything stiff.</p><p>We moved into the aisle after the crowd thinned.</p><p>Lyssa stretched.</p><p>“You like it.”</p><p>“It is competent.”</p><p>“You like it.”</p><p>“The servant is good.”</p><p>“You like it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She smiled like she had won something.</p><p>“I knew it.”</p><p>“You did not know.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“You suspected.”</p><p>“I knew.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>We bought watered wine.</p><p>Mine mostly water.</p><p>Food later.</p><p>Second half.</p><p>The merchant&#x27;s wife now believed she was being haunted by two different dead relatives, only one of whom was her husband.</p><p>This was becoming structurally ambitious.</p><p>Then I smelled smoke.</p><p>Not stage smoke.</p><p>I did not know why I knew that.</p><p>Maybe because the stage smoke earlier had smelled sweet.</p><p>This smelled like hot cloth.</p><p>I looked toward the left side of the stage.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Actor talking.</p><p>Audience listening.</p><p>Lyssa noticed me stop laughing.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Smoke.”</p><p>She sniffed.</p><p>Her expression changed.</p><p>Onstage, the servant entered too early.</p><p>I knew because the magistrate looked at him.</p><p>One heartbeat.</p><p>Then smiled.</p><p>“Ah,” the fast.</p><p>Not actor-fast.</p><p>Work-fast.</p><p>I looked at Lyssa.</p><p>She was already looking.</p><p>“You see it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>A thin line of smoke appeared high near the side wall.</p><p>People in the first rows did not notice.</p><p>Some farther back did.</p><p>Murmur.</p><p>The actors continued.</p><p>Why?</p><p>The servant crossed downstage.</p><p>Too far.</p><p>Blocked the audience&#x27;s view of the left wing.</p><p>Deliberate.</p><p>The magistrate began a story that had not been set up.</p><p>Or maybe I had missed it.</p><p>No.</p><p>Lyssa grabbed my sleeve.</p><p>“We&#x27;re going.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>We stood.</p><p>An usher was already moving down the aisle.</p><p>Not shouting.</p><p>“Side doors, please. Slowly. We&#x27;re clearing the hall.”</p><p>That was worse than shouting.</p><p>Because it meant there was a plan.</p><p>People started standing.</p><p>The actors kept going.</p><p>The magistrate&#x27;s story became louder.</p><p>The servant interrupted him repeatedly.</p><p>Audience laughter turned uneven.</p><p>More people noticed smoke.</p><p>An usher opened another door.</p><p>“Come on,” Lyssa said.</p><p>“I am.”</p><p>We moved.</p><p>She was ahead.</p><p>Of course she was.</p><p>Everyone was ahead.</p><p>My crutches found floor between shoes.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>Swing.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>People pressed from behind.</p><p>Not crushing.</p><p>Yet.</p><p>I hated crowds.</p><p>A man tried to step around my left side, saw the missing lower leg too late, nearly collided with the crutch, apologized, kept moving.</p><p>Lyssa turned.</p><p>“You good?”</p><p>“Yes. Go.”</p><p>Wrong word.</p><p>Not because she abandoned me.</p><p>Because the crowd took permission literally.</p><p>People flowed between us.</p><p>Lyssa slowed.</p><p>Someone behind her said, “Keep moving.”</p><p>She looked back.</p><p>I lifted a crutch slightly.</p><p>Go.</p><p>She went.</p><p>I followed.</p><p>Increasingly behind.</p><p>The aisle narrowed near the door.</p><p>Smoke thickened.</p><p>Not black.</p><p>Gray.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>Somebody coughed.</p><p>A woman started asking whether there was a fire.</p><p>The usher said, “Keep moving, please.”</p><p>Onstage:</p><p>“You cannot arrest a dead man!”</p><p>Huge laugh.</p><p>Perfect line.</p><p>Terrible timing.</p><p>Or perfect timing.</p><p>I could not tell.</p><p>Then something crashed backstage.</p><p>Not stage crash.</p><p>Real crash.</p><p>Audience changed.</p><p>You could feel it.</p><p>The room stopped being entertained and started becoming a crowd.</p><p>Ushers raised voices.</p><p>“Side doors. Chair.”</p><p>There was a chair.</p><p>Prop?</p><p>Real?</p><p>Did not matter.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“I can stand.”</p><p>“Congratulations. me to wait.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>Then moved.</p><p>Slow.</p><p>Painfully slow now because my hands had been gripping too hard from adrenaline and the floor was cluttered.</p><p>Outside air was not medically relevant.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>Hessa sat back.</p><p>“Today we draw.”</p><p>I tried not to look disappointed.</p><p>Failed.</p><p>She noticed.</p><p>“Do you want me to choose a test hand loose.</p><p>Right foot planted.</p><p>Residual limb supported.</p><p>Crutches against the wall where I could see them.</p><p>“Minimal draw,” Hessa said.</p><p>“Nothing else?”</p><p>“Nothing asked.</p><p>“Stable,” Hessa said.</p><p>I held.</p><p>Copper responded.</p><p>No thumb sensation.</p><p>No wrist movement.</p><p>No shaping.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released.</p><p>Hessa waited.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She checked pulse.</p><p>Hand.</p><p>Thumb.</p><p>Grip.</p><p>“Fine?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I watched.</p><p>“You said draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You did was trying to stop changing it.”</p><p>“Everything about it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Were you trying to hold the shape you had?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Were you trying to return it to the original draw?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Were you trying to release?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“What did your body do?”</p><p>“No wrist rotation.”</p><p>“I know what I saw.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>My report.</p><p>“Forearm felt tense.”</p><p>“Muscular?”</p><p>“Maybe. Not strongly.”</p><p>“Hand?”</p><p>“Quiet.”</p><p>“Breathing?”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She wrote that.</p><p>“You are delighted by ignorance.”</p><p>“I am delighted when you stop replacing it.”</p><p>She picked up a charcoal stick.</p><p>My attention sharpened.</p><p>Hessa saw that too.</p><p>“Do not celebrate.”</p><p>“I am not.”</p><p>“You are nineteen. Your entire face is celebrating.”</p><p>She drew one short line on the inside of my right forearm.</p><p>Farther from the wrist than last time.</p><p>Then another line closer to the elbow.</p><p>Two again.</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“One attempt?”</p><p>“If we do it.”</p><p>“If?”</p><p>“I can still decide not to.”</p><p>I shut up.</p><p>Miracle.</p><p>Hessa placed the copper.</p><p>“Different question,” she said.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That was not praise.”</p><p>“What question?”</p><p>“Last time I told you to stop altering while holding the draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You interpreted that as freeze the alteration.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Today, if we proceed, I may ask something narrower.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She pointed to the nearer charcoal line.</p><p>“You will draw. I will tell you whether to alter toward the near or far mark. You will begin one small alteration. Then I will say enough.”</p><p>“Instead of stop.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What does enough mean?”</p><p>“End the deliberate alteration and allow the mana to settle back toward the underlying draw without releasing the draw.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“That is harder.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“It is also different.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Last time I was trying to hold the altered state.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Now you want me to stop maintaining it.”</p><p>“I want to know whether you can stop feeding the deliberate change without dropping everything.”</p><p>That was cleaner.</p><p>Also terrifying.</p><p>“External effect?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Left?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Second attempt if I fail?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Of course.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/111/Ch111_Fast-Coverage-003-C20.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 111." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“What counts as failure?”</p><p>“I will tell you afterward.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You know.”</p><p>“I know some things I would stop for. I do not know every way you can fail before you do it.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>I hated fair.</p><p>She examined my right hand one more time.</p><p>“Any tingling now?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Numbness?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Ready?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Minimal draw.”</p><p>I drew again.</p><p>The second draw of the day felt slightly less crisp.</p><p>Not weaker.</p><p>More aware.</p><p>That could have been attention.</p><p>I said nothing.</p><p>“Stable?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Hessa watched.</p><p>Copper answered.</p><p>“Far mark.”</p><p>I began.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Not thumb.</p><p>Not hand.</p><p>Forearm.</p><p>The alteration gathered as a narrow pressure of awareness, not physical pressure, moving along the inside of the right forearm.</p><p>Not a line exactly.</p><p>More like a region with a direction.</p><p>It approached the far mark.</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>I stopped feeding it.</p><p>That was the instruction.</p><p>Not freeze.</p><p>Not reverse.</p><p>Not release.</p><p>Stop feeding.</p><p>For half a second nothing happened.</p><p>Then the altered region softened.</p><p>Not disappeared.</p><p>Softened.</p><p>The edge nearest my wrist faded first.</p><p>The center remained.</p><p>Then the whole thing seemed to collapse inward.</p><p>My wrist twitched.</p><p>Tiny.</p><p>I felt it.</p><p>Hessa saw it.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released immediately.</p><p>Mana gone.</p><p>The forearm sensation vanished with it.</p><p>My heart was beating harder than the test deserved.</p><p>Hessa touched my wrist.</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Tingling?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Numbness?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Weak?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>I thought.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Anything familiar?”</p><p>“The wrist twitch.”</p><p>“Familiar how?”</p><p>“Movement. Not the setup.”</p><p>“Do not improve the answer.”</p><p>“I am not.”</p><p>She checked grip.</p><p>Fingertips.</p><p>Thumb.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Then she sat.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I waited longer.</p><p>This was abuse.</p><p>Finally:</p><p>“You stopped feeding the alteration.”</p><p>I almost smiled.</p><p>She raised a finger.</p><p>“And then the pattern changed.”</p><p>Smile gone.</p><p>“How?”</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/111/Ch111_Wrist-Twitch-Check.png" alt="Hessa watches Greg&#x27;s wrist closely after a small involuntary movement changes the test." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“I saw the response diminish rather than broaden. Copper response reduced with it. Then your wrist moved.”</p><p>“Did I succeed?”</p><p>“You performed the instruction more closely than last time.”</p><p>“That is not yes.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Is it no?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“You want a category before I have one.”</p><p>“I stopped shaping.”</p><p>“You stopped deliberately feeding the change. I am reasonably confident of that.”</p><p>That landed.</p><p>“Reasonably?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And it settled?”</p><p>“It changed toward less altered. That is what I observed.”</p><p>“Without dropping the draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There.</p><p>Something in my chest lifted.</p><p>Hessa continued before I could turn it into a parade.</p><p>“You also had an involuntary or at least unrequested wrist movement at the end.”</p><p>“Tiny.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No Barrier pattern.”</p><p>“Not one I recognized.”</p><p>“So.”</p><p>“So I have one attempt where the alteration broadened after a stop instruction and one attempt where a differently framed instruction produced diminishing alteration followed by a wrist twitch.”</p><p>“That is better.”</p><p>“It is different.”</p><p>“It can be both.”</p><p>Hessa looked annoyed that I had said something reasonable.</p><p>I enjoyed this.</p><p>“Does this change external effect?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Casting?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Next test?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>My joy survived anyway.</p><p>That annoyed her more.</p><p>“You are not cleared to practice this.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You are not cleared to draw.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You are not cleared to shape.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You are not cleared to reproduce the wrist movement.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Tomorrow no magic.”</p><p>I groaned.</p><p>“One day?”</p><p>“One day.”</p><p>“Then?”</p><p>“Come back the day after tomorrow.”</p><p>“Are we doing this again?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>I stood.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>Hand normal.</p><p>Palms normal.</p><p>Residual limb quiet.</p><p>I took the crutches.</p><p>Hessa said, “Greg.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“You trained yesterday.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You tested today.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Tomorrow does not need to contain Pessa because it cannot contain me.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>She watched me.</p><p>I thought about lying.</p><p>Did not.</p><p>“I might ask Lyssa to do something.”</p><p>Hessa blinked.</p><p>“That sounds medically preferable.”</p><p>“Rude.”</p><p>“Go.”</p><p>I went.</p><p>Outside, Carrow was offensively normal.</p><p>Carts.</p><p>Bread.</p><p>Mud.</p><p>Someone shouting about lamp oil.</p><p>A dog asleep under a bench.</p><p>I had shaped mana.</p><p>I had maybe stopped shaping mana.</p><p>Reasonably.</p><p>Under a different instruction.</p><p>Once.</p><p>In a small supervised test.</p><p>Without a spell.</p><p>I wanted to tell everyone.</p><p>Instead I went to find Lyssa.</p><p>She was working.</p><p>So I waited.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="110.html">← Chapter 87</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="112.html">Chapter 89 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/174.html:178`: <p>I had spent weeks learning to draw mana under Hessa's supervision. I<br>
- `chapters/004.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 3: The Expert — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 3</div><h1>THE EXPERT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The first thing I did the next morning was count my money. The second thing I did was count it again because the number offended me. It did not improve. I sat on the edge of the bed with the coins spread across the blanket in little stacks and tried to remember when silver had become invisible to me. Not metaphorically. Literally. There had been a point in my old life when I stopped counting it. Somebody else handled expenses. Somebody else settled rooms, replaced gear, paid porters, bought supplies, tipped runners, bribed clerks, and quietly moved money around so Greg could continue being Greg without ever needing to wonder whether dinner cost four copper or six.</p><p>That arrangement had seemed efficient. Now it seemed suspiciously like being spoiled. I moved one silver from the left stack to the right. Training. Another. Food. Another. Arlo. Another. Debt. I stopped. That was already more categories than coins.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Too Many Categories" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/004/v28_c04_s01_too-many-categories.png"/></figure><p>"Excellent," I said.</p><p>The room did not object. The shale project had become the most dangerous kind of thing: promising. The sixth disk had barely beaten the control; by the end of the night, Arlo's best result was closer to twenty percent. Failure would have been cleaner. If that result had collapsed on replication, the project could die with dignity. Instead we had a path toward better tests, and no idea whether the final product would take two weeks or two years.</p><p>I had been treating it like short-term money because I wanted it to be short-term money. Arlo could keep working if we slowed the pace. Antonius had financing rights for three months. Nothing about the project demanded that I bleed myself dry this week except impatience. I took a piece of paper and wrote:</p><p>ARWICK / SHALE. LONG TERM.</p><p>Under it:</p><p>DO NOT FEED IT ALL MY MONEY.</p><p>"Very sophisticated."</p><p>The problem was cash. Now.</p><p>I had spent most of yesterday feeling clever for identifying capital as the first bottleneck, then spent borrowed capital like I still had forty years of wealth behind me. Six silver here. Three there. Training. Delivery. Testing. Food. I remembered buying boots once for thirty gold because I liked the buckle. I looked down at my current boots. The left one had a crack near the toe.</p><p>"Different economy."</p><p>Same economy. Different Greg.</p><p>That annoyed me more. I opened the five-year plan. Mana conditioning three times a week. Better food because Hessa had said nutrition mattered. Guild access. Equipment. Teachers. Materials. Information. Every accelerated year had a price attached to it. I needed income that worked now, did not depend on precise future memory, and did not consume the money meant to build magic. I wrote: WHAT AM I GOOD AT?</p><p>My mind answered with careers instead of skills. Warrior. Mage. Investor. Merchant. Teacher. Gambler. Strategist. Each one immediately generated prerequisites, alternate routes, and reasons I could probably do it better this time. Within a minute I had turned earning dinner into a redesign of my life.</p><p>"Stop," I told myself. "Money. Today."</p><p>ACTUALLY GOOD AT.</p><p>That narrowed things. Fighting? I looked at the sword. Sixty-year-old Greg understood timing, distance, fear, and the hundred ugly ways fights went wrong. Nineteen-year-old Greg still had nineteen-year-old speed, strength, conditioning, and habits. I could probably embarrass another Bronze warrior. That was not the same as being worth money. I wrote:</p><p>FIGHTING. BETTER THAN I LOOK. NOT SPECIAL.</p><p>Strategy? Yes. For whom? I had no party, command, or reputation. No one was paying a nineteen-year-old Bronze adventurer to redesign a campaign. I wrote:</p><p>STRATEGY. USELESS WITHOUT PIECES.</p><p>That one hurt. Future knowledge? I stared at it. Yesterday I would have put it first. Today I wrote:</p><p>FUTURE KNOWLEDGE. BIG THINGS. BAD INDEX. EXPENSIVE TO VERIFY.</p><p>Also not immediate. Investing? I almost laughed. Investing required money. I wrote:</p><p>INVESTING. APPARENTLY REQUIRES MONEY.</p><p>Teaching? Maybe. Who would listen? Consulting? Worse. People-reading? I stopped. That one stayed. I was good at people. Not morally. Technically. Faces. Posture. Breathing. The pause before a lie. The difference between fear and caution. Who needed to feel clever. Who needed to feel safe. Which insult would make a fighter reckless. I had built half a career on that before admitting it was a skill.</p><p>Magic had eventually made the reading measurable. Reinforcement exposed tension and fatigue. Barriers told me where someone expected force. But I had been reading people long before magic. Probably before I knew I was doing it. I wrote:</p><p>PEOPLE. GOOD.</p><p>Then underneath:</p><p>TOO GOOD?</p><p>That was not useful financially. Unless I gambled. The thought arrived so cleanly I distrusted it. I leaned back. Cards. Dice. Tables. Not pure games of chance. Not the stupid ones. Anything with betting decisions, bluffing, hidden information, player behavior. I had played constantly in my old life. Not professionally. Socially. Expeditions were boring. Sieges were worse. Give twelve adventurers three weeks in a fortress and eventually somebody invented a drinking game, a card table, or a reason to hate whoever packed the dice. I had been good. Very good. How good? I frowned. That was exactly the kind of memory I had learned to question. I remembered winning. People remember winning.</p><p>I remembered other people complaining. Also not evidence. I remembered being banned from a table in Hareth because the owner believed I was cheating. That was better. Had I been cheating? Not mechanically. I had known when the owner was bluffing. He considered that cheating because the distinction cost him money. I smiled.</p><p>"Okay."</p><p>There was a gambling room near the slaughter lane. Antonius's room. That was bad. Maybe useful. Too visible. If I started winning money under my lender's roof, Antonius would notice exactly how I was paying him. Then again, Antonius already thought I was interesting. More interesting was not necessarily better. I needed a different room. Carrow had several. I knew that because nineteen-year-old Greg had been in most of them. That memory came back with enough detail to be embarrassing. The Broken Pike.</p><p>Closed after a stabbing. Still open now? Probably. The Copper Nail. Too small. The White Dog. I stopped. I could see the table arrangement. Or thought I could. I remembered losing a boot there. Why? Bet. Of course. Young Greg had apparently been an idiot with continuity. I stood. Then sat down again. Money first. How much could I afford to lose? Old Greg would have asked how much he could deploy. Different language. Different survival rate. I separated food, training, and debt reserve, then stared at what remained. A few silver. Enough that losing it would hurt, not enough that a modest win solved much. Which meant I immediately wanted to risk all of it. There he was.</p><p>Greg. I took half. Put the rest away. Then took one more coin. Put it back.</p><p>Progress.</p><p>The White Dog existed. That was the first win. The second was that nobody there knew me. At least nobody important. I entered slowly enough to let the room explain itself. Six tables. Three active. One dice game. Two cards. The air smelled like beer, tallow, wet wool, and the particular anxiety of people pretending money was entertainment. I liked it immediately. That was probably another character flaw. A woman at the nearest table looked up. Did I know her?</p><p>Name? No idea. Future importance? Nothing. Good. I scanned the others anyway. Old man with red nose. Young laborer with scarred knuckles. Merchant apprentice trying too hard to look bored. Two women in dock coats. A man in guild leathers with a silver clasp. Silver rank?</p><p>Decorative clasp. Why did I know that? Because he kept touching it. Pride object. Not rank. I filed him. The dealer at the card table was missing the tip of one ear. Memory tugged. Nothing followed. I stood there too long.</p><p>"Playing?" the dealer asked.</p><p>"I was deciding."</p><p>"About?"</p><p>"Whether you're honest."</p><p>The table laughed. The dealer did not.</p><p>"Sit down."</p><p>I sat. Three-card draw. Simple. Too simple. Good. I bought in small. The first hand I lost. Deliberately? That would have been smarter. I simply had bad cards. Important distinction. The second hand I folded too late because I mistook the merchant apprentice's nervousness for weakness. He had an excellent hand. I paid for the lesson.</p><p>I watched him. He was nervous because he had an excellent hand, not because he was bluffing. Knowing the principle was not knowing the man. Third hand. Dock-coat woman tapped one finger when she wanted someone to raise. Fourth. Red-nose exhaled through his nose before lying. Fifth. Guild-leathers touched his fake silver clasp when he wanted to look confident. I lost two. Won one. Folded three. The dealer watched me watching.</p><p>"First time?" he asked.</p><p>"Today?"</p><p>"Here."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You stare."</p><p>"So I've been told."</p><p>"Bad habit."</p><p>"Depends."</p><p>He dealt. I picked up the cards. Mediocre. Not useless. The merchant apprentice looked at his hand and went still. Very still. Good hand. Red-nose scratched his cheek. Nothing. Dock coat checked the pot before checking anyone else. Interested. Fake Silver touched the clasp. There. Weak. I raised. Merchant apprentice called. Dock coat called. Fake Silver hesitated, then called because pride had entered the hand. Red-nose folded. Next card. Merchant apprentice blinked once. Better. Dock coat relaxed. Worse. Fake Silver touched the clasp again. Still weak. I had not improved. I raised anyway. Not because my cards deserved it.</p><p>Because two players wanted permission to leave and one wanted to prove he could stay. Dock coat folded. Fake Silver called. Of course. The merchant apprentice raised me. There was the problem. Good hand. Very good. I looked at him. He was trying not to breathe. I could beat Fake Silver. Not him. I folded. Fake Silver did not. The merchant apprentice took the pot. Fake Silver swore. I smiled, not because I won, but because the room had become legible. I stayed three hours. I did not win every hand. The others were not stupid. I just stopped making expensive mistakes quickly.</p><p>The patterns changed as people changed. Red-nose's tell shifted after drinking. Dock Coat got reckless when behind. Merchant Apprentice protected profit. Fake Silver could be pushed by disrespect. I used that once.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Reading The Table" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/004/v28_c04_s02_reading-the-table.png"/></figure><p>"Too rich for you?" he asked when I folded.</p><p>"Too boring." </p><p>He stayed in the next hand three raises longer than he should have.</p><p>Ugly. Effective.</p><p>I won. The feeling was familiar. Not the money. The steering. That little shift where another person thought they were making a decision and I knew which pressure had nudged it. Old Greg had called it support when the outcome was heroic, strategy when it was political, negotiation when money moved, flirting when clothes came off. Read the person. Find the lever. Apply pressure. Fake Silver was stacking fewer coins than he had arrived with. Angry at me? At himself. Better. If he blamed me, he might leave. If he blamed himself, he would stay and try to repair the story.</p><p>I disliked how natural that thought felt. I used it anyway. By the end of the third hour, I had nearly tripled the money I brought. Training. Food. Interest. A week, maybe two. My chest tightened with something dangerously close to offense. I had once tipped more after dinner. Now this changed whether I could train next week. My calibration was wrong. Silver was not background noise anymore. Silver was time.</p><p>The realization should have made me conservative. Instead it made me want more. Of course it did. There was a higher-stakes table in the back, deliberately ignored when I entered. Better clothes. More money. One empty chair. I could buy in now. Barely. If I lost, I would walk out with less than I started. If I won. There it was again.</p><p>I stood. Not toward the door. Toward the back table. The game was Crown and Knives. That was more complicated. Good. Hidden cards. Shared cards. Betting rounds. Enough structure that observation mattered more. A man with silver rings looked up.</p><p>"Seat's expensive."</p><p>"How expensive?"</p><p>He named the buy-in. I had it. I should leave. Food secured. Training secured. Debt safer. Leave. I sat down. Apparently forty years of surviving my own decisions had taught me many things except how to stop at enough. The first hour went badly. These players lied with intention. They manufactured tells. One woman touched her necklace when bluffing for three hands, then used the same motion with a real hand to punish anyone who had noticed. I paid for that. A thin man named Osric talked constantly. I assumed distraction. Wrong. He talked more when thinking because silence made him uncomfortable.</p><p>The information was in when he stopped. I learned that after losing another hand. My stack shrank. I felt irritation. Then something worse. Excitement.</p><p>Good players. Finally.</p><p>That thought belonged to old Greg too. The room sharpened. I stopped trying to win money and started trying to understand them. Osric's silences. Necklace woman's false tells layered over real ones. Ring man's habit of staring at the player he wanted to challenge. Fourth player, older woman named Senna, had almost nothing visible. I watched her too hard. She noticed.</p><p>"You planning to marry me?" Senna asked.</p><p>"Not yet."</p><p>"Then stop looking at me like that."</p><p>"I'm learning."</p><p>"Learn quieter."</p><p>The table laughed. I smiled. She did not.</p><p>Senna was the best player. Present-important, not future-important. I watched her hands. Nothing. Breathing. Nothing. Eyes. Minimal. Bet sizing. There. Not a tell. A preference. She hated inefficient bets. When somebody distorted a small pot with an irrational raise, she became more conservative even with good hands. Not fear, disgust. She disliked bad structure. I tested it and lost. Wrong. She had known I was testing. Her eyes flicked to me afterward. Tiny smile. Oh. I liked her. Dangerous in a completely different way.</p><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>By midnight I had recovered the losses and pushed slightly above my first-table winnings. Enough. The cards had priced something I could actually sell now: attention. Fast models of specific people. No future knowledge. No expert needed to verify me. Just a buy-in and a room full of decisions.</p><p>I stood. This time toward the door. Senna looked up.</p><p>"Running?"</p><p>"Stopping."</p><p>"Different?"</p><p>"For me? Apparently," I said.</p><p>She glanced at my stack.</p><p>"You came in small."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You leave small." </p><p>I looked at the coins. Old calibration rose again. Small. She was right. And wrong.</p><p>"Not to me," I said.</p><p>Outside, the night air felt colder. I walked home with the coins heavy in my pocket. A few silver. Nothing to old Greg. Training, food, and time to this one. Both calibrations were still in my head.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Walking Home With Silver" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/004/v28_c04_s03_walking-home-with-silver.png"/></figure><p>Worse, I could already see the next leverage. If I could make this much reliably, how fast could I clear Antonius? Two nights? Three? Bad question. How fast could I clear Antonius while still funding Hessa? Better.</p><p>And did I actually want to clear him? Debt was risk. Interest was waste. Freedom mattered. Antonius was also access, capital, information, a future institution still small enough to talk to. Maybe I should repay enough to prove myself, then borrow again. Larger. Gambling for living and training. Borrowed money for high-upside projects.</p><p>That sounded excellent until I remembered why I was gambling in the first place: my first high-upside project had nearly eaten the rest of my money.</p><p>"Right."</p><p>Present Greg needed rules. Old Greg preferred judgment. Rules were what you gave people whose judgment you did not trust. Apparently I qualified. At the room, I wrote:</p><p>1. FOOD / ROOM / TRAINING MONEY DOES NOT GET INVESTED.</p><p>2. BORROWED MONEY GETS A PURPOSE BEFORE I BORROW IT.</p><p>3. FUTURE MEMORY IS A LEAD, NOT PROOF.</p><p>4. LEAVE THE TABLE WHEN THE DAY IS SOLVED.</p><p>I stared at number four. Then added:</p><p>5. ACTUALLY LEAVE.</p><p>Under that I wrote: WHAT AM I GOOD AT? PEOPLE. LEARNING PEOPLE. THINKING IN SYSTEMS. MAYBE GAMBLING. I paused, then crossed out MAYBE.</p><p>GAMBLING.</p><p>That one had earned its place. I counted the money again. Not enough. Real. Tomorrow I could do this again without asking history to cooperate. I lay down. Then sat up again. One more thought. If I was this good at reading gamblers, what else had I been reading all my life without calling it a skill? Parties. Guild clerks. Merchants. Lovers. Enemies. Audiences. The word audiences sat there longer than the others. I did not know why. Not yet. I wrote it down anyway.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="002.html">← Chapter 2</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="005.html">Chapter 4 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/027.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 21: The Rescuer — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 21</div><h1>THE RESCUER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Senn was faster than she looked. That was inconvenient. She had a broom, work shoes, and thirty-one goats behind a closed gate. None of those things suggested speed. She disappeared around the corner before Cal and I reached it.</p><p>“Left?” he asked.</p><p>“Dyer’s Lane.”</p><p>“That means nothing to me.”</p><p>“Me either.”</p><p>We turned left. Darrowmere changed within one street. The square and command post had been stone, carts, officials, people doing jobs they understood. Here the buildings leaned close. Workshops below. Rooms above. Narrow passages between them. Lines of dyed cloth stretched overhead from upper windows, red and yellow and blue dripping into buckets because somebody had abandoned them halfway through rinsing.</p><p>The street smelled of wet wool, vinegar, smoke, and something metallic. Doors stood open. A bucket rolled in a gutter. No people. That was wrong. Not empty. Abandoned recently. There was a difference. A kettle still steamed on a doorstep. A pair of shoes sat neatly outside one door. Someone had dropped half a loaf in the mud.</p><figure class="chapter-art feature-illustration feature-portrait"><a href="../visual/chapter_art/027/v28_c27_feature_dyers-lane.png" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><img alt="Dyers Lane" decoding="async" height="1402" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/027/v28_c27_feature_dyers-lane.png" width="1122"/></a></figure><p>One long bell. Two short. East breach. Again.</p><p>“Which way?” Cal asked.</p><p>I listened. Senn shouted somewhere ahead. Not words. A name.</p><p>“Mira!”</p><p>We ran. My body objected immediately. Bruised hip. Shoulder. Headache. No sword. No knife. NO CASTING tied to my wrist. Excellent equipment for an emergency. We passed a dye yard with six waist-high vats. Purple liquid had spilled across the stones. A man stood on a roof pulling a ladder up behind him.</p><p>“Inside!” he shouted.</p><p>“We’re looking for a girl!”</p><p>“Everyone is!”</p><p>Useful. Not useful. Cal pointed. Senn. She was at the next intersection, arguing with two Darrowmere watch. They had overturned a handcart across the lane. One held a spear. The other had a crossbow.</p><p>“Senn,” the spearwoman said, “no.”</p><p>“My daughter is there,” Senn said.</p><p>“We sent someone,” the spearwoman said.</p><p>“You sent Jory,” Senn said.</p><p>“Yes,” the spearwoman said.</p><p>“He’s sixteen,” Senn said.</p><p>“He’s watch,” the spearwoman said.</p><p>“He’s sixteen,” Senn said.</p><p>Senn tried to go around. The spearwoman blocked her. Cal slowed. I did too. Good. Competent people already here. Do not become another problem.</p><p>“What house?” I asked.</p><p>Senn pointed past the barricade.</p><p>“Blue shutters. End of lane.”</p><p>The crossbowman said, “Girl’s name?”</p><p>“Mira.”</p><p>“Age?”</p><p>“Twelve.”</p><p>“Alone?”</p><p>“She was with my mother.”</p><p>“Your mother?”</p><p>“Eda.”</p><p>“Age?”</p><p>“Old.”</p><p>“Senn.”</p><p>“Sixty-eight.”</p><p>The crossbowman nodded.</p><p>“Anyone else?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The spearwoman looked at us.</p><p>“Guild?”</p><p>“Bronze,” Cal said.</p><p>She looked at my wrist.</p><p>“No casting?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Weapon?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She looked at Cal’s bandaged arm.</p><p>“Wonderful.”</p><p>“I have a sword.”</p><p>“One arm.”</p><p>“Other one works.”</p><p>Senn said, “Are we finished?” The spearwoman ignored her.</p><p>“Creature crossed roofs near the lane three minutes ago. Another was seen behind the tannery. We have two watch inside pulling residents. You stay here.”</p><p>That was correct. I hated it. Something watched us. I turned. Roofline. Windows. Cloth lines. Nothing.</p><p>“What?” Cal asked.</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>The word came too quickly. He followed my eyes.</p><p>“What did you see?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“That is different.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Senn shouted, “Mira!” A voice answered. Faint.</p><p>“Ma!”</p><p>Senn moved. The spearwoman caught her.</p><p>“Mira!” Senn screamed.</p><p>“Ma!”</p><p>Blue shutters. End of lane. Alive. Good. The crossbowman cupped his hands.</p><p>“Mira! Stay inside!”</p><p>“No!”</p><p>Not ideal. A second voice called from the same direction. Older.</p><p>“Roof!”</p><p>Everyone looked up. Gray moved across red cloth. Not creature. Cloth. Wind. No wind. I stared. The red sheet sagged. Something had crossed the line above it. I had not seen what.</p><p>“There,” I said.</p><p>Crossbowman raised.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>I pointed. Nothing. </p><p>He waited. Nothing. </p><p>Spearwoman said, “Did you see it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“I saw the cloth move.”</p><p>“Could be wind.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There was no wind. I did not say that. She already knew.</p><p>“Back,” she ordered.</p><p>We backed. All of us except Senn, who had to be physically moved. The lane narrowed toward the blue shutters. Three buildings on each side. Dye shed. Cooper. House. Another house. Roof bridges made from planks. People here moved goods above street level. Useful. Dangerous. Something scraped tile. Left. I turned. Nothing. My skin tightened. Not fear exactly. Old sensation. A dungeon corridor after the traps stopped.</p><p>A forest when birds stopped calling. A room where someone had already decided to kill you and was waiting for position. Watched. I knew that feeling. I also knew how often experienced people turned ordinary silence into evidence because they wanted their instincts to be magic. Know. Think. Check. I knew I felt watched. I thought something might be tracking movement from the roofs.</p><p>I could check nothing. Wonderful. A whistle sounded deeper in the lane. Two short. The spearwoman answered with one. A watchman appeared at a doorway halfway down. Young. Jory, presumably.</p><p>“Sella house clear!”</p><p>“Next?”</p><p>“Locked!”</p><p>“Mira!” Senn yelled.</p><p>The blue shutters opened. A girl’s face appeared.</p><p>“Ma!”</p><p>“Stay there!”</p><p>The girl did not stay there. Of course. She disappeared from the window. Senn made a sound that contained several religions. Jory ran toward the blue-shutter house. Something moved above him. This time I saw enough. Not shape. Shadow. Wrong direction.</p><p>“Jory!”</p><p>He looked back. Bad.</p><p>“Roof!”</p><p>He looked up. Worse. A gray body came down behind him. The crossbow snapped. Bolt struck wall. Creature landed. Jory ran. Good. No fight. He ran toward us. Creature followed. Spearwoman lowered her weapon.</p><p>“Clear!”</p><p>We moved aside. She had the line. Jory passed. Creature came. She thrust. Not at chest. Low. Front leg. The creature changed direction. Too fast. Exactly as before. But she expected it. Her spear moved with it. Darrowmere had learned too. Point cut the shoulder. Creature screamed and went up the wall. Crossbowman fired. Miss. Creature reached roof. Gone. Nobody chased. Excellent.</p><p>Jory bent over breathing. The spearwoman slapped the back of his head.</p><p>“You looked,” she said.</p><p>“You yelled,” Jory said.</p><p>“Not me,” she said.</p><p>He looked at me. I raised my hand.</p><p>“Sorry.”</p><p>“Why yell if I’m not supposed to look?”</p><p>Fair. Spearwoman said, “Next time run first.”</p><p>“Next time?”</p><p>“Move.”</p><p>Jory moved. They had adapted in hours. </p><p>Senn said, “My daughter.”</p><p>“Yes,” the spearwoman said. “Now we know the roof route.”</p><p>She pointed to the blue house.</p><p>“Jory, rear access?” she asked.</p><p>“Alley connects dye shed,” Jory said.</p><p>“Crossbow, roof cover,” she ordered.</p><p>The man nodded. She looked at Cal.</p><p>“Can you hold a door?” she asked.</p><p>“Yes,” Cal said.</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>"You?"</p><p>“I can also hold a door,” I said.</p><p>“No magic?”</p><p>“No magic.”</p><p>“Good. You two come.”</p><p>Senn said, “Me.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I know the house.”</p><p>“Tell us.”</p><p>“Back door sticks. Kitchen window opens outward. Stairs turn right. My mother sleeps downstairs because of her knee. Mira’s room is above.”</p><p>The spearwoman nodded.</p><p>“Anything dangerous inside?”</p><p>“Eda.”</p><p>The spearwoman almost smiled.</p><p>“Stay.”</p><p>We went. Not down the lane. Through the dye shed. Smarter. The building was dark and warm. Vats filled most of the floor. Blue wool hung from racks. A cat watched us from a shelf and seemed unimpressed by the emergency. The spearwoman finally gave us her name.</p><p>“Iris.”</p><p>Cal said, “Cal.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I heard.”</p><p>I disliked that. Iris pointed to a rear door.</p><p>“Jory takes alley. Cal holds here. Greg with me.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You’re unarmed.”</p><p>“That usually argues for farther away.”</p><p>“You ask useful questions.”</p><p>That was not enough armor. We entered the alley. Narrow. Brick on one side. Wood on the other. Overhead, two planks connected buildings. I looked up. Nothing. Watched. Again. Not from ahead. Behind? I turned. Cal stood in the dye shed doorway. Beyond him, racks. Cat. Nothing.</p><p>“What?” Iris whispered.</p><p>“I feel watched.”</p><p>“That a magic thing?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Useful?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then keep it.”</p><p>I liked her too. This was ridiculous. We moved. The blue house’s back door was twenty yards away. </p><p>Jory reached it first. Tried latch. Stuck. Of course. He shoved. Nothing. </p><p>Iris said, “Window.” Kitchen window. Outward. </p><p>Jory lifted it. A gray head appeared inside. No. Old woman. White hair. She hit him with a pan. Jory fell backward.</p><p>“Eda!” Iris hissed.</p><p>“Who are you?”</p><p>“Watch!”</p><p>“Prove it.”</p><p>Jory sat in the alley holding his forehead.</p><p>“Ma’am.”</p><p>Eda looked at him.</p><p>“Oh. Jory.”</p><p>“You know me?”</p><p>“You stole pears.”</p><p>“When I was nine.”</p><p>“You stole pears.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Open the door,” Iris said.</p><p>“It sticks.”</p><p>“We know.”</p><p>Eda disappeared. Door opened thirty seconds later. She had a knife in one hand.</p><p>“Mira’s upstairs.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“She went for the box.”</p><p>“What box?”</p><p>“Her father’s.”</p><p>Senn had not mentioned a box. Of course. People never remembered the object until the object became the problem. Iris pointed.</p><p>“Jory, take Eda.”</p><p>“I can walk,” Eda said.</p><p>“Then walk with Jory.”</p><p>“I don’t like Jory.”</p><p>“You know him.”</p><p>“Unfortunately.”</p><p>They left. Iris looked at me.</p><p>“Stairs.”</p><p>I looked up. Watched. Not feeling now. Certainty? No. Still feeling. The house creaked. Ordinary wood. Outside, a crossbow snapped. Everyone froze. One shot. No whistle. Iris waited. Then moved. We climbed. Right turn. Senn had been exact. At the top, a short hall. Mira’s door open. No girl.</p><p>“Mira,” Iris called quietly.</p><p>Something knocked. Back room. We entered. Mira was under the bed. Not hiding. Reaching. Her entire arm disappeared beneath it.</p><p>“I almost have it.”</p><p>Iris closed her eyes.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“The box.”</p><p>“Leave it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Mira.”</p><p>“My dad made it.”</p><p>There it was. Not rational. Not irrational either. Twelve. Father. Box. Iris looked at me. I knew what she wanted. Move the girl. Not optimize the box. I crouched.</p><p>“Mira.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Who are you?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“That’s a stupid name.”</p><p>“Today has been difficult enough.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/027/Ch027_Fast-Coverage-003-A16.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 27." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>She stared. Good. Attention.</p><p>“Your mother is outside.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“She hit a watchwoman with a broom.”</p><p>“No she didn’t.”</p><p>“Not yet.”</p><p>Mira smiled despite herself.</p><p>“Come out.”</p><p>“I can reach it.”</p><p>The house roof creaked. Not wood. Weight. Iris heard it. Her eyes went up.</p><p>“Mira. Now.”</p><p>The girl froze. There. Fear finally got through. She pulled her arm out. No box. I grabbed her wrist. Iris grabbed my coat.</p><p>“No running.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Roof.”</p><p>Right. Movement triggers? Maybe. Creature could be above. We moved slowly into the hall. Scrape. Overhead. Following. Mira squeezed my hand.</p><p>“Is it one?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Did you see it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then how do you know?”</p><p>“I don’t.”</p><p>Good answer. Bad comfort. Downstairs. Halfway. Something hit the roof. Hard. Dust fell. Mira screamed. We ran. No more slow. Kitchen. Back door. Jory waiting at alley mouth.</p><p>“Go!”</p><p>Iris pushed Mira toward him. The girl ran. I followed. Something crashed through the upstairs window. Glass behind us. Cal shouted from the dye shed.</p><p>“Move!”</p><p>We moved. Mira reached Jory. Jory grabbed her. Roof tiles shattered. Creature landed in the alley between us and the dye shed. Not the one Iris cut. No shoulder wound. Fresh. It did not attack. That was worse. It looked at Mira. Then me. Then Iris. Still. The first still creature I had seen. Black eyes. No visible white. Nostrils opening and closing.</p><p>Smelling? Listening? Thinking? My skin went cold. Watched. All chapter. No. All lane. Was this it? Impossible to know. The creature tilted its head. Not animal-curious. That was interpretation. Dangerous. Do not humanize unknown behavior. Iris lowered her spear. The alley was too narrow. Good for spear. Bad for turning. Jory had Mira behind him. Cal on far side. Creature between.</p><p>“Back,” Iris said.</p><p>We backed toward the house. Creature stayed. One step. It matched. Not charged. Matched.</p><p>“Greg,” Iris whispered.</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Better. My wrist tag brushed my skin.</p><p>NO CASTING.</p><p>I had mana. Not much. Enough for one stupid thing. No. If I broke it the first time danger became inconvenient, it had never been a restriction. Iris shifted spear point. Creature’s eyes moved to it. There. Attention. Maybe.</p><p>“Jory,” I said.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Take Mira.”</p><p>“I have her.”</p><p>“Not you. Cal.”</p><p>Cal understood. He moved sideways. Creature’s head followed. Not Mira. Movement. Maybe. Jory transferred Mira to Cal. Creature tracked Cal. No. Tracked Mira? Could not tell.</p><p>“Take her through the shed.”</p><p>Cal did. Creature tensed. Iris moved the spear. It looked back. Attention could be pulled. That was enough. Not truth. Enough.</p><p>“Now,” Iris said.</p><p>She stepped forward. Not thrust. Occupied space. Creature compressed. I knew what came next.</p><p>“Left.”</p><p>Iris went left before asking. Creature exploded right. Past us. Not toward Mira. Up the wall. Gone. We did not chase. We ran. Through the dye shed. Cat still there. Outside. Barricade. Senn saw Mira. Everything else stopped mattering. She hit the girl. One open hand against the shoulder.</p><p>Then pulled her in so hard Mira disappeared against her dress.</p><p>“You stupid, stupid, stupid child.”</p><p>“I got the box.”</p><p>Senn pulled back.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>Mira reached inside her coat. Small wooden box. She had gotten it after all. I stared.</p><p>“When?”</p><p>Mira looked at me like I was stupid too.</p><p>“With my other hand.”</p><p>Of course. Senn started crying. Then laughing. Then both. Eda arrived behind them with Jory.</p><p>“I told her to leave it.”</p><p>“You helped her hide it,” Senn said.</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“You always help her.”</p><p>“She has good instincts.”</p><p>“She went upstairs during a breach.”</p><p>“Except today.”</p><p>Again. Iris was already reporting to the crossbowman. Creature in alley. No attack. Observed tracking movement or person, uncertain. Exited roofward. No pursuit. I looked back toward Dyer’s Lane. Red cloth overhead. Blue shutters. Empty windows. Nothing. Still watched. The feeling had not gone. That mattered. Or it did not. Cal came beside me.</p><p>“You still feel it?”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“How did you know?”</p><p>“You’ve checked the roofs fourteen times.”</p><p>“Fourteen?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I looked again. Nothing.</p><p>“Could be the creatures.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be people hiding.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be you hit your head.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be nothing.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He waited. I hated him for learning the method.</p><p>“What do you think?” he asked.</p><p>I looked at the roof where the creature had disappeared. Then farther. Beyond it. A chimney. Bell tower. Laundry lines. Windows. Too many places for eyes.</p><p>“I think something has been watching how we move.”</p><p>“Creature?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Person?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Magic?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>Cal nodded.</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Iris heard us.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing confirmed,” I said.</p><p>“Then report the feeling separately.”</p><p>I looked at her. She shrugged.</p><p>“People survive by noticing things before they can prove them. They die by treating the noticing like proof.”</p><p>That was annoyingly good. We returned west with Senn, Mira, Eda, and the remaining watch. Nobody attacked us. The bells stopped before we reached the square. That should have made me feel better. It did not. At command, Doven took the breach report. Two creatures confirmed inside the wall. One driven out. One unaccounted for. No deaths. Three minor injuries. One missing box recovered despite explicit instructions.</p><p>Doven looked at Mira. She held it tighter. He did not ask. Then </p><p>Iris said, “Greg has an unconfirmed observation.” </p><p>I glared at her. </p><p>She waited. Doven looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I could have made it sound better. Instinct. Experience. Pattern recognition. Predator behavior. I had words that made uncertainty wear a uniform. I did not use them.</p><p>“I felt watched from the time we entered Dyer’s Lane.”</p><p>“By what?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Did you see anything?”</p><p>“Several movements consistent with creatures. Nothing that explains the entire feeling.”</p><p>“Magic?”</p><p>“Nothing detected.”</p><p>“Were you checking?”</p><p>“No casting. No detection method.”</p><p>“Could it be nerves?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could it be a creature?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could it be a person?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Doven wrote something. That was all.</p><p>“What did you write?”</p><p>He turned the paper.</p><p>UNCONFIRMED: POSSIBLE OBSERVATION FROM ROOFS / MOVEMENT TRACKING.</p><p>No monster. No watcher. No certainty. Good. I nodded. Doven looked at my wrist.</p><p>“You cast?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>That surprised him. It surprised me too.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Alden sat against the far wall. Still there. Still furious about it. He looked at me.</p><p>“Anything happen?”</p><p>I looked at the NO CASTING tag. Then at my empty sword belt. Then at the blood still under my fingernails.</p><p>“A goat stood on me.”</p><p>Alden waited.</p><p>“That’s all?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Thought so.”</p><p>I sat beside him. Outside, Darrowmere resumed making noise. Hammers. Carts. People. Someone shouting about missing chickens. The bell did not ring. I looked at the window. Nothing looked back. That was not the same as nothing being there.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="026.html">← Chapter 20</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="028.html">Chapter 22 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/028.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 22: The Guest — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 22</div><h1>THE GUEST</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Darrowmere charged refugees for soup. One copper. I learned this because Alden had no copper.</p><p>“I have copper,” he said.</p><p>“You have a silver.”</p><p>“That is money.”</p><p>“It is too much money for soup.”</p><p>“I can get change.”</p><p>The woman behind the pot looked at him.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Alden looked at me. I looked at the woman. She had a ladle. I had learned enough today.</p><p>“Two soups,” I said.</p><p>“One copper each.”</p><p>I paid. Alden took his bowl.</p><p>“You owe me.”</p><p>“One copper.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You owe Antonius gold.”</p><p>“That is unrelated.”</p><p>“Is it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>We sat on the edge of a dry fountain in Darrowmere’s central square and ate. The soup contained barley, onion, cabbage, and something that had once been optimistic about becoming meat. It was excellent because it was hot, not because it was good.</p><p>The sun had gone down behind the western roofs. Smoke still marked the east, but less than before. The bells had not rung for nearly an hour. People had begun doing evening things. That was stranger than the monsters.</p><p>A shopkeeper shuttered half his windows and left the other half open. A woman swept broken glass into a pile. Two watchmen argued about where to put a lantern. A boy carried three loaves through the square and sold all of them before reaching the other side. Somebody had erected a chalk board outside the grain office.</p><p>ROOMS NEEDED.</p><p>ROOMS OFFERED.</p><p>ANIMALS HELD.</p><p>MISSING PERSONS.</p><p>WORK CREWS.</p><p>The handwriting changed every few lines. Names accumulated. Names disappeared. Darrowmere was surviving administratively. I ate. Alden ate faster. His left arm stayed close to his body despite all his complaints about the restriction. Good.</p><p>“You’re staring,” he said.</p><p>“At what?”</p><p>“The board.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I am reading it.”</p><p>“You’ve read it four times.”</p><p>That seemed excessive. I looked at my bowl instead.</p><p>“Where are we sleeping?”</p><p>Alden stopped eating. Ah. There it was. We had arrived without bedrolls, spare clothes, a return plan, or a contract assigning lodging. My shirt had been cut off. I was wearing a borrowed gray undershirt from the infirmary that was too short in the arms.</p><p>My sword was still on the road unless someone had recovered it. My knife was also on the road, though in a different location. I had one copper less than before. Alden had one copper debt more. We had been very busy becoming less prepared.</p><p>“Guild hall?” Alden asked.</p><p>“Full.”</p><p>“Inn?”</p><p>“Probably full.”</p><p>“Stable?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why not?”</p><p>“Because I have standards.”</p><p>“You rode in a boat on a wagon.”</p><p>“That was transportation.”</p><p>Alden finished his soup.</p><p>“Stable.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>We checked the Guild hall. Full. Not metaphorically. There were people sleeping under the registration table. The clerk inside pointed us toward Temple House. Temple House was full. Temple House pointed us toward three inns. The first inn had no rooms.
