The second had floor space for six copper each.</p><p>“Six?” Alden asked.</p><p>The innkeeper looked at him.</p><p>“Floor.”</p><p>“Not bed?”</p><p>“Floor.”</p><p>“Blanket?”</p><p>“Two copper.”</p><p>“Each?”</p><p>“Blanket.”</p><p>Alden looked at me. </p><p>I said, “Stable.” </p><p>He smiled. I hated him. The third inn had no rooms, no floor, no stable, and one woman willing to rent us the use of a chicken shed for four copper if we did not disturb the chickens. We returned to the square. The chalk board had changed. ROOMS NEEDED now had seventeen more marks.</p><p>A man stood beside it shouting.</p><p>“Anyone with loft space, spare room, covered yard, dry shed, put your street and number. No promises. Watch may inspect. Guild will pay partial if assigned.”</p><p>Alden said, “Guild will pay?”</p><p>“Apparently.”</p><p>“We should have waited.”</p><p>“We did.”</p><p>“No. Before soup.”</p><p>“That has nothing to do with lodging.”</p><p>“It’s all money.”</p><p>That sounded like Antonius. I disliked it. A woman at the board turned.</p><p>“Bronze?”</p><p>“Yes,” Alden said.</p><p>She looked at our wrist tags. Then at our injuries.</p><p>“Working?”</p><p>“Apparently not,” I said.</p><p>“Can you walk?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then working.”</p><p>She handed us a piece of chalk.</p><p>“Name.”</p><p>I wrote Greg. Alden wrote Alden Marr.</p><p>“City?”</p><p>We gave it.</p><p>“Need?”</p><p>“Two places to sleep.”</p><p>“Together?”</p><p>Alden looked at me. I looked at him.</p><p>“No,” we said simultaneously.</p><p>The woman did not react.</p><p>“Any animals?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Children?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Medical restrictions?”</p><p>Alden held up his tag. I held up mine. She read them.</p><p>“Interesting.”</p><p>“It is not.”</p><p>She marked something.</p><p>“Can either of you cook?”</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>Alden said, “No.” </p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“You can cook.”</p><p>“I can heat food.”</p><p>“That is cooking.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The woman said, “Can either of you cook without setting anything on fire?”</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>Alden hesitated.</p><p>“Why did you hesitate?”</p><p>“I was deciding whether frying counts.”</p><p>She wrote one name. Mine.</p><p>“Wait.”</p><p>“You said yes.”</p><p>“For what?”</p><p>“Work lodging.”</p><p>“What work?”</p><p>“Kitchen.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You need a room.”</p><p>“I need sleep.”</p><p>“You need a room first.”</p><p>Alden started laughing. The woman pointed at him.</p><p>“You can carry water one-handed.”</p><p>His laughter stopped.</p><p>“No lifting left,” he said.</p><p>“Bucket in right.”</p><p>He considered.</p><p>“That seems legal.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>We were assigned to the Golden Sheaf. Not an inn. A bakery. The owner had two rooms above the ovens normally used by seasonal workers. Both seasonal workers were currently with family west of town. The rooms were available. The price was three hours of evening work. Each. I objected on economic grounds. Alden objected because he was tired. The board woman ignored us both.</p><p>The Golden Sheaf was four streets from the square. Warmth hit us before the door opened. Bread. Yeast. Flour. Woodsmoke. Butter. For one dangerous second, I would have agreed to anything. The owner was named Brina.</p><p>She was short, square, gray-haired, and covered in flour from wrists to eyebrows. She looked at us.</p><p>“Which one cooks?”</p><p>I raised my hand.</p><p>“No casting,” she said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good. Magic ruins proofing if idiots use heat spells.”</p><p>“I was not going to use magic.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/028/Ch028_Fast-Coverage-003-A17.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 28." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“Everyone says that until they get impatient.”</p><p>“I do not know heat magic.”</p><p>She paused.</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>Alden leaned against the doorframe.</p><p>“What do I do?”</p><p>“Water.”</p><p>He sighed.</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>“Right hand.”</p><p>He looked at her.</p><p>“How does everyone know?”</p><p>“Tag.”</p><p>He looked at the tag as though betrayed. We worked. Not heroically. I chopped onions. Then carrots. Then cabbage. Then more onions. Brina made tomorrow’s soup in a pot large enough to drown a child. I did not mention that comparison.</p><p>Alden carried water from the courtyard pump one bucket at a time. He tried two once. Brina pointed at his wrist. He put one down. No argument. Interesting. The bakery had not closed because of the breach. It had changed. Bread for normal customers ended at midday.</p><p>After that, Brina switched to coarse loaves for watch, Guild, displaced families, and anyone holding a meal chit. The town paid some. The Guild paid some. Temple House paid some. Some people paid nothing. Brina kept three ledgers. I asked why. She told me to chop. I chopped. Twenty minutes later she explained anyway.</p><p>“Town rate. Guild rate. Charity.”</p><p>“Different prices?”</p><p>“Different debts.”</p><p>“Who pays charity?”</p><p>“I do until I don’t.”</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“It means chop.”</p><p>I chopped. Alden returned with water.</p><p>“Why are you smiling?”</p><p>“I’m not.”</p><p>“You are.”</p><p>“Work.”</p><p>“That’s upsetting.”</p><p>Brina pointed at the pump. He left. The kitchen had five other people. None were employees. A cooper’s wife kneaded dough. A boy from the tannery washed bowls. An elderly man cut turnips badly. A watchwoman on break ate standing up while labeling sacks.</p><p>Nobody asked us about the creatures. For nearly an hour, the monsters did not exist. There were onions, bowls, flour, and the question of whether the second soup pot had enough salt. I tasted it.</p><p>“Needs salt.”</p><p>Brina tasted it.</p><p>“Not yet. It reduces another hour.”</p><p>“Then why ask me?”</p><p>“I wanted another tongue on it before I added anything.”</p><p>I liked her less. Then she gave me the heel of a fresh loaf with butter. I reconsidered. My headache eased. Not gone. Better. The NO CASTING tag remained on my wrist. At one point a stack of bowls began to slide. My hand moved. Mana did not. I caught them with my other hand. Three broke. Brina looked at the pieces.</p><p>“Could’ve been twelve.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She handed me a broom. Good. I swept. Something moved outside the rear window. I looked. Courtyard. Pump. Wall. Alden. Nothing else. He noticed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>He followed my eyes anyway. The watcher feeling had faded in the square. Here it returned. Not strong. A pressure between my shoulders. The sense that if I turned quickly enough I would catch something withdrawing. </p><p>I turned quickly. Nothing. </p><p>Alden said, “You’re doing it again.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Still?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you want me to check?”</p><p>That was a good question.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because then we have two people staring at roofs instead of one.”</p><p>He accepted that. Also interesting. We finished the kitchen work after dark. Brina inspected our hands. Not metaphorically. Hands. Alden’s right palm had pump blisters. Mine smelled permanently of onion.</p><p>“Good enough,” she said.</p><p>“Room?”</p><p>“Upstairs.”</p><p>“Bed?”</p><p>“Mattress.”</p><p>“Blanket?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I nearly cried. Not actually. Possibly. The rooms were tiny. Mine had a narrow mattress, a washbasin, a chair with one short leg, and a window overlooking the rear alley. Alden’s was across the hall. I washed. The water turned gray. Then pink. Then gray again. I discovered bruises I had not previously negotiated with. Hip. Ribs. Shoulder. Knee. Palm. My body had submitted an itemized complaint.</p><p>I lay down. The mattress was too soft. I hated it. Then I slept. For eleven minutes. Someone knocked. I opened my eyes. Dark. Knock.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>Alden. I got up. Opened door.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>He held a copper. I stared.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Soup.”</p><p>I stared harder.</p><p>“I owe you.”</p><p>“You woke me to repay one copper?”</p><p>“You said I owed you.”</p><p>“I did not mean tonight.”</p><p>“You didn’t specify.”</p><p>I took the copper.</p><p>“Go away.”</p><p>He smiled.</p><p>“Good night.”</p><p>I closed the door. Lay down. Counted to perhaps twenty. Knock. I opened it again.</p><p>“If this is interest, I will kill you.”</p><p>Alden was not smiling.</p><p>“Bell.”</p><p>I listened. Nothing. Then one stroke. Not alarm pattern. Single. Pause. Single. Pause.</p><p>“What is that?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>We went downstairs. Brina was already at the front door. She opened it. People stood in the street listening. Single bell. Pause. Single. An old man across the road said, “Found.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Missing.”</p><p>Another bell.</p><p>“Found alive?” Alden asked.</p><p>The man shrugged.</p><p>“Found.”</p><p>The town had a bell for that. Of course it did. Brina closed the door.</p><p>“Bed.”</p><p>“That’s it?” I asked.</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>“Morning.”</p><p>She went upstairs. Alden looked at me. I looked at him. Bed. Correct. We went. I closed my door. Lay down. The alley outside was quiet. No bell. No shouting. No claws. I could smell bread through the floorboards. My channels ached less. My body ached more. I had a copper from Alden. My sword was still missing. Tomorrow existed. That was enough.</p><p>I closed my eyes. Watched. The feeling came back. Not from the alley. Not the roof. Somewhere. I opened my eyes. Dark room. Window. Chair. Washbasin. Nothing. I waited. Nothing happened. Five minutes. Maybe ten. I almost slept. Then something tapped the window. Once. I was awake immediately. No mana. No sword. No knife.</p><p>NO CASTING.</p><p>I did not move. Tap. Not again. Only once. Could have been wood cooling. Could have been a branch. There was no tree outside. Could have been a bird. At night. Could have been nothing. I waited. Eventually, I got up. Slowly. I did not open the window. I looked through it. Alley. Roofline. Bakery wall. Moonlight on stone. Nothing. Then I looked down.</p><p>On the outer sill sat a small piece of bread.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Bread On The Sill" decoding="async" height="335" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/028/v28_c28_s01_bread-on-the-sill.png" width="302"/></figure><p>The heel. Butter side up. I stared. Brina had given me one exactly like it downstairs. That meant nothing. Bread existed in bakeries. People dropped bread. Birds carried things. Children did strange things. Someone could have placed it there before I entered the room. Except I had looked out this window while washing. The sill had been empty. I knew that. I thought I knew that.</p><p>Check. Could I prove it? No. I did not touch the bread. I closed the curtain. Then I moved the chair under the door handle. Not because I was afraid. Because chairs were free. I lay down again. I did not cast. I did not investigate. I did not wake Alden.</p><p>For a long time, I listened to Darrowmere breathe around me. Ovens below. Someone coughing through the wall. A cart passing far away. A dog barking twice. Normal sounds. Eventually I slept. In the morning, the bread was gone.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="027.html">← Chapter 21</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="029.html">Chapter 23 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/040.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 32: The Tester — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 32</div><h1>THE TESTER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Dinner was fish stew. I did not ask what fish. This was growth. Or cowardice. The stew had potatoes, onions, something green, and enough salt to make the water afterward necessary rather than optional. I ate two bowls, went upstairs, checked my hands, checked my ribs, checked my channels, and did not check anything else. No sinkstone notes. No manufacturing list. No Arlo.</p><p>No Silas Marris. I slept. Morning made that decision look better. My right palm had closed enough that gripping no longer hurt unless I squeezed hard. My left blister had decided to become ugly rather than painful. Ribs quiet. Channels quiet. Mild stiffness in my legs from the spar. Nineteen-year-old recovery remained offensive.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Pell Vessa Workshop" decoding="async" height="169" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/040/v45_c40_pell-vessa-workshop.png" width="477"/></figure><p>Useful. I ate. Then I looked at the regulator. Arlo had asked for measurements. I had measurements. That was enough reason to go. I brought the device, my notes, and no questions about sinkstone. This lasted until I reached his door. Arlo’s workshop was louder than usual. Hammering from the back. A scraping wheel. Someone swearing about ceramic. Normal. I entered. Arlo was not at the regulator bench.</p><p>Vessa was. Arlo stood near the front with a man holding a brass lamp assembly. The customer was angry. Not theatrically. Expensively.</p><p>“It failed twice,” the customer said.</p><p>Arlo said, “Yes.”</p><p>“You repaired it,” the customer said.</p><p>“Yes,” Arlo said.</p><p>“It failed again,” the customer said.</p><p>“Yes,” Arlo said.</p><p>“That is not repair.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The man stared. I stopped just inside. Vessa saw me. She put one finger to her lips. Not because silence was required. Because this was good. I stayed. The customer set the lamp on the counter. Hard.</p><p>“Then what did I pay for?”</p><p>“First repair.”</p><p>“Which failed.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then refund it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because the first fault was repaired.”</p><p>The customer looked ready to become louder. Arlo turned the lamp. Pointed.</p><p>“First fault here.”</p><p>Small crack in the fuel collar.</p><p>“Replaced.”</p><p>Then another point.</p><p>“Second fault here.”</p><p>A blackened contact near the ignition housing.</p><p>“Different.”</p><p>“You expect me to believe it broke twice by coincidence?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Arlo paused.</p><p>“I expect it broke twice because it is bad.”</p><p>Vessa coughed into her hand. The customer looked at her. She became extremely interested in a file. Arlo continued.</p><p>“I can repair this fault.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Three copper.”</p><p>“I already paid four.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“For a bad lamp.”</p><p>“For a repair.”</p><p>The man looked at the lamp. Then Arlo. Then me. I had no role. Good.</p><p>“What would you do?” he asked.</p><p>Damn. Arlo looked at me. </p><p>Vessa looked at me. The customer waited. I could answer. The lamp was probably not worth repeated repair if failures were distributed. Maybe replace. Maybe inspect full assembly first. Maybe the customer wanted reliability more than lowest cost. Maybe Arlo knew the lamp better. </p><p>I said, “Ask him.” </p><p>The customer frowned.</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“No. Ask whether he would repair it if it were his.”</p><p>Arlo’s face changed. Not much. The customer looked at him.</p><p>“Well?”</p><p>Arlo picked up the lamp. Turned it. Looked at the base.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>There.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Body is thin. Heat warped one side. Collar repair holds. Contact can be replaced. Something else will fail.”</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>Arlo shrugged.</p><p>“Could be tomorrow. Could be a year.”</p><p>“Then why offer repair?”</p><p>“Because you asked for repair.”</p><p>The customer stared. Then laughed once. Not happily.</p><p>“Do you sell lamps?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Of course not.”</p><p>He took the lamp.</p><p>“Three copper?”</p><p>“For this fault.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He left. Arlo watched the door close. Then looked at me.</p><p>“You cost me three copper.”</p><p>“You did that.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Would you have repaired it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You said you would not if it were yours.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>“Interesting.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Vessa laughed. Arlo pointed at my bag.</p><p>“Measurements?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was the end of the lamp. No moral. No business philosophy. Just three copper not earned. I gave him the notes. He read them standing. Vertical. Tilted. Horizontal. Tap test. Cold water. No hot. He read that twice.</p><p>“Why no hot?”</p><p>“Tired.”</p><p>He looked up.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>That annoyed me.</p><p>“Why good?”</p><p>“Because tired measurements are bad.”</p><p>“I could have measured accurately.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“I dislike maybe.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He set the notes down.</p><p>“Horizontal worse.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Expected.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“You knew?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“That is not what expected means.”</p><p>“I expected orientation to matter.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>He took my regulator. Held it sideways.</p><p>“The settling pocket.”</p><p>Right. Gravity. The recess that gave flow somewhere to be wrong also had orientation. Of course.</p><p>“How much worse did you expect?”</p><p>“Didn’t know.”</p><p>“Then my measurement matters.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Good. He read the tap test again.</p><p>“Repeat?”</p><p>“Three times.”</p><p>“Same?”</p><p>“Same direction. Not same amount.”</p><p>He nodded.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“What does it change?”</p><p>“Fixture.”</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not regulator?”</p><p>“Maybe regulator.”</p><p>Arlo put the regulator in a clamp.</p><p>“Fixture first. If it still flutters, then regulator.”</p><p>“That is sensible.” Not the old clamp. A new one. Fourth fixture? No. Different bench. </p><p>He tapped the table. Flow line fluttered. Not much. Then he put a folded cloth beneath the fixture feet. Tapped again. Less flutter. </p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Isolation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That does not fix use.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It fixes measurement.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Good. Separate the tool from the test. I liked that.</p><p>“What if the use environment vibrates?”</p><p>“Then regulator needs to tolerate it.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Depends on use.”</p><p>“Mine?”</p><p>“You tell me.”</p><p>There. Ownership again. I had wanted low-flow control for magic work eventually. But what actual environment? Bench? Field? Body? Armor? Moving carriage? I had not specified. Future devices had context built into memory. Present device did not.</p><p>“What did I ask you to build?”</p><p>Arlo looked at me.</p><p>“Better low-flow regulator.”</p><p>“That is vague.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You built it anyway.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Interesting.”</p><p>Clean. I laughed. </p><p>Vessa said, “He also wanted to beat Tere’s old one.” </p><p>Arlo looked offended.</p><p>“No,” Arlo said.</p><p>“Yes,” Vessa said.</p><p>“Not beat,” Arlo said.</p><p>“What?” Vessa asked.</p><p>“Improve,” Arlo said.</p><p>“That is beat with paperwork.”</p><p>I liked her. Arlo ignored us.</p><p>“What do you want it for?”</p><p>I looked at the regulator. Barrier experiments. Mana feed? Not yet. Could be measuring low-output spell components. Could be material testing. Could become something else entirely.</p><p>“I don’t know yet.”</p><p>Arlo nodded. No disappointment.</p><p>“Then test broadly.”</p><p>That was permission to be annoying. Dangerous. I pulled my notes back. Then remembered the other question. Kestrin shale. I had not brought it. It had followed me anyway.</p><p>“Do you use processed kestrin?”</p><p>Arlo did not react. Good.</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>My attention sharpened. Vessa saw. Eyebrows. Fuck.</p><p>“For what?”</p><p>“Kiln packing. Cheap isolation blocks. Some fixture beds.”</p><p>“Mana work?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“What treatment?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>“On?”</p><p>“What you want.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Do you make it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Who does?”</p><p>Arlo shrugged.</p><p>“Stone yards. Kiln suppliers. Ward-material shops.”</p><p>Same broad answer as Edrin. Good.</p><p>“Consistent batches?”</p><p>He looked at me now.</p><p>“Consistent how?”</p><p>“Mana behavior within a narrow band.”</p><p>“How narrow?”</p><p>I stopped. Guild evidence. Do not imply access.</p><p>“Better than cheap material usually deserves.”</p><p>Arlo considered.</p><p>“That is not a number.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then I don’t know.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Is unusually consistent processed shale difficult?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Stone varies.”</p><p>“Treatment?”</p><p>“Also varies.”</p><p>“Heat?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Solution?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Pressure?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Order?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Cooling?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Grain?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I smiled. He frowned.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You like this.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Vessa said, “There he goes.” I ignored her.</p><p>“If you wanted consistent output, where would you spend effort?”</p><p>Arlo stared at me.</p><p>“That is not one question.”</p><p>“Choose.”</p><p>“Sorting.”</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>“Before treatment?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why not control treatment better?”</p><p>“Because bad stone stays bad stone.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“What do you sort for?”</p><p>“For suppression? Grain, porosity, and how much the raw piece varies before treatment.”</p><p>“Not color?”</p><p>“Only if color tracks one of those in the stock you bought.” I changed angle.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/040/Ch040_Fast-Coverage-003-B02.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 40." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“Say you want mild mana suppression.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Hypothetical.”</p><p>Arlo glanced at the notes still in my hand.</p><p>“You did not ask me about processed shale for a hypothetical.”</p><p>I went still.</p><p>“What are you working on?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Bad answer.”</p><p>“I am not working on it.”</p><p>“Worse.”</p><p>Vessa set down her file. Now both interested. I could tell them. Public knowledge: processed kestrin exists, some treated forms retain mana, mild suppression known in trade. Not Guild evidence. No Silas Marris. No Darrowmere.</p><p>“I saw processed shale that behaved more consistently than I expected.”</p><p>True.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Not mine to say.”</p><p>Arlo nodded. Accepted. Good.</p><p>“What did it do?”</p><p>“Suppression. Retention.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Not mine to say.”</p><p>He looked annoyed. Now he understood Edrin’s life. Good.</p><p>“Then what do you want?”</p><p>“Who can make consistent material.”</p><p>Arlo thought. Actually thought. Not performing expertise. His eyes went to the shelves. Then the kiln. Then Vessa. She shrugged.</p><p>“Stone yards can sort,” Vessa said.</p><p>Arlo said, “Kiln people can control heat.”</p><p>“Ward shops can test after,” Vessa said.</p><p>Arlo nodded.</p><p>“Best consistency might not come from one maker.”</p><p>I stopped. There. Supply chain. Not secret master craftsman. Sort here. Treat there. Test elsewhere. Rebatch. Ordinary manufacturing.</p><p>“How would you buy it?”</p><p>Arlo asked.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“If you needed consistent suppression.”</p><p>“I would find whoever makes the best.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared. He continued.</p><p>“I would buy too much cheap stock, test it, keep the good.”</p><p>That was crude. Effective.</p><p>“Wasteful.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Expensive.”</p><p>“Less than making a kiln.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“What if volume is large?”</p><p>“Then contract sorting.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Supplier.”</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>Arlo shrugged.</p><p>“I buy from Dorrin Stone when I need shale.”</p><p>Name. Small. Ordinary.</p><p>“Are they good?”</p><p>“They deliver.”</p><p>“That is not good.”</p><p>“It is very good.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Do they process?”</p><p>“Some. Mostly sell.”</p><p>“Would they know who does?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There. Lead. Easy. Legal. Public. My brain began building. Dorrin Stone. Ask about sorted kestrin. Ask who treats for mana suppression. Do not mention sacks. Do not mention Guild. Compare trade terms. Maybe find Silas Marris indirectly. No. Stop. Arlo watched me.</p><p>“Do not go now.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I need you.”</p><p>That changed everything.</p><p>“For?”</p><p>He pointed at the ceramic-bodied regulator. The cracked one.</p><p>“Still failing.”</p><p>I had forgotten. Good.</p><p>“What do you need?”</p><p>“Hands.”</p><p>I looked at my blisters.</p><p>“Bad timing.”</p><p>“Eyes, then.”</p><p>He set the ceramic regulator on the bench. Hairline crack around inlet. Dark staining. Same as before.</p><p>“What changed?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“That is poor progress.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What have you tested?”</p><p>He handed me a page. Pressure. Heat. Firing. Fluid. Clamp. Assembly torque. Three ceramics. Two glazes. Same crack location in four of seven trials. Not random.</p><p>“Why ceramic?”</p><p>“Customer wants nonmetal body.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Reagent compatibility.”</p><p>“What reagent?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“What do you want me to see?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“You said you need me.”</p><p>“I need another person to watch assembly.”</p><p>That was disappointingly sensible. Vessa said, “I watched.”</p><p>“You assemble.”</p><p>“I can watch.”</p><p>“You correct.”</p><p>“That is watching with value.”</p><p>Arlo looked at me.</p><p>“You don’t know enough.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>Excellent. He wanted ignorance. I sat. Arlo assembled the regulator. Slowly. Not his normal speed. He narrated nothing. Good. Body. Collar. Seal. Inlet. Ceramic housing. He tightened. Stopped. Looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You paused.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Habit.”</p><p>“What habit?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Do it again.”</p><p>He disassembled. Reassembled. Same point. Tiny pause before final collar turn.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Third. Pause.</p><p>“There.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You change grip.”</p><p>Arlo looked at his hand.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Vessa leaned closer. Arlo assembled again. At final collar turn, his thumb shifted from side pressure to top. Small. Why? Ceramic body wanted stability. He was unconsciously bracing.</p><p>“Why do you brace there?”</p><p>“I don’t.”</p><p>“You do.”</p><p>He tried without. The body rotated a fraction in the fixture. Vessa said, “Oh.” </p><p>Arlo stared. The fixture held the collar. Not body. Like regulator fixture four. But ceramic had less tolerance for torsion. Arlo’s hand had been compensating. His hand was part of the fixture. Not repeatable.</p><p>“There,” I said.</p><p>Arlo looked pleased. Very pleased. Dangerously.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>We ran it. Vessa assembled. Different grip. Less rotation. Arlo assembled with deliberate body support. Less. Not solved. Better. He wrote. No lesson. No correction. Just finding a thing. I forgot Dorrin Stone for almost an hour. That might have been the most interesting part.</p><p>By the time Arlo stopped, my stomach had started making decisions.</p><p>“Food,” Vessa said.</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“That was not for you.”</p><p>Arlo looked at her. She pointed at the door.</p><p>“Both.”</p><p>We left. Arlo did not. Vessa came back, grabbed his sleeve, and pulled. He resisted for two steps. Then went. I followed because apparently I had been included. The food stall was around the corner. Rice. Roasted vegetables. Thin slices of pork. Arlo paid for his. Vessa paid for hers. I paid for mine. No one offered. Good. We ate standing. I remembered Dorrin Stone halfway through the pork.</p><p>“Dorrin Stone.”</p><p>Arlo looked annoyed.</p><p>“You remembered.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“They close early.”</p><p>I looked at the sun. He was right. Good.</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>Vessa said, “What are you buying?”</p><p>“Questions.”</p><p>“Expensive.”</p><p>“Usually.”</p><p>She nodded. No interest beyond that. Arlo finished eating.</p><p>“Bring regulator next time.”</p><p>“I brought it today.”</p><p>“Next time.”</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Vibration.”</p><p>“Mechanical?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Mana?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. I could wait. Again. Suspicious. We returned to the workshop. I collected my regulator and notes. The ceramic problem remained on the bench. Arlo had work. Vessa had work. I had a stone supplier name. Not a conspiracy. Not an answer. A place that sold rocks. Excellent. Outside, I considered going to Dorrin Stone anyway. Closed soon did not mean closed.</p><p>Could hurry. Could arrive before shutter. Could ask one question. Could get one name. Then another. Old pattern. One more. I looked at my hands. Better. Not good. My stomach full. Body tired in a clean way. Tomorrow existed. I went home by the long route. Not because it was efficient. Because the weather was good.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="039.html">← Chapter 31</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="041.html">Chapter 33 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/091.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 73: The Beginner — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 73</div><h1>THE BEGINNER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Hessa sent for me the next morning.</p><p>I did not assume this meant magic.</p><p>This was maturity.</p><p>It lasted until I reached her door.</p><p>Then I assumed it meant magic.</p><p>The note had been brief.</p><p>COME AFTER BREAKFAST.<br/>BRING NOTHING.</p><p>Bring nothing was either very good or very bad.</p><p>If she wanted me to cast, I did not need equipment.</p><p>If she wanted to tell me I was still not casting, I also did not need equipment.</p><p>Efficient woman.</p><p>I knocked.</p><p>“Come.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg at Hessa’s table during the first post-loss magic assessment." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/091/Ch91_Hessas-Test-Table.png"/></figure><p>Hessa was at the long table by the window with three cups, a shallow ceramic dish, and a bowl of water.</p><p>No crystals.</p><p>No wire.</p><p>No chalk.</p><p>No measuring frame.</p><p>No Barrier plates.</p><p>Nothing interesting.</p><p>I looked at the table.</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“Stop inventorying it.”</p><p>“I was looking.”</p><p>“You can look while sitting.”</p><p>“That is unfair.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat.</p><p>The chair was worse than mine.</p><p>This was now a category of knowledge I possessed.</p><p>Hessa pushed one of the cups toward me.</p><p>Tea.</p><p>I picked it up.</p><p>“Why am I here?”</p><p>“To answer a question.”</p><p>“Mine?”</p><p>“Eventually.”</p><p>She took a drink.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>This was another skill I had been developing.</p><p>Not well.</p><p>“What question?”</p><p>Hessa put her cup down.</p><p>“Does it still feel like your foot is there?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How often?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>“On?”</p><p>“Attention. Movement. Sometimes nothing I can identify.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>I looked at the shallow dish.</p><p>Empty.</p><p>“Cold. Burning. Cramping. Pressure. Position.”</p><p>“Position?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Explain.”</p><p>“Sometimes the foot feels planted. Sometimes twisted. Sometimes like the ankle is bent. Once I woke up and felt the whole foot hit the floor.”</p><p>“After it was gone.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Any sensation while using magic?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>I corrected.</p><p>“I haven't used magic.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then stop sounding offended.”</p><p>“I am not offended.”</p><p>“You are.”</p><p>“I am interested aggressively.”</p><p>“That is offended with paperwork.”</p><p>I drank tea.</p><p>She was improving.</p><p>Or I was easier to mock.</p><p>Probably both.</p><p>Hessa reached for the bowl of water.</p><p>She put one finger into it.</p><p>Then withdrew it.</p><p>“Cold.”</p><p>“I can see condensation.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She slid the bowl toward me.</p><p>“Right hand.”</p><p>I put two fingers in.</p><p>Cold.</p><p>“Left.”</p><p>I switched.</p><p>Cold.</p><p>“Right foot.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>She looked back.</p><p>“That seems difficult.”</p><p>“Your right foot, Greg.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>I took off my right shoe.</p><p>The floor was cool.</p><p>Hessa moved the bowl down.</p><p>I put my toes in.</p><p>Cold.</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Left foot.”</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>I stared harder.</p><p>She pulled the bowl back onto the table.</p><p>“What was that?”</p><p>“A question.”</p><p>“That was not a question.”</p><p>“It answered one.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“Whether you would try.”</p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>Closed it.</p><p>Opened it again.</p><p>“That is insulting.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“I would not put a nonexistent foot in water.”</p><p>“You nearly stood on one.”</p><p>“That was different.”</p><p>“You tried to step on one while kissing a girl.”</p><p>“That was private.”</p><p>“Nerin told me.”</p><p>“Of course he did.”</p><p>“Medical information.”</p><p>“Then why do you know about the kissing?”</p><p>“He enjoyed that part.”</p><p>I made a note to kill Nerin.</p><p>Later.</p><p>Hessa tapped the table.</p><p>“Your body can attempt an old movement before your attention corrects it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I wanted to know whether instruction could do the same.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“You noticed.”</p><p>“Obviously.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She took another drink.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>The question I wanted to ask was sitting directly behind my teeth.</p><p>I let it stay there.</p><p>Hessa noticed.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Ask.”</p><p>“Can I cast?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>There it was.</p><p>I had expected it.</p><p>Still unpleasant.</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Why not?”</p><p>“Because I don't know what changed.”</p><p>“Channels?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Body map?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Neither?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“That is not satisfying.”</p><p>“It is accurate.”</p><p>I put my shoe back on.</p><p>This took longer than it used to.</p><p>Not much.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>Hessa waited.</p><p>No assistance.</p><p>Good.</p><p>When I finished, she said, “I can check some things without having you cast.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What things?”</p><p>“Basic channel response.”</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was magic.</p><p>Technically.</p><p>Not casting.</p><p>Still.</p><p>My pulse increased.</p><p>Nineteen was inconvenient.</p><p>Fifty-something years of memory and the body still reacted to permission like a dog hearing a cupboard open.</p><p>“What do I do?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“That is becoming a theme.”</p><p>“Sit square.”</p><p>I adjusted.</p><p>She came around the table.</p><p>“Hands on your thighs.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“Close your eyes.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“So you stop trying to help.”</p><p>“I can stop trying to help with my eyes open.”</p><p>“No, you can't.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>I closed them.</p><p>The room changed.</p><p>Not magically.</p><p>Sound.</p><p>Street outside.</p><p>Cart wheel over stone.</p><p>Someone calling something about onions.</p><p>Hessa's steps.</p><p>Then her hand touched my right shoulder.</p><p>Two fingers.</p><p>Light pressure.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>She moved to my left shoulder.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Upper arm.</p><p>Forearm.</p><p>Wrist.</p><p>I knew this kind of examination only broadly.</p><p>Not enough to predict it.</p><p>Good.</p><p>She touched the center of my chest.</p><p>Something moved.</p><p>Not power.</p><p>Attention.</p><p>No.</p><p>That was too vague.</p><p>I felt the familiar internal readiness that came before drawing mana, except smaller and incomplete, like hearing the first note of a song and knowing the next one without singing it.</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>“I didn't.”</p><p>“You started.”</p><p>“I thought.”</p><p>“You started.”</p><p>I opened my eyes.</p><p>Hessa's fingers were still against my shirt.</p><p>“What did you do?”</p><p>“Very little.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Close your eyes.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>Annoying woman.</p><p>She repeated it.</p><p>Shoulder.</p><p>Arm.</p><p>Wrist.</p><p>Chest.</p><p>This time I did not follow the sensation.</p><p>It remained.</p><p>Faint.</p><p>Not imagined.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>She moved her fingers lower along the right side of my ribs.</p><p>The readiness shifted.</p><p>Then hip.</p><p>Right thigh.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Nothing at the shin.</p><p>Ankle.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Foot.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Obviously.</p><p>She moved back up.</p><p>Left hip.</p><p>Left thigh.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Then stopped.</p><p>I knew where her hand was from pressure through the trousers.</p><p>Below the knee there was no contact.</p><p>There could not be.</p><p>But my left foot felt cold.</p><p>I opened my eyes.</p><p>Hessa was standing beside me.</p><p>Her hand was nowhere near the residual limb.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>She withdrew.</p><p>“What did you feel?”</p><p>“Cold.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Left foot.”</p><p>Her face did not change.</p><p>That was worse than if it had.</p><p>“Did you do that?”</p><p>“I touched your left knee.”</p><p>“That is not what I asked.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did you use magic?”</p><p>“A little.”</p><p>“On the knee?”</p><p>“Near it.”</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“Not yours.”</p><p>“Obviously.”</p><p>“Then why ask?”</p><p>“Specificity.”</p><p>She returned to her chair.</p><p>I looked at my missing lower leg.</p><p>Nothing visible.</p><p>No glow.</p><p>No sensation now.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because once is information.”</p><p>“Twice is better information.”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Usually.”</p><p>“Not when the subject is already leaning into the result.”</p><p>“I am sitting.”</p><p>“You know what I mean.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>I hated that.</p><p>“What does it mean?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Does it mean the channel is still there?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Does it mean the body map carries channel expectation?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Does it mean your magic triggered phantom sensation without any channel below the knee?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Could you tell the difference?”</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>Bad chair.</p><p>My chair was better.</p><p>This was not relevant.</p><p>Hessa watched me.</p><p>“You're disappointed.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I am furious.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Because this is useful.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And you are stopping.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Because I want to continue.”</p><p>“Partly.”</p><p>“That is vindictive.”</p><p>“Partly.”</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>Very slightly.</p><p>I had not known Hessa could do that.</p><p>Disturbing.</p><p>“Other reason?”</p><p>“You have spent weeks learning what your body does when you aren't directing it.”</p><p>I said nothing.</p><p>“Today I need to know what it does when you aren't directing magic.”</p><p>I looked at the empty ceramic dish.</p><p>“What was that for?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>She shrugged.</p><p>“Gives you somewhere to look.”</p><p>“That is evil.”</p><p>“It worked.”</p><p>I had spent the first five minutes trying to infer a test from a dish.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>Excellent.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Greg studying notes and test materials after Hessa’s channel-response check." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/091/Ch91_Notes-After-Channel-Test.png"/></figure><p>“What did you learn?”</p><p>“That you can feel a basic channel prompt through the trunk.”</p><p>“I knew I could feel magic.”</p><p>“Before.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Before is not now.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>She continued.</p><p>“You responded along the right side in a way I expected.”</p><p>“What does expected mean?”</p><p>“Broadly intact.”</p><p>My pulse increased again.</p><p>She raised one finger.</p><p>“Do not turn that into cleared.”</p><p>“I was turning it into encouraging.”</p><p>“That is allowed.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“And left?”</p><p>“Your response above the knee was present.”</p><p>“Broadly intact?”</p><p>“Broadly.”</p><p>“Below?”</p><p>“I did not test below.”</p><p>“You can't touch below.”</p><p>“I don't need to touch skin to test every channel response.”</p><p>That stopped me.</p><p>I knew that.</p><p>Of course I knew that.</p><p>But the sentence opened several doors at once.</p><p>Hessa saw it happen.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I have a question.”</p><p>“You have twelve.”</p><p>“Can channels persist through absent tissue?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Has anyone studied amputation?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was new.</p><p>I sat forward.</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>“People.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Not here.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Different places.”</p><p>“What did they find?”</p><p>“Different things.”</p><p>“That is aggressively unhelpful.”</p><p>“It is also true.”</p><p>“Give me one.”</p><p>She considered.</p><p>“Some practitioners report changed flow after limb loss. Some report no meaningful change. Some cannot return to prior forms. Some can. Some develop pain with channel use. Some don't. Records are bad.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because people lose limbs in wars, accidents, monsters, infections, failed magic, punishment, work. They are not all mages. The mages are not all trained the same. The injuries are not the same. The amputations are not the same. The follow-up is not the same. And most people care whether the patient can live, not whether a Barrier architecture remains elegant.”</p><p>I sat back.</p><p>That was fair.</p><p>Also rude.</p><p>“Below-knee specifically?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Barrier specialists?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Dynamic support?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Counter-architecture?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Barely.</p><p>This was the first time since the amputation that the problem had become larger than me in a useful way.</p><p>Not unique.</p><p>Not solved.</p><p>Not even especially well documented.</p><p>But other people had lost limbs and used magic afterward.</p><p>Some had returned.</p><p>Some had not.</p><p>Some differently.</p><p>That should have comforted me.</p><p>Instead it made me want records.</p><p>“Do not go looking for records.”</p><p>I looked at Hessa.</p><p>“I didn't say anything.”</p><p>“You leaned.”</p><p>“That is not speech.”</p><p>“It is with you.”</p><p>“Are there records in Carrow?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Guild?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Private?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She let the silence sit.</p><p>I could feel my left foot again.</p><p>Not cold.</p><p>Present.</p><p>Heel on floor.</p><p>It was not on the floor.</p><p>I looked down.</p><p>The sensation weakened when I looked.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not interesting.</p><p>Not yet.</p><p>Hessa followed my gaze.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Foot feels planted.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Position only?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“After the test?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did it start before you looked?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>That was all.</p><p>No conclusion.</p><p>I wanted one badly enough that my teeth hurt.</p><p>“When do we test again?”</p><p>“Three days.”</p><p>“Why three?”</p><p>“Because I said three.”</p><p>“Physiological reason?”</p><p>“Scheduling.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>She had work.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Same test?”</p><p>“Some of it.”</p><p>“Casting?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Mana draw?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>She pointed at me.</p><p>“Maybe means maybe.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You don't.”</p><p>“I do.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“Maybe means maybe.”</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>“Good enough.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>I had not intended to.</p><p>Hessa's mouth moved again.</p><p>Almost smile.</p><p>She stood.</p><p>Done.</p><p>I stood too.</p><p>Hands to crutches.</p><p>Right foot planted.</p><p>Left knee bent.</p><p>The phantom foot tried to remain on the floor for half a second as my body rose.</p><p>It produced a strange stretching sensation through an ankle that did not exist.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Not because I was falling.</p><p>Because I wanted to notice.</p><p>Then I finished standing.</p><p>Hessa watched.</p><p>“Anything?”</p><p>“Old geometry.”</p><p>“Meaning?”</p><p>“Foot thought it stayed down while I stood.”</p><p>“Thought?”</p><p>“Felt.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>I adjusted the crutches.</p><p>“When you write this down, don't write ‘channel response below knee.’”</p><p>“I wasn't going to.”</p><p>“What will you write?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Patient annoying.”</p><p>“That lacks diagnostic precision.”</p><p>“Patient consistently annoying.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>I went to the door.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>I turned.</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“No experiments.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“No trying to reproduce what I did.”</p><p>“I don't know what you did.”</p><p>“That has never stopped you.”</p><p>Also fair.</p><p>I opened the door.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Three days?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I nodded.</p><p>That was enough.</p><p>Outside, Carrow continued without caring that my left foot had felt cold when a mage touched my knee.</p><p>A cart blocked half the street.</p><p>Someone had dropped onions.</p><p>A dog was eating one and regretting it.</p><p>I stood in the doorway for a moment with both crutches planted.</p><p>Three days.</p><p>Not clearance.</p><p>Not a theory.</p><p>Not even a result I could name safely.</p><p>But it was the first appointment about magic that ended with another appointment about magic.</p><p>I went home before I could improve it.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="090.html">← Chapter 72</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="092.html">Chapter 74 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/171.html:542`: <p>"How much mana?"</p>
- `chapters/171.html:650`: <p>Not much mana.</p>
- `chapters/122.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 97: The Reacher — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 97</div><h1>THE REACHER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Hessa had covered the tray.</p><p>That was new.</p><p>Not dramatic.</p><p>A square of gray cloth over the part where the copper usually sat.</p><p>I noticed before I sat down.</p><p>She noticed me noticing.</p><p>“Hands first.”</p><p>“That is not copper.”</p><p>“Hands.”</p><p>Right thumb.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Fingers.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Wrist.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Forearm.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>She pressed along the inside of the arm, then checked grip, fingertips, wrist movement.</p><p>“Yesterday?”</p><p>“Theatre.”</p><p>“Magic?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Symptoms?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Training?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fall?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Near fall?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Residual limb?”</p><p>“Baseline.”</p><p>“Phantom?”</p><p>“Ordinary.”</p><p>“Anything unusual below the left knee?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hand urge?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I looked at the cloth.</p><p>She did not.</p><p>This was deliberate cruelty.</p><p>“Do you want to know what is under it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She wrote another line.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You are enjoying this.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You are lying.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>She closed the notebook.</p><p>Then removed the cloth.</p><p>Copper.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>Also a narrow glazed tile.</p><p>A small upright wooden frame.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/122/Ch122_Single-Thread-Apparatus.jpg" alt="Hessa watches a single suspended thread beside Greg&#x27;s supported right forearm during the bounded assessment." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>And from the top of the frame hung a single dark thread.</p><p>The thread ended above the tile.</p><p>Nothing touched it.</p><p>I stared.</p><p>Hessa watched my face.</p><p>“That is external.”</p><p>“It is a thread.”</p><p>“It is outside my body.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Is this clearance?”</p><p>“For one question.”</p><p>I stopped breathing for a moment.</p><p>Not intentionally.</p><p>Hessa&#x27;s expression sharpened.</p><p>“Breathe.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“One question,” she repeated. “One attempt. Under my instruction. This is not casting clearance. It is not Barrier clearance. It is not independent external work. It is not permission to reproduce the test.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Say the rest.”</p><p>“Left shaping remains excluded.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No independent draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No independent shaping.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No independent external attempt.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No spell.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>I looked at the thread again.</p><p>It was extremely unimpressive.</p><p>Perfect.</p><p>“What is the question?”</p><p>“Whether you can deliberately extend a small altered response beyond the boundary of the right forearm without releasing the underlying draw.”</p><p>I looked back at her.</p><p>“Extend.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not release.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Not push.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Not cast.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Not Barrier.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“How far?”</p><p>She pointed.</p><p>The thread hung less than a finger-width from where my right forearm would rest beside the frame.</p><p>“That far.”</p><p>“That is not a measurement.”</p><p>“It is enough of one.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“I measured before you arrived.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>Cruel woman.</p><p>“How far?”</p><p>“Three quarters of an inch from skin to thread when your arm is in position.”</p><p>Better.</p><p>“Why thread?”</p><p>“Light. Visible. Harmless. If it moves, we can see direction. If it does not move, we have a clean absence to discuss.”</p><p>“Air.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Breathing.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Table vibration.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Crutch movement.”</p><p>“You will be seated.”</p><p>“Door.”</p><p>“Closed.”</p><p>“Window.”</p><p>“Closed.”</p><p>“Your sleeve.”</p><p>“Rolled above the elbow.”</p><p>“My hand.”</p><p>“Still.”</p><p>“Your hand.”</p><p>“Not near it.”</p><p>“Copper response.”</p><p>“Separate observation.”</p><p>I stared at the apparatus.</p><p>“You thought about this.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That should not have been surprising.</p><p>It was.</p><p>I had spent weeks wanting an external test.</p><p>Hessa had apparently spent at least some portion of that time deciding what one would need to mean.</p><p>The thread did not look like magic.</p><p>It looked like sewing.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>“What counts?”</p><p>Hessa pointed at the tile beneath it.</p><p>“There is a charcoal line directly below the thread&#x27;s resting position.”</p><p>I leaned closer.</p><p>There was.</p><p>“If the thread moves visibly away from rest while you are holding the requested state, I record direction and duration.”</p><p>“How much movement?”</p><p>“Visible.”</p><p>“That is subjective.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can we mark distance?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because your first external question is whether there is any reproducible-looking change worth measuring more precisely later.”</p><p>“Reproducible-looking is dangerous language.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“Because one attempt cannot establish reproducibility.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I liked her less when she agreed quickly.</p><p>“And if it moves once?”</p><p>“We record that it moved once.”</p><p>“External effect?”</p><p>“We record an observed external movement during the attempt.”</p><p>“That is cowardly.”</p><p>“That is accurate.”</p><p>“And if it does not move?”</p><p>“We record no observed external movement.”</p><p>“Failure.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It is literally failure to move the thread.”</p><p>“It is failure to move the thread if moving the thread is the goal.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“The goal is to learn whether your current control can produce an observable external change under this instruction.”</p><p>“That is moving the thread with extra words.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I knew this argument.</p><p>I was going to lose it.</p><p>“What stops the test?”</p><p>“Any thumb tingling. Any urge to curl or spread fingers. Wrist movement. Weakness. Cold. Numbness. Pain. Familiar broad pattern. Any left-side change that is not ordinary phantom sensation. Any sense that you are trying to complete Barrier. Any urge to release forcefully. Any change you cannot describe well enough for me to decide whether to continue.”</p><p>“That last one is hostile.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One attempt.”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“If nothing happens, no second attempt?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“If I know what I did wrong?”</p><p>“Especially no.”</p><p>I sat.</p><p>She positioned my right forearm on a folded cloth beside the frame.</p><p>Not touching.</p><p>The thread hung near the inside of the forearm.</p><p>Three quarters of an inch suddenly looked enormous.</p><p>I could bridge it with a fingertip.</p><p>Not allowed.</p><p>My hand rested open on the table beyond my forearm.</p><p>Hessa adjusted the copper on the other side.</p><p>“Before draw.”</p><p>The thread was still.</p><p>Mostly.</p><p>Nothing in a room was perfectly still.</p><p>Tiny tremor.</p><p>Maybe air.</p><p>Maybe vision.</p><p>The charcoal line gave me a reference.</p><p>“Breathe normally,” Hessa said.</p><p>“That will move it.”</p><p>“Then we observe baseline first.”</p><p>We did.</p><p>I breathed.</p><p>The thread moved almost imperceptibly once.</p><p>Toward me.</p><p>Then back.</p><p>“Baseline movement,” Hessa said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I breathed.</p><p>Nothing obvious.</p><p>Again.</p><p>Tiny movement.</p><p>Different direction.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Annoying.</p><p>“Do not hold your breath during the attempt.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“I am telling you anyway.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Minimal draw.”</p><p>I drew.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Familiar enough to recognize.</p><p>Not easy.</p><p>Not automatic.</p><p>Copper responded.</p><p>Right forearm.</p><p>Ordinary phantom left foot.</p><p>No unusual extension.</p><p>No thumb.</p><p>No fingers.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>The thread remained thread.</p><p>“Small alteration. Right forearm. Toward the charcoal mark on your skin.”</p><p>There was a small mark near the wrist-side area again.</p><p>I shaped.</p><p>Localized.</p><p>Not perfect.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Copper changed.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Alteration present. Small. Slightly broader toward elbow than the mark, but not shifting.”</p><p>“Motor?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Left?”</p><p>“Ordinary.”</p><p>“Good. Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>The thread did nothing.</p><p>This was not yet the external instruction.</p><p>My heart had accelerated anyway.</p><p>That was inconvenient.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Heart rate.”</p><p>“I can see.”</p><p>“Does that matter?”</p><p>“It may matter to you. Not enough to stop.”</p><p>Fine.</p><p>She watched my hand.</p><p>Then the copper.</p><p>Then the thread.</p><p>“Now listen carefully.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“Do not release.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do not increase the internal alteration.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do not try to move your hand, wrist, or fingers.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Keep the underlying draw active.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“From the existing altered region only, attempt the smallest extension you can toward the thread.”</p><p>I stared at the thread.</p><p>“Extension.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Across the gap.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop if it feels like force.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop if it becomes broad.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop if I say stop.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>“Reach.”</p><p>I tried.</p><p>Nothing happened.</p><p>Not to the thread.</p><p>Internally, the alteration changed.</p><p>I felt it narrow.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not narrow.</p><p>Lengthen?</p><p>Dangerous word.</p><p>The edge nearest the thread became more distinct.</p><p>I did not feel anything outside the skin.</p><p>I did not know what outside should feel like.</p><p>The thread remained still.</p><p>“Report,” Hessa said.</p><p>“Near edge sharper. Maybe narrower behind it.”</p><p>“External sensation?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Motor?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Continue only the same instruction. Do not increase force.”</p><p>I tried again.</p><p>Small.</p><p>The internal altered region seemed to lean toward the gap.</p><p>That was metaphor.</p><p>No.</p><p>It changed asymmetrically toward the thread.</p><p>Better.</p><p>Copper response changed.</p><p>The thread moved.</p><p>Tiny.</p><p>Toward my arm.</p><p>I froze.</p><p>Wrong.</p><p>Not release.</p><p>Not stop draw.</p><p>Hessa said, “Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>The thread returned toward the charcoal line.</p><p>My heart was loud.</p><p>“Did you breathe differently?”</p><p>“I don&#x27;t know.”</p><p>“Good answer. Hold.”</p><p>The alteration remained.</p><p>No motor.</p><p>No thumb.</p><p>No cold.</p><p>“Again. Same extension. No more.”</p><p>I tried.</p><p>The thread did not move.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>I wanted to try harder.</p><p>Did not.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Internal asymmetry toward thread. No external sensation. No movement I can see.”</p><p>“I saw none.”</p><p>“First movement?”</p><p>“I saw it.”</p><p>“Cause?”</p><p>“Unknown.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I hated that.</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>“One attempt.”</p><p>“This is the same attempt.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>I maintained draw.</p><p>Maintained alteration.</p><p>Tried the same smallest extension.</p><p>The thread moved again.</p><p>Not much.</p><p>This time sideways.</p><p>Not toward me.</p><p>To my left.</p><p>Then stopped.</p><p>Hessa immediately said:</p><p>“RETURN.”</p><p>External question over.</p><p>I obeyed.</p><p>Not release.</p><p>Reduce alteration.</p><p>The thread settled.</p><p>I did not watch it.</p><p>Right forearm.</p><p>RETURN.</p><p>The altered region diminished.</p><p>Wrist-side edge softened.</p><p>Center dimmed.</p><p>No motor urge.</p><p>No elbowward shift I could detect.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Reducing. No motor. No thumb.”</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>The alteration became uncertain.</p><p>“I cannot tell if residual remains.”</p><p>“Underlying draw?”</p><p>“Still present. Higher confidence.”</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>Hessa watched copper.</p><p>Then my hand.</p><p>Then thread.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released.</p><p>She took my right hand immediately.</p><p>Open.</p><p>Close.</p><p>Thumb.</p><p>Fingers.</p><p>Wrist.</p><p>Grip.</p><p>No symptom.</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Numb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Urge?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Left?”</p><p>“Ordinary phantom.”</p><p>“Anything external now?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>The thread hung above its charcoal line.</p><p>I wanted to accuse it of something.</p><p>Hessa wrote.</p><p>I could not read upside down from this angle.</p><p>Probably intentional.</p><p>“Well?”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“I am sitting.”</p><p>“Then continue.”</p><p>Hostile.</p><p>She wrote longer than usual.</p><p>“What did you see?”</p><p>“I will tell you.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“When I am done writing what I saw before hearing what you want me to have seen.”</p><p>That was fair.</p><p>Horrible.</p><p>I looked at the thread.</p><p>First movement toward my arm.</p><p>Could be breath.</p><p>Second sideways.</p><p>Could be air.</p><p>Could be table.</p><p>Could be nothing.</p><p>Could be magic.</p><p>The last possibility was too large.</p><p>I tried to make it smaller.</p><p>Observed movement.</p><p>Unknown cause.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Hessa put the pencil down.</p><p>“Your report first.”</p><p>I gave it exactly.</p><p>Minimal draw.</p><p>Small alteration.</p><p>Near edge became more distinct after REACH.</p><p>Internal response became asymmetric toward thread.</p><p>No external sensation.</p><p>First visible thread movement toward arm.</p><p>I did not know whether breathing changed.</p><p>Second extension produced no observed movement.</p><p>Third produced a small sideways movement.</p><p>Then RETURN.</p><p>Alteration reduced.</p><p>No unwanted motor response.</p><p>No thumb.</p><p>No unusual left phantom.</p><p>Release normal.</p><p>Hessa nodded.</p><p>“My observation is close.”</p><p>“Close how?”</p><p>“Copper changed when you attempted extension.”</p><p>“That is expected.”</p><p>“Not necessarily.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“The internal altered response appeared to change directionally.”</p><p>“You can see that?”</p><p>“I can see enough through copper response to say it changed. Direction is partly your report.”</p><p>Important.</p><p>“The thread moved twice during the extension portion.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Once toward you. Once sideways.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It also showed small baseline movement before draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So?”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/122/Ch122_Fast-Coverage-005-01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 122." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“So I cannot attribute either movement to you.”</p><p>Disappointment arrived cleanly.</p><p>Not devastating.</p><p>Just there.</p><p>“Then no external effect.”</p><p>“No established external effect.”</p><p>“That is different wording.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did the test fail?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What did it establish?”</p><p>“That I can ask you to attempt a bounded extension without you immediately releasing, broadening into the familiar pattern, recruiting your hand, or losing the underlying draw.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>She continued.</p><p>“And when I ended the external question, you returned the alteration without the previous unwanted responses.”</p><p>“That is internal control.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So we learned internal control during an external test.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And the external result is unknown.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>I looked at the thread.</p><p>“You planned this.”</p><p>“I hoped for interpretable information.”</p><p>“You got the wrong information.”</p><p>“I got information.”</p><p>“Practitioner.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>“Am I cleared for external testing now?”</p><p>“You were cleared for this external test.”</p><p>“That is not what I asked.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Can we repeat it?”</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Day after?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“How many living days?”</p><p>“Two.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because this was your first supervised attempt to deliberately extend an altered response beyond your body.”</p><p>“And nothing happened.”</p><p>“Unknown.”</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>“No. It is less satisfying.”</p><p>Same thing.</p><p>Not same thing.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>“Two full no-magic days?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then assessment?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could the next assessment repeat the thread?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could it use something else?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could it return to internal control?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could you decide external testing was premature?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You are impossible.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at the apparatus.</p><p>“Can I ask whether the sideways movement is more interesting than the movement toward me?”</p><p>“You can ask.”</p><p>“Is it?”</p><p>“Not enough to matter.”</p><p>“Because breath would more likely move it away?”</p><p>“Do not build airflow theory from your chair.”</p><p>“I know airflow.”</p><p>“You do not know this room&#x27;s airflow well enough.”</p><p>“Window closed.”</p><p>“Door closed.”</p><p>“Still convection.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Body heat.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Your movement.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Table vibration.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Thread twist.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Static?”</p><p>She paused.</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>I hated the universe.</p><p>“So the thread can move for six reasons.”</p><p>“More.”</p><p>“And magic is one candidate.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“Possibly possibly.”</p><p>“That is where we are.”</p><p>I wanted a clean event.</p><p>A spark.</p><p>A twitch that happened exactly when I reached and nowhere else.</p><p>A thread leaping sideways three times in identical direction.</p><p>Something I could own.</p><p>Instead I had two tiny movements and a woman professionally refusing to let me have them.</p><p>Good.</p><p>No.</p><p>Accurate.</p><p>Probably good later.</p><p>Still irritating now.</p><p>Hessa uncovered the charcoal reference under the thread and checked where it rested.</p><p>“Back at baseline?”</p><p>“Approximately.”</p><p>“Approximately?”</p><p>“Thread has twist.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>“The first external magical test of my life may have been defeated by sewing.”</p><p>“It was not defeated.”</p><p>“Thread twist.”</p><p>“Is real.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“That is why we test small things.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Because small things reveal all the ways measurement is annoying.”</p><p>“Among other reasons.”</p><p>She removed the frame.</p><p>That felt abrupt.</p><p>The external world disappeared from the tray.</p><p>Copper remained.</p><p>I watched her put the thread apparatus on a shelf.</p><p>“Can I touch it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I meant later.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you will inspect the thread.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And the frame.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And the tile.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And then attempt to determine airflow.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And then arrive next time with a theory.”</p><p>I considered lying.</p><p>Did not.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>She made me sit another ten minutes.</p><p>Ordinary hand movement only.</p><p>No ritual.</p><p>She caught me checking the thumb once.</p><p>“Did it feel wrong?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then stop.”</p><p>I drank water.</p><p>Reached for the cup.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Grip.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Crutches.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Three ordinary steps.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>No finger urge.</p><p>No wrist movement.</p><p>No strange left phantom.</p><p>Hessa watched.</p><p>“Two days.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No magic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Living.”</p><p>“Poorly specified.”</p><p>“Consistently effective.”</p><p>“That is not established.”</p><p>She pointed at the door.</p><p>I left.</p><p>Outside, Carrow had not changed.</p><p>This was offensive.</p><p>I had just attempted to affect something outside my body with mana.</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>Technically I had attempted.</p><p>The something had moved.</p><p>Maybe because of me.</p><p>Maybe because rooms contained air.</p><p>A cart passed.</p><p>Someone shouted about fish.</p><p>Two children were arguing over a hoop.</p><p>I stood near Hessa&#x27;s doorway and tried to decide what I felt.</p><p>Pleased.</p><p>Annoyed.</p><p>Hungry.</p><p>That seemed manageable.</p><p>Theatre was west.</p><p>Guild another direction.</p><p>Lyssa would be working or not.</p><p>Pessa had her own day.</p><p>Tomorrow had no magic.</p><p>The day after also had no magic.</p><p>Then Hessa.</p><p>I could spend forty-eight hours thinking about thread.</p><p>Absolutely not.</p><p>I started walking.</p><p>West.</p><p>Then stopped.</p><p>Not because theatre was wrong.</p><p>Because I was hungry and the food stall I wanted was east.</p><p>I turned east.</p><p>This was not symbolic.</p><p>It was lunch.</p><p>Probably.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="121.html">← Chapter 96</a><a
