- `chapters/097.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 79: The Variable — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 79</div><h1>THE VARIABLE</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Hessa did not ask about Holl.</p><p>This was suspicious.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg at Hessa’s table for the second supervised minimal mana draw." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/097/Ch97_Second-Mana-Draw.png"/></figure><p>She put the copper strip on the table.</p><p>Same strip.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>I leaned closer.</p><p>“Did you mark it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“How do you know it is the same one?”</p><p>“I don't.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“That seems bad.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Repeatability.”</p><p>“We are not testing the copper.”</p><p>“We are using the copper to test me.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So if the copper changes, the measurement changes.”</p><p>“It confirms draw. It does not measure you.”</p><p>I sat back.</p><p>That distinction was irritating.</p><p>Good.</p><p>The chair was still bad.</p><p>Also good.</p><p>Hessa pointed at my bread.</p><p>“You ate.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Recently?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Bread.”</p><p>“That explains the bread.”</p><p>“Pepper stew earlier.”</p><p>“How much earlier?”</p><p>“Yesterday.”</p><p>“That is not recently.”</p><p>“I ate other things.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>“Food.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>I had become Jorren.</p><p>This was catastrophic.</p><p>“Breakfast. Bread. Cheese. Apple.”</p><p>“Water?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Sleep?”</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>“Leg?”</p><p>“Closer to normal.”</p><p>“Closer?”</p><p>“Still slightly fuller than before Pessa's session.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Heat?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Drainage?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hands?”</p><p>“Warm from getting here. Fine.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>No standing.</p><p>I knew before she said it.</p><p>“Seated.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“You sound disappointed.”</p><p>“I am practicing emotional range.”</p><p>“No, you're not.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>She sat opposite me.</p><p>No stones today.</p><p>No tricks.</p><p>Copper strip.</p><p>Tea.</p><p>Her notebook.</p><p>I looked at the notebook.</p><p>“You wrote last time?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“What happened.”</p><p>“Can I see?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because then you'll try to reproduce what I wrote instead of what happened.”</p><p>“That is deeply insulting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She held the copper loop around two fingers.</p><p>Flat end toward me.</p><p>“Same amount as last time.”</p><p>“How exact?”</p><p>“Not exact.”</p><p>“Then how do I know?”</p><p>“You don't.”</p><p>“That seems like a problem.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Hessa waited.</p><p>This was the thing I liked about her.</p><p>Not kindness.</p><p>Though she had some.</p><p>Not patience.</p><p>She had less.</p><p>She would say when the method was bad.</p><p>Not useless.</p><p>Not invalid.</p><p>Bad in a specific way.</p><p>We did not have a calibrated instrument for Greg.</p><p>Greg was unfortunately the instrument.</p><p>“Ready?” she asked.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I reached.</p><p>Mana came more easily this time.</p><p>Not more mana.</p><p>Less hesitation.</p><p>Chest.</p><p>Shoulders.</p><p>Arms.</p><p>Right side.</p><p>Hip.</p><p>Thigh.</p><p>Lower leg.</p><p>Foot.</p><p>Left hip.</p><p>Thigh.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Then nothing.</p><p>I almost broke the draw.</p><p>Nothing below the knee.</p><p>Not the organized fullness.</p><p>Not cold.</p><p>Not occupied.</p><p>My ordinary phantom foot was there because my ordinary phantom foot was often there, but magically, internally, whatever word applied, the sequence stopped.</p><p>At the knee.</p><p>My heart sped.</p><p>“Hold,” Hessa said.</p><p>I held.</p><p>The mana remained.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Steady.</p><p>The copper strip did nothing visible.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>I waited for the absent foot to change.</p><p>It did not.</p><p>I tried not to wait.</p><p>This was impossible once I had noticed myself waiting.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released.</p><p>Mana settled away.</p><p>Hessa lowered the copper.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I told her.</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I hated the sound of the pen.</p><p>“That's different.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Did you confirm the draw?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Same?”</p><p>“Broadly.”</p><p>“Broadly is doing too much work.”</p><p>“It is earning its pay.”</p><p>“Was the left-above-knee response present?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Below?”</p><p>“I did not establish anything below.”</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“You said repeat assessment.”</p><p>“We repeated it.”</p><p>“One trial.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Yesterday was one trial.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So we have two trials with different subjective results.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is almost maximally unhelpful.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It is close.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What did we learn?”</p><p>“That the below-knee sensation is not inevitable.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>That was something.</p><p>Hessa pointed at me with the pen.</p><p>“And?”</p><p>I thought.</p><p>“That I can complete a minimal draw without it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was more important.</p><p>I disliked that too.</p><p>I had been treating the sensation as the interesting part.</p><p>Because it was strange.</p><p>Strange attracts thought.</p><p>But the draw had worked.</p><p>Again.</p><p>Without the strange thing.</p><p>“So the sensation may be irrelevant.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Attention-dependent.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Body map.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Some channel effect that varies.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Position was the same.”</p><p>“Mostly.”</p><p>“Mostly?”</p><p>“You arrived more tired yesterday.”</p><p>“I arrived more tired today.”</p><p>“You arrived more hurried yesterday.”</p><p>“I came from Holl today.”</p><p>“That was today.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>Right.</p><p>Holl had been less than an hour ago.</p><p>Pepper stew yesterday.</p><p>My internal calendar had become soup.</p><p>Hessa watched me.</p><p>“You need more sleep.”</p><p>“I slept.”</p><p>“Enough?”</p><p>“I said enough.”</p><p>“That is not a number.”</p><p>“Neither is broadly.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>Fair hit.</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>She did not.</p><p>Probably internally.</p><p>“Did you think about Holl during the draw?” she asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Before?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“During?”</p><p>“No. During I was waiting for my foot.”</p><p>“Then you were not distracted.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Good?”</p><p>“It removes one story.”</p><p>“Does it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She shrugged.</p><p>“Maybe you were less anticipatory because you were distracted before. Maybe more because you knew the test. Maybe neither matters. We cannot tell.”</p><p>“You are enjoying this.”</p><p>“A little.”</p><p>Monster.</p><p>She poured tea.</p><p>I drank.</p><p>No second draw.</p><p>Apparently.</p><p>I waited anyway.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Greg beside assessment notes and instruments after an inconsistent result." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/097/Ch97_Variable-Notes.png"/></figure><p>Hessa wrote another line.</p><p>Then closed the notebook.</p><p>“That is all.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“We have time.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I am here.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You are here.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The copper is here.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“This is a conspiracy.”</p><p>“Against what?”</p><p>“Sample size.”</p><p>Hessa leaned back.</p><p>“What would a third draw tell you?”</p><p>“If the sensation happens.”</p><p>“And if it does?”</p><p>“Two of three.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>Closed it.</p><p>“If it doesn't?”</p><p>“One of three.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>I hated this.</p><p>“Not much.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“It would tell us repeatability.”</p><p>“No. It would give us one more observation.”</p><p>“Which contributes to repeatability.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So.”</p><p>“So your body is still recovering from training, you hurried here, and we do not know the cost of repeated draws yet.”</p><p>“The first two did nothing.”</p><p>“You mean you noticed nothing.”</p><p>Fine.</p><p>“Also,” she said, “you are now emotionally invested in producing or not producing the foot sensation.”</p><p>“I am not.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“I am scientifically interested.”</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>I drank tea.</p><p>The phantom left foot felt slightly turned inward.</p><p>I adjusted a foot that did not exist.</p><p>The sensation corrected.</p><p>Body map.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>No.</p><p>Just body map as a description.</p><p>Not cause.</p><p>I had learned something from Hessa.</p><p>This was unfortunate.</p><p>“What next?” I asked.</p><p>“Not magic.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Today.”</p><p>“You said maybe vary position.”</p><p>“I said maybe.”</p><p>“You and Pessa have coordinated vocabulary.”</p><p>“We meet weekly to discuss how to annoy you.”</p><p>“I knew it.”</p><p>She ignored me.</p><p>“Your swelling is almost settled.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Go home. Or work. Or eat. Do not train today.”</p><p>“Pessa decides training.”</p><p>“Then tell Pessa I think stacking training after a draw today is stupid.”</p><p>“That sounds like deciding training.”</p><p>“That sounds like medical advice.”</p><p>“You said you own magic.”</p><p>“I also own telling you when I think you are being stupid.”</p><p>“That jurisdiction is dangerously broad.”</p><p>“Go.”</p><p>I did not go.</p><p>I looked at the copper.</p><p>“What does it actually do?”</p><p>Hessa sighed.</p><p>Victory.</p><p>“Copper is easy to observe for a small induced response if I know what I am looking for.”</p><p>“What response?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“You will start watching the copper.”</p><p>“It doesn't visibly change.”</p><p>“You'll still watch.”</p><p>True.</p><p>“Is it detecting mana?”</p><p>“Not generally.”</p><p>“Your mana?”</p><p>“Not exactly.”</p><p>“My draw?”</p><p>“Close enough.”</p><p>“That is terrible.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can it false positive?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“False negative?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then why use it?”</p><p>“Because I am not using it alone.”</p><p>There.</p><p>That was the answer.</p><p>I looked at her hands.</p><p>“You're sensing too.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And watching me.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And asking subjective report.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And checking physical response.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And comparing across days.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So copper is one witness.”</p><p>Hessa's expression changed.</p><p>Barely.</p><p>“One witness,” she said.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I liked that.</p><p>Not enough to write it down.</p><p>Probably later.</p><p>“Can I ask about records?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“One question.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You gave me one last time.”</p><p>“That created expectations.”</p><p>“Did anyone report inconsistent missing-limb sensation during draw?”</p><p>Hessa stared.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She should say no.</p><p>Not because the answer was no.</p><p>Because she had said no questions.</p><p>“Some reports describe inconsistent sensation,” she said.</p><p>I won.</p><p>Then she continued.</p><p>“The records are bad enough that I do not know whether they mean the same thing you mean.”</p><p>Victory revoked.</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Nothing?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Potentially.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She pointed at the door.</p><p>I stood.</p><p>Both crutches.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>Push.</p><p>No phantom mistake.</p><p>No magical sensation.</p><p>Just standing.</p><p>At the door I stopped.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Day after.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I want a boring day between.”</p><p>I considered objecting.</p><p>Then I thought about Holl.</p><p>Same lot.</p><p>Do not change the fixture yet.</p><p>Track bench.</p><p>Wait.</p><p>This was not the same problem.</p><p>I almost made it the same problem.</p><p>Caught it.</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Day after,” I said.</p><p>Hessa narrowed her eyes.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You agreed too fast.”</p><p>“I am growing.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>I opened the door.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>I turned.</p><p>“No draw.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“I will not draw mana without you.”</p><p>“Or another practitioner I explicitly clear to supervise.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>That was new.</p><p>“Are you planning to clear someone?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why add it?”</p><p>“Because rules should say what they mean.”</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>“Day after.”</p><p>“Day after.”</p><p>Outside, I had nowhere urgent to be.</p><p>Again.</p><p>This was becoming suspicious.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Greg alone with his notebook after the supervised assessment." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/097/Ch97_After-the-Variable.png"/></figure><p>I stood on the street and considered the Guild, home, food, Lyssa, Jorren, Pessa, Holl, absolutely nothing, and several bad ideas.</p><p>The second draw had worked.</p><p>The interesting sensation had not.</p><p>I was happier about the first fact than unhappy about the second.</p><p>This seemed healthy.</p><p>I distrusted it immediately.</p><p>Then I went to find lunch.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="096.html">← Chapter 78</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="098.html">Chapter 80 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/020.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 17: The Volunteer — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 17</div><h1>THE VOLUNTEER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Jorren hit me before I could apologize. This was efficient. I had arrived at the yard late enough that the afternoon shadows had moved noticeably and early enough that Jorren had not yet decided to leave. He stood in the packed dirt with two wooden swords, one in each hand. He threw one at me. I caught it badly. He hit me with the other.</p><p>“Late,” he said.</p><p>“I was delayed by professional obligations.”</p><p>“You were talking.”</p><p>“Professionally.”</p><p>He hit me again. The sky had been gray when I left the guild. I had noticed. That was the embarrassing part. There were clouds above the western roofs, low and thick enough that anyone with eyes could have identified them as weather. The air had gone damp. The yard smelled like dirt instead of dust. I had classified all of that as background.</p><p>Then Jorren struck my shoulder and the first drop of rain hit my nose. I looked up. He hit me in the ribs.</p><p>“You keep doing that,” he said.</p><p>“Looking at the sky?”</p><p>“Looking somewhere else.”</p><p>“It started raining.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Another drop landed on my cheek. Then five. Then fifty. The yard changed in less than a minute. People cursed and gathered coats. A pair of Bronze adventurers abandoned a wrestling match and ran laughing toward the covered arcade. Someone near the equipment shed shouted about bows. The dry dirt darkened in irregular circles, then all at once. Jorren lowered his sword.</p><p>“We’re done.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Rain.”</p><p>“I know what rain is.”</p><p>“Good. Go inside.”</p><p>I looked at the ground.</p><p>“We can still train.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>He pointed with the wooden sword. The packed yard had already gone slick on top.</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“So you’re bad enough when the ground stays where you put your feet.”</p><p>“That feels personal.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>Rain drummed against the shed roof. I shifted my stance experimentally. My right boot slid half an inch. Jorren stared at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>Jorren pointed at my boot.</p><p>“It slipped. That is enough information.”</p><p>“I wanted to know how much,” I said.</p><p>He took the sword out of my hand.</p><p>“Enough that training is over.” Training over. I hated weather. Not rain. Rain was fine. Weather was a system that changed plans without consulting me. I followed Jorren beneath the arcade. Alden was there. Of course he was.</p><p>He sat on a low stone wall with his red scarf tucked inside his leather coat and a meat pie in one hand. His hair was wet enough to suggest he had made no effort to avoid the rain.</p><p>“You’re late,” he said.</p><p>“I’ve already been punished.”</p><p>Jorren leaned the wooden swords against the wall.</p><p>“Not enough.”</p><p>Alden looked toward the yard.</p><p>“So tomorrow?” Alden asked.</p><p>“No,” Jorren said.</p><p>Alden frowned. I did too. Jorren looked between us.</p><p>“What?” Jorren asked.</p><p>“We were training tomorrow,” Alden said.</p><p>“Outside,” Jorren said.</p><p>“There’s an inside,” Alden said.</p><p>“Not for what I wanted,” Jorren said.</p><p>“What did you want?” I asked.</p><p>Jorren ignored me. Rainwater began running off the tiled roof in a continuous curtain. Alden took another bite of pie.</p><p>“Could use the covered loading yard,” Alden said.</p><p>“Too narrow,” Jorren said.</p><p>“The old horse court?” Alden asked.</p><p>“Stone,” Jorren said.</p><p>“South wall?” Alden asked.</p><p>“Mud,” Jorren said.</p><p>Alden chewed.</p><p>“Warehouse?” Alden asked.</p><p>Jorren looked at him.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You didn’t even ask which one.”</p><p>“I know enough,” Jorren said.</p><p>I looked from one to the other.</p><p>“What exactly were you planning?”</p><p>Jorren sighed.</p><p>“Distance.”</p><p>Alden smiled. Ah. Jorren had spent yesterday showing Alden what happened when he committed too quickly after gaining an advantage. Today, apparently, he intended to widen the problem.</p><p>“How much distance?” I asked.</p><p>“Enough that he has to decide whether to close it.”</p><p>Alden pointed his pie at Jorren.</p><p>“He means run.”</p><p>“I mean move,” Jorren said.</p><p>“You mean run while you hit me,” Alden said.</p><p>“If you let me.”</p><p>Alden grinned. That was a yes. Rain erased the yard. Not literally. The fence remained. The posts remained. The practice dummies remained, increasingly miserable. But the space Jorren wanted was gone. Plans changed. I disliked how quickly both men accepted that.</p><p>“Could train something else,” I said.</p><p>Jorren looked at the flooded yard.</p><p>“Not what I planned,” Jorren said.</p><p>“Footwork,” I said.</p><p>“On wet stone or mud?” Jorren asked.</p><p>I looked at the arcade floor.</p><p>Jorren shook his head.</p><p>“Your feet are the problem on dry ground. We do this another day.”</p><p>Alden laughed. I considered leaving. Then thunder rolled somewhere beyond the western wall. Not close. Close enough that everyone under the arcade paused for half a breath. The rain strengthened. A stable boy ran across the yard with a blanket over his head.</p><p>A woman at the guild door shouted, “Canal road’s flooding again.” That got my attention. Jorren saw it.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I haven’t moved.”</p><p>“You did the face.”</p><p>Everyone knew the face now. This was intolerable. The guild door opened again and the ink-thumbed clerk stepped beneath the arcade. Her hair had begun escaping whatever arrangement usually kept it obedient.</p><p>“Anyone assigned west road, river path, or lower canal, check the board,” she called. “Two escorts delayed. One canceled. Ferryman’s refusing the south crossing until the water drops.”</p><p>A chorus of complaints answered her. She did not care. Alden stood.</p><p>“What about the tannery run?” Alden asked.</p><p>“Delayed,” the clerk said.</p><p>“How long?” Alden asked.</p><p>“Tomorrow morning if the road drains,” the clerk said.</p><p>“I had that,” Alden said.</p><p>“You have it tomorrow morning,” the clerk said.</p><p>“I have training tomorrow morning,” Alden said.</p><p>The clerk looked at Jorren.</p><p>“You?” she asked.</p><p>Jorren nodded. She looked back at Alden.</p><p>“Then you don’t,” the clerk said.</p><p>Alden opened his mouth. Closed it. I enjoyed this enormously.</p><p>“Weather,” I said.</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Shut up.”</p><p>The clerk scanned the arcade.</p><p>“Need two Bronze for an indoor reassignment.”</p><p>Nobody moved. That was interesting.</p><p>“What kind?” I asked.</p><p>Jorren said, “Greg.” The clerk pointed at me.</p><p>“You volunteered.”</p><p>“I asked.”</p><p>“Close enough.”</p><p>Alden stepped beside me.</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>The clerk looked at him.</p><p>“You too?”</p><p>He shrugged.</p><p>“My job drowned.”</p><p>“Your job is delayed.”</p><p>“Temporarily drowned.”</p><p>She considered us. Then Jorren. Jorren shook his head.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Excellent,” the clerk said. “Two Bronze.”</p><p>“What are we doing?” I asked.</p><p>“Moving flour.”</p><p>Alden stared. I laughed. The clerk did not.</p><p>“East storehouse roof started leaking. Quartermaster wants the dry sacks shifted before the water reaches them. Four copper each. Probably an hour.”</p><p>Alden looked toward the rain. Then at me.</p><p>“This is your fault.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“You asked for weather.”</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“You looked happy.”</p><p>“I’m happy now.”</p><p>“That’s worse.”</p><p>Jorren picked up the wooden swords.</p><p>“Go move flour.”</p><p>“You’re not coming?” I asked.</p><p>“I have somewhere dry to be.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Not moving flour.”</p><p>He left. I watched him go. Alden said, “I liked him less before I knew him.”</p><p>“That’s unusual.”</p><p>“For him?”</p><p>“For knowing people.”</p><p>We followed the clerk inside. The east storehouse belonged to the guild, which meant it had been designed by someone who believed stairs were a moral test. Three flights down, one corridor across, through a courtyard that was technically covered but leaked anyway, then up another narrow stair into a long room lined with sacks. The leak was obvious.</p><p>Water dripped through three places in the roof and ran down a support beam. A quartermaster with a shaved head stood among six laborers. He pointed.</p><p>“Those two rows to the inner wall. Leave the marked sacks. Don’t stack higher than shoulder. If anything tears, stop.”</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>“Hero work.”</p><p>“You recovered a goat.”</p><p>“It was a difficult goat.”</p><p>We started moving flour. The first sack weighed enough to make my body remind me that being nineteen did not mean being strong. I got it onto my shoulder. My left leg wobbled. Alden took two. I hated him immediately.</p><p>“Show-off.”</p><p>“Efficient.”</p><p>“You’re carrying them wrong.”</p><p>He stopped. I had not meant to say that. The quartermaster looked over. Alden said, “How?” I pointed.</p><p>“You’re letting the second one pull your shoulder back. Fine for ten steps. Bad for fifty.”</p><p>He adjusted.</p><p>“Like this?”</p><p>“Worse.”</p><p>He adjusted again.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Annoyingly better.”</p><p>He walked away. The quartermaster stared at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You a porter?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then carry.”</p><p>Fair. I carried. The work settled into a rhythm. Lift. Walk. Set. Return. Rain hammered the roof. The sound changed the room. Conversation had to happen closer. Footsteps disappeared beneath it. The air smelled of wet wood, flour dust, wool, and the faint mineral scent that came when old stone finally got enough water to remember it had once been mud. I liked it.</p><p>Not the carrying. The rain. There was something satisfying about a whole city being forced to admit the sky existed. Alden passed me going the other way.</p><p>“Tomorrow’s training is fucked.”</p><p>“Delayed.”</p><p>“Same thing.”</p><p>“No. One implies emotional injury.”</p><p>“I’m emotionally injured.”</p><p>“You’ll recover.”</p><p>“What are we doing instead?”</p><p>“Moving flour.”</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>He looked genuinely dissatisfied. Three weeks ago, Alden had wanted Gold because Gold was above Bronze. Platinum because Platinum was above Gold. S because I had put the letter in front of him. Now he was irritated because he had expected to learn something specific and weather had taken it away. Good. Dangerous word. Useful. Worse word. I lifted another sack. Alden caught me watching.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“That’s your lying nothing.”</p><p>“I have several.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>He walked away. The leak spread, not dramatically. A dark line moved across one roof plank and became a second drip. The quartermaster cursed.</p><p>“Move the back row too.”</p><p>Everyone groaned. I set my sack down. The new drip landed directly on the cord. Water darkened the fibers. I stared. Cord. Mouth. Closure. Seal. Wrong sack. Ordinary flour. Probably. The association was enough.</p><p>“What?” Alden asked.</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Different nothing.”</p><p>I crouched beside the sack. The cord had swollen slightly where wet. No magic. No visible structure. I touched it. The knot tightened under my finger. Not by itself. Wet fiber. Simple. Still. Something about the South Canal seal had responded when its knot was disturbed. Edrin had called the sack ordinary and the closure not. What counted as disturbance? Pulling? Loosening?</p><p>Cutting? Wet cord changing shape? I stood. The quartermaster was watching me.</p><p>“If you are done with the cord, move the sack,” the quartermaster said.</p><p>“I had a thought,” I said.</p><p>“Have it at the inner wall,” the quartermaster said.</p><p>I did. The next sack went faster. Then the next. On the sixth trip, one of the laborers slipped. Not badly. His heel hit a wet patch near the leaking beam. The sack on his shoulder shifted. He caught himself against the wall. I saw the movement before it finished. Weight going left. Knee collapsing inward. Sack continuing. A small intervention could have changed it.</p><p>Barrier at the heel. No. Too slow. At the sack. Angle. Not stop. Redirect. I gathered mana. Then the laborer recovered on his own. I let the mana go. Nothing happened. Alden had seen.</p><p>“You were going to cast.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why didn’t you?”</p><p>“He didn’t need me.”</p><p>Alden looked at the laborer, who was already swearing at the wet floor. Then back at me.</p><p>“Huh.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“That’s my line.”</p><p>“I have several.”</p><p>I disliked him. We carried more flour. Half an hour later, the rain had not weakened. The storehouse had become a map of buckets. The quartermaster moved us to a third row. My shoulders burned. Alden had stopped carrying two sacks at once. I noticed. He noticed me noticing.</p><p>“Shut up.”</p><p>“I said nothing.”</p><p>“You were about to.”</p><p>“I was about to congratulate you on learning.”</p><p>“Fuck off.”</p><p>That was friendship adjacent. Possibly. Or murder adjacent. The distinction could wait. We reached the last six sacks. A loud crack came from above. Everyone froze. Not thunder. Wood. The quartermaster looked up.</p><p>“Out.”</p><p>Nobody argued. That mattered. We moved. One laborer grabbed a sack. The quartermaster slapped it out of his hands.</p><p>“Leave it.”</p><p>We filed toward the door. I looked back. Water poured through the new split in the roof. Not a collapse. Yet. The support beam beneath it had gone dark with water. The crack had opened along a joint. I knew nothing about roofs. Important. I knew load. Some. Magic load. Different. Probably. Alden caught my coat.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I’m going.”</p><p>“You’re staring.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Do it outside.”</p><p>He pulled. I went. That mattered too. We reached the corridor. The quartermaster counted heads. Seven laborers. Two adventurers. Him. Ten.</p><p>“Good,” he said. “Nobody goes back until the carpenter looks.”</p><p>“What about the flour?” one laborer asked.</p><p>“It’s flour.”</p><p>That answer pleased me. The man looked horrified.</p><p>“It’s thirty silver of flour.”</p><p>The quartermaster shrugged.</p><p>“It’s not ten people.”</p><p>Better answer. Alden leaned against the wall. Rainwater ran down his hair from the courtyard crossing.</p><p>“So,” he said. “Four copper?”</p><p>The quartermaster looked at him.</p><p>“You moved the flour.”</p><p>“Most of it.”</p><p>“You get paid.”</p><p>Alden nodded. I said, “That’s your concern?”</p><p>“I’m wet.”</p><p>“We’re indoors.”</p><p>“I was wet earlier.”</p><p>“You chose not to avoid it.”</p><p>“That doesn’t make me less wet.”</p><p>The quartermaster left to find the carpenter. The laborers dispersed toward a kitchen. Alden and I remained in the corridor.</p><p>“What now?” he asked.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Training tomorrow.”</p><p>“Still thinking about that?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked toward the courtyard. Rain fell in silver ropes beyond the arches. The yard would be mud tomorrow even if the sky cleared.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Muddy Guild Yard" decoding="async" height="334" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/020/v28_c20_s01_the-muddy-guild-yard.png" width="300"/></figure><p>Jorren’s distance drill was gone. At least for a day. Maybe two. I could imagine trying to recreate it somewhere else. Warehouse. Covered market. Long corridor. Bad surfaces. People. Costs. Permission. Or we could do something else. The obvious answer annoyed me because it was obvious.</p><p>“We train what the weather gives us.”</p><p>Alden frowned.</p><p>“That sounded wise.”</p><p>“I apologize.”</p><p>“What does the weather give us?”</p><p>I looked at the wet stone.</p><p>“Bad footing.”</p><p>His smile returned.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“That’s Jorren’s no.”</p><p>“You’ve known him four days.”</p><p>“It’s a good no.”</p><p>I laughed. Then I thought about it properly. Bad footing was useful. It was also a stupid thing to practice at speed when my ankle still failed under dry conditions and Alden’s preferred method of learning involved discovering the boundary with his face. Hessa would kill me. Jorren would help.</p><p>“No,” I agreed.</p><p>Alden looked disappointed.</p><p>“Something else.”</p><p>Rain. Plans changed. What remained? Decision. Timing. Commitment. Distance could be simulated without running. Maybe.</p><p>“Coins,” I said.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“We need coins.”</p><p>“For training?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>I checked my purse. Not many.</p><p>“Your coins.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You’re richer than me.”</p><p>“I made twelve copper yesterday.”</p><p>“I made twelve before that.”</p><p>“You spent some.”</p><p>“So did you.”</p><p>“On food.”</p><p>“That’s spending.”</p><p>“It keeps me alive.”</p><p>“Luxury.”</p><p>Alden stared at me.</p><p>“Your training is terrible.”</p><p>“You haven’t seen it yet.”</p><p>“Good point.”</p><p>The guild clerk found us before I could explain. She carried two wooden tokens.</p><p>“Payment.”</p><p>Alden held out his hand. She gave him one. I held out mine. She kept it.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You volunteered.”</p><p>“That does not remove compensation.”</p><p>“I wanted to see your face.”</p><p>She gave me the token.</p><p>“This guild is corrupt.”</p><p>“Cash desk closes at fifth bell.”</p><p>“What time is it?”</p><p>She looked toward the rain.</p><p>“Later than it looks.”</p><p>Weather had eaten the light. I disliked that too. Alden pocketed his token.</p><p>“Coins.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“If the yard’s bad.”</p><p>“And if it clears?”</p><p>“Jorren hits you.”</p><p>“He hits you too.”</p><p>“Mostly me.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He started toward the stairs.</p><p>“Where are you going?”</p><p>“Cash desk.”</p><p>“We could talk about the exercise.”</p><p>“After I have money.”</p><p>“That is reasonable.”</p><p>He stopped.</p><p>“You coming?”</p><p>I looked toward the corridor leading back to the east storehouse. Carpenter. Roof. Wet cord. Load. No. Not my roof. Not my flour. Not my seal. The South Canal sacks were behind a locked guild door with a warder who knew more about current seals than I did. Hessa had told me to stop when told. The quartermaster had told us out.</p><p>Jorren had told me training was over. This was becoming oppressive. I followed Alden. At the cash desk, we traded the wooden tokens for four copper each. Alden immediately spent one on two hot buns from a woman sheltering beneath the guild entrance. He handed me one. I looked at it.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You carried flour.”</p><p>“So did you.”</p><p>“I bought two.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I wanted two.”</p><p>“Then why are you giving me one?”</p><p>He had already bitten into his.</p><p>“Because I bought two.”</p><p>This was not an explanation. I took the bun. It was hot enough to hurt my fingers. We stood beneath the guild awning and watched rain fill the street gutters. People ran under cloaks. Carts moved slower. A horse refused a puddle with the absolute conviction of an animal whose opinions outweighed commerce. Tomorrow had changed. The tannery run had changed. Training had changed.</p><p>The guild board had changed. A roof had changed. A sack of flour had become more valuable because water was falling in the wrong place. None of it was dramatic. That was the interesting part. I bit into the bun. Alden said, “What are the coins for?” I chewed.</p><p>“Distance.”</p><p>“You said we can’t run.”</p><p>“We don’t need to.”</p><p>He waited. I took two coppers from my purse and put them on the stone ledge between us, about a foot apart.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Two Coppers" decoding="async" height="334" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/020/v28_c20_s02_two-coppers.png" width="303"/></figure><p>“Pick one.”</p><p>He reached. I slapped his hand.</p><p>“What the fuck?”</p><p>“Too fast.”</p><p>“You said pick one.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>He stared at me. I smiled. Rain hammered the awning.</p><p>“Tomorrow,” I said.</p><p>His eyes narrowed. Then he smiled too.</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>That was not reassuring. I ate the rest of my bun. Across the street, runoff struck the curb, split around a loose stone, and joined itself again on the other side. I watched it for one second too long. Alden followed my gaze.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Water.”</p><p>“I know what water is.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He waited. I kept walking. Not every question needed to become an experiment today. The rain followed us home anyway.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="019.html">← Chapter 16</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="021.html">Chapter 18 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

- `chapters/017.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 13: The Investigator — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 13</div><h1>THE INVESTIGATOR</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>I read the contract.</p><p>Alden had not lied about it. This disappointed me slightly, because correcting him would have been satisfying.</p><p>The posting occupied half a sheet on the Bronze board beneath a request to clear mud wasps from a chimney and above a notice concerning a mule that had learned to bite only guild members. South Canal, Verran Grain Stores. Night intrusion on three occasions. Two sacks missing the first night, four the second, three the third. Rear boards damaged. Mud tracks near the canal wall. No watchman injured because no watchman had seen anything. Owner wanted the loss stopped and, if possible, the responsible party identified.</p><p>Two Bronze minimum. Eighteen copper each if human theft was confirmed and materially interrupted. Twelve if vermin or animal. Additional recovery payment at owner's discretion.</p><p>The important line was lower down.</p><p>Do not pursue onto canal after dark without licensed water support.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Wait" decoding="async" height="357" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/017/v28_c17_s12_the-wait.png" width="290"/></figure><p>I read that twice.</p><p>The ink-thumbed clerk watched me from behind the counter.</p><p>"You planning to memorize it?" she asked.</p><p>"I am appreciating the sentence everyone else will ignore."</p><p>"Which one?"</p><p>I pointed.</p><p>She looked at the line, then at me. "That one exists because Bronze adventurers kept falling in."</p><p>"How many?"</p><p>"Enough to get a sentence."</p><p>Alden leaned against the counter beside me. "I read that part."</p><p>"Did you appreciate it?"</p><p>He tapped the warning with one finger. "I noticed the water-support part."</p><p>The clerk snorted.</p><p>I looked over the rest again. "Any previous reports from the neighboring stores?"</p><p>"No confirmed theft. One owner says he heard scraping two nights ago. Another says Verran invented the whole thing to get the guild to subsidize a watchman."</p><p>"Does Verran have enemies?"</p><p>"He sells grain."</p><p>"So yes."</p><p>"Everyone has enemies if you ask enough questions," she said. "Bronze board, Greg."</p><p>I liked her more every time she told me to stop doing something.</p><p>Alden tapped the bottom of the posting. "Are you done?"</p><p>"Almost."</p><p>"You said that before you started reading the back."</p><p>"There was writing on the back."</p><p>"There were payment initials on the back."</p><p>"Which are writing."</p><p>He looked at the clerk. "Is he always like this?"</p><p>"I charge extra for opinions."</p><p>That was sensible.</p><p>I signed beneath Alden's name.</p><p>Jorren's space remained blank.</p><p>He had actual work, which I had initially interpreted as an inconvenience and then, after several minutes of thought, recognized as a life independent of mine. Progress remained humiliating.</p><p>Alden watched me notice the empty line.</p><p>"We only need two," he said.</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"You looked like you were counting missing furniture."</p><p>"Jorren is useful furniture."</p><p>"Tell him that."</p><p>"I intend to survive the week."</p><p>The clerk slid the posting copy toward us. "Verran expects you before dusk. If you damage his stock, he will attempt to deduct it from your pay. He cannot do that without arbitration, but he will attempt it with enthusiasm."</p><p>"Anything else?" I asked.</p><p>"Yes. Don't fall in the canal."</p><p>Alden picked up the paper. "We appreciate the sentence."</p><p>I hated him a little.</p><p>We reached South Canal while the sun was still above the roofs.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Third Sack" decoding="async" height="357" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/017/v28_c17_s11_the-third-sack.png" width="330"/></figure><p>The district smelled like wet stone, old rope, fish, grain dust, horse piss, and money too practical to wash itself. Warehouses stood shoulder to shoulder along the canal, broad brick or timber structures with loading doors facing both street and water. Cranes leaned over the dark green canal at intervals. Barges moved slowly beneath them, pushed by poles or dragged from the towpath when the channel narrowed.</p><p>Verran Grain Stores occupied a long two-story building with a faded wheat sheaf painted over the street doors. The canal side sat on stone footings with a narrow loading ledge just above the water. Three high windows had shutters. One lower section of wall had newer boards among older gray ones.</p><p>A man was waiting outside with his arms folded.</p><p>He was perhaps forty-five, thick through the middle, with a trimmed beard and a coat too good for unloading grain but too dusty for a merchant who stayed behind a desk.</p><p>"Merek Verran," he said. His eyes went to Alden's red scarf, then to me. "You're the guild?"</p><p>Alden lifted the contract copy.</p><p>Verran frowned.</p><p>I said, "Bronze contract for the night intrusion. Greg. Alden."</p><p>"You're young."</p><p>"The guild charges more for old people."</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>Verran did not laugh. That was useful information.</p><p>"Come inside," he said.</p><p>The warehouse was larger than it looked from the street. Rows of stacked sacks formed aisles between timber posts. Wheat, barley, oats, rye. Some marked for mills, some for bakers, some with merchant stamps I recognized and some I didn't. The air was dry enough to itch the back of my throat.</p><p>A woman with a lantern was checking a tally board near the rear wall.</p><p>"Nella," Verran called. "Show them the damage."</p><p>She turned.</p><p>Nella was perhaps thirty, narrow-faced, sleeves rolled above strong forearms. She looked at us, then at Verran.</p><p>"You could show them."</p><p>"I have invoices."</p><p>"You always have invoices."</p><p>"That's why we still have a warehouse."</p><p>Nella set down the tally board. "Come on."</p><p>Alden smiled at me as we followed her.</p><p>"Don't," I whispered.</p><p>"I didn't say anything."</p><p>"Your face did."</p><p>At the canal wall, Nella crouched beside the newer boards.</p><p>"First morning, this one was cracked," she said, touching a vertical plank. "Second time, two were loose. We replaced them. Third time, somebody had worked the bottom nails out of the new boards."</p><p>I crouched beside her.</p><p>The boards were thick enough that rats were not the explanation unless the rats had acquired tools and labor organization. The bottom edges showed fresh scraping. The nails had been driven again, but one hole was enlarged.</p><p>"From which side?" I asked.</p><p>"That's the argument," Nella said.</p><p>Verran had followed us after all. "Outside," he said.</p><p>Nella pointed at the inner face. "Some marks are here."</p><p>"Because they pushed the boards inward," Verran said.</p><p>"Or because somebody inside loosened them," Nella said.</p><p>Verran's mouth tightened. "Nobody inside is stealing from me."</p><p>That was not evidence.</p><p>I looked at Nella. "Who has keys?"</p><p>"Verran. Me. Night watch. Two senior loaders."</p><p>"Who was here on the three nights?"</p><p>"Different people."</p><p>Verran said, "Which is why it isn't my staff."</p><p>"Or somebody inside knows the route," Alden said.</p><p>Verran turned on him. Alden stayed crouched by the boards and pressed one loose nail with his thumb.</p><p>I had the sudden urge to see how long they would continue.</p><p>Nella saved us. "The missing sacks came from this section."</p><p>She led us twenty feet along the wall to a stack of barley.</p><p>Nine sacks over three nights. Not the nearest sacks to the damaged boards. Not the most expensive grain either.</p><p>I walked the route from the damaged wall to the stack.</p><p>Alden watched me.</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"You're doing the face."</p><p>"Which face?"</p><p>"The one where you're somewhere else."</p><p>"I'm here."</p><p>"Physically."</p><p>Nella looked between us.</p><p>"Do you have a plan yet, or are you still looking?"</p><p>"Still looking," Alden said.</p><p>"Good. Tell me before you move anything," Nella said.</p><p>I crouched beside the lowest sacks. The floorboards were dusty. Grain dust, boot marks, drag lines from normal work. Nothing clean enough to become revelation because warehouses had the unfortunate habit of containing workers.</p><p>"How heavy?" I asked.</p><p>Nella answered without checking. "Barley sacks, about seventy pounds when full. These are a little under because Verran cheats the measure."</p><p>"I do not cheat the measure," Verran said.</p><p>"You round," Nella said.</p><p>"Everyone rounds," Verran said.</p><p>"Down," Nella said.</p><p>Alden coughed into his fist.</p><p>I touched one sack.</p><p>Heavy enough that one person could carry it. Awkward enough that nine sacks meant repeated trips or some way to move them without crossing much floor.</p><p>"Any spilled grain outside?"</p><p>"A little on the ledge after the second night," Nella said.</p><p>"Tracks?"</p><p>"Mud. One clear boot. Maybe another. Water smeared most of it."</p><p>"Boat?"</p><p>Verran said, "Obviously."</p><p>"Then why does the contract say tracks near the canal wall instead of boat?"</p><p>He opened his mouth.</p><p>Nella answered. "Nobody saw one."</p><p>Good.</p><p>Alden walked back to the damaged boards and pressed his palm against one.</p><p>"If they come from outside, they have to open this quietly, climb in, cross to the sacks, carry them back, climb out, close enough of it that the watch doesn't notice until morning."</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>He looked toward the stacked barley.</p><p>"Why not take the sacks nearest the wall?"</p><p>Better.</p><p>"Exactly."</p><p>Alden smiled.</p><p>I disliked how pleased that made me.</p><p>Verran folded his arms. "So what does that mean?"</p><p>"Nothing yet," I said.</p><p>Alden said, "It means whoever is doing it wants those sacks."</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He shrugged. "Or somebody inside hands them over."</p><p>Also possible.</p><p>Nella asked, "What do you want us to do?"</p><p>That was the actual question.</p><p>I looked at the warehouse, the doors, the rear boards, the windows, the canal ledge. My mind immediately offered twelve arrangements. Hide among sacks. Roof observation. Outside watch. Flour on floor. Thread on boards. Mark sacks. Move target grain. Put one of us inside and one outside. Ask neighboring warehouse for roof access. Borrow a boat. Do not borrow a boat because sentence.</p><p>Alden went back to the damaged boards and worked one thumbnail into the widened nail hole while I thought.</p><p>He did not fill the silence.</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>Or maybe I was already inventing a version of him that improved on schedule because I wanted the story to be satisfying.</p><p>Annoying thought.</p><p>I cut the list.</p><p>"We stay inside," I said. "Leave the warehouse looking normal. Don't change the stack. Don't add an obvious trap. Nella, can the night watch stay on his usual route?"</p><p>"Her," Nella said. "Sima tonight."</p><p>"Can Sima stay on her usual route and not come in here unless there's a fire?"</p><p>"Probably."</p><p>Verran frowned. "Why?"</p><p>"Because if whoever is stealing knows the watch pattern, changing it tells them tonight is different."</p><p>Alden nodded. "And if it's someone inside?"</p><p>"Then they already know we're here unless Verran kept his mouth shut."</p><p>Everyone looked at Verran.</p><p>He looked offended.</p><p>Nella said, "He didn't."</p><p>Of course.</p><p>"Then we assume the thieves may know guild adventurers are present," I said. "Which means they either skip tonight, change method, or think Bronze means manageable."</p><p>Alden's grin appeared.</p><p>"Don't enjoy that," I said.</p><p>"I didn't say anything."</p><p>"Your face did."</p><p>Nella looked at me. "You two really do that?"</p><p>"Apparently."</p><p>We ate before dark because fighting hungry is stupid and waiting hungry is worse.</p><p>Verran provided bread, hard cheese, and an apple each after Nella reminded him that the contract required reasonable access to water and facilities during overnight work. He disputed whether food counted as a facility. Nella gave us the bread anyway.</p><p>Alden ate sitting on a grain sack despite three available stools.</p><p>"So," he said, "what do I do tonight?"</p><p>"Your job."</p><p>"Helpful."</p><p>"You wanted training. This is better training than me narrating your shoulders."</p><p>He took a bite of apple. "You're going to narrate my shoulders anyway."</p><p>"Only if they become interesting."</p><p>"They're excellent shoulders."</p><p>"Historically significant."</p><p>The words escaped before I could stop them.</p><p>Alden's chewing slowed.</p><p>Fuck.</p><p>Not because the phrase revealed anything. People said historically significant about buildings, arguments, hangovers, and occasionally shoulders if they were sufficiently pleased with themselves.</p><p>But I had heard the second meaning.</p><p>Alden swallowed. "You really are strange."</p><p>"I've been told."</p><p>"By who?"</p><p>"Everyone with sustained exposure."</p><p>He accepted that.</p><p>We settled behind a row of wheat sacks with sightlines toward the damaged wall and the barley stack. I disliked hiding behind grain because grain burned, collapsed, spilled, attracted vermin, and had no respect for tactical dignity. Alden disliked it because there was nothing to do.</p><p>For the first hour, he whispered twice.</p><p>For the second, once.</p><p>By the third, he had become personally offended by darkness.</p><p>"This is adventuring?" he murmured.</p><p>"Mostly."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"People tell stories wrong."</p><p>"Almost always."</p><p>He shifted his weight.</p><p>I touched his boot with mine.</p><p>"Stop."</p><p>"My leg's asleep."</p><p>"Then it is finally contributing."</p><p>He stared at me in the dark.</p><p>I could barely see his expression, but I felt the insult.</p><p>Somewhere near the street side, a board creaked.</p><p>Alden went still.</p><p>We listened.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>A rat appeared at the end of the aisle, paused, and looked directly at us.</p><p>Alden's hand moved toward his sword.</p><p>I caught his wrist.</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>I looked at the rat.</p><p>The rat washed its face.</p><p>Alden slowly lowered his hand.</p><p>I leaned close enough to whisper, "Excellent threat assessment."</p><p>"It surprised me."</p><p>"It weighs eight ounces."</p><p>"Could be magical."</p><p>"Then we're underpaid."</p><p>The rat left.</p><p>Alden waited several breaths before whispering, "You don't know how much that rat weighed."</p><p>"Closer than you."</p><p>Another hour passed.</p><p>Then I heard scraping.</p><p>Not from the damaged boards.</p><p>Below us.</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>Alden heard it too. His head turned toward the canal wall.</p><p>Scrape.</p><p>Pause.</p><p>Scrape.</p><p>Wood against wood, low and controlled.</p><p>The bottom edge of the wall shifted.</p><p>Not the replaced boards.</p><p>Three feet to the left, an older plank moved inward less than an inch.</p><p>Alden started to rise.</p><p>Then stopped.</p><p>His weight settled back.</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He did not look at me.</p><p>Good.</p><p>The plank moved again.</p><p>A thin iron hook slid through the gap.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="The Hook" decoding="async" height="357" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/017/v28_c17_s13_the-hook.png" width="273"/></figure><p>It lay flat against the floor.</p><p>A rope followed.</p><p>No person entered.</p><p>The hook disappeared beneath the nearest stack, moving slowly along the floor as somebody outside manipulated it.</p><p>Not toward the barley.</p><p>Past it.</p><p>I watched the rope angle change.</p><p>The hook snagged something behind the stack.</p><p>A soft thump.</p><p>Then another.</p><p>Alden leaned close.</p><p>"They're pulling them."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"From outside."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Then how do they choose the sacks?"</p><p>That was the question.</p><p>The rope tightened.</p><p>A sack shifted behind the barley stack and slid into view.</p><p>Not barley.</p><p>A smaller sack, dark canvas, maybe forty pounds.</p><p>Nella had not shown us that.</p><p>The sack scraped toward the wall.</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>I could see the decision forming in him.</p><p>Go now.</p><p>Catch the hand on the hook.</p><p>Seize initiative.</p><p>Spend it.</p><p>He stayed still.</p><p>The sack reached the wall.</p><p>The plank opened wider.</p><p>A hand appeared.</p><p>Then an arm.</p><p>Then the sack was dragged through the gap and vanished.</p><p>Alden's jaw tightened.</p><p>He hated waiting.</p><p>So did I.</p><p>The rope returned.</p><p>Second pass.</p><p>This time the hook traveled to the same place.</p><p>Another dark sack shifted.</p><p>I counted the grain stacks between us and the wall. Too much obstruction for a clean rush. Alden could reach the opening faster than I could. Current Greg could not rely on old speed. Fine.</p><p>We did not need old speed.</p><p>We needed to know how many.</p><p>The second sack vanished.</p><p>Voices outside, too low to distinguish.</p><p>At least two.</p><p>Maybe three.</p><p>The hook returned a third time.</p><p>Alden breathed through his nose.</p><p>I almost smiled.</p><p>Yesterday, he would have spent the advantage.</p><p>Today, he was holding it so hard it hurt.</p><p>The third sack began to move.</p><p>Then something changed outside.</p><p>A whisper, sharper.</p><p>The rope stopped.</p><p>Alden's eyes flicked toward me.</p><p>They knew.</p><p>Maybe a sound. Maybe Sima's route. Maybe one of them had seen movement through a crack.</p><p>The rope jerked backward.</p><p>"Now," I whispered.</p><p>Alden moved.</p><p>He did not charge the wall.</p><p>That surprised me.</p><p>He sprinted down the aisle toward the rear loading door.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Very good.</p><p>I went the other direction because my body could not beat him to the same place and duplicating a faster man is an excellent way to become decorative.</p><p>The hook snapped free of the sack.</p><p>Outside, wood banged.</p><p>I reached the damaged wall as the old plank was pulled outward.</p><p>A face appeared in the gap.</p><p>Young man. Wet hair. Wide eyes.</p><p>He saw me.</p><p>"Shit."</p><p>"Accurate."</p><p>He shoved the plank back.</p><p>I drove my shoulder into it.</p><p>Old Greg would have reinforced the impact through hip, knee, Barrier brace, and a tiny force layer at the contact point.</p><p>Current Greg had a shoulder.</p><p>The plank hit me back hard enough to make my teeth click.</p><p>I swore.</p><p>The gap opened anyway.</p><p>A hand came through holding the iron hook like a weapon.</p><p>He thrust blindly.</p><p>Too fast for my shoulder.</p><p>Slow enough for my mind.</p><p>Barrier.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Not stop.</p><p>Angle.</p><p>I gathered mana.</p><p>The pathway felt thin and unpleasantly bright inside my skull. I shaped the smallest plane I could manage, not in front of me, but beside the hook's path.</p><p>The hook struck it.</p><p>For less than a heartbeat, the Barrier existed.</p><p>The iron point kicked sideways.</p><p>Instead of catching my cheek, it tore my sleeve.</p><p>Pain flashed behind my eyes.</p><p>The Barrier vanished.</p><p>I grabbed the shaft with both hands.</p><p>"Mine," I said.</p><p>The thief pulled.</p><p>I pulled back.</p><p>This was not sophisticated magic.</p><p>This was two idiots fighting over a hook through a wall.</p><p>I had missed this profession.</p><p>Outside, someone shouted.</p><p>Alden.</p><p>Then a crash.</p><p>The hook went slack.</p><p>I yanked it through the gap and dropped it.</p><p>The plank opened.</p><p>The wet-haired man tried to squeeze through backward, apparently deciding the warehouse was safer than whatever Alden was doing outside.</p><p>I helped him make that decision by grabbing his collar and pulling.</p><p>He came through badly, hit the floor, rolled, and kicked me in the thigh.</p><p>My leg folded.</p><p>I fell on him.</p><p>This was not part of any formal technique I remembered.</p><p>It worked.</p><p>He punched me in the ear.</p><p>I punched him in the mouth.</p><p>That also worked, though less elegantly.</p><p>He twisted under me.</p><p>I felt the old answer arrive.</p><p>Pin wrist. Reinforce elbow. Barrier at shoulder. Shift weight. Lock hip.</p><p>No.</p><p>One thing.</p><p>I trapped his right wrist against the floor with both hands and put my knee on his forearm.</p><p>Ugly.</p><p>Current.</p><p>He bucked.</p><p>I stayed on him.</p><p>"Stop," I said.</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>"Also current."</p><p>Footsteps hammered through the warehouse.</p><p>Alden appeared at the aisle entrance dragging another man by the back of his coat.</p><p>His red scarf was gone.</p><p>He had blood on one knuckle and an expression of enormous satisfaction.</p><p>"Got one."</p><p>"So did I."</p><p>The man under me tried to throw me off.</p><p>I nearly lost him.</p><p>Alden looked at the situation.</p><p>"Do you?"</p><p>"Help."</p><p>He laughed and did.</p><p>We tied both men with warehouse cord.</p><p>Nella arrived carrying a short cudgel and a lantern. Sima, the night watchwoman, came behind her with a crossbow held low but ready.</p><p>Verran appeared last, because owners often arrived at exactly the point where other people had made the danger manageable.</p><p>"Where are the sacks?" he demanded.</p><p>Nella looked at the bound men.</p><p>"Good evening to you too."</p><p>Alden wiped his knuckle on his trousers. "Two went outside. Third is there."</p><p>He pointed.</p><p>The dark sack sat halfway between the hidden stack and the wall.</p><p>Verran stared at it.</p><p>Then his face changed.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>Nella saw it too.</p><p>"That's not grain," she said.</p><p>Nobody moved for a moment.</p><p>I looked at Verran.</p><p>"What is it?"</p><p>"Nothing relevant to your contract."</p><p>Alden laughed once.</p><p>Not humor.</p><p>"They broke into your grain warehouse three nights to steal the thing that's not relevant?"</p><p>Verran's jaw tightened.</p><p>Nella walked to the sack.</p><p>"Don't," Verran said.</p><p>She stopped.</p><p>That was the first time all evening he had said something and she obeyed immediately.</p><p>Interesting again.</p><p>The wet-haired thief on the floor smiled through a split lip.</p><p>"Tell them."</p><p>Verran looked at him.</p><p>"Shut up."</p><p>The thief smiled wider.</p><p>I suddenly cared much less about the canal.</p><p>That was dangerous.</p><p>The contract.</p><p>Identify and materially interrupt the intrusion.</p><p>We had two thieves.</p><p>At least one more outside.</p><p>Two sacks already removed.</p><p>The guild specifically prohibited canal pursuit without licensed water support.</p><p>I looked at Alden.</p><p>He was already looking toward the loading door.</p><p>Outside, a pole knocked against stone.</p><p>A boat pushing away.</p><p>His weight shifted.</p><p>Here it was.</p><p>The next move.</p><p>He could run.</p><p>He could chase.</p><p>He could try to jump onto a departing skiff from a dark canal ledge because he was twenty-one and fast and had recently discovered that success felt good.</p><p>I did not say anything.</p><p>Alden looked toward the door.</p><p>Then at the two bound men.</p><p>Then at the sack.</p><p>He exhaled.</p><p>"Fuck."</p><p>He stayed.</p><p>Something inside me lit up. Not pride. Ownership trying to disguise itself as pride.</p><p>I looked away before I could enjoy it too cleanly.</p><p>Sima went to the canal door and peered through a narrow viewing slit.</p><p>"Skiff," she said. "Three people maybe. Heading east."</p><p>Alden asked, "Can you identify it?"</p><p>"Dark hull. Short mast down. No lamp. Half the canal owns one."</p><p>"Then they're gone," he said.</p><p>The sentence cost him something.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Also not mine.</p><p>Nella crouched beside the dark sack without touching it.</p><p>"Verran."</p><p>He rubbed a hand over his beard.</p><p>"It's seed grain."</p><p>The thief laughed.</p><p>Nella looked at him. "No, it isn't."</p><p>Verran's eyes closed briefly.</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>I did not know, and for once that felt useful.</p><p>"Open it," Nella said.</p><p>"No," Verran said.</p><p>"They've stolen two already," Nella said.</p><p>"Which is why we do not open the third in a room full of idiots," Verran said.</p><p>I raised a finger. "That is the first persuasive thing you've said."</p><p>Alden frowned. "What do you think is in it?"</p><p>"If I knew, I would be less interested in not opening it."</p><p>Verran looked at me sharply.</p><p>There.</p><p>Fear.</p><p>Not of thieves.</p><p>Of contents.</p><p>I stood slowly. My head still pulsed from the Barrier. My ear hurt. My thigh hurt. My shoulder would become an argument tomorrow.</p><p>I felt excellent.</p><p>That was probably a warning.</p><p>"We don't open it," I said.</p><p>Nella's mouth tightened. "Why?"</p><p>"Because Verran is scared of it, and I don't know whether he's scared of losing money, getting arrested, being poisoned, being exploded, or having to explain himself. Those are different problems."</p><p>Alden looked at Verran. "Which one?"</p><p>Verran said nothing.</p><p>The wet-haired thief said, "Ask him where he got it."</p><p>Verran kicked him.</p><p>Not hard enough to injure seriously.</p><p>Hard enough to make the room change.</p><p>Alden moved before I did.</p><p>He caught Verran by the front of his coat and shoved him back against a post.</p><p>"Don't," Alden said.</p><p>Quietly.</p><p>Verran stared at him.</p><p>Alden had the advantage.</p><p>I watched his shoulders.</p><p>They stayed down.</p><p>He did not hit him.</p><p>He did not spend it.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Then Alden looked at me.</p><p>"What now?"</p><p>That question felt different than it had in the yard.</p><p>Not obedience.</p><p>Not deference.</p><p>He had acted. He had established the immediate boundary. Now he wanted the next useful piece.</p><p>I looked at the sack.</p><p>At Verran.</p><p>At Nella.</p><p>At the thieves.</p><p>At the canal wall.</p><p>I could feel my mind trying to turn the room into a larger machine.</p><p>Where did the sacks come from? Who wanted them? Why steal only three at a time? Why use a grain warehouse as cover? Was Verran moving something illicit? Dangerous? Valuable? Was the theft targeted recovery rather than theft? Were the thieves employees of whoever originally owned it? Was this guild contract being used to provide armed security for contraband?</p><p>Seventeen reasons.</p><p>Maybe more.</p><p>I breathed.</p><p>Actual job.</p><p>"We secure the prisoners," I said. "We send Sima for the city watch and the guild clerk. We do not open the sack. We do not let Verran move it. We write down exactly what happened before everybody has time to improve their story."</p><p>Verran said, "You work for me."</p><p>"No," I said. "You purchased a guild contract. Different relationship."</p><p>Nella smiled.</p><p>Alden released Verran.</p><p>"I like that distinction."</p><p>"Of course you do."</p><p>Sima left through the street door.</p><p>We waited.</p><p>The wet-haired thief gave his name as Ors. The other refused his. Ors claimed Verran had stolen the sacks first. Verran claimed Ors was a canal thief and liar. Nella claimed Verran was a cheap bastard but had never previously stored anything she wasn't allowed to inventory.</p><p>That last part interested me most.</p><p>"You didn't know these were here?" I asked.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"How many?"</p><p>She counted the hidden stack with her eyes. "Five left, if those are all of them. Eight before tonight."</p><p>Three nights of theft.</p><p>Two. Four. Three grain sacks reported missing.</p><p>But the thieves had taken something else.</p><p>I looked at Verran.</p><p>"Did any grain actually disappear?"</p><p>He said nothing.</p><p>Nella's face went flat.</p><p>"Merek."</p><p>He looked at her.</p><p>That relationship had history I did not own.</p><p>Good.</p><p>"I needed the guild here," he said.</p><p>Alden laughed in disbelief.</p><p>I did not.</p><p>It made too much sense.</p><p>"You invented the grain losses," I said.</p><p>"I lost property."</p><p>"Property you didn't want described on a guild posting."</p><p>"Correct."</p><p>"So you lied about grain."</p><p>"I simplified."</p><p>I stared at him.</p><p>Somewhere, Antonius would have appreciated the audacity and despised the execution.</p><p>Nella looked like she might murder him before the thieves got another chance.</p><p>"You made me recount barley for three mornings," she said.</p><p>Verran had the good sense to look more frightened of her than of us.</p><p>Alden turned to me. "Does that change our pay?"</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He shrugged. "Important question."</p><p>It was.</p><p>"Probably upward if the clerk is in a good mood."</p><p>"Does she have those?"</p><p>"We'll discover something tonight."</p><p>The city watch arrived first, two officers with leather coats and the exhausted expressions of people who had been promised a grain theft and received a room full of lies.</p><p>The guild clerk arrived ten minutes later.</p><p>She walked in, looked at the bound thieves, the damaged wall, Verran, the dark sack, Alden's bloody knuckle, my torn sleeve, and Nella's face.</p><p>Then she looked at me.</p><p>"You read the contract."</p><p>"I did."</p><p>"And somehow this still happened."</p><p>"The contract was misleading."</p><p>She looked at Verran.</p><p>"Was it?"</p><p>He began explaining.</p><p>She held up one ink-stained finger.</p><p>"Stop."</p><p>He stopped.</p><p>I loved competence.</p><p>The clerk took statements separately.</p><p>Mine first.</p><p>Then Alden's.</p><p>Then Nella's.</p><p>Then Verran's.</p><p>Then the prisoners after the watch formally took custody.</p><p>She did not open the sack.</p><p>She did not let Verran move it.</p><p>She sent a runner for a licensed appraiser and another guild officer with authority above Bronze contracts.</p><p>I watched the process and felt something settle pleasantly in my chest. I had not solved it. I did not have to.</p><p>That was new enough to be suspicious.</p><p>Alden stood beside me near the street door.</p><p>"You knew she'd do that?" he asked.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You looked smug."</p><p>"I predicted competence."</p><p>"That's knowing."</p><p>"No. It's betting on a process."</p><p>He considered that.</p><p>"You really like processes."</p><p>"They complain less than people."</p><p>"People are more fun."</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He grinned.</p><p>There was probably a song about that grin somewhere in my damaged future memory.</p><p>I got nothing.</p><p>Good.</p><p>The clerk eventually came over with her ledger.</p><p>"Human theft confirmed," she said. "Eighteen copper each. Verran's false material description creates a contract violation. Additional six copper hazard and misrepresentation adjustment."</p><p>Alden's eyebrows rose.</p><p>"Twenty-four?" Alden asked.</p><p>"Each," the clerk said.</p><p>"I like arbitration," Alden said.</p><p>"You haven't experienced arbitration," the clerk said.</p><p>"I like the threat of arbitration," Alden said.</p><p>She ignored him and looked at me. "You used magic?"</p><p>I touched the torn sleeve.</p><p>"Tiny Barrier. Redirected a hook."</p><p>"Injury?"</p><p>"Pride. Ear. Shoulder. Thigh. Mostly pride."</p><p>"He punched you?" Alden asked.</p><p>"You were outside."</p><p>"I thought you had him."</p><p>"I did eventually."</p><p>The clerk made a note. "Get the ear looked at if you start hearing bells."</p><p>My stomach dropped.</p><p>For one stupid second, the warehouse disappeared.</p><p>A bell cracking.</p><p>A red scarf dark with something that was not shadow.</p><p>Voices singing too loudly.</p><p>...last bell broke...</p><p>Then grain dust, lantern light, Alden beside me.</p><p>Present.</p><p>The clerk was still writing.</p><p>Alden was watching me.</p><p>"What?" he asked.</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>He did not believe me.</p><p>He also did not ask again.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>Outside, the canal had gone almost black. Lamps reflected in broken lines across the water. A barge moved somewhere farther east, its pole tapping stone.</p><p>Alden rolled two copper pieces across his knuckles while we walked back toward the guild district.</p><p>"You were right," he said.</p><p>"I usually am."</p><p>"About waiting."</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He kept his eyes on the street.</p><p>"We got two because we waited," he said. "Would've gotten one if I'd moved on the first sack. Maybe none."</p><p>There it was. My mind assembled the lesson automatically.</p><p>I could name the principle, strengthen it, give him a rule to carry into the next fight.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>"That's it?"</p><p>"That's it."</p><p>"No speech?"</p><p>"Do you need one?"</p><p>He thought.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then I'm saving us both time."</p><p>He nodded slowly.</p><p>We walked another half block.</p><p>"You waited too," he said.</p><p>"I am very disciplined."</p><p>"You fought a man through a wall over a hook."</p><p>"After waiting."</p><p>Alden laughed.</p><p>I laughed too.</p><p>My head hurt. My ear rang faintly. I had twenty-four copper coming, a torn sleeve, two new bruises, and no idea what Verran had been hiding in those sacks.</p><p>Alden had taken one correction into the field and used it when I was not beside him telling him what to do.</p><p>That satisfied me. Too much.</p><p>I looked at him and saw present possibilities: footwork, patience, command, the way he asked questions after acting, the way people looked at him when he made a decision, the way he had stopped himself at the canal door.</p><p>I could do a great deal with that. There I was again.</p><p>Alden tossed one copper into the air and caught it.</p><p>"Tomorrow?"</p><p>"What about tomorrow?"</p><p>"Training."</p><p>"With Jorren?"</p><p>"If he'll come."</p><p>"He has a life."</p><p>Alden looked genuinely surprised.</p><p>"Does he?"</p><p>"Apparently. I found out recently."</p><p>"Shame."</p><p>We reached the corner where our routes split.</p><p>Alden started left, then stopped.</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You did the face again when she said bells."</p><p>The street felt colder.</p><p>I could lie.</p><p>Harmless Greg had several options.</p><p>Old Greg had better ones.</p><p>I was tired.</p><p>"I know," I said.</p><p>Alden waited.</p><p>I did not explain.</p><p>After a moment, he nodded.</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>Then he walked away.</p><p>No demand.</p><p>No clever trap.</p><p>No insistence that I owed him the answer because we had bled in the same warehouse.</p><p>That bothered me more than pressure would have.</p><p>I stood there until his red scarf disappeared into the evening crowd.</p><p>Then I realized something else.</p><p>He had asked for training tomorrow.</p><p>Not another contract.</p><p>Not money.</p><p>Not a favor.</p><p>Training.</p><p>I had wanted someone who could do things I couldn't yet.</p><p>Apparently he wanted something from me too.</p><p>That was fair.</p><p>Fair was not the same as safe.</p><p>I turned toward home.</p><p>Behind me, somewhere across the city, a bell marked the hour.</p><p>I did not remember the song.</p><p>I let it ring anyway.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="016.html">← Chapter 12</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="018.html">Chapter 14 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/363.html:590`: <p>No mana.</p>
- `chapters/001.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 1: The Boy — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 1</div><h1>THE BOY</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>I woke up because my back did not hurt. That was wrong.</p><p>Not alarming at first, just wrong. Waking normally involved negotiation. Lower back. Left shoulder. Right knee. The rib that clicked if I slept twisted. None of it terrible. There had simply always been a roll call. This morning, silence. I lay still and waited for the pain to report late.</p><p>I flexed my toes. Too easy. I bent one knee, then the other. Nothing objected.</p><p>I sat up too quickly and nearly laughed. No stiffness. No hand braced against the mattress while my back decided whether we were doing this. The room was unfamiliar for perhaps half a second, and then it was not. Cheap plaster wall. Narrow bed. Washbasin with a crack running down one side. One chair with a coat thrown over it. My sword leaning against the corner.</p><p>The crack in the washbasin caught me first. I remembered cutting my thumb on it. Or thought I did. There had been blood, a towel, somebody laughing. Mara? No. The soap thief next door? Possibly. I looked at my thumb. No scar. Wrong hand, maybe. I checked the other. Nothing. I stared at the basin until the memory stopped being a memory and became a question.</p><p>Maybe it was not my basin. Cheap rooms repeated themselves. Cheap swords did too. I looked at the sword. There should be a nick near the guard. I crossed the room and turned it toward the window. The nick was there. I had made it trying to split kindling because I had been too lazy to find an axe. I remembered being angry about the damage and continuing to use it on firewood anyway. That was harder to dismiss.</p><p>I stopped breathing. "No," I said.</p><p>My voice was wrong too. Higher. Not high. Young. I put both hands in front of my face. The skin was too smooth. No swelling at the knuckles. No pale scar crossing the left palm from the frost-wolf contract. The index finger on my right hand was straight. I bent it. Straight. I bent it again. Still straight.</p><p>That finger should have leaned slightly inward from a badly healed fracture. I remembered refusing to have it reset because there had been another descent the next morning. I remembered the healer calling me an idiot. I remembered years of pretending I barely noticed the angle. The memories were clear enough. The finger disagreed with all of them. I got out of bed too fast. My body rose with me instead of sending three separate complaints to management. I crouched. Lower. Stood. Did it again.</p><p>"What the fuck?"</p><p>I jumped once. That was childish. I did it again. The floorboards creaked.</p><p>A voice from the other side of the wall shouted, "Some of us are sleeping!"</p><p>I knew that voice. Or thought I did. I froze. The name would not come. I knew the irritation. I knew I had once shared this wall with somebody. I knew he snored. I knew he borrowed soap and never returned it. Name? Nothing.</p><p>That bothered me enough to send me back to the washbasin. The little oval mirror above it was spotted around the edges. I leaned close. The face in it was mine. That was obvious. It was also wrong. Dark hair. Too much of it. No gray. No crease beside the mouth. No scar under the chin. I touched my jaw. The reflection copied me. I opened my mouth. Closed it. Turned my head. Same face. Mine, except far too young.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg confronting his nineteen-year-old reflection." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/001/v28_c01_s01_the-mirror.png"/></figure><p>The missing name next door and the face in the mirror did not fail in the same direction. One memory was incomplete. The other was much too complete. I knew what my face should look like. I also knew I could be wrong about details. That distinction suddenly mattered. Recognition was evidence, not proof.</p><p>So I made myself slow down. Body first. Room second. Date third. Explanation later. Start with things I could check. If I was dreaming, details might slide. If something magical had altered my body, the room should not have changed with it. If my memory was damaged, the physical objects did not care. I did not need the correct explanation yet. I needed one that survived the next test.</p><p>I looked at myself again. Lean. Young. A little underfed. Shoulders I had once considered broad and now recognized as the optimistic beginning of broad. I lifted my shirt. Flat stomach. I had forgotten that. I pressed a thumb against an old injury site. Nothing. My body kept answering the same way.</p><p>"Hello," I told the mirror. </p><p>The boy looked pleased with himself. Apparently some things survived whatever this was. Dream, curse, head injury, some magical effect. None explained everything. An extremely committed brothel also occurred to me and lasted several seconds.</p><p>I checked the room for evidence of the last one. No. Too poor. More importantly, staging the room would not explain the hand, the voice, the scars, or why I remembered this place in fragments that felt older than the face looking back at me. I found my trousers. One problem at a time.</p><p>Dressing became another test. No stiffness. No careful weight shift. No moment with one hand braced against the chair while my hip decided whether it had an opinion. I pulled on one boot and stopped. Cheap leather. Hard sole. Badly stitched heel. No waterproofing worth the word. I remembered this kind of boot. Mine. Early. Not necessarily this exact pair. I searched the coat. Three copper. A bent lockpick I had no business owning. A Bronze guild token. I sat down with the token in my palm.</p><p>Bronze. For a long moment, I stared at it like it had personally insulted me. Then I laughed. "Bronze."</p><p>The laughter turned strange in the middle. Not sadness. Not yet. Disbelief.</p><p>Another token existed in my memory: black enamel over star-metal, heavy enough that new adventurers sometimes asked if it was ceremonial. Seven people in the world had held that rank when I finally reached it. I could see the thing in my hand and remember the weight of the other one. Both memories insisted they belonged to me. Fine. The Bronze token was here. Start there.</p><p>I turned it over. Scratched initials on the back. Mine. Current, or at least physically present. I went to the window. Carrow. I knew the street. The street did not quite match itself. The southern row of shops was missing. The guild roof still had old red tiles. A chimney stood where I remembered a three-story apothecary. I checked one landmark, then another. Familiar. Wrong. Not random wrong. Earlier wrong.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg holding his Bronze token over younger Carrow." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/001/v28_c01_s02_bronze-younger-carrow.png"/></figure><p>That was too large a thought. I backed away from it. Window later. Room now. I opened the wardrobe. Two shirts. One coat. Training leathers. Sword belt. Warrior gear. I closed the wardrobe. Opened it again. Still warrior gear. Bronze gave me one boundary. Warrior gear gave me another. Whatever explanation I eventually accepted had to account for me owning equipment from a part of my life I remembered as finished.</p><p>I tried the smaller question. When had I still been doing this? Warrior first. Magic later. I could remember the order much better than the dates. Twenty-four? Twenty-five when I finally stopped pretending the sword was going to become more than it was? The answer came with the uncomfortable fuzziness of a story I had retold too many times. Useful.
