Not enough.</p><p>I pulled the sword from the corner. Cheap steel. One-handed. Balanced badly toward the tip. I remembered loving it. That annoyed me. I swung once, careful of the ceiling. Feet. Shoulder. Wrist. The movement came back from somewhere deeper than recollection. Not excellent. Never excellent. Competent. The body knew the weapon too.</p><p>"I was still doing this." The sentence helped. It did not explain the room, but it gave me another boundary. I was young enough that I still expected to become a warrior. That meant before magic. Before support. Before Barrier.</p><p>Barrier. For one stupid moment, I remembered the clean version. I became a support mage at twenty-five because I finally understood what I was. Elegant. Very professional. The sort of sentence somebody would put beneath a portrait. I stared at the sword.</p><p>"Wait a second." That was not how it happened. There had been jokes. Taverns. A ridiculous fashion. Everybody learning Barrier because someone had discovered that the cheapest defensive spell in the guild curriculum had a use considerably more popular than stopping goblins. Sex.</p><p>I sat down again. "Oh, for fuck's sake."</p><p>History had improved the story. I had not discovered magic because I was called by destiny. I had learned Barrier because I wanted a cleaner, easier way to avoid making babies. And I had been good at it. No. I frowned. That was the polished version too. My first Barrier had been garbage. Thin. Uneven. Flickered at the edge.</p><p>The strange part was not that I cast a perfect spell. I had not. It was that once someone corrected me, I rarely made the same mistake twice. Then I started correcting things nobody had pointed out, changing things just to see what happened. For months, I thought that was normal because Barrier was supposed to be easy.</p><p>There was another correction buried inside that memory. I had spent years telling people I discovered a gift for support magic. That was not quite true either. I discovered a gift for understanding systems that happened to express itself through magic. Barrier was merely the first system simple enough for me to see all the moving parts at once.</p><p>That memory gave me another date marker and proved why memory was dangerous. I could remember the lesson and still misremember the story around it. Younger than twenty-five, then. Probably. My face said much younger. The Bronze token agreed. The city outside was starting to agree too. But all of that was chronology. There was a smaller test sitting right in front of me.</p><p>Magic. If I was merely remembering my body wrong, mana should still answer the way I remembered. If something had changed me, maybe the response would tell me how. I closed my eyes and reached for the old internal sensation. Not Barrier. Nothing ambitious. Just enough response to know what was there. In memory, the motion was as ordinary as flexing a hand. Here, I got a headache and a faint tingling in my palm. I stopped immediately. "Shit."</p><p>Expected: mana. Actual: almost nothing. That did not tell me why. Injury, interference, an untrained body, something stranger. Fine. The useful part was the mismatch. My memories knew how to do something this body apparently did not. Another contradiction, not an answer. </p><p>I put the sword across my knees and let the largest possibility sit there without naming it. Either an absurd amount of my past had been rebuilt around me, including my body, or I was somehow standing inside an earlier version of my own life. Both explanations were ridiculous. One was beginning to require fewer exceptions. "Check," I said, and searched the desk. Old guild notices. Receipts. A letter from somebody whose handwriting I recognized before the name. Maren. No. Mara? I unfolded it. Mara. The date at the top meant almost nothing by itself. I found a guild notice and compared them.</p><p>Then another notice. Then another. I counted backward from something I did remember clearly: the siege of East Verrel, famous enough that nobody who lived through the next forty years forgot the year. The arithmetic gave me a number. I did it again.</p><p>Nineteen.</p><p>"You're kidding." One document could be wrong. Three could share the same calendar. I checked the guild token issue date. Nineteen. I checked the letter again. Nineteen.</p><p>The room. The sword. Bronze. The old roof tiles. The missing apothecary. The face. The straight finger. Nineteen. The memories on the other side of those facts did not disappear. The crooked finger belonged to fifty-eight. The body in the mirror belonged to nineteen. I did not know how both could be mine. I knew they were.</p><p>I stood very slowly. Then grinned. Somehow, impossibly, I was back at nineteen with the rest of my life still in my head. Call the mechanism a curse, a miracle, time displacement, divine stupidity, whatever survived checking later. The mechanism could wait. The result could not. I laughed again, and this one came from somewhere wild. I had decades back. A whole second life. For perhaps five minutes, I did nothing intelligent. I stretched. Ran in place. Touched my hair. Checked my teeth. Looked at myself in the mirror twice more. There were other observations I will leave to the dignity of historical record, except to say that nineteen-year-old bodies are aggressively enthusiastic about being nineteen.</p><p>"Outstanding," I told the mirror. The mirror agreed. Then I thought of my mother. </p><p>The joy stopped. Not because I expected her to be downstairs. I knew better. I thought I knew better. Memory can be cruel when hope gets involved. </p><p>I sat at the desk and forced myself to calculate. My parents had died before nineteen. Both. Years before.</p><p>The reset had not gone far enough. I sat there for a while. No miracle there. No reunion. No impossible knock on the door. I needed something clearer than hope, so I found paper.</p><p>Paper helped. Paper made impossible things administrative. Once something could be written beneath a heading, it became a problem instead of an omen. I had built campaigns that way. Businesses too. Relationships, less successfully. People generally disliked discovering they had become a column in one of my plans.</p><p>That thought made me wonder who I had been seeing at nineteen. Someone. Probably several someones if I was being charitable toward my younger self's ambition and uncharitable toward his judgment. I could not remember. That was alarming for about half a second, then merely embarrassing. Apparently I remembered wars better than women who had once seen me naked. There was a lesson in that somewhere. I declined to find it.</p><p>At the top I wrote: WHAT DO I KNOW?</p><p>Then beneath it: WHAT DO I THINK I KNOW?</p><p>Then: WHAT CAN I VERIFY?</p><p>I stared at those headings. "Very professional."</p><p>Under KNOW, I wrote the siege of East Verrel. The Red Winter. The collapse of the Northern Gate. Three names that would eventually become famous. A war. A plague. Then I stopped. I knew those things had happened. I did not know, without checking, whether I had the years right, whether I was remembering the first cause or the version everyone repeated later, or whether one of those famous names was currently a child. KNOW was already becoming a narrower category than I wanted. I paused. People.</p><p>Who was alive now? Who was already important? Who was still nobody? Who had I known personally? Who had I only known by reputation? I wrote a separate heading: PEOPLE WHO MATTER.</p><p>I hated the heading immediately. Too honest. I left it.</p><p>Alive was the strange word. My mind kept sorting people into dead and not-dead using information that had not happened yet. A man could be eating breakfast three streets away while my first instinct labeled him dead. A woman I remembered at sixty might currently be twelve. Someone I had mourned for thirty years might not have made the decision that killed them yet. That was not useful information in the clean way I wanted it to be. It was emotional contraband.</p><p>Then another thought arrived. What about the people I had never met because they died before I became important enough to cross their path? Historians had names. Guild records had names. Disasters had casualty lists. There might be brilliant people walking around right now whose only historical contribution, in my memory, was dying too early. I wrote a fourth heading before I could talk myself out of it: PEOPLE I MISSED.</p><p>Who had died before I ever met them? I started writing names and crossing them out. Soren. Did I know Soren yet? No. Maybe. I remembered Soren at thirty-something. Scar on the left arm. Laugh like gravel. Hated pears. I could see the scar more clearly than I could place the year. That was apparently how this was going to work.</p><p>Had he always hated pears? Why did I remember that? Did it matter? Probably not. I wrote: SOREN - LATER IMPORTANT. CURRENTLY ?</p><p>Then Mira. I stared at the name. Did I know her at nineteen? No. I did not think so. That was not the same as no. Future Mira existed in my head with the dangerous confidence of somebody I had known too well; the beginning of that memory was mostly missing. Current Mira, wherever she was, might be a child. Or in another city. Or someone entirely unlike the person I remembered. I wrote: MIRA - DO NOT ASSUME.</p><p>That felt useful. Then I looked at the list again. Too many names. Too many ghosts who were not ghosts anymore. I imagined walking into a room, seeing some young idiot, and realizing he would eventually command armies. Or ruin a kingdom. Or save one.</p><p>Would I tell him? Would I help? Would I use him? That answer came too quickly. Of course I would use him. I set the charcoal down. "Excellent." Second chance. Same bastard. I made another heading: MISTAKES.</p><p>That list came faster than I liked. A party I abandoned. A contract I took because I wanted the money and pretended it was strategy. A healer I pushed until she collapsed because I knew she could do more. A swordsman I kept angry because he fought better angry. People I had lied to because the lie made them useful. People who died because they trusted me. People who survived because they trusted me.</p><p>That was the ugly part. My methods had worked often enough to become philosophy. I stopped writing. S-class Greg had not been a saint. He had been useful. Extremely useful. Those are not the same thing. I stood and walked to the window again. A boy crossed the street below carrying a bundle of rope. I watched him too long.</p><p>Did I know him? No. Maybe. His face triggered nothing. I still tracked him until he disappeared around the corner. That was going to become a problem. Every person now came with a question.</p><p>Who are you? Did you matter? Did I know you? Did you die? Did you become somebody? Did I make you into something? Did you make me? The boy looked up once before turning the corner. Caught me staring. He frowned. I waved. He walked faster.</p><p>"Fair."</p><p>I returned to the desk. Now career. What had I actually been doing at nineteen? Warrior. Bronze. Slow. That much felt solid. The order around it did not.</p><p>I remembered the shape of those years more than the sequence. Training. Cheap contracts. Trying to become stronger through repetition because that was what warriors did. Getting marginally better. Then more marginally better. Then discovering at twenty-five that I had spent years pushing the wrong door. Twenty-five felt right. Probably. I almost wrote it under KNOW, reconsidered, and left it under THINK. I should skip those years. Obviously. Magic now. Barrier now. Support now. Except I had already tried the smallest magical test I knew, and this body had answered with a headache and a tingling palm.</p><p>That mattered. I understood the theory more deeply than some professors ever would, but understanding was not capacity. My channels had not been trained. My body had not spent six years accumulating the foundation that made Barrier possible. The morning had given me one result, not permission to pretend the problem was solved. Knowledge was not embodiment. Annoying.</p><p>Could I accelerate the magical foundation? Probably. How much? Unknown. I wrote: MANA CONDITIONING - START NOW.</p><p>Then: WARRIOR YEARS - MOSTLY SKIP.</p><p>I paused. Mostly. Those years had not been entirely wasted. Warrior Greg had learned how fighters moved. How shields failed. How fear changed timing. How much a man could hear while somebody tried to cut his head off. Later, support Greg had known what frontliners needed because he had spent years being a mediocre one. I crossed out MOSTLY SKIP and wrote: KEEP USEFUL PARTS. Better.</p><p>Then money. Money was easy. I wrote that confidently and stared at the page. Was it? The confidence had arrived before the evidence. That was becoming familiar.</p><p>What exactly did I remember that made money today? Not eventually. Today. The Red Winter was decades away. Antonius Vale's rise was useless without access. A famous mana crystal shortage happened... when? I frowned. No idea. A shipping company became huge because of something involving southern grain. Was that this decade? Later? I could remember the company logo. Not the date. Apparently memory had retained the parts that made good stories and discarded the parts useful for buying lunch.</p><p>"Wonderful." Forty years of future knowledge and I could not remember next week's price of onions. That was probably healthy. I leaned back.</p><p>Wrong question. What happens tomorrow? Bad question. What becomes valuable later, and why? Better.</p><p>That I could answer. Or thought I could. Infrastructure. Mana access. Certain dungeon materials people currently treated as waste. Specific institutions. Certain people. Support training itself, eventually. I began another list. Then another. The desk disappeared beneath paper. Halfway down one page I moved an item from KNOW to THINK. Two lines later I moved another from THINK to CHECK. Some ideas were memory. Some were inference built on memory. Some were probably complete bullshit wearing a familiar face. I marked them differently: KNOW. THINK. CHECK.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg building a written framework from unreliable future memory." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/001/v28_c01_s03_know-think-check.png"/></figure><p>By midday, I had a plan. A sensible plan. It would take perhaps twelve years. I stared at twelve. Too long. I started cutting. I did not need to learn warrior lessons twice. Ten. I knew which guild paths were dead ends. Nine. I knew which kinds of teachers mattered. Eight. I could begin mana conditioning early. Seven. Certain introductions could happen years sooner. Six. I stared at six. The number irritated me.</p><p>"Five." I wrote it. </p><p>The room offered no encouragement. Five years to reach the beginning of what had taken me decades. Ridiculous. Aggressive. Possible? Maybe. That was enough.</p><p>The first bottleneck was capital.</p><p>Capital immediately made me think of equipment. Equipment made me think of enchanted steel. Enchanted steel made me remember how obscenely cheap early mana-conductive alloys had once been before military procurement discovered them. For three glorious seconds I thought I had found my fortune. Then I tried to place the alloy in time and remembered the irritating part: it had not been invented yet. Probably. I chased the memory backward and got a workshop smell, a military procurement argument, and no inventor. I wrote it down anyway. Not as an investment. Under CHECK. Could it be invented early? By whom? Did I remember enough to point somebody toward it? Probably not. Still, the page gained another branch.</p><p>This was the danger and the opportunity. I did not have one future. I had forty years of loose threads, and pulling any one of them might lead to money, catastrophe, or a memory of a dinner conversation that had never been important in the first place.</p><p>That gave the plan an order. First, get enough money that I could stop selling my days one cheap contract at a time. Second, use that money to buy training, food, equipment, and access while I started conditioning mana years early. Third, verify the pieces of the future I actually remembered before betting on them. Only after that did I get to play with famous names, wars, guild politics, or any of the grand nonsense my older self had once moved through. I did not need to rebuild sixty-year-old Greg today. I needed to make nineteen-year-old Greg harder to trap tomorrow.</p><p>Nineteen-year-old Greg had three copper. Sixty-year-old Greg knew what money could do. Better food. Training. Equipment. Travel. Access. Time. Most importantly, options. I did not want wages. I wanted leverage. The obvious answer was borrowing. The sensible answer was borrowing a little. I wrote a number. Looked at it. Crossed it out. Wrote a larger one. Crossed that out. Then wrote an amount so offensive that I laughed.</p><p>"Reasonable." It was not. I knew a lender. Or rather, I knew what he became. Present version? Unknown. Current habits? Unknown. How much he would lend an arrogant nineteen-year-old Bronze warrior with three copper? Probably nothing. Still. That was a present problem. Present problems could be worked. I folded the papers. </p><p>Then unfolded them and removed PEOPLE WHO MATTER. Too incriminating. Then put it back.</p><p>If I was going to become the same manipulative bastard again, hiding the list from myself would not help. I looked once more at the mirror. Young. Alive. Unfinished. The old life felt impossibly far away and uncomfortably close. I had no reputation, no magic, no network, no proof.</p><p>Just forty years of experience, a nineteen-year-old body, a Bronze badge, and the deeply irritating conviction that this was still more than enough. Good work, Greg. I grabbed the coat. Then went looking for money.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><span class="is-disabled">← Previous</span><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="002.html">Chapter 2 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/064.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 51: The Patient — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell story-threshold story-threshold-major"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 51</div><h1>THE PATIENT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p><strong>The cart ride hurt less than being lifted.</strong> This was not because the cart ride hurt less. It was because somebody had given me something. I asked what. The healer said, “Don't worry about it.” Bad answer.</p><p>“What?” I asked.</p><p>“Poppy, willow, three drops gray tincture,” the healer said.</p><p>“How much poppy?” I asked.</p><p>“Enough,” she said.</p><p>“That's not a unit.”</p><p>“Good. You're awake.”</p><p>I hated her. The cart hit a seam in the road. White. Everything became white. Then gray. Then the healer's hand was on my shoulder.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stay.”</p><p>“I am literally in the cart.”</p><p>“Stay awake.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>That. I stayed. Mostly. My left leg existed as pressure. Not pain exactly. Pressure too large to fit inside a leg. Something had wrapped it. Splinted it. There was blood. I knew because I could smell it. Iron. Wet cloth. Poppy. Street. Horse. My right boot was still on. This became important for no reason.</p><p>“Did you take my left boot?”</p><p>The healer looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“My boot.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Tam fixed it.”</p><p>She stared.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“One copper.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>I closed my eyes.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Still here.”</p><p>The Guild infirmary had a blue door. I had never noticed. That seemed unfair. People carried me through it. Not the cart. A litter. Four hands. Maybe six. Ceiling. Doorframe. Lamp. Whitewashed wall. Someone said, “Trauma room.” Someone else said, “Hessa Marr.” Good. I tried to sit. Three people objected. One physically.</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>“I know her.”</p><p>“Wonderful.”</p><p>“I need to tell her one cast.”</p><p>The woman holding my shoulder said, “You can tell her later.”</p><p>“No. Yesterday one. Today one.”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“Coin. One breath. Clean.”</p><p>She looked at another healer.</p><p>“Is he confused?”</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>That was not helpful. They cut my trousers. I objected. Not because of modesty.</p><p>“Those are good trousers.”</p><p>No one cared. Scissors went through the left leg. Cloth opened. I looked. Someone put a hand in front of my face. I moved it. Then wished I had not. My lower leg did not look like a leg. That was the simplest version. Below the knee, the shape was wrong in several directions. Skin opened along the inner side. Bone. Maybe tibia.</p><p>Too much blood despite the wrap. Swelling already changing everything. Foot pale. Not white. Pale. Wrong. My toes looked farther away than they should.</p><p>“Can you feel this?”</p><p>A healer touched the foot.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>“Here?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Here?”</p><p>Pause.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Don't guess.”</p><p>“I am not.”</p><p>I was. He pressed a toenail. Color returned slowly. Very slowly. He looked at the woman beside him. They did not need to say anything.</p><p>“Pulse?” I asked.</p><p>“Quiet.”</p><p>“That's not a pulse.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Dorsal?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Do you know what you're asking?”</p><p>“Apparently.”</p><p>“Nothing reliable.”</p><p>“Posterior?”</p><p>“Nothing reliable.”</p><p>Good. No. Not good. Information.</p><p>“Warmth?”</p><p>“Cooler than the other.”</p><p>“How much blood?”</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>Everyone used terrible units. A woman with silver threaded through black hair entered. Not Hessa. She wore a dark apron and no Guild badge I could see. Surgeon. Probably. She looked at the leg. Then me.</p><p>“Gregory?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I'm Sera Dain.”</p><p>“Surgeon?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Hessa is coming?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>The question surprised me. Because Hessa knew. Because Hessa knew my channels. Because Hessa knew I was not nineteen in any useful way except all the ways that mattered now.</p><p>“She knows my magic.”</p><p>Sera nodded.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She examined the leg. Hands. Questions. Touch. Pressure. I answered. Some answers were probably wrong. She stopped the bleeding more effectively. Not magically. Clamp. Pressure. Something tied. Pain arrived in a new shape. I made a noise. Not words. Someone gave me more poppy.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>No one answered. Sera said, “Greg. Look at me.” I did.</p><p>“The leg is badly crushed.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>“Both bones are broken in multiple places. One is open. There is extensive muscle damage. I am concerned about the main blood vessels below the knee.”</p><p>“Concerned meaning?” I asked.</p><p>“I don't have useful flow to the foot,” Sera said.</p><p>“Can you restore it?” I asked.</p><p>“Maybe,” she said.</p><p>Maybe. Good word. Honest word.</p><p>“What determines?”</p><p>“What I find when I open it. How much vessel is intact. How much muscle is viable. Nerve damage. Contamination. Whether the tissue continues bleeding when we release pressure.”</p><p>“And healing?”</p><p>“Helps.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Not enough to answer the question you actually mean.”</p><p>Good surgeon.</p><p>“What do I mean?”</p><p>“Can magic save your leg.”</p><p>I looked at my foot.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I hated maybe now.</p><p>“What can it do?”</p><p>“Help close smaller vessels. Support damaged tissue that still has blood. Reduce some swelling. Help after bone is aligned. Improve healing after debridement.”</p><p>“Can it regrow vessel?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Nerve?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Muscle?”</p><p>“Not if it's dead.”</p><p>“Bone?”</p><p>“Not missing bone.”</p><p>“Can it bridge?”</p><p>“Small defects, sometimes, with support. Not what I can see here.”</p><p>Good. Information.</p><p>“What is the salvage threshold?”</p><p>Sera looked at me for a long second.</p><p>“Not one threshold.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Time without flow.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Crush extent.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Contamination.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Nerve.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Systemic risk.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Infection later.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Function if saved.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I knew this. Not this exact medicine. The structure. A limb could be technically present and still be a terrible limb. A limb could kill you while people were congratulating themselves for preserving it. Old Greg had seen that. Battlefields. Dungeon exits.</p><p>People carried three days because nobody wanted to say the word. Amputation. I had said it before. To other people. Sometimes gently. Sometimes not.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>Hessa. She came in fast. Not running. Hessa did not run. She crossed the room, looked at my face once, then the leg. Her expression changed. Small. Enough.</p><p>“You were due in five days,” she said.</p><p>“Scheduling problem.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I used one cast.”</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“One breath. Coin. External reference. Clean.”</p><p>“Symptoms?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Yesterday one. Also clean.”</p><p>“I know about yesterday.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Pessa.”</p><p>Of course. I laughed. Bad idea. Pain. Hessa put two fingers against my wrist. Then neck. Then temple. Not magic first. Pulse. Eyes. Breathing.</p><p>“Channels?”</p><p>“Quiet.”</p><p>“Any casting after injury?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Sera said, “You know his baseline?”</p><p>“Yes,” Hessa said.</p><p>“Any reason healing support is unsafe?” Sera asked.</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“His channels are immature relative to what he thinks they should be.”</p><p>Sera's eyebrows moved.</p><p>“Useful version.”</p><p>“Low reserve. Do not use him to power anything. External healing only. Small staged work. Watch head pressure and tremor.”</p><p>Good. No temporal explanation. Professional enough. Sera nodded.</p><p>“Can you support tissue assessment?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“I'm going to touch the leg.”</p><p>“Bold.”</p><p>“Shut up.”</p><p>There she was. She put one hand above the knee. One near the ankle without pressing the crushed section. Closed her eyes. Mana moved. Not mine. Warm. Faint. Then sharper. I knew enough healing theory to know I should not try to interpret what she was doing. I did anyway. Flow. Response. Tissue. Maybe. Hessa opened her eyes.</p><p>“Sera.”</p><p>They moved two steps away. I could still hear. Probably because they forgot I had ears.</p><p>“Upper calf responds.”</p><p>“Lower?”</p><p>“Patchy.”</p><p>“Foot?”</p><p>“Very little.”</p><p>“Can you distinguish compression from disruption?”</p><p>“Not reliably.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I said, “Excellent bedside manner.” Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“You asked for units in the cart.”</p><p>“How do you know that?”</p><p>“The healer complained.”</p><p>Traitor. Sera said, “We need to operate.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Now.”</p><p>“Salvage attempt?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There. Hope. Dangerous thing.</p><p>“What odds?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I don't have a useful number.”</p><p>“Estimate.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No,” Hessa said.</p><p>I looked between them. Cowards. Professionals. Same shape sometimes.</p><p>“What happens if you find it isn't salvageable?”</p><p>Sera answered.</p><p>“I stop trying to preserve tissue that will threaten you.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>Her face did not change.</p><p>“If the damage is too extensive, I amputate below the knee if I can. Above if I have to.”</p><p>There. The room stayed the same. Lamp. White wall. Cut trousers. My right boot. Below the knee. Better than above. That thought arrived immediately. Efficient. Useful. Disgusting.</p><p>“Greg?”</p><p>“I heard.”</p><p>“I need consent.”</p><p>“For exploration and salvage attempt?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And amputation if necessary?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at my left foot. It was still there. Pale. Dirty. One toenail cracked. I had not known that. Maybe from the wheel. Maybe old. My brain wanted to inventory. Length. Level. Bone. Vessel. Future gait. Armor. Sword stance. Barrier stance. Stairs. Roads. Alden. No. Not yet.</p><p>“Can you wake me before deciding?”</p><p>Sera's answer came too quickly.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because if I reach that decision, delaying to wake you may cost blood, tissue level, or your life.”</p><p>“Can Hessa decide?”</p><p>Hessa said, “No.” I looked at her.</p><p>“I know you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That's why.”</p><p>Fuck. Sera waited. No pressure. That made it worse.</p><p>“Below knee if possible.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Preserve length if it doesn't compromise viable tissue.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do not preserve useless length for appearance.”</p><p>Sera's face tightened slightly. Not pity. Recognition maybe.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do not take above knee because it's easier.”</p><p>“I won't.”</p><p>“Do not keep dead tissue because I'm nineteen.”</p><p>“I won't.”</p><p>Hessa said, “Greg.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You are negotiating with a surgeon who already knows her job.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then stop.”</p><p>I looked at Sera.</p><p>“Sorry.”</p><p>“Accepted.”</p><p>I signed. My hand shook. Not channels. Body. I hated that more. They prepared me. Clothes. Blanket. More drugs. Someone took my right boot. I objected again.</p><p>“Both?”</p><p>“You can't operate in one boot.”</p><p>“I am not operating.”</p><p>No one appreciated this. Hessa stayed near my head.</p><p>“Who needs to know?” she asked.</p><p>“About what?”</p><p>“That you're here.”</p><p>“No one.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Antonius will notice debt work eventually.”</p><p>“That's next week.”</p><p>“Alden.”</p><p>“Next week.”</p><p>“Your lodging?”</p><p>“Paid.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I hated the word.</p><p>“Jorren maybe.”</p><p>“Maybe?”</p><p>“He'll tell Sevren.”</p><p>“Do you want that?”</p><p>I thought.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Then:</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>Hessa nodded.</p><p>“Then I will tell Jorren you were injured and are in surgery. Nothing else until we know.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Arlo?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Antonius?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Alden?”</p><p>I closed my eyes.</p><p>“He'll hear.”</p><p>“From whom?”</p><p>“City.”</p><p>“That's not a person.”</p><p>“It behaves like one.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/064/Ch064_Fast-Coverage-003-A02.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 64." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Hessa almost smiled.</p><p>“Jorren first.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“My gloves.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Yard.”</p><p>“I will save the kingdom.”</p><p>“They were seven copper.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Everyone knows.”</p><p>Terrible city. Sera returned.</p><p>“Ready.”</p><p>No.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>They moved me. Ceiling again. Different door. Hessa walked beside me.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If it comes off.”</p><p>She waited. I had nothing. That was the problem.</p><p>“If it comes off,” I said again.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>Not therapist. Just true. Then the drugs took the room apart.</p><p>*</p><p>I woke because my left foot hurt. This was encouraging for perhaps half a second. Then I remembered. My left foot burned. Toes. Arch. Heel. All of it. Too hot. Too tight. I tried to move it. Nothing. Panic arrived before thought. I sat up. Or tried. Hands caught me.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>Hessa.</p><p>“Foot.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“My foot.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“It hurts.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“That's good.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I looked at her. The room was dimmer. Different bed. Blanket over me. I looked down. My right leg made a shape under the blanket. My left did too. Shorter. Much shorter. No. The burning foot remained. I could feel every toe. I could feel the little toe curled wrong. I could feel pressure under the heel. There was no foot-shaped blanket.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She did not lie.</p><p>“Below the knee.”</p><p>No. I pulled the blanket. She caught my wrist.</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>“Move.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Move.”</p><p>A surgeon's voice from somewhere.</p><p>“Let him see.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/064/Ch064_Fast-Coverage-006-01.jpg" alt="A loose sketch-style story scene from Chapter 64." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Sera. Hessa released me. I pulled the blanket. Bandages. My left thigh. Knee. Then thick wrapped dressing ending below it. Not far below. Enough. No shin. No ankle. No foot. My foot hurt. My foot was not there. This was a contradiction. I stared.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>Sera came closer.</p><p>“About a handspan below the knee joint.”</p><p>“Centimeters?”</p><p>She blinked. Wrong world.</p><p>“Handspan.”</p><p>“Whose?”</p><p>“Mine.”</p><p>I laughed. It sounded bad.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Not good. Below knee. Length. Knee preserved. Useful. The inventory started. I let it. Knee. Thigh. Hip. Balance changed. Lever gone. Mass gone. Proprioception wrong. Wound. Healing. Socket. No. Not yet.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>Sera sat. Not beside me. Near.</p><p>“We opened the lower leg. The main artery was torn across a crushed segment. The companion vessels were badly damaged. Muscle in the deep lower compartments was nonviable. The tibia was fragmented over too much length for stable reconstruction with the tissue available. The major nerve was also severely crushed.”</p><p>“Could you bridge the artery?”</p><p>“Not across the damaged length with what we had and still have viable coverage.”</p><p>“Graft?”</p><p>“Not here. Not safely. And blood flow alone would not have solved the muscle, nerve, bone, and contamination.”</p><p>“Could healing have kept the muscle?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Could you have waited?”</p><p>Sera said, “No.”</p><p>“How long did you try?”</p><p>“Long enough.”</p><p>“That isn't a unit.”</p><p>Hessa closed her eyes. Sera said, “A little under an hour after opening before I made the decision.”</p><p>“What changed?”</p><p>“We found the vessel injury extended farther than the external wound suggested. The crushed muscle did not respond after decompression and restored proximal flow. The bone fragments had stripped tissue over a long section. Continuing would have meant more blood loss for a limb I did not believe could become viable.”</p><p>“Believe.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Not know. Medicine. I hated it.</p><p>“What chance?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“What chance did you discard?”</p><p>Sera did not flinch.</p><p>“A small one that the foot could have remained attached for some period. A smaller one that it would have remained alive. Smaller again that it would have become useful. Against a significant chance of infection, tissue death, repeated surgery, higher amputation later, or you becoming much sicker.”</p><p>There. Decision. Not certainty. I looked at the bandage.</p><p>“You chose.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I told you to.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Fuck. That was worse. Maybe better. No. Nothing.</p><p>“Did you preserve the knee?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I can see that.”</p><p>“Then stop asking questions you can answer.”</p><p>I looked at her. Hessa said, “I like her.”</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>Sera checked the dressing.</p><p>“Bleeding is controlled. Hessa assisted with staged healing after the amputation, not before the decision. Bone end is covered. Muscle closure is viable. Skin closure is partial because I want drainage and reassessment.”</p><p>“Infection?”</p><p>“Risk.”</p><p>“Next?”</p><p>“Rest. Fluids. Food when you can keep it down. Dressing checks. Another look tomorrow. No standing.”</p><p>“I have another leg.”</p><p>“No standing.”</p><p>“Crutches?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“We'll see.”</p><p>Bad phrase.</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>“Some of what you're feeling is the wound.”</p><p>“And the foot?”</p><p>“Your nerves and brain still expect it.”</p><p>“Phantom.”</p><p>Sera looked at me.</p><p>“You know the word?”</p><p>“Different word where I learned it.”</p><p>Hessa watched me. Careful. Sera said, “It may change. Burning, pressure, position, itching. It may come and go.”</p><p>“Can healing fix it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Of course. I lay back. The absent foot was still clenched. I tried to unclench it. Nothing happened. I tried again. Nothing. My body had an instruction with no destination. That frightened me more than the bandage. I closed my eyes. Bad. The wheel came back. Timber plate. Drop. Cart. Turn. Barrier. Slat snapping away. Clearance. Almost. I opened my eyes. Hessa was still there.</p><p>“Was the Barrier wrong?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did it move me the wrong way?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did I miss the cart?”</p><p>“You missed the cart body.”</p><p>“The wheel.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could I have gone left?”</p><p>“I wasn't there.”</p><p>“Ressa?”</p><p>“Outside earlier.”</p><p>“Dorn?”</p><p>“Also.”</p><p>“Marn?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>I needed geometry. Positions. Times. If I could find the wrong decision, the room would make sense. Hessa said, “Not now.”</p><p>“You don't know what I'm doing.”</p><p>“Yes, I do.”</p><p>“Then tell me.”</p><p>“You're trying to turn the yard into a problem you can solve after the answer is already your leg.”</p><p>I stared at her. Too close to therapy. But Hessa looked irritated, not gentle. Better.</p><p>“I need to know.”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“What if I made the wrong call?”</p><p>“Then you made it yesterday.”</p><p>Fuck.</p><p>“What if I didn't?”</p><p>“Then you still don't have a foot.”</p><p>Worse. Good Hessa. I turned my face toward the wall. Someone had painted over a crack. Poorly. I could still see it. The foot burned. My heel pressed into a mattress it could not touch. Time passed. Maybe. I slept. Maybe. When I woke again, Jorren was sitting in the chair. He had food. Of course. He looked terrible. Not crying. Just wrong.</p><p>“Hey,” he said.</p><p>“That's weak.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>He put the food down. Soup. I smelled it. My stomach turned.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“Who told you?”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Who did you tell?”</p><p>“Sevren.”</p><p>“Only?”</p><p>“Octavia was with him.”</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>“Alden heard from somebody at the Guild before I found him.”</p><p>City.</p><p>“Antonius?”</p><p>“No idea.”</p><p>“Arlo?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. Jorren looked at the blanket. Then deliberately looked at my face. That was worse than staring.</p><p>“You can look.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“When I came in.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>He swallowed.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“Cart.”</p><p>“I know cart.”</p><p>“Wheel.”</p><p>“I know wheel.”</p><p>“Then why ask?”</p><p>“Because people ask stupid things when their friend loses a leg.”</p><p>Friend. I looked away.</p><p>“Apparently.”</p><p>He sat. No speech. Good. After a while he said, “You missed drinks.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Tonight.”</p><p>“No. Drinks were yesterday.”</p><p>He blinked.</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>“Idiot.”</p><p>“Poppy?”</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>“Not a unit.”</p><p>I looked at him. He smiled. Small. Someone had told him. Traitors everywhere.</p><p>“My room?”</p><p>“What about it?”</p><p>“Food.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Eggs.”</p><p>“You're worried about eggs?”</p><p>“They go bad.”</p><p>“I'll eat them.”</p><p>“Those are my eggs.”</p><p>“Then I'll cook them.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“Gloves.”</p><p>“Dorn has them.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“He brought your things.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Seven copper.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>Terrible city. Jorren stayed. Not forever. Long enough. When he left, the room got larger. Hessa came back later. Or maybe she had never left for long. She checked my channels. Quiet. She checked the dressing with Sera. No crisis. Good. I hated good. At some point I remembered the calendar.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Five days.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You scheduled me in five days.”</p><p>She stared. Then understood.</p><p>“We'll reschedule.”</p><p>“I might be here.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So technically convenient.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Sleep.”</p><p>I did not. Not immediately. The absent foot hurt. The real leg hurt. My back hurt. My mouth was dry. The room smelled like boiled cloth and medicine. I thought about the calendar pinned beside the mirror. Road days crossed out. Hessa. Alden. West Storehouse. Blank spaces. The page was wrong now. Not destroyed. Wrong. That was somehow harder. I had spent months treating wrong plans as invitations.</p><p>Update. Adjust. Rebuild. Better information. New constraints. I knew how to do that. I was very good at it. I did not want to. That was new. I lay still. My left foot burned where there was no left foot. For once, I let the problem remain unsolved.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="063.html">← Chapter 50</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="065.html">Chapter 52 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/286.html:218`: <p>I did not use mana.</p>
- `chapters/286.html:245`: <p>The wall was warm, not burning. No smoke. No smell. No cracking. No visible active mana. The floor was dry. The shelf could stay away from it for now. There was no reason to turn a household oddity into an emergency.</p>

- `chapters/286.html:484`: <p>"For not touching old seal with mana?"</p>
- `chapters/034.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 27: The Helper — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 27</div><h1>THE HELPER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Arlo was not testing my regulator. He was using it to hold up a shelf.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Regulator Shelf Support" decoding="async" height="324" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/034/v45_c34_regulator-shelf-support.png" width="251"/></figure><p>I stood in the workshop doorway with the wrapped improved piece in my hand and watched a narrow brass regulator, almost identical to mine, wedged beneath the left corner of a wooden rack. The rack held ceramic cups. One cup was cracked. Two were marked with charcoal. A third contained screws. Arlo looked up from a bench.</p><p>“You’re late.”</p><p>“You sent yesterday.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I was in Darrowmere.”</p><p>“I heard.”</p><p>“You knew that when you sent the message?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then I am not late.”</p><p>“You are here after I needed you.”</p><p>“That is a different accusation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He went back to work. I entered. The workshop had changed. Not dramatically. The same benches. Same kiln smell. Same metal filings in the floor cracks. Same collection of tools arranged according to a system I still could not infer. But one wall now held six regulators instead of two. Three brass. One dark iron. One ceramic-bodied.</p><p>One that looked like it had been made by someone angry at circles. Arlo had not been waiting for me. Good. I set my wrapped regulator on the only clear corner of the bench. He pointed without looking.</p><p>“Not there.”</p><p>I moved it.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Hot.”</p><p>I touched the bench. Hot. Young reflexes pulled my hand back before thought finished. Arlo looked over.</p><p>“Functional?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Your hand says otherwise.”</p><p>“Bench.”</p><p>“Your wrist.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>LIMITED CASTING.</p><p>“Small, low-load only.”</p><p>“How small?”</p><p>“Coin-sized has been clean.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>“Three yesterday. Two today.”</p><p>He stopped filing.</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Symptoms?”</p><p>“Pressure after five breaths.”</p><p>“Then you are not casting.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Everyone liked the restriction except me. Arlo wiped his hands on his apron.</p><p>“Give me the piece.”</p><p>I unwrapped it. He took it. No ceremony. Turned the adjustment screw twice. Held it to the light. Then placed it beside another regulator. Mine looked better. Not prettier. More finished. The channel edges were cleaner. The brass body had been filed down around the housing. The screw sat tighter. Arlo had added two tiny marks near the collar.</p><p>“What changed?”</p><p>“Everything small.”</p><p>“That is not useful.”</p><p>“It is accurate.”</p><p>He picked up the other regulator.</p><p>“This is the first fixture.”</p><p>Then mine.</p><p>“Second fixture.”</p><p>He pointed to the shelf support.</p><p>“Third.”</p><p>I stared at the regulator under the shelf.</p><p>“You improved the fixture three times.”</p><p>“Four.”</p><p>“Where is four?”</p><p>He pointed at the kiln. A woman I had not noticed was kneeling beside it. She wore a leather apron over a blue shirt and had both arms inside the open lower access panel. Not literally inside. Up to the elbows. Enough. She looked over.</p><p>“Don’t point at me.”</p><p>Arlo lowered his hand.</p><p>“Vessa.”</p><p>I knew the name. Arlo’s shop. Chalk notes. Fixture work. She had been part of the place before I understood the place. Vessa pulled one arm free.</p><p>“Greg?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The regulator boy.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Arlo said, “Yes.” </p><p>I looked at him. He had already returned to the bench. </p><p>Vessa smiled.</p><p>“Good. Hold this.”</p><p>She handed me a metal plate. It was heavier than expected. My nineteen-year-old wrist dipped. I caught it with both hands. She noticed. Did not comment.</p><p>“Flat,” she said.</p><p>I held it flat. She slid back under the kiln.</p><p>“What am I holding?”</p><p>“Door plate.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I need both hands.”</p><p>Reasonable. Arlo set three regulators in a row.</p><p>“Comparison.”</p><p>I looked at the plate.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I am occupied.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was apparently not contradictory. Arlo connected the first regulator to a small hand-pump assembly. No mana. Good. A glass tube rose from the apparatus with ink marks at regular intervals. He pressed the pump. Air moved through. A bead inside the tube climbed. Stopped. He wrote a number. Second regulator. Pump. Bead. Number. Mine. Pump. Bead. Number. He frowned. I became interested.</p><p>Vessa said from beneath the kiln, “Plate.” I had tilted it. I corrected. Arlo pumped again. Same result.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>He pointed at the glass tube.</p><p>“Same band again.”</p><p>I moved closer.</p><p>“Too narrow?”</p><p>“Narrower than the other fixtures.” Hostile city.</p><p>“What is wrong with the number?”</p><p>“Too good.”</p><p>I shifted my grip on the plate. That phrase had caused problems before.</p><p>“How too good?”</p><p>He showed me. I understood enough of the marks. The first regulator had variable low-flow behavior. The second was tighter. Mine held a narrower band. Much narrower.</p><p>“That is good.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You said too good.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Explain.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared. </p><p>He picked up mine. Turned the screw. Pump. Number. Turned. Pump. Number. Again. Again. The numbers stayed close. Not identical. Close. Arlo’s frown deepened. </p><p>Vessa said, “If you make him more interested, he’ll drop my plate.”</p><p>“I will not.”</p><p>My arms were beginning to tire. Not much. Enough. The plate was not designed to be held for this long. My body knew before my pride did. Vessa’s hand emerged.</p><p>“Give.”</p><p>I gave. She took the full weight one-handed from an awkward angle. Competence. Not magical. Just practiced. I liked watching it. She fitted the plate into place. Two bolts. Turn. Check. Loosen. Shift. Turn. No wasted motion.</p><p>I nearly asked why she had loosened the first bolt after tightening it. Did not. She was working.</p><p>Arlo said, “Greg.”</p><p>I looked back. He had disassembled my regulator.</p><p>“You could ask.”</p><p>“You brought it for comparison.”</p><p>“That does not imply destruction.”</p><p>“It is not destroyed.”</p><p>“It is in five pieces.”</p><p>“Six.”</p><p>He lifted the collar. Six. I moved closer. The internal channel looked different. Not the shape I remembered. Arlo had added a tiny recess near the inlet.</p><p>“What is that?”</p><p>“Problem.”</p><p>“What problem?”</p><p>He pointed at the first regulator.</p><p>“Low flow pulses.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not from supply.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“Hand pump.”</p><p>Right. No mana source. No spell variability. Mechanical isolation. Good.</p><p>“So internal.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Cavitation?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>Wrong word. Later word? Different field? I searched memory. Fluid behavior. Bubbles. Pressure. Not necessarily useful here.</p><p>“Nothing. Air pocket?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Flex?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Valve chatter?”</p><p>He paused.</p><p>“Closer.”</p><p>Good. He held the tiny adjustment screw between finger and thumb.</p><p>“At low opening, the screw does not stay where the fixture says it stays.”</p><p>“Movement?”</p><p>“Very small.”</p><p>“From pressure?”</p><p>“From everything.”</p><p>He tapped the bench.</p><p>“Vibration. Pump. Hand. Floor.”</p><p>I looked at the regulator.</p><p>“So the recess stabilizes the screw?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He pointed to the recess.</p><p>“It gives the flow somewhere to be wrong.”</p><p>I stopped. That was interesting.</p><p>“Explain.”</p><p>He sighed. Not annoyed. Arlo’s version of pleased.</p><p>“The first fixture tried to make the opening exact.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It isn’t.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The second made the screw better.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Still isn’t.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The third changes the channel around the bad opening.”</p><p>I looked at the recess. A tiny side volume. The flow could fluctuate at the screw and then settle before the outlet. Not fixing the unstable part. Absorbing its error. My brain lit. Buffer. No. Different. Similar. I thought of sinkstone. Cheap buffers always lie about what they keep. Not now. Arlo was here. This was his thing.</p><p>“What did the fourth fixture change?”</p><p>Arlo looked toward Vessa. She had closed the kiln panel.</p><p>“Ask her.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“What did the fourth fixture change?”</p><p>Vessa stood.</p><p>“Arlo.”</p><p>He looked offended. She wiped soot from her forearm.</p><p>“The first three held the body too hard.”</p><p>Arlo said, “Not too hard.”</p><p>“They marked the brass,” Vessa said.</p><p>“Cosmetic,” Arlo said.</p><p>“They distorted the housing,” Vessa said.</p><p>“Barely,” Arlo said.</p><p>“Enough,” Vessa said.</p><p>Arlo looked at me.</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>Vessa continued.</p><p>“Fourth holds the collar and lets the body sit.”</p><p>“Less clamping force?”</p><p>“Different clamping.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because he kept making the same good regulator in the fixture and a worse one after he took it out.”</p><p>I looked at Arlo. He did not deny it. That was funny. I smiled.</p><p>“Do not,” he said.</p><p>“I said nothing.”</p><p>“You made the face.”</p><p>Vessa laughed again. Arlo pointed at her.</p><p>“You missed it too.”</p><p>“Twice.”</p><p>“Three.”</p><p>“Second one was your filing.”</p><p>“It was not.”</p><p>Their argument continued without me. Good. I looked at the six regulators on the wall. The progression was visible now. Not invention. Iteration. Fixture. Measurement. Failure. Change. Another failure. Someone else noticing the housing distortion. Change again. My original contribution had been small. A question about low flow. A use case. Maybe an insistence. Arlo had done the rest. No. Arlo and Vessa.</p><p>Probably Tere somewhere before that. The workshop had grown around the problem without me. I liked that more than I expected.</p><p>“What do you need from me?” I asked.</p><p>Arlo stopped arguing.</p><p>“Nothing,” Arlo said.</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“You sent for me.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“For nothing?”</p><p>“For the regulator.”</p><p>“You said comparison.”</p><p>“I compared it.”</p><p>“You could have asked someone to bring it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then why me?” I asked.</p><p>Arlo looked down at the regulator.</p><p>“You own it.”</p><p>That was all. Not expertise. Not future knowledge. Property. I had built a larger role for myself because I was used to being useful. Embarrassing. Vessa said, “He also wanted to know if you broke it.” </p><p>Arlo looked at her.</p><p>“That was secondary.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“You expected me to break it?”</p><p>“You use things.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/034/Ch034_Fast-Coverage-003-A21.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 34." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“That is what they are for.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then why phrase it like criticism?”</p><p>“It wasn’t.”</p><p>Right. Clean relationship to work. I picked up the first regulator.</p><p>“Can I?”</p><p>Arlo nodded. I turned the screw. Felt the loose point. Then mine. Tighter. Not because the screw itself was dramatically better. Because the outlet behavior cared less about the screw’s tiny instability.</p><p>“Does it work with liquid?”</p><p>Arlo said, “Some.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“Water.”</p><p>“Oil?”</p><p>“Bad.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Thick.”</p><p>“Alcohol?”</p><p>Vessa said, “Better use for alcohol.” Arlo ignored her.</p><p>“Not tested.”</p><p>“Mana solution?”</p><p>“Not tested.”</p><p>My attention sharpened.</p><p>Arlo set the regulator beside the hand pump.</p><p>“Mechanical behavior first. Mana after we know what this does without it.”</p><p>“That is sensible.”</p><p>“That is sensible.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I dislike it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Arlo began reassembling mine. I watched his hands. Fast. Not elegant. Effective. He dropped the collar. Caught it against his apron before it hit the floor. Young me would have pretended not to notice. Old me would have categorized dexterity and failure rate. Present me laughed. Arlo looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You laughed.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You dropped it.”</p><p>“I caught it.”</p><p>“That is why.”</p><p>He stared. </p><p>Vessa said, “He’s been outside too much.” Maybe. Arlo finished the assembly. </p><p>Then handed me a small paper packet.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Washers.”</p><p>I opened it. Six thin rings. Different thicknesses.</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Testing.”</p><p>“I cannot cast.”</p><p>“Not magic.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“What do I test?”</p><p>“Use it.”</p><p>“With what?”</p><p>He shrugged.</p><p>“Whatever you use it for.”</p><p>“That is dangerously broad.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you want measurements?”</p><p>“If you can.”</p><p>“Failure notes?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Temperature?”</p><p>“If relevant.”</p><p>“Flow medium?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Orientation?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Duration?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“External vibration?”</p><p>Arlo paused. Then nodded.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I smiled. There it was. Not a lesson. A problem. My body leaned toward the bench before I decided to. Arlo saw.</p><p>“You cannot stay.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I have work.”</p><p>“So do I.”</p><p>“Not here.”</p><p>I looked around. Vessa had reopened the kiln panel. Arlo was already reaching for a ceramic-bodied regulator. A customer waited near the front now, holding a cracked lantern assembly. I had not heard him enter. The workshop did not need me.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>I wrapped my regulator. The customer stepped aside to let me pass. Then </p><p>Arlo said, “Wait.” </p><p>I turned. </p><p>He held up the ceramic-bodied piece.</p><p>“Do you know why this fails?”</p><p>I looked. Hairline crack around the inlet. Dark staining.</p><p>“Heat?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pressure?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Bad firing?”</p><p>Vessa said, “Careful.” </p><p>I looked at her. </p><p>She smiled. </p><p>Arlo said, “Not firing.”</p><p>“Then I don’t know.”</p><p>He nodded.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I don’t either.”</p><p>He put it back on the bench. That was apparently the entire exchange. I waited. Nothing.</p><p>“You asked me just to see if I knew?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You know strange things.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Do you want me to think about it?”</p><p>“If you want.”</p><p>There. Permission. Not assignment. Not need. I looked at the crack again. Wanted to. Very much. Also sword. Food. Hessa’s restriction. Antonius’s warning. Sinkstone. Silas Marris. Berren. The crack was small. Interesting. Not mine.</p><p>“I’ll think about it later.”</p><p>Arlo nodded. No disappointment. That made leaving easier. Outside, late afternoon had turned the workshop lane gold. My arms still remembered the weight of Vessa’s kiln plate. A mild tremor lived in the muscles near my elbow. Not mana. Just fatigue. Nineteen-year-old body. I rolled my shoulders. It felt good. That surprised me. Not the soreness. The work. Holding something heavy because another person needed both hands.</p><p>No optimization. No leverage. No future consequence. Useful for thirty seconds. Then done. I walked toward the east market. The smith Alden had recommended occupied half an open-front shop between a cobbler and a seller of cooking pots. A woman was already at the stone.</p><p>My sword lay nowhere because I had not given it to her yet. She was sharpening a butcher’s cleaver. I waited. She did not look up. Good. The wheel hissed. Metal. Water. Wheel. Her left hand controlled angle. Right hand pressure. Three passes. Check. Two passes. Check. She wiped the blade. Handed it to the butcher.</p><p>“Tomorrow for the other two.”</p><p>“I need one tonight.”</p><p>“You have one.”</p><p>“I need two.”</p><p>“Then come tomorrow.”</p><p>He paid. Left. She looked at me.</p><p>“Sword.”</p><p>I handed it over. She drew it halfway. Looked at the chip.</p><p>“Two copper.”</p><p>“Alden said.”</p><p>“Red scarf?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Three copper.”</p><p>“He said.”</p><p>“He talks.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She pulled the blade fully.</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>“He said basic edge today.”</p><p>She looked at the light. Then at me.</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I’m done.”</p><p>I looked at the wheel. Still spinning. Three blades on the rack. A hammer on the bench. Shop open.</p><p>“You are open.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“But done.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I understood the words. Not the system. She pointed at her right wrist. Slight swelling. Not dramatic.</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>There. Physical limit. Not mine. Hers. I handed her two copper. She put the sword behind the counter. No negotiation. Old me would have priced urgency. Young me might have argued because I wanted the sword. Present me had another swordless evening. Fine.</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>She nodded. I left. Halfway down the lane, I realized I had not asked her name. That was probably healthy. Not everyone needed to become a person I collected. Then I stopped. No. That was stupid. Names were not ownership. I turned back.</p><p>The butcher had been replaced by a pot seller asking about a knife. The smith was already working. I could interrupt. I did not. Tomorrow. At the corner, someone called my name. I turned.</p><p>Jorren sat outside a narrow drink shop with one boot on the empty chair opposite him. He lifted his cup.</p><p>“You look unemployed.”</p><p>“I have done three jobs today.”</p><p>“You look bad at them.”</p><p>“I was excellent at beans.”</p><p>He moved his boot. Invitation. I looked at the regulator under my arm. Arlo had work. Smith had stopped. Antonius had no urgency. Hessa had restricted casting. I could go home and write notes about sinkstone. I could think about the ceramic crack. I could list questions for Edrin. I could calculate Silas Marris possibilities. Jorren drank. Did not repeat the invitation.</p><p>I sat.</p><p>“What is that?” he asked.</p><p>“Regulator.”</p><p>“Magic?”</p><p>“Eventually.”</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He pushed a second cup toward me. I looked at it.</p><p>“You ordered for me?”</p><p>“No. Man left.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Wife came.”</p><p>“Emergency?”</p><p>Jorren shrugged.</p><p>“She looked like one.”</p><p>I drank. Bitter. Cheap. Good.</p><p>“What did you do today?” I asked.</p><p>“Worked.”</p><p>“At?”</p><p>“Dock gate.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Money.”</p><p>“Anything interesting?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I waited. He looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing happened?”</p><p>“Cart axle broke.”</p><p>“That is something.”</p><p>“Not to me.”</p><p>“What was in the cart?”</p><p>“Turnips.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>Jorren stared. I drank. He laughed.</p><p>“There he is.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You went away.”</p><p>“I am sitting here.”</p><p>“Your face left.”</p><p>Everyone. Everyone could see it.</p><p>“What did it do?”</p><p>“Turnips became important.”</p><p>“They might be.”</p><p>“They weren’t.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“Because they were turnips.”</p><p>I considered arguing. Did not. Jorren leaned back.</p><p>“You fight monsters?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You alive?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Alden?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then decent.”</p><p>That was not how evaluation worked. It was how his did. He drank. I drank. The regulator sat under my arm. The ceramic crack waited in Arlo’s workshop. My sword waited behind a smith’s counter. Sinkstone waited for Edrin’s tests. Silas Marris existed whether I investigated them or not. For perhaps ten minutes, nothing required me. This was inefficient. I stayed anyway.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="032.html">← Chapter 26</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="035.html">Chapter 28 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/105/Ch105_Campfire-Companions.png"/></figure><p>Hessa made me put my right hand on a towel.</p><p>This was worse than the curved copper.</p><p>The towel was folded twice on the table beside the bad chair.</p><p>Clean.</p><p>White.</p><p>Ordinary.</p><p>I looked at it.</p><p>Then at Hessa.</p><p>“Hand on the towel,” she said.</p><p>“Why the towel?”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>I sat.</p><p>My thumb had behaved since yesterday.</p><p>No tingling after I left Hessa.</p><p>None while Jorren found a piece of roast pork large enough to justify his new knife.</p><p>None during dinner.</p><p>None upstairs.</p><p>None overnight.</p><p>None dressing.</p><p>None at breakfast.</p><p>I had written this in paragraphs because civilization had rules.</p><p>Hessa took the notebook.</p><p>She read.</p><p>“You wrote ‘thumb remained a thumb.’”</p><p>“It did.”</p><p>“That is not a symptom report.”</p><p>“It establishes continuity.”</p><p>“It establishes that you are annoying.”</p><p>She handed the notebook back.</p><p>“Hand.”</p><p>I gave her the right one.</p><p>Temperature.</p><p>Pulse.</p><p>Pressure along the thumb.</p><p>Wrist.</p><p>Forearm.</p><p>Grip.</p><p>Fingertips.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>“Any recurrence?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Any numbness?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Weakness?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Grip trouble?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Anything you have not told me because you decided it was unrelated?”</p><p>I considered.</p><p>“My right calf is no longer sore from Pessa.”</p><p>“That was not what I meant.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>She did not.</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She put my hand back on the towel.</p><p>Palm up.</p><p>“Leave it there.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because today I want it quiet.”</p><p>My pulse changed.</p><p>Not much.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>“We are drawing.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And shaping?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>There it was.</p><p>I had expected disappointment.</p><p>It arrived.</p><p>Clean.</p><p>Immediate.</p><p>Annoying.</p><p>“Because of the tingling.”</p><p>“Because I have a new observation and I don't want to add another one before I understand the first as well as I reasonably can.”</p><p>“You cannot understand it from waiting.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Then.”</p><p>“Do not turn that into permission.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>“What does draw-only tell you?”</p><p>“One thing, if we're lucky.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Whether a minimal draw, without deliberate alteration, immediately reproduces the hand symptom today.”</p><p>“That is very narrow.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If it does not?”</p><p>“Then it does not.”</p><p>“That is not useful.”</p><p>“It is exactly as useful as it is.”</p><p>“If it does?”</p><p>“Then it does.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“You want me to promise interpretation before the observation.”</p><p>“I want to know what the observation would mean.”</p><p>“It would mean what happened.”</p><p>“That is infuriating.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The straight copper strip was on the table.</p><p>No curved one.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>I looked at my right hand on the towel.</p><p>“Why the towel?”</p><p>“So I can see whether you move your hand.”</p><p>“You could see it on the table.”</p><p>“Your hand rests differently on wood.”</p><p>“Does that matter?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“You are changing a variable.”</p><p>“I am making it easier for you to relax your hand.”</p><p>“That is changing a variable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So this is not a clean comparison.”</p><p>“There is no clean comparison.”</p><p>Pessa would like her.</p><p>I did not say this either.</p><p>Hessa moved the copper strip close to my forearm.</p><p>Not thumb.</p><p>“Minimal draw.”</p><p>I closed my eyes.</p><p>“Keep the right hand quiet.”</p><p>“It is quiet.”</p><p>“Keep it that way.”</p><p>I drew.</p><p>Mana arrived.</p><p>Familiar now.</p><p>That word required caution.</p><p>Familiar did not mean normal.</p><p>Chest.</p><p>Shoulders.</p><p>Arms.</p><p>Right side.</p><p>Left thigh.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Ordinary phantom foot.</p><p>Nothing unusual below the knee.</p><p>The right hand remained warm against the towel.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>No pressure.</p><p>No urge to turn the wrist.</p><p>No spreading into the palm beyond whatever ordinary draw sensation belonged there.</p><p>I noticed myself looking for Barrier.</p><p>Not magically.</p><p>Mentally.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Hessa said, “Report.”</p><p>“Draw stable.”</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>“Right hand unchanged.”</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>“No thumb tingling.”</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>“No unusual below-knee sensation.”</p><p>She did not react.</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released.</p><p>Mana went.</p><p>Right hand still there.</p><p>Thumb still a thumb.</p><p>“Do not move.”</p><p>“I wasn't.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She set the copper down.</p><p>Then we waited.</p><p>I opened my eyes.</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>“Until I stop.”</p><p>“That is not a unit.”</p><p>“You do not need one.”</p><p>“I could estimate.”</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>I stared at the wall.</p><p>The wall was aggressively uninformative.</p><p>A crack ran from near the window frame toward the ceiling.</p><p>I had seen it before.</p><p>Or thought I had.</p><p>Maybe it had grown.</p><p>This was not my jurisdiction either.</p><p>I looked at my hand.</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>“I am looking.”</p><p>“Look somewhere else.”</p><p>“This is medically authoritarian.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at Hessa instead.</p><p>She was writing.</p><p>“What are you
