the pen down.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>I looked at the wall again.</p><p>My thumb did not tingle.</p><p>The longer it did not tingle, the more I wanted it to.</p><p>Not because I wanted injury.</p><p>Because no symptom was not an answer.</p><p>A symptom was also not an answer.</p><p>This was a poor system.</p><p>“How long now?”</p><p>Hessa ignored me.</p><p>I counted breaths.</p><p>Then stopped counting because that was functionally timing.</p><p>Personal record.</p><p>Someone knocked at the outer door.</p><p>Nerin answered.</p><p>Voices.</p><p>A child coughed.</p><p>Not dramatically.</p><p>Twice.</p><p>Then there was the sound of a chair scraping.</p><p>Life continued outside the experiment.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I hated that too.</p><p>Hessa looked at my hand.</p><p>“Anything?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Move the fingers normally.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>Once.</p><p>Thumb to nothing.</p><p>Just open.</p><p>Close.</p><p>“No tingling.”</p><p>“Grip.”</p><p>I squeezed her fingers.</p><p>Released.</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Wrist.”</p><p>She had me bend it once each direction.</p><p>No pain.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>“Stand.”</p><p>“What about observation?”</p><p>“Stand.”</p><p>Both crutches.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/105/Ch105_Towel-to-Crutch.png" alt="Greg transfers his right hand from the test towel to the right crutch grip under Hessa&#x27;s observation." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Right hand left the towel and took the right crutch grip.</p><p>Immediate pressure through palm.</p><p>Thumb around handle.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>I stood.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>“Walk to the door.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“That is a test.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You forbade me from changing grip to test.”</p><p>“I forbade you from testing yourself.”</p><p>“Different because you are here.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Authority is convenient.”</p><p>“Walk.”</p><p>I walked to the inner door and back.</p><p>Ordinary pace.</p><p>Two crutches.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>Turn.</p><p>Not Pessa's turn.</p><p>Just a turn.</p><p>I did not analyze it.</p><p>Mostly.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I went.</p><p>Back.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Last.”</p><p>Third.</p><p>No tingling.</p><p>She had me sit.</p><p>Right hand back on towel.</p><p>“You just tested crutch use.”</p><p>“I observed a small amount of ordinary crutch use immediately after a draw.”</p><p>“That is testing crutch use.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could have said that.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“You said walk.”</p><p>“That was the instruction.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>“What does it mean?”</p><p>“That you completed a minimal draw and a few minutes of ordinary crutch use without immediate thumb tingling.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“And nothing else yet.”</p><p>“Nothing?”</p><p>“Nothing else.”</p><p>“You are cruel.”</p><p>“I am careful.”</p><p>“Same texture.”</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>Tiny.</p><p>Then gone.</p><p>“Can we shape?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why not? The thumb is fine.”</p><p>“The thumb is fine right now.”</p><p>“Which is what we wanted.”</p><p>“It is one thing we wanted.”</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>“Time.”</p><p>“We have time.”</p><p>“Not in this room.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>Bad chair.</p><p>Same enemy.</p><p>“You want another day.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because the second tingling episode happened later during ordinary life, not during the immediate observation after shaping.”</p><p>“So immediate draw-only plus crutch use not reproducing it tells us nothing about delayed recurrence.”</p><p>“It tells us it did not happen immediately.”</p><p>“You are impossible.”</p><p>“I am repetitive.”</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>She folded the towel.</p><p>Experiment over.</p><p>I watched her put it aside.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“No magic tomorrow.”</p><p>“Day after?”</p><p>“Come back.”</p><p>“For shaping?”</p><p>“For assessment.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“I know what you want.”</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“To try the thumb again.”</p><p>That was too small.</p><p>I shook my head.</p><p>Her expression changed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I want to know if I can still learn magic.”</p><p>The room got quiet.</p><p>Not theatrically.</p><p>The child in the outer room coughed again.</p><p>Hessa's face did not soften.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I did not want soft.</p><p>“You are learning,” she said.</p><p>“I failed.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is not what I mean.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“I mean casting.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Barrier.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Other spells.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Being able to use mana without someone sitting six feet away with copper.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>I hated how calm she was.</p><p>“I was good at this.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not the best.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“But good.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And now I put mana in the wrong part of my hand and everyone is pleased.”</p><p>“I was not pleased.”</p><p>“I was.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>“That matters.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There.</p><p>Not enough.</p><p>Enough to continue.</p><p>I looked at my right hand.</p><p>“Do you think I can?”</p><p>Hessa took time.</p><p>This was worse than an immediate no.</p><p>“I think you have already shown that you can draw mana repeatedly.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You deliberately altered it once.”</p><p>“Wrong.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You stopped when the alteration began to move somewhere you did not intend.”</p><p>I looked up.</p><p>“That matters?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>More than I had given it.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>“You recognized something familiar and stopped before it became more.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You reported the hand symptom.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You did not reproduce it yourself.”</p><p>“I considered several excellent methods.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You don't know.”</p><p>“I know you.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>She continued.</p><p>“These are all things I need before I let you do more.”</p><p>“That is not an answer.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Do you think I can cast again?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>There.</p><p>Clean.</p><p>I nodded.</p><p>It hurt less than I expected.</p><p>Or differently.</p><p>“Do you think I cannot?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>“You asked.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“Would you rather I lie?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then stop looking offended.”</p><p>“I can be offended by reality.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>We sat.</p><p>After a moment I said, “If the old pattern keeps taking over, how do you tell whether I am learning anything new?”</p><p>“I don't, from one attempt.”</p><p>“I mean eventually.”</p><p>“Eventually I would want you to make a deliberate change that is not simply the first movement of something you already know.”</p><p>“That was the thumb.”</p><p>“That was the question.”</p><p>“And I failed it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So we repeat until I don't.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I glared.</p><p>She ignored it.</p><p>“Repetition can teach the thing we are trying to observe,” she said.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>There was the ugly part.</p><p>If I practiced the thumb enough under supervision, then eventually succeeding would not necessarily show that I could make an unfamiliar deliberate change. It could show that I had trained a new tiny form.</p><p>“That contaminates the test.”</p><p>“It changes the question.”</p><p>“Same problem.”</p><p>“No. Problems are allowed to change.”</p><p>I looked at the towel.</p><p>“So you might not repeat the same instruction.”</p><p>“I might.”</p><p>“Or you might change the target.”</p><p>“I might.”</p><p>“Different finger.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Left hand.”</p><p>“Not yet.”</p><p>That answer was immediate.</p><p>I noticed.</p><p>“Because of the missing-side question?”</p><p>“Because I do not need to add that question yet.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>Separate.</p><p>I liked her more when she refused to make the interesting connection.</p><p>“So the goal isn't to teach me thumb magic.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“That would be a terrible specialty.”</p><p>“It would.”</p><p>“Very limited market.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>We sat.</p><p>The bad chair supported me badly.</p><p>The towel sat folded beside the copper.</p><p>No magic.</p><p>No answer.</p><p>Still.</p><p>Something had changed.</p><p>Not in the thumb.</p><p>In the question.</p><p>Before the accident, magic competence had been a ladder.</p><p>Draw.</p><p>Shape.</p><p>Spell.</p><p>Better spell.</p><p>More efficient.</p><p>More power.</p><p>Different conditions.</p><p>Failure meant find the error and train it.</p><p>Now the uncertainty lived lower.</p><p>Could I even perform the thing at all?</p><p>My brain immediately tried to build probabilities from four draws and one failed localization.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Not because Hessa told me.</p><p>Because the numbers were garbage.</p><p>That was growth.</p><p>Or exhaustion.</p><p>“Can I train with Pessa today?”</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“Do you want to?”</p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>Closed it.</p><p>That was not the medical answer.</p><p>“You are becoming annoying.”</p><p>“I learned from you.”</p><p>“I asked whether you want to.”</p><p>I checked.</p><p>Body.</p><p>Right calf fine.</p><p>Hip fine.</p><p>Hands fine.</p><p>Residual limb baseline.</p><p>Thumb normal.</p><p>I could.</p><p>That was not want.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then don't.”</p><p>“What if I want to later?”</p><p>“Ask Pessa.”</p><p>“Medically?”</p><p>“I have no objection based on what I see today. If the thumb tingles again before then, reconsider.”</p><p>“Reconsider means?”</p><p>“Use judgment.”</p><p>“That is dangerously vague.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Are you sure?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>Hessa stood.</p><p>Appointment over.</p><p>At the door I stopped.</p><p>“Why did you ask if I wanted to train?”</p><p>She was cleaning the copper strip.</p><p>“Because you asked if you could.”</p><p>“That is not usually how medicine works.”</p><p>“It was not a medical question anymore.”</p><p>I thought about that.</p><p>Dangerous.</p><p>Useful.</p><p>Probably both.</p><p>“Day after tomorrow.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Assessment.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Possible shaping?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I groaned.</p><p>Nerin laughed from the outer room.</p><p>I left.</p><p>Outside, Carrow was wet.</p><p>Not raining.</p><p>It had rained while I was inside.</p><p>The stones shone dark.</p><p>Roof edges dripped.</p><p>A wagon had cut brown tracks through the street.</p><p>I stood under the awning for a moment.</p><p>No destination.</p><p>Pessa was possible.</p><p>Guild possible.</p><p>Jorren possible.</p><p>Lyssa possible if she was not working, which she probably was.</p><p>Home possible.</p><p>Food definitely possible.</p><p>I chose food first because uncertainty consumed calories.</p><p>This was medically established by hunger.</p><p>I bought a meat roll from a stall and ate it walking slowly toward the Guild.</p><p>My thumb did not tingle.</p><p>I refused to care.</p><p>This lasted until the second bite.</p><p>Then I cared.</p><p>Still no tingling.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>At the Guild, Merrin was at the front desk.</p><p>He looked up.</p><p>“Work?”</p><p>I almost said yes.</p><p>Not because I wanted work.</p><p>Because he had offered a category.</p><p>Work was easy to become.</p><p>Useful.</p><p>Requested.</p><p>Paid.</p><p>Contained.</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“Receipt comparison. Ground floor. Sitting. Maybe an hour.”</p><p>Perfect.</p><p>Exactly the kind of thing I could do.</p><p>I looked toward the side room.</p><p>Then at the meat roll.</p><p>Then back at Merrin.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He blinked once.</p><p>“All right.”</p><p>That was it.</p><p>No inquiry into my recovery.</p><p>No disappointment.</p><p>He turned to the next person.</p><p>I stood there holding food.</p><p>This had happened before.</p><p>Still weird.</p><p>Jorren was not there.</p><p>Alden was not there.</p><p>Pessa was somewhere beyond the yard, maybe.</p><p>No one required me.</p><p>I finished the meat roll.</p><p>Then I went upstairs.</p><p>Not lodging upstairs.</p><p>Guild upstairs.</p><p>Stopped.</p><p>No.</p><p>That was stupid.</p><p>I did not need to climb stairs to prove I could make an unproductive choice.</p><p>I turned around.</p><p>Ugly turn.</p><p>Worked.</p><p>Outside again.</p><p>A boy was floating folded paper boats down the gutter left by the rain.</p><p>Not a child I knew.</p><p>One boat caught under a cart rut.</p><p>He poked it with a stick.</p><p>Missed.</p><p>Poked again.</p><p>Freed it.</p><p>The boat spun once and continued.</p><p>I watched until it vanished under a bridge stone.</p><p>Then I walked home.</p><p>The keeper was repairing a loose hinge on the pantry door.</p><p>She had the pin out and was tapping it straight against the floor with a small hammer.</p><p>“Need help?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>I sat at the bottom table.</p><p>She hammered.</p><p>I watched.</p><p>After a while she said, “You have somewhere to be?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>Hammer.</p><p>Turn pin.</p><p>Hammer.</p><p>Check.</p><p>“Could be better.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“Door still opens.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She put the pin back.</p><p>The hinge squeaked.</p><p>She frowned.</p><p>Removed it again.</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Useful nothing?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She went back to work.</p><p>My thumb steps.</p><p>Slow.</p><p>Rail.</p><p>Crutches.</p><p>Right leg.</p><p>Pause at the landing.</p><p>No drama.</p><p>In my room, the repaired tavern chair sat by the window.</p><p>I sat.</p><p>Carrow outside.</p><p>Wet roofs.</p><p>People moving.</p><p>Someone shouted about onions in the distance.</p><p>Possibly the same seller.</p><p>Probably not.</p><p>The world contained many onion This was because I had become wise. Also because it rained. Mostly rain. Not Darrowmere rain. City rain. Steady enough to turn the street outside my lodging into brown water and make everyone with somewhere to be reconsider how urgently they needed to be there.</p><p>I stood under the front awning with my coat on and watched it. Dorrin Stone sold rocks. Rocks would survive. I went back upstairs. This felt excellent for almost twelve minutes. Then I started thinking. Sorted kestrin shale. Treatment. Testing. Rebatching.</p><p>If Arlo was right, consistency might be manufactured without improving the actual process much. Buy enough variation, measure after, throw away the wrong behavior. Or sell the wrong behavior somewhere else. Nothing was waste if there was another tolerance band. Future artificers did this constantly. Not specifically with sinkstone. With everything. Mana glass. Conductive salts. Barrier inks. Bone ash. Cheap cores.</p><p>The sophisticated version had specifications, batch certificates, testing houses, arguments about standards, bribes, fraud, and at least one murder I vaguely remembered because someone had substituted powdered shell for something expensive. Maybe. Different decade. Different city. Possibly not murder. Memory was helpful. I stopped. Rain. Rocks. Later. I checked my hands. Better again.</p><p>The left blister had dried flat. Right palm still tender under pressure. I wrapped neither. Normal use.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Dorrin Stone Sorted" decoding="async" height="169" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/041/v45_c41_dorrin-stone-sorted.png" width="549"/></figure><p>Hessa would approve. Probably. I did not need Hessa’s approval to possess hands. That sentence sounded defensive even internally. I ate another breakfast. Rain tax. By the time it weakened, the morning had become late enough that Dorrin Stone would definitely be open and early enough that Arlo could not accuse me of arriving after closing. Good range.</p><p>I took the regulator because Arlo had said bring it next time. Then realized I was not going to Arlo. I left it. The note looked absurdly ordinary. Gloves. A week ago I would have treated them as equipment. A month ago I would have treated them as an expense. Old Greg would have had somebody else buy six pairs and forgotten what they cost.</p><p>I wanted a pair that fit. That was different. Tomorrow I would stand under the north freight arch and watch something clear something else by inches. Then I would go to Arlo and see what was inside a regulator. After that, maybe food. Maybe Jorren. Maybe nothing.</p><p>There were enough tomorrows now that I had started arranging them. I left the notebook open long enough for the ink to dry. Then took it again. No reason. Put it down. Left. Came back. Put it in the bag. Fine. Dorrin Stone occupied a long yard north of the kiln district. I knew I was close before I saw the sign because the road became worse. Stone carts. Heavy wheels. Broken edges. Mud packed with pale grit.</p><p>The yard itself had a waist-high wall and an open gate wide enough for two carts if neither driver valued the paint.</p><p>A board above it read:</p><p>DORRIN STONE</p><p>CUT. BROKEN. SORTED. DELIVERED.</p><p>Promising. Inside were rocks. A lot of rocks. This should not have surprised me. It did. Blocks stacked by size. Broken stone in bins. Pale limestone. Dark slate. Red aggregate. Gray shale. White chips. Sand under canvas.</p><p>Three workers moved a slab using rollers and language that would have improved Mara’s drink shop. Nobody looked magical. Good. I stood out of the way. A cart came through behind me. I moved farther out of the way. A woman carrying a slate board saw me.</p><p>“You buying?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Kestrin shale.”</p><p>She pointed without stopping.</p><p>“Back left.”</p><p>I followed the direction. Three bins. One mostly fist-sized chunks. One smaller broken pieces. One dark fine aggregate.</p><p>Labels:</p><p>KES RAW</p><p>KES SORT</p><p>KES FINES</p><p>Easy. I looked. Raw varied wildly. Color. Veins. Porosity. Some almost smooth. Some crumbly. Sorted looked less variable. Not identical. Closer. A man with a shovel said, “Don’t climb in.”</p><p>“I wasn’t.”</p><p>He pointed at the bin edge.</p><p>“Then stay on this side.”</p><p>“I need to ask about processed material.”</p><p>“Office.”</p><p>He pointed. I went to the office. It was not an office. It was a roof with three walls, a counter, two stools, and enough paper to prove civilization had made a mistake. An older woman sat behind the counter with silver hair braided down her back. She was eating an apple and writing numbers. I waited. She finished the number. Not the apple.</p><p>“Yes?”</p><p>“I’m looking for processed kestrin shale.”</p><p>“What process?”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Mana suppression.”</p><p>She bit the apple.</p><p>“Mild?”</p><p>“Potentially.”</p><p>“Packing?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Ward bed?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Heat sink?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>She stopped chewing.</p><p>“What are you making?”</p><p>“I don’t know yet.”</p><p>“Then you don’t know what you’re buying.”</p><p>Correct.</p><p>“I’m asking who processes it.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because Arlo Arwick said you might know.”</p><p>Dorrin stopped with the apple halfway to her mouth. Recognition, not suspicion.</p><p>“Arlo still owes for two bins.”</p><p>Interesting. Not my business.</p><p>“Does he?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I’ll tell him.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because he knows.”</p><p>Fair. She finished chewing.</p><p>“I’m Dorrin,” she said.</p><p>Person. Company. Of course.</p><p>“Greg,” I said.</p><p>“I know,” Dorrin said.</p><p>I waited. She pointed at my bag.</p><p>“Arlo’s regulator boy.”</p><p>Hostile network.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What do you want with kestrin?”</p><p>“I saw a processed batch with unusually consistent magical behavior.”</p><p>True.</p><p>“Whose?”</p><p>“Not mine to say.”</p><p>“Then I can’t tell you if it’s unusual.”</p><p>Also true.</p><p>“I’m not asking you to identify it.”</p><p>“You’re asking me to identify who could make it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is identifying it with extra steps.”</p><p>I liked her. Annoying.</p><p>“I’m asking generally.”</p><p>“Generally, lots.”</p><p>“How lots?”</p><p>She looked toward the yard.</p><p>“Raw kestrin?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Comes from six quarries if you count the bad one.”</p><p>“Which is the bad one?”</p><p>“All of them depending what you need.”</p><p>Arlo had relatives everywhere.</p><p>“Who sorts?”</p><p>“We do. Two other yards. Some processors buy raw and sort themselves.”</p><p>“By what?”</p><p>“Color. fracture. density if someone pays. Vein. grain. Sometimes reaction.”</p><p>“Mana reaction?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>She stared at me.</p><p>“Test it.”</p><p>“With?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>I smiled. She did not.</p><p>“Low line?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Contact?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Heat first?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Who pays for reaction sorting?”</p><p>“People who need it.”</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>There. Limit.</p><p>“Customer privacy?”</p><p>“Customer boredom. Mine.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“How much does reaction sorting add?”</p><p>“What grade?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“What tolerance?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“What size?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Then somewhere between one copper and too much.”</p><p>Useful. Not numerical. I looked back toward the bins.</p><p>“Do you process here?”</p><p>“Break. wash. sort. Some heat drying. No active treatment.”</p><p>“So no soaking.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“No mana exposure.”</p><p>“Not intentionally.”</p><p>“No controlled heating beyond drying.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Who does active treatment?”</p><p>“Kilns. Ward shops. Two chemical yards.”</p><p>“Names?”</p><p>She looked at me. I waited. This was public trade information. Probably. She could still say no.</p><p>“Buying?”</p><p>“Questions.”</p><p>“That’s not buying.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“What is the cheapest amount of sorted kestrin you sell?”</p><p>She pointed at a small sack under the counter.</p><p>“One copper.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Enough to make you regret carrying it.”</p><p>I bought it. Transactional clarity. She put my copper in a box.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Now you are a customer.”</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>“Who treats for suppression?”</p><p>“Suppression specifically?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Bale Ward Supply sells treated bed stone. Kett’s Kiln does heat work for three shops. Varo Chemical does salt treatment, but I don’t know if they sell direct.”</p><p>Three. My brain expanded. Bale. Kett. Varo. Which sorts before? Which tests after? Which rebatches? Which buys from Dorrin? Which might sell to North Quay? Which works with Silas Marris? No. Dorrin tapped the one-copper sack with two fingers.</p><p>“You bought one sack and I gave you three names.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Start with those.”</p><p>“I was going to ask for more.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>I laughed. She bit the apple again.</p><p>“Which would you ask first?”</p><p>I said it before thinking.</p><p>“Bale.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Finished product.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Why not Kett?”</p><p>“Processing without specification tells me less.”</p><p>Another nod.</p><p>“Why not Varo?”</p><p>“Could be upstream of several products.”</p><p>She looked almost interested.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Bale first.”</p><p>That was not evidence. It was a trade person’s judgment. Useful.</p><p>“Do they make their own?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Some?”</p><p>“Some bought.”</p><p>“From?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Right. I looked at the sack I had purchased.</p><p>“Is this reaction sorted?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then what did I buy?”</p><p>“Size and visible quality.”</p><p>“What visible quality?”</p><p>“Less crumbly. Lower obvious vein. Fairly even pieces.”</p><p>“Why would Arlo buy it?”</p><p>“He buys cheaper.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“What does he buy?”</p><p>“Raw broken.”</p><p>“Because he can tolerate variation?”</p><p>“Because he is cheap.”</p><p>Both could be true.</p><p>“Does he owe you for two bins of raw broken?”</p><p>Dorrin stared.</p><p>“Not your business.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Good. A worker came to the counter.</p><p>“North cart wants the pale cut,” he said.</p><p>Dorrin said, “Second stack, not first. First is Brin order.” The worker left. Her attention moved with him. Conversation over. I could feel it. One more question. No. I picked up the sack. Heavy. Not terrible. Maybe twenty pounds. My hands noticed. I shifted it against my hip. Dorrin saw.</p><p>“Carry from bottom.”</p><p>I adjusted. Better.</p><p>“Thanks.”</p><p>She had already returned to numbers. I left. The rain had stopped completely. The yard smelled like wet stone. I stood outside with one copper less and twenty pounds of material I did not need. This was familiar. Young Greg behavior. Buy thing because curiosity. Carry thing because pride. Discover later that thing had nowhere to go. Old Greg had improved. Mostly by having other people carry things.</p><p>I walked. Bale Ward Supply was east. I knew roughly where. Could go now. I had three names. Dorrin had explicitly recommended Bale first. Efficient. Logical. I turned east. Then the sack shifted. My right palm hurt. Not badly. Enough. I stopped.</p><p>Why was I carrying twenty pounds of shale to a ward shop? No reason. Could leave it home. Could give it Arlo. Could test it later. Could ask Dorrin to deliver. Too late. I kept walking. Young Greg. Definitely. At the next corner someone shouted my name. Not Alden. Not Jorren. Nessa. She stood under a striped awning with the laundry basket.</p><p>Food basket. Probably.</p><p>“You look stupid,” Nessa said.</p><p>“I am carrying rocks,” I said.</p><p>“I can see,” Nessa said.</p><p>“That is why,” I said.</p><p>She looked at the sack.</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“Kestrin shale.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Research.”</p><p>“Worse.”</p><p>She had three wrapped parcels in the basket and a bundle of green onions sticking out beneath a cloth.</p><p>“Where’s Jorren?”</p><p>“Working.”</p><p>“You know?”</p><p>“He has a job.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You don’t?”</p><p>“I have several.”</p><p>“Then why rocks?”</p><p>Excellent question.</p><p>“I bought them.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/041/Ch041_Fast-Coverage-003-B03.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 41." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“That wasn’t the question.”</p><p>I liked her less when she was accurate. She handed a parcel to a man who approached from the side. He gave her two copper. No discussion. Routine.</p><p>“Chicken?” I asked.</p><p>“Pork.”</p><p>“Good?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Honest.”</p><p>“Two copper.”</p><p>“I ate.”</p><p>“Then don’t buy.”</p><p>Again. Simple.</p><p>“What are you doing?” I asked.</p><p>“Selling food.”</p><p>“After?”</p><p>“Taking this basket back before my sister decides it belongs to me permanently.”</p><p>“Does she still do laundry?”</p><p>Nessa looked at me.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Right. People did not change professions because I had met them once.</p><p>“Where are you going with the rocks?”</p><p>“Bale Ward Supply.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“They sell treated bed stone.”</p><p>She waited. I had answered the surface question. Apparently not enough.</p><p>“For mana suppression.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Curiosity.”</p><p>“There.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“That’s the answer.”</p><p>She shifted the basket.</p><p>“You make everything sound like work.”</p><p>I looked at the sack.</p><p>“It is work.”</p><p>“Are you paid?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then maybe not.”</p><p>She left. No invitation. No lesson. Just basket. I continued east. Her sentence followed. Are you paid? Bad standard. Arlo was not paid to improve his regulator until someone bought it. Edrin was paid to investigate evidence. I was not paid to care.</p><p>Old Greg had spent enormous portions of his life on unpaid curiosity. Some became power. Some became disasters. Some became nothing. Still worth doing. Maybe. Bale Ward Supply had a proper sign. Blue-painted letters. Clean windows. Shelves visible inside. Much more respectable than Arlo. Suspicious. I entered with the sack. A bell rang.</p><p>A young man behind the counter looked at the sack, then at me.</p><p>“We sell that.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then why bring your own?”</p><p>Good start.</p><p>“I have questions.”</p><p>He sighed. Dorrin had prepared me.</p><p>“Can I buy something first?”</p><p>His expression improved.</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“What is the cheapest treated kestrin you sell?”</p><p>He pointed at a tray of gray pellets.</p><p>“Bed fill. Three copper a scoop.”</p><p>“How much is a scoop?”</p><p>He showed me. Small. Maybe two pounds. Dorrin’s twenty pounds for one copper. Processing and selection multiplied price quickly.</p><p>“Suppression grade?”</p><p>“Basic.”</p><p>“Consistency?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“For what?”</p><p>There it was again.</p><p>“I’m comparing manufacturing approaches.”</p><p>“Are you a maker?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Guild?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Student?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Of?”</p><p>“Magic.”</p><p>“That is not a trade.”</p><p>Hessa would like him.</p><p>“I’m Greg.”</p><p>He paused.</p><p>“Barrier Greg?”</p><p>No.</p><p>“Why does everyone call me things?”</p><p>He shrugged.</p><p>“Alden talks.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Do you know Alden?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Worse.</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“Customer mentioned him.”</p><p>The city was becoming dangerous. I pointed at the tray.</p><p>“Do you make this?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Who does?”</p><p>“Supplier.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Customer privacy. Actual this time.</p><p>“Can you tell me how it is specified?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Good. He reached beneath the counter and produced a card. Not secret. Sales information.</p><p>BASIC BED KESTRIN</p><p>LOW REACTIVITY VARIANCE</p><p>DRY USE</p><p>NO HIGH-HEAT GUARANTEE</p><p>REPLACE AFTER HEAVY EXPOSURE</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>“Low variance measured how?”</p><p>“House test.”</p><p>“What test?”</p><p>“Not mine.”</p><p>“Who knows?”</p><p>“Master.”</p><p>“Here?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>I wanted to ask where. No.</p><p>“What does heavy exposure mean?”</p><p>“Depends on application.”</p><p>I laughed. He looked confused.</p><p>“Sorry.”</p><p>“Do you want a scoop?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Why? Because I was stupid. Three copper. I paid. Now I had twenty-two pounds of kestrin shale. Excellent. He put the treated pellets in a paper packet. I held one through the paper. Similar size to seized material? Maybe. Could not compare directly. Do not invent.</p><p>“Can I ask who supplies if I’m not asking about a customer?”</p><p>“You are asking about our supplier.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Do you sort after receiving?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>There.</p><p>“What for?”</p><p>“Broken pieces. Color. Bad surface. Some batches get line checked.”</p><p>“Every piece?”</p><p>He laughed.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Sample?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>I smiled again. He became concerned.</p><p>“Are you all right?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Do you ever rebatch?”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Combine lots after testing to hit a narrower behavior range.”</p><p>He frowned.</p><p>“Master might.”</p><p>Not his knowledge. Stop.</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>He nodded, relieved. I left. Two places. One raw supplier. One retail ward supplier. No Silas Marris. No Darrowmere. No suspicious reaction. No secret symbol. No one ran when I said kestrin. Good. I had also spent four copper. All of the millrace money. One copper at Dorrin. Three at Bale. I stopped in the street. Four copper. Half a day in cold water.</p><p>Goat. Reeds. Blisters. Mud. Converted into rocks. I laughed. A woman carrying folded cloth walked around me. Reasonable. Old Greg would have called this investment. Young Greg would have called it buying interesting things. Present Greg had no defense. I shifted the sack again. Heavy. I should have taken it home before Bale. Obviously. I started back. Halfway, I passed a delivery cart marked DORRIN STONE.</p><p>I stopped. The driver stopped because I was staring.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>He drove on. Delivery. The sign had literally said delivered. I had carried twenty pounds across the city because I had failed to read the fourth word. Excellent. At my lodging, the keeper saw the sack.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“No rocks upstairs.”</p><p>“It is one sack.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Last tenant cracked a floor tile.”</p><p>“With twenty pounds?”</p><p>“With stupidity.”</p><p>Different load. Same mechanism.</p><p>“Where can I put it?”</p><p>She pointed behind the desk.</p><p>“Until tomorrow.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“One copper.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“For storage?”</p><p>“For rocks.”</p><p>“That is not a category.”</p><p>“It is now.”</p><p>I paid. Five copper spent. The millrace had become negative one. This was getting better. I carried the small treated packet upstairs. Set it on the desk. Did not test it. I did not have Edrin’s equipment. I could make a tiny mana line. No. That would be deliberate testing. Hessa had allowed small utility, not repeated load experiments. Also uncontrolled comparison would tell me almost nothing.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I wrote:</p><p>DORRIN STONE</p><p>raw / sorted / fines sort by visible quality, size, sometimes density, grain, reaction does not actively treat Bale Ward Supply Kett’s Kiln Varo Chemical Dorrin recommends Bale first for finished suppression product</p><p>BALE</p><p>basic bed kestrin low reactivity variance dry use no high-heat guarantee replace after heavy exposure supplier undisclosed some receiving inspection some batches line checked rebatching unknown</p><p>Then:</p><p>SPENT 5 COPPER TO LEARN ROCKS ARE HEAVY.</p><p>Accurate. I sat back. The manufacturing chain had not narrowed. It had widened. Quarries. Stone yards. Sorters. Kilns. Chemical treatment. Ward suppliers. Testing. Retail. Potential rebatching. Delivery. Customers. Any unusually consistent batch could have become consistent at several points. Or multiple. Good. Harder. Better. I thought of Silas Marris. Trading company. Moves goods. Magical goods sometimes. Could sit anywhere in that chain without making anything.</p><p>Could own finished product. Could contract processing. Could simply buy. No evidence. Leave it. I thought of Darrowmere. Altered kestrin. Different inclusions. Different behavior. Could enter from another branch entirely. Leave it. I thought of Bale’s master arriving tomorrow. Could go back. Ask about house test. Supplier maybe still private. Kett’s Kiln. Varo Chemical. Three directions. Six. Nine. Face. No one was there to tell me.</p><p>I could still feel it. I closed the notebook. Outside, someone shouted about a missing dog. A cart wheel hit a pothole. The lodging keeper argued with a delivery boy. My hands did not hurt much anymore. My channels were quiet. I had rocks downstairs costing rent. Tomorrow I could ask better questions.</p><p>Tonight I had to figure out how to stop owning twenty pounds of shale. That was a different problem. Probably Arlo.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="040.html">← Chapter 32</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="042.html">Chapter 34 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/104.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 82: The Adviser — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 82</div><h1>THE ADVISER</h1></header><article class="prose"><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg standing alone above a broad valley and city beyond, in a reflective pause." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/104/Ch104_Valley-Overlook-Reflection.png"/></figure><p>My thumb did not tingle in the morning.</p><p>This was disappointing.</p><p>Not medically.</p><p>Medically, it was excellent.</p><p>Scientifically, it was almost useless.</p><p>Emotionally, I wanted the thumb to do something interesting and was mature enough not to admit this to Hessa.</p><p>I wrote:</p><p>No tingling overnight. None on waking. Right hand normal.</p><p>Then I stopped.</p><p>I had briefly considered adding:</p><p>Tested by touching thumb to each fingertip.</p><p>I had not done that as a test.</p><p>I had buttoned my shirt.</p><p>This distinction mattered.</p><p>The dark green shirt had buttons.</p><p>Therefore ordinary dressing had become evidence.</p><p>Dangerous.</p><p>I closed the notebook.</p><p>Breakfast was porridge.</p><p>The keeper had put dried apple in it, which improved porridge by giving the mouth occasional reasons to continue.</p><p>I ate two bowls.</p><p>My right calf still remembered Pessa but had downgraded its complaint to background commentary. Hip similar. Residual limb baseline. Hands fine.</p><p>I had no Hessa appointment.</p><p>I could ask Pessa to train.</p><p>I wanted to.</p><p>I also wanted to tell Jorren that I had shaped mana badly.</p><p>These wants competed for perhaps twelve seconds.</p><p>Jorren won because he would be more impressed.</p><p>This was not true.</p><p>That was why it was funny.</p><p>I found him at the Guild.</p><p>He was arguing with Alden about boots.</p><p>Not metaphorically.</p><p>Actual boots.</p><p>Alden had one foot on a bench and was pulling the laces tight enough to restrict future generations.</p><p>Jorren stood over him.</p><p>“That is too tight.”</p><p>“It is not.”</p><p>“Your foot is changing color.”</p><p>“It is not.”</p><p>“It looks frightened.”</p><p>“Feet cannot look frightened.”</p><p>“That one can.”</p><p>Alden saw me.</p><p>“Tell him.”</p><p>I looked at the boot.</p><p>“What am I telling him?”</p><p>“That it's fine.”</p><p>Jorren said, “That he's strangling his foot.”</p><p>“I am not qualified.”</p><p>“You have a foot,” Alden said.</p><p>“One.”</p><p>Alden lowered his head.</p><p>Jorren closed his eyes.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>Alden said, “I walked into that.”</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>“Fuck.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Jorren pointed at me.</p><p>“You did that on purpose.”</p><p>“I answered accurately.”</p><p>“Monster.”</p><p>Alden loosened the boot.</p><p>“Pessa says new boots always feel wrong.”</p><p>“That does not mean remove circulation,” Jorren said.</p><p>“They're not new.”</p><p>“Then why are we doing this?”</p><p>“The heel slips.”</p><p>“Ah.”</p><p>That was different.</p><p>I leaned my crutches against the bench long enough to sit.</p><p>Alden demonstrated by standing and taking three steps.</p><p>The heel lifted.</p><p>Not much.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>“Sock?” I asked.</p><p>“Same socks.”</p><p>“Laces?”</p><p>“Same.”</p><p>“Boot stretched?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>Jorren said, “His foot shrank.”</p><p>“My foot did not shrink.”</p><p>“Have you been measuring it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then we cannot rule out spontaneous foot reduction.”</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>“Why are you friends with him?”</p><p>“I was lonely.”</p><p>Jorren put a hand over his heart.</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>This was going well.</p><p>Alden sat again and retied the boot differently.</p><p>I watched.</p><p>Then remembered why I had come.</p><p>“I shaped mana.”</p><p>Jorren said, “Good.”</p><p>There it was.</p><p>Exactly.</p><p>I hated him.</p><p>Alden's head snapped up.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>“Wait. Actually?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Yesterday.”</p><p>“What did you do?”</p><p>“I failed to move mana into my thumb.”</p><p>Silence.</p><p>Jorren frowned.</p><p>“That is less impressive.”</p><p>“Hessa phrased it that way too.”</p><p>Alden sat completely still.</p><p>“You shaped?”</p><p>“Altered.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Hessa says altered.”</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“It means I performed a minimal supervised draw, then deliberately attempted to localize a very small amount into the pad of my right thumb.”</p><p>Jorren looked at my thumb.</p><p>I put it in my lap.</p><p>He grinned.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You hid it.”</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“You did.”</p><p>“You looked at it.”</p><p>“Because you said thumb.”</p><p>“That does not give you jurisdiction.”</p><p>Alden said, “Did it work?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“The mana moved broadly into my palm and wrist. My wrist rotated. Forearm engaged. It felt like the beginning of Barrier.”</p><p>Alden's face changed.</p><p>He understood that.</p><p>Not the medical caution.</p><p>The casting.</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“Possibly. Hessa will not confirm it from one attempt.”</p><p>“But you felt it.”</p><p>“I felt something I recognized as the beginning of the setup.”</p><p>“That is Barrier.”</p><p>“Apparently not in a court of Hessa.”</p><p>Jorren leaned against the table.</p><p>“Did anything come out?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did you make a shield?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did you explode?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then this is a disappointing story.”</p><p>“I shaped mana.”</p><p>“You failed your thumb.”</p><p>“I altered mana.”</p><p>“You failed your thumb.”</p><p>Alden was still staring.</p><p>“Can you do it again?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Can't or aren't allowed?”</p><p>“Not allowed.”</p><p>“Could you?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>That quieted him.</p><p>Good question.</p><p>I did not know.</p><p>The answer made the success feel smaller and larger at the same time.</p><p>Jorren tapped his own thumb against the table.</p><p>“Does it hurt?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It tingled yesterday.”</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He tapped again.</p><p>I watched.</p><p>He noticed.</p><p>“Want to touch it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Want me to move mana into it?”</p><p>“You cannot.”</p><p>“Neither can you.”</p><p>Alden laughed so hard he had to sit back down.</p><p>I stared at Jorren.</p><p>“That was good.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“I dislike you.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>Alden said, “When can you try again?”</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>“Shaping?”</p><p>“Assessment. Probably same instruction. Maybe.”</p><p>“Can I watch?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You didn't ask Hessa.”</p><p>“I am not asking Hessa.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>Because I did not want Alden there.</p><p>The answer arrived immediately.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>Not because he was annoying.</p><p>He was.</p><p>Not because it was private.</p><p>Maybe partly.</p><p>Mostly because Hessa's room was one of the few places where my competence was allowed to be tiny without becoming social.</p><p>A failed thumb was funny with Jorren afterward.</p><p>During?</p><p>No.</p><p>“I don't want you there.”</p><p>Alden blinked.</p><p>Then shrugged.</p><p>“All right.”</p><p>That easy.</p><p>No injury.</p><p>No argument.</p><p>I had spent more effort preparing the refusal than he spent receiving it.</p><p>Jorren watched me.</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He did not say anything.</p><p>Good friend.</p><p>Terrible person.</p><p>Alden stood and tested the boot again.</p><p>Heel still slipped.</p><p>“Still wrong.”</p><p>Jorren pointed.</p><p>“See?”</p><p>“It's better.”</p><p>“It is less wrong.”</p><p>“That is better.”</p><p>I looked at the boot.</p><p>“Is the problem the boot or the lacing?”</p><p>Alden said, “Boot.”</p><p>Jorren said, “Foot.”</p><p>I said, “Excellent. We have learned nothing.”</p><p>Alden kicked the bench.</p><p>Not hard.</p><p>“Pessa told me to fix it before tomorrow.”</p><p>That mattered.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because it rubbed yesterday.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Heel.”</p><p>“Skin broken?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then fix the boot.”</p><p>“I am trying.”</p><p>Jorren said, “He has been trying for twenty minutes.”</p><p>“I have been here seven.”</p><p>“It has felt like twenty.”</p><p>Alden pulled the boot off.</p><p>The heel inside was visibly worn smoother than the other.</p><p>There.</p><p>Actual evidence.</p><p>Jorren picked it up.</p><p>“Leather's gone soft.”</p><p>Alden took it back.</p><p>“Can it be fixed?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>They both looked at me.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I am not becoming the boot expert because I noticed the boot.”</p><p>Jorren said, “You used to know leather.”</p><p>“I knew enough leather to make poor decisions confidently.”</p><p>“You had boots.”</p><p>“I had two.”</p><p>Alden glanced down.</p><p>Then up.</p><p>He did not apologize.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I appreciated that too.</p><p>“Tam?” he asked.</p><p>I thought of my damaged left boot and the salvage leather Tam still had.</p><p>“Tam works leather.”</p><p>“Would he look?”</p><p>“Probably if you pay him.”</p><p>Jorren said, “Solved.”</p><p>“No. Referred.”</p><p>“Same thing if you're lazy.”</p><p>Alden put on his other boot and carried the bad one.</p><p>“I'll go.”</p><p>“You have training?” I asked.</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“Pessa?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“You coming?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I had not decided until I said it.</p><p>That was interesting too.</p><p>I could have asked Pessa.</p><p>Hessa had no medical objection.</p><p>My body was baseline.</p><p>Pessa might have trained me.</p><p>But I had trained two days ago.</p><p>I had shaped yesterday.</p><p>Tomorrow Hessa again.</p><p>I did not want every open day assigned to improvement.</p><p>This was suspiciously healthy thinking.</p><p>I rejected it on principle.</p><p>“I have things to do.”</p><p>Jorren said, “Do you?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Alden laughed.</p><p>Then left with the boot under his arm.</p><p>Jorren waited until he was out the door.</p><p>“So.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I didn't say anything.”</p><p>“You were going to.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Show me your thumb.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He held out his hand.</p><p>I stared at it.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Thumb.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I want to see the magical thumb.”</p><p>“It looks like a thumb.”</p><p>“I have never seen a magical one.”</p><p>“It is not magical.”</p><p>“It had mana in it.”</p><p>“Poorly.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>I put my right hand on the table.</p><p>He examined it with absurd seriousness.</p><p>Turned his head.</p><p>Leaned closer.</p><p>Did not touch.</p><p>“Remarkable.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>“Strong shape.”</p><p>“It is a thumb.”</p><p>“Good color.”</p><p>“Jorren.”</p><p>“Five stars.”</p><p>I pulled my hand back.</p><p>He laughed.</p><p>Then, without transition:</p><p>“Come help me buy a knife.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I don't know what kind of knife.”</p><p>“Neither do I.”</p><p>“That makes me less useful.”</p><p>“You are not being hired.”</p><p>“What is it for?”</p><p>“Food.”</p><p>“You have a knife.”</p><p>“Mine is terrible.”</p><p>“You cut LIAR pepper stew with it.”</p><p>“That was a spoon.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>He pushed away from the table.</p><p>“Come.”</p><p>I considered Pessa again.</p><p>Not as obligation.</p><p>As option.</p><p>Then Jorren.</p><p>“Why me?”</p><p>“Because Alden will buy the largest one.”</p><p>“That is true.”</p><p>“Octavia will tell me exactly what freight cooks use and then make me feel stupid.”</p><p>“Also plausible.”</p><p>“Nessa will sell me one from under the counter and I don't want to know why she has it.”</p><p>I stood.</p><p>“Lyssa?”</p><p>“At work.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“I saw her this morning.”</p><p>Independent schedules.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>“Sevren?”</p><p>“Road.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“This is not agreement.”</p><p>“You stood up.”</p><p>“That is not agreement.”</p><p>“It is with you.”</p><p>I hated that Pessa had spread.</p><p>We went to the market.</p><p>Jorren did not need a knife.</p><p>This became clear at the third stall.</p><p>He wanted a knife.</p><p>Different category.</p><p>His current knife cut food.</p><p>It was small, plain, and apparently offended him aesthetically.</p><p>“You want a nicer knife.”</p><p>“I want one that feels good.”</p><p>“That is not the same as needing one.”</p><p>“I never said need.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>There.</p><p>He had me.</p><p>I had recently purchased a shirt because I liked it.</p><p>I had no standing to prosecute desire.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“I did not approve.”</p><p>“You stopped objecting.”</p><p>“Different.”</p><p>He picked up a narrow kitchen knife with a dark wooden handle.</p><p>The seller remained unnamed because I had learned that not every human being required permanent storage in my head.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img balance.</p><p>Not by waving it.</p><p>Good.</p><p>He held it.</p><p>Turned it.</p><p>Set it down.</p><p>Picked up another.</p><p>“What are you looking for?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“That is reassuring.”</p><p>“I'll know.”</p><p>This was the kind of statement I distrusted professionally and understood personally.</p><p>He tried six.</p><p>Rejected two immediately.</p><p>Kept returning to the dark-handled one.</p><p>“Buy that one.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You keep picking it up.”</p><p>“That doesn't mean it's best.”</p><p>“You are buying a food knife, not appointing a magistrate.”</p><p>“What if the other one is better?”</p><p>“Better how?”</p><p>He looked at the other one.</p><p>“Steel.”</p><p>“Do you know that?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Edge?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Handle?”</p><p>“Dark one.”</p><p>“Weight?”</p><p>“Dark one.”</p><p>“Price?”</p><p>He asked.</p><p>The dark one cost more.</p><p>Not catastrophically.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>Jorren frowned.</p><p>“There.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Now you have an actual tradeoff.”</p><p>“I liked it better before money.”</p><p>“Most things are improved by excluding price.”</p><p>He put both knives down.</p><p>We walked to another stall.</p><p>Then another.</p><p>He tried more.</p><p>None displaced the dark-handled knife in his head.</p><p>I could tell because he compared every handle to it without saying so.</p><p>I said nothing.</p><p>Personal record.</p><p>At the fourth stall, my right thumb tingled.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Not dramatic.</p><p>Same mild sensation.</p><p>Pad and side of thumb.</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>I did not squeeze it.</p><p>Did not touch fingertips.</p><p>Did not flex repeatedly.</p><p>I simply noticed.</p><p>Jorren had picked up a knife.</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Thumb.”</p><p>His face lost the joke.</p><p>“Tingling?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Bad?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“I am fine.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>There was a crate beside the stall.</p><p>I sat.</p><p>Annoying when friends became reasonable.</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>“Just started.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Numb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You sound like Hessa.”</p><p>“I listened.”</p><p>That shut me up.</p><p>We waited.</p><p>The tingling faded.</p><p>Perhaps a minute.</p><p>Perhaps less.</p><p>I did not time it.</p><p>This was heroic.</p><p>“Gone.”</p><p>Jorren looked at my hand.</p><p>“Still buying knife.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You're not going to Hessa?”</p><p>“She said report if it returns.”</p><p>“That sounds like going to Hessa.”</p><p>“It does.”</p><p>“You can report after the knife.”</p><p>He stared.</p><p>I reconsidered.</p><p>“No. You're right.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“That was unpleasant.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>We turned back.</p><p>I did not feel ill.</p><p>No more plausible.</p><p>Or shaping aftereffect.</p><p>Or attention.</p><p>Or nothing.</p><p>I refused to rank them.</p><p>This was getting absurd.</p><p>Hessa was not pleased to see me.</p><p>Not thumb.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Hand.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Grip.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Temperature.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>No tingling now.</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>“I did not time it.”</p><p>She looked pleased.</p><p>This was insulting.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I knew you'd say that.”</p><p>“What were you doing?”</p><p>“Walking through the market with Jorren.”</p><p>“Crutches?”</p><p>“No, Hessa. I flew.”</p><p>She stared.</p><p>“Yes. Crutches.”</p><p>“Any unusual grip?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Carrying anything?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Right hand dominant on crutch?”</p><p>“Not exclusively. Both.”</p><p>“Any wrist pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Forearm?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>“Does this change tomorrow?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I hated the word reduced.</p><p>Not disappeared.</p><p>Reduced.</p><p>Jorren leaned against the wall behind me.</p><p>Hessa looked at him.</p><p>“You are?”</p><p>“Jorren.”</p><p>“I know who you are.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>“He's the knife problem,” I said.</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“What knife problem?”</p><p>“No problem.”</p><p>Jorren said, “I was buying a knife.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Food.”</p><p>Hessa blinked.</p><p>I watched her decide not to ask.</p><p>Professional excellence.</p><p>She pointed at me.</p><p>“If the tingling returns again today, come back.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If it returns and persists, come back.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If you get numbness, weakness, coldness, pain, or trouble gripping, come back.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No rehearsal.”</p><p>“I won't.”</p><p>She looked at Jorren.</p><p>“If he starts experimenting, stop him.”</p><p>Jorren brightened.</p><p>“I have authority?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Damn.”</p><p>“You have hands.”</p><p>“So does he.”</p><p>“Yes, but apparently his are busy.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>Hessa did not.</p><p>We left.</p><p>Outside, Jorren said, “I like her.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“She gave me a civilization.</p><p>We walked back toward the Guild.</p><p>My thumb did not tingle.</p><p>I did not check it.</p><p>Jorren carried the knife like he had acquired a minor title.</p><p>“Worth it?” I
