- `chapters/383.html:404`: <p>No one knew Hessa would kill me verbally if I called moving light mana without evidence.</p>
- `chapters/038.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 32: The Patient — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 32</div><h1>THE PATIENT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The four copper lasted until dinner. This was not because I spent four copper. I spent one. The other three remained in my pocket while I sat on the edge of my bed and stared at my hands. Blisters. Two on the right. One on the left. Small. Ordinary. Embarrassing.</p><p>I had once held Barriers against things that could break stone. Now a hooked pole had injured me. Not badly. Still. I pressed the skin beside the largest blister. Pain. Useful. I stopped. Testing pain by making pain was stupid. Hessa would have said so. Jorren would have laughed first.</p><p>Alden would have asked whether I was trying to lose a fight to my own palm. Berren would have said the blister was probably afraid of him. Too many people had acquired voices in my head. That seemed unhealthy. I washed. The water turned gray. Mud had reached places mud should not reach. My ribs ached when I bent. Shoulders worse. Forearms worse than shoulders.</p><p>Right calf tight. No channel pain. No pressure behind the eyes. No heat. Good. One clean Barrier. Very small. Exactly enough. I wanted to cast another. Not because I needed one. Because I could. This was the problem with getting permission. Before permission, restraint had structure. After permission, there was choice. Annoying. The regulator sat on the desk. Mechanical test. Water. No mana.</p><p>Useful. I looked at the washbasin. Then my hands.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Hands" decoding="async" height="296" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/038/v45_c38_hands.png" width="274"/></figure><p>Then the bed. The bed won. I woke after dark. Not planned. Still dressed. One boot on. One boot off. Face against the blanket. My neck hurt. Young body recovered quickly if given the chance. It also demanded the chance with violence. I sat up. Hunger. Again. Nineteen was mostly hunger pretending to be a personality. I found bread. Hard. Cheese. Harder.</p><p>Ate both. No cooking. No strategy. The room had cooled. Street noise below had thinned to occasional carts and arguments. I took the regulator from the desk. Arlo had asked for use. Mechanical. Flow medium. Orientation. Duration. Temperature if relevant. External vibration. I could test with wash water. I found a cup. Then stopped. Dirty water. No. Fresh. I went downstairs. The lodging keeper was counting coins behind the front desk.</p><p>She looked at the cup.</p><p>“Water?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Pump.”</p><p>“Outside?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It’s dark.”</p><p>She looked at me. I went outside. The public pump stood thirty paces away. Three people were there. A woman filling two buckets. A boy with a jug. An old man rinsing something that looked like turnips. Turnips. Jorren. I smiled. The old man saw.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>He moved his turnips away from me. Reasonable. I waited. No urgency. The woman finished first. The boy spilled half his jug and started again. I could have helped. Did not. He knew how. Eventually my turn. I filled the cup. Then another.</p><p>Back upstairs, I fitted the regulator between a small funnel and a narrow tube improvised from a cleaned quill shaft. Ugly. Functional. First test. Vertical. Water. Room temperature. No vibration. The flow was too fast to show much. I adjusted. Slower. Better. The regulator held. Not perfectly. Small pulses. Less than the first design. I wrote it down. Second test. Tilted. Flow changed.</p><p>Not much. Interesting. Third. Horizontal. Worse. I frowned. Then remembered Arlo’s face. Too good. No. Different. I tapped the table lightly. Flow fluttered. Stopped. Fluttered again. External vibration. There. Useful. Not magic. Simple. I recorded it. Then I wanted to know whether thicker liquid changed behavior. Oil. No. Arlo said bad. Could test anyway. Not tonight. I wanted to know whether temperature mattered.</p><p>Cold water. Hot water. Easy. No. Bed. My hands hurt. Tomorrow. I wrapped the regulator again. That felt like progress too. Stopping before exhausting the question. Maybe. Or I was tired. More likely. I slept properly. Morning arrived with consequences. Hands worse. Shoulders better. Ribs about the same. No headache. No channel symptoms. Good. I ate before leaving. Two eggs. Bread.</p><p>Something green that might have been an herb and might have been a leaf the cook had regretted. Still food. At Hessa’s, the fourteen-year-old boy from before was already there. He stood with both hands around a clay cup. Nothing happened. </p><p>Hessa said, “Again.”</p><p>He breathed. Focused. A faint warmth appeared against my face. Not visible. Barely there. The boy smiled. Then lost it.</p><p>Hessa said, “Good.” He looked disappointed.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“But I got it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He frowned. I liked him. Hessa looked at me. I stopped smiling. The boy noticed.</p><p>“You’re Greg.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You’re the Barrier one.”</p><p>That phrasing was new.</p><p>“Apparently.”</p><p>He looked at my hands.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“Millrace.”</p><p>“Monster?”</p><p>“Reeds.”</p><p>He stared. Hessa looked almost pleased. The boy left. His disappointment went with him. No dramatic lesson. Just a boy who wanted another try. I sat on the mat. Hessa checked my hands first.</p><p>“Blisters.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What did you do?”</p><p>“Work.”</p><p>“That is not an explanation.”</p><p>“Millrace clearing.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Casting?”</p><p>“One small Barrier.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Yesterday afternoon.”</p><p>“Symptoms?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“After?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Overnight?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Alcohol?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She checked pulse. Eyes. Palm. Then stepped back.</p><p>“Barrier.”</p><p>I formed one. Coin-sized. Low. Three breaths. Release. Clean. Again. Four breaths. Release. Still clean.</p><p>“Larger,” she said.</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“How much larger?”</p><p>“Hand.”</p><p>Good. Palm-sized. I shaped it. Not dense. Not hard. Just there. Three breaths. The channels noticed. Not pain. Load. Familiar now. Release. Hessa waited.</p><p>“Anything?”</p><p>“Pressure one.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Behind eyes.”</p><p>“Gone?”</p><p>“Mostly.”</p><p>She waited another ten seconds.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Gone.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I wanted to. Very much. I formed the Barrier. Same size. Same load. Two breaths. Pressure one. Then two. I dropped it. Immediate. Good. Hessa said nothing. I sat. Waited. Pressure faded.</p><p>“Good,” she said.</p><p>“For stopping?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is a low standard.”</p><p>“For you, no.”</p><p>Fair. She checked again.</p><p>“No more Barrier today.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“That was two.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I can do more.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So why not?”</p><p>“Because yesterday was physical fatigue and one tiny cast. Today you showed clean recovery and repeatable symptom onset under larger load. That is enough information.”</p><p>I hated information when it ended experiments.</p><p>“What can I cast?”</p><p>“Small utility. No sustained Barrier. No repeated load testing.”</p><p>“So still restricted.”</p><p>“You are recovering.”</p><p>“Semantics.”</p><p>“Body.”</p><p>Worse. I looked at my hands. Blisters. She saw.</p><p>“Those matter too.”</p><p>“To magic?”</p><p>“To you.”</p><p>“I can hold a sword.”</p><p>“For how long?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Good answer.”</p><p>I disliked that too. The planned spar was tomorrow. Alden. Berren. Short rotating rounds. No chasing. No extending after call. Good structure. My body was not ready for twenty minutes. Maybe ten. Maybe less. Tomorrow would decide.</p><p>“Do I spar?”</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“With?”</p><p>“Alden and Berren.”</p><p>She knew Alden by now. Not well. Enough.</p><p>“Berren is the bitten one?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then all three of you are injured.”</p><p>“That makes it fair.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It makes it symmetrical.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I smiled. She did not.</p><p>“Light rounds if you wake clean. No Barrier unless you can do it without pressure. If pressure starts, stop casting. If ribs worsen, stop. If your hands open, stop.”</p><p>“My hands will not open.”</p><p>She looked at the blisters.</p><p>“Those.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Wrap?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“Eat.”</p><p>“I eat.”</p><p>“You forget.”</p><p>“I remember eventually.”</p><p>“That is not eating.”</p><p>Fine. I left with more permission and fewer fantasies. Outside, the morning was bright and cool. I had no immediate appointment. That was dangerous. Antonius? Possible. Arlo? Regulator data. Edrin? No message. Sinkstone? Still interesting. Silas Marris? Still not today. Jorren? Working dock gate. Alden? South farms escort. Berren? Probably foot. I could go back to my room. Test the regulator. Write notes.</p><p>Rest. Or Antonius could find work and pay down debt. Debt won. Mostly because it existed even when I ignored it. I went west. Rusk was not at the storehouse. A worker I recognized from the bean day said, “Vale office.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>He pointed upstairs. Of course. Antonius sat at the desk with three ledgers open and a woman in a green coat standing beside the window. I stopped in the doorway. Antonius looked up.</p><p>“You.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You have mud on your boots.”</p><p>“Yesterday.”</p><p>“That is not better.”</p><p>The woman in green looked at me. Not interested. Good. </p><p>Antonius said, “Wait downstairs.” </p><p>I did. No questions. That felt strange enough that I noticed. Downstairs I helped Jalen move two crates because he asked. Not Antonius work. No pay. One crate was heavy. My hands objected. I adjusted grip. Used forearms. Bad. Still got it moved.</p><p>Jalen said, “You’re the bean man.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You found the drain.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Bean man.”</p><p>Fine. We stacked the crates. Then another worker asked me to hold a ledger while she checked labels. I held it. That was all. Ten minutes. Fifteen. No one came for me. I could leave. I did not. The storehouse had its own rhythm. Cart in. Cart out. Numbers shouted. Cloth moved. Oil checked. Someone cursed a broken wheel. No mystery. I watched a boy perhaps sixteen count bundles badly.</p><p>He skipped one. I knew because I had counted too. Then he started over without anyone telling him. Caught it. Good. I said nothing. Antonius came down eventually. The woman in green left by the side door. He looked at the crates.</p><p>“Did I hire you?”</p><p>“No.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/038/Ch038_Fast-Coverage-003-A25.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 38." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“Then why are you moving things?”</p><p>“Jalen asked.”</p><p>“Did he pay you?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Antonius looked at Jalen. Jalen looked busy.</p><p>“Interesting,” Antonius said.</p><p>“That word is dangerous from you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What work?”</p><p>He handed me a folded sheet. Inventory transfer. Verran customers. Two had taken temporary space. One had not. Soap maker.</p><p>“Check twelve crates.”</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Damage. Seal condition. Count. Nothing magical.”</p><p>“Why me?”</p><p>“You are here.”</p><p>That was becoming a system. I checked. Twelve crates. Three dented. One seal cracked. No contents exposed. Count correct. Soap smelled through wood. Antonius reviewed my sheet.</p><p>“Four copper?”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Millrace.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“Guild contracts are posted.”</p><p>“You track my income?”</p><p>“I track people who owe me money.”</p><p>“That is disturbing.”</p><p>“It is debt.”</p><p>He looked at my hands.</p><p>“Blisters.”</p><p>“Everyone sees everything.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He turned the sheet over.</p><p>“Did you enjoy it?”</p><p>I stopped. That question was worse than money.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>He looked at my hands.</p><p>“You came back with blisters and still sound pleased about four copper.”</p><p>Hostile city.</p><p>“I enjoyed parts.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>He nodded. No follow-up. That annoyed me.</p><p>“You don’t care?”</p><p>“Should I?”</p><p>“I expected analysis.”</p><p>“I have work.”</p><p>Good. He moved to the next ledger. I stood there. Antonius looked up.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Then go.”</p><p>I almost did. Then remembered.</p><p>“Silas Marris.”</p><p>His expression changed a fraction.</p><p>“If this is about pursuing them, don't.”</p><p>“I only said the name.”</p><p>“And I am telling you the boundary before you make it my problem.”</p><p>“I have not pursued them.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Edrin has not sent word.”</p><p>“Also good.”</p><p>“You sound invested.”</p><p>“I am invested in you continuing to owe me money.”</p><p>“There.”</p><p>“Go rest.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Is that concern?”</p><p>“It is asset maintenance.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>I left. Outside the west storehouse, I had three copper from the millrace. Still. Antonius had not taken them. Interesting. He could have. Debt payment. He did not. Maybe because I had not offered. Maybe because he preferred scheduled payment.</p><p>Maybe because collecting every coin immediately reduced my capacity to work. Systems. No. Not now. I bought lunch. Two copper. Too much. Meat pie. Actually good. Worth it. One copper left from the four.</p><p>I sat on a low wall near the canal and ate. No one I knew nearby. No work. No appointment. The regulator in my bag. I took it out. Mechanical test. Fine. I found a public pump again. This time I tested cold water in three orientations. Vertical. Tilted. Horizontal. Recorded.</p><p>Then held the body in one hand and tapped the tube with the other. Vibration. Flow flutter. Same direction. Repeatable enough. Good. A woman waiting for the pump stared at me.</p><p>“What is that?”</p><p>“Regulator.”</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Low flow.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Move.”</p><p>Right. I moved. Sat on the wall again. The result was small. Arlo would like it. Maybe. I wanted to test hot water. Could. Not needed now. I wrapped the device. Stopped. Again. This stopping thing was becoming suspicious. I ate the last bite of pie. Then realized I had nowhere I needed to be. Could go home. Could walk. Could find Jorren after his shift.</p><p>Could check if Alden was back. Could visit Arlo. Arlo had asked for measurements. I had measurements. That was an actual reason. I headed toward his workshop. Halfway there, I changed direction. Not because Arlo could wait. Because I was tired. Actually tired. Hands. Shoulders. Ribs. Channels. All separate. All voting. The room won again. I went home. No revelation. No discipline.</p><p>Just fatigue. I slept for an hour. When I woke, someone had pushed a folded note under the door. I stared at it from the bed. White paper. No seal. No blood. Probably not catastrophe. Good. I picked it up.</p><p>EDRIN.</p><p>Not from Edrin. The handwriting was cleaner. Guild clerk.</p><p>GREG.</p><p>SAYE REQUESTS YOUR PRESENCE TOMORROW AFTERNOON IF AVAILABLE.</p><p>BLIND COMPARISON COMPLETE.</p><p>NO URGENCY.</p><p>I read it twice. No urgency. Again. Apparently the entire city had decided to weaponize that phrase. Tomorrow afternoon. After the spar. If the spar happened. If Hessa’s conditions held. If Berren’s foot held.</p><p>If Alden returned from south farms without inventing a new injury. The sinkstone question had waited. Edrin had done the work without me. Now there was a result. Good. I put the note on the desk. Did not open my notebook. Did not write possibilities. Not yet. My hands hurt. The regulator waited. The note waited. Tomorrow waited. I lay back down.</p><p>For once, waiting did not feel like losing time.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="037.html">← Chapter 31</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="039.html">Chapter 33 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/037.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 30: The Laborer — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 30</div><h1>THE LABORER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>I decided at noon. This was later than Berren wanted and earlier than Antonius would have respected. The decision itself was not difficult. Four copper. Meal. Half a day. Possible river lizards. The difficulty was admitting that none of those explained why I wanted to go.</p><p>I had work available elsewhere. Arlo had given me a regulator to test. Antonius could always find something that needed counting, moving, pricing, or arguing over. Edrin had actual magical material under examination. Hessa would see me the next morning if my channels remained quiet.</p><p>The millrace paid less than several better uses of my time. I went to the Guild anyway. Berren had already signed my name. I stared at the sheet. He stood beside me on his rebuilt boot.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You signed my name.”</p><p>“You said maybe.”</p><p>“That is not yes.”</p><p>“It was becoming yes.”</p><p>“You cannot sign other people onto contracts.”</p><p>“You can erase it.”</p><p>I looked at the clerk. The ink-thumbed clerk looked back at me.</p><p>“Can I erase it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Berren smiled. The clerk continued.</p><p>“I can strike it and note declined.”</p><p>Berren stopped smiling. I considered. There it was. Permission. Actual choice. I could walk away. I looked at the contract again.</p><p>WEST MILLRACE GATE.</p><p>CLEARING AND WATCH.</p><p>TWO BRONZE MINIMUM.</p><p>THREE PREFERRED.</p><p>FOUR COPPER EACH.</p><p>MEAL PROVIDED.</p><p>My name sat beneath Berren’s in handwriting that did not resemble mine.</p><p>“Leave it.”</p><p>Berren smiled again. I pointed at him.</p><p>“Do not do that again.”</p><p>“Unless you mean yes?”</p><p>“Especially then.”</p><p>The clerk said, “Initial.”</p><p>I initialed beside the false signature. Now it was my mistake. Better. We left through the west gate just after noon with a mill worker named Ossin and a handcart full of rope, two shovels, a pry bar, three hooked poles, and enough bread to make the contract’s meal clause technically true.</p><p>Ossin was fifty or close to it, thick through the chest, gray beard cut short, left thumb missing above the first joint. He walked faster than Berren. This annoyed Berren. I enjoyed it. The west mill sat less than three miles outside the city where a narrow river had been bullied into usefulness. The main channel continued south.</p><p>The millrace split west through a stone gate and ran beside a low embankment toward a broad timber building whose wheel had stopped. No wheel meant no grinding. No grinding meant sacks waiting. Sacks waiting meant people losing money. Ordinary catastrophe. Six workers were already at the gate. None looked relieved to see adventurers. Good.</p><p>A woman in rolled trousers stood knee-deep in the race with a hooked pole. She looked at Berren’s boot.</p><p>“No,” she said.</p><p>Berren stopped.</p><p>“What?” Berren asked.</p><p>“You’re not going in,” she said.</p><p>“I’m hired.”</p><p>“You’re hired to clear and watch.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You can watch from dry stone.”</p><p>“I can clear.”</p><p>“You can clear from dry stone.”</p><p>He looked at me. I did not help. The woman pointed at a pile of debris jammed against the gate. Branches. Reeds. Two broken boards. A dead goat. That last part complicated the smell.</p><p>“Water came up two nights ago,” she said. “Gate dropped crooked. Debris packed behind it. We need the channel clear enough to lift and reseat.”</p><p>“Why adventurers?” I asked.</p><p>“Because last time Dovan got bit.”</p><p>A worker on the bank lifted his trouser leg. Two small scars above the ankle.</p><p>“River lizard,” he said.</p><p>“How large?”</p><p>He held his hands about two feet apart.</p><p>Berren looked disappointed.</p><p>I liked him less for three seconds.</p><p>The woman said, “You kill anything that comes out. Mostly you pull rubbish.”</p><p>“Who controls the lift?”</p><p>“I do.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“What’s your name?”</p><p>“Etta.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I know. Guild slip.”</p><p>Right. Berren said, “Berren.”</p><p>“I know. Limp.”</p><p>He frowned. I smiled. Etta handed me a hooked pole.</p><p>“Start there.”</p><p>No briefing. No theory. Work. The first branch came free easily. The second did not. I planted my feet on wet stone and pulled. Nothing. Adjusted angle. Pulled again. The branch shifted half an inch. My ribs complained. Not sharply. Enough. I changed hands. Berren reached for the pole.</p><p>“I have it.”</p><p>“You don’t.”</p><p>“I do.”</p><p>“You stopped pulling.”</p><p>I let him take the upper grip. He braced from the dry bank. We pulled together. The branch came free suddenly. Both of us nearly went backward. Ossin caught Berren by the collar. I caught myself. Berren looked at him. Ossin released him.</p><p>“Four copper,” he said.</p><p>Apparently that explained gravity. We dragged the branch onto the bank. Then another. Then reeds. Then a length of fence. Etta identified it as a chicken run from upstream.</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“Mine.”</p><p>She kept working. Of course. The dead goat required rope. Berren volunteered. Etta said no. He argued. She pointed at his boot. He said the foot was fine. She said she did not care. He looked at me. Again. </p><p>I said, “She controls the lift.”</p><p>“That has nothing to do with the goat.”</p><p>“It means this is her worksite.”</p><p>He stared at me. I was right. Also irritating. He knew both.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>He took watch on the bank with one of the hooked poles. I tied the goat. Badly. Not dangerously. Just inefficiently. Ossin watched me redo the knot twice.</p><p>“Adventurer?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not sailor.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He took the rope. One loop. Under. Back. Tight. The goat came out. I watched his hands.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>He showed me. I copied. Wrong. Again. Better. Third time. Good enough. Ossin nodded. That pleased me more than it should have. Young Greg had known knots. Probably. Future Greg knew several. My hands did not. Or knew different ones.</p><p>Memory offered a dungeon harness knot involving two loops and a locking turn. Wrong application. I left it alone. By the time the main debris pile was half cleared, my shirt was wet through from sweat and spray. The day was warm. The water was cold. My shoulders burned. Forearms worse. No mana. No spell pressure. Just work. I had forgotten how direct that could be.</p><p>Pull. Lift. Carry. Throw. Again. Nothing abstract. Nothing waiting thirty years to matter. At one point I stood ankle-deep in the race holding a broken board while Etta cut away reeds tangled around it. The current pushed against my calves. Not hard. Persistent. My young legs adjusted constantly. Tiny corrections. Heel. Knee. Hip. Balance happened before thought. Interesting. I almost started analyzing it.</p><p>Then the board slipped. Etta said, “Hold.” </p><p>I held. Better use of attention. A river lizard appeared after perhaps an hour. Berren saw it first.</p><p>“Left.”</p><p>I turned. Gray-green body between stones. Long tail. Flat head. Maybe eighteen inches. Not two feet. It opened its mouth. Small teeth. Angry. Berren raised the hooked pole. The lizard ran at him. He stepped back. Good. Not because of fear. Because his right foot did not want the turn. The lizard changed direction toward the water. I could cast. Tiny Barrier.</p><p>Coin-sized. Redirect at the nose. Easy. Probably. No. Etta threw a shovel. Not the blade. The flat side struck the lizard behind the head and knocked it into the shallows. Ossin grabbed the tail with a hook and flung it onto the far bank. It ran away. Berren stared. Etta retrieved her shovel.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>Berren said, “We’re here for that.”</p><p>“You were slow,” Etta said.</p><p>“I was not,” Berren said.</p><p>“You were,” Etta said.</p><p>He looked at me. I had seen it. He knew. His first movement had been correct. His second had hesitated because the lizard was smaller than the threat he had prepared for. He had expected fight. Etta expected nuisance. Different objective. I could explain that. He already looked annoyed enough to be thinking. </p><p>I picked up reeds. </p><p>Berren said, “Nothing?”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You always have something.”</p><p>“I am working.”</p><p>He narrowed his eyes. Then laughed.</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>We kept working.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Four Copper Millrace" decoding="async" height="506" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/037/v45_c37_four-copper-millrace.png" width="762"/></figure><p>Ten minutes later another lizard surfaced beside my boot. I moved faster than thought. Young reflex. My foot came up. The lizard darted. I put a coin-sized Barrier on the stone beside its head. Not in front. Beside.</p><p>It turned away from the pressure change and ran straight into Berren’s waiting hook. He lifted. Not hard. Just enough to redirect it onto the far bank. The lizard vanished into grass. Berren looked at me.</p><p>“That was magic?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Terrible.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He smiled. I did too. No pain. No pressure. Channels quiet. One small cast. Done. I wanted another. There were no lizards. Inconsiderate. The gate itself was worse than the debris. Once enough rubbish had been cleared, Etta had two workers fit a chain to the upper beam. Ossin and I took the capstan. Berren moved toward us. Etta pointed at the bank.</p><p>He stopped.</p><p>“I can turn a capstan.”</p><p>“You can also tear your foot open.”</p><p>“It is closed.”</p><p>“For now.”</p><p>“I am being paid four copper.”</p><p>“So watch four-copper lizards.”</p><p>He muttered something. She ignored him. The capstan moved. Slow. Wood complained. Chain tightened. The gate lifted three inches. Water punched through beneath it. Everyone shouted at once. Not panic. Coordination.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>“Left brace.”</p><p>“Clear.”</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>The race changed shape around my legs. Current stronger. Cold water to my knees. My body reacted. Heart faster. Grip tighter. Balance. The gate rose another inch. A mass of reeds and mud tore loose and hit me in the thigh. I nearly fell.</p><p>Ossin leaned into the bar and caught my shoulder with his missing-thumb hand.</p><p>“Feet.”</p><p>I reset. Again. No embarrassment. No time. Work. The gate came up enough for Etta to see beneath it.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/037/Ch037_Fast-Coverage-003-A24.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 37." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>We stopped. She crouched in the water. Reached under. I watched. Not because I wanted to improve her. Because she knew what she was doing. She felt along the stone channel with both hands. Then swore.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Pin seat chipped.”</p><p>One of the workers swore too. Berren called from the bank, “Bad?” </p><p>Etta stood.</p><p>“Annoying.”</p><p>Good category.</p><p>“What does that change?” I asked.</p><p>“We can reseat it. Won’t hold clean.”</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>“Maybe a week. Maybe a month.”</p><p>“Then?”</p><p>“Mason.”</p><p>“Why not mason now?”</p><p>Etta set one wet hand on the gate.</p><p>“Because the mill is stopped now.”</p><p>Right. Objective. Get wheel moving. Perfect gate later. I knew this. Still asked. She pointed at a box of wooden wedges.</p><p>“We set temporary. Then clear the lower run.”</p><p>I looked at the chipped seat. Could Barrier support it? Small contact point. Temporary load. No. Too much sustained pressure. Wrong tool. Could a tiny Barrier help position the wedge? Maybe. Not necessary. Etta had hands. Workers had wedges. I carried one. The first was too thick. Etta shaved it with a knife. Second fit. Third braced. They lowered the gate. It settled crooked.</p><p>Less crooked than before. Water entered the millrace in a controlled sheet. The wheel downstream moved. One turn. Stopped. Then another. Then kept going. Everyone watched. Not reverently. One worker immediately shouted toward the mill. Someone inside shouted back. Machinery began making noise. The contract was not done. Of course.</p><p>The lower run had accumulated debris while the wheel was stopped. We walked it. Berren limped more. Not dramatically. Enough. I said nothing. He saw me see.</p><p>“Don’t.”</p><p>“I didn’t.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>We found a clogged screen behind the mill. Leaves. Straw. A dead chicken. Etta looked at it.</p><p>“Not mine.”</p><p>Important. We cleared it. By then my hands hurt. Blisters beginning at the base of two fingers. I stared at them. Ridiculous. I had fought creatures in Darrowmere. A millrace was injuring me with wood. Young body. Soft hands. Old memories. I wrapped one palm with cloth. Ossin saw.</p><p>“Tomorrow’s worse.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Hands know.”</p><p>That sounded mystical. It was probably callus. Berren said, “Mine are fine.” </p><p>I looked. His hands were callused. Hook work. Weapon work. Current body experience. Not future. Actual. He had something I did not. That bothered me. Then pleased me. Then bothered me that it pleased me. Complicated. At the lower screen, Berren finally got to work. Dry bank. Hooked pole. He was good.</p><p>Not extraordinary. Good. He knew how to catch debris without burying the hook. Knew when to pull and when to twist. Knew how to let current help. Dema’s hook boy. His pride made more sense when the skill was visible outside class.</p><p>He caught a branch, shifted his grip, and rolled it over the stone lip. Clean. I watched. He noticed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You were staring.”</p><p>“Competence.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You are good at that.”</p><p>He looked suspicious.</p><p>“At hooks?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>Good. No false modesty. He hooked another branch.</p><p>“I’m better from a cart.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Moving angle.”</p><p>That interested me. He saw.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Day after.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You said tomorrow before.”</p><p>“Day after.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>He had forgotten. Or I had. We worked another hour. No more lizards. No monster. No hidden magical mechanism. No suspicious mark beneath the gate. No future-important stranger. Just mud. At some point I realized I was having fun. This was unacceptable. The work was repetitive. The pay mediocre. My shoulders hurt.</p><p>Berren complained about his foot every time Etta could not hear and denied it whenever she could. Ossin told the same story twice about a flood from twelve years ago. The mill workers argued about whose dead chicken had entered the screen. Nobody solved it. I was having fun. Not constantly. Enough. Old Greg had remembered Bronze work as waiting. Jobs before real jobs.</p><p>Money before real money. Training before real competence. People before important people. That was not entirely false. Some of it had been awful. Some contracts were stupid. Some employers cheated. Young Greg had wasted money, chased praise, picked fights, slept through mornings, and confused being busy with becoming good.</p><p>He had also stood in cold water with other idiots and dragged a goat out of a millrace for four copper. Maybe that had been a life too. I pulled another mat of reeds free. It slapped me in the face. Berren laughed so hard he had to sit. I threw mud at him. Bad throw. Hit Ossin. Silence. I looked at Ossin.</p><p>Mud on his shirt. He looked at me. Then picked up a handful.</p><p>“Oh no.”</p><p>He hit me in the chest. Berren nearly fell off the bank laughing. Etta shouted from upstream.</p><p>“If one of you falls in, I am not paying extra.”</p><p>Work resumed. Mostly. The meal was bread, hard cheese, pickled onions, and cold pork. Excellent. Not objectively. Hunger. We ate sitting on the embankment with the wheel turning behind us. Berren removed his right boot. The sock had a small red stain near the bite. I saw. He saw me see.</p><p>“Shut up.”</p><p>“I said nothing.”</p><p>Ossin said, “You’re bleeding.” </p><p>Berren looked betrayed. </p><p>Etta came over. She looked once.</p><p>“You’re done.”</p><p>“We’re eating.”</p><p>“After eating.”</p><p>“There’s still lower bank.”</p><p>“We have six people.”</p><p>“I’m contracted.”</p><p>“You watched. You cleared. You’re done.”</p><p>He looked at the four-copper contract as if the paper might defend him. I knew exactly what he wanted. Not money. Not entirely. He wanted to finish. To prove the bite had not removed him from ordinary work. Accurate read. Probably. I could support that. Tell Etta he could remain on dry watch. Help rewrap the foot. Adjust tasks. Keep him useful.</p><p>I understood the problem. Therefore I knew what should happen next. There. I ate an onion. Berren looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You’re thinking.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“About my foot.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Don’t.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>He waited. Maybe expecting more. I ate cheese. Etta walked away. Berren swore quietly. Then rewrapped the foot himself. Not well. Not terribly. He put the boot back on. Sat. Stayed. No one praised him. Good.</p><p>After the meal I returned to the lower bank with Ossin. Berren remained under a tree with the hooked pole across his knees. Watch duty. Still part of the contract. Not the part he wanted. His problem. I checked twice to see whether he was still there. He was. The second time he caught me. He raised one finger. Not the polite one.</p><p>I laughed. By late afternoon the race ran clean enough that Etta called it. Not clean. Enough. Important distinction. The wheel turned steadily. The gate leaked around the chipped seat. A mason would come tomorrow. The dead goat was someone else’s problem now.</p><p>We walked back toward the city with wet boots and sore shoulders. Berren limped badly enough that Ossin put the handcart beside him. Berren refused. </p><p>Ossin did not argue. He simply kept the cart there. After half a mile Berren sat on it. No announcement. Ossin pulled. </p><p>I took the other handle. </p><p>Berren said, “This is humiliating.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He did not get off. The cart was heavier with him. My arms were already tired. I could feel every incline. Young body. Real weight. No optimization fixed it. We switched with Ossin twice.</p><p>At the west gate, the Guild clerk checked the work slip. Etta had marked complete. Four copper. Actual coins. One meal. Half a day. I held the money in my palm. Not much. Enough to sharpen a sword twice. Enough for bad beer and bad chicken and several mistakes. Berren took his four.</p><p>“Worth it.”</p><p>“Your foot is bleeding.”</p><p>“Still worth it.”</p><p>“Those statements can coexist.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I liked that answer. Ossin headed back toward the mill with the empty cart. He had not been paid four copper. He worked there. Different economics. I almost asked his wage. Did not. Berren noticed.</p><p>“You were going to ask him something.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Not important.”</p><p>He looked suspicious. Then shrugged. We stood inside the gate. His aunt’s bakery room waited somewhere. My room waited. Hessa tomorrow. Spar day after if bodies cooperated. I had four copper. Blisters. Mud dried on my shirt. One clean Barrier cast with no symptoms. And no new information about anything important. I felt excellent. That was probably a problem. Not today.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="036.html">← Chapter 29</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="039.html">Chapter 31 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/337.html:146`: <p>Not mana I could feel directly.</p>
- `chapters/103.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 81: The Shaper — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 81</div><h1>THE SHAPER</h1></header><article class="prose"><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/103/Ch103_Two-Copper-Strips.png" alt="Two narrow copper strips lie ready on Hessa&#x27;s assessment table in front of Greg." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Hessa had two copper strips.</p><p>This seemed aggressive.</p><p>I looked at them.</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Two strips,” I said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why two?”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat.</p><p>The chair remained bad.</p><p>I appreciated that some things in life had standards.</p><p>My right calf was mildly sore from Pessa.</p><p>Not pain.</p><p>Work.</p><p>Hip similar.</p><p>Hands fine.</p><p>Residual limb baseline.</p><p>I told Hessa before she asked.</p><p>She asked anyway.</p><p>“What did Pessa do?”</p><p>“Made me turn.”</p><p>Hessa waited.</p><p>“That is the medically relevant summary.”</p><p>“Fall?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Near fall?”</p><p>“One skid. One hop. She caught my arm.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Swelling after?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“Baseline.”</p><p>“Hands?”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>No questions about circles.</p><p>No questions about left turns.</p><p>No questions about my theory.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Different jurisdiction.</p><p>Still not saying it.</p><p>Hessa examined the residual limb.</p><p>Nothing interesting.</p><p>Then she sat across from me.</p><p>Two copper strips on the table.</p><p>One straight.</p><p>One bent into a shallow curve.</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Those are different.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because they are.”</p><p>“That is not enough information.”</p><p>“It is for now.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>“What are we doing?”</p><p>“Drawing.”</p><p>I tried not to look disappointed.</p><p>Failed.</p><p>Hessa saw.</p><p>“First.”</p><p>My pulse improved.</p><p>“First?”</p><p>“Minimal draw. Same as before.”</p><p>“Then?”</p><p>“If it is boring, maybe something else.”</p><p>There it was.</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>My least favorite word.</p><p>I closed my eyes.</p><p>Hessa used the straight copper strip.</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>Mana came.</p><p>Easier again.</p><p>Chest.</p><p>Shoulders.</p><p>Arms.</p><p>Right side.</p><p>Left thigh.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Below the knee, nothing unusual.</p><p>Ordinary phantom foot present.</p><p>No magical extension I could distinguish.</p><p>Hold.</p><p>Release.</p><p>Done.</p><p>Boring.</p><p>Beautiful.</p><p>Hessa asked the usual questions.</p><p>No pain.</p><p>No heat.</p><p>No cold.</p><p>No pressure.</p><p>No cramping.</p><p>No unintended shaping.</p><p>Residual limb unchanged.</p><p>Hands unchanged.</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She put the straight copper aside.</p><p>Picked up the curved one.</p><p>My heart began doing something embarrassing.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Eyes open.”</p><p>I opened them.</p><p>She placed the curved strip in front of me.</p><p>Not touching.</p><p>Just there.</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>“Copper.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then we're making progress.”</p><p>I refused to reward that.</p><p>“What does the curve do?”</p><p>“Nothing useful.”</p><p>“Then why?”</p><p>“Because you have never trained with it.”</p><p>I went still.</p><p>There.</p><p>The shaping test.</p><p>Maybe had become now.</p><p>Hessa watched my face.</p><p>“This is not casting clearance.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“It is not permission to shape outside this room.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“It is not permission to repeat whatever happens.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“I am allowed to attempt exactly what you instruct while you supervise. Nothing else.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I looked at the copper.</p><p>“What am I doing?”</p><p>“Draw the same small amount.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Hold it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then move the smallest amount you can deliberately distinguish into the pad of your right thumb.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“That is shaping?”</p><p>“It is deliberate alteration.”</p><p>“Routing.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You hate categories.”</p><p>“I hate categories before evidence.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Why thumb?”</p><p>“Right side is intact. Thumb is small. It is not part of any spell form I know you trained as a distinct first step.”</p><p>“What if it is?”</p><p>“Is it?”</p><p>I searched memory.</p><p>Barrier.</p><p>Pulse.</p><p>The ugly little fire-light thing.</p><p>Early academy exercises.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not specifically thumb pad.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“And the curved copper?”</p><p>“I am going to hold it near your thumb.”</p><p>“To detect the change?”</p><p>“To give me another witness.”</p><p>“Does the curve matter?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why curve it?”</p><p>“So you do not unconsciously treat it as the same test.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“That is manipulative.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>She held the curved copper near my right hand.</p><p>Not touching.</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I drew.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Familiar.</p><p>Hold.</p><p>“Now,” she said, “do not make a spell. Do not reach outward. Do not increase the draw. Put only enough mana into the pad of your right thumb that you can tell you changed something.”</p><p>This sounded easy.</p><p>That was the problem.</p><p>I reached for the change.</p><p>My body knew what to do.</p><p>Too well.</p><p>Mana shifted down the arm.</p><p>Not to the thumb.</p><p>Across the palm.</p><p>Wrist rotated slightly.</p><p>Forearm tightened.</p><p>Something in my chest opened.</p><p>Barrier.</p><p>Not the spell.</p><p>The beginning.</p><p>The old setup.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Hessa said, “Release.”</p><p>I already was.</p><p>Mana dropped away.</p><p>My breath came faster.</p><p>Nothing hurt.</p><p>Hessa put the copper down.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“I failed.”</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>Fine.</p><p>“Draw stable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I attempted to move a small amount toward right thumb.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Instead the mana spread into the palm and wrist.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Forearm engaged.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“My wrist rotated.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then I felt the beginning of Barrier setup.”</p><p>“Did you shape Barrier?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did mana leave the body?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did you increase draw?”</p><p>“I don't think so.”</p><p>“I didn't observe a meaningful increase.”</p><p>“Copper?”</p><p>“Responded.”</p><p>“To what?”</p><p>“The redistribution.”</p><p>My pulse jumped.</p><p>“So I shaped.”</p><p>Hessa raised one finger.</p><p>“You altered.”</p><p>“That is shaping.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“You deliberately attempted one alteration. The result was not the alteration I asked for.”</p><p>I looked at my thumb.</p><p>Normal thumb.</p><p>Traitor.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“One attempt tells us almost nothing.”</p><p>“It told us something.”</p><p>“That old pattern is automatic.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“I felt Barrier.”</p><p>“You felt something you recognized as Barrier setup.”</p><p>“That is the same thing.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It is very close.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>Bad chair.</p><p>Excellent enemy.</p><p>“What did you see?”</p><p>Hessa took her time.</p><p>“Stable draw. Then a broader shift through the right hand than requested. Wrist and forearm movement. Channel change consistent with deliberate alteration. No external release. No spell completion. No concerning physical response.”</p><p>“And Barrier?”</p><p>“I am not inside your head.”</p><p>“You know my Barrier form.”</p><p>“I know parts of your casting habits from before.”</p><p>“Did it look like Barrier?”</p><p>“It looked familiar.”</p><p>There.</p><p>Good enough.</p><p>Bad enough.</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>Hessa frowned.</p><p>“Why are you happy?”</p><p>“I shaped mana.”</p><p>“You failed the instruction.”</p><p>“I shaped mana badly.”</p><p>“That is true.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>She let me.</p><p>Not long.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/103/Ch103_Fast-Coverage-003-C15.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 103." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Then she checked my hand.</p><p>Temperature.</p><p>Pulse.</p><p>Grip.</p><p>No tremor.</p><p>Residual limb.</p><p>No change.</p><p>Phantom foot?</p><p>Normal.</p><p>No organized fullness.</p><p>No extension.</p><p>Nothing relevant.</p><p>Good.</p><p>The left leg had contributed nothing unusual.</p><p>I appreciated its restraint.</p><p>“What now?”</p><p>“Tea.”</p><p>“That is not a magical progression.”</p><p>“It is today.”</p><p>She poured.</p><p>I took the cup with the right hand.</p><p>My thumb worked.</p><p>This felt absurdly meaningful.</p><p>“Does this count as clearance?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I know. I wanted to hear you say it.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Consistency.”</p><p>She drank.</p><p>I looked at the curved copper.</p><p>“Why did it respond if I did the wrong thing?”</p><p>“Because it was not checking success. It was helping me confirm that something changed.”</p><p>“So it cannot tell thumb from palm.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Could you?”</p><p>“Broadly.”</p><p>“Broadly.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I hated that word less now.</p><p>“What would success have looked like?”</p><p>“To you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“A smaller localized change with less accompanying wrist and forearm pattern.”</p><p>“And if I can't?”</p><p>“We find out.”</p><p>“Could the old pattern be impossible to suppress?”</p><p>“We do not know.”</p><p>“Could it be useful?”</p><p>“Later question.”</p><p>“Could relearning involve replacing old forms?”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“Could old forms be adapted?”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“Could Barrier eventually come back?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>That was the real question.</p><p>I had hidden it badly.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I exhaled.</p><p>Not because I expected more.</p><p>Because maybe was not no.</p><p>Dangerous.</p><p>She saw that too.</p><p>“Do not build a future out of one failed thumb.”</p><p>“That is a cruel sentence.”</p><p>“It is accurate.”</p><p>I drank tea.</p><p>The excitement did not go away.</p><p>Neither did the irritation.</p><p>Good combination.</p><p>“What is next test?”</p><p>“Probably the same instruction.”</p><p>“Same thumb?”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“Same position?”</p><p>“Probably seated.”</p><p>“Same copper?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Why not tomorrow?”</p><p>“I want a boring day between attempts.”</p><p>“Delayed effects.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then when?”</p><p>“Day after tomorrow.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“You are obsessed with boring days.”</p><p>“I am interested in delayed effects.”</p><p>“There were none before.”</p><p>“Before was draw only.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>This was different.</p><p>Tiny.</p><p>Still different.</p><p>“Can I train with Pessa tomorrow?”</p><p>“Medically, if you remain at baseline, I do not object to you asking her.”</p><p>“Same answer.”</p><p>“Same question.”</p><p>“Can I tell her I shaped?”</p><p>“You can tell her what happened.”</p><p>“She will say she doesn't care.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>“Can I tell Jorren?”</p><p>Hessa looked confused.</p><p>“Why are you asking me?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“You may tell your friend you failed to move mana into your thumb.”</p><p>“That wording is hostile.”</p><p>“It is accurate.”</p><p>I thought about Jorren's response.</p><p>Probably:</p><p>Good.</p><p>That was somehow irritating in advance.</p><p>“Can I write it down?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Paragraphs?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No table?”</p><p>She stared.</p><p>“Sorry.”</p><p>I finished the tea.</p><p>Hessa checked my hand once more.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Stand.”</p><p>Both crutches.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>Push.</p><p>No problem.</p><p>My right thumb tingled.</p><p>I froze.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She was immediately attentive.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Thumb tingling.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Very mild.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Numb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She touched the thumb.</p><p>Then fingers.</p><p>Had me squeeze.</p><p>Release.</p><p>Touch each fingertip.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>“Still?”</p><p>“Yes. Less.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>We waited.</p><p>The tingling faded.</p><p>“Gone.”</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I looked at the notebook.</p><p>“Concerning?”</p><p>“Not currently.”</p><p>“Relevant?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Delayed effect?”</p><p>“Immediate minor effect.”</p><p>“Could be from gripping the crutch.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be from shaping.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be attention.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>She did not.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Report if it returns.”</p><p>“I will.”</p><p>“No self-test.”</p><p>“I will not.”</p><p>“No thumb experiments.”</p><p>“I will not.”</p><p>“No Barrier rehearsal.”</p><p>“I will not.”</p><p>“No trying to reproduce the wrist movement without mana as a magical exercise.”</p><p>I paused.</p><p>“That is very specific.”</p><p>“Because I know you.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>I left.</p><p>Outside, I looked at my right thumb.</p><p>Not because I was testing it.</p><p>Because it was attached to my hand.</p><p>Important legal distinction.</p><p>I had shaped mana.</p><p>Badly.</p><p>Into the wrong place.</p><p>With an old reflex trying to take over.</p><p>Possibly.</p><p>One tiny deliberate failure.</p><p>I was so happy I nearly walked into a barrel.</p><p>The barrel did not care.</p><p>Carrow remained consistent.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="100.html">← Chapter 80</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="104.html">Chapter 82 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
