- `chapters/039.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 31: The Partner — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 31</div><h1>THE PARTNER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>My hands were better. Not good. Better. The right blister had flattened overnight. The left one had become tender in a way that suggested it wanted attention and would resent receiving it. My ribs were quiet until I twisted. My channels were quiet until I used them. Alden arrived before I finished breakfast. Berren arrived after. This told me everything important about both men.</p><p>Alden leaned against the doorframe in his red scarf and looked at the bread in my hand.</p><p>“You eating?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That sounded like Hessa.”</p><p>“Terrifying.”</p><p>Berren appeared behind him with a different boot. Not repaired. Different. Older leather, wider toe, ugly enough to be comfortable. He saw me looking.</p><p>“My aunt’s.”</p><p>I looked at his feet.</p><p>“Your aunt has large feet.”</p><p>“Uncle’s.”</p><p>“Then why say aunt’s?”</p><p>“Her house.”</p><p>Reasonable. He walked almost normally. Almost.</p><p>“Foot?”</p><p>“Closed.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He frowned.</p><p>“You’re pleased?”</p><p>“Pain means you can feel it.”</p><p>“That is the worst good news.”</p><p>Alden pushed off the frame.</p><p>“Guild yard.”</p><p>We went. No one asked whether we still wanted to spar. We had already spent too much time arranging it. The Guild practice yard was busy. Dema Rusk had one side occupied by six Bronze adventurers working shield rotations. Two people I did not know were throwing weighted ropes at posts. Someone had broken a practice spear and was pretending not to have.</p><p>Alden claimed a narrow strip near the rear wall. Not claimed. Asked.</p><p>A Guild attendant looked at our weapons, looked at Berren’s foot, and said, “Light.”</p><p>Alden said, “Light.”</p><p>Berren said nothing.</p><p>Good. We used blunted practice swords. My repaired real sword stayed belted at the wall. That mattered more than expected. The practice blade felt wrong. Weight close. Balance not. Grip thicker.</p><p>Young hands noticed immediately. Blisters noticed more. I wrapped both palms. Alden watched.</p><p>“Rules,” Alden said.</p><p>He had thought about them. Good.</p><p>“One minute rounds. Clean touch ends exchange, reset immediately. Three exchanges, then switch.”</p><p>Berren said, “That is not a round.”</p><p>“It is ours,” Alden said.</p><p>“No chasing after clean touch,” Alden continued. “No extending after call. No head shots. No hard shots to Greg’s ribs. No low attacks on Berren’s right.”</p><p>Berren objected.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Alden pointed at Berren’s rebuilt boot.</p><p>“It is injured.”</p><p>“I can defend it.”</p><p>“Not the point.”</p><p>“What is the point?”</p><p>“Practice tomorrow too.”</p><p>Good. Berren disliked it. Accepted. Alden looked at me.</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“Small only.”</p><p>“Use?”</p><p>I thought. Hessa had said no Barrier unless I could do it without pressure. Yesterday palm-sized repeated load had produced pressure. Coin-sized utility had been clean.</p><p>“Coin-sized. One per exchange maximum. If pressure starts, none.”</p><p>Berren looked delighted.</p><p>“That is terrible.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Alden said, “First Greg and Berren.” Of course. </p><p>We stepped in. </p><p>Berren smiled. </p><p>I did not. My body did. Heart faster. Weight lighter. Hands alive. The yard narrowed. Not mentally. Physically. Distance. Feet. Shoulders. Blade.</p><p>Berren’s right foot was protected, but not hidden. He had changed his stance since the bakery. Less weight on it. More square through the hips. That created other problems. Potential. No. Fight. Alden lifted a hand.</p><p>“Go.”</p><p>Berren came first. Not reckless. Good. Short step. Blade outside. He wanted me to read the obvious line and give him the inside. I did. Then changed. Too slow. His practice blade touched my shoulder.</p><p>“Berren.”</p><p>Alden called it. Berren stepped back immediately. Good. No extra flourish. No grin until after. Then grin.</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Second exchange. I knew the bait now. He knew I knew. Different fight. He came outside again. I did not give the inside. He kicked my blade. Not with the injured foot. Left. Good. My grip shifted against the blister. Pain. Tiny. Enough. He saw. Changed target. Hand. I retreated.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Three Way Spar" decoding="async" height="160" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/039/v45_c39_three-way-spar.png" width="497"/></figure><p>Young legs got me there. Barely. I put a coin-sized Barrier beside his blade, not against it. The pressure changed the line a fraction. His cut missed my fingers. My practice sword touched his chest.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>Reset. Berren looked at the empty air where the Barrier had been.</p><p>“That is disgusting.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>Alden said, “Again.” No symptoms. Third. </p><p>Berren did not attack. Interesting. He waited. He wanted me to build. </p><p>I did. Bad. Old habits. Control the exchange. Set conditions. </p><p>He stepped only when I committed. </p><p>Then turned the entire thing into a close collision. Shoulder. Blade trapped. My ribs said no. I disengaged before contact. He could have followed. Did not. </p><p>Alden called, “Berren.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“That was not a touch.”</p><p>“You left.”</p><p>Fair. Berren nodded. No argument. Two to one. I wanted another. Alden stepped between us.</p><p>“Switch.”</p><p>I hated his system. Therefore it was good. Alden and Berren. I moved to the wall. My channels were quiet. Hands less so. Berren reset. Alden’s stance had changed too. Not dramatically. His repaired shoulder was no longer guarded. He held the practice sword loosely. Berren attacked. Alden gave ground. Berren pressed. Old Berren would have chased harder. Current Berren stopped after the second step.</p><p>Alden had expected third. I saw it in his hips. Berren saw too. He cut across. Touch. Berren. Alden laughed. Not embarrassed. Actually pleased.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Second exchange. Alden changed immediately. No assumption that Berren would repeat. Good. He took center. Berren tried to angle. Alden touched forearm. One each. Third. Longer. Not because either stalled. Because both stopped giving away first answers. Berren’s foot limited his rightward exit. Alden knew. Did not attack it.</p><p>Instead he used the limit to predict where Berren would choose to go. Different. Permission within rules. He drove him left. Berren knew he was being driven. Went anyway. Then dropped his weight and turned the exit into an entry. Bad foot held. Barely.</p><p>His blade touched Alden’s side at the same time Alden touched his shoulder. Both stopped. They looked at me. I looked at Alden.</p><p>“You’re running this,” I said.</p><p>He frowned.</p><p>“Both,” Alden said.</p><p>Berren said, “Coward.”</p><p>“Both,” Alden repeated.</p><p>Done. Switch. Me and Alden. This was more dangerous. Not physically. Informationally. He knew me better. I knew him better. That was the problem. Alden smiled.</p><p>“Go.”</p><p>I waited. He waited. Berren groaned.</p><p>“Fight.”</p><p>Alden moved. No opening test. Direct. Fast. My body knew the line. My memory knew three counters. My current body could execute one and a half. I chose the half. Mistake. His blade touched my upper arm.</p><p>“Fuck.”</p><p>Alden stepped back.</p><p>“You picked something you can’t do.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He knew. Of course. Second exchange. I simplified. No future technique. No clever sequence. Step. Parry. Cut. He was faster. I was earlier. Different advantage. My blade touched his sleeve a fraction before his reached my shoulder. Greg. Maybe. Alden looked at Berren. </p><p>Berren said, “Greg.”</p><p>Good. Third.</p><p>Alden changed rhythm. Slow first. Then fast.</p><p>I recognized it. He had learned that from someone else.</p><p>Not me. Dema? Jorren? His south-farm escort? No idea. Good. I tried to solve it while moving. Bad. He saw my attention leave my feet. His boot hooked mine lightly. Not a trip. Enough. My balance broke. Young body recovered. Almost. His blade touched my chest. Alden. He grinned.</p><p>“You stopped watching my feet.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>Berren laughed. Switch. We continued. Short rounds worked. Annoyingly well. No one got enough time to settle. Every time I started building a reliable model, the person changed. Then the person came back changed by someone else. Berren learned that my tiny Barrier wanted a prepared angle.</p><p>He started making me spend attention on lines I could not profitably redirect. Alden learned that Berren’s restraint had improved enough that baiting overcommitment no longer worked reliably. I learned that Alden had developed a delayed second tempo I had never taught him. Then I learned it was not stable yet. Then he stopped using it. Good. Berren’s foot worsened after the fourth rotation.</p><p>Not dramatically. His rightward movement shortened. Alden saw. I saw. Berren saw us see.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Alden said, “Last rotation.” </p><p>Berren shifted once on the rebuilt boot, opened his mouth, then closed it.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>That was new. Or maybe not. Maybe I had only known him in situations where he wanted to prove he could continue. Last rotation. Berren and me. My palms hurt. Ribs warm. Channels still quiet. I could cast. I wanted to. Did not. First exchange. He expected magic. I gave him none. Touched wrist. Greg. Second. He expected no magic. Coin-sized Barrier at the edge of his guard.</p><p>Tiny. His blade shifted. Not enough. He adapted through it. Touched my shoulder. Berren. Good. Pressure behind eyes. One. Small. There. No more magic. Third. No cast. He did not know I had stopped. That mattered. He kept respecting the possibility. Interesting. I almost used that to build a trap. Then remembered this was a spar. Not a proof. I attacked. He defended.</p><p>We collided close. His foot slipped. Not injury. Sweat on packed dirt. I caught his upper arm. </p><p>He caught mine. Both of us stayed up. </p><p>Alden called, “Done.” No touch. No winner. </p><p>Berren looked disappointed for half a second. Then his foot reminded him of reality. He sat. </p><p>I sat too. Alden remained standing. Show-off.</p><p>“How was south farms?” I asked.</p><p>He blinked. Not expecting that.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“That is not information.”</p><p>“You ask too many questions.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He drank water.</p><p>“Two wagons. Seed grain. One wheel problem. Farmer argued about route. Nothing attacked us.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Paid three copper.”</p><p>Berren said, “I got four.”</p><p>“You got carried home in a cart.”</p><p>“Luxury transport.”</p><p>Alden looked at his boot.</p><p>“You’re bleeding again,” Alden said.</p><p>Berren looked down. Small red mark.</p><p>“Fuck,” Berren said.</p><p>“Lara?”</p><p>I asked. He looked at me.</p><p>“How do you know her name?”</p><p>“Bakery.”</p><p>“That was Nara.”</p><p>“Your sister is Lara.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Your aunt?”</p><p>“Vessa.”</p><p>I froze. No. Different Vessa. Probably. City names repeated. Arlo’s Vessa. Berren’s aunt Vessa. Could be same. Do not connect because names.</p><p>“How old?”</p><p>Berren stared.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>Alden saw my face.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I said nothing.”</p><p>“You found a thing.”</p><p>“I found a name.”</p><p>“Leave it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Berren looked between us.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing,” both of us said.</p><p>Good. We rested. No dramatic conclusion. Scores were meaningless because rotations changed. Alden had probably won more exchanges. Berren had surprised both of us. I had used two Barriers total. Second produced mild pressure. Useful. Not good. Useful. My hands had held. Ribs had held. Body tired. Alive. Hessa would approve of stopping. Probably. That was disturbing. Alden left first. He had somewhere to be.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“Lunch.”</p><p>“With?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“People.”</p><p>Jorren’s answer. Hostile.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>He left. Berren stood carefully.</p><p>“I’m going to my aunt’s.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Don’t.”</p><p>“I said good.”</p><p>“That sounded medical.”</p><p>“It was social.”</p><p>“Worse.”</p><p>He limped away. I was alone. Afternoon. Edrin. The Guild annex was already busy when I arrived. Not crisis busy. Paper busy. Two clerks. One constable. A woman arguing about a confiscated charm. The blue door stood open. Edrin was inside. Three dark sacks still occupied the stone table. Not in the same positions.</p><p>The Darrowmere sample sat in a shallow ceramic tray under a glass cover. Gray-black fragments. Small. Glass inclusions. Similar. Very similar. My brain wanted yes. That was dangerous. Edrin pointed at a chair.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“I am not tired.”</p><p>“You look tired.”</p><p>“I sparred.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat. She looked at my hands.</p><p>“Blisters.”</p><p>“Millrace.”</p><p>She did not ask. Good. The ink-thumbed clerk from before sat at the side desk. The watch constable was different. No Verran. No Nella. Good. This was not theater. Edrin lifted two sheets.</p><p>“Blind comparison.”</p><p>I leaned forward.</p><p>“No touching.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You say that often.”</p><p>“Because you say that often.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She put the first sheet down.</p><p>“Physical comparison first. Darrowmere fragments are kestrin shale.”</p><p>There. Connection. Maybe.</p><p>“Processed?”</p><p>“Some treatment.”</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“Unknown.”</p><p>“Same as sinkstone?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Too fast. I stopped. Edrin continued.</p><p>“Or not established.”</p><p>Better. She pointed to columns.</p><p>“Composition overlaps. Base stone matches common kestrin shale within what our assay can distinguish.”</p><p>“Common?”</p><p>“Very.”</p><p>“How common?”</p><p>“Road fill in some districts. Cheap furnace lining. Packing. Drainage beds. Low-grade building mix.”</p><p>That widened everything. Good.</p><p>“Glass inclusions?”</p><p>“Not the same.”</p><p>I leaned closer. The seized sinkstone pellets had pale veins and porosity. The Darrowmere fragments had glassy specks.</p><p>“Different process?”</p><p>“Maybe. Different heat. Different additive. Different source stone. Different contamination.”</p><p>“Mana behavior?”</p><p>She looked at me. There. Main result.</p><p>“Different.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>“Completely?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Of course. Edrin placed the second sheet.</p><p>“Both suppress a low test line at close range.”</p><p>My pulse increased.</p><p>“Amount?”</p><p>“Sinkstone more.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Depends on batch.”</p><p>“Darrowmere?”</p><p>“Weak.”</p><p>“Residual charge?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Duration?”</p><p>“Darrowmere fragments retained measurable residue from test exposure for twenty-three minutes.”</p><p>“Sinkstone?”</p><p>“Hours in some samples.”</p><p>“Same signature?”</p><p>“That question is too broad.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Same absorption behavior?”</p><p>“Not enough to say.”</p><p>“Release?”</p><p>“Darrowmere sample showed no measurable release under the conditions we used.”</p><p>“Conditions?”</p><p>“Heat, pressure, fresh mana line, dead line, salt wash.”</p><p>Good tests.</p><p>“Sinkstone?”</p><p>“Variable release under two conditions.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you do not need every detail.”</p><p>“I disagree.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The clerk did not look up. Probably had heard this before. I looked at the fragments. Kestrin shale. Processed somehow. Weak suppression. Residual retention. Not same glass. Not same behavior. Could still be related. Could be unrelated. Could be same broad material family with different treatment.</p><p>Could be road debris that happened to be mildly mana-reactive because kestrin shale did that naturally.</p><p>“Untreated control?”</p><p>Edrin nodded. Good.</p><p>“What did it do?”</p><p>“Very weak suppression. No retained residue above our threshold after three minutes.”</p><p>So Darrowmere fragments were not simply raw stone. Probably.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/039/Ch039_Fast-Coverage-003-B01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 39." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“What treatment evidence?”</p><p>“Heat alteration. Surface vitrification. Trace salts.”</p><p>“Which salts?”</p><p>“Mixed.”</p><p>“Intentional?”</p><p>“Unknown.”</p><p>“Could road exposure do it?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Could wagon fire?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Could processing?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could creature biology?”</p><p>She paused.</p><p>“Unknown.”</p><p>Important.</p><p>“Was fragment embedded?”</p><p>“Recovered from wound cavity.”</p><p>“I know. Where in cavity?”</p><p>“Between damaged tissue and a broken rib.”</p><p>“Could have entered with weapon?”</p><p>“No weapon fragment recovered from that wound.”</p><p>“Could have entered when body hit road?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could creature have swallowed it?”</p><p>“Wrong location for that theory.”</p><p>“Could it have been carried in tissue before wound?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Evidence?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. No connection. Not yet. My brain hated that. It wanted shape. Silas Marris sacks. Processed mineral. Darrowmere fragments. Creatures. Watcher. Road. No. Separate until proven. Edrin watched me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“You stopped.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I can make them related very easily.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“That would not make them related.”</p><p>She nodded. No praise. Good.</p><p>“What do you think?”</p><p>I asked. Edrin leaned back.</p><p>“Same cheap stone family.”</p><p>“That is all?”</p><p>“No. Both altered enough to behave differently from untreated control.”</p><p>“Same alteration?”</p><p>“No evidence.”</p><p>“Same maker?”</p><p>“No evidence.”</p><p>“Same purpose?”</p><p>“No evidence.”</p><p>“Same supply chain?”</p><p>“No evidence.”</p><p>“Darrowmere connection to Silas Marris?”</p><p>“No evidence.”</p><p>Each answer hurt in a satisfying way. Clean.</p><p>“What do you know?”</p><p>She pointed at the sheets.</p><p>“That.”</p><p>I smiled. She frowned.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You are pleased.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“The result is useful.”</p><p>“It is inconclusive.”</p><p>“Those are not opposites.”</p><p>Edrin looked at me for a moment. Then nodded once. Maybe. The clerk brought another tray. Three small pieces of untreated kestrin shale. Ugly gray stone. Rubbish. I looked. Future memory shifted. Cheap buffers always lie about what they keep. Still no mechanism. But the base material itself was mildly reactive. Present people knew that. Processing amplified or changed it. Different processes could produce different families of behavior.</p><p>That mattered without connecting Darrowmere to Silas Marris.</p><p>“Who processes kestrin shale in the city?”</p><p>Edrin said, “Several people.” My attention sharpened.</p><p>“There.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Face.”</p><p>Fuck.</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>“Kilns. Ward-material suppliers. Cheap artificing shops. Some metalworkers use treated shale as packing. Glassmakers sometimes buy specific grades.”</p><p>“Names?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I am not giving you a scavenger hunt.”</p><p>“I can find them.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then why not save time?”</p><p>“Because this is Guild evidence.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Can I investigate independently?”</p><p>“You can ask legal questions in public places.”</p><p>“That sounds like permission.”</p><p>“It is a description of law.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>She slid one sheet away.</p><p>“Do not represent yourself as Guild.”</p><p>“I would not.”</p><p>“Do not imply access to seized evidence.”</p><p>“I would not.”</p><p>“Do not tell people Darrowmere creatures contain sinkstone.”</p><p>“I definitely would not.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Because we do not know that.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can I say processed kestrin shale exists?”</p><p>“That is public knowledge.”</p><p>“Can I say it retains mana?”</p><p>“Some treated forms. Also public to people in the trade.”</p><p>Interesting. Less secret than Greg had made it. Future significance had inflated present novelty. Again.</p><p>“What is actually unusual about the seized material?”</p><p>Edrin looked at the sacks.</p><p>“Consistency.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>“Across pellets?”</p><p>“Yes. Within each sack, behavior is unusually narrow for cheap processed shale.”</p><p>Arlo. Too good. No. Different field. But manufacturing consistency mattered.</p><p>“Batch control.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“Professional process.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“Expensive?”</p><p>“Not necessarily.”</p><p>“Skilled?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There. That was the thread. Not monsters. Not conspiracy. Manufacturing. Someone had taught rubbish to remember magic. And done it consistently.</p><p>“What about the three sacks differing?”</p><p>“Still true.”</p><p>“Different exposure history?”</p><p>“Possible.”</p><p>“Different batch treatment?”</p><p>“Possible.”</p><p>“Different storage?”</p><p>“Possible.”</p><p>“Can you distinguish?”</p><p>“Not yet.”</p><p>I wanted to help. I wanted to design tests. I wanted to ask Arlo whether he knew anyone processing kestrin shale. I wanted Antonius’s Silas Marris business contacts. I wanted North Quay records. I wanted Ors. Six directions. Face expanding. Edrin saw.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You do not work here.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>That landed differently now. Not exclusion. Boundary. Also relief. Someone else owned the evidence problem. I could be curious without becoming responsible. Unfamiliar.</p><p>“What do you need from me?”</p><p>I asked. Edrin considered.</p><p>“Nothing today.”</p><p>There it was again. Arlo. Nothing. Edrin. Nothing. The city had become alarmingly capable without me.</p><p>“Then why summon me?”</p><p>“You asked for the comparison.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I told you the result.”</p><p>That simple. I sat back. My ribs hurt. Hands hurt. Mild pressure from the morning Barrier had been gone for hours. Berren was probably being bullied by family into resting. Alden was eating lunch with people who were none of my business. Edrin had evidence. Arlo had regulators. Antonius had ledgers. I had no assigned role.</p><p>“What happens next?” I asked.</p><p>Edrin looked at the tray.</p><p>“We test the three seized batches separately under controlled charge.”</p><p>“And Darrowmere?”</p><p>“Stored.”</p><p>“No more tests?”</p><p>“Not unless there is a reason.”</p><p>That offended my curiosity. It was also correct. The Darrowmere fragment had answered the current question. Same enough to be interesting. Different enough to prove nothing. Stop. I stood. </p><p>Edrin said, “Greg.” </p><p>I waited.</p><p>“If you learn who is producing unusually consistent sinkstone, tell me.”</p><p>There. A role. Small. Legal. Not exclusive.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I want to know.”</p><p>I smiled. She pointed at the door.</p><p>“Go.”</p><p>I went. Outside, afternoon light hit hard after the annex. The city continued. Carts. Bread. A dog barking at a wheel. Someone arguing about onions. I had learned something important. Maybe. Not that Darrowmere connected to Silas Marris. Not that the creatures carried sinkstone. Not that the sacks explained anything east. The opposite, almost. The world had refused to collapse into one answer.</p><p>Good. Annoying. Good. I started toward Arlo’s workshop. Then stopped. My hands hurt. Tomorrow’s spar was already today. No. Spar done. Time had moved. I laughed. A passerby looked at me. Reasonable. Arlo could wait until tomorrow. So could the manufacturer. So could Silas Marris. I went to find dinner.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="037.html">← Chapter 30</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="040.html">Chapter 32 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/022.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 16: The Trainee — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 16</div><h1>THE TRAINEE</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The guild gave me a free seat because Merek Verran was a liar. This was not how they described it. The ink-thumbed clerk called it a hazard adjustment.</p><p>“Your contract was materially misrepresented,” she said. “The guild can refund part of the filing share or issue training credit.”</p><p>“How much training credit?”</p><p>“Eight copper.”</p><p>“How much refund?”</p><p>“Six.”</p><p>“Training.”</p><p>She marked the credit card.</p><p>“Eight copper, expires at the end of the month.”</p><p>“Why offer the worse option?”</p><p>“It costs us less.”</p><p>I stared at her. She stared back.</p><p>“That was refreshingly honest.”</p><p>“It also expires at the end of the month.”</p><p>“Less refreshing.”</p><p>She slid a small card across the desk.</p><p>FIELD FAILURE AND PARTY RECOVERY</p><p>BRONZE CONTINUING PRACTICE</p><p>Third bell to sixth. Hall Two. Instructor: Dema Rusk. I read it twice.</p><p>“Party recovery?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Who teaches this?”</p><p>“It says.”</p><p>“I mean what kind of training?”</p><p>“The kind where you attend and find out.”</p><p>“Can Alden come?”</p><p>“If Alden pays eight copper.”</p><p>“He won’t.”</p><p>“Then probably not.”</p><p>I pocketed the card.</p><p>“Jorren?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She returned to her ledger. I made it three steps.</p><p>“Is there food?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“That should be on the card.”</p><p>“Go away.”</p><p>Hall Two smelled like wet wool, old wood, and twenty-seven adventurers who had all decided they were dry enough.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Continuing Education" decoding="async" height="335" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/022/v28_c22_s01_continuing-education.png" width="302"/></figure><p>The rain had stopped sometime before dawn, but the city was still carrying it. Cloaks hung from pegs. Boots left dark prints across the floor. Two windows had been opened despite the cold because somebody near the back smelled like horse. Rows of benches faced a chalk board. I stopped in the doorway. This was a classroom.</p><p>I had spent decades becoming one of the strongest support adventurers alive, died, returned to my nineteen-year-old body, discovered my magic was pathetic, accumulated debt, found future-important people before they became future-important, and nearly had my face opened by an iron hook. Apparently the second life also contained professional development. A woman at a registration table held out her hand.</p><p>“Card.”</p><p>I gave it to her. She checked my name against a list.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Company?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Party?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She looked up.</p><p>“Independent?”</p><p>“For now.”</p><p>She marked something.</p><p>“Prior recovery certification?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Field medicine?”</p><p>“Informal.”</p><p>“That means no.”</p><p>“That seems harsh.”</p><p>“It means no.”</p><p>She handed me a slate, a piece of chalk, and a folded strip of yellow cloth.</p><p>“What’s this?”</p><p>“Keep it.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You’ll find out.”</p><p>I loved and hated that answer. I found a seat in the third row. The man beside me was perhaps thirty, with a broken nose that had healed sideways and a bronze guild pin polished bright enough to signal either pride or boredom. He looked at my slate.</p><p>“First time?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Third.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Company pays.”</p><p>“That is not a reason to suffer.”</p><p>“It is when they pay me for the day too.”</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>“What’s your name?”</p><p>“Berren.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>I disliked that.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You’re hook boy.”</p><p>I closed my eyes.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“South Canal?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Hook through the wall?”</p><p>“Near the wall.”</p><p>“You fought him through it.”</p><p>“For part of the fight.”</p><p>Berren grinned.</p><p>“Hook boy.”</p><p>“I have made a mistake coming here.”</p><p>“You haven’t met Rusk yet.”</p><p>At exactly third bell, a woman shut the hall doors. Not the instructor. The instructor was already standing at the front. Dema Rusk was broad through the shoulders, maybe fifty, with gray hair cut short and a face that had acquired its lines through repeated disappointment. She wore no armor. A wooden whistle hung from her neck. On the board behind her were four words.</p><p>STOP.</p><p>COUNT.</p><p>MOVE.</p><p>DECIDE.</p><p>She looked at us.</p><p>“Who here has recovered a party member under active threat?”</p><p>Hands went up. Mine did not. I had recovered hundreds. Not in this body. Not under this certification. Interesting question.</p><p>“Who has been recovered?”</p><p>More hands. Mine went halfway up before I stopped. Old body. Current body. Was that yes? Rusk saw me.</p><p>“You.”</p><p>“Complicated.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The room laughed. She pointed at the board.</p><p>“Today is not about winning fights. It is not about healing. It is not about courage. If you want courage, go to a tavern and pay someone to sing at you.”</p><p>A few people smiled. Rusk did not.</p><p>“This is about what happens after the plan fails.”</p><p>That got quieter.</p><p>“Most Bronze deaths do not happen because nobody knew how to swing a sword. They happen because something changed and the party kept executing the old plan.”</p><p>I sat straighter. That was good. Annoyingly good. Rusk tapped STOP.</p><p>“First failure. You do not stop.”</p><p>COUNT.</p><p>“Second failure. You do not know what you still have.”</p><p>MOVE.</p><p>“Third. You move the wrong person, the wrong direction, at the wrong time.”</p><p>DECIDE.</p><p>“Fourth. Nobody decides what happens next.”</p><p>A man in the first row raised his hand.</p><p>“What if the leader’s down?”</p><p>“Then somebody else decides.”</p><p>“What if nobody knows enough?”</p><p>“Then somebody decides badly.”</p><p>A few people shifted. Rusk said, “A bad decision everyone can follow is often safer than five excellent decisions executed separately.” I felt something old move in me. Not memory. Recognition. There were exceptions. Many. I could build twelve objections before she finished the sentence: terrain, magical interference, split objectives, unknown threat, specialized roles, command failure, deliberate decentralization. All true. All useless to a room full of Bronze adventurers learning how not to die in a ditch.</p><p>I shut up. Berren glanced at my untouched slate.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You stopped writing.” Rusk divided us into groups of four. My group contained Berren, a young woman named Lio who carried a bow taller than she was, and a bald man named Cass who announced within thirty seconds that he was a shieldman. Not that he used a shield. That he was a shieldman. It was apparently metaphysical. Our first exercise was insulting.</p><p>One person lay on the floor. One person was injured. One was disoriented. One was functional. Rusk blew the whistle. We had to get everyone across a chalk line. No magic. No weapons. No running. I was functional. Of course. Berren lay down. Lio clutched one arm. Cass spun once in place because apparently that represented disorientation.</p><p>I said, “Cass, take Berren’s shoulders. Lio, good arm under his knees. I’ll guide.” Cass said, “I can carry him.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I’m stronger than her.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So I carry him.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because if you fall, we lose both of you.”</p><p>Cass frowned. Rusk blew the whistle again.</p><p>“Dead,” she said.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“All four.”</p><p>“We were talking.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That seems unfair.”</p><p>“Threat disagreed.”</p><p>Reset. Second attempt. I gave fewer words. We crossed. Rusk marked something on her slate. I wanted to see it. She turned it away. Second exercise added a fifth person represented by a sandbag.</p><p>“Equipment,” Rusk said.</p><p>“What kind?” someone asked.</p><p>“Expensive.”</p><p>The room laughed.</p><p>“Leave it,” she said.</p><p>Half the room objected. Good. That was the point. Our sandbag died heroically. Cass mourned it. Third exercise gave us six wooden disks representing spells, supplies, injuries, and time. Now I was interested. Too interested. I began rearranging them. Berren slapped my hand. I stared at him.</p><p>“Too fast,” he said.</p><p>I had created a monster.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Rusk said wait for the whistle.”</p><p>“I was organizing.”</p><p>“You were cheating.”</p><p>“I was preparing.”</p><p>“Hook boy cheats at school.”</p><p>“I hate you.”</p><p>The whistle blew. We turned the disks.</p><p>HEALER: CONSCIOUS, NO MANA.</p><p>FIGHTER: LEG INJURY.</p><p>SCOUT: MISSING.</p><p>EXIT: UNKNOWN.</p><p>THREAT: NOT VISIBLE.</p><p>TIME: THREE MINUTES.</p><p>My mind opened. Too wide. Find scout? No. Establish exit. Inventory mobility. Healer useful without mana? Knowledge, hands. Fighter can move? Leg injury unspecified. Threat not visible means not absent. Three minutes until what? Unknown.</p><p>“What does three minutes mean?” I called.</p><p>Rusk said, “You have three minutes.”</p><p>“Until what?”</p><p>“Decide without knowing.”</p><p>Excellent. Terrible. Cass said, “Find scout.”</p><p>“No,” I said.</p><p>Lio said, “Exit first.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Berren pointed to the fighter disk.</p><p>“Can he walk?”</p><p>Rusk said, “With help.”</p><p>“Then move,” I said.</p><p>“Where?” Cass asked.</p><p>We had no exit. Good. I smiled. Cass stared.</p><p>“Why are you happy?”</p><p>“This is a good problem.”</p><p>“It’s a terrible problem.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Lio said, “Backtrack.” </p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“We know where we came from.”</p><p>There it was. Not clever. Not perfect. Known.</p><p>“Backtrack,” I said.</p><p>Cass frowned. “Scout?”</p><p>“Mark and return if we can.”</p><p>“What if he’s alive?”</p><p>“What if all four of us die looking?”</p><p>Cass did not like that. Neither did I. That mattered. Rusk blew the whistle.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>She went group by group. Some searched for the scout. Some split. One tried to fortify in place. One spent two minutes arguing whether the missing scout counted as abandoned. Rusk did not tell us the right answer. Instead she asked what information each choice assumed. That was better. Much better. When she reached us, she looked at Lio.</p><p>“Why backtrack?”</p><p>“Known route.”</p><p>“Risk?”</p><p>“Threat may be behind us.”</p><p>“Greg?”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“How do you know my name?”</p><p>“Registration exists.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Risk?”</p><p>“Moving the injured fighter costs speed. Backtracking may take us toward whatever separated the scout. We also don't know whether the known route is still open.”</p><p>“Then why choose it?”</p><p>“Because unknown exit plus unknown threat plus missing scout gives us too many unresolved variables. Known route removes one.”</p><p>Rusk nodded.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>Fine. I wanted more than fine. That was embarrassing. At fourth bell, we took a break. There was no food. I complained to Berren. He produced dried apple from his pocket.</p><p>“You knew.”</p><p>“Third time.”</p><p>“This is corruption.”</p><p>“This is experience.”</p><p>Everyone in the city had agreed on phrases without me. I bought two pieces from him for one copper.</p><p>“Company pays you and you sell food to people who didn’t bring any.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You’re going to be rich.”</p><p>“No. I’m Bronze.”</p><p>Fair. The hall doors opened. A guild runner entered. He did not look frightened. That was why I noticed him. Frightened runners were easy. This one looked focused. He crossed to Rusk and spoke quietly. She listened. Asked one question. He answered. She looked toward the registration woman. The woman left. Training resumed. Nothing happened. That was the first sign. The fifth exercise was physical.</p><p>Yellow cloth meant injured leg. We tied it above the knee and had to move through a line of benches while another group rolled padded balls at us. Not hard. Not dangerous. Humiliating. My current body was better at being nineteen than it had been three weeks ago. That did not make it good. I ducked one ball. Caught another. Tried to pivot around a bench.</p><p>My right foot planted. My body expected reinforcement that did not exist. I stumbled. Berren caught my coat.</p><p>“Got you.”</p><p>“I had it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I was recovering.”</p><p>“You were becoming floor.”</p><p>We kept moving. A ball struck my shoulder. </p><p>Lio shouted, “Leave him.”</p><p>“Correct,” Rusk called.</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>“Excuse me?”</p><p>“You’re ambulatory.”</p><p>“I was hit.”</p><p>“With cloth.”</p><p>“It was emotionally significant.”</p><p>“Move.”</p><p>We moved. Halfway through, Cass went down deliberately. Now we had a choice. </p><p>I started toward him. </p><p>Lio said, “Line first.” </p><p>I stopped. She was right. Again. This was becoming irritating. </p><p>We crossed the line, established the safe side, then went back two together. Rusk blew the whistle.</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>I looked at Lio.</p><p>“How long have you been Bronze?”</p><p>“Seven months.”</p><p>“Party?”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/022/Ch022_Fast-Coverage-003-A14.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 22." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“Usually my sister and two cousins.”</p><p>“What does your sister do?”</p><p>“Bosses us around.”</p><p>“That may be a class feature.”</p><p>Lio smiled.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>At fifth bell, another runner came. Different runner. Wet boots. No rain outside. Mud from somewhere else. He went directly to Rusk. This conversation lasted longer. The room noticed. Not everyone. Enough. </p><p>Rusk asked, “Confirmed?” The runner said something too quiet to hear. Rusk looked at the doors. Then at us.</p><p>“Ten-minute break.”</p><p>That was wrong. We had not been scheduled for one. People stood. Conversation rose. I stayed seated. Berren stretched.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Face.”</p><p>“Runner.”</p><p>“What about him?”</p><p>“Wet boots.”</p><p>Berren looked toward the door.</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“It stopped raining.”</p><p>“Ground’s wet.”</p><p>“Not here.”</p><p>He stared at me.</p><p>“You need hobbies.”</p><p>I had hobbies. Most were currently impossible. The registration woman returned carrying a stack of paper. She and Rusk spoke. Two other guild staff entered. One began taking names from a board near the wall. Not ours. Companies. Available parties. I stood. Berren grabbed my sleeve.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Water.”</p><p>“You have some.”</p><p>“More water.”</p><p>“You’re lying.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He let go. I walked toward the hall door. Rusk stepped in front of it.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“This is becoming a city motto.”</p><p>“Break is inside.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I said so.”</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>Her expression did not change.</p><p>“Something that is not currently your assignment.”</p><p>That phrasing was familiar.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Road?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Town?”</p><p>Her eyes moved. Tiny. Enough. I knew better than to spend it. Mostly. I returned to my bench. That surprised her. It surprised me too. </p><p>Cass said, “What’s happening?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Didn’t ask?”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“I still don’t know.”</p><p>Berren handed me another piece of dried apple. Free. That was how serious things had become. The ten-minute break lasted seventeen. When Rusk resumed, two seats were empty. A pair from the back row had been called out. She did not explain. The final exercise began with a map. A bad map. One road. One stream. Three buildings. A bridge. A wooded slope.</p><p>Rusk placed four markers near the buildings.</p><p>“Your party is returning from a routine escort.”</p><p>She placed six more markers on the road.</p><p>“Civilians.”</p><p>Then three at the bridge.</p><p>“More civilians.”</p><p>Then five behind them.</p><p>“More.”</p><p>Someone said, “From what?” </p><p>Rusk looked at him.</p><p>“Does it matter yet?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“If we know what they’re running from.”</p><p>“You don’t.”</p><p>A murmur moved through the room. Rusk continued.</p><p>“The civilians are moving toward you. They disagree about what happened. One says animals. One says monsters. One says bandits using trained animals. One says the town watch told everyone to leave. One says nobody told anyone anything.”</p><p>My skin tightened. Not memory. Attention. Rusk said, “You have four party members. One cart. Two injured civilians already aboard. Your contract is to deliver the cart.” </p><p>Cass raised his hand.</p><p>“To where?”</p><p>“Here.”</p><p>She tapped the far edge of the map.</p><p>“Through them?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What town?” I asked.</p><p>Rusk looked at me.</p><p>“This is an exercise.”</p><p>That was not an answer. The room had changed. Everyone knew it. Not because of the map. Rusk was using something fresh. Berren leaned toward me.</p><p>“Face.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>Rusk gave us five minutes. The groups began arguing. Go forward. Turn back. Question civilians. Protect cart. Abandon cart. Send scout. Do not send scout. Find authority. There was no authority. Good. Bad. Real. I looked at the map. The stream crossed the road before the bridge. Wooded slope to the north. Three buildings clustered south.</p><p>“What are the civilians carrying?” I asked.</p><p>Rusk looked at me.</p><p>“Whatever they could.”</p><p>“Animals?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Wagons?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Children?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Uniform direction?”</p><p>“Mostly.”</p><p>“Any injuries?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“From what?”</p><p>“Different answers.”</p><p>There. That was the problem. Not monsters. Information. The first useful fact was that people were leaving. Everything else was story. I looked at my group.</p><p>“We don’t go through them,” I said.</p><p>Cass said, “Contract.”</p><p>“Cart doesn’t move through a frightened crowd,” I said.</p><p>Berren nodded.</p><p>“Turn?” Berren asked.</p><p>“Not yet,” I said.</p><p>Lio pointed at the buildings.</p><p>“Get off the road,” Lio said.</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>“Then what?” Lio asked.</p><p>I looked at the map.</p><p>“Count,” I said.</p><p>Rusk heard. Her eyes flicked toward the board at the front.</p><p>STOP.</p><p>COUNT.</p><p>MOVE.</p><p>DECIDE.</p><p>Damn her.</p><p>“Count what?” Cass asked.</p><p>“People. Injuries. Direction. Who saw what personally. Who heard it. How long ago. Which road they used.”</p><p>Berren said, “That’s a lot.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“We have a cart.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“We’re Bronze.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What if the monsters arrive while you’re interviewing refugees?”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“Then we learn something.”</p><p>He laughed once.</p><p>“Terrible answer.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Rusk blew the whistle. Exercise over. Nobody relaxed. She stood at the front.</p><p>“For those of you who noticed, yes. The scenario was adapted from a report received during class.”</p><p>The room went silent. There it was. Fire. Not literal. Not yet.</p><p>“Where?” someone asked.</p><p>Rusk looked toward the registration table. The woman there had stopped pretending to organize paper.</p><p>“Darrowmere,” Rusk said.</p><p>I knew the name. Not from the future. From a road sign. A market ledger. Somebody at Antonius’s warehouse had mentioned wool from there. A town east and north. Close enough for carts. Far enough that I had never been.</p><p>“What happened?” Lio asked.</p><p>“We do not know.”</p><p>A man in the back said, “You said monsters.”</p><p>“I said civilians are saying monsters.”</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“We do not know.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>“We do not know.”</p><p>“Is the town evacuated?”</p><p>“We do not know.”</p><p>The repetition changed the room. People wanted facts. The guild had uncertainty. Rusk continued.</p><p>“What we know is that travelers began arriving at North Gate shortly after fourth bell. More have followed. Some are from Darrowmere. Some are from farms along the road. At least one wagon has injured people. The city watch is managing the gate. The guild has been asked for additional hands.”</p><p>“How bad?” Cass asked.</p><p>Rusk looked at him.</p><p>“That is another version of a question we cannot answer yet.”</p><p>Someone swore softly. Outside the hall, a bell rang. Not a memory bell. A real one. Two short strokes. Pause. Two more. </p><p>People looked toward the door. </p><p>Berren said, “Gate call.” </p><p>Rusk nodded.</p><p>“Training is ending early.”</p><p>Nobody complained about the missing hour. That was impressive.</p><p>“Those already assigned today remain assigned unless recalled. Unassigned Bronze do not run to North Gate because you heard the word monsters.”</p><p>Several people looked offended. Correctly accused.</p><p>“You report to the board. You take instructions. You do not become another problem.”</p><p>Her eyes found mine. This was discriminatory. Also reasonable. The doors opened. Noise entered. Not panic. Activity: boots, voices, a clerk calling company names, someone asking for blankets, someone else asking how many beds the guild infirmary had.</p><p>The world had become larger while we sat in a classroom moving wooden disks. I stood. My first impulse was North Gate. My second was Antonius. Freight. Roads. Darrowmere goods. People arriving meant carts, food, rooms, money, missing workers, stories. My third was Alden. Of course it was. My fourth was Hessa. My fifth was the board. Too many. I stopped. Rusk was collecting slates.</p><p>I handed her mine.</p><p>“What do I do?”</p><p>She looked at me. It was a stupid question. A useful one.</p><p>“Are you assigned?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then check the board.”</p><p>“After?”</p><p>“Do what it says.”</p><p>“What if it says nothing?”</p><p>“Then you are not needed yet.”</p><p>I hated that answer. She saw.</p><p>“Recovery starts before the disaster reaches you,” she said. “Sometimes that means staying out of the road.”</p><p>I looked past her. The hall emptied around us.</p><p>“What if they need more people later?”</p><p>“Then you will still exist later.”</p><p>Also irritating. Also good. I nodded. At the board, three new postings were being written.</p><p>NORTH GATE SUPPORT.</p><p>INFIRMARY CARRY.</p><p>ROAD INTAKE RUNNERS.</p><p>No monster contract. No rescue expedition. No glorious emergency. People needed bodies moved, names recorded, water carried, messages run. I read each posting. Then I read them again. A voice behind me said, “Greg?” Alden.</p><p>His replacement escort had apparently returned early. Mud marked both boots to the ankle. His red scarf was tied at his wrist again. He looked at the board.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“Darrowmere.”</p><p>“What happened there?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>He looked at me. That answer had become easier. Not easy. Easier. Behind him, two women entered the guild supporting an older man between them. Travel dust covered all three. Not rain. One woman was crying. The other was singing under her breath. I could not hear the words. Only the tune. Simple. Four notes. Again. Four notes. The older man snapped, “Stop that.”</p><p>She stopped. Alden looked at me. I had gone still. Not because I knew the song. I did not. I knew the shape of songs that started this way. One frightened person repeating something because silence was worse. By tomorrow there would be words. By next week there might be verses. Most would be wrong. Some would survive longer than facts.</p><p>“What?” Alden asked.</p><p>I looked at the board. NORTH GATE SUPPORT needed six Bronze. Four names already filled the line. I picked up the pen.</p><p>“Nothing yet,” I said.</p><p>Then I signed.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="019.html">← Chapter 15</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="023.html">Chapter 17 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/077.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 62: The Sorter — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 62</div><h1>THE SORTER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The morning wound check took twelve minutes. I timed it because I was bored. Nerin did not appreciate this.</p><p>“Eleven fifty-two.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“From unwrap to rewrap.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Data.”</p><p>“On what?”</p><p>“Your efficiency.”</p><p>“Get out.”</p><p>The limb was less swollen than last night. Incision dry. No heat. No spreading redness. No new drainage. The dark/questionable margin that had occupied so much of my attention a few days ago was now mostly just part of the healing edge. Still watched. Not gone.</p><p>Sera's instruction through Nerin was boring:</p><p>Ground-floor activity fine. Use transport. No repeated stairs for entertainment. One controlled ascent later only if swelling remained modest. Wound check tomorrow. I asked whether sitting for two hours counted as activity.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Dangerous?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Useful answer.”</p><p>“Depends how you sit.”</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>Knee position. Pressure. Shift periodically. Do not let residual limb hang unsupported too long if it increases throbbing. Simple. I could visit Holl. I did not need permission from Sera to think. Apparently I needed instructions for chairs now. Fine. The cart cost two copper. I paid. No protest. Holl had chairs. This improved my opinion of him immediately. Not enough chairs.</p><p>One. Still. I took it.</p><p>“Morning,” Holl said.</p><p>“Morning.”</p><p>“You look different.”</p><p>“Hair?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Rude.”</p><p>He looked at the crutches. Then at my face.</p><p>“Can you work?”</p><p>“Not why I'm here.”</p><p>“Good. I don't have work.”</p><p>Excellent start. His place smelled like stone dust, damp wood, and the faint mineral bitterness I associated with cheap kestrin. Not Arlo's workshop. Less metal. More trays. Holl had a long bench against one wall with shallow wooden boxes divided into squares. Pieces of pale gray stone sat in some compartments. Others held brass tags. A balance. A mana bead fixture. Reference tiles.</p><p>A little clamp. Nothing dramatic. Commercial. Good.</p><p>Duration unknown. I had not asked because this was not a job. Progress.</p><p>“What do you actually sell?” I asked.</p><p>Holl stopped.</p><p>“That your greeting now?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He wiped his hands.</p><p>“Kestrin?”</p><p>“Your business.”</p><p>“I sort and certify cheap suppression stock for people who don't want to pay for better stone,” Holl said.</p><p>There.</p><p>“Certify what?” I asked.</p><p>“Range.”</p><p>“Not exact value.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“How wide?”</p><p>“Depends what they buy.”</p><p>He pointed to three trays.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Holl and Greg working over the sorting and testing pieces." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/077/svgPLG_Ch77_Holls-Sorting-Test.png"/></figure><p>“Lamp shops want one thing. Ward repair crews another. Cheap cabinet lining another.”</p><p>“Kestrin in cabinets?”</p><p>“Small lockboxes. Not good ones.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because people are cheap.”</p><p>Universal force.</p><p>“What do they need from the stone?”</p><p>“Enough suppression to matter. Not so much variation that one piece behaves like another material entirely.”</p><p>“So bands.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What do you measure?”</p><p>“Response against reference bead. Recovery after removal. Sometimes repeat exposure if customer pays.”</p><p>That last part made my brain move. Do not. General. Holl continued.</p><p>“Mostly I buy lots cheap, reject obvious bad pieces, test samples, then sort.”</p><p>“Samples or every piece?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>There.</p><p>“What are you trying to make faster?”</p><p>He smiled.</p><p>“Finally.”</p><p>I leaned back. Chair stable. Good.</p><p>“Tell me.”</p><p>He brought over a tray. Twenty pieces maybe. Thumb-sized to palm-sized.</p><p>“Dorrin lot.”</p><p>I recognized nothing specific. Good.</p><p>“Raw?”</p><p>“Sorted raw. Untreated.”</p><p>“You treat?”</p><p>“Sometimes. Mostly I send treatment out or sell to people who do their own.”</p><p>“Bale?”</p><p>“Sometimes buys finished sorted stock. Sometimes brings treated stock for checking.”</p><p>Known. Good.</p><p>“So your fast test problem is raw acceptance?”</p><p>“Partly.”</p><p>“Treatment adjustment?”</p><p>“Not usually mine.”</p><p>“Final sorting?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Two of three. Good.</p><p>“What costs time?”</p><p>“Setting each piece. Reading bead. Waiting. Recording. Resetting reference.”</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>“About half a minute for rough band if stone behaves. Longer if it doesn't settle.”</p><p>Half minute. Commercially enormous at volume.</p><p>“How many pieces?”</p><p>“Lot like this? Hundreds. Bigger, thousands.”</p><p>There.</p><p>“Every piece?”</p><p>“Not usually.”</p><p>“Why not?”</p><p>“Because then cheap stone stops being cheap.”</p><p>Exactly.</p><p>“So you sample.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And if sample looks too broad?”</p><p>“Reject lot, renegotiate, or sort more deeply.”</p><p>“False rejection cost?”</p><p>Holl looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“If your quick test says bad lot and lot is actually usable, what does that cost?”</p><p>“Money.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>He rolled eyes.</p><p>“Depends price. Sometimes I can buy cheaper because seller wants it gone.”</p><p>“False acceptance?”</p><p>“Worse.”</p><p>“Customer complaint.”</p><p>“Or return.”</p><p>“Or failure in use.”</p><p>“For cheap uses, usually complaint before catastrophe.”</p><p>Good. Not high stakes. Mostly.</p><p>“So faster test doesn't need exact measurement.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What decision?” I asked.</p><p>“Which pile,” Holl said.</p><p>There. Simple.</p><p>“Accept. Reject. Test more.”</p><p>Holl nodded.</p><p>“And for individual pieces?”</p><p>“Sell band A, B, C. Reject.”</p><p>Classification. Not exact property.</p><p>“How many bands?”</p><p>“Usually three.”</p><p>“Why three?”</p><p>“Because four doesn't pay.”</p><p>Excellent. I laughed. He looked pleased. There. Economics. Not physics.</p><p>“What have you tried?”</p><p>Holl brought out a brass frame. Two reference tiles fixed at opposite ends. Mana bead suspended in middle. A sliding tray beneath.</p><p>“You move piece under. Compare bead displacement against references.”</p><p>“Simultaneous?”</p><p>“Nearly.”</p><p>“Faster than reset?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Problem?”</p><p>“Geometry.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Piece size changes distance.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Shape.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Moisture.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Position.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Operator.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Temperature?”</p><p>“Less than you think at this rough level.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“What do you need?” I asked.</p><p>“Something a worker can use without me,” Holl said.</p><p>There. Not fastest possible. Transferable.</p><p>“Training time?”</p><p>“An hour, maybe two.”</p><p>“Decision error?”</p><p>“I'd tolerate one band wrong sometimes. Not reject good as bad too often. Definitely not sell weak as strong too often.”</p><p>Asymmetric errors. Good.</p><p>“So false acceptance worse than false rejection.”</p><p>“For upper band, yes.”</p><p>“Could bias thresholds.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He had thought of it. Competent.</p><p>“Why haven't you?”</p><p>“Because the bead reading drifts with piece position enough that biasing threshold doesn't fix operator inconsistency.”</p><p>There. Actual problem. I leaned forward. My residual limb bumped chair edge. Pain. I stopped. Adjusted. Holl waited. No comment. Good.</p><p>“Can you constrain position?”</p><p>“Pieces aren't same shape.”</p><p>“Constrain one surface?”</p><p>“Which surface?”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>He smiled.</p><p>“That's where I got.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“What about mass?”</p><p>“Correlates badly.”</p><p>“Thickness?”</p><p>“Better. Still not enough.”</p><p>“Volume?”</p><p>“Too slow.”</p><p>“Water displacement?”</p><p>“Wet stone changes behavior.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>He had tried. Good.</p><p>“Destructive?”</p><p>“For raw acceptance, maybe.”</p><p>Holl nodded slowly.</p><p>“I can break samples.”</p><p>“There.”</p><p>“For final sorting, no.”</p><p>“Different tests.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>This was the thing. One faster cheap test might be wrong question.</p><p>“What if raw acceptance uses destructive sample test and final sorting uses rough nondestructive banding?”</p><p>“That is already two tools.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I asked for one.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Cheap.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Could one fixture have two modes?”</p><p>“More parts.”</p><p>“Still maybe cheaper than labor.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>There. Maybe. I looked at the brass frame. Not touching.</p><p>“Can I?”</p><p>Holl handed it over. Good. I held frame on my lap. Light enough. The sliding tray had side rails. Reference tiles fixed. Mana bead hung from a small arch.</p><p>“Why slide piece?”</p><p>“So bead stays fixed.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“Why flat tray?”</p><p>“Because stone sits on things.”</p><p>“Shape changes height.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What if reference is not absolute position?”</p><p>Holl looked.</p><p>“Meaning?”</p><p>I did not know yet. Danger. Fine.</p><p>“If operator doesn't read bead displacement directly. If operator only asks whether it crosses a mark.”</p><p>“I tried marks.”</p><p>“On bead path?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Still position drift.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“What if you deliberately exaggerate difference?”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>There. I thought. Barrier? No. Magic design? Maybe. No casting. Also Holl's tool. Could use two references bracketing threshold. Already.</p><p>“Could make the test answer one threshold at a time.”</p><p>Holl frowned.</p><p>“Instead of three bands at once?”</p><p>“Yes. First pass: strong enough for upper? Second: strong enough for middle? But then more passes.”</p><p>“Slower.”</p><p>“Unless first pass removes most.”</p><p>“Lot distribution matters.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He had records.</p><p>“What's typical distribution?”</p><p>“Depends lot.”</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>He pulled ledger. Good. Not secret. Commercial. We looked. Recent lots. Rough percentages. Some mostly middle. Some broad. One mostly weak. One tight around middle. Interesting. Do not think seized. Too late. Internal narrowness. No. Different. Ordinary commercial lots could sometimes be tight. Not nearly same issue. Stay.</p><p>“If most pieces middle, threshold sequence could reduce passes.”</p><p>Holl said, “Weak versus usable first.”</p><p>“Then upper among usable,” I said.</p><p>“Yes,” Holl said.</p><p>“Two binary decisions.”</p><p>“Instead of one three-band reading.”</p><p>“Could be easier for operator.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>There. We both stared at fixture. No revelation. Good.</p><p>“How do you set threshold?”</p><p>“Reference tile.”</p><p>“One?”</p><p>“For each.”</p><p>“Could physically swap reference.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Worker doesn't interpret magnitude. Only left/right of reference.”</p><p>“That's what I want.”</p><p>“Then why bead in middle?”</p><p>Holl looked offended.</p><p>“Because it shows response.”</p><p>“I know. Could make response comparative mechanically.”</p><p>“Magic isn't mechanical.”</p><p>“No, but display can be.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>I did not know. Good.</p><p>“Maybe two beads.”</p><p>He stopped.</p><p>“Same ambient?”</p><p>“Same fixture.”</p><p>“One reference stone, one test stone?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Compare beads.”</p><p>“Operator asks which moves more.”</p><p>“Beads vary.”</p><p>“Matched pair?”</p><p>“Cost.”</p><p>“Calibration.”</p><p>“Cost.”</p><p>“Still.”</p><p>Holl took frame back. He was thinking. Good.</p><p>“Two channels also interact.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Could shield.”</p><p>“With what?”</p><p>“Kestrin.”</p><p>We both laughed. That was stupid. Maybe not. No.</p><p>“Metal divider?”</p><p>“Mana field doesn't care about thin brass enough.”</p><p>“Distance.”</p><p>“Bigger fixture.”</p><p>“Cost.”</p><p>There. Tradeoffs. Good. No miracle. Holl put frame down.</p><p>“What did you come here for?”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“This.”</p><p>“No. Why now?”</p><p>Ah.</p><p>“Edrin reminded me of testing.”</p><p>Careful. True. Not details.</p><p>“What testing?”</p><p>“General.”</p><p>He stared.</p><p>“Guild?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Also true.</p><p>“Can't say?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. Holl nodded. No pressure.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>Boundary survived. My brain immediately wanted to ask whether he had ever seen extremely narrow commercial lots. Could. General? Maybe. Dangerously close. Do not. Not necessary for Holl's problem. I did not ask. That was harder than expected.</p><p>“Your faster test,” I said. “What would success actually be?”</p><p>Holl thought.</p><p>“Worker sorts twice as much in a day with no meaningful increase in customer returns.”</p><p>There. Excellent.</p><p>“That's better than faster.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you track returns by band?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“By worker?”</p><p>He paused.</p><p>“Not consistently.”</p><p>There.</p><p>“Start.”</p><p>He frowned.</p><p>“That doesn't make test faster.”</p><p>“No. Tells you whether operator is actually problem.”</p><p>“I know operator is problem.”</p><p>“Which operator?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Fuck.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Maybe fixture drift. Maybe training. Maybe one worker. Maybe all.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/077/Ch077_Fast-Coverage-003-B22.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 77." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“I have three people.”</p><p>“Then cheap experiment.”</p><p>He was already reaching for ledger. Good.</p><p>“Don't redesign tool yet.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Who are you?”</p><p>“Recovering.”</p><p>“Badly.”</p><p>“Medium.”</p><p>He pulled another ledger. Worker marks existed on some batches. Not all. Enough to start maybe. We spent twenty minutes reconstructing three recent lots. Not perfect. One worker had more upper-band returns. Maybe. Small sample. Another worked slower but fewer returns. Third almost no data. No conclusion. Good.</p><p>“Need prospective record,” Holl said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Same lot split between workers.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Same fixture?”</p><p>“If you want operator.”</p><p>“Different fixtures if you want fixture.”</p><p>“I have one.”</p><p>“Convenient.”</p><p>He glared. I smiled. This was fun. I forgot my leg. Actually. For maybe ten minutes. Then I stood. Or tried. Both hands went toward table. Crutches were against wall. Right. Holl caught one before it fell.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“I am leaving.”</p><p>“Then use sticks.”</p><p>“Crutches.”</p><p>“Fancy sticks.”</p><p>I hated him. I retrieved them. Standing took more effort than arrival. Shoulders tired. Right thigh okay. Residual limb aching from sitting too long with knee bent. Different problem.</p><p>“How long was I here?”</p><p>Holl looked at clock.</p><p>“Two hours.”</p><p>Fuck.</p><p>“Thought one.”</p><p>“You talk.”</p><p>“My shop.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Chair helped?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>There it was. I pointed. He looked confused. Fine.</p><p>“Pay?”</p><p>Holl asked.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You did useful work.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“No?”</p><p>“I came because you invited testing conversation.”</p><p>“And you spent two hours.”</p><p>“Not contracted.”</p><p>He considered.</p><p>“Food?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He handed me two small meat pies from shelf. Cold.</p><p>“Consulting fee.”</p><p>“That is not a fee.”</p><p>“Then don't eat them.”</p><p>I put both in coat pocket. Carrying solved.</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“Come back after I have records.”</p><p>There. Not schedule.</p><p>“Ask me.”</p><p>He smiled.</p><p>“Don't reserve it?”</p><p>Fuck. Carrow.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>*</p><p>Before I left, Holl made me watch one of his workers use the current fixture. Her name was Iris. Maybe twenty-five. Short hair. Stone dust on both sleeves. She had clearly done this more than I had. Good.</p><p>Holl gave her ten pieces from a tray and said nothing else. She slid first piece beneath bead. Waited. Compared. Brass tag into middle box. Second. Upper. Third. She rotated it once before testing.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“Flat side.”</p><p>There. Operator already compensating.</p><p>“Always same side?”</p><p>“No. Flattest.”</p><p>Subjective. Good. Fourth piece rocked. She wedged a tiny wood chip under one edge. I looked at Holl. He looked at me. Exactly. Position problem. Iris tested. Middle. Fifth. Weak. Sixth. She frowned. Retested after wiping tray. Different result.</p><p>“Dust?” I asked.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Maybe?”</p><p>Iris shrugged.</p><p>“Could've sat wrong first time.”</p><p>There. Fixture. Operator. Surface. Dust. No single variable. Good.</p><p>“How long have you done this?”</p><p>“Eight months.”</p><p>“Fast?”</p><p>“Faster than him.”</p><p>She pointed at Holl. Holl looked offended.</p><p>“More accurate?”</p><p>“Depends who asks.”</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>“What would make this easier?”</p><p>I asked. Iris answered immediately.</p><p>“Stop making me decide close ones.”</p><p>There. Not faster. Decision burden.</p><p>“What do you do now?”</p><p>“Put aside.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>“Bad lot, many. Good lot, few.”</p><p>“Then Holl retests?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Holl nodded.</p><p>“That pile is my time.”</p><p>Ah. Fast worker sorting could shift ambiguous cases to expert. Two-stage system already existed informally.</p><p>“What if tool only made obvious cases faster and left close ones for you?”</p><p>Holl looked.</p><p>“That is what it does now.”</p><p>“No. Worker still spends time deciding whether close.”</p><p>Iris nodded.</p><p>“True.”</p><p>“Could mark an uncertainty zone.”</p><p>Holl frowned.</p><p>“Then more pieces come to me.”</p><p>“Maybe. But worker throughput rises.”</p><p>“My throughput falls.”</p><p>“Total system.”</p><p>There. He hated phrase. Good.</p><p>“How many ambiguous?”</p><p>“Track it,” I said.</p><p>Iris said, “Please.” Holl glared at both of us. Excellent. No invention. Measurement first. I liked Iris. Not enough to make her recurring. She returned to work. Holl said, “You are expensive in notebooks.”</p><p>“You paid me in pie.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>The cart ride back was excellent because I sat. This was now an opinion I held strongly. My arms had done enough. Holl's problem moved in my head. Not sinkstone. Mostly. Binary thresholds. Operator variation. Commercial error asymmetry.</p><p>Throughput measured as usable correct sorting per labor day, not seconds per piece. Good. Edrin's problem sat adjacent. Measurement and selection. Could faster sorting explain narrow batches? Maybe. No. Do not infer from existence of generic sorting problem to seized chain. Different evidence. I knew that. My brain did not care. I wrote nothing in cart. Also progress.</p><p>*</p><p>At lodging, the keeper had put my current notebook on kitchen table.</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“You left it.”</p><p>“I had it.”</p><p>“You had the small one.”</p><p>Right. Two notebooks. Bad system. I ate one meat pie. Cold. Good.</p><p>“Work?”</p><p>keeper asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You got paid in pie.”</p><p>“Not work.”</p><p>“Sounds like work.”</p><p>“It was consultation.”</p><p>She stared. I stopped. Oh. That word. Maybe. No. Not profession. Not job. Conversation.</p><p>“Pie.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She took half of second pie. Theft.</p><p>*</p><p>Sera's note allowed one controlled ascent if swelling remained modest. It was not modest. Not terrible. More than morning. Two hours sitting plus crutches plus travel. No. I did not attempt stairs. No spotter anyway. Good. Storage room again. My room remained upstairs. Fine.</p><p>I was tired enough not to care much. That itself felt like information.</p><p>*</p><p>Before Edrin arrived, I tried to move the chair from kitchen to storage room. Why? Because I wanted it there. No deeper reason. I stood. Two crutches. Chair. Right. Could drag chair with crutch tip? Bad. Could hook chair leg with right foot while seated? Maybe. Could ask keeper? She was outside. I stared at chair. Then left it. Five minutes later keeper returned.</p><p>“Can you move that?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She moved it. No commentary. I hated how easy this was. Then I remembered Holl's worker and ambiguous pile. Not every task needed one person from start to finish. No. That was almost philosophy. Chair moved. Enough. I sat in it. Better. Edrin came near evening. Not because Holl. She had Guild business nearby. Apparently. Carrow. She saw me downstairs.</p><p>“Did you go?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Holl?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What did you tell him?”</p><p>“Nothing protected.”</p><p>“What did you ask?”</p><p>“What he actually sells.”</p><p>Good. Her face said good without saying it. Excellent. I summarized Holl's business. Sort and certify cheap suppression stock. Range, not exact value. Raw acceptance and final sorting. Three commercial bands because four does not pay.</p><p>Sampling because testing every piece makes cheap stone expensive. Faster test goal: roughly double worker throughput without meaningful increase in returns. Current fixture suffers geometry and operator inconsistency. Potential experiment: track return/error rates by worker and split same lot prospectively before redesigning tool. Edrin listened.</p><p>“Anything about my investigation?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Anything you want to tell me?”</p><p>There. Different. I thought.</p><p>“Holl's problem makes one thing more plausible in general.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Consistency can be purchased with labor.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Already knew.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Anything new?”</p><p>“Measurement doesn't have to be exact if decision is categorical.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Explain.”</p><p>“If someone wants narrow behavior, maybe they don't need exact numerical response. They need a fast enough accept/reject threshold around tolerance.”</p><p>“That could lower cost.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Does Holl have that?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Can he?”</p><p>“Unknown.”</p><p>“Does this connect him to seized stock?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Immediate. Good. Edrin nodded.</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>There. Valued. Not needed.</p><p>“What are you doing next?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“Not telling you.”</p><p>“Rude.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Can I ask why?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>She left. I did not follow. Physical impossibility not required. I simply did not. Good.</p><p>*</p><p>Sevren was north. Jorren working late. Alden training. Arlo and Vessa had explicitly banned me. I had no social visitor. This was fine. For about twenty minutes. Then boring. I ate second half of stolen meat pie? No. Keeper had eaten it. Criminal. I ordered stew. Paid.</p><p>Read cheap adventure pamphlet again. The marsh serpent still made no sense. Good.</p><p>*</p><p>After dinner, I copied Holl notes. Not every detail.</p><p>Actual useful:</p><p>HOLL SELLS SORTED/CERTIFIED CHEAP SUPPRESSION STOCK.<br/>CUSTOMERS BUY RANGE/BAND, NOT EXACT VALUE.<br/>RAW ACCEPT + FINAL SORT.<br/>3 BANDS BECAUSE 4 DOESN'T PAY.<br/>FAST TEST SUCCESS = MORE CORRECT SORTING PER WORKER/DAY, NOT FASTEST READING.<br/>ERRORS ASYMMETRIC.<br/>TRACK WORKER + RETURNS BEFORE TOOL REDESIGN.<br/>BINARY THRESHOLDS MAY BE EASIER THAN 3-BAND MAGNITUDE.</p><p>Then separate page:</p><p>EDRIN:<br/>MEASUREMENT NEED NOT BE EXACT IF TOLERANCE DECISION IS CATEGORICAL.<br/>DOES NOT CONNECT HOLL.</p><p>Important. I underlined last line. Once. No arrows. Good.</p><p>*</p><p>My phantom foot started burning near bedtime. Not pressure. Burning. First strong burning in a few days. Fatigue. Probably. Hessa had said worse with fatigue. I knew. Knowing did nothing. I rubbed actual thigh. No effect. Shifted. No effect. Put blanket over residual limb. No effect. Swore. Slight effect emotionally. The phantom toes curled. I could feel nails. There were no nails.</p><p>Fuck. I sat. Breathing. Not magical. Not experiment. Wait. It faded after maybe fifteen minutes. Long enough. Short enough. I was tired. The room was downstairs. My room upstairs. No stair attempt. Correct. I hated correct. Then slept.</p><p>*</p><p>I woke once in the night because somebody came down the stairs. New rail creaked at one post. Tiny. Wood settling? Fastener? I listened. No second sound.</p><p>My brain immediately supplied:</p><p>LOOSE POST.<br/>FAILURE.<br/>FALL.</p><p>No. Lerris had installed. Stringer sound. Rail used all day. One creak. Could inspect tomorrow. Could ask keeper if others noticed. Did not need to wake carpenter. I lay there. The west-river report existed upstairs. I could not reach it without stairs anyway. Good. Physical constraint as anti-rumination tool. Terrible. I slept again.</p><p>Morning came with the second meat pie absent because theft remained permanent. The keeper denied wrongdoing.</p><p>“You gave it.”</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“You put it on table.”</p><p>“That's not law.”</p><p>“Kitchen law.”</p><p>Terrible. My residual limb was less swollen. Good. No drainage. No heat I could detect. Wound check later. No hurry. I had nowhere scheduled. Holl had records to gather. Edrin had her investigation. Arlo and Vessa had their crooked mount face. Alden had Pessa. Sevren had north roads. Jorren had work.</p><p>I had a cup of tea and one stairwell between me and my bed. This was not nothing. It was also not a crisis. The Guild runner arrived while I was eating. Of course. He had a folded posting slip. I stared.</p><p>“Job?”</p><p>“Clerk said ask.”</p><p>Good. Not reserve.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Archive comparison. Two hours. Seated. Tomorrow or day after. Guild records room.”</p><p>I did not take slip yet.</p><p>“Stairs?”</p><p>“Records room ground floor.”</p><p>“Chair?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Carrying?”</p><p>“Ledgers brought to table.”</p><p>“Pay?”</p><p>“Three copper.”</p><p>“Privy?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Ask.”</p><p>He sighed.</p><p>“Same floor, back corridor.”</p><p>“Threshold?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>There. Unknown. My brain started. Stop. Archive comparison. Not mill frame.</p><p>“Tell clerk I'll answer after wound check.”</p><p>Runner nodded. No offense. Good. He left. The keeper looked at me.</p><p>“Work?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>She smiled. I pointed. She laughed. I drank tea. Interesting problem could wait. Job could wait. Stairs could wait. Not forever. Just long enough to ask what mattered. That was not wisdom. It was breakfast.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="076.html">← Chapter 61</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="078.html">Chapter 63 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

- `chapters/012.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 9: The Researcher — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 9</div><h1>THE RESEARCHER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>A spoon is an underrated investigative instrument. It is terrible at cutting. Mediocre at prying. Excellent at making the person who gave it to you feel safer than he should. I turned Antonius's spoon over in my hand.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Antonius Spoon" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/012/v28_c12_s01_antonius-spoon.png"/></figure><p>"Water."</p><p>Antonius kept the cup beside his ledger.</p><p>"Tell me what you need it for first."</p><p>"I don't know yet."</p><p>"Then start with the spoon."</p><p>I leaned back. This was the problem with Antonius. He had begun learning me. Not understanding me. That would have been intolerable. Learning the shape of the next mistake.</p><p>"Plate." </p><p>He considered.</p><p>"Wood or ceramic?"</p><p>"Ceramic."</p><p>Antonius handed me a shallow wooden dish instead.</p><p>"Use this."</p><p>"Why not ceramic?"</p><p>"Because I eat from the ceramic ones."</p><p>I looked around the office. Antonius Vale, future owner of a black tower that would eventually become synonymous with money, leverage, and decisions made behind closed doors, currently had a favorite spoon and protected his crockery. Useful historical information.</p><p>"Wood."</p><p>He gave me a shallow wooden dish. I set it beside the green shard. The material was roughly the size of two fingers laid together. Translucent at the edges. Cloudier toward the center. The black veins did not sit on the surface. They ran through it. Not stone. Or not only stone. I pressed the spoon gently against one corner. Nothing. Hard. More pressure. </p><p>Antonius said, "Greg."</p><p>"I'm using the spoon."</p><p>"You're using my desk." </p><p>I moved the dish beneath it.</p><p>"Better?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Specific criticism improves performance."</p><p>"Don't break anything."</p><p>"That is not specific enough."</p><p>"Don't break the green thing, the dish, the spoon, the desk, yourself, me, the building, or anything I own." </p><p>I paused.</p><p>"Define own."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Fine." I pressed again. </p><p>The shard shifted. The black line inside seemed to move. </p><p>I stopped. Antonius noticed.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Maybe nothing."</p><p>"That's not your face for nothing."</p><p>"I have several faces."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>That should have bothered me more than it did. I lifted the shard with the spoon and rolled it a fraction. The vein had not moved. Light. Probably. I angled it toward the window. Green. Black. A memory scratched at the back of my skull. Canvas walls. Blood. A brass mortar. Someone grinding. Not the black part. The voice was female. Older?</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Not The Black Part" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/012/v28_c12_s02_not-the-black-part.png"/></figure><p>No.</p><p>Tired. I could see hands but not a face. Green powder in a folded paper. Someone coughing. Then nothing. Memory was generous with atmosphere and stingy with answers.</p><p>"Do you have a lamp?"</p><p>Antonius glanced at the one behind him.</p><p>"No flame near the shard."</p><p>"I wasn't going to burn it."</p><p>"Then tell me what the light changes before I move it." </p><p>I looked at the shard.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>No fire.
