- `chapters/025.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 19: The Defender — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 19</div><h1>THE DEFENDER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The first creature came over the wall sideways.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Creature Crosses The Wall" decoding="async" height="335" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/025/v28_c25_s01_creature-crosses-the-wall.png" width="302"/></figure><p>Not climbed. Not jumped. Sideways. One moment the top of the orchard wall was empty. The next, four gray limbs hooked over the stones and something long pulled itself across without changing pace. The driver shouted. The horses saw it. Everything happened at once. Our wagon lurched left. Alden grabbed the rail. I grabbed Alden. The rider from the timber yard drew his sword.</p><p>The creature dropped into the road. Dog was wrong. Wolf was wrong. It had the head for either if you looked quickly and wanted the world to make sense. Narrow muzzle. Dark mouth. Ears pressed flat. Then the body ruined it. Too long through the ribs. Forelegs slightly shorter than the rear.</p><p>Joints folding close to the body, then opening farther than they should. Gray hide with strips of coarse black hair along the spine. It landed without the impact its size deserved. Smooth. That was what the potter had meant. The horses screamed.</p><p>“Hold them!” the driver yelled.</p><p>The wagon turned harder. The left wheels struck the ditch. Alden went over the side. I caught cloth. His red scarf. Wrong thing. It tore free. Alden hit the road shoulder and rolled. The creature turned. Too fast. Exactly too fast. Not speed. No preparation. Its front half pointed at the horses. Then at Alden. No visible shift between. My hand was already up.</p><p>Mana. Too much thought. Small. Brief. What needs to move? Not creature. Alden. No. Creature’s mouth. It lunged. I cast. A Barrier the size of my palm appeared beside its muzzle.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Palm Sized Barrier" decoding="async" height="335" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/025/v28_c25_s02_palm-sized-barrier.png" width="300"/></figure><p>Not in front. Beside. The creature struck it at an angle. The Barrier shattered. Pain snapped behind my eyes. The head moved three inches. Enough. Its teeth closed on Alden’s coat instead of his throat. Alden shouted and drove his boot into its chest. The creature dragged him.</p><p>“Greg!”</p><p>I jumped from the wagon. Bad decision. Necessary decision. Maybe. The rider reached us first. His sword came down across the creature’s back. Steel cut hide. Black blood sprayed. Blood. Useful later. Not now. The creature released Alden and folded. That was the only word.</p><p>Its body compressed under itself, legs disappearing, spine bending, then it exploded sideways into the rider. He flew. Sword gone. Alden came up on one knee. I drew mine. I was a Bronze warrior. I had been an S-class support adventurer. Neither fact made my current sword arm faster. The creature came at me. I knew where to cut. I could not get there.</p><p>I stepped back. Its first claw missed my stomach. Second caught my belt. Leather snapped. I hit it with the sword guard. Useless. Alden slammed into its side. Both went down.</p><p>“Stop winning the first part!” I shouted.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Get off it!”</p><p>Alden rolled away. The creature’s rear leg kicked through the space where his ribs had been. Good. He learned. The rider recovered his sword.</p><p>“Back!”</p><p>We backed. The creature did not pursue. It crouched in the road. Black blood ran down one side. Its breathing was wrong too. Fast. Then still. Fast. Then still. The wagon horses were half in the ditch. Driver fighting reins. Relief cargo shifting. Rusk was not with us. Of course he was not. Boat delivered. Employment ended. Problem ours. No. Problem local.</p><p>We had a rider. Driver. Alden. Me. Creature.</p><p>“Name?” I shouted at the rider.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Your name.”</p><p>“Cal.”</p><p>“Cal, can you fight it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How sure?”</p><p>He stared at me.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Yes, now.”</p><p>“Six.”</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>“Alden?” I asked.</p><p>“Seven,” Alden said.</p><p>“Greg?” Alden asked.</p><p>“Three,” I said.</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“That low?”</p><p>“Current body.”</p><p>The creature moved. Conversation over. Cal went left. Alden went right. I stayed behind them. Support. There. That felt different. Not safer. Correct.</p><p>“Don’t chase if it breaks,” I said.</p><p>Alden said, “I know.” The creature sprang at Cal. He set his sword. Wrong.</p><p>“Move!”</p><p>Cal moved. Late. Claws raked his sleeve. Alden cut the creature’s rear leg. Shallow. It spun. Again no transition. Alden had expected it this time. He ducked. Good. I saw the pattern. Not enough. Creature attacks. Compresses. Changes direction without normal footwork. How? Magic? Anatomy? Both? Check later. It went for Alden. He retreated. Three steps. Fourth would put him against wagon wheel.</p><p>“Left!”</p><p>He went left without asking why. The creature followed. Cal struck from behind. Blade bit deeper. Black blood. The creature screamed. High. Almost human. The horses lost what remained of their minds. One reared. Harness snapped. The wagon shifted.</p><p>“Driver!” I shouted.</p><p>“I know!”</p><p>He did. Of course he did. Stop narrating other professions. The free horse kicked. The creature flinched. Interesting. Sound? Movement? Horse? No time. It bolted toward the orchard wall. Alden took one step after it. Stopped. Good. Cal did not. He chased.</p><p>“Cal!”</p><p>He reached the wall as the creature climbed. It did not climb like an animal. Front claws struck stone. Rear legs folded. Then it flowed upward. Cal stabbed. Missed. The creature vanished over. Silence. Not silence. Horses. Driver. My breathing. Alden’s breathing. Cal swearing.</p><p>“Everyone alive?” I asked.</p><p>“Yes,” Alden said.</p><p>“Yes,” Cal said.</p><p>Driver shouted, “Horse!” Right. One horse was loose. Alive. Running east. The other three were tangled but standing. The wagon leaned into the ditch. Relief cargo still aboard. </p><p>I looked at Alden. Blood on coat.</p><p>“Yours?”</p><p>He checked.</p><p>“Don’t know.”</p><p>“Check.”</p><p>“I’m fine.”</p><p>“Check.”</p><p>He did. Torn coat. Scratches along shoulder. No bite. Cal had three claw lines on his forearm. Bleeding. Not deep.</p><p>“Wrap that.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>Good. The orchard wall stood ten feet away. Creature beyond. Maybe leaving. Maybe circling. Maybe three creatures. Three seen. We had encountered one. I remembered the rider’s report. Three seen. Not three total. The road behind us was open. The road ahead bent between orchard walls. Darrowmere smoke beyond. The loose horse had disappeared around that bend. Alden picked up his red scarf from the dirt.</p><p>Torn. He looked at it. Something inside me went cold. Future. Red scarf dark. Bell cracking. No. Not this. I knew that. I knew nothing.</p><p>“Alden.”</p><p>He tied the torn scarf around his wrist.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>He stared at me.</p><p>“Bad face?”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>A sound came from the orchard. Not the scream. Branches. Cal raised his sword. Alden raised his. I did too. Wrong. My sword was not where I belonged. I lowered it slightly.</p><p>“Back to wagon.”</p><p>Cal said, “We can kill it.”</p><p>“Maybe,” I said.</p><p>“It’s hurt,” Cal said.</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>“We hurt it,” Cal said.</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>“So finish,” Cal said.</p><p>Alden looked at him. Then at me. There it was. First advantage. Spend it. </p><p>I said, “No.” Cal’s jaw tightened.</p><p>“It’ll hit someone else.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“Then we kill it.”</p><p>“Or it pulls us over the wall and there are two more.”</p><p>Branches moved. Closer. Cal backed toward the wagon. Good. Not agreement. Compliance. Enough. The driver had a knife out and was cutting a twisted trace.</p><p>“What do you need?” I asked.</p><p>“Five minutes.”</p><p>“You have one.”</p><p>“Then I need a miracle.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Ask for something smaller.”</p><p>He almost hit me. Fair.</p><p>“Hold those three horses. Keep them from pulling sideways. Get the cargo off the left rear.”</p><p>That I could do.</p><p>“Alden.”</p><p>“Cargo.”</p><p>We moved. Canvas first. Medical chest. Blankets. Cal kept watch. The orchard branches stopped moving. Worse. We shifted weight. The wagon rose slightly. Driver freed the trace.</p><p>“Can it roll?”</p><p>“If the wheel’s sound.”</p><p>“Is it?”</p><p>“Find out.”</p><p>He climbed down into the ditch. I hated that.</p><p>“Cal, watch wall. Alden, road east.”</p><p>“What about west?”</p><p>“I have west.”</p><p>Alden glanced at my sword.</p><p>“You said three.”</p><p>“Three is not zero.”</p><p>He nodded. That felt worse than an argument. The driver kicked the wheel. Checked hub.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>“Two minutes.”</p><p>We did not have two minutes. I knew because the second creature came from behind us. Alden saw my face change. He turned.</p><p>“Greg?”</p><p>“West!”</p><p>The creature ran low along the road. Different. Smaller. Same gray hide. Black spine. Bloodless. Fresh. Cal pivoted from the wall. Too far. Alden was closest. He moved to intercept.</p><p>“No!”</p><p>He stopped. The creature did not want him. It wanted the horses. Of course. Livestock. Sheep. Mule. Horse. Pattern.</p><p>“Let it choose!” I shouted.</p><p>Nobody understood. The creature accelerated. The driver was under the wagon.</p><p>“Out!”</p><p>He rolled. The creature launched at the nearest horse. I saw the line. Harness. Horse neck. Creature. Not enough mana to stop mass. Do less. The horse tried to rear. Harness trapped it. That was the danger. Not teeth yet. Harness. I cast at the buckle. Tiny Barrier. Wrong angle. It flashed and vanished. Nothing. Again. Pain. No. Information. I needed touch.</p><p>Distance too far. Alden reached the horse. He slashed the trace. Leather half cut. Creature three strides. Cal running. Two. Alden cut again. Trace snapped. Horse twisted free. One. The creature leapt. Horse moved. Creature hit wagon rail. Wood exploded. The entire wagon rocked. I fell. The creature landed inside the cargo bed. With us. Too close. No architecture. No elegant support.</p><p>Sword. I thrust. Blade entered shoulder. The impact drove the hilt into my palm. Creature screamed. Its head snapped toward me. I tried to pull sword free. Stuck. Bad. Claws came. Alden hit its neck with both hands on his sword. Not cut. Hit. The creature slammed sideways. My sword tore free. Black blood across my shirt. I fell backward over the medical chest.</p><p>The creature turned on Alden. Cal climbed onto the wagon from behind and stabbed down. His blade entered between ribs. Deep. The creature convulsed. Alden jumped back. Cal tried to pull free.</p><p>“Leave it!”</p><p>He did. Good. The creature folded around the sword. Then unfolded. Straight up. For one impossible second it stood almost vertical, front claws against nothing. I saw the underside. Pale. Hairless. And a line of small hard ridges along the sternum. Not natural? Could be natural. No time. It threw itself out of the wagon. Hit road. Ran. Cal’s sword still in it.</p><p>Alden started after. Stopped. Again. Good. The creature made ten yards. Twenty. Then its front legs failed. It rolled. Once. Twice. Still. Nobody moved.</p><p>“Is it dead?” Alden asked.</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“That’s not an answer.”</p><p>“It’s the answer you get.”</p><p>Cal jumped down.</p><p>“Wait.”</p><p>He stopped. I looked at the orchard wall. First creature. Still somewhere. Maybe.</p><p>“Driver?” I called.</p><p>“Wheel’s fine,” the driver said.</p><p>“Horses?” I asked.</p><p>“Three here. One gone,” he said.</p><p>“Can we move?” I asked.</p><p>“Not with traces like this,” he said.</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>“Ten minutes if nobody attacks me.”</p><p>Alden laughed once. Not because it was funny. Adrenaline. His hands were shaking. Mine too. Cal’s bleeding had soaked the cloth around his arm.</p><p>“Sit,” I told him.</p><p>“I’m fine.”</p><p>“You’re leaking.”</p><p>“So are you.”</p><p>I looked down. Black blood. Not mine. Mostly. My belt had cut skin at the hip. Palm torn. No serious wound. Headache growing. Channels felt hot. Two casts. One useful. One failed. Maybe three if I counted the first muzzle redirect. Three. Too many? Not yet. Could become too many. A bell rang ahead. One. Then another. Darrowmere. Not song. Alarm. Cal looked east.</p><p>Alden looked east. The driver did not. He kept working. Good man.</p><p>“Greg,” Alden said.</p><p>“I hear it.”</p><p>The bell rang again. Different rhythm from North Gate. Three quick. Pause. Three. Cal said, “That’s road warning.”</p><p>“You know?”</p><p>“Darrowmere uses three for road.”</p><p>“Which road?”</p><p>“This one.”</p><p>Excellent. A rider appeared around the eastern bend. No. Horse. Loose horse. Ours. It came back at a gallop. Saddle empty because it had no saddle. Harness trailing. Blood on one flank. The horse passed the dead creature. Shied. </p><p>Nearly went into the wall. </p><p>Then kept coming. Behind it, something moved at the bend. One. Two. Three gray shapes. </p><p>Alden said, “That’s bad.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Cal reached for his sword. It was still in the dead creature.</p><p>“Also bad.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The driver looked up.</p><p>“How long?” I asked.</p><p>“Not ten minutes.”</p><p>“How long now?”</p><p>He stared at the approaching creatures.</p><p>“One.”</p><p>Good. One minute. Known.</p><p>“What needs to happen?”</p><p>“Reconnect lead pair. Tie off broken trace. Get us straight.”</p><p>“Alden, help him.”</p><p>Alden looked at the creatures. Then at me.</p><p>“You?”</p><p>“Cal and I buy one minute.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>There was no time for that.</p><p>“You’re better with harness.”</p><p>“I’m better with sword.”</p><p>“So is Cal.”</p><p>Cal said, “Debatable.” The creatures were closer. </p><p>Alden did not move. </p><p>I grabbed his coat.</p><p>“Do the job only you’re standing next to.”</p><p>That was not philosophy. It was geography. He moved. Good. Cal picked up my fallen sword. I drew the knife from my belt. Three creatures. Maybe the first wounded one among them. Maybe not.</p><p>“Plan?” Cal asked.</p><p>“Don’t win.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Make them hesitate.”</p><p>“With what?”</p><p>I looked at the dead creature. Then the horses. Then the orchard walls. Then the relief canvas.</p><p>“Fire?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Magic?”</p><p>“Bad.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>The creatures slowed. That mattered. They saw the dead one. Smelled blood. Recognized? Maybe. One moved left. One right. Third stayed center. Pack behavior. Or coincidence. I backed toward the wagon.</p><p>“Cal. Throw the sword.”</p><p>“My sword?”</p><p>“Your sword is in that.”</p><p>“My other sword.”</p><p>He looked at mine in his hand.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“At what?”</p><p>“Center one. Don’t hit it.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Make it move.”</p><p>He understood. Good. He threw. Bad throw. Good enough. Sword struck road in front of center creature. It flinched sideways. The right creature accelerated. Reaction. Not coordinated? Maybe. I threw the knife at the right one. Missed by feet. Also good enough. It changed line. We were not hurting them. We were spending their certainty.</p><p>“Again?” Cal asked.</p><p>“We are out of swords.”</p><p>“Bad plan.”</p><p>“Temporary plan.”</p><p>Behind us, harness buckles clattered. Alden shouted, “Thirty!” Thirty seconds. </p><p>The left creature ran at us. </p><p>Cal stepped forward.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He stepped back. Good. I gathered mana. Headache sharpened immediately. Too much. Small. What part? Eyes? No. Foot. Not stop. Change. The creature hit full speed. I waited. Too long. Too close. Now. Barrier. Coin-sized. At ground level. Not under paw. Beside. Its front foot clipped the edge. The Barrier vanished. Creature stumbled. Not fell. One bad step. Cal kicked dirt into its face.</p><p>That was not what I expected. It worked. The creature veered.</p><p>“Twenty!” Alden yelled.</p><p>Center creature came. No mana. Not safely. Sword? No. Knife? Gone. Cal had nothing. Dead creature had sword. Relief cargo. Blankets. Canvas. Rope. Rope. I grabbed the loose coil from the road. Too slow. Cal grabbed the other end without being asked. We stretched it between us.</p><p>“This is stupid,” he said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The creature came. We dropped the rope. Not trip. Never trip something that could jump. It jumped anyway. Good. Expected obstruction. It cleared the rope. We moved apart. The creature landed between us. Past us. Closer to wagon. Bad. Alden appeared. Not with sword. With a blanket. He threw it over the creature’s head. I laughed. Actually laughed. The creature thrashed.</p><p>“Go!” Alden shouted.</p><p>Driver whipped reins. The horses pulled. Wagon moved. Alden jumped onto the rear. Cal grabbed the side. I ran. Current body. Mud. Headache. No belt. Wonderful. The blanketed creature tore free. I reached the wagon. Alden caught my wrist. Pulled. I hit the rear board chest-first. Could not climb.</p><p>“Greg!”</p><p>“I know!”</p><p>He hauled. Cal grabbed my coat. Between them I got over. The wagon accelerated. Not fast. Fast enough. The three creatures followed. One fell back. Then another. The last stayed. Long gray body. Smooth stride. Black hair. It came alongside the rear wheel. Alden raised his sword.</p><p>“Don’t!”</p><p>“It’s here!”</p><p>“Wheel!”</p><p>He looked. Understood. If he struck and it hit the wheel, if it jammed, if the wagon turned... He did not swing. The creature lunged. At him. I grabbed the back of his coat and pulled. Teeth closed on air. Then the road widened. Darrowmere watch appeared ahead. Six people. Spears. Crossbows. Green coats.</p><p>“Down!” someone shouted.</p><p>We dropped. Crossbows snapped. One bolt missed. One struck the creature’s flank. It screamed and peeled away. The watch did not chase. Excellent. They formed around the wagon instead. One ran beside us.</p><p>“Keep moving!”</p><p>Driver shouted, “Happy to!” We passed the first barricade. Then the second. Then a ditch lined with sharpened stakes. Then people. Real people. Watch. Guild. Farmers. Carts. Smoke. A burning shed somewhere east. Darrowmere. The wagon finally slowed inside a stone yard. </p><p>I stayed on the floor. </p><p>Alden stayed beside me. </p><p>Cal sat against the rail. Nobody spoke for several breaths. Then </p><p>Alden said, “Three?”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You said you were a three.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That was a three?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He considered this.</p><p>“I hate your scale.”</p><p>“Reasonable.”</p><p>Cal started laughing. Then Alden. Then me. It hurt. Everything hurt. A watchwoman climbed onto the wagon.</p><p>“Nemi sent word you might be coming.”</p><p>I stopped laughing.</p><p>“Nemi Caul?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“She made it?”</p><p>“She’ll be angry you asked.”</p><p>Good. The watchwoman looked at the black blood across us.</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>“Four,” Cal said.</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“Three at the end. One first. One killed. Could be overlap.”</p><p>The watchwoman nodded. Good. She understood counting.</p><p>“Dead one?”</p><p>“Road, about a mile west.”</p><p>“Marked?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Sword in it,” Cal said.</p><p>She looked at him.</p><p>“Expensive marker.”</p><p>“It was a good sword.”</p><p>“Then you’ll want the recovery team.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“You Greg?”</p><p>I did not like that.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Nemi said there was a young Bronze asking useful annoying questions.”</p><p>Alden made a sound. I ignored him. The watchwoman pointed toward a long low building.</p><p>“Get checked. Then report.”</p><p>“For what?”</p><p>She looked east. The bell rang again. Three quick. Pause. Three.</p><p>“Because that was the easy road.”</p><p>My laughter stopped. Behind the eastern wall, something screamed. Not one creature. Several. Alden stood. I stood more slowly. My channels burned. My palm bled. My sword was somewhere on the road. I had one knife less than before. Darrowmere had more monsters than answers. Good. No. Not good. Interesting. That was worse.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="024.html">← Chapter 18</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="026.html">Chapter 20 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/182.html:210`: <p>The mana came easier than it had before the road, though I no longer<br>
- `chapters/182.html:492`: <p>The mana sat where it sat.</p>
- `chapters/019.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 15: The Bystander — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 15</div><h1>THE BYSTANDER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The guild had put my sacks behind a locked door.</p><p>This was reasonable.</p><p>I disliked it immediately.</p><p>The ink-thumbed clerk was at the front desk when I arrived. She looked up from a ledger, saw me, and looked toward the clock on the wall.</p><p>“You were here yesterday,” the clerk said.</p><p>“I know,” I said.</p><p>“The South Canal material is no longer on your contract,” she said.</p><p>“I have a question,” I said.</p><p>She closed the ledger.</p><p>“Then ask one. I may still tell you it is watch business now.”</p><p>I considered denying this.</p><p>“What happened to the South Canal sacks?”</p><p>She closed the ledger.</p><p>“That question.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“They were transferred.”</p><p>“To whom?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What were they?”</p><p>“If we knew that, I imagine the report would say.”</p><p>“Can I see the report?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I leaned on the counter.</p><p>She pointed at my arm.</p><p>I stopped leaning.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you are not assigned to it.”</p><p>“I found them.”</p><p>“You found a warehouse wall and then became involved in a fight behind it.”</p><p>“That is an uncharitable summary.”</p><p>“It is a guild summary.”</p><p>“Those are often the same thing.”</p><p>She opened the ledger again.</p><p>I did not move.</p><p>After several seconds she sighed.</p><p>“You were paid.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The watch took custody.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The owner is being questioned.”</p><p>“Merek Verran.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The sacks?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I am asking because if they are dangerous, somebody should know before opening them.”</p><p>“They have not been opened.”</p><p>That was something.</p><p>“Why not?”</p><p>Her eyes narrowed.</p><p>I had done it again.</p><p>One useful answer, immediately converted into three more questions.</p><p>I smiled apologetically.</p><p>It did not help.</p><p>“Because the warder told us not to,” she said.</p><p>“What warder?”</p><p>A voice behind me said, “Me.”</p><p>I turned.</p><p>The woman standing there was perhaps forty, perhaps older, with gray threaded through black hair at both temples and the compact shoulders of someone who had spent years carrying things other people assumed magic made weightless. She wore a dark blue guild coat with a stitched silver square at the collar. A leather case hung from one shoulder.</p><p>Her left hand was stained purple from the first knuckle down.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Warder Arrives" decoding="async" height="334" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/019/v28_c19_s02_the-warder-arrives.png" width="302"/></figure><p>Not ink.</p><p>Reagent.</p><p>I looked at the hand.</p><p>She noticed.</p><p>“Problem?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You stared.”</p><p>“I was identifying the stain.”</p><p>“Were you?”</p><p>“Trying.”</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>I looked again.</p><p>Purple at the skin folds. Darker around the nail beds. No blistering. Faint metallic smell, unless that was the case.</p><p>I knew six purple reagents.</p><p>I thought I knew eleven.</p><p>Three of them would have removed the skin.</p><p>“Something used for ward tracing,” I said.</p><p>The woman looked at the clerk.</p><p>“This is the Bronze from South Canal?”</p><p>“Yes,” the clerk said.</p><p>“I’m Greg,” I said.</p><p>“I read the incident note,” the woman said.</p><p>That was becoming less flattering.</p><p>She shifted the leather case higher on her shoulder.</p><p>“Edrin Saye. Guild warder.”</p><p>I waited for recognition.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>No future title.</p><p>No tavern song.</p><p>No ruined city.</p><p>Just Edrin Saye.</p><p>That was pleasant.</p><p>“What did you find on the sacks?” I asked.</p><p>“A sealed closure I cannot identify yet,” Edrin said.</p><p>“Dangerous?” I asked.</p><p>“Unknown. Which is why they stay closed,” Edrin said.</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“A seal.”</p><p>“That is a category.”</p><p>“So is warder.”</p><p>I liked her slightly less.</p><p>Which was promising.</p><p>“Can I see it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you’re not assigned to it.”</p><p>I looked at the clerk.</p><p>She looked delighted.</p><p>“This place has a culture problem.”</p><p>Edrin walked toward the side hall.</p><p>I followed.</p><p>The clerk said, “Greg.”</p><p>“I’m only walking.”</p><p>“Somewhere else.”</p><p>Edrin stopped at the hall entrance and looked back at me.</p><p>“What did you see at the warehouse?”</p><p>That was permission.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>I joined her.</p><p>The clerk muttered something about Bronze adventurers and administrative decay.</p><p>I told Edrin what I had actually seen. Three dark sacks among ordinary grain stock. Heavier than they looked when one thief dragged one. No obvious dust. No smell I remembered. The thieves had targeted them specifically. Merek Verran had lied about the nature of the thefts, or at least omitted enough that the distinction was becoming philosophical.</p><p>Edrin listened without interrupting.</p><p>“What did you touch?” she asked.</p><p>“The warehouse.”</p><p>“The sacks.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“The men?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“With magic?”</p><p>“One of them indirectly.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>I explained the hook.</p><p>Her expression did not change.</p><p>“Show me.”</p><p>“With a hook?”</p><p>“With your hand.”</p><p>I held my fingers apart to show the size of the Barrier.</p><p>She looked at the space between them.</p><p>“That small?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because my head is also small.”</p><p>She stared at me.</p><p>“Relative to a warehouse door.”</p><p>“Ah.”</p><p>She resumed walking.</p><p>“Good instinct.”</p><p>That pleased me enough that I distrusted it.</p><p>The side hall ended at another desk, this one occupied by a young man copying numbers from one page to another. Edrin signed something. He unlocked a heavy door and stepped through.</p><p>I followed.</p><p>She turned.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You said show you.”</p><p>“I said show me the Barrier.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>“Outside.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>I backed out.</p><p>The door closed.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>The young man copied numbers.</p><p>I read them upside down until he put his hand over the page.</p><p>“That’s rude,” I said.</p><p>“So is reading.”</p><p>“I wasn’t reading. I was noticing.”</p><p>He moved the page farther away.</p><p>Edrin returned carrying a square of rough wood about the size of my palm.</p><p>She shut and locked the door behind her.</p><p>The wood had a black line painted across it.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not painted.</p><p>Burned.</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>“Training tile?” I asked.</p><p>“Testing tile,” Edrin said.</p><p>“What does it test?” I asked.</p><p>“Whether you can hold one fixed Barrier while I change the pressure,” Edrin said.</p><p>“I’m beginning to understand why the guild employs you.”</p><p>She held it out.</p><p>“Barrier between your hand and the tile. Do not touch the tile. Do not cast through it. Do not try anything clever.”</p><p>“That last one is vague.”</p><p>“It is intentionally broad.”</p><p>Hessa had infected the city.</p><p>I raised my hand.</p><p>“Fixed?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>“Until I tell you.”</p><p>I gathered mana.</p><p>The morning’s beans had left my channels tired in a way that was easy to mistake for readiness. They felt warm. Open.</p><p>That was not the same thing as strong.</p><p>I formed a small Barrier between my palm and the tile.</p><p>It came more easily than I expected.</p><p>Too easily.</p><p>I almost changed it.</p><p>Shorter duration. Less feed. See if the same shape could exist without the full anchor.</p><p>Do not experiment, Hessa had said.</p><p>I held the ordinary form.</p><p>Edrin moved the tile forward until it touched the Barrier.</p><p>Pressure arrived.</p><p>Not much.</p><p>My channels noticed anyway.</p><p>“Hold,” she said.</p><p>I held.</p><p>The tile pressed harder.</p><p>The Barrier trembled.</p><p>My first instinct was to reinforce.</p><p>My second was to change the angle and let the tile slide.</p><p>My third was to shorten the structure and pulse it against the movement.</p><p>All three were old answers.</p><p>Or future answers.</p><p>Or answers I had invented this morning because a bean had moved two fingers and I was an idiot.</p><p>I held.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released.</p><p>The spell vanished.</p><p>Edrin looked at me.</p><p>“You wanted to move it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why didn’t you?”</p><p>“You told me not to.”</p><p>“That usually work?”</p><p>“Recently.”</p><p>She handed the tile to the young man.</p><p>“Your Barrier is weak.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Very weak.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Your placement is better than your output.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You’re irritating.”</p><p>“I’ve heard that.”</p><p>“Your release is strange.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What about it?”</p><p>“You cut it clean.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She waited.</p><p>I hated when competent people learned my tricks.</p><p>“What does that mean here?” I asked.</p><p>“Here?”</p><p>“In current guild instruction.”</p><p>Her eyes narrowed.</p><p>Careful.</p><p>“What do they call it?”</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>“That’s all?”</p><p>“What do you want us to call it?”</p><p>I almost said termination architecture.</p><p>I was not certain that was the right century.</p><p>Or the right school.</p><p>Or a real term.</p><p>I had once argued for three hours about whether a Barrier ended when mana feed stopped or when the boundary ceased behaving as a boundary.</p><p>I remembered the argument.</p><p>I did not remember which side I had been on.</p><p>That seemed unfair.</p><p>“Nothing,” I said.</p><p>Edrin studied me for another second.</p><p>Then she said, “Most beginners let a spell die.”</p><p>“I didn’t.”</p><p>“No. You ended it.”</p><p>A small thrill ran through me.</p><p>Not because I had impressed her.</p><p>Well.</p><p>Partly because I had impressed her.</p><p>Mostly because the distinction survived.</p><p>Something old in my hands still existed even when the power did not.</p><p>“What happens if they end it badly?” I asked.</p><p>“Usually nothing.”</p><p>“Usually.”</p><p>“Waste. Residual tension. Sometimes a rebound if the structure is under load.”</p><p>“What kind of rebound?”</p><p>She smiled for the first time.</p><p>“Not one you are cleared to test,” Edrin said.</p><p>“I was asking,” I said.</p><p>“And I am keeping the answer attached to the person responsible for the ward,” Edrin said.</p><p>Edrin picked up the tile.</p><p>“The seal on your sacks is under load.”</p><p>Everything else disappeared.</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“I said no.”</p><p>“You just told me.”</p><p>“I told you enough to explain why we have not opened them.”</p><p>A seal under load.</p><p>I knew what that could mean.</p><p>I knew too many things it could mean.</p><p>Containment.</p><p>Compression.</p><p>Preservation.</p><p>Transfer.</p><p>A condition held in place.</p><p>A boundary carrying something that wanted to become something else.</p><p>Or current warders used under load differently than I did.</p><p>Know.</p><p>Think.</p><p>Check.</p><p>“What does it do?” I asked.</p><p>“We don’t know.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>That was the correct answer.</p><p>I hated it.</p><p>“What do you know?”</p><p>Edrin considered me.</p><p>“The sack itself is ordinary cloth. The closure is not. There’s a narrow structure around the cord and mouth. Old enough to be dirty, not old enough for me to call it ancient. It responds when the knot is disturbed.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Pressure changes.”</p><p>“Mana?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Direction?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Heat?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Sound?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did you test movement?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“It means I am the warder.”</p><p>I shut my mouth.</p><p>That took effort.</p><p>Edrin continued.</p><p>“The seal is stable while the sack remains closed. I can trace part of the boundary. I cannot identify the full condition. I do not know whether opening it releases something, destroys something, marks something, or merely tells somebody the sack was opened.”</p><p>“Could be preservation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be theft protection.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be a trigger.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be badly made.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“You considered that?”</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>That should not have surprised me. It did. Annoying.</p><p>“Have you seen the structure before?” I asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Any family resemblance?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“To what?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I breathed out.</p><p>“You enjoy this.”</p><p>“I enjoy you not knowing.”</p><p>“That is unprofessional.”</p><p>“It is one of the profession’s smaller pleasures.”</p><p>The side door opened.</p><p>The ink-thumbed clerk leaned through.</p><p>“Vale is here.”</p><p>I turned.</p><p>Of course he was.</p><p>Antonius stood in the front hall wearing a dark coat and the expression of a man who had arrived to collect money and discovered me instead.</p><p>His eyes moved from me to Edrin.</p><p>Then to the testing tile.</p><p>Then back to me.</p><p>“No,” he said.</p><p>“I haven’t asked anything.”</p><p>“That has never protected me.”</p><p>Edrin asked, “You know him?”</p><p>Antonius looked at her.</p><p>“He owes me money.”</p><p>“That explains a great deal.”</p><p>“It explains nothing,” I said.</p><p>Antonius ignored me.</p><p>“What are you doing here?” Antonius asked.</p><p>“I found something,” I said.</p><p>“You always find something.”</p><p>“That sounds complimentary.”</p><p>“It is not.”</p><p>The clerk returned to her desk.</p><p>“Mr. Vale, your appointment is with Master Crenn.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then why are you talking to Greg?”</p><p>Antonius looked at me.</p><p>“I ask myself that regularly.”</p><p>He started toward the stairs.</p><p>I followed.</p><p>He stopped.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>This was becoming repetitive.</p><p>“I only need one thing.”</p><p>“You need many things. That is the problem.”</p><p>“The South Canal sacks.”</p><p>Antonius’s face did not move.</p><p>That was movement.</p><p>“You know about them,” I said.</p><p>“I know there was an incident.”</p><p>“You know more than that.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You didn’t ask what sacks.”</p><p>Edrin made a small sound behind me.</p><p>I could not tell whether it was approval or regret.</p><p>Antonius looked at me for several seconds.</p><p>Then he said, “Walk.”</p><p>We left the guild.</p><p>That was not what I had expected.</p><p>Outside, he turned toward the market without asking whether I was coming.</p><p>I came.</p><p>“What did you find?” he asked.</p><p>I told him about the seal.</p><p>Not every detail.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>Antonius listened.</p><p>“Did you touch it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Everyone keeps sounding surprised.”</p><p>“Experience.”</p><p>“Hessa said something similar.”</p><p>“Who is Hessa?”</p><p>“No one.”</p><p>Antonius glanced sideways.</p><p>I had done that badly.</p><p>He did not pursue it.</p><p>That was worse.</p><p>“What do you know about Merek Verran?” I asked.</p><p>“He rents two canal warehouses. Owns neither. Grain, lamp meal, dried beans in winter, sometimes wool.”</p><p>“Sometimes dark sealed sacks.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Sealed Sacks" decoding="async" height="334" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/019/v28_c19_s01_the-sealed-sacks.png" width="303"/></figure><p>“I had not heard that part.”</p><p>“Debts?”</p><p>“Everyone has debts.”</p><p>“To you?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Competitors?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Enemies?”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“That is not useful.”</p><p>“It is more useful than inventing one.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He had become irritatingly quotable.</p><p>“Why are you here?”</p><p>“Appointment,” Antonius said.</p><p>“At the guild?” I asked.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“For?” I asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I sighed.</p><p>We crossed between two vegetable carts.</p><p>Antonius said, “The watch asked three lenders whether Verran had recently sought unusual credit.”</p><p>“Did he?”</p><p>“Not from me.”</p><p>“Why ask lenders?”</p><p>“Because merchants lie to guards differently than they lie to creditors.”</p><p>“That is beautiful.”</p><p>“No, it is ordinary.”</p><p>“Those are not mutually exclusive.”</p><p>He ignored that.</p><p>“Verran has been paying his storage rent on time. His grain volume is down. His cart traffic is not.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“That’s interesting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why do you know his cart traffic?”</p><p>“I have a warehouse on the same canal.”</p><p>Of course he did.</p><p>“How far?”</p><p>“Far enough that you are not going there.”</p><p>“I didn’t ask.”</p><p>“You were about to.”</p><p>I had been.</p><p>We reached a tea stall.</p><p>Antonius bought tea.</p><p>One cup.</p><p>I looked at it.</p><p>He drank.</p><p>“You could have bought two.”</p><p>“You owe me money.”</p><p>“This feels vindictive.”</p><p>“It costs one copper.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>He took another drink.</p><p>I hated him.</p><p>“What do you think is in the sacks?” I asked.</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Guess.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you will turn my guess into a plan.”</p><p>“That is insulting.”</p><p>“It is preventative.”</p><p>I looked back toward the guild.</p><p>Seal under load.</p><p>Unknown condition.</p><p>Ordinary cloth.</p><p>Targeted theft.</p><p>Reduced grain volume. Stable cart traffic.</p><p>My mind assembled six possibilities.</p><p>Seven.</p><p>Nine.</p><p>I discarded three.</p><p>Rebuilt two.</p><p>Antonius watched me.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“I’m not doing anything.”</p><p>“You are borrowing against information you do not have.”</p><p>That landed.</p><p>I disliked when he used my own problems in new contexts.</p><p>“I could learn more.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“By waiting.”</p><p>“Terrible method.”</p><p>“Frequently profitable.”</p><p>I thought of Alden in the warehouse.</p><p>Wait one move.</p><p>The correction had worked because Alden's instinct was to spend advantage immediately.</p><p>Mine was apparently to spend uncertainty.</p><p>That was rude.</p><p>I drank imaginary tea.</p><p>Antonius finished the real one.</p><p>“What happens now?” I asked.</p><p>“The guild warder examines the seal. The watch questions Verran. Somebody checks manifests. Somebody checks carts. Somebody checks whether the sacks came through a gate legally.”</p><p>“And me?”</p><p>“You do whatever Bronze adventurers do when not interfering with investigations.”</p><p>“Get hit?”</p><p>“Preferably somewhere else.”</p><p>He started walking again.</p><p>“Tomorrow I’m training.”</p><p>“With Jorren?”</p><p>“And Alden.”</p><p>Antonius stopped.</p><p>Not dramatically.</p><p>One step simply failed to become the next.</p><p>“Marr?”</p><p>There it was again.</p><p>Not bells.</p><p>Not music.</p><p>A name entering a room before the person did.</p><p>“You know him?”</p><p>Antonius resumed walking.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“That was a bad no.”</p><p>“It was an accurate no.”</p><p>“You reacted.”</p><p>“I recognized the surname.”</p><p>My attention sharpened.</p><p>“Hessa did too.”</p><p>Antonius looked at me.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No one.”</p><p>“You are poor at that.”</p><p>“I am improving.”</p><p>“Who is Hessa?”</p><p>“My magic instructor.”</p><p>“You have a magic instructor.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Since when?”</p><p>“Before you knew me.”</p><p>“That is reassuring.”</p><p>“It should be.”</p><p>“It is not.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>He said nothing about Marr.</p><p>I let three steps pass.</p><p>Four.</p><p>This was restraint.</p><p>It felt awful.</p><p>“What does Marr mean to you?” I asked.</p><p>Antonius sighed.</p><p>“A family name.”</p><p>“I had gathered.”</p><p>“An old one.”</p><p>“How old?”</p><p>“Older than either of us.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“You asked.”</p><p>“Rich?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Noble?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Guild?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“That is three different answers.”</p><p>“It is a large family.”</p><p>Ah.</p><p>That changed the shape of the problem.</p><p>Not solved.</p><p>Changed.</p><p>“Hessa said many people share names.”</p><p>“She was right.”</p><p>“Do you know Hessa Marr?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Alden?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Any Marr?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I considered pressing. Antonius looked at me. I did not.</p><p>At the next corner Antonius turned toward the river.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>He looked back.</p><p>“Aren’t you coming?”</p><p>“You told me to do something else.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“I am.”</p><p>Suspicion entered his face.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I have training.”</p><p>“That is tomorrow.”</p><p>“My training.”</p><p>“With Jorren?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did you forget?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I had.</p><p>Not entirely.</p><p>I had remembered it as a thing in the category of today, which was not the same as remembering the hour.</p><p>Antonius saw this.</p><p>His mouth moved.</p><p>“Do not.”</p><p>“I said nothing.”</p><p>“You were about to enjoy that.”</p><p>“I was.”</p><p>He walked away.</p><p>I headed toward Jorren.</p><p>Halfway there, I passed a mason repairing the corner of a courtyard wall.</p><p>He had set a plank across two low stacks of brick. On the plank sat a bucket of mortar. Each time he needed mortar, he stepped onto the plank, took what he needed, stepped down, and returned to the wall.</p><p>The plank bent under his weight.</p><p>Not much.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>The mason looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>I looked at the plank.</p><p>A Barrier was not a plank. It could take load, but brief load and continuous load were not the same problem. The hook had touched mine for less than a breath. The bean for less. Edrin’s tile had stayed against the fixed plane long enough for my channels to complain. I thought I knew why. I needed to test it. Not now.</p><p>I kept walking.</p><p>Three steps later I turned back.</p><p>The mason had returned to work.</p><p>I looked at the plank again.</p><p>“What if you didn't hold the weight?” I murmured.</p><p>The mason straightened.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You said something.”</p><p>“I was talking to the wall.”</p><p>He stared at me.</p><p>“That normal for adventurers?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I continued toward Jorren.</p><p>I was late.</p><p>He would hit me.</p><p>That was useful.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>Behind my eyes, a bean moved one finger.</p><p>A hook moved one inch.</p><p>A testing tile pressed against a wall that wanted to become something else.</p><p>And somewhere behind a guild door, three sacks remained closed because nobody yet knew which part of the seal mattered.</p><p>For once, neither did I.</p><p>I smiled all the way to training.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="018.html">← Chapter 14</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="022.html">Chapter 16 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

- `chapters/346.html:157`: <p>Mana shape felt wrong.</p>
- `chapters/346.html:352`: <p>"Any mana use by you?"</p>
- `chapters/101.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 81: The Waiting Man — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 81</div><h1>THE WAITING MAN</h1></header><article class="prose"><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg moving on crutches through a wet city alley at night." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/101/Ch101_Rainy-Alley-Walk.png"/></figure><p>Hessa was not there.</p><p>This was unexpected because the appointment was at Hessa's rooms, and Hessa was usually the part of Hessa's rooms that made them useful.</p><p>The door was unlocked.</p><p>Nerin was inside.</p><p>She looked at me, looked toward the back room, then held up one finger.</p><p>“Wait.”</p><p>“Is she with someone?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Should I come back?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>That was all I got.</p><p>I sat.</p><p>The bad chair remained bad.</p><p>Consistency.</p><p>There were sounds from behind the closed inner door.</p><p>Not dramatic sounds.</p><p>Movement.</p><p>A basin set down.</p><p>Low voices.</p><p>Once, Hessa said, “Again.”</p><p>Then silence.</p><p>I looked at the copper strip on the side table.</p><p>It was not the same strip.</p><p>Or maybe it was and had been moved.</p><p>I did not touch it.</p><p>Personal record.</p><p>Nerin was sorting folded cloth into three piles.</p><p>I watched.</p><p>She noticed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You're counting.”</p><p>“I am not.”</p><p>“You looked at each pile.”</p><p>“That is not counting.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>I knew.</p><p>I refused to answer.</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>The inner door opened.</p><p>A man came out with his right hand wrapped from palm to wrist.</p><p>He was older than me by enough that I could not estimate it usefully.</p><p>His face was pale.</p><p>Hessa came behind him.</p><p>“Keep it dry today.”</p><p>He nodded.</p><p>“If the fingers go cold, blue, or numb, come back.”</p><p>Another nod.</p><p>“Not tomorrow. Come back.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He left.</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“You're early.”</p><p>“I am exactly on time.”</p><p>She looked at the wall clock.</p><p>“You're early by three minutes.”</p><p>“That is not early in a meaningful sense.”</p><p>“It is three minutes.”</p><p>“I waited longer than three minutes.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So I was not early for the appointment that actually occurred.”</p><p>Hessa closed her eyes.</p><p>Nerin laughed into the cloth.</p><p>“Come back in half an hour,” Hessa said.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Half an hour.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I need to clean the room, write notes, eat something, and sit down.”</p><p>“You are sitting now.”</p><p>“I am standing.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>She pointed at the door.</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>She looked tired.</p><p>Not injured.</p><p>Not collapsing.</p><p>Just tired.</p><p>This was somehow more persuasive.</p><p>“Half an hour?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Exactly?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Between half an hour and forty-five minutes.”</p><p>“That is a range.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I can work with a range.”</p><p>“I know. Go.”</p><p>I went.</p><p>The street had nothing prepared for me.</p><p>This was rude.</p><p>I could not go far because thirty to forty-five minutes was long enough to start something and short enough to make starting it stupid.</p><p>I bought a small meat pie.</p><p>Then another because the first was small in the way merchants use the word small to mean insulting.</p><p>I ate sitting on the edge of a dry horse trough.</p><p>The stone was cold.</p><p>My residual limb felt normal.</p><p>My hands felt normal.</p><p>Everything felt normal.</p><p>I considered what Hessa had been doing.</p><p>Hand injury.</p><p>Maybe burn.</p><p>Maybe crush.</p><p>Maybe magic.</p><p>Not my business.</p><p>This phrase was getting suspiciously easy.</p><p>I finished the second pie.</p><p>There were still twenty minutes.</p><p>I watched a dog fail to steal cabbage.</p><p>The dog had a strategy.</p><p>It waited until the cabbage seller turned.</p><p>Then approached from the side.</p><p>The problem was that the dog was white and the stall cloth was dark blue.</p><p>Also the seller had apparently met the dog before.</p><p>“Don’t.”</p><p>The dog stopped.</p><p>Waited.</p><p>Seller turned.</p><p>Dog moved.</p><p>“Don’t.”</p><p>This happened four times.</p><p>The dog did not update.</p><p>I respected commitment.</p><p>At thirty-seven minutes, I returned.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/101/Ch101_Hessa-Eats-Bread.png" alt="Hessa eats bread at her worktable while Greg waits with his crutches." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Hessa was eating bread.</p><p>I stopped in the doorway.</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“You said half an hour to forty-five minutes.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It has been thirty-seven.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I am inside the interval.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>Nerin was gone.</p><p>The inner room smelled faintly of boiled cloth and something metallic.</p><p>The examination cot had fresh covering.</p><p>Hessa finished the bread.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>This was difficult.</p><p>She drank water.</p><p>I continued waiting.</p><p>This was more difficult.</p><p>Finally she said, “How are you?”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“That answer has never helped anyone.”</p><p>“Residual limb baseline. No swelling after yesterday because yesterday I did nothing strenuous. Hands fine. Right calf and hip fine. No change in phantom symptoms after the last draw. No pain, cold, heat, cramping, pressure, or persistent extension. I wrote it down.”</p><p>“In paragraphs?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I used semicolons.”</p><p>“I don't care.”</p><p>“You cared about tables.”</p><p>“I care about you not turning every sensation into a private experiment.”</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She stood.</p><p>“Leg.”</p><p>Same examination.</p><p>Wrapping off.</p><p>Skin.</p><p>Temperature.</p><p>Pressure.</p><p>Questions.</p><p>Nothing interesting.</p><p>She rewrapped it.</p><p>Then sat.</p><p>I looked at the copper strip.</p><p>She did not pick it up.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She still did not pick it up.</p><p>“Are we drawing?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“No?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I don't want to.”</p><p>That was not an acceptable medical explanation.</p><p>I said this.</p><p>She leaned back.</p><p>“I treated someone before you.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>“It required sustained channel work.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>There.</p><p>Relevant.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Not your business.”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>“I am not concerned that I would hurt you.”</p><p>“That sounds promising.”</p><p>“I am also not interested in supervising an unnecessary test while I am tired enough to know I am tired.”</p><p>I looked at the copper strip.</p><p>“Unnecessary.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“We scheduled it.”</p><p>“We scheduled an assessment.”</p><p>“Which has included a draw.”</p><p>“Previously.”</p><p>“You changed the plan.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Because you are tired.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I considered this.</p><p>It was irritating.</p><p>Also correct.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>“Would the draw itself be dangerous?”</p><p>“I just told you I am not concerned I would hurt you.”</p><p>“So why not?”</p><p>“Because the question is not whether I can probably supervise it adequately.”</p><p>I hated the word probably.</p><p>Hessa saw that.</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>“You want margin.”</p><p>“I want my judgment to be boring.”</p><p>That was annoyingly good.</p><p>I looked at her hands.</p><p>No tremor.</p><p>No visible problem.</p><p>She was not impaired.</p><p>She was simply declining to spend expertise at the edge of what she considered useful.</p><p>“What did you learn from examining me?”</p><p>“That you had no concerning delayed effect from the last draw.”</p><p>“That matters.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So this appointment still produced information.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I brightened.</p><p>Hessa pointed at me.</p><p>“Do not become pleased because I found a way to make cancellation sound productive.”</p><p>“I am not.”</p><p>“You are.”</p><p>“A little.”</p><p>She sighed.</p><p>“When next?”</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Day after?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why not tomorrow?”</p><p>“Because there is no urgency.”</p><p>“There is to me.”</p><p>“That is not the same thing.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>Bad chair.</p><p>Still bad.</p><p>“Three successful draws.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No delayed effects.”</p><p>“So far.”</p><p>“Variable subjective sensation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No shaping.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I paused.</p><p>“Are we getting closer to shaping?”</p><p>Hessa was quiet.</p><p>Not long.</p><p>Long enough.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I felt my entire body become more attentive.</p><p>She saw it.</p><p>“Do not do that.”</p><p>“Do what?”</p><p>“Turn one word into permission.”</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“You inhaled like a hunting dog.”</p><p>“That is insulting.”</p><p>“It was accurate.”</p><p>“Maybe means what?”</p><p>“It means I am beginning to think about what the first shaping test would need to be.”</p><p>There.</p><p>Not clearance.</p><p>Not a plan.</p><p>Still.</p><p>There.</p><p>“What would it be?”</p><p>“I have not decided.”</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Immediate.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Too familiar.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“That seems like an advantage.”</p><p>“For performance, perhaps. Not for the first question I want answered.”</p><p>“What question?”</p><p>“Whether you can deliberately alter drawn mana in a very small way without falling into an old trained pattern.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>That made sense too quickly.</p><p>Barrier was not merely a spell.</p><p>It was practiced.</p><p>Repeated.</p><p>Body-known.</p><p>Possibly exactly the wrong thing if she wanted to distinguish deliberate shaping now from the machinery of prior habit.</p><p>“You don't want automatic.”</p><p>“I don't want more variables than I need.”</p><p>“What kind of shaping?”</p><p>“I said I have not decided.”</p><p>“Direction?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Compression?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Release pattern?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Sorry.”</p><p>I was not sorry.</p><p>I was extremely interested.</p><p>She knew.</p><p>“That is not clearance,” she said.</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You may not practice drawing.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You may not try to feel the edge of shaping without drawing.”</p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I closed it.</p><p>That had been a good idea.</p><p>Apparently not.</p><p>“You may not rehearse Barrier mentally as a magical exercise.”</p><p>“That is impossible to define.”</p><p>“Then don't deliberately sit there imagining the mana sequence.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“You are criminalizing thought.”</p><p>“I am telling you not to train.”</p><p>“Thought is not training.”</p><p>“Yours is.”</p><p>Unfair.</p><p>Possibly fair.</p><p>“What can I do?”</p><p>“Live until the day after tomorrow.”</p><p>“That seems broad.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can I cook?”</p><p>“If the keeper permits it.”</p><p>“He did.”</p><p>“Then apparently.”</p><p>“Cards?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Work?”</p><p>“If someone pays you.”</p><p>“Pessa?”</p><p>Hessa considered.</p><p>“Tomorrow, if your body remains at baseline, I have no medical objection to you asking her.”</p><p>Important wording.</p><p>“No medical objection.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not clearance.”</p><p>“Pessa decides whether she wants to train you.”</p><p>Different jurisdiction.</p><p>I did not say it.</p><p>Personal record.</p><p>Hessa stood.</p><p>Appointment over.</p><p>I remained seated.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I am adjusting to the fact that I came here for magic and received no magic.”</p><p>“You received an examination.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And a future maybe.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>That was malicious.</p><p>“You did that intentionally.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I stood.</p><p>Both crutches.</p><p>No phantom step.</p><p>No unusual sensation.</p><p>No magic.</p><p>At the door I stopped.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“The man before me.”</p><p>Her face changed slightly.</p><p>Closed.</p><p>“Not your business.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>I hesitated.</p><p>“Is he all right?”</p><p>She considered that too.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was enough.</p><p>I left.</p><p>Outside, the white dog was across the street.</p><p>It had acquired cabbage.</p><p>I had missed the breakthrough.</p><p>The dog saw me looking and ran.</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>No draw.</p><p>No shaping.</p><p>No answer.</p><p>A maybe.</p><p>Apparently that was enough to ruin the rest of my day in the best possible way.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top"
