- `chapters/139.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 108: The Subject — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 108</div><h1>THE SUBJECT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Hessa had moved the towel. I noticed before I sat down. Not far. Perhaps two fingers toward the end of the table. I put both crutches against the wall and looked at it. Hessa was grinding something in a small stone bowl. The room smelled bitter and green, with something sharper underneath that caught in the back of my nose. Morning light came through the narrow window beside her shelves and made every suspended bit of herb dust unnecessarily visible.</p><p>"You moved the towel."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"It was wet."</p><p>I looked at her. She kept grinding.</p><p>"You replaced it."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"In a different position."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"It is farther down the table."</p><p>Hessa stopped. She looked at the towel. Then at me. Then back at the towel.</p><p>"It is a towel, Gregory."</p><p>"That is not an answer."</p><p>"It is the only answer you are getting before you sit down."</p><p>I sat. The cot creaked under me. Hessa resumed grinding. I looked at the towel. Yesterday I had performed in front of an audience. Today I was suspicious of folded linen. This seemed like a decline.</p><p>"How was the show?" Hessa asked.</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>"You know about the show?"</p><p>"I know you went."</p><p>"That is not the same thing."</p><p>"No."</p><p>She scraped the crushed leaves into a small paper fold. I waited. She did not ask again.</p><p>"Parts were good," I said.</p><p>"Mm."</p><p>"Parts were bad."</p><p>"Sounds like a show."</p><p>"You've been?"</p><p>"To shows?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"No. I've spent my entire life avoiding rooms with chairs."</p><p>I frowned. Hessa glanced at me.</p><p>"That was a joke."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"You looked injured."</p><p>"I was determining whether you were mocking Teren."</p><p>"I don't know Teren."</p><p>"Then probably not."</p><p>She put the paper fold aside and washed the pestle in a basin. Water tapped against stone. Somewhere below us, a door opened hard enough to rattle the window, followed by a man's voice complaining about somebody's cart. Carrow was awake. I had slept badly. Not because of magic. That distinction mattered. I had spent too much of the night remembering an audience laughing. Also not laughing. The not laughing had been more educational. Possibly. I had no idea. Then there was the trip. Five days. Maybe six. East. Temporary.</p><p>There was an old municipal hall there with a roof I had wanted to see before I died the first time. That was a perfectly legitimate reason to travel. The theatre was also going. Coincidence. Mostly.</p><p>"Sleep?" Hessa asked.</p><p>"Enough."</p><p>"How much?"</p><p>I told her.</p><p>"Water?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Food?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Alcohol?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Pain?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Cramping?"</p><p>"Ordinary."</p><p>"Residual limb?"</p><p>"Baseline."</p><p>"Right hand?"</p><p>"Normal."</p><p>"Forearm?"</p><p>"Normal."</p><p>"Phantom?"</p><p>"Ordinary."</p><p>She dried her hands.</p><p>"You said ordinary very quickly."</p><p>"It is ordinary."</p><p>"You checked?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>That was not entirely true. I had noticed. Noticing was not checking. Probably. Hessa watched me for another moment, then wrote something.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"You wrote."</p><p>"I often do."</p><p>"What did you write?"</p><p>"That you answered too quickly."</p><p>"That contaminates the record."</p><p>"It is the record."</p><p>I disliked her profession. Hessa pulled the stool over and sat beside the cot. The copper strip was already on the small tray. So was charcoal, paper, and the same narrow measuring cord she had used before. No thread apparatus. Good. I had not expected it. I was still glad.</p><p>"What are we doing?"</p><p>"Drawing mana."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Then shaping."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Then reporting."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"And then?"</p><p>"We stop."</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>"That is the entire assessment?"</p><p>"If nothing interesting happens."</p><p>"That is barely an assessment."</p><p>"You have become very difficult to impress."</p><p>"Nineteen draws."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Fifteen shaping attempts."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Three external attempts."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"And now we're going backward."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"We are doing something I could already do."</p><p>"That is not backward."</p><p>"It is not forward."</p><p>Hessa leaned over and tapped the paper with one finger.</p><p>"Last time you gave me a more detailed description of the neutral shape than you had before the directional tests."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"The neutral shape was not neutral in the way you assumed."</p><p>"I did not assume it was symmetrical."</p><p>"You drew it symmetrical."</p><p>"Because I thought it was."</p><p>"Excellent. We have located the assumption."</p><p>I shut my mouth. She continued.</p><p>"If your ordinary shaped state already has a more distinct wrist-side boundary, then a later report that the wrist-side boundary became more distinct under instruction means less than it would if the starting shape were even."</p><p>"It still changed."</p><p>"Perhaps."</p><p>"It did."</p><p>"You reported that it did."</p><p>I hated that sentence too. Hessa did not look pleased about saying it. That made it worse. She set my right forearm onto the folded towel. The position was familiar. Palm down, forearm supported, elbow free enough that I was not pressing hard into the table edge. I looked at the towel.</p><p>"It is different."</p><p>Hessa closed her eyes.</p><p>"Gregory."</p><p>"Two fingers."</p><p>"You may leave."</p><p>"I didn't say it invalidated the test."</p><p>"You are looking at cloth instead of your arm."</p><p>"I can do both."</p><p>"That is precisely the problem."</p><p>Fair. I looked at my arm. Hessa adjusted the copper strip.</p><p>"Minimal draw."</p><p>I breathed. Reached. Mana came. Not dramatically. It had stopped feeling dramatic several assessments ago, which was probably dangerous in its own way. There. Present. Contained. The copper responded.</p><p>"Confirmed," Hessa said.</p><p>I held. Right side normal. Hand normal. Thumb quiet. No motor urge. No cold. No pain. My left phantom foot existed somewhere below the cot, vague and familiar and completely uninvolved.</p><p>"Shape," Hessa said.</p><p>I formed the small alteration in the right forearm. No direction. No external reach. Just the shape. It gathered slowly enough that I could feel the temptation to help it. I did not. There.</p><p>"Hold."</p><p>I held.</p><p>"Report."</p><p>"Localized. Similar size to last time."</p><p>"Similar is interpretation. Edges."</p><p>Right. I closed my eyes. Not because I needed to. Because the room became less annoying.</p><p>"Wrist-side boundary is clearest."</p><p>Hessa said nothing.</p><p>"Upper edge less distinct. Elbow side softer. Lower edge..."</p><p>I waited.</p><p>"Lower edge is difficult."</p><p>"Meaning?"</p><p>"I can tell where I think it stops. I cannot tell whether I'm feeling the end of the shape or the point where my attention stops being useful."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"That wasn't a success."</p><p>"It was a report."</p><p>Fine.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/139/Ch139_Forward-Coverage-004-01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 139." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>"Anything changing?"</p><p>I waited. The shape stayed. Or mostly stayed. The upper edge felt broader than it had at the start. I did not like that.</p><p>"Upper edge may be spreading."</p><p>"May?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Direction?"</p><p>"Not instructed."</p><p>"I asked what direction."</p><p>"Oh. Toward the outside of the forearm. Slightly."</p><p>"Other edges?"</p><p>"Wrist side still clearest. Elbow side soft. Lower unclear."</p><p>Hessa wrote. I could hear the charcoal moving. Scritch. Pause. Scritch. It was surprisingly irritating.</p><p>"Draw it," she said.</p><p>"With my left hand?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"My left hand draws badly."</p><p>"It drew badly last time."</p><p>"So we are preserving the variable."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>I opened my eyes. Hessa put the paper where I could reach it without moving my right forearm. I took the charcoal in my left hand. The first line looked like a potato.</p><p>"This is useless."</p><p>"Continue."</p><p>I drew the wrist-side edge darker. Then the upper edge. Then the softer elbow side. The lower boundary got a broken line because I did not trust it. Hessa watched the paper, not my face.</p><p>"Done?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Look at the prior one."</p><p>She turned over a sheet beside her ledger. My drawing from the last assessment. I looked between them. Oh. The wrist-side boundary was dark in both. The elbow side was soft in both. The upper edge was not identical, but it was close enough that I could not dismiss it as nothing. The lower edge on the old drawing had been cleaner. Or I had drawn it cleaner. Those were not the same fact.</p><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"One more neutral shape."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Same setup."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because you are already comparing."</p><p>"That is the point."</p><p>"Not while you are holding mana."</p><p>I looked at my right arm. Fuck.</p><p>"Return," Hessa said.</p><p>I reduced the shape. The wrist-side edge softened first. Again. Not completely. The center faded. Upper edge lingered. I continued the same return without separately correcting it.</p><p>"Report."</p><p>"Wrist side reduced. Center reduced. Upper edge remains clearer."</p><p>"Continue."</p><p>I did. The remaining edge softened. Then I reached the familiar ugly point where I could not tell whether something remained or whether I was searching for it because Hessa had asked me to.</p><p>"Uncertain."</p><p>"Hold draw."</p><p>I held the underlying mana. The shaped alteration was either gone or below my confidence.</p><p>"Copper?"</p><p>"Draw remains," Hessa said.</p><p>"Release."</p><p>I released. The mana went. Nothing jumped. Nothing hurt. Nothing moved outside me. No thread trembled. No revelation occurred. Hessa waited anyway. She checked my hand, wrist, forearm, breathing, residual limb, and the things she always checked even when I was increasingly convinced she could do half of it by glaring.</p><p>"Anything?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Stand."</p><p>I reached for the crutches. She watched me rise. Right foot planted. Hands loaded. Hips came forward. Normal. I settled.</p><p>"Anything?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Walk."</p><p>I went to the window and back. The room was not large enough to make this dignified.</p><p>"Anything?"</p><p>"My dignity is declining."</p><p>"Baseline."</p><p>I looked at her. She wrote it down.</p><p>"You did not."</p><p>"I did."</p><p>"Hessa."</p><p>She smiled without looking up. Barely. That was worse than laughter. I sat again. She put the two drawings side by side. They were not identical. They were also not very different. I leaned closer.</p><p>"If that's the ordinary geometry," I said, "then the directional tests are weaker."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Not gone."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Because there were changes after instruction."</p><p>"Reported changes."</p><p>"Yes, yes."</p><p>"And because the prior tests were not mapped this way before the instruction, we cannot compare their starting geometry at the same level of detail."</p><p>I stared at the pages. That annoyed me more than if she had simply said the tests were bad. Bad could be discarded. These were not bad. They were incomplete. Much worse.</p><p>"So we repeat them."</p><p>"Eventually."</p><p>"With a pre-map."</p><p>"Possibly."</p><p>"Same position."</p><p>"Possibly."</p><p>"Same towel."</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>"I will preserve the sacred towel."</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>"I'll label it."</p><p>"That would actually help."</p><p>"I regret speaking."</p><p>She stacked the papers. I watched her. There was still something missing.</p><p>"What did today establish?"</p><p>"Establish is too strong."</p><p>"Fine. What did today support?"</p><p>"That your neutral shaped state may have a repeatable asymmetry under this setup."</p><p>"May."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Wrist-side boundary more distinct."</p><p>"In two detailed reports."</p><p>"And upper edge changes without directional instruction."</p><p>"In both assessments, though not identically."</p><p>"So anatomy?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"Support pressure?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"Arm position?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"Natural magical geometry?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"Expectation?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"Day variation?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>I sighed.</p><p>"You really do have one answer."</p><p>"I have several. You keep asking questions with the same answer."</p><p>I looked at the two drawings again. Then I remembered the wagon. Not because it had anything to do with my forearm. Because it was leaving. Tomorrow, apparently. I had known that before coming here. I had not intended to bring it up until after the assessment. That was sensible. The assessment was medical and magical. The theatre was theatre. Separate.</p><p>"Hessa."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I haven't asked."</p><p>"You changed your voice."</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>"What does that mean?"</p><p>"You have an administrative question."</p><p>"I do not have an administrative voice."</p><p>"You absolutely do."</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/139/Ch139_Forward-Coverage-004-02.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 139." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>I considered objecting. That would delay the question.</p><p>"The theatre is leaving Carrow tomorrow."</p><p>Hessa's hand stopped over the ledger.</p><p>"For how long?"</p><p>"Five days. Maybe six."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>I told her. She knew the town. Of course she did. Hessa knew every place within a week's travel where somebody had once broken a wrist badly.</p><p>"Why are you telling me?"</p><p>"Because I might go."</p><p>"Might?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>She waited. I disliked silence when other people used it deliberately.</p><p>"I want to see the municipal hall," I said.</p><p>Hessa nodded.</p><p>"The roof was rebuilt twice."</p><p>"Mm."</p><p>"The original load paths are strange."</p><p>"I'm sure."</p><p>"And the theatre is performing there."</p><p>"An extraordinary coincidence."</p><p>I looked at her. She remained completely serious.</p><p>"I would be traveling with them."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"There would be wagons."</p><p>"I know what theatres use."</p><p>"Do you?"</p><p>"No. But I know what roads use."</p><p>Fair.</p><p>"I wouldn't test anything independently."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I wouldn't draw."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I wouldn't shape."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I wouldn't cast."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"I am enjoying this part."</p><p>I shifted on the cot.</p><p>"What I am asking is whether going changes your restrictions."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>My stomach tightened. Hessa closed the ledger.</p><p>"You will be somewhere else."</p><p>"That is not what I meant."</p><p>"It is what I mean. If you are injured, sick, exhausted, or develop a new symptom, I am not there."</p><p>"I understand."</p><p>"Do you?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You said you slept enough this morning."</p><p>"I did."</p><p>"You slept badly."</p><p>I stopped. She had not asked whether I slept well. Only how much. Annoying woman.</p><p>"I slept enough badly."</p><p>"That sentence is why I worry about you."</p><p>"You don't worry about me."</p><p>"No."</p><p>She began wrapping the charcoal in cloth.</p><p>"I simply arrange my professional decisions around the possibility that you will do something stupid."</p><p>"That sounds like worry."</p><p>"It is risk management."</p><p>She tied the cloth twice. Too tightly for something she did not care about. I did not mention it.</p><p>"So can I go?"</p><p>"I don't control where you travel."</p><p>"That is evasive."</p><p>"It is accurate. I control what magical work I supervise and what I clear you to do."</p><p>"And?"</p><p>"And you remain uncleared for independent draw, shaping, casting, Barrier work, external testing, or whatever clever category you invent because you think it isn't technically one of those."</p><p>"I wasn't going to."</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>"I wasn't."</p><p>She kept looking.</p><p>"I probably wasn't."</p><p>"Better."</p><p>I rubbed my palm against my trouser leg.</p><p>"If I go, when is the next assessment?"</p><p>"When you return."</p><p>"That could be six days."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"We've been working on a shorter cadence."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"So the gap changes the sequence."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>I waited. Hessa waited back.</p><p>"You're not going to tell me not to go."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Do you want me to?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then this is an odd complaint."</p><p>"I expected you to object."</p><p>"I object to unsupervised magic. I object to you converting uncertainty into permission. I object to you pretending symptoms don't count because they interfere with your plans."</p><p>"I don't do that."</p><p>She looked at me. Fine.</p><p>"Not consistently."</p><p>"Better."</p><p>She stood and carried the bowl to the shelf. I looked at the drawings again. Six days without an assessment. Possibly. Five. The theatre had chairs in other towns. Apparently. Also shopkeepers. I could stay. That would be easier. Known room. Known stairs. Hessa. Guild. Pessa. Lyssa. Jorren. Work if it appeared. Theatre again when they came back, assuming they came back when expected. Nothing required me to leave Carrow. That was important. I was not being forced onto a road. I was not fleeing anything.</p><p>I was not chasing work I needed to survive. I was not even formally part of the troupe. There were excellent reasons not to go.</p><p>"Hessa."</p><p>She turned.</p><p>"If I travel tomorrow, is today the last assessment before I leave?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>I nodded.</p><p>"That is irritating."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>She came back to the table and pushed the newer drawing toward me.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Take it."</p><p>I stared.</p><p>"You keep the records."</p><p>"I have the record."</p><p>She tapped her ledger.</p><p>"Take the drawing."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"So when you spend six days thinking about it, you can at least think about the thing you actually reported."</p><p>I picked it up.</p><p>"That sounds like permission to analyze it."</p><p>"No magic."</p><p>"I said analyze."</p><p>"No reconstructing the sensation."</p><p>"I can't promise not to remember my own arm."</p><p>"You know the difference."</p><p>I did. Mostly. I folded the paper once. Hessa immediately said, "Don't." I unfolded it.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"You just folded through the wrist boundary."</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>"You said the drawing isn't independent evidence."</p><p>"It isn't."</p><p>"Then why does the fold matter?"</p><p>"Because now I have to wonder whether you will later remember the fold as part of the line."</p><p>I looked at the charcoal mark. Then at her.</p><p>"That is extremely annoying."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>She gave me a scrap of stiff paper to carry it between. I slid the drawing inside. At the door I collected my crutches.</p><p>"Hessa."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"If I go east, and nothing changes, I come back and we continue?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Same restrictions."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Same question?"</p><p>"We'll see."</p><p>I opened the door.</p><p>"And Gregory?"</p><p>I looked back. She had already reopened the ledger.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Go because you want to go."</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>"I told you. The municipal hall."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"The roof is genuinely interesting."</p><p>"I believe you."</p><p>"And I'm useful to the theatre."</p><p>"I didn't ask."</p><p>"They need the sword."</p><p>"Gregory."</p><p>"And possibly the Shopkeeper."</p><p>"Leave my office."</p><p>I did. The street outside was brighter than I expected. A produce cart blocked half the lane, and two women were arguing over whether a basket of onions belonged to one of them or to a shop three doors down. Someone had hung wet shirts from an upper window. They snapped in the breeze above the street like surrender flags nobody respected. I tucked Hessa's drawing safely inside my coat. The theatre left tomorrow. I had an entire day to decide whether I was going. I turned west.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="138.html">← Chapter 107</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="140.html">Chapter 109 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/005.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 4: The Warrior — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 4</div><h1>THE WARRIOR</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>I paid Hessa first. That was new. Not paying people. I had always paid people eventually. Paying the sensible thing before the interesting thing. I put the training money aside before breakfast, counted what remained, and felt briefly pleased with myself. Then I went gambling. Three nights later, I had more money than I had possessed since waking up. Five nights later, I had less. This was not, strictly speaking, the gambling's fault. The distinction mattered to me. It did not matter to the coins. The gambling worked. That was the problem.</p><p>The White Dog became easy faster than it should have. Not easy enough to demand money from the universe. Cards remained cards. Bad hands and stupid luck still existed. A drunk dockworker once called a bet he had absolutely no business calling and drew the one card that could save him. I disliked him personally for almost six minutes. But individual people were astonishingly repetitive.</p><p>Give me an hour and I knew who protected winnings, who chased losses, who bluffed when embarrassed, who lied better after drinking, who needed to be seen as fearless, who watched the cards, who watched the pot, and who watched me. The last group was dangerous. So I moved rooms.</p><p>The White Dog one night. The Copper Nail the next. A guild game behind a cooper's shop. A private table I got invited to because Osric apparently decided losing money to me was more enjoyable when accompanied by better wine. I won. Not always. Enough.</p><p>Silver became less frightening. Then, almost immediately, less real. That was how fast my brain betrayed me. The first few winnings had been food. Training. Rent. Breathing room. The next few became capital. Capital became possibility. Possibility became permission. I funded another round of Arlo's tests. Reasonable. I bought better food because Hessa had told me to. Also reasonable. I replaced my cracked boots. Still reasonable.</p><p>Then I bought a sword. That required more explanation. I already owned a sword. Technically. The object in my room had an edge, a hilt, and a history of being used on firewood. It was a sword in the same sense that I was currently a mage. Potentially. I wanted something balanced. Not expensive. There was a difference. I knew the difference. I had spent decades around excellent weapons. That should have helped. It did help.</p><p>A little. It also convinced me to spend far more than I had intended because I could feel every defect in the cheaper blades. The third sword I tested pulled slightly forward. The fourth had a grip too narrow for my hand. The fifth was competent. I should have bought the fifth. The sixth was beautiful. Not jeweled. Not ceremonial. Nothing stupid. Just balanced.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Sixth Sword" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/005/v28_c05_s03_the-sixth-sword.png"/></figure><p>The kind of balance you did not notice until you picked up something worse afterward. I made three cuts in the shop's practice lane. The blade stopped where I wanted it. My wrist remembered things. My shoulder remembered more. Something in my chest opened.</p><p>"Oh," I said.</p><p>The smith looked at me.</p><p>"You buying it?"</p><p>I looked at the price. That was too much silver. Old Greg said it was nothing. Young Greg's coin purse said otherwise. I bought it. On the walk home I constructed a very sophisticated argument explaining why this was an investment in accelerated martial development. By the time I reached my room, I almost believed it. I added a line to the board.</p><p>WARRIOR?</p><p>I looked at the word until the question mark annoyed me. Warrior Greg was familiar. I knew how he stood. What he wore. What he did when frustrated. Give him a sword and a problem with a face and the world became wonderfully narrow. Maybe I wanted the profession. Maybe I wanted the role because I already knew how to disappear inside it.</p><p>Why not? The question had been bothering me since Hessa's first assessment. I had accepted my first life's shape too quickly. Warrior first. Plateau. Barrier. Support. Versatility. S-class. That sequence had become biography, and biography had quietly become destiny. But it had not been destiny the first time. It had been a collection of decisions made by a younger, stupider Greg with less information. I knew why warrior Greg had plateaued.</p><p>Mostly. Probably. That last word irritated me. I wrote:</p><p>WHY WAS I ONLY AN OKAY WARRIOR?</p><p>Strength? I had been strong enough. Speed? Courage? Unfortunately abundant. Technique? I paused.</p><p>That was the word. I had never been elegant. I had been effective enough to pass stat checks, as a Silver-ranked swordswoman whose name I could no longer remember had once put it. Greg wins because Greg can afford the hit. Because his reinforcement is better. Because his barrier catches the mistake. Because the other man gets tired first. Because somebody let Greg prepare. Later, once I had magic, I had humiliated better swordsmen by making the contest unfair. I liked doing that.</p><p>There was something delicious about watching a technically superior fighter realize the duel had become a mathematics problem he had not agreed to solve. People called it dirty. I called it winning. But before magic? I had been okay. Just okay.</p><p>Which raised an interesting question. How much better could I be if I learned it correctly this time? I knew what elite footwork looked like. I knew why good fighters conserved motion. I knew what panic did to breathing. I knew how shields failed. I knew what angles killed people. I had watched monsters move. I had watched S-class warriors move.</p><p>More importantly, I had spent decades making those warriors better. You learned a great deal about mechanics when your job was to amplify someone without tearing their muscles apart. Maybe first-life Greg had lacked education more than potential. Flattering theory. I liked it immediately. Dangerous. I wrote it down anyway. The guild practice yard charged by the hour. Of course it did.</p><p>I paid. Silver. A stupid amount of silver for access to sand, posts, battered shields, and men who smelled like leather. I did not care. I wanted to move. That was the part the board could not solve. I was tired of sitting. Tired of remembering. Tired of explaining to Arlo what I thought might happen. Tired of Hessa telling me to breathe slowly while trying to feel something that had once answered me like another limb. Tired of cards. Even winning at cards involved sitting down. I wanted my body to do something.</p><p>More specifically, I wanted to be somebody who did things. The borrower waited. The investor watched Arlo. The student breathed on command. The gambler sat and studied faces. The warrior moved. So I trained. For twenty minutes, I was a genius. My stance was cleaner than I remembered. My grip changed automatically. I stopped loading my shoulder before cuts.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Back In The Yard" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/005/v28_c05_s01_back-in-the-yard.png"/></figure><p>I shortened movements I had once made dramatically because nineteen-year-old Greg had apparently believed enemies were impressed by commitment. I moved around a post and saw mistakes before I made them. This was going to work. Of course it was. Why had I ever doubted it? I was not relearning swordsmanship. I was correcting it. Different thing. Faster thing. I worked through basic cuts.</p><p>Transitions. Recovery. Advance. Retreat. Pivot. Again. Again. Again. My body learned quickly. Not magically. But quickly enough that I could feel old understanding finding new joints. I laughed. Actually laughed. A man training two lanes over glanced at me. I did not care. This was good. This was movement. This was mine. Then my legs started shaking. Not metaphorically.</p><p>I stepped back after a cut and my rear leg failed to put me where my mind had already decided I would be. I stumbled. Caught myself. Looked down. My legs offered no explanation. I tried again. Slower. The movement worked. Again. Faster. My calf tightened. My thigh burned. My lungs had started working much harder than I had noticed.</p><p>Right.</p><p>Nineteen-year-old body. Bronze conditioning. Not sixty-year-old knowledge in an S-class chassis.</p><p>"Fine." I rested.</p><p>For almost a minute. Then started again. That was the first mistake. The second was deciding fatigue made the test more useful. The third was noticing a broad-shouldered Bronze warrior watching me and asking if he wanted to spar. He looked at my token. Then at me.</p><p>"Sure."</p><p>That tone. I knew that tone. Young. Confident. He thought I was going to be easy. Wonderful. His name was Jorren. Or Joran. No, Jorren. He told me twice. I forgot once because I was watching his feet. He had better conditioning than me. Probably stronger. His guard was too high. He planted before committing. His right shoulder tightened before a heavy cut. I knew him in thirty seconds.</p><p>Not him. His fight. Close enough. We used blunted practice swords. First exchange, he hit me. I got up anyway. I had seen it coming. That was irritating. Seeing and moving were not the same thing. I reset. Second exchange, I made him miss. Third, I touched his ribs. Fourth, he hit my shoulder. Fifth, I touched his wrist. He frowned. Sixth, I let him think he had found the shoulder again, stepped inside the line, and put the practice blade against his throat.</p><p>He froze. I smiled. There it was. That old pleasure. Not winning. The moment someone realized the contest they thought they understood was not the contest they were in.</p><p>"You've done this before," Jorren said.</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You're Bronze."</p><p>"So are you."</p><p>"That's not what I meant." I liked him slightly more for that. We went again. I won the next exchange. Lost the next two.</p><p>Won another. Then lost badly because my foot dragged half a beat behind the decision. Jorren's practice sword hit my ribs. I went down. The sand was warm. I lay there staring upward. My mind had known exactly what to do. My body had simply declined. That was old. I had just forgotten it. Jorren offered a hand.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Jorren Makes The Point" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/005/v28_c05_s02_jorren-makes-the-point.png"/></figure><p>"You all right?"</p><p>"Excellent," I said.</p><p>Jorren kept his hand out and waited for me to prove it.</p><p>"I'm fine."</p><p>That was more believable. I took his hand. He pulled me up.</p><p>"You're weird."</p><p>"I've heard that."</p><p>Jorren said, "You fight like an old man." </p><p>I stared at him. </p><p>He laughed.</p><p>"Not slow. Just... you know."</p><p>"Like you already know what I'm going to do."</p><p>Oh. That was interesting.</p><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>Jorren lowered the practice sword. His eyes went to my chest, then my shaking legs.</p><p>"Maybe tomorrow."</p><p>I disliked him again. On the walk back, my ribs hurt. My legs hurt. My shoulder hurt. I felt fantastic. I added another training session the next day. That cost money.</p><p>Then another. Money. I paid a Silver-ranked instructor for an hour because I wanted someone better than Jorren. More money. The instructor corrected my stance twice, my recovery six times, and told me my instincts were ahead of my mechanics. I considered that confirmation. It was also criticism. I mostly heard confirmation. I gambled that night and won enough to cover it. So I booked him again. Then lost at cards the following night.</p><p>Not much. Enough. The next night I won. The night after that I lost badly. That one was my fault. I knew it while doing it. The table was new. Higher stakes. The players were better. I had already lost twice and should have left. Instead I stayed because I had learned them. Almost. Almost was an expensive word. I had Senna's voice in my head. Learn quieter. I had my own rule on the wall.</p><p>LEAVE THE TABLE WHEN THE DAY IS SOLVED.</p><p>The day was not solved. That became my excuse. I chased. Not cards. Information. One more hand and I would understand the man across from me. One more and I would know whether the twitch near his mouth meant excitement or irritation. One more. One more. He knew I was studying him. I did not realize he was studying me. That cost me. A lot. I walked home with less money than I had started the week with.</p><p>Still fine. Annoying. Recoverable. I had Hessa money set aside. Except I had spent part of it on the second sword lesson. Not all. Some. The distinction felt important until I counted. I stared at the coins.</p><p>"That's inconvenient." I could win it back. That was the worst sentence I had thought all week. I knew it immediately. I went gambling the next night anyway. I won. I paid Hessa. I bought food.</p><p>I put more money into Arlo because one of his tests had improved again and stopping now seemed idiotic. Then I found a set of used vambraces at a price I considered absurdly low. They were absurdly low. I bought them. Good purchase. Still money. A week became a pattern. Win. Spend. Invest. Train. Lose. Win. Borrow against what I expected to win. That last part happened quietly. Antonius made it easy. Of course he did.</p><p>"You've been paying on time," Antonius said.</p><p>"I told you I would."</p><p>"You've also been borrowing again."</p><p>"Capital efficiency."</p><p>"Is that what we're calling it?"</p><p>"Do you have a better term?"</p><p>"Compulsion."</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>Antonius did not answer. The smile stopped feeling like an argument.</p><p>That should have mattered more. We sat in the same back room where he had first decided I was worth risking money on. The room looked smaller now. Or I felt larger. Dangerous distinction. Antonius tapped the ledger.</p><p>"Shale."</p><p>"Long-term."</p><p>"Magic training."</p><p>"Investment."</p><p>"Sword instruction."</p><p>"Also investment."</p><p>"Gambling."</p><p>"Income," I said.</p><p>Antonius looked up.</p><p>"You're very good at naming things."</p><p>"I've had practice."</p><p>"Are you good at any of them?"</p><p>That irritated me. Which meant it was a good question.</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Which?" </p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>People. Gambling. Learning. Strategy. Swordsmanship, potentially. Magic, eventually. Investing, once properly capitalized. The answer became less impressive the longer it took. When nobody told me what problem to solve, I generated enough problems to occupy a committee.</p><p>Antonius waited with one finger on the ledger while I assembled a committee's worth of answers and failed to choose one.</p><p>"Several," I said.</p><p>That got the smallest smile.</p><p>"That's what worries me."</p><p>"I can service the debt."</p><p>"You can service today's debt."</p><p>"Same thing," I said.</p><p>Antonius did not answer. He turned the ledger toward me.</p><p>I disliked how little room that left me.</p><p>Numbers. Actual numbers. I hated actual numbers when they disagreed with conceptual numbers. My original loan. Interest. Second advance. Third. Payments. Another advance. Fees. The sword instructor I had paid through a guild note because I had been short that afternoon. Arlo's material order. A gambling stake Antonius's man had covered when I arrived without enough coin because I knew the table was good. I stared at that one.</p><p>"I borrowed to gamble?"</p><p>"You told Rusk it was working capital."</p><p>I said, "It was." </p><p>Antonius leaned back.</p><p>"You're very good at naming things."</p><p>Right.</p><p>I counted mentally. Then again. The debt was not catastrophic. Not yet. But it had grown. More importantly, I did not have the money to clear it. I had assets. Sort of. A promising material project. Training. A good sword. Used vambraces. Skills. Potential. None of those were coins. Antonius preferred coins. Reasonable.</p><p>"When is the next payment?" I asked. He told me.</p><p>Soon. I nodded.</p><p>"I can make that."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>That surprised me. Antonius folded his hands.</p><p>"The question is what you do after."</p><p>"Continue."</p><p>"Of course."</p><p>"What would you suggest?"</p><p>"Stop borrowing." </p><p>I laughed. </p><p>He did not.</p><p>"Oh."</p><p>"Pay me. Gamble with your own money. Train with your own money. Buy garbage rocks with your own money."</p><p>"Kestrin shale."</p><p>"Garbage rocks."</p><p>"It's going to matter."</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"It will."</p><p>"Then it can matter slowly."</p><p>That was almost exactly what I had told myself. I resented him for stealing it.</p><p>"I need speed."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>The answer was obvious. Because I had already lost forty years once. Because every month I wasted was a month I could have compressed. Because somewhere ahead were wars, collapses, dungeons, people I had failed, people I could reach earlier, mistakes I could prevent, opportunities that would disappear if I arrived late. Because being nineteen again did not feel like having extra time. It felt like being behind. I said none of that.</p><p>I said, "I have plans." </p><p>Antonius watched me.</p><p>"Everyone with debt has plans." </p><p>I left irritated.</p><p>Pay this amount. By this time. Stop inventing twelve reasons the debt was strategically interesting. I was much less comfortable with a smaller board. That irritation lasted until Hessa made me hold a mana response for four breaths instead of three. Then I forgot Antonius entirely.</p><p>Four. Not much. Everything. My hand tingled. The sensation was still pathetic compared with what I remembered. But it was mine. Afterward I went directly to the practice yard. That was stupid. Hessa had told me not to. Specifically. Mana conditioning taxed the body. Sword training taxed the body. Recovery mattered. I knew recovery mattered. I had lectured people about recovery. I had magically forced people through failed recovery and watched the consequences. But I felt good.</p><p>Young. Alive. Moving. So I trained. The Silver instructor was unavailable. Jorren was there. He grinned when he saw me.</p><p>"Old man."</p><p>"Statue."</p><p>"You plant your feet."</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>"See? Emotional too."</p><p>We sparred. I was better. Noticeably. That was all the evidence I needed. My timing had improved. My body was catching up. Not quickly enough, but catching. I baited his heavy right twice. Punished it twice. The third time he adjusted. I adjusted back.</p><p>Better.</p><p>He clipped my arm. I touched his chest. He swept my leg. I fell. Got up. Again. For a while there was no future. That was what I liked. No forty-year index. No names. No debts. No people who were dead but currently alive. There was Jorren's shoulder. My foot. His breath. Distance. Move.</p><p>I had forgotten how clean action could be. Maybe that was why I had become a warrior the first time. Not because I was good at it. Because I liked it. That realization bothered me. I had spent years telling the story differently. Young Greg wanted glory. Young Greg was stupid. Young Greg thought swords were impressive. All true. Incomplete. Young Greg liked moving. So did I. Jorren came in high. I stepped left.</p><p>Pivot. Drive through. Perfect. Except my leg did not move. For half a heartbeat the movement existed perfectly in my head and nowhere else. My mind had already completed the step. My exhausted leg had not. Jorren hit me in the chest. I landed on my back hard enough to knock the breath out of me. I stared at the sky and felt offended by biology.</p><p>"Greg?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"Fine," I wheezed. </p><p>He leaned over me.</p><p>"Excellent," I added. He continued staring.</p><p>"That means yes."</p><p>Warrior Greg did not stay in the sand because his legs were tired. That was exactly the sort of stupid sentence Warrior Greg believed. I believed it too. I went home exhausted. I should have slept. Instead I counted money.</p><p>Bad.</p><p>Very bad. Payment soon. Hessa due after that. Arlo wanted another material batch. The sword instructor had offered a discounted block of five sessions if I paid upfront. Discounted. That made it economical. I wrote the amount down. Then stared at it. Progress. I crossed it out. Then wrote it again smaller. Potentially. I needed money. I knew how to make money.</p><p>Cards. Simple. I went out. The table was wrong. I knew that within twenty minutes. I stayed. The first player was unreadable because he was drunk enough that his own intentions changed between looking at his cards and placing the bet. The second was good. The third was better. The fourth was lucky. I hated the fourth. I lost. Not badly. Then badly. Then recovered half.</p><p>That should have been the exit. Instead I saw the line. The second player protected large pots. The third attacked weakness. The lucky idiot was overconfident. I could turn them against each other. I stayed. An hour later, I owed the table. Not much. Enough. I signed a note. Sensible? Probably not. I walked outside. Rusk was waiting. Antonius's man. Large. Quiet. I had met him twice. He looked at me. I looked at him.</p><p>"That's efficient," I said.</p><p>"Antonius wants to see you."</p><p>I asked, "Now?" </p><p>Rusk looked at the sky.</p><p>"Do you have another appointment?" </p><p>I considered lying. He knew I did not. People-reading worked both ways.</p><p>I said, "Reasonable." Antonius had the new note before I arrived. Of course he did. He placed it beside the ledger. Did not speak. I sat.</p><p>Also did not speak. That lasted longer than I liked. Finally </p><p>I said, "Temporary." </p><p>Antonius nodded.</p><p>"Winnable."</p><p>Another nod.</p><p>"I know what I did wrong."</p><p>That got him.</p><p>"I stayed after the table changed," I said.</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>"That's exactly what happened."</p><p>"You think your problem is the game."</p><p>"It was a gambling loss," I said.</p><p>Antonius pushed the ledger toward me.</p><p>"Your problem is you think being able to explain a mistake means you can afford it." </p><p>I stared at him. That was annoyingly good.</p><p>"I can make the payment."</p><p>"Tomorrow?" Antonius asked.</p><p>I calculated.</p><p>Maybe. He saw the calculation.</p><p>"No," Antonius said.</p><p>"I didn't answer."</p><p>"You did."</p><p>I looked at the ledger again. There were too many numbers now. Not enormous numbers. That was the humiliating part. I had once moved sums that would make this entire room look like pocket change. Now a few silver in the wrong direction had become a man across a desk deciding what happened to my week. I hated it. I hated him a little. Mostly I hated the scale. Antonius tapped the note.</p><p>"You'll work it." </p><p>I looked up.</p><p>"You heard me."</p><p>"I can gamble it back."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>That stopped me. Antonius leaned forward.</p><p>"That's why you're not going to." </p><p>I laughed once. </p><p>He did not.</p><p>"You don't get to decide whether I gamble."</p><p>"I decide what happens when you owe me money you cannot pay."</p><p>"I can pay."</p><p>"Not tonight."</p><p>Silence. There it was. The contract. Creditor labor. I remembered the phrase because I had considered it almost funny when I signed. Eight days. Thirty-five percent. If I defaulted, labor at Antonius's direction until the balance was satisfied. At the time I had been thinking about future industries. Now I was thinking about hauling crates.</p><p>"Excellent," I said. </p><p>Antonius smiled.</p><p>There was no warmth in it.</p><p>"Tomorrow morning."</p><p>"What am I doing?"</p><p>"Whatever I need."</p><p>"I have training."</p><p>"Move it."</p><p>"Hessa doesn't move."</p><p>"Then pay me," Antonius said.</p><p>I looked at the ledger.</p><p>Could not. Not without borrowing. From him. That seemed structurally unsound. Antonius watched the realization arrive.</p><p>"You wanted capital," he said. "Now you get to learn what it costs." I wanted to tell him I already knew. I had financed expeditions.</p><p>Negotiated credit. Built ventures. Watched kingdoms borrow against tax years that had not happened yet. I understood debt. Conceptually. Apparently conceptually was doing a lot of work in my second life. I stood.</p><p>"How long?"</p><p>"Until I trust the numbers again."</p><p>"That's not a number."</p><p>"I dislike you."</p><p>"I can live with that." I walked to the door.</p><p>Antonius said, "Greg." </p><p>I turned. </p><p>He looked at the sword at my hip.</p><p>"Nice sword." </p><p>I looked down at it. The sixth sword.</p><p>Beautiful balance. Excellent purchase. Investment in accelerated martial development. I had bought it with money I did not have. For the first time, it looked expensive.</p><p>"Fuck you," I said. </p><p>Antonius laughed.</p><p>Outside, I started walking home. My legs hurt from training. My ribs hurt from Jorren. My hand still held the faint memory of mana. The sword moved comfortably at my hip. Both legs worked. For now, everything worked. That was the problem. Cards. Memory. Investments. Bodies. People. Me.</p><p>Tomorrow Antonius owned my morning. Hessa owned part of my afternoon. Arlo wanted money I no longer had. The gambling tables were temporarily forbidden unless I wanted to discover how patient Antonius really was. And Warrior Greg, apparently, was back.</p><p>That was comforting in a way I did not entirely trust. There was always another Greg available when the current one became inconvenient. I had spent most of my life calling that adaptability. For now, I still liked the word. Halfway home, I caught myself thinking about how to make creditor labor useful. I stopped walking.</p><p>The thought remained. Antonius had already supplied the walls. I only had to inspect what was inside them. People. Routes. Goods. Clients.</p><p>Debtors. Information. Access. Useful became leverage. Leverage became options. I smiled, remembered what Antonius had just said, and let the smile fade. Mostly.</p><p>"Still," I said.</p><p>And kept walking.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="004.html">← Chapter 3</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="007.html">Chapter 5 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/375.html:259`: <p>No mana.</p>
- `chapters/085.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 70: The Arbiter — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 70</div><h1>THE ARBITER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>My leg objected to the north road before breakfast.</p><p>Not dramatically. Dramatic would have been easier to classify.</p><p>The residual limb was swollen enough that the dressing felt tighter, sore along the lower margin, and warm only in the ordinary sense that the rest of me was also warm. No new redness. No drainage. No smell. No fever. I checked twice because the first check had produced an answer I disliked rather than an answer I distrusted.</p><p>Still dry.</p><p>Good.</p><p>My right thigh hurt in places I had not assigned responsibility to yesterday. Lower back too. Hands were better than after a long crutch day. Shoulders were better. Apparently travel redistributed suffering instead of eliminating it.</p><p>Useful.</p><p>I wrote that down beneath DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.</p><p>The keeper put porridge in front of me and looked at the notebook.</p><p>“You writing about your holiday?”</p><p>“It was four hours.”</p><p>“Long holiday.”</p><p>“I delivered nothing.”</p><p>“You ate an apple.”</p><p>“That was not labor.”</p><p>“You watched other people labor.”</p><p>“Educational.”</p><p>She snorted.</p><p>I had planned to spend the morning downstairs. Planned was generous. I had decided not to go anywhere until the swelling reduced and then had immediately begun constructing exceptions.</p><p>Guild if requested.</p><p>Infirmary if necessary.</p><p>Food if unavailable here.</p><p>Alden if he arrived with blood.</p><p>Lyssa if she arrived without blood.</p><p>Fire.</p><p>Structural collapse.</p><p>Unusually interesting noise.</p><p>The last category made the entire system suspect.</p><p>Somebody knocked.</p><p>The keeper looked at me.</p><p>I looked at the door.</p><p>“Interesting noise,” she said.</p><p>“Shut up.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg studying Holl’s testing sheets and working notes." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/085/Ch85_Holls-Working-Sheets.png"/></figure><p>Holl came in carrying a wooden box under one arm and three folded sheets in the other hand.</p><p>He stopped when he saw me at the table.</p><p>“Good. Sitting.”</p><p>“I do that now.”</p><p>“So I heard.”</p><p>He put the box on the table hard enough to make my cup jump.</p><p>The keeper looked at the cup, then at Holl.</p><p>“Sorry,” he said.</p><p>She went back to the stove.</p><p>Holl sat opposite me and pushed the papers across the table.</p><p>“You said write it down.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“No. I did.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>Prospective records.</p><p>Worker. Lot. Throughput. Ambiguous pieces. Returns or banding errors.</p><p>I had not thought about them yesterday.</p><p>That was probably healthy.</p><p>I unfolded the first sheet.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Greg working through testing figures at a cluttered table." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/085/Ch85_Arbiter-Calculations.png"/></figure><p>Holl had made columns.</p><p>Bad columns.</p><p>They were still columns.</p><p>“You did this yourself?”</p><p>“Iris started it.”</p><p>“She started it. I changed it because she writes too small.”</p><p>“Your writing is larger.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Those are not synonyms.”</p><p>He ignored me.</p><p>I read.</p><p>Six working days. Four lots. Two regular testers plus Holl on close pieces. Pieces sorted into three behavior bands. Set-asides counted. Rechecks counted separately on two days and not on the others because apparently measurement systems also required supervision.</p><p>There were return marks at the bottom.</p><p>Three.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“Three customer returns?”</p><p>“Three pieces returned. Two customers.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Wrong behavior.”</p><p>“Wrong band?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Confirmed?”</p><p>Holl tapped the box.</p><p>I looked at it.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You came here with rocks.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“My leg hurts.”</p><p>“You're sitting.”</p><p>“That is not the same as volunteering my table for magic testing.”</p><p>Holl stared at me.</p><p>I stared back.</p><p>This was satisfying.</p><p>He leaned back.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>That was less satisfying. I had expected resistance and prepared several excellent arguments.</p><p>“What do you want from me?” I asked.</p><p>“Look at the records.”</p><p>“Only?”</p><p>“Only.”</p><p>I pulled the second sheet closer.</p><p>There were numbers.</p><p>Numbers were dangerous because they looked like answers before anyone had asked a question.</p><p>Lot one: low ambiguity. Fast throughput. No returns.</p><p>Lot two: high ambiguity. Slow throughput. One returned piece.</p><p>Lot three: moderate ambiguity. Fast throughput. Two returned pieces.</p><p>Lot four: very high ambiguity. Very slow throughput. No returns yet.</p><p>I read again.</p><p>Then the worker lines.</p><p>Iris was faster than the other regular tester.</p><p>Not slightly.</p><p>Enough that I would have noticed if I had been paying her.</p><p>Her ambiguity rate was also higher.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>The other tester set aside fewer pieces and processed fewer per hour.</p><p>Holl's rechecks converted some ambiguous pieces into saleable stock and rejected others.</p><p>“Which worker made the three returned calls?” I asked.</p><p>Holl pointed.</p><p>Two Iris. One other tester.</p><p>“Were those pieces marked ambiguous before sale?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Close?”</p><p>“Don't know.”</p><p>“You don't know?”</p><p>“I didn't record every piece's original tray position and prayer history, Greg.”</p><p>“Reasonable.”</p><p>He narrowed his eyes.</p><p>“That sounded insulting.”</p><p>“It wasn't.”</p><p>It mostly wasn't.</p><p>I went back to the sheets.</p><p>The obvious answer was Iris was faster because she threw more uncertain pieces at Holl.</p><p>The second obvious answer was that this was bad.</p><p>The third obvious answer was that I had learned nothing from the last year.</p><p>“What happens to set-asides?” I asked.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="A hand sorting small testing pieces and marks on a work surface." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/085/Ch85_Testing-Pieces-and-Marks.png"/></figure><p>“Holl tests them,” Holl said.</p><p>“You are Holl.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What happens after you test them?”</p><p>“Band, reject, or hold.”</p><p>“Hold for what?”</p><p>“Better lot. Customer question. Sometimes I sell them as mixed suppression if somebody doesn't care.”</p><p>“At what price?”</p><p>“Less.”</p><p>“How much less?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>“On?”</p><p>“Customer.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>I looked at the lot totals again.</p><p>“Your expensive resource isn't the fixture.”</p><p>Holl's face changed slightly.</p><p>Not agreement. Attention.</p><p>“Keep going.”</p><p>I hated when people said that because it made me want to perform certainty.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>The keeper put bread between us without being asked. Holl took a piece. I took a piece. Nobody paid her immediately, which meant either trust or criminality.</p><p>“Maybe,” I said, “your expensive resource is you.”</p><p>“Obviously.”</p><p>“Not your skill generally. Your close-piece time.”</p><p>He chewed.</p><p>I pointed at lot four.</p><p>“This lot had the worst ambiguity and no returns.”</p><p>“Yet.”</p><p>“Yes. Yet. But you spent...”</p><p>I counted marks.</p><p>“Nearly twice as much recheck time on it as lot three.”</p><p>“Bad stone.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“It was bad stone.”</p><p>“Fine. Bad stone. But if Iris is faster because she sends more close calls to you, that might be good or bad depending on what her time costs, what your time costs, what rejects cost, and what a wrong band costs.”</p><p>Holl stopped chewing.</p><p>I continued because stopping now would have been cowardice.</p><p>“And returns may not be the right error measure.”</p><p>“They're errors.”</p><p>“They are some errors. A customer can receive a piece at the edge of a band and never notice. Another customer can return a technically correct piece because their use is sensitive. A wrong piece might be consumed before anyone complains. A rejected piece might have been saleable. You don't see false rejects in returns.”</p><p>Holl looked at the sheets.</p><p>I looked too.</p><p>There it was.</p><p>The dangerous feeling.</p><p>I understand this.</p><p>Therefore I know what should happen next.</p><p>I could feel the sentence assembling.</p><p>Change the fixture.</p><p>Change the thresholds.</p><p>Give Iris a separate close category.</p><p>Price lots by expert-time burden.</p><p>Test a sample of rejects.</p><p>All plausible.</p><p>None mine yet.</p><p>“What decision are you trying to make?” I asked.</p><p>Holl looked up.</p><p>“Thought that was your question.”</p><p>“It is. Answer it.”</p><p>He considered.</p><p>“Whether to change anything.”</p><p>“Too broad.”</p><p>“Whether Iris is too loose.”</p><p>There.</p><p>Not the fixture.</p><p>Not the entire business.</p><p>Iris.</p><p>I read the numbers again with the actual question attached.</p><p>Different document.</p><p>“Then this doesn't answer it.”</p><p>Holl grunted.</p><p>“It tells you she's faster and sends you more close pieces. It tells you two returned pieces came from her calls. It doesn't tell you whether she makes more wrong calls per hundred clear decisions than the other tester.”</p><p>“Can calculate.”</p><p>“Not from this.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because the lots differ.”</p><p>He frowned.</p><p>I tapped lot two, then three.</p><p>“If she handled more of the ugly material, comparing raw returns is nonsense. If she handled easier material, same problem the other direction. Also you recheck her ambiguous pieces. Those are not her final calls.”</p><p>Holl leaned forward.</p><p>“What do you need?”</p><p>Need.</p><p>Another dangerous word.</p><p>I nearly answered with a list.</p><p>Instead I asked, “What would you do if she is too loose?”</p><p>“Tell her to tighten.”</p><p>“And if that slows her down?”</p><p>“Fine if returns stop.”</p><p>“What if returns don't change?”</p><p>“Then I tell her to go faster again.”</p><p>I smiled despite myself.</p><p>“Good experimental design.”</p><p>“Don't call it that.”</p><p>“Fine. Business annoyance.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>I looked at the box.</p><p>“What are those?”</p><p>“The three returns and six pieces I pulled because I wanted comparison.”</p><p>“No testing.”</p><p>“You said.”</p><p>“Can I look at them without mana?”</p><p>Holl shrugged.</p><p>“Rocks don't bite.”</p><p>“Several rocks bite.”</p><p>“Not these.”</p><p>He opened the box.</p><p>Nine pieces of dull gray kestrin sat in cloth dividers. Cheap suppression stone looked disappointing even when it was causing expensive questions. The pieces differed in shape, surface, thickness. Two had chalk marks. One had a chipped corner.</p><p>I did not touch them.</p><p>“Which are returns?”</p><p>Holl pointed.</p><p>I looked.</p><p>Nothing visible distinguished them from the others.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Or useless.</p><p>Often the same thing.</p><p>“Do customers buy pieces or behavior?” I asked.</p><p>“Behavior.”</p><p>“You price by band.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do they care how close a piece is to the band edge?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Do you know which before sale?”</p><p>“Usually.”</p><p>Usually.</p><p>I rubbed my thumb against the bread crust.</p><p>“Then maybe there are two questions.”</p><p>Holl groaned.</p><p>“I came here for fewer questions.”</p><p>“Terrible choice.”</p><p>“What two?”</p><p>“Is Iris making worse calls? And are you selling the same tolerance to customers who don't actually need the same tolerance?”</p><p>He stared at me.</p><p>I immediately regretted the second question.</p><p>Not because it was bad.</p><p>Because it was interesting.</p><p>Interesting questions were how I acquired unpaid employment.</p><p>Holl reached for the papers.</p><p>“That's useful.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You always say maybe after the useful part.”</p><p>“Because you haven't tested it.”</p><p>“I'm not testing customers.”</p><p>“You already do. With invoices.”</p><p>He gave me a flat look.</p><p>I ate bread.</p><p>The keeper came past, saw the stones, and stopped.</p><p>“No magic.”</p><p>Holl and I both said, “No magic.”</p><p>She looked at me specifically.</p><p>“I said no magic.”</p><p>“You say many things.”</p><p>Then she left.</p><p>Holl smiled.</p><p>“Strong institutional authority.”</p><p>“You don't know the half of it.”</p><p>I pushed the papers back toward him.</p><p>“Don't change Iris from this.”</p><p>“I wasn't going to fire her.”</p><p>“I didn't say fire.”</p><p>“You're already arguing against blaming her.”</p><p>“I thought you might blame the worker because worker is an easy variable.”</p><p>Holl's expression hardened.</p><p>“She is an easy variable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And sometimes the worker is the problem.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That mattered.</p><p>I had a tendency to become suspicious of obvious answers after discovering hidden ones. This was merely the inverse stupidity.</p><p>Holl tapped the page.</p><p>“So how do I know?”</p><p>I looked at the totals.</p><p>“You own the process.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You know the cost of a wrong band.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You know what amount of recheck time annoys you enough to matter.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then pick a narrow comparison you can actually run without ruining the work.”</p><p>He waited.</p><p>I waited too.</p><p>He frowned.</p><p>“You're not going to tell me?”</p><p>“I can suggest.”</p><p>“Suggest.”</p><p>“Same lot. Split enough ordinary pieces between Iris and the other tester that material difference matters less. Keep their ambiguous piles separate. You recheck a small sample of each person's clear calls too, not only the pieces they flag. Then compare wrong clear calls, ambiguity, throughput, and your time.”</p><p>Holl considered it.</p><p>“Costs product.”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Costs me.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>He nodded.</p><p>That was the correct response to ignorance. Disturbing.</p><p>“And customer tolerance?” he asked.</p><p>“Ask them what decision the stone supports.”</p><p>“They'll tell me they need good stone.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Useless.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“So maybe ask what happens if the suppression is a little high or low.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“That sounds like work.”</p><p>“It is your business.”</p><p>“Thought you liked work.”</p><p>“I like other people's work at a safe distance.”</p><p>He laughed once.</p><p>The residual limb throbbed hard enough that I shifted in the chair.</p><p>Holl noticed.</p><p>Not dramatically. His eyes went down, then back up.</p><p>“You done?” he asked.</p><p>I wanted to say no.</p><p>The box was open.</p><p>Nine stones.</p><p>Three returns.</p><p>A business problem with actual data and a worker whose performance might be misread by the wrong denominator.</p><p>This was excellent.</p><p>Also my leg hurt.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The word annoyed me less than expected.</p><p>Holl folded the sheets.</p><p>“That's it?”</p><p>“You asked me to look.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“I looked.”</p><p>“What do I owe you?”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“For what?”</p><p>Holl stared at me.</p><p>Right.</p><p>Professional interaction.</p><p>I had somehow forgotten money while discussing somebody else's money.</p><p>“How long have you been here?” I asked.</p><p>The keeper answered from the stove.</p><p>“Forty minutes.”</p><p>Holl looked at her.</p><p>She shrugged.</p><p>“I have ears.”</p><p>I considered.</p><p>This was not Guild work. Holl had come to me. No transport. No magic. Judgment, not testing. Forty minutes.</p><p>“One copper.”</p><p>Holl reached into his purse.</p><p>Then stopped.</p><p>“Too little.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“You're arguing upward?”</p><p>“I pay Iris more than that for an hour when she's testing.”</p><p>“She's doing skilled production work.”</p><p>“So were you.”</p><p>“I ate your bread.”</p><p>“My bread?” the keeper said.</p><p>“Our bread,” I corrected.</p><p>“Two copper,” Holl said.</p><p>I almost objected.</p><p>Then didn't.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>He put two copper on the table.</p><p>The keeper took one.</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>“Bread,” she said.</p><p>“That was not one copper of bread.”</p><p>“Table fee.”</p><p>“You have never charged a table fee.”</p><p>“New policy.”</p><p>Holl was already closing the box.</p><p>“You're encouraging her.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Get out.”</p><p>He stood.</p><p>At the door he looked back.</p><p>“Same lot. Sample clear calls too.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Don't change Iris yet.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Ask customers what happens if they're wrong.”</p><p>“Approximately.”</p><p>He nodded.</p><p>Then he left with his stones and bad columns.</p><p>The room became quiet again.</p><p>I looked at the remaining copper.</p><p>One copper net after extortion.</p><p>Still more than yesterday's professional income.</p><p>Yesterday's professional income had been negative.</p><p>I had paid for transport to go nowhere useful and look at yellow cloth.</p><p>Today a testing shop owner had brought work to my breakfast table because something I had asked him to record had produced a question he wanted help answering.</p><p>The two facts did not cancel each other.</p><p>That seemed important enough that I refused to write it down.</p><p>I elevated my leg on the other chair.</p><p>The keeper put another piece of bread beside me.</p><p>“Free?” I asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I ate it anyway.</p><p>*</p><p>By afternoon the swelling had reduced.</p><p>Not gone. Reduced.</p><p>I stayed downstairs.</p><p>This was partly discipline and partly because the stairs had become less interesting now that I knew I could use them under controlled conditions. Competence had ruined a perfectly good obsession.</p><p>I reread Holl's numbers from memory.</p><p>That was a mistake.</p><p>I did not have the papers.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I could reconstruct the broad pattern but not the exact counts. Also good. It prevented me from solving a business that was currently walking away from me in a wooden box.</p><p>I opened my notebook instead.</p><p>NORTH ROAD: WHITE FLOWERS IN DITCH.</p><p>DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.</p><p>CART VIBRATION COSTS MORE THAN EXPECTED.</p><p>Below that I wrote:</p><p>HOLL: COMPARE DECISIONS, NOT JUST PEOPLE.</p><p>I stared at it.</p><p>Too neat.</p><p>I crossed out HOLL.</p><p>Then I crossed out the whole sentence.</p><p>The keeper saw me.</p><p>“Bad?”</p><p>“Annoying.”</p><p>“What was it?”</p><p>“Something true enough to become false if I liked it too much.”</p><p>She considered that.</p><p>“Sounds like you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I turned the page.</p><p>Blank.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Someone outside shouted about onions.</p><p>A cart rolled past.</p><p>Upstairs, a door opened and shut.</p><p>My leg hurt less than it had that morning.</p><p>I had one copper from work I had not gone looking for.</p><p>I had spent yesterday on a road for no reason that would survive an invoice.</p><p>Tomorrow remained offensively unassigned.</p><p>I left the page blank.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="084.html">← Chapter 69</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="086.html">Chapter 71 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
