- `chapters/186.html:443`: <p>"That's not mana."</p>
- `chapters/213.html:36`: <p>I had lost a leg, joined a theatre, moved paper with mana, acquired<br>
- `chapters/213.html:385`: <p>The gathered mana crowded toward the wrist side.</p>
- `chapters/291.html:191`: <p>Gray hair tied high. Thick forearms. Leather apron. No visible mana tool.</p>
- `chapters/291.html:320`: <p>No mana.</p>
- `chapters/094.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 76: The Subject — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 76</div><h1>THE SUBJECT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>My hands were fine.</p><p>My residual limb was slightly more swollen than the morning before, but not enough to worry me and enough that Pessa would have worried me.</p><p>This created a scheduling problem.</p><p>Pessa had said come back if the leg was not more swollen.</p><p>It was more swollen.</p><p>Slightly.</p><p>Hessa had said three days.</p><p>Three days had happened.</p><p>I went to Hessa.</p><p>This was not choosing magic over training.</p><p>Pessa had given a condition.</p><p>My body had answered it.</p><p>I disliked this because it was reasonable.</p><p>Hessa opened the door, looked at me, and said, “You trained.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“With Pessa.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Yesterday?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She looked down.</p><p>Not at the missing leg.</p><p>At the wrapping.</p><p>“More swollen?”</p><p>“Slightly.”</p><p>“Then why are you here?”</p><p>“You said three days.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“Do you want me to leave?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>She let me in.</p><p>The useless ceramic dish was gone.</p><p>I noticed immediately.</p><p>Hessa noticed me noticing.</p><p>“Disappointed?”</p><p>“It was a strong instrument.”</p><p>“It held almonds after you left.”</p><p>“That explains nothing.”</p><p>“It held almonds.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg at the table during Hessa’s supervised mana-draw assessment." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/094/Ch94_Copper-Strip-Assessment.png"/></figure><p>The table had a narrow copper strip on it now.</p><p>Also three small stones.</p><p>Not crystals.</p><p>River stones, gray and ordinary, each about the size of the last joint of my thumb.</p><p>A cup of tea.</p><p>One chair.</p><p>I looked around.</p><p>“Where's yours?”</p><p>“I'll stand.”</p><p>“That seems aggressive.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat.</p><p>The chair remained bad.</p><p>Consistency.</p><p>Hessa picked up the copper strip.</p><p>It was thin enough to bend but not flimsy. One end had a small loop. The other was flat.</p><p>“What is that?”</p><p>“Copper.”</p><p>“I know copper.”</p><p>“Congratulations.”</p><p>“What does it do?”</p><p>“Very little.”</p><p>“Good. We are progressing.”</p><p>She put it down.</p><p>“First, leg.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Not magic.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She checked the residual limb with the same practical lack of ceremony she used for everything else.</p><p>Wrapping off.</p><p>Skin.</p><p>Temperature.</p><p>Pressure.</p><p>Questions.</p><p>Any new pain?</p><p>No.</p><p>Drainage?</p><p>No.</p><p>Heat?</p><p>No.</p><p>Throbbing after training?</p><p>Some.</p><p>How long?</p><p>Settled by evening.</p><p>Swelling this morning?</p><p>Slightly above previous morning.</p><p>She pressed along the upper calf that remained.</p><p>Not hard.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Here?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Here?”</p><p>“Tender.”</p><p>“New?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Training today?”</p><p>“Pessa said not if more swollen.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I was going to tell her.”</p><p>“You were going to negotiate.”</p><p>“I was going to report.”</p><p>“And then?”</p><p>“Potentially negotiate.”</p><p>Hessa rewrapped the limb.</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She washed her hands.</p><p>Then she sat in the chair that had apparently existed behind me the entire time.</p><p>I looked.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You said you'd stand.”</p><p>“I changed my mind.”</p><p>“That is allowed?”</p><p>“For me.”</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>She put the three stones in a line.</p><p>“Tell me what they are.”</p><p>“Stones.”</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Why good?”</p><p>“Because I don't want you identifying them.”</p><p>“Then why ask?”</p><p>“To see if you would pretend.”</p><p>“I do not pretend.”</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“Professionally.”</p><p>She continued looking.</p><p>“Usually.”</p><p>She pushed the first stone toward me.</p><p>“Pick it up.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“Anything?”</p><p>“Stone.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Cool. Smooth on one side. Rougher on the other.”</p><p>“Magic.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Put it down.”</p><p>Second stone.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Third.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>She moved them around.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>“Eyes closed.”</p><p>I closed them.</p><p>She put one in my palm.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Another.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Third.</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>I opened my eyes.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You decided maybe after I changed the order.”</p><p>“I felt something.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Expectation.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That is not magic.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She took the stones away.</p><p>“What are they?”</p><p>“Stones.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Completely ordinary?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That was insulting.”</p><p>“It was necessary.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because today you want a result.”</p><p>I said nothing.</p><p>She was right.</p><p>That was irritating enough without confirmation.</p><p>Hessa picked up the copper strip.</p><p>“This is also ordinary.”</p><p>“Why should I believe you now?”</p><p>“You shouldn't.”</p><p>Good answer.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Greg concentrating over Hessa’s sparse assessment table." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/094/Ch94_Subject-at-the-Table.png"/></figure><p>She looped the copper around two fingers of her left hand and held the flat end toward me.</p><p>“Mana draw.”</p><p>My heart did the cupboard thing.</p><p>Again.</p><p>I hated that metaphor now.</p><p>“Mine?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Casting?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Less than you used to pull before deciding whether to cast.”</p><p>That was very little.</p><p>“From where?”</p><p>“Your normal draw.”</p><p>“That is not a place.”</p><p>“You know what I mean.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>The first movement inward.</p><p>Not a spell.</p><p>Not shaping.</p><p>Not Barrier.</p><p>Just drawing enough mana into active control that the channels woke.</p><p>I had done it thousands of times.</p><p>Maybe tens of thousands.</p><p>The remembered number was unreliable.</p><p>The body memory was not.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>Hessa saw me thinking.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“I haven't started.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>I put both hands flat on my thighs.</p><p>“What does the copper do?”</p><p>“If I tell you, you'll try to make it do that.”</p><p>“That suggests it does something.”</p><p>“Very little.”</p><p>“Your favorite amount.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She held it out.</p><p>“Close your eyes.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I reached.</p><p>Nothing happened.</p><p>Not nothing.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“You stopped,” Hessa said.</p><p>“It didn't feel like the old draw.”</p><p>“How was it different?”</p><p>I considered.</p><p>“Enough that I waited for the old shape instead of following this one.”</p><p>“Good. Again without waiting for it.”</p><p>I closed my eyes again.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>Draw.</p><p>This time I did not wait for the remembered shape.</p><p>Mana came.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Familiar.</p><p>Wrong.</p><p>I inhaled sharply.</p><p>“Hold,” Hessa said.</p><p>I held.</p><p>Not a spell.</p><p>No shaping.</p><p>Just presence.</p><p>The internal sensation was like standing in a room after someone moved the furniture.</p><p>Everything still existed.</p><p>Not everything was where my body expected.</p><p>The draw settled through my chest, shoulders, arms.</p><p>Down the right side.</p><p>Hip.</p><p>Thigh.</p><p>Lower leg.</p><p>Foot.</p><p>Left hip.</p><p>Thigh.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Then my awareness continued.</p><p>That was the problem.</p><p>It continued into calf.</p><p>Ankle.</p><p>Foot.</p><p>All of which felt present.</p><p>Not physically present.</p><p>Magically?</p><p>No.</p><p>I did not know.</p><p>The left foot felt full.</p><p>Not cold.</p><p>Full was the wrong word.</p><p>Occupied.</p><p>“Release,” Hessa said.</p><p>I released.</p><p>The sensation vanished from both sides at once.</p><p>My phantom foot remained.</p><p>Ordinary phantom foot.</p><p>If ordinary was the word.</p><p>I opened my eyes.</p><p>Hessa was looking at the copper strip.</p><p>It had not changed.</p><p>“What did you feel?”</p><p>I told her.</p><p>All of it.</p><p>She asked me to repeat the sequence without interpretation.</p><p>Chest.</p><p>Shoulders.</p><p>Arms.</p><p>Right side.</p><p>Left side.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Continued sense below the knee.</p><p>Foot.</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Burning?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pressure?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Different from your normal phantom?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>I hated the question.</p><p>“More organized.”</p><p>“Meaning?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“No, not good.”</p><p>“Accurate.”</p><p>She set down the copper.</p><p>“What did you see?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“What did you feel?”</p><p>“I told you.”</p><p>“I mean me.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>I had forgotten she was doing something.</p><p>Excellent subject behavior.</p><p>“What did you feel?”</p><p>“A draw.”</p><p>“Helpful.”</p><p>“Broadly clean.”</p><p>My pulse accelerated.</p><p>Hessa lifted a finger.</p><p>“Broadly.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Your trunk response was normal enough.”</p><p>“Normal enough.”</p><p>“Right side too.”</p><p>“And left?”</p><p>“Above the knee, present.”</p><p>“Below?”</p><p>She looked at the copper strip.</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>I exhaled through my nose.</p><p>“Did the copper tell you nothing?”</p><p>“It told me something.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“That you drew mana.”</p><p>“I knew that.”</p><p>“I wanted independent confirmation.”</p><p>“Of whether I was lying?”</p><p>“Of whether what you experienced corresponded to a draw.”</p><p>I paused.</p><p>That was different.</p><p>“Did it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How does copper do that?”</p><p>“Very little.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She almost smiled.</p><p>“Again?” I asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“One draw.”</p><p>“You had one draw.”</p><p>“That is a terrible sample.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So again.”</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is less cautious than three days.”</p><p>“No. The first test was whether anything obvious happened after prompting your channels. Nothing obvious did. Today was whether you could make a minimal draw without shaping.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The word landed harder than it should have.</p><p>I had drawn mana.</p><p>After the amputation.</p><p>I had drawn mana.</p><p>Not cast.</p><p>Not shaped.</p><p>Not tested Barrier.</p><p>But drawn.</p><p>I looked down at my hands.</p><p>No glow.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“What do you know?”</p><p>“That this is not clearance.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That it does not establish below-knee channels.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That the phantom sensation could be body map, channel expectation, attention, or some combination we haven't separated.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That one successful minimal draw does not tell us whether repeated draw causes pain, fatigue, asymmetry, instability, or delayed effects.”</p><p>Hessa nodded.</p><p>“That was annoyingly good.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“And I drew mana.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There it was again.</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>I could not help it.</p><p>Hessa let me.</p><p>That mattered.</p><p>She did not immediately crush the moment into caution.</p><p>She gave me perhaps three seconds.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“Fuck.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I knew you were waiting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>She handed me tea.</p><p>I drank.</p><p>My left foot felt normal.</p><p>Normal phantom.</p><p>Heel against floor.</p><p>Toes slightly curled.</p><p>I looked at the actual floor.</p><p>The sensation weakened.</p><p>“Foot?”</p><p>Hessa asked.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“After release?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Different?”</p><p>“Not now.”</p><p>“Write that later.”</p><p>“I thought I wasn't supposed to turn this into a research project.”</p><p>“You're the patient. Patients can remember symptoms.”</p><p>“Subject.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Today I was the subject.”</p><p>“You were annoying in either role.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>We sat for a minute.</p><p>I wanted to ask about Barrier.</p><p>I did not.</p><p>I wanted to ask whether a channel could terminate at the knee.</p><p>I did not.</p><p>I wanted to ask whether mana could follow remembered anatomy.</p><p>I did not.</p><p>This was almost physically painful.</p><p>Hessa watched.</p><p>“You can ask one.”</p><p>“One?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>I considered.</p><p>Not the most interesting question.</p><p>The most useful.</p><p>“What would make you stop?”</p><p>She looked at me differently.</p><p>Good question, apparently.</p><p>“Pain that concerns me. Heat. New swelling that doesn't fit physical activity. Channel response I don't understand enough to repeat safely. Draw instability. Symptoms that persist after release. Anything that suggests shaping is happening when I didn't ask for shaping.”</p><p>“Why would shaping happen?”</p><p>“That was your one.”</p><p>“Cruel.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She drank tea.</p><p>I thought about stopping conditions.</p><p>This was familiar.</p><p>Not the magic.</p><p>The structure.</p><p>Define failure before the test.</p><p>Holl.</p><p>Fixtures.</p><p>West River.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not everything needed to become everything else.</p><p>Still useful.</p><p>“What happens tomorrow?”</p><p>“Same draw.”</p><p>“That's all?”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“Probably?”</p><p>“If it is boring, we may vary position.”</p><p>“What position?”</p><p>“Seated. Standing if your leg is settled.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“You know Pessa has me training.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Do you talk?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“About me?”</p><p>“When relevant.”</p><p>This should have bothered me more than it did.</p><p>“Who owns tomorrow?”</p><p>“I own magic.”</p><p>“And Pessa owns movement.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What if both want the same body?”</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“You own the body.”</p><p>I went still.</p><p>She continued before I could turn it into something larger.</p><p>“So tell Pessa what happened. Tell me what Pessa does. Neither of us gets to pretend the other load doesn't exist.”</p><p>That was practical.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Less profound.</p><p>Better.</p><p>“Can I train tomorrow?”</p><p>“Ask Pessa.”</p><p>“Medically.”</p><p>“Your swelling decides more than I do.”</p><p>“I hate distributed authority.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>I finished the tea.</p><p>When I stood, the phantom left foot felt planted again.</p><p>I noticed before moving.</p><p>Both crutches.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>Stand.</p><p>The phantom stayed where it was for a moment and then seemed to lift with me.</p><p>No stretching ankle this time.</p><p>Different.</p><p>I told Hessa.</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>No theory.</p><p>At the door she said, “Eat.”</p><p>“I eat.”</p><p>“You forget after magic.”</p><p>“I haven't done magic in weeks.”</p><p>“You forgot before.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“And no testing alone.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Not even draw.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Not even because you already did it once.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>I sighed.</p><p>“I will not draw mana without you.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I opened the door.</p><p>Outside, the street was bright enough to make me squint.</p><p>I had expected the first return of mana to feel larger.</p><p>Trumpets.</p><p>Revelation.</p><p>A clean answer about what my body was now.</p><p>Instead I had tea in my stomach, slightly swollen tissue under wrapping, sore hands from yesterday, and one successful draw I was forbidden to repeat.</p><p>I was absurdly happy.</p><p>I went to find Pessa.</p><p>Not to train.</p><p>To report.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="093.html">← Chapter 75</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="096.html">Chapter 77 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

- `chapters/003.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 3: The Investor — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 3</div><h1>THE INVESTOR</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Buying garbage turned out to be the easy part. Toma sold me a cart of Kestrin shale for two silver and the expression of a woman who had just discovered that fools could be harvested. I paid another copper to have it delivered to Arlo's workshop, which left me standing in the east market with borrowed money in my pocket and the unpleasant awareness that every coin now had Antonius Vale attached to it.</p><p>Garbage had always been underrated. Not philosophically. Literally. Adventurers were terrible at distinguishing "worthless" from "not currently worth carrying." I had made money on that distinction later. Bones nobody wanted until necromantic licensing changed. Slime residue before preservative alchemy improved. Broken cores once artificers learned to laminate them. The shale was not unique. It was simply the first future waste product my nineteen-year-old purse could reach.</p><p>That thought nearly sent me back toward the guild salvage yard to start buying every cheap material I vaguely remembered becoming useful. I stopped myself before enthusiasm became inventory. One experiment first. If I could not make one cart of remembered garbage profitable, owning six different kinds of remembered garbage would merely make me a collector.</p><p>The order had not changed. Prove the shale. Protect enough of the idea that I could profit from it. Pay Antonius before the interest or the man himself became a larger problem. Then divert part of whatever remained into mana conditioning. Money first, magic second, because being the greatest support mage in my old life meant very little while my current body could not cast a useful spell and my current purse could not afford to teach it.</p><p>Arlo was the technical gate. Antonius was the financial clock. Magic was still an expense I could not afford. Keep the chain narrow. Find out which assumption failed first.</p><p>Eight days. Thirty-five percent. If the experiment failed, my labor belonged to him until the debt was cleared. I had accepted worse contracts. That was not comforting. Arlo was less pleased to see the shale than Toma had been to sell it.</p><p>"You actually bought it," Arlo said.</p><p>"I said I would," I told him.</p><p>He looked past me at the cart.</p><p>"I thought you meant enough to test."</p><p>"Most of them should stop," I said.</p><p>Arlo looked past me at the cart. "That's too much."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"No, Greg. I mean physically. I don't have room for that."</p><p>I turned and looked at his workshop. He was right. Arwick Works was currently a room with ambitions. One bench. Two kilns, one of which looked old enough to remember monarchy. Shelves crowded with lamp regulators, cracked ceramic housings, brass fittings, wire, powdered reagents, and several objects I could not identify despite having lived through the next forty years. That pleased me. Not everything needed to become a memory.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg realizing the cart of Kestrin shale will not fit Pell’s workshop." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/003/v28_c03_s01_cart-too-much-shale.png"/></figure><p>"How much do you need?" I asked.</p><p>"For a test? A bucket," Arlo said. </p><p>I looked at the cart. </p><p>The carter looked at me.</p><p>"Take the rest back," I told the carter.</p><p>"Paid delivery," the carter said.</p><p>"I know," I said.</p><p>"Delivery goes one way," he said.</p><p>"Of course it does," I said.</p><p>Arlo folded his arms. I paid for the lesson. By the time the shale was stacked badly beside his rear wall, my elegant investment thesis had acquired hauling fees, storage problems, and a man named Hobb who charged three copper to move something I had just paid someone else to move. I wrote that down too.</p><p>The hauling mistake irritated me because future knowledge could not fix it. I knew the shale became valuable. I did not know how much space Arlo had behind his workshop, what Hobb charged, or how many times I could afford to move the same stupid rocks. Grand history was cheaper in my head than one bad delivery in the present. Old Greg had learned logistics eventually. Young Greg was apparently paying tuition twice.</p><p>NOT EVERYTHING SCALES.</p><p>Arlo read over my shoulder.</p><p>"Are you writing lessons?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"I'm preventing myself from becoming stupid twice," I said.</p><p>"Does that work?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Historically? No," I said.</p><p>Arlo gave me the look again. People had several for me already: nineteen-year-old talking like an old man, Bronze adventurer knowing too much outside his profession, stranger staring at a face as if searching for something behind it. Arlo had developed his own. Brilliant or insane, with growing evidence for both.</p><p>"Six silver," he said.</p><p>"For the test," I said.</p><p>"For my time," Arlo corrected.</p><p>"You said six yesterday," I said.</p><p>"Six for my time. Same as yesterday," Arlo said.</p><p>I counted the coins onto his bench. It hurt. That was useful. In my old life, by the end, six silver had been invisible. I had spent more than that on wine I did not particularly like because someone important had selected the bottle. Now I watched each coin leave my hand. Capital had weight again. So did mistakes. Arlo picked up a shale chip. "Tell me exactly what you think this does."</p><p>I almost told him. Not the whole truth. The future was not a truth I could hand him. But I nearly gave him the answer as I remembered it. Then I stopped, because I did not remember the answer. I remembered filter housings. I remembered the Arwick stamp.</p><p>The loan agreement folded inside my coat seemed suddenly heavier. I touched it to make sure it was still there, then wondered why. Antonius did not need the paper to remember I owed him. I did. The document was less a contract than a physical reminder that every clever idea currently had a clock attached to it.</p><p>Eight days sounded generous when I was sitting across from him. Inside Arlo's workshop, watching six silver become somebody else's afternoon, it sounded like a very short week. I remembered somebody explaining, years after the discovery, that the shale's trace mana made it useful for binding residue during high-heat processing. That was not a formula. It was a story about a formula.</p><p>I pulled the memory apart anyway. Who had been talking? Workshop or banquet? Was the speaker an artificer or merely somebody repeating the explanation badly? Had the useful property been binding residue, or resisting it? The more I pushed, the less trustworthy the detail became. Good. Better to discover that at a bench than after betting the rest of the loan.</p><p>"What?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"I was about to pretend I knew more than I do."</p><p>Arlo looked at the shale chip in my hand.</p><p>"Then start with what you actually know." He waited. </p><p>I picked up a chip.</p><p>"I think the trace mana is the useful part. Powdered. Suspended in a ceramic mix or laid as a layer. Heat activates something. Maybe the structure changes. Maybe it just exposes more surface."</p><p>"Those are different mechanisms."</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"Which one?"</p><p>"I don't know."</p><p>Arlo's expression flattened. I pointed at him. "That is why you're being paid."</p><p>"No. I'm being paid to test a hypothesis."</p><p>"Excellent. We have several."</p><p>Arlo shook his head.</p><p>"You have guesses. Give me the one you want tested first."</p><p>He muttered something about adventurers and began working. I stayed. Arlo objected. I stayed anyway, not because I needed to supervise him, but because I needed to see what the present knew. That distinction mattered within the first hour. Arlo ground the shale much finer than I expected. He washed part of it. Heated another portion dry. Mixed samples into two cheap clay bodies and one better ceramic paste. He kept notes in a narrow hand and labeled everything. I understood perhaps half of what he was doing. That bothered me more than it should have.</p><p>I had assumed the advantage lived in the answer. Arlo kept showing me otherwise. I knew the shale mattered; he knew how to make that claim survive contact with a kiln. Old Greg had rarely been the best person in the room at every task. He had been very good at finding the person who was.</p><p>That was closer to support than I wanted to admit. I had planned around artificers, healers, scouts, and killers for decades. I knew enough about their disciplines to coordinate them. Enough was dangerous. It was very easy to mistake knowing what an expert needed for being the expert.</p><p>"What?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Nothing," I said.</p><p>"You keep looking at me," Arlo said.</p><p>"I have a memorable-face problem," I said.</p><p>"Your face?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Other people's."</p><p>Arlo held out one hand. "You've been staring at my hands for five minutes."</p><p>"I was trying to remember someone," I said.</p><p>True, but incomplete. I was trying to decide whether Arlo belonged on the list in my head. If his surname really became the Arwick mark I remembered, this cramped workshop was the beginning of something. If not, he was still the man doing the work in front of me.</p><p>"Me?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Possibly," I said. </p><p>He set the cup down.</p><p>"That's unsettling," Arlo said.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"Do you do that with everyone?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Currently," I said.</p><p>"Why?" Arlo asked.</p><p>I considered telling him that one day his surname might be stamped on equipment used across three kingdoms. Instead I said, "I was away from Carrow a long time."</p><p>"You're nineteen," Arlo said.</p><p>"Emotionally," I said.</p><p>Arlo stared. I smiled. He returned to the kiln. By afternoon, the first samples had failed. One cracked. One warped. One smelled terrible. The fourth did absolutely nothing interesting. I watched Arlo scratch a line through it.</p><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>"You paid for one test," Arlo said.</p><p>"I paid for your time," I said.</p><p>"You paid for six silver of my time," Arlo said.</p><p>"How much time remains?" I asked.</p><p>He looked at the window. "Enough to tell you this was a bad idea."</p><p>I felt the first real pinch of fear. Not panic. Arithmetic. Antonius's money sat in my pocket becoming smaller. The shale was supposed to matter. I knew that. No. I thought I knew that. I went outside. The alley behind the cooper smelled like wet wood and horse piss. I leaned against the wall and closed my eyes. Filter housing. White ceramic. Blue maker's stamp.</p><p>ARWICK.</p><p>Was it Kestrin shale? I searched. A banquet thirty years later. Someone talking beside me while I watched a duchess lie badly about a border dispute. Wrong memory. Workshop. Smoke. A woman with burned fingertips. Not Arlo. Arwick. Was her name Arwick? I could hear myself saying, "Use the old Kestrin mix." Maybe. Or "Don't use the old Kestrin mix." Fuck. Memory offered confidence without subtitles. I opened my eyes. This was exactly the trap. I had remembered the outcome and reconstructed the cause. The reconstruction was good enough to interest Arlo. That did not make it true. I could lose the loan. Fine. I could work it off.</p><p>One bad memory did not erase forty years. It did change what I was allowed to buy with them. Memory could generate leads. Arlo's bench got to decide which ones survived.</p><p>"Greg," Arlo said. Arlo stood in the doorway.</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"Come look," he said.</p><p>The fifth sample had not worked either. The sixth had. Not dramatically. No glow. No miraculous transformation. Arlo had run a cheap alchemical wash through a porous ceramic disk containing a small percentage of powdered shale. The liquid collected below was clearer than the control. Barely. But measurably. Arlo ran it again. Same result. He stopped talking. That was when I knew we had something.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Pell and Greg watching the sixth filtration disk produce a repeatable result." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/003/v28_c03_s02_sixth-disk.png"/></figure><p>I stared at the disk and remembered another successful test from much later in life. Different project. Different people. We had celebrated the first positive result for an entire night and discovered the next morning that it came from contamination in the measuring vessel. I had learned two things: never celebrate before replication, and never let Daro choose the celebratory liquor. Daro. Was Daro alive now? Almost certainly. Where? No idea. I nearly wrote his name down before remembering I was standing in Arlo's workshop and had no paper in my hand.</p><p>"How good?" I asked.</p><p>"Not good," Arlo said.</p><p>"Better?" I asked.</p><p>"Yes," Arlo said.</p><p>"How much better?" I asked.</p><p>"I need proper measures," Arlo said.</p><p>"Guess," I said.</p><p>"I don't guess," Arlo said.</p><p>"Everyone guesses. Professionals write the guess down," I said. </p><p>He glared at me.</p><p>"Ten percent?" I asked.</p><p>My heart kicked. Ten percent was enough. Not for the future product I remembered. Not yet. Enough for proof. Arlo looked at the disk. Then at the shale. Then at me.</p><p>"Where did you get this idea?" Arlo asked. </p><p>I smiled. </p><p>He did not.</p><p>"Greg," Arlo said.</p><p>Arlo Arwick. Lamp repairer. Small workshop. Good hands. Careful notes. Future surname, maybe. I still did not know whether he became rich, whether somebody inherited the name, or whether I was remembering the wrong Arwick entirely. What did I owe the man in front of me if my memory had pointed me toward work he had not found yet? Inconvenient question. I answered a different one.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Pell turning the successful experiment into a dangerous question for Greg." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/003/v28_c03_s03_pell-asks-where.png"/></figure><p>"How quickly can you improve it?" I asked.</p><p>Arlo's mouth tightened.</p><p>"That's not what I asked," Arlo said.</p><p>"I know," I said.</p><p>"Where did you get the idea?"</p><p>"From something I saw a long time ago," I said.</p><p>"You were a child a long time ago," Arlo said.</p><p>"I was very observant," I said.</p><p>"Greg," Arlo said. </p><p>I leaned over the bench.</p><p>"If I tell you I don't have an answer you will believe, will you stop asking?" I asked.</p><p>"No," Arlo said.</p><p>"Then we've discovered another stable property," I said.</p><p>He should have thrown me out. Instead he looked back at the sample. Curiosity beat suspicion, for now.</p><p>Useful. I hated how quickly the word appeared.</p><p>Interested, I corrected. Better.</p><p>"What do you need?" I asked.</p><p>"Better clay. Controlled heat. Different ratios. Proper test reagents," Arlo said.</p><p>"Cost?" I asked. </p><p>He named a number. </p><p>I swore. </p><p>Arlo smiled for the first time all afternoon.</p><p>"You wanted research."</p><p>"I wanted profitable research."</p><p>"Those are different."</p><p>"Apparently."</p><p>I checked the remaining silver. I could fund it. Barely. Then I would have almost nothing left. The sensible move was to take the weak positive result back to Antonius and ask for more capital. The better move was to improve the result first. The Greg move was to do both while pretending there was no distinction.</p><p>"I need a written statement," I said.</p><p>Arlo frowned. "Of what?"</p><p>"What we tested. What happened. Your estimate that further trials are justified," I said.</p><p>"I'm not putting my name on your sales pitch," Arlo said.</p><p>"Not a sales pitch. A technical observation," I said.</p><p>"For whom?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"A lender," I said.</p><p>"You borrowed the money?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Obviously," I said. </p><p>Arlo stared at me.</p><p>"How much?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Enough," I said.</p><p>"From who?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Antonius Vale," I said. </p><p>He put both hands on the bench.</p><p>"You borrowed from Vale to buy garbage."</p><p>"When you say it like that, it sounds irresponsible," I said.</p><p>"It is irresponsible," Arlo said.</p><p>"Then say it more quietly," I said.</p><p>Arlo walked to the other side of the workshop and stood there. I watched him think and felt the roles assembling anyway. Cautious artificer. Technical credibility. Future manufacturer. Partner. Asset. No. Arlo. A person named Arlo who wanted his work to remain his.</p><p>I had always been good at turning people into roles because roles were easier to arrange than people. Arlo was especially tempting because his surname already occupied some unknown place in my future.</p><p>"If I write anything, it says exactly what happened. No claims. No projections."</p><p>"Perfect," I said.</p><p>"And my name stays attached to the work," Arlo said.</p><p>That surprised me, mostly because nineteen-year-old Greg would have tried to own the idea. Old Greg knew better. Mostly.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>Arlo narrowed his eyes. "That easy?"</p><p>"No. I'm growing," I said.</p><p>"Into what?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"Unclear," I said.</p><p>He wrote the statement. I took it to Antonius before sunset. His storage-room office still had the ham. The scarred man from yesterday was there too; his name, I learned, was Rusk. Nothing surfaced when I searched for him. On the walk over I rehearsed the argument three ways, then caught myself rehearsing for the Antonius I remembered rather than the one I had actually met.</p><p>So I changed the plan. Give him the evidence. Let him ask. Watch what present Antonius cared about. Yesterday I had been a Bronze adventurer selling confidence. Today I had Arlo's name on a test that had produced a measurable effect. Not a business. Evidence.</p><p>Antonius looked at me long enough that </p><p>I said, "What?"</p><p>"You keep looking at people like that?"</p><p>"I have a memorable-face problem."</p><p>"Your face?"</p><p>"Other people's." </p><p>He held out his hand. I gave him Arlo's note.</p><p>He read it twice.</p><p>"Ten percent."</p><p>"Approximately."</p><p>"Meaning?"</p><p>"Meaning it worked badly."</p><p>Rusk laughed.</p><p>Antonius looked at me. "And you came here proud."</p><p>"I came here early."</p><p>"What do you want?"</p><p>"The rest of the loan I asked for."</p><p>"No," Antonius said.</p><p>"Half."</p><p>"No," Antonius said.</p><p>"A quarter."</p><p>"No," Antonius said. </p><p>I sat back.</p><p>"You're being difficult."</p><p>"I gave an unsecured loan to a Bronze adventurer yesterday. Today he returned with a piece of paper saying his garbage is slightly less useless than expected."</p><p>"That is a cruel summary of scientific progress."</p><p>Antonius slid the paper back.</p><p>"You owe me."</p><p>"I know," I said.</p><p>"Then why would I increase my exposure?"</p><p>"Because yesterday you were lending against me. Today you're lending against evidence."</p><p>"Bad evidence."</p><p>"Better than no evidence."</p><p>He almost smiled.</p><p>I leaned forward.</p><p>"And because if you don't, I'll find someone else."</p><p>Rusk stopped laughing. Antonius did smile then.</p><p>"You think you can?"</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>Could I? Probably. Maybe. There were merchants. Guild factors. Alchemists. Arlo himself if I could convince him to risk his workshop. I did not know their current names. I did know how money behaved around opportunity. That was enough to make the threat credible to me. Antonius studied my face.</p><p>"Who?"</p><p>"I don't know yet."</p><p>Rusk barked a laugh. Antonius's smile widened.</p><p>"At least you're an honest liar."</p><p>"I've had practice."</p><p>"At nineteen?" I shrugged. </p><p>He drummed two fingers on the desk.</p><p>"What is the actual play?"</p><p>There. Not the loan. The play. I liked him more for asking. Yesterday the shale had been remembered garbage. Now it was a weak result, a technical witness, and a reason to ask for another round of capital. That was enough.</p><p>"We prove the filtration effect. If it's material, we secure supply before anyone cares. Arlo develops the process. We sell the process, manufacture the filters, or license both depending on capital."</p><p>"We."</p><p>"Whoever pays."</p><p>"You've already promised Arwick a share?"</p><p>"His name stays on the work."</p><p>"That's not a share."</p><p>No. It wasn't. I disliked that Antonius noticed.</p><p>"What does he get?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"I haven't decided."</p><p>"Has he?"</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Then you're not partners."</p><p>"I didn't say we were." </p><p>Antonius leaned back. For a moment I saw the older man inside him. Or projected him there.</p><p>"How much do you think the idea is worth?" he asked.</p><p>I nearly answered with the future. A fortune. Wrong. Today it was worth one weak test and a cart of garbage.</p><p>"Nothing yet." </p><p>Antonius nodded.</p><p>"Good." He opened the cabinet. Not the full amount. More than I expected.</p><p>"I want first refusal on financing," he said.</p><p>"Limited."</p><p>"First refusal."</p><p>"For thirty days."</p><p>"Six months."</p><p>"Two."</p><p>"Four."</p><p>"Three."</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>"And if you sell the process during that period without offering it to me first, the debt doubles."</p><p>"That's predatory," I said.</p><p>"Yes," Antonius said.</p><p>"Good. I was worried you were losing your touch," I said.</p><p>His eyes narrowed again. I needed to stop doing that. He pushed the silver across. The shale might eventually solve the money problem. It would not solve my body. In my first life I had spent six more years pretending the sword was going to make me exceptional. I had no interest in repeating that delay.</p><p>"What do you know about mana conditioning?"</p><p>That question surprised him.</p><p>"Nothing," Antonius said.</p><p>"Who in Carrow does?"</p><p>"Guild."</p><p>"Anyone better?"</p><p>"Why?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"I want to learn magic."</p><p>Rusk looked at my sword. Antonius looked at my Bronze plate.</p><p>"You're a warrior."</p><p>"Allegedly."</p><p>"You cast?"</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Then why now?"</p><p>Because six years from now a sexual fad would accidentally reveal that I had wasted my youth.</p><p>"Career development." </p><p>Antonius laughed. Actually laughed. That was new.</p><p>"Go to the guild," he said. "Ask for Hessa Marr."</p><p>The name hit. Hessa. I went still. Antonius noticed. Of course he did.</p><p>"You know her?"</p><p>Did I? Old woman. White braid. Cane. No. Instructor. Barrier. Someone yelling at me. Not Hessa. Maybe. I could see a funeral. Whose?</p><p>"Hessa Marr," Antonius repeated. I searched harder. That only made it worse. There was something there. A memory with no label.</p><p>"I know the name."</p><p>"From?"</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>"Unreliable people."</p><p>Rusk groaned. Antonius waved me out. I left with more borrowed silver and a name that would not stop scratching at the inside of my skull. The guild was busiest at dusk. Parties returning. Contracts closing. Healers complaining. Porters weighing salvage. The smell of sweat, oil, wet leather, cheap stew, and minor triumph. Home. That word arrived before I could stop it. For most of my first life, guild halls had been home. Not this one. All of them. The noise settled something in me. Then Sella saw me.</p><p>A shield hit the floor somewhere to my left. The sound dragged up a memory of a different guild hall, a different shield, and a man named Corren insisting the dent proved he'd blocked a troll. It had been an ogre. I had corrected him in front of six people because I enjoyed being right more than I enjoyed Corren. He never forgave me. I could not remember whether he survived the Northern Gate.</p><p>That was happening constantly now. Noise became people. Smells became campaigns. A laugh could turn into a dead friend until I looked over and found a stranger. I had wanted forty years of experience back. Apparently it came without a search function.</p><p>"You."</p><p>"Me."</p><p>She was behind the counter now. That felt wrong. Later Sella had possessed an office, three assistants, and the terrifying ability to make veteran captains apologize for forms they had not yet failed to file. Now she was sorting contract slips.</p><p>"What do you want?" she asked.</p><p>"Hessa Marr." </p><p>Sella stopped. That was not encouraging.</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"I was told to ask for Hessa Marr."</p><p>"Who told you?"</p><p>"Vale."</p><p>Her expression worsened.</p><p>"Of course."</p><p>"Do you know him?"</p><p>"Everybody knows him."</p><p>Not yet, I thought. I leaned closer.</p><p>"How well?" </p><p>Sella leaned away.</p><p>"There. You're doing it again."</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"Looking at me like you're trying to remember where you buried me."</p><p>"That is disturbingly specific."</p><p>"Who are you?"</p><p>"Greg," I said.</p><p>"I know your name."</p><p>"Progress."</p><p>She did not smile. I looked at her and tried, deliberately this time, not to search the future. Sella now. Young clerk. Ink on her fingers again. Hair pinned badly because she had probably redone it during shift. A small burn on her wrist. Tired. Annoyed. Competent enough that three people had asked her questions while we were speaking and she answered all three without losing my thread. That was useful information too.</p><p>"Hessa?" I asked.</p><p>"Training annex. Basement."</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>"Greg," Sella said. </p><p>I turned.</p><p>"If Vale sent you, don't sign anything without reading it."</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>"I never do."</p><p>"You look exactly like someone who does."</p><p>Fair. The training annex had six practice rooms. Hessa Marr occupied the smallest. I knew her when I saw her. Not personally. Historically. That was different. Hessa Marr had written the Marr Primer. No. Had she? The primer was Marr. H. Marr. I had used it later when retraining a noble's son whose tutors had filled his head with expensive nonsense. I had complained about it. What had I complained about? Too conservative. Excellent foundations. Terrible diagrams. I smiled. Hessa looked up from a ledger. She was perhaps forty. Broad face. Hair tied in a knot. Sleeves rolled to the elbow. No cane. Of course no cane.</p><p>I did not remember Hessa as a beloved mentor. I remembered Marr attached to foundational instruction, and Antonius had independently sent me to her. Good enough to test. I needed her to tell me what this nineteen-year-old body actually had and what it lacked.</p><p>"Can I help you?"</p><p>I stared. </p><p>She sighed.</p><p>"Is there something on my face?"</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Then stop."</p><p>"Sorry." I sat opposite her.</p><p>"Antonius Vale said you teach mana conditioning."</p><p>"Vale sends me people he wants injured."</p><p>"Comforting."</p><p>"What do you want?"</p><p>"To learn."</p><p>"Magic?"</p><p>"Eventually."</p><p>"Have you tested?"</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Why not?"</p><p>"I was busy being wrong about my career." </p><p>Hessa looked at the sword on my hip.</p><p>"Warrior?"</p><p>"Allegedly." </p><p>She held out her hand.</p><p>"Token."</p><p>I gave her the Bronze plate.</p><p>She checked it.</p><p>"Two years registered."</p><p>That answered a question I had not thought to ask. Two years. Seventeen. I had joined at seventeen. Yes. That felt right. Another piece clicked into place. Hessa pushed the token back.</p><p>"You've been active?"</p><p>"Enough," I said.</p><p>"Injuries?"</p><p>"Not currently."</p><p>"Mana exposure?"</p><p>"Dungeons."</p><p>"Formal channel work?"</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Spell attempts?"</p><p>"One."</p><p>Her eyes sharpened.</p><p>"When?"</p><p>"This morning."</p><p>"What spell?"</p><p>"Barrier."</p><p>"Without conditioning?"</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"Why?" Hessa asked.</p><p>"Optimism."</p><p>"Result?"</p><p>"Headache. Tingling hand."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"Good?"</p><p>"You didn't rupture anything."</p><p>"Excellent standard." </p><p>She stood.</p><p>"Come here."</p><p>The test was humiliating. Not because it hurt. Because I knew exactly what she was testing and my body failed every expectation my mind supplied. Mana response. Poor. Channel definition. Almost nonexistent. Reservoir. Small. Control. Interesting. Hessa repeated that one.</p><p>I knew what a good mana response looked like. I had coached it, enhanced it, planned around fractions of efficiency most adventurers never noticed. Now Hessa asked my own body for the magical equivalent of lifting a finger and the response arrived late, weak, and slightly confused.</p><p>For one stupid instant I wanted to tell her who I became. Not because it would help. Because I wanted the room corrected. I wanted the hierarchy restored. I wanted her to understand that the boy failing a beginner's exercise had once stood among seven S-class adventurers in the world. The impulse was so childish that I almost laughed. There he was. Greg. Still desperate for the audience to know when he was impressive.</p><p>"Again," I said. I did. </p><p>She watched my hand.</p><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>Third time.</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"Who taught you?"</p><p>"No one."</p><p>"Don't lie."</p><p>"I'm not."</p><p>"You adjusted."</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"How?"</p><p>"You told me what was wrong."</p><p>"I told you the sensation was collapsing toward the thumb."</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"Most beginners don't know what that means."</p><p>I almost said, It was obvious. That sentence had cost me years the first time. So I shut my mouth. Hessa noticed that too.</p><p>"What were you going to say?"</p><p>"Nothing useful."</p><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>We repeated the exercise. My capacity was terrible. My control was not. Not good. Not yet. But the shape was there. The old mind inside a young magical body. Hessa sat down.</p><p>"You're strange."</p><p>"I've had a productive day."</p><p>"You cannot cast Barrier."</p><p>"I know," I said.</p><p>"You may be able to in a few months." </p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>Months.</p><p>I had not brought my old reservoir back. I had not smuggled S-class power into a young body. What I had brought was recognition: I understood what Hessa was correcting and could adjust faster than a true beginner. I could not skip the foundation. I might stop wasting years building it by accident.</p><p>At twenty-five, during the Barrier craze, I had learned quickly because six years of dungeon exposure and physical training had already done work I had never noticed. Hessa had just put a timetable on doing that work deliberately.</p><p>Months. My plan changed while she was still speaking.</p><p>"What if I train every day?"</p><p>"Then you'll injure yourself."</p><p>"Twice a day?"</p><p>"Did you hear me?"</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"No, you heard words." </p><p>I smiled. </p><p>Hessa did not. Good instructor.</p><p>"What is the fastest safe progression?" I asked.</p><p>"Why?" Hessa asked.</p><p>"I dislike waiting."</p><p>"That is not a reason."</p><p>"It has governed most of civilization."</p><p>"Three sessions a week. Daily breath work. Dungeon exposure counts, but only if you're not exhausted. Nutrition."</p><p>"Four sessions."</p><p>"Three."</p><p>"I'll pay."</p><p>"Then you can pay for three."</p><p>"You're difficult."</p><p>"So I've been told."</p><p>I thought of the silver in my coat. Research. Debt. Training. Food. I had wanted capital because capital bought time. Now every use of it competed with another.</p><p>"Three," I said.</p><p>Hessa named the fee. I winced. She smiled. Apparently everyone enjoyed this part. I paid for the first week. When I returned to Arlo's workshop, it was dark. He was still there. Three new disks sat beside the kiln.</p><p>"You're late," he said.</p><p>"You missed me."</p><p>"No," Arlo said.</p><p>"Results?"</p><p>"Better."</p><p>That word hit harder than it should have. Arlo showed me. Not ten percent. Closer to twenty. Still crude. Still inconsistent.</p><p>Real.</p><p>I laughed. Arlo did not. Then he did, a little. I looked at the disks, the shale, the notes, Arlo's tired face, and my mind began moving. Supply. Tests. Ownership. Guild salvage contracts. Manufacturing. Licensing. Antonius. Arwick. How much could I secure before anyone else noticed? How fast could Arlo improve it? Who did I need? Who could I cut out? The thoughts came cleanly. Comfortably. Arlo was saying something. I had stopped listening.</p><p>"Greg," Arlo said. </p><p>I looked up.</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"I said if this becomes something, I'm not your employee."</p><p>I blinked. Had I said something aloud? Apparently my face had.</p><p>"I didn't say you were."</p><p>"You looked at my workshop like you were measuring it."</p><p>I glanced around. I had been.</p><p>"Sorry."</p><p>"No, you're not."</p><p>"If we continue, we decide terms before the next round."</p><p>My first instinct was irritation. My second was respect. My third was calculation.</p><p>Dangerous. Useful. Person. I exhaled.</p><p>"All right."</p><p>"All right?"</p><p>"Tomorrow. We write terms." </p><p>Arlo looked suspicious.</p><p>"Fair terms."</p><p>More suspicious.</p><p>"I know what fair means."</p><p>"Do you?"</p><p>That landed somewhere old. Faces. People I had pushed because I could. People I had made stronger. People I had made useful. People who had thanked me and hated me, sometimes in the same conversation. I looked at Arlo. Not Arwick Works. Not a stamp on a future filter. Arlo, in a rented room, after spending his entire day testing my stupid idea because curiosity had gotten its teeth into him.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>Then, because the truth deserved precision:</p><p>"I think I do." </p><p>Arlo nodded slowly.</p><p>"Tomorrow."</p><p>I left. Carrow was dark and wet, lanterns reflected in the street. I had begun the day with three copper. I ended it in debt to a future crime lord, financially entangled with an artificer whose future I only half remembered, enrolled in magical conditioning six years ahead of schedule, and carrying a technical result that might become valuable if my memory had not lied about everything around it. A sensible person would have called that unstable. I called it momentum.</p><p>The next move was not another miracle. It was keeping these pieces together long enough for one of them to start paying for the others. That was probably the first mistake.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="002.html">← Chapter 2</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="004.html">Chapter 4 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/054.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 42: The Interpreter — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 42</div><h1>THE INTERPRETER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p><strong>I woke with a wooden horse watching me.</strong> This was unsettling. Its head was too small. Its legs were too thick. The carver had given it one eye slightly higher than the other, which made it look suspicious of the washbasin. I liked it more in daylight.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="The badly carved wooden horse watching Greg from the table." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/054/svgPLG_Ch54_Horse-Watches-Back.png"/></figure><p>Bad sign. My head hurt. Not badly. Cheap drink hurt differently at nineteen. Old Greg could drink. Old Greg had also spent years building the sort of tolerance that was probably just slow poisoning with better furniture. Current Greg had three cups and a headache. Useful. I drank water. Then more water. My hand was better.</p><p>The larger blister had flattened under Hessa's wrap. The smaller one had become less interesting. My beard still surprised me when I looked in the mirror. Better. Still my face. Probably. Someone knocked. I stared at the door. Nobody should know I was awake. Another knock.</p><p>“Greg?”</p><p>Woman. Not Hessa. Not Vessa. Not Octavia. I opened the door. The lodging keeper stood there holding a folded note.</p><p>“You have mail,” she said.</p><p>“That's ominous,” I said.</p><p>“You owe me nothing for it,” she said.</p><p>“Less ominous.”</p><p>She handed it over.</p><p>“Boy left it.”</p><p>“What boy?”</p><p>“A boy.”</p><p>“Description?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Fair. I closed the door. The note was Guild paper. Not Guild handwriting. Greg, If you are still interested in the stone, I have something worth showing you. Not urgent. Edrin.</p><p>Below that:</p><p>AFTER MIDDAY.</p><p>Good. Not urgent. She had written it. I read it again. Still not urgent. I put it on the table beside the horse. Then made breakfast. That was harder than it should have been. The note existed. I could feel it existing. Stone. Sinkstone. Three seized batches. Narrow behavior inside each sack. Different behavior between sacks. Processed kestrin. Darrowmere fragments not the same thing.</p><p>Dorrin sorting. Bale rejection. Holl's brass line. Kett. Varo. Testing. Rebatching. Silas Marris. I cracked an egg. Shell went into the bowl. I removed it. The note remained on the table. Not urgent. I ate two eggs and bread. Then washed the bowl. Then cleaned my knife. Then stopped. This was ridiculous. It was still morning. I had time.</p><p>I could go immediately and wait outside Edrin's room for three hours like a dog with a technical question. No. I put the note in my pocket. Then went outside. The city had already started without me. Good. I walked to the river. Not because I needed to. Because yesterday I had liked it. This was becoming suspicious.</p><p>The same low wall was occupied by an old man repairing a basket. I sat farther down. Boats moved. Workers shouted. A gull stole something and was pursued by a child with unrealistic confidence. I watched. My brain tried to turn the river into freight capacity. I refused.</p><p>Then it tried to identify which barges could carry treated stone without water exposure. I refused less successfully. Fine. The sinkstone existed. I was allowed to think about it. I was not required to chase it every minute. That distinction remained irritating. A courier came down the river road. Dark hair. Long stride. No. Not Sevren. I noticed anyway. Also irritating.</p><p>I stayed until the sun moved enough that sitting became hot. Then I went to the Guild. Not Edrin. Contract hall. I wanted to see if my name was still on the lane-support slip. It was not visible. Of course it was not visible. The availability notes lived behind a desk. I nearly asked. Then didn't. There were jobs on the board.</p><p>The pigs were gone. Someone had accepted them. I felt relief for reasons I could not defend. Alden was not in the yard. Jorren was not there. Berren was. He sat on a bench lacing his right boot. The wrap was gone. He saw me.</p><p>“Face.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You changed it.”</p><p>I touched my beard.</p><p>“Apparently.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“You look twelve.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>He stood. Put weight on the foot. No wince. Good. I looked away before he could catch me checking. He caught me anyway.</p><p>“Still attached.”</p><p>“I can see that.”</p><p>“Want to spar?”</p><p>I looked at my hand. Then at his foot.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He nodded. No insult. That was concerning.</p><p>“Why not?”</p><p>“Hessa said no pressure work yesterday.”</p><p>“That's magic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Sword isn't magic.”</p><p>“My hand.”</p><p>He looked.</p><p>“Ah.”</p><p>“Also your foot,” I said.</p><p>“My foot's fine,” Berren said.</p><p>“Then why are you lacing it like you're negotiating?” I asked.</p><p>He stopped. Looked at me.</p><p>“Fuck you,” Berren said.</p><p>Good. He sat again. I sat beside him.</p><p>“What happened to the pigs?”</p><p>“What pigs?”</p><p>“Contract.”</p><p>“No idea.”</p><p>“Someone took it.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>We sat. A pair of Copper adventurers crossed the yard carrying a rolled net between them. One was bleeding from the ear. Nobody seemed concerned. Berren watched them.</p><p>“You drinking tonight?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Jorren?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Tam?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“You went upstairs?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How was it?”</p><p>“People.”</p><p>He laughed.</p><p>“That bad?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>That answer surprised both of us. Berren finished his boot.</p><p>“I'm going east yard.”</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Training.”</p><p>“With Alden?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. He stood.</p><p>“See you.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>He left. Independent. I liked that too. This was getting out of hand. By midday I had successfully accomplished almost nothing. I bought lunch. A meat pie. Then another because one was not enough. Nineteen. Expensive metabolism. Worth it. After midday, I went to Edrin. Her workroom smelled the same. Stone dust. Oil. Something sharp from the reagent cabinet. The table was different.</p><p>Three shallow trays sat in a row. Each held dark gray pellets. Sinkstone. Seized stock. I stopped at the threshold. Edrin looked up from a ledger.</p><p>“You came.”</p><p>“You said worth showing.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“Was that manipulative?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Good. She pointed to the stool. I sat. She did not begin. Instead she finished the line she was writing. Then another. Then sanded the ink. I waited. Progress. She closed the ledger.</p><p>“Before you ask, no, I don't know who made it.”</p><p>“I wasn't going to ask first.”</p><p>“What were you going to ask first?”</p><p>“Whether those are the three seized batches.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Separated?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Same sacks?”</p><p>“Representative samples from each.”</p><p>“Chain of custody?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“You're getting worse.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Debatable.”</p><p>She moved the first tray forward.</p><p>“Batch one.”</p><p>The pellets looked ordinary. Gray. Some darker. Small broken pieces. Nothing that said magical contraband. She placed a mana bead beside the tray. Not touching. The bead glowed faintly. Then she slid three pellets into a narrow brass cup around it. The glow dimmed.</p><p>“Expected.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She removed them. The glow recovered. Then she placed three different pellets from the same tray. Same dimming. Not identical. Close. Third set. Close.</p><p>“Still narrow,” I said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She moved to batch two. Same procedure. Stronger dimming. Three sets. Again narrow within the batch. Batch three. Weakest immediate suppression. But Edrin did not stop. She removed the pellets. The bead stayed dim. I leaned forward.</p><p>“Retention,” I said.</p><p>“Yes,” Edrin said.</p><p>“How long?” I asked.</p><p>“Depends batch,” she said.</p><p>She handed me a sheet. Numbers. Good numbers. Not perfect. Batch one suppressed moderately, recovered quickly. Batch two suppressed strongest, retained some effect for several minutes. Batch three suppressed least during contact but left the longest residual effect after removal. I read it twice.</p><p>“These are different products.”</p><p>Edrin moved the trays apart with one finger each.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Different treatment targets. Intended uses. Makers.”</p><p>“Maybe, maybe, maybe.”</p><p>I looked up.</p><p>“You enjoy this.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Lie. Small one. I read again. Within each batch, the spread was narrow. Between batches, behavior was meaningfully different. That part we already knew. The new part was the shape. Not simply more or less sinkstone. Different response profiles.</p><p>“Same raw stone?”</p><p>Edrin pushed another page toward me.</p><p>“Visually and by simple density, close enough that I wouldn't separate origin.”</p><p>“Close enough isn't same.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Mineral inclusions?”</p><p>“Not enough sample destruction authorized.”</p><p>Right. Evidence had owners. Even seized evidence.</p><p>“What did you find?”</p><p>She tapped the bottom of the sheet. I read. After three repeated exposure cycles, batch one drifted. Not much. Batch two drifted more. Batch three barely changed. I looked at the trays.</p><p>“Durability.”</p><p>“Or exhaustion.”</p><p>“Or release behavior.”</p><p>“Or something else.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“That's what was worth showing.”</p><p>I sat back. Three batches. Three profiles. Narrow inside. Different under repeated use. This was not random cheap treated shale thrown into sacks. Probably. I hated probably.</p><p>“Professional specification,” I said.</p><p>“Likely.”</p><p>“Not merely sorting.”</p><p>“Likely.”</p><p>“Could still be post-treatment sorting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be one process with three target ranges.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be three processes.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be three suppliers.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be one supplier selling grades.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be customer specification.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be Silas Marris buying whatever was available and the sacks just happened to be internally consistent.”</p><p>Edrin looked at me.</p><p>“Less likely.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Finally.</p><p>“How much less?”</p><p>“Enough that I would spend time on the alternatives first.”</p><p>There. Professional judgment. Not proof. Useful. I looked at batch three. Longest residual effect. Lowest immediate suppression. Interesting. Dangerous word.</p><p>“What happens if you mix them?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“I was asking.”</p><p>“You were asking with your hands.”</p><p>My right hand had moved toward the trays. I put it in my lap.</p><p>“Fair.”</p><p>“We are not mixing seized evidence because you're curious.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“Temporarily.”</p><p>Vessa's word. Edrin's mouth twitched.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I looked at the three trays.</p><p>“Have you tested treated commercial kestrin against them?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I turned.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>She reached under the table. Fourth tray. Pale gray. More uniform in appearance.</p><p>“Where from?”</p><p>“Guild stores.”</p><p>“Supplier?”</p><p>“Bale.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Which product?”</p><p>“Basic bed.”</p><p>Same class as mine.</p><p>“Lot?”</p><p>“Different from yours unless you've been stealing Guild stock.”</p><p>“I have not.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She ran the bead test. Commercial Bale basic bed dimmed the bead weakly. Consistent enough. Recovery immediate. Repeated cycles showed little drift. Different. Clearly.</p><p>“Fine bed?”</p><p>“Not yet.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I have a budget.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Eight copper retail.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Could requisition.”</p><p>“I could.”</p><p>“You haven't.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because basic already answers the first question.”</p><p>Which was? I waited. She waited. I found it.</p><p>“Whether ordinary commercial treated kestrin naturally looks like seized stock.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It doesn't.”</p><p>“Not this ordinary commercial product.”</p><p>Good correction. Not all commercial. This one. I wrote it. Edrin watched.</p><p>“You've been somewhere.”</p><p>“Many places.”</p><p>“Your questions are less bad.”</p><p>“Bale.”</p><p>“Ah.”</p><p>“Holl.”</p><p>“I know Holl.”</p><p>“Everyone knows Holl.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“What did he tell you?”</p><p>I hesitated. Supplier privacy. Nothing secret about basic process categories.</p><p>“Bale buys treated stock, rejects, sorts, tests by line and bead, sometimes rebatches. Low variance means commercial tolerance, not identical pieces. Piece testing is possible but too expensive for cheap stock under ordinary methods.”</p><p>Edrin nodded.</p><p>“Reasonable.”</p><p>“He said unusually narrow individual behavior could come from better raw sorting, better process control, narrow source lots, more testing and rejection, post-treatment response sorting, or luck.”</p><p>“Also reasonable.”</p><p>“And blending for bulk behavior, but that wouldn't necessarily narrow individual pellets.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at the seized trays.</p><p>“Your test uses groups of three.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Have you tested individuals?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Of course. She handed me another page. The spread was still narrow. Not identical. Narrow. That mattered.</p><p>“Piece-level consistency.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So blending alone doesn't explain it.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>Unless pieces were individually sorted before blending. Still.</p><p>“Did Holl know Silas Marris?”</p><p>“As a trading company.”</p><p>Edrin's eyes sharpened.</p><p>“Reaction?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did you ask suppliers?”</p><p>“He refused.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Why good?”</p><p>“Because I don't want you charming merchants into violating customer privacy for an investigation you don't own.”</p><p>There it was. I felt the objection before I formed the answer.</p><p>“I wouldn't charm.”</p><p>She stared. Fine.</p><p>“I might persuade.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>I looked at the trays. I understood the problem. Not fully. Enough to see the next useful questions. Who treated the stone? Who specified the ranges? Who tested individual pieces? Who paid enough to make that economical? Who needed batch three's strange low-suppression, long-residual profile? The questions were sitting there. I could go to Varo. I could ask Kett. I could ask Holl who bought fine bed.</p><p>I could ask Antonius what kinds of customers paid for controlled material. I could ask Silas Marris directly. That last thought was especially stupid. I could do all of it. Some of it might work. That was the dangerous part. Edrin watched my face.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“That's never true.”</p><p>“I know what I would do next.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I told her. Not all of it. The legal version.</p><p>“Find processors who can produce narrow response ranges. Ask what controls cost. Ask whether they test before or after treatment. Ask what kind of customer pays for individual response consistency. Then compare capabilities to these profiles without naming the evidence.”</p><p>Edrin listened. Then said, “Good.” I waited.</p><p>“But?”</p><p>“No but.”</p><p>That was worse.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“That's what I would do too.”</p><p>There. Permission-shaped object. My brain reached for it immediately.</p><p>“I can go to Varo.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stopped. Edrin smiled. Not kindly.</p><p>“Why not?”</p><p>“Because I said your next questions are good. I did not assign them to you.”</p><p>There. Exact. Clean. I leaned back.</p><p>“That was fast.”</p><p>“You're predictable.”</p><p>“Unfair.”</p><p>“You stood up.”</p><p>I looked down. I had. Halfway. I sat fully. Edrin folded her hands.</p><p>“I am going to Varo.”</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because this is my investigation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And because if they know something, they are more likely to answer a Guild warder with evidence authority than a nineteen-year-old Bronze who looks like he's trying to buy rocks.”</p><p>“I do buy rocks.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Arlo complained.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Not seriously.”</p><p>That was unacceptable.</p><p>“What did he say?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Edrin.”</p><p>“No.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/054/Ch054_Fast-Coverage-003-B15.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 54." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>I hated competent people. She gathered the test sheets. I watched.</p><p>“You asked me here because?”</p><p>“You had been thinking about consistency before I had.”</p><p>“That's not an answer.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“You wanted my interpretation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“And you gave me useful questions.”</p><p>“Which you are going to ask.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I sat with that. This was exactly the kind of thing Old Greg would have hated. Someone else taking the next step. Using my thinking. Owning the action. Potentially getting the answer first. Good. I hated it. Also good.</p><p>“Can I come?”</p><p>Edrin considered.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I felt the disappointment immediately. Not strategic. I wanted to see Varo. I wanted to hear the answers. I wanted to watch the process. I wanted the rocks. Probably not the rocks. Some of the rocks.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I don't know what kind of conversation it will be.”</p><p>“I can stay quiet.”</p><p>She laughed. Actually laughed.</p><p>“That is insulting.”</p><p>“I can.”</p><p>“You can for perhaps six minutes.”</p><p>“Seven.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I looked at the trays again.</p><p>“Will you tell me what you learn?”</p><p>“If I can.”</p><p>“That's vague.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Because investigation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Privacy.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Evidence.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Annoying.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I sighed.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>Edrin started returning the trays to sealed boxes. I stood. This time because the meeting was over. At the door she said, “Greg.” I turned.</p><p>“If you independently encounter information about controlled sinkstone production in the course of normal work, tell me.”</p><p>“That was already the rule.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why repeat it?”</p><p>“Because you just tried to turn my trip to Varo into your trip to Varo.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Normal work.”</p><p>“Normal work.”</p><p>“Not manufactured work.”</p><p>She pointed at me.</p><p>“Especially that.”</p><p>I left. Outside, the afternoon felt brighter than necessary. I wanted to go to Varo. Badly. Three streets south from Bale. Not far. I knew where it was now. I could walk past. That was not going. I started walking. South. This was suspicious. I told myself I was going home. Home was not south. I adjusted. West. Then stopped. This was pathetic.</p><p>A cart passed carrying empty clay jars. A woman shouted at someone from an upstairs window. A dog slept in a patch of sun. Nobody cared whether I went to Varo. I cared. That was enough to make the decision difficult. I turned north. Guild. No. That was substitution. I turned east. River. Also substitution.</p><p>I stood in the intersection until a driver shouted at me.</p><p>“Move!”</p><p>I moved. Toward food. Reliable. I bought fried dough with onions. Too hot. Burned my tongue. Good. While I ate, someone bumped my shoulder.</p><p>“New face.”</p><p>Sevren. I turned. He was carrying a courier tube under one arm and half a pear in his hand.</p><p>“Old face.”</p><p>“Less beard.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He looked at it critically.</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Everyone says that.”</p><p>“Then you should trust the evidence.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He bit the pear.</p><p>“Working?”</p><p>“Not currently.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“I need help.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“With what?”</p><p>He held up the courier tube.</p><p>“Nothing important.”</p><p>“That is not reassuring.”</p><p>“I need to return a ladder.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Why do you have a ladder?”</p><p>“I don't.”</p><p>“Then how are we returning it?”</p><p>“We have to get it first.”</p><p>I looked at him. He ate pear.</p><p>“Whose ladder?”</p><p>“Octavia's.”</p><p>That seemed unlikely.</p><p>“She owns a ladder?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Sevren.”</p><p>“It's complicated.”</p><p>“Is it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“North cloth yard.”</p><p>“Where does it go?”</p><p>“West courier shed.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I borrowed it.”</p><p>“From the west courier shed.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And left it at the north cloth yard.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Roof.”</p><p>I waited. He waited. This was not enough information. It was also probably all the information required.</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Now would be good.”</p><p>I looked south. Varo existed. Edrin was going tomorrow. Not mine. Sevren had a ladder. Apparently.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>He smiled. Not triumphant. Just pleased. We walked north.</p><p>“What was the roof?”</p><p>“Loose route board.”</p><p>“You climbed onto a roof to fix a route board.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“It was hanging.”</p><p>“Was that your job?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I looked at him. He looked at me.</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>“I didn't say anything.”</p><p>“You made the face.”</p><p>Everyone knew the face. Terrible.</p><p>“Did you fix it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did you break anything?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did leaving the ladder there create a problem?”</p><p>“Only for the people who own the ladder.”</p><p>“Which is a problem.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And now you're fixing it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I considered.</p><p>“You're very annoying.”</p><p>“I've heard.”</p><p>We reached the north cloth yard. The ladder leaned exactly where he said. A woman at the gate saw Sevren.</p><p>“You came back.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Miracle.”</p><p>“Temporary.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Who's this?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Ladder.”</p><p>That was apparently enough. We took one end each. The ladder was long. Not heavy. Awkward. Sevren took the front. I took the back. We walked. At the first corner, he turned too sharply. My end hit a post.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>He stopped.</p><p>“You need wider.”</p><p>“I know now.”</p><p>“You knew before.”</p><p>“I knew conceptually.”</p><p>I laughed despite myself. We adjusted. Second corner clean. Third corner, a fruit cart blocked half the lane. I stopped. Sevren looked back.</p><p>“Can fit.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not with the awning.”</p><p>He looked. Measured with eyes. Then lifted his end.</p><p>“Over?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because my end will hit the sign.”</p><p>He looked back. Right. He lowered it. We backed up. Took another street. Greg model one. Sevren zero. I enjoyed this too much. At the next lane, a delivery cart blocked us. Sevren did not stop.</p><p>He ducked his end under the cart's rear rail, rotated the ladder through the open space behind the wheel, and said, “Up.” I lifted. The ladder passed diagonally through a gap I had already categorized as unusable. We were through. He looked back.</p><p>“Conceptually.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>Sevren one. Greg one. Good. We returned the ladder. The courier shed clerk looked at Sevren.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Returned.”</p><p>“You borrowed it yesterday.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You said one hour.”</p><p>“Time passed.”</p><p>The clerk pointed at a chalk board. Sevren's name was written under EQUIPMENT.</p><p>Beside it:</p><p>LADDER.</p><p>He took the chalk and erased it.</p><p>“Resolved.”</p><p>The clerk looked at me.</p><p>“He does this.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You've known him how long?”</p><p>“Not long enough.”</p><p>Sevren handed me the rest of the pear. I looked at it.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I'm done.”</p><p>“That is not how gifts work.”</p><p>“It's how pears work.”</p><p>I ate it. We left. At the corner Sevren said, “Drink?” I considered. My tongue hurt from fried dough. My head had only recently stopped hurting from last night.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He nodded.</p><p>“Food?”</p><p>“I ate.”</p><p>“Walk?”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>He shrugged. There. No objective. I almost said no. Then didn't.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>We walked. Not toward Varo. That helped. Sevren told me about a courier horse named Bishop who had learned to stop at a bakery even when the route did not include the bakery. I told him that was training failure. He said it was initiative. We argued for six streets. Neither changed position.</p><p>At one point he stopped to help a woman lift a crate onto a cart. No discussion. No optimization. Lift. Done. She thanked him. He kept walking. I noticed. Did not make a philosophy. Mostly. At the river split, Sevren looked north.</p><p>“I have a delivery.”</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You forgot?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He tapped the courier tube. Right. His actual life.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“North quay.”</p><p>“Need help?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. He started away. Then turned.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing yet.”</p><p>“That is not a plan.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then why ask?”</p><p>“To see if you're busy.”</p><p>I thought about Edrin going to Varo. Not with me. Arlo might have regulator work. Guild might call. Hessa might want the hand checked. Jorren existed. Alden existed. Everything existed.</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>Sevren nodded.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He left. Same answer. Different person. I watched him go for perhaps two seconds too long. Then went home. The wooden horse was still beside the washbasin. I put Edrin's note beneath it so it would not blow away. The horse was not heavy enough for this job. It slid. I repositioned it. Still bad. I found a cup. Better. The note stayed.</p><p>Edrin would go to Varo tomorrow. Without me. That remained irritating. I could live with irritating. Probably. I sat on the bed. My body was tired in an ordinary way. My hand barely hurt. My beard itched at the jaw. My tongue was burned.</p><p>I had spent the day learning something important about sinkstone and returning a ladder. The ladder had been more fun. I did not write that down.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="053.html">← Chapter 41</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="055.html">Chapter 43 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/014.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 10: The Escort — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 10</div><h1>THE ESCORT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Jorren hit me in the ribs three more times before he decided I was learning.</p><p>I disagreed with his metric.</p><p>"Again," he said.</p><p>"I have ribs," I said.</p><p>"Good.
