Use them," Jorren said.</p><p>"That is not what ribs are for," I said.</p><p>Jorren raised the practice sword. I raised mine. This time I did not look at his shoulders.</p><p>That sounds stupid. It was not. I had spent decades learning to read the first honest movement in a body. Shoulders lied less than hands. Hips lied less than shoulders. Feet lied least of all, except when someone was very good, in which case everything lied and you started looking at breathing, rhythm, distance, intent, terrain, allies, exits, mana, fatigue, injury, and whether the bastard had a second knife.</p><p>Jorren had one wooden sword. No mana. No second knife.</p><p>Probably. I looked at his feet. He stepped.</p><p>My mind produced six answers. I chose one I could actually perform. Block. Simple. Ugly. Correct.</p><p>Wood cracked against wood. The impact traveled through my wrist, but my sword stayed where I had put it. Jorren's eyebrows moved. That was all the warning I got before he kicked my ankle. I fell.</p><p>"Fuck."</p><p>Jorren nudged the practice sword away from my shoulder.</p><p>"Better."</p><p>"Which part?" I asked.</p><p>"The part before you fell."</p><p>I rolled onto my back and stared at the sky. "Excellent. I am improving in increasingly narrow portions of combat," I said.</p><p>Jorren planted the end of his practice sword beside my head. "You stopped trying to win," he said.</p><p>I turned my head. He was serious.</p><p>"I am always trying to win."</p><p>"No. Usually you're trying to prove you already know how."</p><p>That was an unpleasantly crowded category of people who could apparently diagnose me now. I sat up. "Hessa has been talking to you."</p><p>"Who?"</p><p>"Never mind."</p><p>Jorren offered his hand. I took it and stood. The training yard was mostly empty. Two boys were wrestling badly near the fence. An older woman in a leather vest was teaching a girl how to fall without putting her wrist down. Somewhere behind the guild building, somebody was hammering metal in a rhythm that made me want to count it. Jorren handed both practice swords to the yard keeper.</p><p>"Come on," he said.</p><p>"Where?" I asked.</p><p>"Job," Jorren said.</p><p>I stopped. Jorren kept walking.</p><p>"Jorren."</p><p>He looked back.</p><p>"What job?" I asked.</p><p>"Easy one," Jorren said.</p><p>Every scar I had ever acquired developed an opinion.</p><p>"There are no easy jobs," I said.</p><p>"There are," Jorren said.</p><p>"No. There are jobs where the problem hasn't introduced itself yet," I said.</p><p>Jorren sighed. "You want to go back to adventuring?"</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"You've complained about it every time I've seen you."</p><p>"That is how I express commitment," I said.</p><p>"Then come," Jorren said.</p><p>I followed him through the guild hall. I had been in buildings like this for most of my first life. Different city, different hall, same architecture of organized desperation. Boards. Benches. Ink. Mud. People pretending not to listen to other people's negotiations. The better halls had clerks who understood that adventurers were essentially mobile disasters requiring paperwork. Carrow's hall was not one of the better halls.</p><p>It was fine. Bronze work covered most of the near board. Deliveries. Escorts. Pest clearing. Missing livestock. Guard shifts. Recovery work. A request to find a man's blue coat, which had somehow acquired a reward large enough to imply the coat contained either money, evidence, or a marriage. I looked at the higher boards.</p><p>Jorren stepped in front of me.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I was looking," I said.</p><p>"Look lower," Jorren said.</p><p>"That is philosophically hostile," I said.</p><p>"Bronze," Jorren said.</p><p>"I know my rank," I said.</p><p>"Do you?" Jorren asked.</p><p>I smiled at him. He did not smile back. Fine.</p><p>Jorren led me to a clerk with ink on both thumbs. She was perhaps thirty, with close-cut hair and the expression of someone who had already heard every explanation for why a contract had gone wrong.</p><p>"Replacement," Jorren said.</p><p>The clerk looked at me. "Name?"</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Full."</p><p>"Gregory."</p><p>She waited.</p><p>"Gregory is full enough," I said.</p><p>Jorren rubbed his face. The clerk looked at him.</p><p>"Greg," he said.</p><p>"Greg what?"</p><p>I considered several surnames I had used in my first life. That was a bad sign.</p><p>"Just Greg," I said.</p><p>The clerk stared at me, then wrote something. I leaned over. She covered the page.</p><p>"Stay on your side of the counter."</p><p>"You're writing about me," I said.</p><p>"And you'll see the contract when I hand it over."</p><p>I liked her.</p><p>"Contract?" I asked.</p><p>She pulled a sheet from beneath the counter. "Mara Venn. Mill road. Two miles north. Wagon escort and collection. One damaged axle reported. Cargo is iron fittings and lamp oil. Client wants two Bronze bodies because the road has had thefts."</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Contract" decoding="async" height="352" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/014/v28_c14_s01_the-contract.png" width="330"/></figure><p>"Bandits?" I asked.</p><p>"Thieves," the clerk said. "If they were organized enough to be bandits, the rate would be higher."</p><p>"How many thefts?" I asked.</p><p>"Three reported."</p><p>"Over what period?"</p><p>"Greg," Jorren said.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>The clerk answered anyway. "Nine days."</p><p>"Same location?" I asked.</p><p>"Within half a mile."</p><p>"Time?" I asked.</p><p>"Late afternoon twice. Unknown once."</p><p>"Violence?" I asked.</p><p>"One driver shoved. One knife shown. No injuries reported."</p><p>"Number of offenders?" I asked.</p><p>"Two to four."</p><p>"Description?" I asked.</p><p>"Young."</p><p>"That's not a description," I said.</p><p>"It is when nobody agrees on anything else."</p><p>I looked at the contract. Mara Venn. Mill road. Damaged axle. Iron fittings. Lamp oil. Collection.</p><p>"Why is the wagon still there?" I asked.</p><p>"Axle cracked yesterday," the clerk said. "Venn left one hand with it and came back to arrange repair."</p><p>"Cargo stayed?" I asked.</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Overnight?" I asked.</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>Jorren looked at me. I looked at the clerk.</p><p>"Still easy?" I asked.</p><p>She shrugged. "Probably." I hated probably.</p><p>"What does collection mean?" I asked.</p><p>"Bring wagon and cargo to Venn's yard. Repairman is already going."</p><p>"Who's the repairman?" I asked.</p><p>"Venn's."</p><p>"Who is with the wagon?" I asked.</p><p>"Her nephew."</p><p>"Age?" I asked.</p><p>The clerk paused.</p><p>"Sixteen."</p><p>I closed my eyes. </p><p>Jorren said, "Don't."</p><p>"I'm not doing anything."</p><p>"Your face."</p><p>"Pay?" I asked.</p><p>"Eight copper each."</p><p>I stared. The clerk stared back.</p><p>"Eight," I said.</p><p>"Bronze work," Jorren said.</p><p>"I remember Bronze work paying badly," I said.</p><p>"Then why are you surprised?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"Memory improves things," I said.</p><p>The clerk slid the contract toward us. "Take it or don't." I wanted the job. That was the embarrassing part.</p><p>Eight copper was insulting. The threat was small. The cargo was boring. There was no dungeon, no magical salvage, no future-important artificer, no lender whose name survived forty years in my memory. A wagon had a broken axle. A sixteen-year-old was sitting beside it.</p><p>Someone needed to bring both home. I signed. The clerk looked at my signature.</p><p>"Gregory?" the clerk asked.</p><p>"Greg," I said.</p><p>"You signed Gregory," she said.</p><p>"Administrative identity is complicated," I said.</p><p>"Not here," she said.</p><p>Jorren signed beneath me. The clerk stamped the sheet.</p><p>"Return before dark if possible," she said. "If there is a serious threat, leave the wagon. Cargo is insured."</p><p>I paused.</p><p>"Insured by whom?"</p><p>Jorren grabbed my shoulder.</p><p>"We're leaving."</p><p>"I was curious," I said.</p><p>"That is the problem," Jorren said.</p><p>We left. Outside, Jorren handed me a short sword in a plain leather sheath. I weighed it.</p><p>"Guild issue?" I asked.</p><p>"Mine," Jorren said.</p><p>"You carry two?" I asked.</p><p>"Because people forget theirs," Jorren said.</p><p>"I didn't forget," I said.</p><p>"You came to spar," Jorren said.</p><p>"Correct," I said.</p><p>"Then I saved you a walk," Jorren said.</p><p>I buckled it on. The weight was familiar. Not this sword.</p><p>A sword. My body changed slightly when the belt settled. Shoulders.</p><p>Stride. Attention. Jorren's eyes dropped once to the sword belt, then returned to the road.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You stand different with a sword on," Jorren said.</p><p>"Different how?"</p><p>"Like you're already measuring the next step."</p><p>We walked north. The city thinned into workshops, yards, then scattered houses. The road was dry enough that wagon ruts had hardened into ridges. Fields opened beyond low stone walls. A line of trees followed a creek to the east. I counted distances without meaning to. Wall to ditch. Ditch to tree line. House to bend.</p><p>Places someone could wait. Places someone could run. Jorren walked as if we were going to buy bread.</p><p>"You aren't looking," I said.</p><p>Jorren kept his eyes on the road.</p><p>"I am."</p><p>"At what?"</p><p>He stepped around a broken rut without looking down.</p><p>"The road."</p><p>"Specifically?"</p><p>"Everything."</p><p>"That is not specific."</p><p>Now he glanced at me. "You think because I don't twitch my head at every bush, I'm not looking?" I considered that.</p><p>"Possibly," I said.</p><p>"You do too much," Jorren said.</p><p>"Frequently," I said.</p><p>"No. With your eyes," Jorren said.</p><p>That was new. I looked ahead.</p><p>"What do you mean?" I asked.</p><p>"You keep checking things you've already checked," Jorren said.</p><p>"Things change," I said.</p><p>"Not every three breaths," Jorren said.</p><p>Fair. I forced myself to stop scanning. Immediately hated it.</p><p>A cart approached from the north. Farmer. Empty crates. One wheel wobbling. Driver tired. No threat. I checked behind it. Jorren made a sound.</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"You did it again," Jorren said.</p><p>"The cart could conceal someone," I said.</p><p>"It didn't," Jorren said.</p><p>"Because I checked," I said.</p><p>Jorren shook his head. We walked another hundred paces. I tried something else.</p><p>Instead of searching for threats, I let the road exist.</p><p>Birds.</p><p>Wheel marks.</p><p>Old dung.</p><p>Fresh dung.</p><p>Broken branch.</p><p>Two sets of boot prints near the ditch. A place where grass had been flattened. I stopped.</p><p>Jorren took three more steps before looking back.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>I pointed. He looked.</p><p>"People sat there."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Recently."</p><p>"Probably."</p><p>"Watching the road?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>I crouched. No dramatic revelation appeared. No blood.</p><p>No secret symbol. No conveniently dropped bandit schedule. Two people had sat in grass.</p><p>One had eaten an apple. The core lay near the ditch. I picked it up.</p><p>Jorren said, "Useful?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then put it down."</p><p>I put it down. Growth. We kept walking.</p><p>The wagon appeared around the next bend. One rear wheel had been removed. The axle rested on a block of stone. A narrow-shouldered boy sat on the wagon bed with a cudgel across his knees. He saw us and stood too fast.</p><p>"Guild?"</p><p>"Yes," Jorren called.</p><p>The boy relaxed. Then saw me. His expression became less relaxed.</p><p>I had that effect sometimes. A stocky woman was kneeling beside the axle with a tool roll open on the ground. Gray threaded her dark hair. She looked up once, assessed us, and returned to the cracked wood.</p><p>"You're late," she said.</p><p>"We took the contract ten minutes ago," Jorren replied.</p><p>"Then the guild's late."</p><p>"Probably."</p><p>I liked her too. The boy jumped down.</p><p>"I'm Tavin."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>He looked at Jorren.</p><p>"Jorren."</p><p>The woman spoke without looking up. "Lara Holt."</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Broken On The Road" decoding="async" height="352" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/014/v28_c14_s02_broken-on-the-road.png" width="290"/></figure><p>"Repair?" I asked.</p><p>"Cracked axle. Hold that clamp if you want to help."</p><p>I crouched beside her. She looked at me.</p><p>"Do you know axles?"</p><p>"Some."</p><p>"Enough to help?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"Then hold that."</p><p>She handed me a clamp. This was how useful people recruited you. No speech.</p><p>No assessment. Object. Task.</p><p>I held the clamp. The axle had split lengthwise near the wheel seat. Lara had fitted a shaped iron strap around it and was drilling pilot holes for bolts.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Hold That" decoding="async" height="352" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/014/v28_c14_s03_hold-that.png" width="273"/></figure><p>"Temporary?" I asked.</p><p>"To Venn's yard."</p><p>"Cargo weight?"</p><p>"Too much."</p><p>"Can we unload?"</p><p>"Into what?"</p><p>Fair. Jorren walked around the wagon. Tavin followed him.</p><p>I listened while Lara worked.</p><p>"Anyone come by last night?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"Three carts," Tavin said. "One shepherd. Two men."</p><p>"What men?"</p><p>"Walking."</p><p>"Stop?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Look at the wagon?"</p><p>"Everyone looks at a broken wagon."</p><p>Good answer.</p><p>"Recognize them?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>Lara tightened the strap.</p><p>"Hold."</p><p>"I am holding."</p><p>"Better."</p><p>I adjusted.</p><p>"Like that?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>She drilled. Wood curled out in pale ribbons. I smelled lamp oil from the wagon.</p><p>Not leaking. Just present. My mind offered fire.</p><p>I ignored it. Iron fittings and lamp oil. Why transport together?</p><p>Because people transported whatever needed transporting. Not everything was a clue. That was harder to remember than it should have been.</p><p>Lara fitted the first bolt.</p><p>"Other side."</p><p>I moved. She worked quickly. Competently.</p><p>No interest in me beyond whether my hands were useful. Pleasant.</p><p>"How long have you done this?" I asked.</p><p>"Since before you were born."</p><p>I nearly laughed.</p><p>"Probably."</p><p>She looked up. I shut my mouth. Not today.</p><p>When the strap was secured, Lara stood and rolled her shoulders.</p><p>"It'll hold if he doesn't drive like an idiot."</p><p>Tavin said, "I don't." Lara looked at him. Tavin corrected himself.</p><p>"I won't."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>We refitted the wheel. That required more lifting than I wanted. My mind knew exactly where to stand and how to use leverage. My back knew it was nineteen and therefore believed consequences were fictional. My arms knew the truth.</p><p>By the time the wheel seated, I was sweating. Jorren noticed. I hated him.</p><p>"You all right?" he asked.</p><p>"Excellent."</p><p>"That's not what I asked."</p><p>"Then yes."</p><p>Lara packed her tools. "I'll walk back."</p><p>"No cart?" I asked.</p><p>"Came with the milk wagon."</p><p>"That passed us."</p><p>"Then I suppose I'm walking."</p><p>She did not seem bothered. Independent problem solved. She had repaired the axle. She had another job somewhere else. We were not the center of her day.</p><p>I liked that. Tavin climbed onto the driver's bench. Jorren looked at me.</p><p>"Front or rear?"</p><p>"Rear."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Cargo access."</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>He took front. I walked behind the wagon as it started. Slow.</p><p>Painfully slow. The repaired axle creaked. Lara walked beside me for the first quarter mile, then turned down a farm lane with a brief wave.</p><p>"Good luck," she said.</p><p>"With the thieves?" I asked.</p><p>"With him."</p><p>She pointed at Tavin. Tavin shouted something impolite. Lara kept walking.</p><p>The road curved. I watched the tree line. Once.</p><p>Then stopped. We reached the flattened grass. The apple core was still there.</p><p>Shocking. Tavin drove past. Nothing happened.</p><p>Another hundred paces. Nothing. I began to feel stupid.</p><p>This was healthy. My first life contained thousands of hours like this. Walking. Waiting. Escorting something nobody wanted. Guarding doors nobody attacked. Searching rooms containing exactly what rooms normally contained. Memory compressed those hours.</p><p>Danger survived. Boredom did not. That distortion mattered.</p><p>If I remembered adventuring primarily as the moments when something happened, then present me was going to expect the world to provide narrative density it had never promised. The wagon rolled. A bird screamed from a fence post.</p><p>I did not draw my sword. Growth. Then the rear wheel jerked.</p><p>The wagon lurched. Tavin shouted. I moved before thought.</p><p>Hand on sword. Step left. Eyes up.</p><p>Road. Ditch. Trees.</p><p>No attackers. Jorren was already at the horse.</p><p>"Stop!" he called.</p><p>Tavin pulled the reins. The wagon settled crooked. I looked at the repaired wheel.</p><p>Still attached. The opposite rear wheel had sunk into a soft patch at the road edge. Not an ambush.</p><p>Mud. I felt betrayed. Jorren looked at me.</p><p>"Threat?"</p><p>"Earth."</p><p>"Should I stab it?"</p><p>"Give me time."</p><p>Tavin climbed down.</p><p>"I can get it out."</p><p>"Wait," Jorren said.</p><p>The boy stopped. Jorren crouched beside the wheel. I looked at the road.</p><p>The soft patch was odd. Most of the surface was hard. This section had been disturbed.</p><p>Not wet. Loosened. I crouched.</p><p>Jorren touched it.</p><p>"Someone dug here."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>Tavin's face changed. I looked toward the ditch. There.</p><p>A narrow trench, covered badly with dust and dry grass, running from the wheel rut toward the ditch. Not enough to trap a wagon permanently. Enough to slow it.</p><p>Enough to make a driver climb down. Jorren stood.</p><p>"Now you can look at bushes."</p><p>I already was. Nothing. No movement.</p><p>No figures. No attack. That was worse.</p><p>"They're not here," Tavin said.</p><p>"Maybe," I replied.</p><p>Jorren gave me a look. I corrected myself.</p><p>"We don't see anyone."</p><p>Better. I walked ten paces back. The road behind us curved out of sight.</p><p>Ahead, another bend. Fields west. Trees east.</p><p>If I wanted to rob a wagon, I would not attack while two armed escorts were visible. If I wanted to rob a wagon and saw two armed escorts, I might wait. If I had prepared the soft patch, I knew the route.</p><p>Maybe I had another one. I stopped. That was branching.</p><p>What was the problem? Get wagon home. Not catch thieves.</p><p>Not solve nine days of road crime. Not become Sheriff Greg. Wagon.</p><p>Home. I turned back.</p><p>"Get the wheel out. Keep moving."</p><p>Tavin blinked. "That's it?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Shouldn't we find who did it?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"Stop doing that."</p><p>He smiled. We unloaded two crates of iron fittings. Heavy.</p><p>Not impossibly heavy. I hated honest labor. We laid a board beneath the wheel, pushed, cursed, pushed again, and got the wagon back onto hard road.</p><p>I wanted to inspect the ditch. I did not. I wanted to follow the trench.</p><p>I did not. I wanted to mark the location, circle through the trees, identify observation points, estimate offender numbers, compare boot prints to the flattened grass, question nearby farms, and build a pattern of attacks. I did one of those things.</p><p>I marked the location in my head.</p><p>Useful.</p><p>Bounded.</p><p>Then we reloaded the crates. Tavin climbed up. Jorren said, "I'll take rear."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because you're thinking."</p><p>"I can think and walk."</p><p>"That's what worries me."</p><p>I took front. The next half mile was uneventful. Then I saw a man beside the road.</p><p>Young. Maybe twenty. Brown shirt.</p><p>No visible weapon. He was kneeling beside a basket with turnips spilled around it. I hated him immediately.</p><p>Not personally. Structurally. Tavin slowed.</p><p>"Don't," I said.</p><p>The boy looked at me. "He's dropped his stuff."</p><p>"I see."</p><p>The man looked up.</p><p>"Wheel broke?" he called.</p><p>"No," I replied.</p><p>Jorren had moved closer behind the wagon. The man picked up a turnip.</p><p>"Need a hand?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>Tavin whispered, "He's just helping."</p><p>"He hasn't helped."</p><p>The man stood. Hands visible. No weapon.</p><p>Alone. Maybe. I looked at the ditch.</p><p>Then the trees. Then stopped myself. What did I know?</p><p>A young man. Basket. Turnips.</p><p>Near road. Three thefts. Prepared soft patch behind us. Nothing else.</p><p>"Keep moving," I said.</p><p>Tavin frowned but flicked the reins. The wagon rolled. The man watched us pass.</p><p>I watched him. He smiled. Not friendly.</p><p>Not unfriendly. Just a smile. We went around the bend.</p><p>Jorren caught up.</p><p>"You think him?"</p><p>"I think he exists."</p><p>"Useful."</p><p>"I have insufficient information."</p><p>"Better."</p><p>We continued. A minute later, footsteps ran behind us. I turned.</p><p>The turnip man came around the bend. Alone. Running.</p><p>"Hey!"</p><p>My hand went to the sword. Jorren's did not. That irritated me.</p><p>The man slowed twenty paces away.</p><p>"You dropped this."</p><p>He held up a small iron bracket. Tavin looked back.</p><p>"Shit."</p><p>One of the cargo pieces. Probably bounced loose when we unloaded. The man approached carefully and held it out.</p><p>I took it.</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>He looked at my hand on the sword.</p><p>"You're welcome."</p><p>Then he jogged back toward his turnips. I stood there. Jorren said nothing.</p><p>I waited. Nothing.</p><p>"Say it," I said.</p><p>"Say what?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"Whatever your face is saying," I said.</p><p>Jorren smiled. "My face did nothing." I hated everyone. We reached Mara Venn's yard before dark.</p><p>The yard sat behind a low warehouse with racks of iron stock under an awning. Three workers came out when Tavin shouted. A woman with a red scarf and forearms like a blacksmith's walked straight past us to the repaired axle. Mara Venn, presumably. She crouched.</p><p>Touched the strap. Looked at Tavin.</p><p>"You drove slow?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Mostly," Jorren said.</p><p>Tavin glared at him. Mara stood.</p><p>"Cargo?"</p><p>"All there," Tavin said.</p><p>I held up the bracket.</p><p>"Almost."</p><p>Tavin's face fell. Mara took it.</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"Road."</p><p>"Lost?"</p><p>"Recovered."</p><p>"By?"</p><p>I considered saying a suspicious turnip merchant.</p><p>"Man on the road found it."</p><p>Mara nodded once.</p><p>"Good."</p><p>She did not care about my emotional journey. Reasonable. We helped unload. Again. Eight copper.</p><p>I had forgotten how much Bronze adventuring involved carrying things. When the last crate hit the warehouse floor, Mara handed Jorren a signed contract slip.</p><p>"Trouble?" Mara asked.</p><p>Jorren looked at me. I answered.</p><p>"Someone loosened part of the road to catch a wheel."</p><p>Mara's attention sharpened.</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>I described the bend.</p><p>"Anyone there?" Mara asked.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"See anyone suspicious?" Mara asked.</p><p>I thought of turnips.</p><p>"No one I could identify as involved," I said. Good. True. Boring.</p><p>Mara looked at Tavin. "You stay off that road alone."</p><p>"I was fine."</p><p>"You stayed beside a wagon full of oil overnight with a stick."</p><p>"It was a good stick."</p><p>Mara stared. Tavin looked down.</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>"Guild know?" Mara asked.</p><p>"Not yet," Jorren said.</p><p>"Tell them," Mara said.</p><p>"We will," Jorren said.</p><p>Mara handed Tavin the iron bracket.</p><p>"You check every crate before the next run."</p><p>He nodded. That was his problem now. Not mine.</p><p>We walked back toward the guild. The sun had dropped low enough to stretch our shadows across the road. I felt good.</p><p>Annoyingly good. No monster. No dungeon.</p><p>No brilliant solution. No future knowledge converted into money. We had brought a wagon home.</p><p>Jorren said, "You almost did well."</p><p>"There it is."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"The insult."</p><p>"You kept moving."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You didn't chase."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You didn't interrogate the turnip man."</p><p>"I considered it."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"How?"</p><p>"Your face."</p><p>"Fuck off."</p><p>Jorren laughed. We reached the disturbed patch again. I stopped.</p><p>He stopped beside me.</p><p>"Now?" I asked.</p><p>"Now what?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"Contract is complete," I said.</p><p>"Not until we file," Jorren said.</p><p>"Nearly complete," I said.</p><p>"No," Jorren said.</p><p>I looked at the ditch.</p><p>"Five minutes," I said.</p><p>"No," Jorren said.</p><p>"Three," I said.</p><p>"No," Jorren said.</p><p>"One," I said.</p><p>Jorren sighed.</p><p>"One," Jorren said.</p><p>I smiled. We inspected the road. Not the forest.</p><p>Not the entire crime. The road. The loosened patch had tool marks beneath the dust. Narrow blade. Shovel or spade. The little trench toward the ditch did not drain anywhere useful. It was camouflage for displaced soil.</p><p>Jorren crouched beside a print.</p><p>"Boot," Jorren said.</p><p>"Excellent," I said.</p><p>"Shut up," Jorren said.</p><p>The print was partial. Small. Worn heel.</p><p>Another near it. Larger. At least two people had worked the patch.</p><p>Maybe. Could have been one person wearing two boots of different sizes, which would be impressive for several reasons. I looked toward the flattened grass farther back.</p><p>"Same?"</p><p>"Can't tell," Jorren said.</p><p>"Neither can I," I said.</p><p>That felt worth saying. We stood. One minute.</p><p>Done. At the guild, the ink-thumbed clerk read Mara's signed slip.</p><p>"Trouble?"</p><p>Jorren pointed at me. I gave the report. Location. Disturbed road. Probable deliberate wheel trap. No attack.</p><p>No confirmed suspects. At least one partial boot print, possibly two people involved. The clerk wrote.</p><p>"Turnip man?" she asked.</p><p>I stared. Jorren laughed so hard he had to lean on the counter.</p><p>"How do you know about the turnip man?" I asked.</p><p>"Three other reports mention him."</p><p>I went still. Jorren stopped laughing. The clerk continued writing.</p><p>"Young. Brown shirt. Sells turnips from a basket."</p><p>"He wasn't selling," I said.</p><p>"Today," the clerk said.</p><p>"He returned dropped cargo," I said.</p><p>"Good," the clerk said.</p><p>"Is he involved?" I asked.</p><p>"We don't know," the clerk said.</p><p>I leaned closer. The clerk looked up. I stopped leaning.</p><p>"What do the other reports say?"</p><p>"One driver saw him before the theft. One after. One buys turnips from him every week and thinks everyone is an idiot."</p><p>"Name?" I asked.</p><p>"Len," the clerk said.</p><p>"Full?" I asked.</p><p>She covered the page.</p><p>"Privacy," the clerk said.</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>"Right," I said.</p><p>The clerk took two stacks of copper from a drawer. Eight each. She pushed mine toward me.</p><p>I looked at it. Eight copper. Actual adventuring income. Pathetic. Beautiful.</p><p>"Anything else?" I asked.</p><p>"Yes," the clerk said.</p><p>She put another contract sheet on the counter. I looked at it. Mill road.</p><p>Observation patrol. Two Bronze. Tomorrow afternoon.</p><p>Jorren groaned. I read the rate.</p><p>"Twelve copper," I said.</p><p>"Don't," he said.</p><p>"I haven't said anything," I said.</p><p>"Your face," Jorren said.</p><p>The clerk tapped the sheet.</p><p>"Interested?" the clerk asked.</p><p>Yes. Immediately. Not because of twelve copper. Because there was now a pattern. A bounded problem. A road.</p><p>A likely pair or small group creating controlled stoppages. A known recurring civilian who might be irrelevant, involved, or simply unlucky enough to sell vegetables where people got robbed. I wanted it.</p><p>Too much. That was information too. I looked at Jorren.</p><p>He was watching me. Not refusing. Waiting.</p><p>I could already feel old Greg building the patrol. Approach routes. Counterambush. Decoy wagon. Hidden positions. Signals. Capture. Interrogation. Maybe magic.</p><p>No. Not magic. Hessa would kill me. Then revive me specifically to stop teaching me.</p><p>I looked at the contract again.</p><p>"What is the job?" I asked.</p><p>"Observation patrol," the clerk said.</p><p>"Observation patrol."</p><p>"Not capture?" I asked.</p><p>"Not unless necessary," the clerk said.</p><p>"Not bait?" I asked.</p><p>"No," the clerk said.</p><p>"Not investigation beyond the road?" I asked.</p><p>"No," the clerk said.</p><p>"Report what we see?" I asked.</p><p>"Yes," the clerk said.</p><p>I nodded.</p><p>"Then yes," I said.</p><p>Jorren looked surprised.</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"Nothing," Jorren said.</p><p>"Your face," I said.</p><p>He signed. I signed beneath him. Gregory again.</p><p>The clerk noticed. She said nothing. Outside, I counted my eight copper into my palm.</p><p>Jorren stretched his shoulders.</p><p>"You happy?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"You look happy," Jorren said.</p><p>"I earned eight copper," I said.</p><p>"You have terrible standards," Jorren said.</p><p>"I once made more money in an hour than this guild probably moves in a month."</p><p>Jorren looked at me. I looked back. That had escaped.</p><p>"Doing what?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"Gambling," I said.</p><p>That was technically possible. He accepted it. Good.</p><p>I put the coins away. Eight copper.</p><p>Tomorrow, twelve more if the road remained boring. Maybe thieves. Maybe no thieves.</p><p>Maybe turnips. I had wanted a dungeon. Instead I had a road.</p><p>That should have felt like failure. It did not. The road had given me something the dungeon could not yet give me safely. A measure.</p><p>Not of old Greg. Not of what I remembered. Of the man who had walked out of Carrow this afternoon with a borrowed sword and too many answers.</p><p>He had seen a trap and not chased the people who made it. He had mistaken a helpful man for a threat and corrected without inventing evidence to save his pride. He had completed the job he was actually paid to do.</p><p>This was an embarrassingly low bar. I had failed lower ones. Jorren started toward the taverns.</p><p>"Drink?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"I have training tomorrow," I said.</p><p>"After," Jorren said.</p><p>"Patrol," I said.</p><p>"After that," Jorren said.</p><p>I considered.</p><p>"One," I said.</p><p>"One what?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"Drink," I said.</p><p>Jorren smiled.</p><p>"Sure," Jorren said.</p><p>"That smile means more than one," I said.</p><p>"It means nothing," Jorren said.</p><p>"Your face," I said.</p><p>He shoved me. I nearly stepped into the street. A cart driver swore at me.</p><p>I swore back. Then followed Jorren toward the tavern. Tomorrow, we were going to watch a road.</p><p>I was already thinking too much about it. Progress had limits.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="013.html">← Chapter 9</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="015.html">Chapter 11 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

- `chapters/033.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 27: The Assessor — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 27</div><h1>THE ASSESSOR</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The west storehouse had acquired a hole. Not a dramatic hole. No fire. No blood. No creature. A section of roof tile had failed above the rear loading bay, taken two battens with it, and deposited rainwater onto forty-three sacks of dried beans. This was apparently my problem. Rusk stood beneath the damage with a clipboard. He looked at my wrist.</p><p>“Limited?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That is not usually the response.”</p><p>“You won’t try to fix the roof.”</p><p>“I know how roofs work.”</p><p>Rusk handed me the clipboard.</p><p>“Then you know it is already covered. Count the sacks.” The top sheet said BEANS. Below that were forty-three lines. </p><p>I looked at the roof. Then the beans. Then Rusk.</p><p>“You sent for me to count wet beans.”</p><p>“Sacks.”</p><p>“That is less interesting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Antonius Vale had three storehouses in West Ward that I knew about, two rented yards, one narrow office, several properties I only understood when rent came due, and a talent for turning other people’s emergencies into categories.</p><p>The west storehouse was mostly grain, dried goods, cheap cloth, lamp oil, and things waiting for someone to decide they were worth moving. Men worked the front bay around us. A handcart rattled over the threshold. Somebody shouted for twine. Nobody cared that I had returned from Darrowmere. Good. Rusk pointed with his pencil.</p><p>“Separate dry, damp exterior, wet through, split, contaminated.”</p><p>“Contaminated by what?”</p><p>“Roof.”</p><p>“That is not contamination.”</p><p>“Pigeon.”</p><p>I looked up. A pigeon looked down.</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>“Do not open sacks unless the exterior is wet enough that we need to inspect contents.”</p><p>“Why me?”</p><p>“Because you can read.”</p><p>“So can you.”</p><p>“I’m doing the cloth.”</p><p>He pointed to the next bay. Six bolts of cheap brown wool sat under a second drip line.</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why not move everything?”</p><p>“We did.”</p><p>I looked again. The sacks were already on pallets away from the leak. Of course. The emergency had happened before I arrived. I had been summoned for aftermath. </p><p>Rusk said, “Vale wants loss estimates before supper.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“He likes numbers before food.”</p><p>“No. Why me?”</p><p>Rusk marked another line on the cloth sheet.</p><p>“You owe him money.”</p><p>There it was. I started counting. Thirty-one dry. Seven damp outside. Three wet through. One split. One pigeon. The pigeon sack was also damp. I argued for two categories. Rusk refused.</p><p>“Loss category is highest expected loss.”</p><p>“That destroys information.”</p><p>“It preserves the information he wants.”</p><p>“Bad system.”</p><p>“Write a note.”</p><p>I wrote a note. Rusk watched.</p><p>“You do that a lot?”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Write notes because the world categorizes wrong.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Seems tiring.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>He went back to the cloth. I inspected the three wet-through sacks. The first smelled normal. The second smelled normal. The third smelled like the canal behind a tannery. I stopped.</p><p>“Rusk.”</p><p>He came over.</p><p>“Smell.”</p><p>Rusk crouched beside the pallet instead.</p><p>“Floor's wet.”</p><p>I looked down.</p><p>Not roof water. Dark moisture had reached six inches down one side. No obvious mold yet. The smell was not the beans. I checked the pallet. Wet. Then the floor. A thin brown trail ran from beneath the rear wall. Not roof water.</p><p>“Drain backflow?”</p><p>Rusk crouched.</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“That makes the roof irrelevant.”</p><p>“It makes two problems.”</p><p>Better. He called a worker over.</p><p>“Jalen. Rear drain.”</p><p>The worker swore.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>Again. Useful word.</p><p>“How often?” I asked.</p><p>Jalen looked at Rusk. </p><p>Rusk said, “Answer him.”</p><p>“Third time this month.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because the drain hates me.”</p><p>“Physical reason.”</p><p>“Street channel backs when the butcher rinses.”</p><p>“Which butcher?”</p><p>“West corner.”</p><p>I knew the shop. Not the butcher.</p><p>“Why hasn’t it been fixed?”</p><p>Jalen stared at me.</p><p>“Because it drains.”</p><p>“Badly.”</p><p>“Still drains.”</p><p>Rusk said, “And because the landlord says street channel is city work, city says our rear connection is private, and Vale says he will not pay twice for the same water.” That sounded like Antonius.</p><p>“What happens to the beans?”</p><p>“Move them. Dry what can be dried. Dump what can’t.”</p><p>“Who decides?”</p><p>“You.”</p><p>I looked at him. He had already returned to the wool.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You found the second water.”</p><p>That was not a qualification. Apparently it was enough. I spent the next hour learning more about wet beans than I had intended to know in either life. Bean quality was not binary. This offended me. Dry sacks were easy. Damp cloth with dry contents could be restitched or transferred. Surface-wet beans could be spread and dried if caught early.</p><p>Deep-wet beans could sour, swell, split, or mold depending on how long they had sat and whether the water was clean. Drain water was not clean. The worker named Jalen knew this. So did an older woman named Mevi who had worked the storehouse longer than Rusk.</p><p>Neither had been asked to make the final loss call before.</p><p>“Why not?” I asked.</p><p>Mevi shrugged.</p><p>“Vale likes one name on a number.”</p><p>“Why Rusk?”</p><p>“He gets blamed neatly.”</p><p>Rusk, across the bay, said, “I can hear you.”</p><p>“Then answer.”</p><p>“Because I get blamed neatly.”</p><p>Good system. Bad job. I crouched beside the split sack.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Wet Bean Storehouse" decoding="async" height="216" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/033/v45_c33_wet-bean-storehouse.png" width="477"/></figure><p>My left knee complained. My ribs were mostly quiet now. Palm healing. Channels quiet.</p><p>LIMITED CASTING.</p><p>I did not need magic to determine that beans sitting in butcher water should not become someone’s dinner.</p><p>“Dump three,” I said.</p><p>Mevi said, “Four.”</p><p>“Which?” I asked.</p><p>She kicked the pigeon sack.</p><p>“The bird one,” Mevi said.</p><p>“Exterior only,” I said.</p><p>“Bird,” Mevi said.</p><p>“The contents are dry,” I said.</p><p>“Bird,” Mevi said.</p><p>“That is not an argument.”</p><p>She looked at me. Then at the pigeon above.</p><p>“Bird.”</p><p>I considered. Future me had eaten things in dungeon camps that made pigeon exposure look ceremonial. Current customers had choices.</p><p>“Dump four.”</p><p>Mevi nodded. No triumph. Just correct. We transferred six damp sacks into clean cloth and marked two for drying. The seventh had a seam beginning to fail. Jalen wanted to restitch it. Mevi wanted a new sack. I wanted to know the cost difference. They both stared at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>Mevi said, “You are his.”</p><p>“I am not.”</p><p>“Vale’s.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Rusk called from the wool, “Debt.”</p><p>“That is different.”</p><p>Jalen said, “How much?” </p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>He nodded as if that confirmed ownership. I stopped discussing it. By the time Antonius arrived, the hole in the roof had been covered with a temporary tar sheet, the rear drain had been blocked from the inside, the beans were separated, and I had produced three pages of numbers. Antonius entered carrying no umbrella. It had not rained for twenty minutes.</p><p>Of course. He took the pages. Read the first. Then the second. Then stopped at my note.</p><p>“Two water sources.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Roof and drain.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Drain again?”</p><p>“You knew?”</p><p>“I own the invoice history.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Why is it still happening?”</p><p>He turned the page.</p><p>“Because the city has not decided it owns the street channel.”</p><p>“And you have not decided you own the rear connection.”</p><p>“I own the rear connection.”</p><p>Rusk looked over. Antonius continued.</p><p>“I do not own the butcher’s rinse water.”</p><p>“That distinction is making your beans wet.”</p><p>“Four sacks.”</p><p>“This time.”</p><p>He looked at me. I knew that look. Not disagreement. Pricing.</p><p>“How much to fix it privately?” I asked.</p><p>“Eight silver if the mason is honest. Twelve if he knows I need it.”</p><p>“And city reimbursement?”</p><p>“Possible.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Not unknown. No. Meaning the answer was useless.</p><p>“Then fix it.”</p><p>Rusk made a small sound. Antonius looked at him.</p><p>“What?” Antonius asked.</p><p>“Nothing,” Rusk said.</p><p>“You disagree?” Antonius asked.</p><p>“No. I enjoy watching other people spend your money,” Rusk said.</p><p>Antonius looked back at me.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because this is the third backflow this month.”</p><p>“That is frequency, not reason.”</p><p>“Because your expected loss is not four sacks.”</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>I looked at the pages. I had not calculated that. Not properly.</p><p>“Depends on rain frequency, butcher use, stock placement, what you store here, and whether someone notices quickly.”</p><p>“So you do not know.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why spend twelve silver?”</p><p>“Because you keep paying Rusk to discover the same problem.”</p><p>Rusk nodded. Antonius ignored him.</p><p>“His wage is already paid.”</p><p>“That is not how cost works.”</p><p>“It is if he is here.”</p><p>I opened my mouth. Stopped. He was doing it on purpose. Maybe. Probably.</p><p>“Fine. Then because the next thing beside that wall might not be beans.”</p><p>“What might it be?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“So now we spend twelve silver protecting imaginary goods.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Antonius smiled slightly. Danger.</p><p>“What would you spend to protect imaginary goods?”</p><p>“Not twelve silver.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>I hated him.</p><p>“Six.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because that is half of twelve.”</p><p>Rusk laughed. Antonius did not.</p><p>“Useful,” he said.</p><p>“That was not useful.”</p><p>“It was honest.”</p><p>He handed the pages back.</p><p>“Get three quotes.”</p><p>“Me?”</p><p>“Rusk.”</p><p>Rusk stopped laughing. Good. Antonius turned toward the office stair.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>I followed. The west storehouse office was above the front bay. One desk. Two chairs. A lockbox. Shelves of ledgers. Window overlooking the street. Antonius sat. I remained standing. He pointed at the chair. I sat.</p><p>“You went to Darrowmere.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You came back.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Eight copper escort?”</p><p>“How do you know that?”</p><p>“Guild relief rates are posted.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Did you get paid?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He opened a ledger. I waited for him to ask about creatures. He did not. He turned three pages.</p><p>“You missed two scheduled work periods.”</p><p>“I was under Guild assignment.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That sounds excused.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“That easy?”</p><p>“You were not hiding.”</p><p>“I expected a fee.”</p><p>“For what?”</p><p>“Disruption.”</p><p>“To me?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You think highly of your importance.”</p><p>I disliked that answer because it was correct in several directions. He wrote something.</p><p>“What is my balance?”</p><p>He looked up.</p><p>“You do not know?”</p><p>“I know approximately.”</p><p>“Approximately is how debt becomes a profession.”</p><p>He read the figure. I did the arithmetic. Less than before. Not dramatically. Enough to feel.</p><p>“Road work counts?”</p><p>“Your payments count.”</p><p>“I meant the missed labor.”</p><p>“No charge.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You did not borrow time.”</p><p>That was irritatingly clean. He closed the ledger.</p><p>“Rusk’s work was the beans.”</p><p>“That was it?”</p><p>“No urgency.”</p><p>Right. I had spent the walk imagining some layered Antonius problem. Wet beans. Of course.</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>He looked at my wrist.</p><p>“Your magic?”</p><p>“Limited.”</p><p>“Meaning?”</p><p>“Small, low-load only. No repeated pressure work. Stop at symptoms. Do not test the limit.”</p><p>“You dislike the last one.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good rule.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“That is why you dislike it?”</p><p>“Partly.”</p><p>He nodded. Then reached under the desk and put a small wooden box between us. I stared.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He paused.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I have had enough boxes.”</p><p>“This one contains nails.”</p><p>I opened it. Nails. Twelve. Ordinary iron. I looked at him.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Arlo.”</p><p>That got me.</p><p>“What about Arlo?”</p><p>“He sent a message yesterday. Your regulator is ready for another comparison run if you are functional.”</p><p>I looked at my wrist.</p><p>“No repeated pressure work.”</p><p>“Then do not cast.”</p><p>“That makes comparison difficult.”</p><p>“His message said bring the device, not magic.”</p><p>“My regulator is at my room.”</p><p>“Then retrieve it.”</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“If you want.”</p><p>No urgency again. I looked at the nails.</p><p>“Why nails?”</p><p>“Rusk needs them.”</p><p>“You carried twelve nails upstairs so you could tell me Arlo sent a message?”</p><p>“I needed the box.”</p><p>I closed it.</p><p>“Your systems are hostile.”</p><p>“They work.”</p><p>Mostly. I stood. </p><p>Antonius said, “One more thing.” There it was. </p><p>I sat again. </p><p>He pulled a folded account sheet from the ledger.</p><p>“South Canal.”</p><p>My attention sharpened.</p><p>“Verran?”</p><p>“His storage business is being inventoried.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You know because you were there?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What did you learn?”</p><p>I considered the line. Edrin had not told me the material was secret. The investigation was active. Verran’s ownership issue mattered commercially. Antonius was not the Guild.</p><p>“What do you already know?”</p><p>His expression changed by almost nothing. Good.</p><p>“Verran stored undeclared magical cargo for a third party. His grain is being transferred to prevent spoilage. Several customers are looking for temporary space.”</p><p>That was public enough.</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>“Three have asked me.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“You want the business.”</p><p>“I want rent.”</p><p>“Same.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Close enough. He slid the account sheet over. Three names. Two grain merchants. One soap maker. Short-term storage needs. Rates. Available capacity. The west storehouse had space if we rearranged lamp oil and cloth. The drain problem suddenly became less imaginary. I looked at him.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/033/Ch033_Fast-Coverage-003-A20.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 33." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“You already decided to fix it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You are getting quotes.”</p><p>“Rusk is getting quotes.”</p><p>“Because you may put transferred Verran customers against the rear wall.”</p><p>“Not against the rear wall.”</p><p>“Because it floods.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So you already agree with me.”</p><p>“I agree information has value.”</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>He smiled. I looked at the customer sheet. One grain merchant needed space by tomorrow. The other in three days. Soap maker uncertain.</p><p>“Why show me?”</p><p>“Because you worked the Verran contract.”</p><p>“You think I know which customers are safe?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then?”</p><p>“I want to know whether the Guild seizure is likely to last.”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“What do you think?”</p><p>There was the dangerous version. Not facts. Judgment. I leaned back. Verran had concealed magical cargo. The cargo belonged to Silas Marris Trading. The Guild and watch were still investigating theft. His grain was being transferred under inventory. Could be days. Could be longer.</p><p>Could resolve tomorrow if the magical cargo proved legal and Verran’s only offense was nondisclosure. Could become worse if ownership was dirty.</p><p>“I would not price long-term,” I said.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Too many unresolved questions. Short storage at a premium. No promise beyond a few days.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>“Three.”</p><p>“Why three?”</p><p>I thought. Because it felt right was not acceptable.</p><p>“Because one customer already needs tomorrow, the second needs three days, and after three days you know whether Verran’s doors are reopening soon enough to compete.”</p><p>Antonius nodded.</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>He wrote three. I had just helped him profit from Verran’s seizure. I felt... Nothing particularly noble. Useful.</p><p>“Do I get paid for that?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You owe me.”</p><p>“Debt is not ownership.”</p><p>“I agree.”</p><p>“Mevi thinks otherwise.”</p><p>“Mevi thinks everyone belongs to whoever signs the wage ledger.”</p><p>“That is concerning.”</p><p>“She has worked here nineteen years.”</p><p>“More concerning.”</p><p>He stood. Meeting over. </p><p>I picked up the nail box. At the door, </p><p>he said, “Greg.” </p><p>I turned.</p><p>“Do not get clever with Silas Marris.”</p><p>I went still. He knew the name. Of course he knew the name.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you made a face.”</p><p>“That is not an answer.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Do you know them?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Business.”</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“The kind where they pay and I provide a service.”</p><p>“Storage?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Credit?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Transport?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“You are being intentionally broad.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Are they dangerous?”</p><p>Antonius considered. That made me pay attention.</p><p>“Everyone is dangerous when the amount is large enough.”</p><p>“Unhelpful.”</p><p>“They are not street thieves.”</p><p>“Company?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Real?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Old?”</p><p>“Older than my business.”</p><p>“Magical goods?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Processed sinkstone?”</p><p>His eyes sharpened. There. I had said too much. Not much. Enough. He sat back down.</p><p>“What is processed sinkstone?”</p><p>I considered lying. Badly.</p><p>“Cheap mana-reactive stone made useful by treatment.”</p><p>“How useful?”</p><p>“Depends on treatment.”</p><p>“You know this from now or later?”</p><p>Silence. Antonius did not know regression. He knew I knew strange things. I had almost answered as if he knew why. Careless.</p><p>“From people who know more than I do,” I said.</p><p>Current enough. He watched me. Then nodded once. Maybe accepted. Maybe stored.</p><p>“What does Silas Marris want with it?” he asked.</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“You know them. You tell me.”</p><p>“I know they move goods.”</p><p>“What goods?”</p><p>“Goods people pay to move.”</p><p>“Hostile system.”</p><p>“Working system.”</p><p>I put the nails under my arm.</p><p>“Have you stored dark sacks for them?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Would you tell me if you had?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Why warn me?”</p><p>“Because you are curious.”</p><p>“That has never concerned you before.”</p><p>“It concerns me constantly.”</p><p>“Yet you employ me.”</p><p>“You are profitable when pointed.”</p><p>There it was. Old Greg would have liked that sentence. Current Greg did too. That was the problem. Antonius continued.</p><p>“Silas Marris is large enough that asking the wrong person the right question will become someone else’s business.”</p><p>“Threat?”</p><p>“Advice.”</p><p>“From you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is suspicious.”</p><p>“Then ignore it.”</p><p>I did not. Outside, Rusk was arguing with a roofer. The roofer wanted nine silver. Rusk wanted five. They had found my six without me. I gave Rusk the nails.</p><p>“Vale says three quotes.”</p><p>“This is one.”</p><p>“What happened to eight through twelve?”</p><p>“He saw the hole.”</p><p>Good. I headed toward my room for the regulator. Not Silas Marris. Arlo. Obligation first had become obligation next. That was probably healthy. I disliked it. At my lodging, the room had remained offensively unchanged. Bed. Washbasin. Mirror. Coat.</p><p>My sword leaned beside the wall, chipped edge still waiting for attention. I found Arlo’s regulator wrapped in cloth at the bottom of my bag. The improved low-flow piece was small enough to fit in my palm. Brass body. Narrow channel. Adjustment screw. No magic required to appreciate good work. I turned it once. Stopped. Hessa’s voice arrived without permission. Do not test where the limit is.</p><p>I had not been going to cast. Probably. I put it back in the cloth. Someone knocked. I opened the door. Alden stood there with his sword on one shoulder and his new red scarf around his neck now instead of his wrist. His left arm still moved carefully. He looked pleased.</p><p>“You found Berren.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“You look pleased.”</p><p>“Everyone knows faces now?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Terrible.”</p><p>He entered without invitation.</p><p>“Berren’s alive.”</p><p>“I knew.”</p><p>“He got bit.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“Minor injury?”</p><p>“Teeth through boot. Didn’t break the foot.”</p><p>That was minor by Guild standards.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“North orchard team.”</p><p>Different contact. Good.</p><p>“What did he see?”</p><p>Alden dropped into the chair.</p><p>“Two. Maybe three. One dead. One ran. He says they don’t like fire.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“Evidence?”</p><p>“They backed from torches.”</p><p>“Could be light.”</p><p>“He said fire.”</p><p>“Could be heat.”</p><p>“He said fire.”</p><p>“Could be people holding fire.”</p><p>Alden grinned.</p><p>“I told him you’d do this.”</p><p>“Do what?”</p><p>“Make a simple thing annoying.”</p><p>“It is already annoying.”</p><p>“He also said one crossed a drainage ditch and the other didn’t.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Doesn’t know.”</p><p>“Width?”</p><p>“Doesn’t know.”</p><p>“Water?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Depth?”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>I reached for paper. Alden slapped his hand over it.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I looked at his hand. He looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I came to tell you Berren is alive.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“No. You knew RETURNED. MINOR INJURY. I am telling you he is alive alive.”</p><p>That was different. I waited. Alden took his hand off the paper.</p><p>“He’s pissed he missed the road fight.”</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>“He says we cheated.”</p><p>“We nearly died.”</p><p>“That’s why.”</p><p>I smiled despite myself.</p><p>“What about Lio and Cass?”</p><p>“Lio never went. Cass took a south relief crew yesterday.”</p><p>Independent motion. Good.</p><p>“Berren coming back to Dema’s class?”</p><p>“Tomorrow if his foot fits in a boot.”</p><p>“Bad criterion.”</p><p>“He knows.”</p><p>Alden looked at the wrapped regulator in my hand.</p><p>“What’s that?”</p><p>“Arlo wants a comparison run.”</p><p>“Magic?”</p><p>“Not necessarily.”</p><p>“You’re limited.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He nodded. No argument. Also new. Then he pointed at my sword.</p><p>“You’re getting that edge fixed.”</p><p>“Eventually.”</p><p>“Today.”</p><p>“I have Arlo.”</p><p>“After.”</p><p>“I have money constraints.”</p><p>He stared at me.</p><p>“You paid for a bad onion pastry.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“You smell like onions.”</p><p>“That was food.”</p><p>“That was a crime.”</p><p>He stood.</p><p>“Smith near the east market. Two copper for a basic edge if the chip isn’t deep.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“I just paid him.”</p><p>“Your edge was worse.”</p><p>“Three copper.”</p><p>I calculated. Two copper. Sword functional but chipped. Darrowmere had demonstrated that a bad edge was not theoretical. I hated practical Alden.</p><p>“After Arlo.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He reached the door.</p><p>“Where are you going?”</p><p>“Food.”</p><p>“You just came here.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“To tell me Berren was alive.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That was all?”</p><p>He looked confused.</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>Nothing. That was the answer. He had found information he wanted. He had come to tell me because I would want it. Then he was leaving. No contract. No lesson. No plan. Friendship was inefficient. I had forgotten how much time it consumed.</p><p>“Nothing,” I said.</p><p>Alden opened the door. Then looked back.</p><p>“Oh. Berren wants to spar when his foot works.”</p><p>“With you?”</p><p>“With us.”</p><p>“I am limited.”</p><p>“He said spar, not cast.”</p><p>“My ribs.”</p><p>“He said when his foot works.”</p><p>“That could be tomorrow.”</p><p>“He’s optimistic.”</p><p>“Dangerously.”</p><p>Alden grinned.</p><p>“Three copper.”</p><p>“Get out.”</p><p>He did. I stood alone with the regulator. Silas Marris. Sinkstone. Darrowmere creatures. Berren’s fire claim. A drainage ditch. Antonius’s warning. Arlo’s comparison. Sword edge. Debt. Too many open threads. Old me would have called that opportunity.</p><p>Old me had also become very good at making other people carry the cost of his opportunities. I wrapped the regulator tighter. Not a revelation. Not reform. Just scheduling. Arlo first. Sword after. Silas Marris not today. I left before curiosity could renegotiate.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="032.html">← Chapter 26</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="034.html">Chapter 28 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/043.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 35: The Porter — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 35</div><h1>THE PORTER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The rocks had to move. This became true before anything else. Not because they mattered. Because the lodging keeper had raised the price.</p><p>“Two copper tomorrow.”</p><p>I stopped halfway through the front room.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“For the sack.”</p><p>“You said one.”</p><p>“I said one yesterday.”</p><p>“That is not how storage works.”</p><p>“It is how my storage works.”</p><p>“You cannot double the price because time passed.”</p><p>“I can remove the rocks.”</p><p>There. Market pressure. Terrible. I looked behind the desk. Twenty pounds of kestrin shale sat exactly where I had left it. Unchanged. Unrepentant. I had Antonius debt work in less than an hour. Arlo’s workshop was in the wrong direction. Dorrin Stone was farther. Throwing it away would cost nothing and solve everything. No. I lifted the sack. My hands were mostly healed.</p><p>Mostly. The weight settled against my forearms.</p><p>“You win.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>I carried the rocks to work. This was not dignified. West Storehouse was already moving when I arrived. Rusk stood near the loading doors with a chalk board in one hand. He looked at the sack.</p><p>“Not in the loading bay.”</p><p>“They are mine.”</p><p>“That is why they are not storehouse inventory.”</p><p>“I need somewhere to put them.”</p><p>“Not here.”</p><p>“I work here.”</p><p>“You owe here.”</p><p>“Related.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I set the sack down beside the wall. Rusk pointed at it.</p><p>“Move.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Outside.”</p><p>“It will get wet.”</p><p>“They are rocks.”</p><p>“Processed later.”</p><p>“They are not processed.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“You wrote Dorrin on the sack.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>I moved them under the exterior awning. Temporary. Free. Excellent. Rusk handed me a pair of work gloves.</p><p>“Today you carry.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>Rusk handed me the gloves.</p><p>“Two loaders are at south yard. Mevi needs another body.”</p><p>“That is clearer.”</p><p>“Good. Work.”</p><p>“What am I carrying?”</p><p>“Whatever Mevi says.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because two loaders are at south yard.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Work.”</p><p>Good. I put on the gloves. They were too large.</p><p>“Smaller?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“Work.”</p><p>Mevi had me move sacks. Not think about sacks. Move them. From incoming pallet to dry platform. From dry platform to numbered row. Bluegrain. Barley. Something called red millet that was not red. The sacks weighed between thirty and sixty pounds. Young body. Good legs. Average technique. Bad pride. Mevi watched me lift the first heavy one.</p><p>“No,” Mevi said.</p><p>I froze with it halfway.</p><p>“What?” I asked.</p><p>“Put it down,” Mevi said.</p><p>I did.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You’re lifting like a rich man.”</p><p>“I have never been rich.”</p><p>“You lift like one.”</p><p>She showed me. Not a lesson. One demonstration. Closer. Hip. Turn. Do not twist under load. Use the sack’s own sag. Let it settle against the body before moving. I copied. Better.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“Good enough.”</p><p>Then she left. That was all. I moved sacks.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Porter" decoding="async" height="329" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/043/v45_c43_the-porter.png" width="283"/></figure><p>Twenty minutes. Thirty. Sweat. Forearms. Back. No mana. No cleverness. The gloves rubbed my healing blister less than expected. One sack had a loose tie. I noticed. Tied it. Wrong knot. It slipped. I used Ossin’s millrace knot instead. Held. Good. Tiny transfer. No one applauded.</p><p>At forty minutes, a cart arrived with six narrow crates marked glass. Rusk called, “Greg.” I put down the grain sack.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Not you.”</p><p>Another Greg? No. A man near the cart looked up. Older. Bald. Greg. Of course. Rusk pointed at him.</p><p>“Glass row.”</p><p>Other Greg nodded. I stared. He saw.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>He was Greg too. This felt unacceptable. He carried glass. I carried grain. The world survived. At the end of the first hour, Mevi handed me water.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“I can keep going.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then why sit?”</p><p>“Because after sitting you keep going better.”</p><p>Fine. I sat on an overturned crate. Other Greg sat two crates away.</p><p>“Greg?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Full?”</p><p>“Gregor.”</p><p>Relief.</p><p>“Why Greg?”</p><p>“Because people have jobs.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“What do you do?”</p><p>“Glass.”</p><p>“That is not a job.”</p><p>“It is today.”</p><p>I liked him. He drank. Then left before I could ask more. Excellent boundaries. I returned to grain. Debt work was supposed to be four hours. Antonius had not appeared. Good. No special function. No request. Just labor. That should have been less satisfying. It was not.</p><p>There was something clean about being told where the sack went. No ambiguity. No hidden optimization. Dry platform. Row three. Stack six. Again. Near midday, the work changed. A shipment of lamp oil arrived. Barrels. Not full-size. Half barrels. Still heavy. Two men rolled them. I was assigned wedges.</p><p>“Wedges?”</p><p>Mevi handed me six triangular blocks.</p><p>“Barrel stops.”</p><p>“I know what wedges are.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>My job was to put wood under round things. Bronze adventurer. Future S-class support mage. Temporal accident. Wedge boy. Fine. The unloading ramp was wet from yesterday’s rain. Not dangerous if used correctly. Everything was dangerous if used incorrectly. First barrel rolled down. Worker controlled rope. Second worker guided. I placed wedge after it settled. Simple. Second. Third. Fourth. On the fifth, the rope handler said, “Hold.”</p><p>Everyone stopped. The barrel had shifted sideways against the ramp rail. Not much. Enough that continuing would scrape the hoop. He adjusted. No Greg. Good. Sixth. Seventh. On the eighth, a cart entered the yard too fast. Horse shied at a dropped plank. Not catastrophe. Noise. The barrel guide looked away. Half second. The barrel rolled. Not free. Rope still held. But faster.</p><p>Toward his ankle. I had a wedge in my hand. Too far. Barrier. Coin-sized. Not against barrel. Against ramp edge beside the hoop. Angle. Contact. The hoop clipped it. Barrier broke immediately. Enough. Barrel shifted an inch. Guide got foot clear. Rope handler stopped it. Done. Pressure? None. Maybe half. Gone. The guide looked at me.</p><p>“Magic?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Then he shoved the barrel back into line. No awe. Correct. Mevi came over.</p><p>“What happened?” she asked.</p><p>“Guide looked away. Barrel moved,” I said.</p><p>“Why?” Mevi asked.</p><p>“Cart noise,” I said.</p><p>She looked at the cart. Then at the ramp. Then at the barrel.</p><p>“Anyone hurt?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Barrel?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She pointed at the unloading lane.</p><p>“Close that side until oil is done.”</p><p>A worker moved a rope across the entry. There. System correction. Not mine. My Barrier had bought an inch. Mevi changed traffic. Better. We finished. At midday, Rusk found me eating bread on the loading step.</p><p>“Vale says two more hours.”</p><p>“I was told four.”</p><p>“You’ve done three.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Two more is five.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is why I said two more.”</p><p>“I did not agree.”</p><p>He looked at me. Fair. Debt work had terms.</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“Not carrying.”</p><p>Suspicious.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Courier.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He handed me a folded receipt.</p><p>“Take this to South Weigh Office. Bring back stamped copy.”</p><p>“That is courier.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I am an adventurer.”</p><p>“You are in debt.”</p><p>Correct.</p><p>“Why me?”</p><p>“Gregor is carrying glass.”</p><p>I looked for Other Greg. Gone. Of course.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Do not lose it.”</p><p>“I have transported civilians.”</p><p>“Paper is easier to lose.”</p><p>Also correct. I took the receipt. South Weigh Office was across half the city. Walking. Good. My body appreciated not lifting. I passed the Guild. Did not enter. Passed the turn toward Bale. Did not turn. Master available. Sinkstone question. Not urgent. Receipt. Simple. I reached South Weigh. Line. Of course. Six people. One clerk. I waited.</p><p>A woman ahead of me had three livestock permits and a chicken under one arm. The chicken hated administration. Reasonable. A man behind me carried a wheel rim. No idea why. The clerk stamped. Signed. Copied. My turn.</p><p>“West Storehouse.”</p><p>Receipt. She read.</p><p>“Wrong office.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“South Weigh handles incoming south-route freight.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/043/Ch043_Fast-Coverage-003-B05.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 43." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“This says South Weigh.”</p><p>“It says South Weight.”</p><p>I looked. Fuck.</p><p>SOUTH WEIGHT CERTIFICATION.</p><p>Not office. A certification company.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Copper Street.”</p><p>Other direction.</p><p>“How far?”</p><p>“Ten minutes.”</p><p>I left. Rusk had said South Weigh. Maybe I heard wrong. Maybe he said South Weight. Difference expensive only in walking. Fine. Copper Street. South Weight Certification occupied one room above a harness shop. I climbed. A man stamped the receipt in twelve seconds.</p><p>“Copy?”</p><p>He made one. Done. I walked back. No revelation. Thirty extra minutes because one letter. Systems. No. Hearing. At West Storehouse, Rusk took the stamped copy.</p><p>“You went to South Weigh.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He laughed.</p><p>“You said South Weigh.”</p><p>“I said South Weight.”</p><p>“You pronounce them the same.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You do.”</p><p>Mevi, passing behind him, said, “He does.” Rusk looked betrayed. Good.</p><p>“Does the extra half hour count?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>“Then I have one and a half left.”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“You said two more after three.”</p><p>“Fine. One and a half.”</p><p>Debt accounting mattered. I returned to work. Not sacks. Inventory marks. Mevi had me chalk incoming lot numbers onto shelf boards while she read them. No thinking. Except when she read 417 and the board already said 471.</p><p>“Wait.”</p><p>She checked. Her page said 417. Board old mark 471. Different lot. We wiped it. Wrote new. No problem. Then one row had no board. I found one. Then chalk broke. I found more. Ordinary work contained infinite small failures. Most did not deserve theory. At the end, Rusk marked my debt ledger. Five hours. I watched.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>He told me the credit. I wrote it in my own notebook. Not approximate. Antonius had infected me. Rusk looked at the rocks outside.</p><p>“Take those.”</p><p>“I was hoping you forgot.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Can I store them here?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because then tomorrow you bring more.”</p><p>“That is unfair.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I lifted the sack. Hands tired. Back tired. Better technique. Still heavy. Arlo. Finally. I carried twenty pounds of shale across Carrow. Again. This time on purpose. Arlo’s workshop was open. Vessa was outside dumping gray water into the gutter. She saw the sack.</p><p>“What did you buy now?”</p><p>“Kestrin.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Too much to keep carrying.”</p><p>“Kestrin.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I bought it.”</p><p>“That does not answer why.”</p><p>“No one accepts that answer.”</p><p>“Because it is bad.”</p><p>She held the door. I went inside. Arlo was at the ceramic bench. He looked up at the sack, then at me.</p><p>Arlo waited.</p><p>“What grade?”</p><p>“Dorrin sorted visible quality. Not reaction sorted.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“About twenty pounds.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Research.”</p><p>“Bad.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Free?” Arlo asked.</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>He pointed at a corner.</p><p>“Put it there,” Arlo said.</p><p>Victory. I set it down. My arms felt suddenly absent.</p><p>“Now you own the problem.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You accepted it.”</p><p>“I accepted stone.”</p><p>“Same.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Fine. He returned to the ceramic regulator. I could ask about Bale. Kett. Varo. I could tell him what I learned. I could ask whether he knew Bale’s house test. Instead I looked at the fixture. New brace. Not mine.</p><p>Arlo and Vessa had added a second body support opposite the collar.</p><p>“You changed it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Better?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>Arlo handed me a page. Seven assemblies. Crack reduced. Not gone. Good. They had continued without me. Of course.</p><p>“Did my observation help?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Simple. No praise. Enough. Vessa said, “Your rocks are leaking dirt.” I looked. Small gray trail from sack seam. Arlo said, “Take them back.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You said free.”</p><p>“They remain free.”</p><p>“They are dirty.”</p><p>“They are rocks.”</p><p>“Outside.”</p><p>I dragged the sack to the rear awning. Arlo allowed that. Barely. I had successfully transferred my storage problem to an artificer. This was perhaps my greatest achievement.</p><p>“What did you do today?” Arlo asked.</p><p>“Carried things.”</p><p>He waited.</p><p>“That’s all?”</p><p>“Mostly.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Again. Everyone approved of labor when it happened to me.</p><p>“I used one Barrier.”</p><p>His attention sharpened.</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Barrel.”</p><p>“Did it work?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Pressure?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“How big?”</p><p>“Coin.”</p><p>“Held?”</p><p>“Broke.”</p><p>“Then how work?”</p><p>“Changed contact angle enough to move the hoop.”</p><p>He nodded. That was all. No demand to see. No lecture. Small. Precise. Directional. Exactly what Hessa wanted. I hated when plans worked. I stayed another ten minutes. Not an hour. Arlo had work. Vessa had work. I had no rocks. Excellent. Outside, late afternoon had turned warm.</p><p>I had spent five hours reducing debt, carried half the storehouse, misdelivered a receipt, used one clean Barrier, and convinced Arlo to inherit twenty pounds of shale. No one had asked me to sort noise. No one had needed a special Greg function. That should have felt like regression. It did not.</p><p>Yesterday Antonius had paid me to decide which problem came first. Today Mevi had paid my debt down by telling me where to put sacks. Both were work. Different role. Same body. I walked home without carrying anything. This felt like wealth.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="042.html">← Chapter 34</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="044.html">Chapter 36 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/362.html:416`: <p>Mana-assisted migration behavior existed.</p>
- `chapters/362.html:424`: <p>"I know ways animals can use mana to move. I don't know which way these do it."</p>
- `chapters/095.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 77: The Taster — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 77</div><h1>THE TASTER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Pessa listened to my report with the expression of someone receiving weather.</p><p>“Slightly more swollen this morning,” I said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You haven't looked.”</p><p>“You're standing differently.”</p><p>I looked down.</p><p>This was useless.</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“More weight right.”</p><p>“I always have more weight right.”</p><p>“More.”</p><p>“Hessa checked it.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“She said no training.”</p><p>“I said no training.”</p><p>“She agreed with you.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I drew mana.”</p><p>Pessa looked at me then.</p><p>Not dramatically.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>“With Hessa?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Once?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Any pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“After?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Leg?”</p><p>“Same.”</p><p>“Hands?”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>That was apparently the entire magical discussion.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>Pessa waited.</p><p>“You don't want to know what it felt like?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“That is almost offensive.”</p><p>“Did Hessa care what it felt like?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then tell Hessa.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Distributed authority remained terrible.</p><p>“When can I train?”</p><p>“When the swelling settles.”</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She stared.</p><p>I left before the word became violent.</p><p>Jorren was outside the Guild eating something red.</p><p>Not red food.</p><p>Red substance attached to food.</p><p>He had a folded piece of flatbread in one hand and the expression of a man who had made a decision too late to reverse it.</p><p>His eyes were watering.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>He swallowed.</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Your face disagrees.”</p><p>“Try this.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He held out the flatbread.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You don't even know what it is.”</p><p>“I know what your eyes are doing.”</p><p>“That could be emotion.”</p><p>“You don't have those.”</p><p>He laughed and then coughed.</p><p>The coughing became worse.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>When he recovered, he pointed down the street.</p><p>“New pepper stall.”</p><p>“New?”</p><p>“New to me.”</p><p>There was a cart under a striped awning with three clay pots set into a bed of hot sand.</p><p>Steam.</p><p>Bread.</p><p>A handwritten board.</p><p>MILD.<br/>HOT.<br/>LIAR.</p><p>I looked at Jorren's food.</p><p>“Liar?”</p><p>He nodded.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I asked for hot.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“He said I looked like a liar.”</p><p>“Reasonable.”</p><p>“He gave me the third one.”</p><p>“You ate it.”</p><p>“I had already paid.”</p><p>This was Jorren.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“One bit.”</p><p>“Worth it?”</p><p>He considered while tears ran down his face.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was also Jorren.</p><p>I had nowhere to be.</p><p>This was dangerous.</p><p>Not in the way Hessa meant.</p><p>I went to the stall.</p><p>The man behind it was old enough to have stopped caring whether customers approved of him and young enough that this was probably personality rather than age.</p><p>I did not ask his name.</p><p>He looked at my crutches.</p><p>Then at my face.</p><p>Then at Jorren.</p><p>“Another liar?”</p><p>“I am generally accurate.”</p><p>“Liar.”</p><p>Jorren made a sound that might have been agreement.</p><p>I looked at the three pots.</p><p>“What is the difference?”</p><p>“Pepper.”</p><p>“That is not enough information.”</p><p>“Then mild.”</p><p>“I didn't say I wanted mild.”</p><p>“You asked questions.”</p><p>“That implies caution?”</p><p>“It implies mild.”</p><p>Jorren leaned against the cart.</p><p>“He does this.”</p><p>The stall man pointed at the board.</p><p>“Mild, hot, liar.”</p><p>“What kind of pepper?”</p><p>He stared at me.</p><p>I had made a mistake.</p><p>Not social.</p><p>Culinary.</p><p>“Red,” he said.</p><p>Jorren laughed.</p><p>I looked into the pots.</p><p>The mild was brown-red.</p><p>Hot was darker.</p><p>Liar looked almost black at the edges where oil gathered.</p><p>It smelled excellent.</p><p>Onion.</p><p>Rendered fat.</p><p>Something sour.</p><p>Cumin?</p><p>No.</p><p>Not cumin.</p><p>A memory arrived from another life.</p><p>Chili.</p><p>Not one dish.</p><p>A thousand arguments pretending to be one dish.</p><p>Beans or no beans.</p><p>Tomato or no tomato.</p><p>Ground meat.</p><p>Chunks.</p><p>Powder.</p><p>Fresh peppers.</p><p>People becoming morally invested in stew.</p><p>Humanity had survived many things it did not deserve to survive.</p><p>“Hot,” I said.</p><p>The stall man nodded once.</p><p>Respect restored.</p><p>He filled a small clay cup.</p><p>Not much.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I paid.</p><p>Jorren watched.</p><p>“You're going to regret that.”</p><p>“You are eating liar.”</p><p>“I regret that.”</p><p>“You said worth it.”</p><p>“Both can be true.”</p><p>Also reasonable.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Greg seated outdoors with food and his notebook nearby." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/095/Ch95_Sitting-by-the-Water.png"/></figure><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Greg standing beside a ship rail, watching the coast and lighthouse beyond." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/095/Ch95_Harbor-Lighthouse-Watch.png"/></figure><p>I sat on the low stone edge of a fountain across from the cart.</p><p>The fountain was dry.</p><p>Probably decorative failure.</p><p>Good seat.</p><p>Crutches beside me.</p><p>Cup in both hands.</p><p>Steam.</p><p>I took a bite.</p><p>Heat.</p><p>Not temperature.</p><p>Pepper.</p><p>Immediate.</p><p>Then meat.</p><p>Onion.</p><p>Sourness.</p><p>A sweetness underneath that I could not place.</p><p>Then more pepper.</p><p>My nose began running.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg and Jorren sitting together after trying the pepper stew." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/095/Ch95_Pepper-Stall-with-Jorren.png"/></figure><p>Jorren sat beside me.</p><p>“Well?”</p><p>I swallowed.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That's all?”</p><p>“What do you want?”</p><p>“You stopped eating.”</p><p>“I swallowed.”</p><p>“Then you stared into the cup.”</p><p>“I was tasting it.”</p><p>This was becoming a conspiracy.</p><p>I took another bite.</p><p>The heat built.</p><p>Not unbearable.</p><p>Enough that each bite made the next one worse.</p><p>Excellent design.</p><p>“What is the sweet thing?” I asked.</p><p>Jorren shrugged.</p><p>“Food.”</p><p>“Helpful.”</p><p>“Ask him.”</p><p>“I did. He said red.”</p><p>“That was pepper.”</p><p>“He will say sweet.”</p><p>Jorren nodded.</p><p>Likely.</p><p>I ate.</p><p>People moved around us.</p><p>Guild traffic.</p><p>A pair of porters arguing about rope.</p><p>A woman carrying six loaves stacked against her chest.</p><p>Two children chasing each other around the fountain until someone shouted from somewhere I could not see.</p><p>A Bronze
