with a dented breastplate.</p><p>A clerk.</p><p>A dog.</p><p>Not the onion dog.</p><p>Different dog.</p><p>Carrow had many dogs and insufficient standards.</p><p>Jorren finished the last of liar.</p><p>He was sweating.</p><p>“Do you have work?” I asked.</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“South warehouse.”</p><p>“What are you doing?”</p><p>“Moving sacks.”</p><p>“That sounds like moving sacks.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Curiosity.”</p><p>“You're going to calculate something.”</p><p>“I might.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I ate another bite.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>“What time?”</p><p>“After midday bell.”</p><p>I looked at the sun.</p><p>“You have maybe an hour.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What are you doing until then?”</p><p>“This.”</p><p>He pointed at the food.</p><p>“You're done.”</p><p>He looked at his empty hand.</p><p>“Then nothing.”</p><p>That sounded suspicious.</p><p>“What do you mean nothing?”</p><p>“I mean I have an hour.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And no work for an hour.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So nothing.”</p><p>I understood every word individually.</p><p>The sentence remained structurally unsound.</p><p>“You could do something.”</p><p>“I am.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Sitting.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>I returned to the stew.</p><p>This was apparently friendship.</p><p>After several minutes, Jorren said, “How's the magic?”</p><p>I nearly answered with everything.</p><p>The copper strip.</p><p>The organized phantom.</p><p>Hessa's stopping conditions.</p><p>The distinction between draw and shaping.</p><p>Instead I said, “I drew mana once.”</p><p>Jorren nodded.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That's all?”</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“You want me to be impressed?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I'm impressed.”</p><p>“You don't sound impressed.”</p><p>He turned to me.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You did a tiny magic thing while sitting in a chair with Hessa watching.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is good.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you want me to shout?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I can.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He inhaled.</p><p>I hit him with my elbow.</p><p>He laughed.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>I smiled despite myself.</p><p>The stall man called across the street.</p><p>“Thinking boy.”</p><p>I looked over.</p><p>He held up a spoon.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You keep staring at the pot.”</p><p>“I am trying to identify something.”</p><p>He pointed the spoon at me.</p><p>“Come.”</p><p>I looked at Jorren.</p><p>He shrugged.</p><p>I collected the crutches.</p><p>Standing from the fountain edge was harder than the chair because the stone was low.</p><p>Right foot close.</p><p>Push.</p><p>Both crutches.</p><p>No problem.</p><p>The residual limb felt full but not worse.</p><p>I crossed.</p><p>The stall man put a drop of something dark on a wooden spoon.</p><p>“Taste.”</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>“Taste.”</p><p>This was how people died.</p><p>Probably not in public pepper stalls.</p><p>I tasted.</p><p>Sweet.</p><p>Dark.</p><p>Sour.</p><p>Fruit.</p><p>“Plum?”</p><p>He grunted.</p><p>“Dried?”</p><p>Another grunt.</p><p>“Cooked down?”</p><p>He took the spoon away.</p><p>“That is three questions.”</p><p>“Those were guesses.”</p><p>“Too many.”</p><p>Jorren had followed.</p><p>“It's plum?”</p><p>The stall man looked offended.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>“Black pear.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>I knew black pears.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Ugly.</p><p>Mostly used dried because fresh they had the texture of wet sand and the flavor of regret.</p><p>“You put black pear in pepper stew.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>He stared.</p><p>I knew the answer before he said it.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>He dipped another spoon into the mild pot and held it out.</p><p>I tasted.</p><p>Same sweetness.</p><p>More obvious without the heat.</p><p>Black pear.</p><p>Once known, impossible to miss.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>The stall man pointed at the liar pot.</p><p>“Now.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I bought hot.”</p><p>“Taste.”</p><p>Jorren said, “Do it.”</p><p>“You are not a neutral party.”</p><p>“I want to watch.”</p><p>Exactly.</p><p>The stall man offered the spoon.</p><p>This was not a challenge.</p><p>It was absolutely a challenge.</p><p>I tasted.</p><p>For perhaps one second, nothing happened.</p><p>Then my mouth became a workplace accident.</p><p>I closed my eyes.</p><p>Jorren started laughing.</p><p>The stall man said, “Liar.”</p><p>I could not speak.</p><p>This was fortunate because several words were available and none improved the situation.</p><p>Heat climbed into my nose.</p><p>My eyes watered.</p><p>My scalp became involved.</p><p>Why was my scalp involved?</p><p>I breathed through my mouth.</p><p>Mistake.</p><p>I breathed through my nose.</p><p>Worse.</p><p>Jorren handed me water.</p><p>The stall man slapped his hand away.</p><p>“No water.”</p><p>I pointed at him.</p><p>He gave me a piece of flatbread.</p><p>I ate it.</p><p>Slight improvement.</p><p>Then another.</p><p>Better.</p><p>The stall man nodded.</p><p>“Now you know.”</p><p>I swallowed.</p><p>“What pepper?”</p><p>“Red.”</p><p>I hated him.</p><p>Jorren was bent over the cart laughing.</p><p>I sat on the fountain again.</p><p>This time I required no philosophical interpretation.</p><p>Sitting was good.</p><p>My mouth slowly returned from war.</p><p>Jorren wiped his eyes.</p><p>“You looked so confident.”</p><p>“I was not confident.”</p><p>“You took the spoon.”</p><p>“That is not confidence.”</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>“Nineteen.”</p><p>He laughed again.</p><p>That was probably the truest thing I had said all day.</p><p>We sat until the bell.</p><p>Not discussing magic.</p><p>Not discussing training.</p><p>Not discussing work.</p><p>At some point the stall man brought over two small pieces of bread with black pear paste on them.</p><p>No charge.</p><p>He handed one to Jorren and one to me.</p><p>“Why?” I asked.</p><p>“Thinking boy learned.”</p><p>“What did I learn?”</p><p>He walked away.</p><p>Jorren bit his.</p><p>“Black pear is good.”</p><p>“I knew black pear existed.”</p><p>“Did you know it was good?”</p><p>I looked at the paste.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not like this.</p><p>I ate it.</p><p>Sweet.</p><p>Sour.</p><p>Smoky from the pot.</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Apparently not.”</p><p>The midday bell sounded.</p><p>Jorren stood.</p><p>“Work.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“You're going to move sacks after liar?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You may die.”</p><p>“Then I won't have to move all the sacks.”</p><p>He started toward the south road.</p><p>No invitation.</p><p>No expectation that I follow.</p><p>He had work.</p><p>I did not.</p><p>“Jorren.”</p><p>He turned.</p><p>“The stall man is wrong.”</p><p>“About what?”</p><p>“I am not a liar.”</p><p>Jorren looked at me for several seconds.</p><p>Then he said, “You told Pessa you weren't going to negotiate.”</p><p>I had told Hessa that.</p><p>Not Jorren.</p><p>“Who told you?”</p><p>He grinned and kept walking.</p><p>I stared after him.</p><p>Carrow was a surveillance state.</p><p>I bought another cup of hot.</p><p>Not liar.</p><p>I had limits.</p><p>This was progress of some kind.</p><p>Probably not the kind Hessa was measuring.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="094.html">← Chapter 76</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="096.html">Chapter 78 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/007.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 5: The Buyer — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 5</div><h1>THE BUYER</h1></header><article class="prose"><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/007/Ch007_Storeroom-Crates.jpg" alt="Antonius carries a crate through the crowded storeroom while Greg studies metal pieces at a workbench." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Antonius was already cleaning when I arrived. This was sufficiently wrong that I stopped in the doorway. He had his sleeves rolled to the elbows, a rag over one shoulder, and a wooden crate in his hands. Dust covered one side of his trousers. There was a streak of something black across his wrist. He looked at me.</p><p>"Sunrise means before the sun has finished rising." </p><p>I looked behind him. Then back at him.</p><p>"What are you doing?"</p><p>"Cleaning."</p><p>"I can see that."</p><p>Antonius shifted the crate toward me.</p><p>"Then take this one."</p><p>He carried the crate past me and set it in the hall. I remained in the doorway. The back storeroom was larger than I expected and worse than Antonius had implied. Shelves leaned under abandoned inventory. Broken furniture had been stacked against one wall. Bundles of cloth sat beside chipped crockery, rusted tools, old ledgers, cracked cases, bent fittings, three wheels of different sizes, and something that might once have been part of a loom. It smelled like dust, oil, damp wood, old paper, and failure. I looked at Antonius again.</p><p>"Why are you cleaning?"</p><p>"Because the room needs cleaning."</p><p>"No." </p><p>He paused.</p><p>"No?"</p><p>"That's not why."</p><p>"It is exactly why."</p><p>"You have employees."</p><p>"So?"</p><p>"Employees clean."</p><p>"Apparently not this room."</p><p>"Then make them."</p><p>"I did." </p><p>I waited. </p><p>He picked up a broom.</p><p>"Poorly." </p><p>I frowned.</p><p>There had to be more. Audit. Theft. Hidden inventory. A test. Something in the room mattered and Antonius wanted to see whether I noticed it. That made sense. I entered. Antonius handed me a second broom.</p><p>"Start there." </p><p>I took it automatically. Then realized what had happened.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"I understand the labor arrangement. I'm questioning the allocation."</p><p>"Sweep first. Question it while you sweep."</p><p>"My time has higher-value uses."</p><p>"Your time currently belongs to me."</p><p>"Temporarily."</p><p>"There it is."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing," Antonius said.</p><p>He swept.</p><p>I stood there holding the broom. This was absurd. Future Antonius Vale had once financed an army without technically financing an army. He had owned pieces of ports through three layers of debt, controlled enough warehouse space to make shortages appear accidental, and supposedly destroyed a noble house by purchasing obligations nobody else thought connected. I did not know how much of that was true. Probably less than people claimed.</p><p>Possibly more.</p><p>The point was that I remembered his name. That alone should have bothered me more than it had. By the end of my first life I had met kings, guildmasters, generals, archmages, merchant princes, criminals, saints, and enough supposedly important people to make importance feel cheap. Most of them had blurred into titles, faces, anecdotes, or nothing at all. Antonius Vale had not. Name. Weight. The sense that rooms changed when he entered them. If S-class Greg remembered you after forty years, you had been good. Powerful. Dangerous. Useful. Something. If he remembered you while forgetting half of what you had actually done, you had probably mattered even more than the surviving memories suggested. Present Antonius was still personally aware of flour. Whatever he became later, I was looking at the early construction of something much larger than I could currently piece together. That man was currently sweeping mouse shit. I watched him.</p><p>Antonius swept another strip of floor before looking over.</p><p>"If you're waiting for the lesson, there isn't one."</p><p>"I didn't say there was."</p><p>"You have the face."</p><p>"What face?"</p><p>"The one where everything around you becomes a metaphor," Antonius said.</p><p>I looked down at the broom.</p><p>"I don't do that."</p><p>"You reorganized my warehouse and called it momentum."</p><p>Fair. I started sweeping. For a while we worked without talking. That was strange too. I expected Antonius to supervise. Instead he moved things. Actually moved them. He knew which crates could be thrown away without opening them. He knew which ledger bundles had to be kept. He knew that a cracked green chest belonged to a dead cooper's account and that the cooper's daughter had six months left to reclaim it.</p><p>"How do you know that?" I asked. </p><p>Antonius did not look up.</p><p>"Know what?"</p><p>"The chest."</p><p>"It's mine."</p><p>"No. It isn't."</p><p>That made him look at me.</p><p>"You just said the daughter can reclaim it."</p><p>"Until winter."</p><p>"So it's collateral."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Then it isn't yours."</p><p>"It is legally."</p><p>"That's not the same thing," I said.</p><p>Antonius stopped sweeping and looked at me.</p><p>"Interesting opinion from a man whose labor I legally own."</p><p>"Temporarily." </p><p>He smiled. I swept harder.</p><p>The room began separating itself in my head. Not physically. Categories. Recoverable collateral. Unsellable collateral. Broken inventory. Records. Tools. Goods nobody remembered. Things Antonius kept because throwing away something once valued felt like admitting the loan behind it had gone bad. Maybe. That last one was inference. Check. I picked up a brass fitting.</p><p>No idea. Put it in the discard crate. A bundle of rotted leather straps. Trash. A chipped ceramic vessel with a narrow throat. Possibly useful. Probably trash. A box of black stones. I stopped.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not stones. Slag. Maybe. I crouched. Antonius kept sweeping. The pieces were porous, glossy in places, ugly as sin. I picked one up. Light. Industrial waste? Smelting residue. Future use? My memory offered three unrelated things at once. Road aggregate. Heat-resistant lining. A tavern in Konia where a drunk metallurgist had explained why old furnaces accidentally produced better insulating material than new ones. Or was that volcanic glass?</p><p>Different material. I turned the piece over.</p><p>"What is this?"</p><p>"Trash."</p><p>"Specific trash."</p><p>"Foundry waste."</p><p>"From where?" </p><p>Antonius pointed with his broom.</p><p>"Discard."</p><p>"Which foundry?"</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Do you know?"</p><p>"No." </p><p>I stared at the black chunk.</p><p>Potential. Not enough information. I put it in a separate pile. Antonius stopped sweeping.</p><p>"That's the trash pile."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"You put trash beside the trash."</p><p>"Different trash."</p><p>"Of course." He resumed.</p><p>Ten minutes later I had six categories. Antonius had two. Keep. Throw away. His system was faster. Mine was better. Probably. The room fought me. Every object suggested something. A bent iron brace reminded me of modular shield frames used during the Western campaigns. Too early. Wrong shape. A cracked lens reminded me of rangefinders. Not invented. Could Arlo use it?</p><p>Maybe. A spool of copper wire was absolutely useful. Antonius said it was corroded. Still copper. A stack of warped wooden plates looked worthless until I realized they were standardized blanks for something. I did not know what. I kept them anyway. Antonius moved them back to discard. I moved them back to keep. He moved them again. I stared at him.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Those might matter."</p><p>"To whom?"</p><p>"I don't know yet."</p><p>"Trash."</p><p>"Potential."</p><p>Antonius moved the plates back toward discard.</p><p>"When you know who wants them, move them back." </p><p>I put them in keep. He let me.</p><p>Victory. Then I found the little box. It was under a broken chair. Wooden. Palm-sized. No lock. I opened it. Inside was a dull gray frame no longer than my palm, two finger-length rods, and a set of tiny stepped plates nested into grooves along one edge. It looked less like a device than the part of a device someone had forgotten to finish. Ugly. Unmarked except for a shallow stamp on one plate.</p><p>A crown?</p><p>No.</p><p>Three teeth. I knew that mark. Maybe. My heart sped up. I picked up the plate. Three teeth. Not a crown. A comb.</p><p>No.</p><p>I had seen it on something. Years from now. Where? Dungeon equipment? Artificer parts? Military? I closed my eyes. Memory did what memory always did when I actually needed it. Nothing useful. Then texture. Rain. Canvas. Someone swearing. A broken mana lantern. A woman with burned fingers saying they should have bought the old fucking... What? I opened my eyes. Antonius was beside me.</p><p>"Trash," Antonius said.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>Antonius nudged the box with two fingers. "Bent precision scrap. Failed artificer. Nobody wanted it. Toss it."</p><p>Antonius kept moving toward the discard pile.</p><p>I looked at the box. Then at Antonius. Then at the box again. For one beautiful second, the correct financial decision was obvious. Say nothing. Put it aside. Ask later whether I could have the trash. Free was an excellent price. I should have done that. Instead I said, "That is potentially extremely valuable."</p><p>Antonius stopped. Fuck. He came back and picked up the gray frame himself.</p><p>I turned one of the stepped plates toward the light. Three teeth. Where had I seen it? Think. Not enough information yet. But the workmanship was wrong for scrap. Tiny grooves. Matched steps. Reference surfaces rather than moving parts. Precision. Old precision.</p><p>"Three silver," Antonius said.</p><p>"Done," I said immediately.</p><p>Antonius kept the frame in his hand.</p><p>"How valuable?" he asked.</p><p>I looked at him. There are questions a sensible man lies to. This was one. I knew that. I understood the incentives perfectly. I had already agreed to three silver. I could say ten. Twenty silver. A gold if I wanted to sound dramatic. Then my memory finally caught on the teeth. Not a device. A reference. Tere. Orlan Tere. Master gauges.</p><p>The thing in Antonius's hand was not meant to do useful work itself. It was meant to tell the tools that did useful work exactly where correct was. And Antonius had asked me a direct numerical question.</p><p>"Forty gold," I said.</p><p>The number sounded so stupid out loud that I wanted to swallow it back. Antonius stopped turning the frame in his hand. I made it worse.</p><p>"At least," I said.</p><p>Silence. Three silver had become forty gold because I had been unable to keep my mouth shut for perhaps twelve seconds.</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>Antonius looked at the frame instead of at me.</p><p>"And you are the right buyer?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Then tell me why it is worth anything," Antonius said.</p><p>I pointed at the nested plates. "I think this is a master calibration gauge. Early mana-regulation work. You don't cast with it. You don't put it in a machine. It sets tolerances on the precision tools that make other fittings. To almost everyone in Carrow, it is a little gray box of useless metal. To the handful of artificers trying to reproduce this standard without rebuilding the reference from scratch? Forty gold is conservative."</p><p>"Think?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"Arlo might be able to identify it. Maybe authenticate it. I recognize the standard, not the condition," I said.</p><p>That was the answer I should have led with. After buying it.</p><p>"Who buys it?" Antonius asked.</p><p>I hesitated. That mattered. I could remember the standard. I could remember the kind of people who cared. I could not yet name the buyer.</p><p>"I can't name one yet," I said.</p><p>Antonius set the frame on the keep shelf, wrote my name on a scrap, and tucked it beneath the box.</p><p>"Five silver," Antonius said.</p><p>"You said three," I said.</p><p>"Before forty gold," Antonius said.</p><p>"Four," I said.</p><p>Antonius picked up the broom.</p><p>"Five," Antonius said.</p><p>The negotiation was over. He was sweeping again. Offensive.</p><p>"Fine. Five," I said.</p><p>"End of week," Antonius said.</p><p>I looked at the box. Five silver for something I believed was worth at least forty gold. An extraordinary purchase. A catastrophic negotiation. Both could be true. Then suspicion arrived.</p><p>"Why was that under a chair?" I asked.</p><p>"Because, Greg, until thirty seconds ago it was trash," Antonius said.</p><p>"Stop saying that," I said.</p><p>Antonius went back to sweeping. I stared at the Tere gauge.</p><p>Forty gold. Maybe more. More than the visible contents of this warehouse put together, if my memory was right. And almost completely useless to me until I found one of the tiny number of people who understood why. That was the important distinction. Value was not the same as usefulness. I returned to work. Twenty minutes later I found a cracked wooden case containing six green glass cylinders. My pulse jumped again. Antonius glanced over.</p><p>"Trash."</p><p>"Wait." </p><p>He sighed.</p><p>The cylinders were cloudy. Each had a metal cap. No mark. I picked one up. Future alchemical storage? Early pressure vessels? Mana cells?</p><p>No.</p><p>Too primitive. Could be rare. Could be important. Could be... I shook one gently. Something rattled. </p><p>Antonius said, "Careful."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"No idea." </p><p>I froze. </p><p>He smiled.</p><p>Bastard. I set it down.</p><p>"What are these?"</p><p>"Old dye cartridges," Antonius said.</p><p>I knew nothing about dye cartridges. Could become useful. Maybe glass composition?</p><p>Caps? I examined one. Antonius watched.</p><p>"Extremely valuable?" I hesitated.</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"How much?" </p><p>I looked again.</p><p>No recognition. No memory texture. Nothing except my own desire not to miss something. That was not evidence.</p><p>"Trash," I said. </p><p>Antonius nodded.</p><p>"Good." </p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>There it was. Something. Test? Had he known about the gray box? I looked toward it. Then at Antonius. He swept.</p><p>"You knew."</p><p>"Knew what?"</p><p>"About the box."</p><p>"I knew it existed."</p><p>"You put me in here to find it."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You're lying."</p><p>"Sometimes."</p><p>"Was that a test?" I asked.</p><p>Antonius stopped.</p><p>The room had become noticeably brighter as we cleared the small window. Dust floated in the beam between us. Antonius rested both hands on the broom.</p><p>"I wanted to know something."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"If everything was valuable to you." I frowned.</p><p>"That's stupid."</p><p>"Is it?"</p><p>"Obviously not everything is valuable."</p><p>"You bought garbage rocks."</p><p>"Kestrin shale is not garbage."</p><p>"You gamble for operating capital."</p><p>"Poor example."</p><p>"You wanted to keep warped wood because it had a shape."</p><p>"Standardization matters."</p><p>"You've tried to save half this room."</p><p>"Less than half."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Fine." He nodded toward the gray box.</p><p>"That came from a man named Orlan Tere."</p><p>Tere. There. The memory snapped into place hard enough that I stopped breathing for a second. Not Teren Coilworks. Orlan Tere. Tere gauges. Tere tolerances. Early mana-regulation hardware had a repeatability problem nobody cared about until suddenly everybody did. Tere had solved part of it too early, too expensively, for a market too small to keep him alive. His workshop failed. The standard did not.</p><p>Years later, other artificers copied the tolerances. Toolmakers copied the reference geometry. The three-tooth mark survived in specialist shops long after almost everyone forgot the man who made it. And the little gray frame on Antonius's shelf was not merely an early fitting. It was the thing used to tell other precision tools what correct looked like. A master reference.</p><p>Forty gold was not collector nonsense. It was replacement-cost nonsense. Rebuilding the reference properly could cost more than buying the surviving original, assuming the buyer trusted it. Antonius watched my face.</p><p>"You know him?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then why do you look like that?"</p><p>Because I remembered his work after forty years despite never knowing the man. That was the same category of evidence as Antonius's name, just narrower. Things that survived in S-class Greg's memory had survived competition. Wars. Breakthroughs. Monsters. People with enough gravity to leave dents. Orlan Tere had left a dent in a technical standard. Antonius Vale had left one in the world.</p><p>"He's important," I said.</p><p>"He owes me eleven silver." </p><p>I blinked.</p><p>"Currently?"</p><p>"No, Greg. Forty years from now." </p><p>I looked at him. </p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>Careful.</p><p>"Where is he?"</p><p>"Gone."</p><p>"Dead?"</p><p>"No idea. Closed the workshop. Left the box and three other crates as collateral. I sold what I could."</p><p>"What was in the other crates?"</p><p>"Tools. Brass. Wire. Two half-built devices."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"Sold."</p><p>"To whom?" I asked.</p><p>Antonius smiled. I hated him.</p><p>"Ledger."</p><p>"Absolutely not."</p><p>"Antonius."</p><p>"Clean."</p><p>I stared toward the shelf. Five silver suddenly felt criminally cheap. Forty gold was conservative if the right artificer understood what the gauge represented. The hard part was not owning the value. The hard part was connecting it to the tiny market capable of recognizing it. Which meant the object solved none of my immediate problems. No rent. No debt payment.</p><p>No mana conditioning. No sword training. No automatic fortune. It was forty gold sitting on a shelf pretending to be five silver until I did more work. Of course it was. Unless my memory was wrong. Unless Orlan himself never mattered and someone else used the name. Unless the mark changed. Unless the story I remembered was retrospective mythology. Still. This was exactly the kind of lead future knowledge was actually good for.</p><p>Not certainty. A lead. Check. Arlo could inspect it.</p><p>Good.</p><p>One problem. I put it down.</p><p>"That was the test?"</p><p>"Partly."</p><p>"What was the right answer?"</p><p>"There wasn't one."</p><p>"Then it's a bad test."</p><p>"I wanted to know whether you'd call everything treasure."</p><p>"I didn't."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"And I recognized the valuable thing."</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"It's valuable."</p><p>"You still don't know what it does."</p><p>"I know who made it."</p><p>"After I told you."</p><p>"I knew the mark."</p><p>"You guessed the mark."</p><p>"I remembered it."</p><p>"Same thing with confidence."</p><p>That was offensive. Also not entirely wrong. I picked up the broom.</p><p>"Why do you care?" I asked.</p><p>Antonius resumed sweeping.</p><p>"About what?"</p><p>"Whether I call everything treasure."</p><p>"Because people who think everything is an opportunity usually end up owing me money." </p><p>I stopped. </p><p>He kept sweeping.</p><p>"That was targeted."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You could have just said that."</p><p>"Would you have listened?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then clean," Antonius said.</p><p>I cleaned.</p><p>The chapter of my life in which Antonius Vale taught me wisdom through sweeping did not occur. He was not teaching me. That became increasingly clear. He simply had a room to clear and wanted to know whether the strange debtor who kept turning assignments into projects could distinguish a real possibility from his own excitement. That was somehow more irritating. I wanted lessons. Lessons meant structure. Lessons meant somebody had arranged the world so the pain produced a useful conclusion. Usually nobody had. Usually there was just pain and whatever you managed to steal from it afterward. I swept under a shelf. Found three copper coins. Antonius held out his hand.</p><p>"Seriously?"</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/007/Ch007_Fast-Coverage-003-C01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 7." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>"My floor," Antonius said.</p><p>I gave him the coins.</p><p>"Loan shark."</p><p>"Lender."</p><p>We worked. At some point the silence stopped feeling like silence. Antonius did not fill rooms unnecessarily. That was another difference between present Antonius and the man I remembered. Future Antonius had barely spoken because people waited for him. Present Antonius barely spoke because he was comfortable not speaking. Maybe that was where it started. Or maybe I was doing the metaphor thing again. I looked at him.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"Good." I kept sweeping.</p><p>An hour later we moved a cabinet together. It was heavier than it looked. Antonius took one end. I took the other.</p><p>"Lift."</p><p>We lifted. No Rusk. No Toma. No employee summoned to do it. Antonius grunted, adjusted his grip, and backed through the doorway. I almost dropped my side because I was thinking.</p><p>"Watch it."</p><p>"I have it."</p><p>"You almost didn't."</p><p>"I was distracted."</p><p>"By furniture?"</p><p>"By you." </p><p>He stopped.</p><p>The cabinet nearly crushed my fingers.</p><p>"Move."</p><p>We set it down in the hall. Antonius straightened.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"You actually work." </p><p>He looked at his dusty hands.</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"No. I mean you work."</p><p>"I understood the sentence."</p><p>"Why?" </p><p>He frowned.</p><p>There was no clever answer waiting. That bothered me.</p><p>"Because it needs doing."</p><p>"You have people."</p><p>"You've mentioned."</p><p>"Your time is worth more."</p><p>"Sometimes."</p><p>"Always."</p><p>"No."</p><p>That answer came immediately. I leaned against the cabinet.</p><p>"Explain."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Antonius," I said.</p><p>He walked back into the room. I followed.</p><p>"You know what everything in your operation does," I said.</p><p>"Not everything."</p><p>"You knew the cooper's chest."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"The grain."</p><p>"After you pointed it out."</p><p>"You know the routes."</p><p>"Some."</p><p>"Inventory."</p><p>"Enough."</p><p>"Tenants."</p><p>"Most."</p><p>"Why?" </p><p>He picked up a broken stool.</p><p>"Because it's my business."</p><p>There. Again. Not a lesson. Just an answer Greg did not like. I had run parties. Organizations. Operations. Campaigns.</p><p>By the end, I had known exactly which person to ask about almost anything. That had felt like mastery. It was mastery, in a way. Delegation was not failure. You could not personally know every strap, ration, spell component, injury, contract, horse, route, and personality in an operation large enough to matter. But I remembered rooms I had stopped entering. Equipment I had stopped touching. People whose names arrived to me attached to functions.</p><p>Quartermaster. Scout. Healer. Negotiator. Replacement. I had known the board. Had I known the pieces? Uncomfortable. Probably enough. That was the sort of answer I gave myself when I wanted a question to stop. Antonius threw the stool into discard.</p><p>"You're doing it."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Metaphor face."</p><p>"Fuck you." He laughed.</p><p>We found lunch in the front office. Bread. Cheese. Pickled onions. Antonius ate at the clerk's desk because the clerk had gone out. I expected him to have better food. Why? Future Antonius had been rich. Present Antonius had flour. Again. Tower. Bricks. I bit into the bread.</p><p>"How old are you?" Antonius asked. </p><p>I looked up.</p><p>There it was.</p><p>"Nineteen."</p><p>"No." I nearly choked.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You're nineteen?"</p><p>"Yes." </p><p>He stared. </p><p>I stared back.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"I thought older."</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>"That wasn't praise."</p><p>"Then fuck you."</p><p>"Twenty-three?"</p><p>"Nineteen." </p><p>He leaned back.</p><p>"That's upsetting."</p><p>"Imagine how I feel."</p><p>Wrong answer. His eyes sharpened. I took another bite. He waited. I chewed.</p><p>"Why would you feel anything?" he asked.</p><p>"Because nineteen is a terrible age."</p><p>"You say that like you've done it before," Antonius said.</p><p>I swallowed.</p><p>"Everyone has been younger."</p><p>"Not everyone talks about it like a disease they recovered from."</p><p>Interesting. Dangerous?</p><p>No.</p><p>Not yet. I could lie. Easy. Hard childhood. Older companions. Military upbringing. Dead parents. Some of it even true. Instead I shrugged.</p><p>"I had to grow up early." </p><p>Antonius watched me.</p><p>That answer worked on most people because people were polite around dead parents. Antonius was not most people.</p><p>"That's not it," Antonius said.</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>"What do you want me to say?"</p><p>"The truth would be novel."</p><p>"From a lender?" He smiled back.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Deflection accepted. Not believed. Different thing. He ate an onion.</p><p>"You're strange with money."</p><p>"I've noticed."</p><p>"You spend like you expect more."</p><p>"I can make more."</p><p>"You lose like you've lost more before." I said nothing.</p><p>"You talk about businesses like you've watched them fail."</p><p>"I've watched businesses fail."</p><p>"At nineteen."</p><p>"Carrow is educational."</p><p>"You don't get impressed by amounts that should impress you."</p><p>"That's because your interest rates are obscene."</p><p>"And then you panic over copper."</p><p>"Copper is currently offensive." </p><p>He laughed quietly.</p><p>Then he looked at me for a long moment. Not interrogation. Indexing. I knew the feeling.</p><p>"What are you?" he asked.</p><p>That was a dangerous question only if I treated it like one.</p><p>"Currently?" I asked.</p><p>Antonius groaned. I smiled.</p><p>"Laborer."</p><p>"Bad one."</p><p>"Improving rapidly."</p><p>"Debtor."</p><p>"Temporary."</p><p>"Gambler."</p><p>"Selective."</p><p>"Warrior?"</p><p>"Again, potentially."</p><p>"Mage?"</p><p>"Eventually."</p><p>"Merchant?"</p><p>"Maybe." He shook his head.</p><p>"You don't know."</p><p>"Know what?"</p><p>"What you are," Antonius said.</p><p>I almost answered immediately. Of course I knew.</p><p>Greg. Support mage. S-class. One of seven. Warrior before that. Leader. Manipulator, if we were being impolite. Dead man. Young man. Borrower. Investor. Expert. Laborer. The answers crowded each other. Antonius tore bread in half.</p><p>"You keep trying jobs like coats," Antonius said.</p><p>I stared at him. That was uncomfortably close.</p><p>"Some coats fit."</p><p>"You buy all of them."</p><p>"Options are useful."</p><p>"Options cost money."</p><p>"Everything costs money with you."</p><p>"That's why I have money." I looked around the cheap office.</p><p>"Do you?" He smiled.</p><p>"More than you."</p><p>Fair. After lunch we went back. The room was almost manageable now. Floor visible. Shelves separated. Discard pile enormous. Keep pile smaller. My uncertain pile had been reduced from twenty-seven items to nine. Antonius had forced me to choose. Not verbally. He simply kept asking:</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>If I had an answer grounded in something, it stayed. If my answer began with "maybe someday," he threw it away. This was barbaric. Also efficient. We reached the last shelf. Three objects. A cracked brass compass. A bundle of narrow iron stakes. A leather case with a broken clasp. Compass first. Needle dead. Trash. Stakes. Could be survey equipment. Could be tent pegs.</p><p>No mark. Trash. Leather case. I opened it. Inside was a set of delicate steel instruments. Calipers. Tiny files. A hand drill. Two shapes I did not recognize. Good quality. Old.</p><p>"Keep," I said.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Precision tools."</p><p>"Broken set."</p><p>"Still tools."</p><p>"Value?"</p><p>"Maybe three silver."</p><p>"One."</p><p>"Two."</p><p>"One."</p><p>"Fine. Keep." </p><p>He put it on the shelf. </p><p>I blinked.</p><p>"That's it?"</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"No argument?"</p><p>"You gave a reason."</p><p>I looked at the case. Then at the gray Tere box. Then at the enormous discard pile. The test had not been whether I knew the future. It had not even been whether I found the valuable thing. It was whether I could stop. That realization annoyed me enough that I did not share it. Antonius looked at me. Metaphor face. I deliberately made my face stupid. He laughed.</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>"Didn't say anything."</p><p>"You were going to."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Liar."</p><p>"Lender."</p><p>We carried the discard outside. Some would be burned. Metal sold by weight. Glass separated. Wood salvaged where possible. Even Antonius's trash had categories once it left the room. Of course it did. At the bottom of the last crate I found a small red scarf. Cheap. Faded. No value. I held it. Memory came without permission. A woman laughing on a balcony forty years from now. Not this scarf. Not even the same shade. Just red cloth. I could not remember her name immediately.</p><p>That hurt. Then I did. Mira.</p><p>No.</p><p>Mira had black hair. This woman was... Gone. The memory dissolved. I stood there holding someone else's worthless scarf and thinking about a woman who had been dead for years and might currently be twelve. Or forty. Or not born. I had no idea.</p><p>"Greg?"</p><p>Antonius. I looked up.</p><p>"Trash," I said. </p><p>He held out the discard sack. I almost put it in.</p><p>Then stopped. Why? No reason. No future value. No technical use. No opportunity. I wanted it. That was different.</p><p>"Can I have this?" I asked.</p><p>Antonius looked at the scarf.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"I don't know," I said.</p><p>Antonius waited. I did not invent one.</p><p>"I just want it."</p><p>Something in his face shifted.</p><p>"Take it," Antonius said.</p><p>I put it in my pocket.</p><p>No ledger. No two silver. No joke. We finished near dusk. An entire day. Gone. No gambling. No sword training. No Arlo. Hessa missed. That last one was bad. I would have to explain. She would say I chose the debt. She would be correct. I hated that in advance. Antonius locked the storeroom. I stood in the hall, dusty, tired, and weirdly satisfied. The room was clean. That should not have mattered.</p><p>It did. One room. One constraint. Finished. My brain immediately tried to expand. Inventory system. Collateral valuation. Storage rotation. Old debtor review. Orlan Tere. Arlo needed to see the box. Could Tere still be in Carrow? Could we find him? If his workshop failed because the market was too early, could I... Stop. I actually stopped. That was new. Antonius noticed.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"You had a thought."</p><p>"I have many."</p><p>"And killed one."</p><p>"Postponed."</p><p>"Of course," Antonius said.</p><p>He locked the front office. </p><p>I pointed toward the storeroom.</p><p>"The Tere box."</p><p>"Two silver."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"End of week."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"If it's trash, I'm still keeping the silver."</p><p>"It isn't."</p><p>"Maybe." </p><p>I smiled.</p><p>"You tested me."</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"I passed," I said.</p><p>Antonius looked at me.</p><p>"Did you?"</p><p>"I found the valuable thing."</p><p>"You found a thing you think will become valuable."</p><p>"Close enough."</p><p>"You also tried to save rotten wood."</p><p>"That was early in the process."</p><p>"And dye cartridges."</p><p>"I threw those away."</p><p>"Eventually."</p><p>"Passed."</p><p>He shook his head. But he was smiling. We stepped outside. The evening air felt cool after the storeroom. Antonius locked the door. I watched him check it twice. Future Antonius had people for this. Present Antonius checked his own lock. I wondered when that changed. I wondered whether it should. Then I wondered whether that was any of my business. Then I wondered whether knowing the answer could make me money. There I was. Antonius started walking.</p><p>"Where are you going?"</p><p>"Home," Antonius said.</p><p>I had never considered that Antonius Vale had a home. That was stupid. Of course he did.</p><p>"Where?" I asked.</p><p>Antonius stopped.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"No reason."</p><p>"Good night, Greg."</p><p>"Do you have a wife?"</p><p>His face went completely blank. Interesting.</p><p>"Good night, Greg."</p><p>"Children?"</p><p>"Go away."</p><p>"That's not a no," I said.</p><p>Antonius walked faster. I laughed.</p><p>"Sunrise tomorrow?" I asked.</p><p>Antonius raised one hand without turning.</p><p>"Ask Rusk."</p><p>That meant yes. Probably. I stood alone outside the warehouse. My hand found the red scarf in my pocket. Worthless. The gray box waited inside. Potentially extremely valuable. Two objects.</p><p>One I could justify. One I could not. I thought about Antonius asking what I was. Then about coats. Then about first-life Greg, who had eventually become so useful that people built plans around him. I had remembered that as leadership. Maybe some of it was. Maybe some of it was simply that someone else had always handed me the problem first. Keep them alive. Win this fight. Fix this spell. Get us through the pass.</p><p>Convince him. Break her. Make this party work. Constraints. I had been very good at constraints. Give me an empty life and apparently I borrowed money, started three careers, bought a sword, gambled, invested in garbage rocks, and argued with a loan shark about warped wood. I laughed. Alone.</p><p>"Excellent."</p><p>A passerby looked at me strangely. Reasonable. I started home. Tomorrow would have a problem. I found that comforting. That was probably something I should worry about. Later.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="005.html">← Chapter 4</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="009.html">Chapter 6 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/006.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 6: The Laborer — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 6</div><h1>THE LABORER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Antonius owned my morning. I objected to this on principle. Not the debt. The morning. Mornings were useful. Hessa preferred them for conditioning because the body was rested. Arlo's workshop was quieter before deliveries began. The guild posted fresh contracts early. Gambling rooms were mostly empty, which made morning excellent for thinking about gambling without actually gambling. Antonius had taken the best part of the day and replaced it with Rusk. Rusk was waiting outside the warehouse when I arrived. He handed me a sack. I looked at it. Then at him.</p><p>"What is this?"</p><p>"Flour."</p><p>"I know what flour is."</p><p>Rusk pointed at the cart.</p><p>"Then carry it."</p><p>The sack weighed perhaps forty pounds. Not difficult. Insulting. I looked past him into the warehouse. Crates. Sacks. Barrels. Two carts. Three laborers. A clerk at a narrow desk. Nothing that looked remotely like the inner machinery of a future financial empire.</p><p>"Where's Antonius?"</p><p>"Working."</p><p>"Doing what?" </p><p>Rusk pointed at the sack.</p><p>I said, "Not that." I disliked Rusk. He had a very economical sense of humor. I picked up the flour.</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"Cart."</p><p>There were two carts.</p><p>"Which?" </p><p>He pointed.</p><p>I carried the sack. This was creditor labor. Apparently Antonius's grand criminal enterprise began with flour. That was interesting for almost ten seconds. Then Rusk handed me another sack. By the sixth, I had developed a theory. Antonius was testing whether I would complain. I therefore did not complain. By the twelfth, I revised the theory. Antonius did not care whether I complained. He needed flour moved. That was worse. I had expected something criminal.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Twelfth Sack" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/006/v28_c06_s02_twelfth-sack.png"/></figure><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Empire Of Flour" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/006/v28_c06_s01_empire-of-flour.png"/></figure><p>Collections, perhaps. Threats. A ledger containing names that would eventually matter. Smuggling. Blackmail. A secret room.</p><p>Instead I was loading flour beside a man named Toma who had a rash on his neck and hummed the same six notes repeatedly. Future Greg knew Antonius Vale as a lender whose influence eventually touched shipping, construction, mercenary companies, city officials, guild contracts, and enough private debt to make three governments nervous. Present Antonius owned two carts and too much flour. I put another sack on the cart.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Inside The Operation" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/006/v28_c06_s03_inside-the-operation.png"/></figure><p>Then another. My shoulder hurt. Sword training yesterday. Excellent scheduling, Greg. Rusk appeared with a crate.</p><p>"Careful."</p><p>"What's in it?"</p><p>"Glass."</p><p>"Valuable?"</p><p>"More valuable if you don't drop it," Rusk said.</p><p>I took the crate. There were markings on the side.</p><p>Lamp chimneys.</p><p>No.</p><p>Medicine bottles? I shifted it. Glass clinked.</p><p>"Where is this going?"</p><p>"North market."</p><p>"To whom?"</p><p>"Doesn't matter."</p><p>"It matters if I'm carrying it."</p><p>"No."</p><p>I said, "Suppose I could improve the route." </p><p>Rusk stared at me. </p><p>I stared back. </p><p>He pointed at the cart. I loaded the crate.</p><p>Fine. Constraint. Move things. I could move things. I was not going to optimize flour. That sentence lasted approximately seven minutes. Then the second cart was loaded badly. Objectively badly.</p><p>Heavy barrels too far rearward. Breakables beside iron fittings. Three deliveries on the same cart arranged in almost the exact opposite order they would be unloaded. I looked at it. Then at the clerk. Then at the cart again. Not my problem. I picked up another sack. The clerk shouted for Toma to move two crates because the East Street order had been placed under the North Market order. Toma stopped humming. He moved them. The flour shifted. One sack tore. White powder spilled across the cart bed.</p><p>Everyone swore. I stood there. Not my problem. Rusk looked at me.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You have a face."</p><p>"I always have a face."</p><p>"Different one," Rusk said.</p><p>I hated observant people.</p><p>I said, "The cart is loaded wrong." </p><p>Rusk looked at the cart.</p><p>"It's loaded."</p><p>"Those aren't the same thing."</p><p>"Will it move?"</p><p>"Probably."</p><p>"Then it's loaded." </p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>Closed it. Picked up another sack. The problem followed me. Not emotionally. Structurally.</p><p>The East Street order was under the North Market order because the clerk loaded by arrival time instead of delivery sequence. The heavy barrels sat rearward because they had arrived last. The glass sat beside iron. Toma had just torn flour digging through a finished load to correct the order. I carried another sack. What was I doing?</p><p>Paying debt. Antonius wanted labor. I wanted time. Could I finish the labor faster? Maybe. I put the sack down.</p><p>"Rusk."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I haven't asked anything."</p><p>"You were going to."</p><p>"I can make this faster."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because Antonius said you work."</p><p>"This is work."</p><p>"This is you trying not to work."</p><p>That was unfair. Accurate. Still unfair.</p><p>I said, "I can reduce loading time." </p><p>Rusk leaned against the cart.</p><p>"By carrying faster?"</p><p>I said, "By making Toma stop moving the same fucking crate three times." </p><p>Toma looked over.</p><p>"I moved it twice."</p><p>"You're about to move it again." </p><p>He looked at the cart. The clerk shouted, "Toma, blue crate needs to come out." Toma looked at me. </p><p>I smiled. </p><p>Rusk sighed.</p><p>"Five minutes."</p><p>Good.</p><p>I went to the clerk.</p><p>I asked, "What are the stops?" </p><p>The clerk looked at Rusk. </p><p>Rusk nodded once. The clerk showed me the sheet.</p><p>Seven stops. Two carts. Approximate weights. Items listed. No route order. I knew Carrow well enough to see the obvious problem immediately. Then I caught myself. Future Carrow. Present Carrow. Roads changed. Shops moved. A bridge I remembered might not exist.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Check.</p><p>"Which streets are blocked?"</p><p>The clerk frowned.</p><p>"None."</p><p>"Market day?"</p><p>"South."</p><p>"Bridge toll?"</p><p>"Which bridge?"</p><p>I asked three more questions. The clerk became irritated. He knew the routes. I did not.</p><p>"Show me how you'd deliver these." </p><p>He did.</p><p>Badly. Not stupidly. Habitually. I used his route knowledge and rearranged the stop order, then the load: last delivery first, heavy weight centered, glass isolated, items grouped by stop. Toma watched.</p><p>"You a carter?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Warehouse?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Merchant?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"What are you?"</p><p>"Currently?" I looked at the flour on my shirt.</p><p>I said, "Apparently this." </p><p>Rusk laughed.</p><p>That was the first time I heard him do it. We reloaded one cart. That cost time. The clerk complained. Rusk let him. Then we took the route. I went because I wanted to see whether I was right. Rusk said I went because Antonius owned my morning. Both could be true. The first stop took half the usual unloading time. I knew that because Toma told me. The second was faster. At the third, we discovered I had put a crate on the wrong cart.</p><p>Not metaphorically. Wrong cart. I had read the clerk's handwriting incorrectly. The other cart was now carrying a North Market delivery toward East Street. I stared at the empty space where the crate should have been. Toma stared at me. Rusk stared at me.</p><p>"Excellent," I said. </p><p>Toma started laughing. I had optimized the system and misplaced the product. That felt familiar. We lost most of the time we had saved fixing it.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Information. The system needed marks large enough that an idiot could not misread them. I was currently the idiot. At the next stop I bought chalk. With my own copper. That hurt more than it should have. I marked each stop with a symbol. Circle. Cross. Two lines. Triangle. Not literacy dependent. Not handwriting dependent. Toma understood immediately. Rusk watched.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"You keep doing that."</p><p>"Doing what?"</p><p>"Getting interested."</p><p>"I am not interested."</p><p>"You bought chalk."</p><p>"That's evidence of frustration."</p><p>We finished the route slightly earlier than usual. Not dramatically. Enough. Back at the warehouse, I expected Antonius to be impressed. He was not there. I had apparently spent half the morning preparing a speech for an absent man. Rusk handed me a broom. I stared at it.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Floor."</p><p>"I just reorganized your delivery process."</p><p>"You also put medicine bottles on the wrong cart."</p><p>"Once."</p><p>"Floor." </p><p>I considered several responses.</p><p>Then swept. Flour had at least felt like labor. Sweeping felt symbolic. I was one of seven S-class people in the world. Would be. Had been.</p><p>Chronology made boasting difficult. I swept around a barrel. The broom caught a nail. I bent down, picked it up, and noticed three more near a broken pallet. That made me look at the pallet. That made me look at the stack beside it. That made me notice the bottom boards were damp. That made me notice the wall behind them was darker than the rest. Water. Small leak.</p><p>Bad storage position. The sacks against that wall were grain. I closed my eyes.</p><p>"No," I said. </p><p>Toma looked over.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing." I kept sweeping.</p><p>Five strokes. Six. Seven. The grain was going to mold. Not today. Eventually. Not my problem. Eight strokes. How much grain? Nine. What did grain cost? Ten. Fuck. I put the broom down. Rusk saw me.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"The wall is wet." He looked.</p><p>"So?"</p><p>"Those sacks shouldn't be there."</p><p>"They've been there for months."</p><p>"That's not the defense you think it is." He came over.</p><p>Touched the wall. Looked at the grain. Then at me.</p><p>"You know grain?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Water?"</p><p>"Yes." He waited. </p><p>I sighed.</p><p>"I know expensive mistakes."</p><p>That afternoon I was late to Hessa. She did not care why.</p><p>"You chose the debt," she said.</p><p>"I chose several things."</p><p>Hessa tapped my wrist.</p><p>"Then leave them outside this room. Again," Hessa said.</p><p>I disliked everyone today. Hessa made me breathe.</p><p>Four counts. Hold. Release. Again. My shoulders were tired from flour. My palms were rough. My back ached. The mana response came weaker than yesterday. I became angry at the warehouse. Then at Antonius. Then at myself. Anger made the response worse. Hessa tapped my wrist.</p><p>"Again."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"Then do it."</p><p>Four counts. Nothing else. No debt. No warehouse. No sword. No Arlo. Breath. Response. Hold. For five breaths, I managed it. Five. I opened my eyes. Hessa nodded. That was all. I wanted applause. Apparently S-class had not cured that either. After training, I should have rested. Instead I went to Arlo. He had three new disks. One cracked.</p><p>One performed worse than the previous batch. One performed slightly better.</p><p>"How much better?" I asked.</p><p>"Not enough to justify that face."</p><p>"What face?"</p><p>"The one where you've already built a factory." </p><p>I looked at him. He was learning me.</p><p>Unfortunate.</p><p>"Slow," Arlo said.</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"You say that like it's an insult."</p><p>"It often is."</p><p>He showed me the notes. I understood perhaps half and remembered enough future terminology to be dangerous. I asked two questions. One was useful. The other revealed I had misunderstood what Arlo was measuring.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Another correction. I left without funding another batch. That was difficult. I was proud of myself for almost an entire street. Then I thought of three cheaper tests Arlo could run. I turned around. Stopped.</p><p>"No."</p><p>A woman passing me gave me a wide berth. Reasonable. The next morning Antonius gave me a list of addresses. Collections. Finally. I smiled. Antonius noticed.</p><p>"Why are you happy?"</p><p>"This is more appropriate."</p><p>"For what?"</p><p>"Your business." He looked around the warehouse.</p><p>"This is my business."</p><p>"No. This is flour."</p><p>"Flour pays."</p><p>"Debt pays better."</p><p>"Sometimes."</p><p>That made me pause. Antonius took the list back before I could read it.</p><p>"Actually, no."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You smiled."</p><p>"So?"</p><p>"I don't like that."</p><p>"You are assigning work based on whether I enjoy it?"</p><p>"Today."</p><p>"That's childish."</p><p>"Carry those." He pointed at a stack of small wooden boxes. </p><p>I stared at him.</p><p>"You were going to send me on collections."</p><p>"I changed my mind."</p><p>"Because I was interested."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>I said, "That is an insane management philosophy." </p><p>Antonius smiled.</p><p>"You're in debt to a loan shark because you borrowed money to gamble."</p><p>"Working capital." </p><p>He laughed.</p><p>Not politely. Actually laughed. I stood there while Antonius Vale, future terror of half the city's merchants, laughed hard enough to put one hand on his desk. This was not how I remembered him. That thought caught. Of course it wasn't. I remembered an older man. Heavier. Quieter. A reputation that entered rooms before he did. This Antonius was what, thirty?</p><p>Maybe less. Still building. Still amused by things. Still personally aware of flour. Antonius wiped his eye.</p><p>"Working capital," he repeated.</p><p>"It was."</p><p>"You lost it."</p><p>"Temporarily."</p><p>That started him again. I disliked him intensely. Also, perhaps, slightly liked him. Dangerous.</p><p>"Boxes," Antonius said.</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"Inventory."</p><p>"What am I doing with them?"</p><p>"Counting." </p><p>I stared. </p><p>He smiled. He was enjoying this now.</p><p>Fine. I counted boxes. There were eighty-three. The ledger said eighty-six. I counted again. Eighty-three. I checked the shelf. Nothing. Asked the clerk. He shrugged. Asked Toma. He thought two had gone out yesterday. Two. Not three. Asked Rusk. He did not know.</p><p>Good.</p><p>A missing box. Finally a problem. I opened the ledger.</p><p>"Don't," the clerk said.</p><p>"I'm counting."</p><p>"With your eyes?"</p><p>"Advanced technique."</p><p>The missing boxes contained lamp oil fittings. Low value individually. Not worth stealing. Probably. Three missing across a month? I checked older entries. Not because Antonius asked. Because the discrepancy annoyed me. Two missing last month. One before that. Always small hardware. Always quantities close enough nobody cared. Not theft? Breakage? Miscounts?</p><p>I looked at receiving. Then dispatch. Different clerks sometimes. Same shelf. I watched for twenty minutes. A laborer came in, took four fittings for a delivery, told the clerk five, then corrected himself after the clerk had already marked five. There. Not crime. Process. Boring. I was disappointed.</p><p>Then I realized boring errors repeated every day became money. That made them less boring. I spent the next hour building a crude token system. Take an item, move a marker. Return an item, move it back. The clerk hated it. Toma liked it because he could see stock without asking. Rusk did not care. Antonius returned while I was arguing with the clerk.</p><p>"What happened to counting?"</p><p>I said, "Your inventory process is bad." </p><p>Antonius looked at the clerk. The clerk looked betrayed.</p><p>"It works," he said.</p><p>"It leaks."</p><p>"How much?" Antonius asked. I told him. </p><p>He looked at the missing quantity. Then at me.</p><p>"That's not much."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"So why do you care?" </p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>Stopped. Because it was wrong. Because I could see the fix. Because once the problem had edges, leaving it ugly felt physically irritating.</p><p>"I don't know."</p><p>That was honest. Antonius's expression changed slightly. Interesting. Not softer. More attentive.</p><p>"Show me."</p><p>So I did. Not the grand version. I had already imagined the grand version. Standardized receiving. Route coding. Inventory zones. Loss tracking. Supplier comparisons. Delivery-time records. Credit risk tied to merchant reliability. Once I started thinking about Antonius's operation, the branches were multiplying again. I wanted to tell him all of it. I nearly did. Then I remembered yesterday's cart.</p><p>One problem. Show the token system. I showed him. Antonius asked three questions. Good questions. One exposed a weakness immediately.</p><p>"What stops someone moving the marker without taking the item?" Antonius asked.</p><p>I stared at the tokens.</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"So your perfect system is theft with decoration."</p><p>"It's not perfect."</p><p>"Yesterday you would have told me it was."</p><p>That irritated me because yesterday I might have. I adjusted. Token attached to the storage position. Clerk moves it when recording. Not laborer. Still imperfect.</p><p>Better.</p><p>Antonius watched me rebuild it.</p><p>"You do this a lot?" he asked.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Turn one thing into six things."</p><p>"I improved your inventory."</p><p>"You reorganized a cart, found a leak, moved my grain, bought chalk, annoyed my clerk, and now you're redesigning the shelf because I told you to count boxes."</p><p>"When you say it like that, it sounds productive."</p><p>"It sounds exhausting."</p><p>"For you?"</p><p>"For everyone." I smiled. </p><p>He did too.</p><p>Not trusting. Definitely not friendly. Curious. That was more useful.</p><p>"Collections tomorrow?" I asked.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because you want to."</p><p>"You're going to run out of unpleasant work." </p><p>Antonius looked around the warehouse.</p><p>"No, Greg. I'm really not."</p><p>The third day he put me on a cart with Rusk and told us to collect overdue rent from three storage tenants. I pointed at him.</p><p>"This is collections."</p><p>"Rent."</p><p>"Debt."</p><p>"Boxes with doors."</p><p>"You're cheating."</p><p>"Get in the cart." </p><p>I did.</p><p>The first tenant paid. The second did not. Rusk knocked. A man opened the door. Thin. Tired. Hands stained blue. Dyer.</p><p>No.</p><p>Ink? Something chemical. He looked at Rusk first. Then me. Dismissed me.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Rusk said the amount. The man said he needed four days. Rusk said two. The man said impossible. I watched. Fear?</p><p>Yes.</p><p>But not of Rusk. Of the door behind him. Interesting. I looked past his shoulder. Shelves. Wrapped bundles. A woman sitting at a table. Child?</p><p>No.</p><p>Young apprentice. Bandaged hand. The man's eyes kept moving toward the back shelf. Not the apprentice. The shelf. Inventory. He had product. Why not sell? Maybe unsellable. Maybe committed. Maybe worth more later. Maybe stolen. My brain branched. I let it. Constraint first. Collect rent.</p><p>"What's on the shelf?" I asked. </p><p>The man looked at me.</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>Lie.</p><p>"Excellent," I said. </p><p>Rusk sighed.</p><p>"What?" the tenant asked.</p><p>"Nothing is usually easier to sell."</p><p>"Who the fuck are you?"</p><p>I said, "Currently? Rent collection." Rusk made a sound that might have been a cough. I stepped slightly sideways so I could see the bundles.</p><p>Dyed cloth. Deep blue. Good color. Expensive? Maybe. I knew nothing about cloth. Important. Do not become a textile expert because you saw blue.</p><p>"What are you waiting for?" I asked. The man said nothing.</p><p>"Buyer?"</p><p>His face changed. There.</p><p>"Buyer is late," I said.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then you're late."</p><p>Silence. Rusk looked at me now. The man rubbed his thumb against his palm. Anxiety.</p><p>"How late?"</p><p>"Two days."</p><p>"How much do they owe you?"</p><p>"That's none of your business."</p><p>"Correct. Your rent is our business. Your buyer is currently standing between those two things." He stared. I could become threatening Greg.</p><p>Easy. Rusk was already doing that by existing. Not needed. I could become sympathetic Greg. Maybe. The man wanted dignity more than sympathy. Different role. Businessman. Fine. I straightened slightly. Changed my voice. Not much. Enough.</p><p>"Your problem isn't that you can't pay. Your problem is that your cash is trapped in cloth for forty-eight hours."</p><p>His eyes narrowed.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I said, "Rusk's problem is that Antonius is owed today." Rusk said nothing.</p><p>Excellent support.</p><p>"So solve both. Partial now. Written date for the rest. Something held against it if the buyer fails."</p><p>The tenant looked at Rusk. Rusk looked at me. I had just invented terms on Antonius's behalf. Potential issue. Rusk said, "What security?" Good man. The tenant looked back at the cloth. Of course. We took two bundles under seal. Not ownership. Security. He paid part. Signed the remainder for three days. On the cart, Rusk drove in silence. </p><p>I waited. Finally </p><p>he said, "Antonius said two days."</p><p>"Three was better."</p><p>"He said two."</p><p>"He would rather get paid."</p><p>"You know that?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"How?"</p><p>Future Antonius?</p><p>No.</p><p>Present Antonius. Flour pays. Small losses matter. He was not a thug pretending to be a financier. He was a financier willing to use thugs. Different thing.</p><p>I said, "He asks about systems before punishment." </p><p>Rusk looked at me. Then back at the road.</p><p>"Sometimes."</p><p>Good.</p><p>Not certainty. Evidence. The third tenant was gone. Empty unit. That was worse. Rusk swore. I looked inside. Dust. Broken crate. Straw. A bent nail. Nothing. No obvious clue. My mind immediately tried to become tracker Greg. I had never been a tracker. I had known trackers. Different thing. I crouched anyway. Footprints? Several. Old. Useless. Cart marks? Maybe.</p><p>I stared. Rusk watched.</p><p>"You know what you're looking at?"</p><p>"No." </p><p>He laughed.</p><p>"Finally."</p><p>"Give me a moment." I looked harder.</p><p>Still nothing. Future knowledge? Tenant name meant nothing. Trade? Metal fittings. Destination possibilities? Too many. I could construct a theory. Several, actually. That was the problem.</p><p>"He left," I said. </p><p>Rusk nodded.</p><p>"Brilliant."</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"No idea."</p><p>"More brilliant." </p><p>I stood.</p><p>That failure bothered me more than it should have. There were no useful constraints. No person to read. No process to inspect. Just absence. Open field. My brain produced possibilities. Dock. South gate. Another lender. Family. Fraud. Fire. Caravan. None were worth anything. I hated it. Rusk noticed.</p><p>"You really don't know."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Thought you knew everything."</p><p>"I know an alarming amount."</p><p>"Not this."</p><p>"Not enough information yet." He grinned.</p><p>Apparently that phrase sounded exactly as defensive as it was. Back at the warehouse, Antonius listened to Rusk's report. First tenant paid. Second restructured. Third gone. Antonius looked at the sealed cloth. Then at me.</p><p>"You took collateral."</p><p>"Temporarily."</p><p>"You extended him an extra day."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Without asking."</p><p>"Also yes."</p><p>"You enjoy being employed?"</p><p>"Not particularly."</p><p>"Interesting strategy."</p><p>"He'll pay."</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"He will."</p><p>"Future knowledge?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>That answer came quickly. Antonius noticed.</p><p>"Then what?"</p><p>"He was protecting the cloth more than he was afraid of Rusk. He has a buyer. The buyer is late. He hates owing us because it makes him look weak, not because he intends to run. He'll pay." Antonius looked at Rusk. Rusk shrugged.</p><p>"Sounded right," Rusk said. Antonius looked back at me.</p><p>"And the third?"</p><p>"Gone."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"No idea." He waited. I hated him.</p><p>"No idea," I repeated. </p><p>Antonius smiled.</p><p>"That hurt."</p><p>"Deeply."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because I was starting to wonder if you believed your own bullshit."</p><p>"I believe most of it."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>There was amusement again. But something else now. Assessment. He was indexing me. I recognized it because I did the same thing to everyone. Debtor? Gambler? Problem? Asset? Person? I almost laughed. There I was doing it again. Antonius leaned back.</p><p>"You don't take this seriously."</p><p>"I take debt seriously."</p><p>"No, you don't."</p><p>"I am literally working it off."</p><p>"Because I made you."</p><p>"That seems unnecessarily semantic."</p><p>"You think this is temporary."</p><p>"It is."</p><p>"Everything is temporary."</p><p>"That's unusually philosophical for a loan shark."</p><p>"I'm not a loan shark." </p><p>I looked around. </p><p>He looked around too.</p><p>"What are you?"</p><p>"I lend money."</p><p>"At thirty-five percent."</p><p>"To people banks won't touch."</p><p>"And take their labor when they fail."</p><p>"Sometimes."</p><p>"Loan shark."</p><p>"Fine." </p><p>He waved it away.</p><p>"But you think you're passing through." </p><p>I did.</p><p>Obviously. A few weeks. Maybe months. Get mana online. Stabilize income. Build capital. Arlo develops the shale. Warrior training accelerates. Then larger moves. Antonius's warehouse was a temporary constraint. Antonius watched all of that happen on my face.</p><p>"You do," he said.</p><p>"I have plans." </p><p>He started laughing.</p><p>Again.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"That's twice you've laughed at my plans."</p><p>"I haven't heard them."</p><p>"Then why are you laughing?"</p><p>"Because every time something goes wrong, you make the plan bigger." </p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>Closed it. Substantially fair. Antonius tapped the ledger.</p><p>"You owed me money. Simple problem."</p><p>"I am solving it."</p><p>"You started a materials venture, became a gambler, hired a magic instructor, bought a sword, started training as a warrior, and somehow redesigned my warehouse."</p><p>"When you summarize it badly, yes."</p><p>"How would you summarize it?" I thought.</p><p>"Momentum," I said. </p><p>Antonius laughed so hard Rusk came in to see what happened. </p><p>I waited.</p><p>Eventually Antonius recovered.</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Yes?"</p><p>"Tomorrow you're cleaning the back storeroom." I stared at him.</p><p>"That's beneath me."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"I could do collections."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"Inventory."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Routes."</p><p>"No."</p><p>I said, "Let me look at your debtor book." </p><p>Antonius stopped smiling.</p><p>"Absolutely not."</p><p>"I could probably identify..."</p><p>"Storeroom."</p><p>"You're wasting me."</p><p>That brought the smile back.</p><p>"Maybe." </p><p>He stood.</p><p>Conversation over. I went to the door.</p><p>Antonius said, "Greg." </p><p>I turned. He was still looking at me with that strange evaluative expression.</p><p>Not trust. Not yet. Something closer to entertainment with potential returns.</p><p>"Don't leave," he said. </p><p>I frowned.</p><p>"Tomorrow?"</p><p>"Carrow."</p><p>That was different. I looked at him.</p><p>"Why?" </p><p>He shrugged.</p><p>"I want to see what you do."</p><p>For once, I had no immediate answer. Antonius smiled.</p><p>"Back storeroom. Sunrise." </p><p>I left.</p><p>On the walk home, I should have been angry about the storeroom. I was. I was also thinking about Antonius. Not future Antonius. This one.</p><p>No.</p><p>Wrong.</p><p>I had never known this version. And I had remembered his name anyway. Through forty years of wars, guilds, catastrophes, and people who could level buildings, Antonius Vale had stayed distinct. I remembered the weight more clearly than the mechanism. Future knowledge kept handing me conclusions about people whose beginnings I had never seen.</p><p>Arlo. Antonius. Maybe half the world. I knew what some of them became. Tomorrow Antonius was giving me a storeroom. One room. One shitty job. I felt my mind settle around it already. I hated that. Then I started wondering what was in the storeroom. Worse.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="005.html">← Chapter 5</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="007.html">Chapter 7 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/142.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 111: The Passenger — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 111</div><h1>THE PASSENGER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Before sunrise, Carrow smelled like horses. Not only horses. Wet stone. Cold ash. Yesterday's beer outside a tavern that had closed recently enough for two men to still be arguing beside it. Bread somewhere I could not see. River damp under everything. But mostly horses.</p><p>I arrived at the theatre with my bag over one shoulder and discovered that I was late. I was not late. The sky was black. Teren had said before sunrise. This was before sunrise. The problem was that theatre people apparently interpreted departure times the way they interpreted scripts. The alley was already full.</p><p>One wagon stood backed almost to the theatre doors, canvas rolled over its top rails. Another waited crooked behind it with a horse that looked personally offended by the hour. Scenery leaned against both walls. A painted window rested upside down on a crate marked COSTUMES, and somebody had put three swords into a basket with a cabbage. I stopped. The cabbage was real.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>The soot-shirt worker looked up from a coil of rope.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>I pointed. He followed my finger.</p><p>"Oh."</p><p>He took the cabbage out.</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>He put it on a chair. That was not better.</p><p>"Gregory!"</p><p>Teren appeared in the theatre doorway carrying a lamp in one hand and a boot in the other.</p><p>"Why do you have one boot?"</p><p>"Not mine."</p><p>"Whose?"</p><p>He looked at it.</p><p>"No idea."</p><p>He threw it into the wagon. A woman inside shouted, "Fuck you."</p><p>"Found your boot."</p><p>"I was wearing the other one."</p><p>"Then you're halfway done."</p><p>Teren disappeared again. I stood in the alley with my bag. This was the organization I had joined. No. Not joined. Traveling with. Important distinction. The servant actor was sitting on the rear edge of the first wagon drinking something from a tin cup. He had a blanket around his shoulders and looked much less cheerful than usual.</p><p>"You came," he said.</p><p>"I said I would."</p><p>"People say things."</p><p>"What are you drinking?"</p><p>"Regret."</p><p>"Is it hot?"</p><p>"Not anymore."</p><p>He moved his cup and made space beside him. I did not sit.</p><p>"Where are the crutches going?"</p><p>He pointed toward the wagon rail. I inspected it. Someone had already tied a broom there.</p><p>"That is where you said."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"There is a broom."</p><p>"We'll move the broom."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>He looked at me over the cup.</p><p>"Gregory."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"The broom will survive."</p><p>I set my bag down. The extra cord was in the top section because I had planned properly. I found it immediately. That felt good. Then I spent several minutes trying to determine the best way to secure two crutches to a wagon that was still being loaded by people who did not respect fixed geometry. Every time I chose a position, someone needed the rail.</p><p>"That's scenery."</p><p>"I can see that."</p><p>"Then move."</p><p>"I am attaching mobility equipment."</p><p>The soot-shirt worker had one end of the painted tower on his shoulder.</p><p>"You can attach it after the tower."</p><p>"The tower blocks the rail."</p><p>"Only until we unload it."</p><p>"That is tomorrow."</p><p>"Exactly."</p><p>I stared at him. He stared back. The tower won. I moved. A second actor I knew mostly as a guard carried a crate past us.</p><p>"Put them inside."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>He jerked his head toward the wagon. I looked. The inside contained three people, four costume trunks, rolled fabric, a basket of kitchen things, two spears, one painted moon, and the cabbage. The cabbage had returned.</p><p>"No."</p><p>The guard shrugged.</p><p>"Then walk."</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>"Morning."</p><p>He kept going. The recurring woman arrived from the street carrying two bags and a long wrapped bundle. Her hair was tied up badly. She looked awake in the technical sense only. She saw me.</p><p>"You're here."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>"You told me there were shopkeepers in other towns."</p><p>She stared for a second. Then remembered.</p><p>"Oh."</p><p>She handed me one of her bags. I nearly dropped it.</p><p>"What is in this?"</p><p>"Shoes."</p><p>"How many feet do you have?"</p><p>"Depends on the show."</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/142/Ch142_Forward-Coverage-004-01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 142." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>She walked into the theatre with the other bag. I looked at the one she had left me. It was heavier than my travel bag. The servant actor sipped his regret.</p><p>"Princess."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"Do you?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>I carried the shoe bag three awkward steps and put it beside the wagon. That counted as loading. Useful. The theatre emptied itself by degrees. Not neatly. Nothing came out in the order I would have chosen. A small table emerged before the legs that belonged to it. Costumes came before the trunk meant to hold them. A rolled backdrop was carried into the alley, returned inside because it was the wrong one, then brought out again because apparently the wrong one was coming too.</p><p>I stopped trying to understand the whole operation. That helped.</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>I turned. Teren stood beside the second wagon with a paper in his hand. Not Gregory. Greg. I waited. He looked at the paper.</p><p>"You're in this one."</p><p>"Which?"</p><p>"Second wagon."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"First is full."</p><p>"It was full twenty minutes ago."</p><p>"Now it is more full."</p><p>"Where do I sit?"</p><p>He pointed. There was no seat.</p><p>"There."</p><p>"That is a crate."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"What is in it?"</p><p>"Curtain weights."</p><p>"How heavy?"</p><p>"Enough."</p><p>"I am not sitting on curtain weights for three hours."</p><p>Teren looked into the wagon.</p><p>"Move the weights."</p><p>"To where?"</p><p>He looked around. I waited. Teren pointed at the first wagon. The servant actor shouted, "No." Teren pointed at the alley. The soot-shirt worker shouted, "No." Teren looked at me.</p><p>"You see the problem."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"That does not solve it."</p><p>"No."</p><p>He walked away. I hated theatre. A little later, the curtain weights went under the rear bench, the rear bench moved forward, two costume trunks traded wagons, the painted moon went flat beneath a stack of fabric, and the crate became a seat after all. Not the curtain-weight crate. A different crate. This one contained cups. I sat carefully. It held. Good.</p><p>My crutches were finally tied along the inner rail beside me, handles forward, cuffs wrapped in a scrap of cloth so the wood would not knock against the wagon every time we hit a rut. I had used one cord. The soot-shirt worker had watched me finish, tugged the knot once, and added a second knot above mine.</p><p>"What was wrong with mine?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"Then why?"</p><p>He had already walked away. I left both knots. The sky had begun turning from black to gray by the time the horses moved. There was no announcement. No speech. No count. Someone shouted that a lantern was still inside. Someone else shouted that it could stay there. The first wagon rolled forward anyway. Our driver swore. The horse moved.</p><p>The wagon lurched hard enough that I caught the rail with both hands. A cup inside my crate rattled. Then another. Then all of them. We rolled out of the alley. That was departure. I looked back once. The theatre doors were still open.</p><p>Teren stood in them with the lamp, shouting at someone I could not see. For one alarming moment I thought we had left him. Then he ran after the wagon carrying the unidentified boot. He climbed onto the back of the first wagon while it was moving. Nobody reacted. Carrow passed slowly around us. Shuttered shops. Dark upper windows. A baker carrying a tray through a side door. A woman sweeping yesterday out of a doorway.</p><p>The streets I knew looked narrower from the wagon because I was not choosing where to put my feet or crutches. I was simply being carried through them with cups under my ass. The city gate appeared. We went through. No one stopped us. Then Carrow was behind us. I turned forward. The road was terrible. Not immediately. For perhaps fifty yards it was acceptable. Then the paving ended. The wagon dropped into a rut. Every cup beneath me jumped.
