- `chapters/190.html:376`: <p>Something warm moved through my chest that had nothing to do with mana.</p>
- `chapters/125.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 100: The Test Case — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 100</div><h1>THE TEST CASE</h1></header><article class="prose"><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/125/Ch125_Two-Thread-Test.jpg" alt="Hessa records the motion of two suspended threads while Greg holds his forearm still at the assessment table." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Hessa had two threads. I disliked this immediately. They hung from the same wooden frame. Dark. Thin. One over the glazed tile beside the place my right forearm would go. The other farther away.</p><p>Not much farther. Enough. The gray cloth was folded on the side table. The copper was already out. Hessa was writing. I sat. She kept writing. I looked at the threads.</p><p>“Hands first,” Hessa said.</p><p>“I was observing.”</p><p>“Observe after I have your baseline.”</p><p>She finished the line.</p><p>“How are your hands?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>“Right calf?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>“Residual limb?”</p><p>“Baseline.”</p><p>“Phantom?”</p><p>“Ordinary.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Fingers?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Any urge to curl them?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Wrist?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>She held out her hand. I gave her mine. Right. She checked grip, thumb, fingers, wrist. Then left. Then residual limb.</p><p>Then the ordinary questions again in slightly different words because Hessa enjoyed catching lies I was not telling.</p><p>“Yesterday?”</p><p>“Theatre.”</p><p>“No magic?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Day before?”</p><p>“Lyssa.”</p><p>“No magic?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You understand that theatre using magic is not you using magic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good. I asked because your face did something.”</p><p>“There was a window.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“I did not touch it.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>She went back to the table. I stared at the two threads.</p><p>“Why two?”</p><p>“Because one annoyed me.”</p><p>“That is not a scientific reason.”</p><p>“It is an excellent medical reason.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“The first test told me less about external effect than I wanted.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It told me more about your control than I expected.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That does not make the external result better.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You are saying that too quickly.”</p><p>“I still know.”</p><p>She pointed at the farther thread.</p><p>“This one is not for you.”</p><p>“Then why is it there?”</p><p>“For me.”</p><p>“That is irritating.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She rolled my right sleeve above the elbow. The charcoal mark today was not the same. Still wrist-side. Slightly higher. A short line. Not the circle. Not the old line. New enough. I noticed.</p><p>Hessa tapped the new mark.</p><p>“Use today's line.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She drew a second charcoal line on the glazed tile. One beneath each resting thread. The near thread hung approximately where the first had. The far one hung perhaps four inches beyond it. Both moved slightly while she worked.</p><p>One turned. Stopped. The other shifted sideways. Stopped. Hessa waited. I waited. She opened the door. Both moved. She closed it. Waited. She crossed the room heavily. The far thread trembled. Near one moved less.</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>“Table vibration,” I said.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You walked near the far leg.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“On purpose?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She opened the window a finger width. Both threads shifted. Near first. Far second. She closed it.</p><p>“Air.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She stood beside the apparatus without touching it. The near thread drifted slightly toward her sleeve. Then away.</p><p>“Heat.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Static.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Why are we doing this again?”</p><p>“Because I am not asking the same question.”</p><p>I looked at the two threads.</p><p>“You are comparing them.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is the same question with a control.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It is literally a control.”</p><p>Her mouth moved. Almost smile. Dangerous.</p><p>“What is the question?” I asked.</p><p>“Whether the thread closest to the altered region behaves differently from a second thread exposed to as much of the same room as I can manage.”</p><p>“That is a control.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I said that.”</p><p>“You said it was the same question.”</p><p>“It is related.”</p><p>“Everything is related if you talk long enough.”</p><p>I considered the horse. Did not say it. Good. Hessa put the copper in position.</p><p>“Rules.”</p><p>“Minimal draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Right forearm only.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Small localized alteration at the marked region.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Maintain underlying draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If instructed, REACH from existing altered region only, smallest extension toward the near thread.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No release.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No push.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No Barrier.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No hand, wrist, finger movement.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No increase in internal alteration.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop if it feels like force.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop if it broadens.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stop when you say stop.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Far thread is not a target.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No attempt to influence both.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No attempt to compensate for room movement.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I paused.</p><p>“That last one was not in the first test.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Because now there are two.”</p><p>“Because now you know enough to be dangerous in a boring way.”</p><p>“That is rude.”</p><p>“That is medicine.”</p><p>She had me breathe normally for several minutes. I watched. Near thread moved. Far thread moved. Sometimes together. Sometimes not. Once both shifted left almost simultaneously. Once the near thread moved toward my empty chair before I sat.</p><p>Useful. Annoying. Hessa wrote everything.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat. Right forearm beside the near thread. Three quarters of an inch. Approximately. I did not measure. Hessa would kill me.</p><p>“Do not stare at the thread.”</p><p>“Where should I look?”</p><p>“My hand.”</p><p>She held two fingers above the copper.</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>“For you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I breathed. Ordinary. Phantom left heel present. No relevance. Right hand loose. No thumb. No fingers.</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I did. Minimal. Still strange. Less strange than months ago. More dangerous than it felt. Copper answered. Not strongly. Enough that Hessa watched it. Underlying draw stable.</p><p>“Shape.”</p><p>Small. Right forearm. Charcoal line. The altered response appeared. Localized. Slightly broader than the mark on the upper side. I reported it.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. No motor. No thumb. No left change. Hessa watched.</p><p>“How certain?”</p><p>“High.”</p><p>“Not maximum?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She waited. Long enough that I started wondering whether this was the entire test.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“REACH.”</p><p>Smallest extension. Toward the near thread. Not force. Not push. Not more. Different. The near edge became more distinct. As before. The alteration felt asymmetric. Toward the thread.</p><p>“Near edge sharper,” I said.</p><p>“Continue same amount.”</p><p>Same amount was impossible. I attempted not to change what I was doing. Copper shifted. Hessa's eyes moved. Not to me. Past me. Probably thread. I did not look.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>“RETURN.”</p><p>Immediately. I reduced the altered response. Near edge softened. Center dimmed. No elbow shift. No urge. No wrist. Underlying draw remained.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released. Ordinary arm. Hessa touched my wrist.</p><p>“Open.”</p><p>I opened.</p><p>“Close.”</p><p>Closed.</p><p>“Thumb.”</p><p>Moved.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Fine. Then she let me look. Near thread rested slightly right of its charcoal line. Far thread rested slightly left of its line.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“You tell me.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“You were not watching.”</p><p>“That was intentional.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So tell me.”</p><p>She checked my forearm again before answering.</p><p>“During baseline, both moved repeatedly.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“During your draw, both moved once.”</p><p>“Together?”</p><p>“Near first. Far followed.”</p><p>“Air.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“During shape?”</p><p>“Neither enough to record.”</p><p>“REACH?”</p><p>“The near thread moved toward your arm.”</p><p>My chest did something. Small. I hated that she saw it.</p><p>“The far thread?”</p><p>“Did not move at that moment.”</p><p>I stared. Hessa raised one finger.</p><p>“Keep it bounded.”</p><p>“What happened next?”</p><p>“While you maintained the same instruction, the near thread stopped. Then the far thread moved left.”</p><p>“Near?”</p><p>“Stayed.”</p><p>“So differential.”</p><p>“One differential observation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then keep it at one.”</p><p>I looked at the near thread. It did not move. Of course.</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It means the nearer thread showed one movement toward your arm during REACH that the farther thread did not show at the same moment.”</p><p>“That is better.”</p><p>“Than what?”</p><p>“Than both moving.”</p><p>“Only if the question is whether they moved together.”</p><p>“The question is whether the near one behaved differently.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It did.”</p><p>“Once.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then that is data.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Useful data.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“It is more useful than the first test.”</p><p>There. I waited. She did not continue.</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“And I still cannot attribute it to mana.”</p><p>I exhaled. The far thread moved. Hessa pointed at it.</p><p>“That.”</p><p>I looked. It settled.</p><p>“Fuck.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be breath.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I was farther from that one.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be convection.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Static.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Table vibration.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Thread twist.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could be mana.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at her. She looked back. That yes was worse than no.</p><p>“Then what changed?”</p><p>“My confidence that the test can produce interpretable information.”</p><p>Not my confidence that you moved it. Different. I knew. Still annoying. She tapped the farther thread lightly with a wooden stick. It spun.</p><p>“Last time, one thread moved and we had no local comparison.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Today I saw a moment when the near thread behaved differently from the far thread.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I also saw other moments when they behaved differently without magic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That matters.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I pointed at the apparatus.</p><p>“Why not put another thread the same distance on the other side?”</p><p>“Other side of what?”</p><p>“My arm.”</p><p>“Then it would not be exposed to the same local conditions.”</p><p>“It would be closer.”</p><p>“To different skin, different room position, different heat pattern, different movement.”</p><p>“Then put one on each side of the same altered region.”</p><p>“With what space?”</p><p>I looked. Not much.</p><p>“Smaller frame.”</p><p>“And now you have changed the frame.”</p><p>“That is solvable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“So I may do that later.”</p><p>I hated later. Hessa continued.</p><p>“Controls are not magic truth machines. They remove some explanations and leave others.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then say what today's second thread cannot tell us.”</p><p>I looked at it.</p><p>“It cannot tell us whether the near movement was mana.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“It cannot fully match local heat.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Or static.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Or tiny air differences.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Or thread-specific twist.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Or whether the two threads respond identically to the same disturbance.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So it is a bad control.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“It is an incomplete control.”</p><p>“That sounds like a polite bad control.”</p><p>“It is a control for some questions and not others.”</p><p>Of course. Everything with Hessa eventually became jurisdiction. Even thread.</p><p>“You are angry.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You are disappointed.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“I would prefer established external effect.”</p><p>“I would prefer a patient who does not build conclusions out of wishes.”</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“You almost did.”</p><p>“That is different.”</p><p>“Barely.”</p><p>She covered the apparatus with the gray cloth. I objected.</p><p>“With my face?”</p><p>“With your entire body.”</p><p>“You said the test was more interpretable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then repeat it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“One supervised external attempt today.”</p><p>“You did not say one before.”</p><p>“I am saying it now.”</p><p>“That is cheating.”</p><p>“I am the doctor.”</p><p>“You use that too much.”</p><p>“I use it exactly enough.”</p><p>She returned to the desk. I sat. My forearm felt normal. Which was good. Boring. Good.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I have not asked.”</p><p>“You want to know when.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“No magic tomorrow.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“One day?”</p><p>“One day.”</p><p>“Then?”</p><p>“Assessment.”</p><p>“External?”</p><p>“Assessment.”</p><p>“You are doing that deliberately.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I thought about arguing. I did not. Not wisdom. I had already lost. She wrote.</p><p>“Thirteenth successful minimal supervised draw.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/125/Ch125_Fast-Coverage-005-01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 125." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>There was the count.</p><p>“Ninth supervised deliberate shaping attempt?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Second supervised external attempt?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“External effect?”</p><p>“Unestablished.”</p><p>I hated the word. It was correct.</p><p>“Internal control?”</p><p>“Still encouraging.”</p><p>“Encouraging.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not improved?”</p><p>She looked up.</p><p>“You established a small altered region at a shifted target, attempted one bounded REACH, RETURNed promptly, maintained the underlying draw, and showed no motor recruitment, broadening, thumb symptom, elbowward shift, or unusual left response.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That supports repeatability of the control sequence under a slightly changed setup.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is improvement in confidence.”</p><p>“Not effect.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“You sound like you are trying to punish the word.”</p><p>“I am.”</p><p>“Tomorrow you live.”</p><p>“I have been doing that.”</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>“What exactly are you protecting against now?”</p><p>She considered me for a moment. Not because she did not know. Because she was deciding how much to say.</p><p>“Accumulation.”</p><p>“Of what?”</p><p>“Unknowns.”</p><p>“That is not a symptom.”</p><p>“No. It is why I do not stack tests.”</p><p>She pointed at my right forearm.</p><p>“You have had repeated small draws, repeated shaping, a new external instruction, and now a second external attempt. Your immediate exams are reassuring. That does not mean I know every delayed cost.”</p><p>“There hasn't been one.”</p><p>“So far.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good. Keep helping me preserve that sentence.”</p><p>I did not like this either. It was difficult to argue against a strategy whose main evidence was that nothing bad had happened.</p><p>“You could just say you are cautious.”</p><p>“I have.”</p><p>“Many times.”</p><p>“And yet.”</p><p>Fine. She gave me ten minutes. No magic. Ordinary hand movement. Cup. Grip. Crutch. She watched me pick up the cup.</p><p>“Stop checking your thumb.”</p><p>“I wasn't.”</p><p>“You checked.”</p><p>“I moved it.”</p><p>“You checked by moving it.”</p><p>“That is how thumbs work.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>At the door she said:</p><p>“Do not buy thread.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“I own thread.”</p><p>“Do not hang it from anything.”</p><p>“I was not going to.”</p><p>“Do not ask the theatre for theirs.”</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>“How do you know about theatre thread?”</p><p>“I know about thread.”</p><p>“That is not what I asked.”</p><p>“Go live.”</p><p>I went. The morning had become late enough that the Guild was busy. I did not have a reason to go there. I went anyway. Jorren was eating an apple on the front steps.</p><p>Of course. He looked at me.</p><p>“Hessa?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Alive?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Boring.”</p><p>I sat beside him. Not gracefully. He did not help. Correct. He took another bite.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“Nothing established.”</p><p>“That sounds expensive.”</p><p>“It was free.”</p><p>“Then you got your money's worth.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“No?”</p><p>“I got one movement.”</p><p>“You said nothing established.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“Then you got one unestablished movement.”</p><p>“That is not a thing.”</p><p>“It is clearly a thing. You have one.”</p><p>I looked at him. He bit the apple again.</p><p>“What did the other movement do?”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You said one movement.”</p><p>“I did not say there were two threads.”</p><p>“There were two threads?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then this story is already too complicated.”</p><p>“It is not complicated.”</p><p>“There are twice as many threads as yesterday.”</p><p>“Two days ago.”</p><p>“Worse.”</p><p>I almost explained the control. He held up the apple.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You asked.”</p><p>“I regret it.”</p><p>“You cannot ask a technical question and then refuse the answer.”</p><p>“I just did.”</p><p>“That is socially irresponsible.”</p><p>“Eat something.”</p><p>I looked at him. He offered the apple. I took it. One bite. Returned it. He frowned.</p><p>“You eat like a thief.”</p><p>“You offered.”</p><p>“I offered generosity. You took geometry.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“That bite was too large.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It changed the apple.”</p><p>“That is what biting does.”</p><p>He inspected the missing section.</p><p>“Damage.”</p><p>I almost explained the two-thread control. Did not. Not because Jorren would not understand. Because I did not want to. I wanted lunch.</p><p>“Are you working?” I asked.</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Warehouse.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>He smiled. Good. We sat. People went into Guild. People came out.</p><p>Merrin passed carrying three ledgers and said:</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>“Merrin.”</p><p>No offer. No task. Good. A courier I did not know argued with a clerk about a damaged seal. A woman in a red coat shouted that somebody had moved her cart. Someone had.</p><p>The cart was across the street. The argument continued anyway. Jorren finished the apple.</p><p>“You going theatre?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Lyssa?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Pessa?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“You have a demanding schedule.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What are you doing now?”</p><p>“Lunch.”</p><p>“You don't have lunch.”</p><p>“I am about to.”</p><p>“That is not lunch.”</p><p>“It will become lunch.”</p><p>He stood.</p><p>“I have work.”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“Later became now.”</p><p>I looked at the sun.</p><p>“That is poor scheduling.”</p><p>“That is time.”</p><p>He left. No theft. Unusual. I bought stew. Sat near the Guild wall. A cart passed. Then another. No ancient beast. No dangerous authority. No impossible old-world recognition. Just Carrow. I ate. The thread entered my head after three bites.</p><p>Near moved. Far did not. Then later far moved. Could be mana. Could be room. Could be me. Could be nothing. I wanted another test. Tomorrow contained no magic. Fine. The theatre was west.</p><p>Lyssa might be anywhere. Pessa might be busy. Work existed. I finished the stew. For once, I did not decide what the rest of the day meant. I stood. Then waited because my right crutch tip had landed on a cabbage leaf.</p><p>I moved it six inches. Better. Current state. Continue.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="124.html">← Chapter 99</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="126.html">Chapter 101 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/046.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 38: The Friend — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 38</div><h1>THE FRIEND</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The next morning I had four copper and no appointment. This was dangerous. Appointments made decisions. No appointment meant Bale. Kett. Varo. Arlo. Guild. Antonius. Jorren. Alden. Hessa in two days, assuming no symptoms. Breakfast. Breakfast won because it was closest.</p><p>I spent one copper on eggs, bread, and something the cook called sausage. It was shaped like sausage. That was enough. Three copper. I sat near the window and opened my notebook.</p><p>DORRIN.</p><p>BALE.</p><p>KETT.</p><p>VARO.</p><p>Then:</p><p>VALE / RUSK.</p><p>WEST ORCHARD.</p><p>HESSA 2 DAYS.</p><p>Too many directions. I drew no arrows. Progress. Someone dropped into the chair opposite me. Jorren. He had wet hair, a dark shirt with one sleeve rolled higher than the other, and a bruise along his jaw.</p><p>“You look organized.”</p><p>“I am.”</p><p>“Bad.”</p><p>“What happened to your face?”</p><p>“Door.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Man near a door.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>He stole half my bread.</p><p>“Buy your own.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“Then why mine?”</p><p>“Yours was closer.”</p><p>Strong argument.</p><p>“What are you doing?”</p><p>“Deciding.”</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>I closed the notebook.</p><p>“What are you doing?”</p><p>“Eating your breakfast.”</p><p>“After.”</p><p>“Sleeping.”</p><p>“Before?”</p><p>“Worked.”</p><p>“Dock gate?”</p><p>“Finished.”</p><p>“Finished today?”</p><p>“Finished forever.”</p><p>That got my attention.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“Nothing. Job finished.”</p><p>Right. Work ended without catastrophe.</p><p>“Next?”</p><p>“Don't know.”</p><p>“How can you not know?”</p><p>Jorren stared.</p><p>“Because I don't.”</p><p>Reasonable. He ate my bread.</p><p>“Guild later.”</p><p>“For work?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Training?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Drink?”</p><p>“Definitely.”</p><p>“At what time?”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>This was useless. I liked it.</p><p>“Come spar.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He stopped chewing.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You sick?”</p><p>“Sore.”</p><p>“From?”</p><p>“Road job.”</p><p>“You fought?”</p><p>“Pig.”</p><p>He stared. I explained. Bad decision. By the end, Jorren was laughing loudly enough that the cook looked over.</p><p>“I did not fight the pig.”</p><p>“You used magic.”</p><p>“To redirect.”</p><p>“You used magic on a pig.”</p><p>“Small magic.”</p><p>He wiped his eyes.</p><p>“Fuck.”</p><p>“I hate you.”</p><p>“Come spar.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Hessa said no deliberate load testing.”</p><p>“Swords aren't magic.”</p><p>“My shoulders are sore.”</p><p>He looked offended.</p><p>“You're nineteen.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“Apparently nineteen-year-olds have shoulders.”</p><p>He considered.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>Unexpected.</p><p>“Fine?”</p><p>“Walk.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Come on.”</p><p>He stood. I looked at the remaining egg. Then at him.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Market.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Need boots.”</p><p>He walked away. I took the egg. No appointment. Fine. We went to the market. Not East Market where Dara worked. South market. Cheaper. Louder. More cloth. More food. More people selling things from blankets. Jorren's boots looked fine. I told him.</p><p>“They leak.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Bottom.”</p><p>“That is where boots should not leak.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Repair.”</p><p>“Already did.”</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I want new boots.”</p><p>There. Preference. Not optimization.</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“Boot kind.”</p><p>I stopped asking. The first seller had twelve pairs. Jorren tried three. Rejected all.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Wrong.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Wrong.”</p><p>Second seller had better leather. More expensive. Jorren tried one pair and walked six steps.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I watched his foot. Heel slipped slightly.</p><p>“Too wide.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I can help.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I already did.”</p><p>“You can shut up.”</p><p>I did. Third stall. Jorren found brown boots with reinforced toes. He put them on. Walked. Bent. Jumped once. Seller looked alarmed. Jorren said, “Good.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Eleven copper.”</p><p>Jorren had nine. Of course. He closed his fist around the coins before I could count them again.</p><p>“Don't.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You are counting my copper.”</p><p>I was. He took the boots off. Seller said, “Ten.” Jorren said, “Nine.”</p><p>“Ten.”</p><p>“Nine and old boots.”</p><p>The seller looked at the old boots.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Leather.”</p><p>“Bad leather.”</p><p>“Still leather.”</p><p>“Wet.”</p><p>“Not now.”</p><p>They argued. I stayed out. This was difficult. Seller eventually said nine and old boots. Jorren paid. Done. No Greg. Excellent. He put on new boots. Old boots stayed.</p><p>“Happy?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He looked at me suspiciously.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You didn't negotiate.”</p><p>“Not my boots.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>That felt like a test I had not known I was taking. We walked. Jorren's stride changed slightly. Longer. He liked them. He did not say. At the next street, he stopped at a knife stall.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You have no money.”</p><p>“I can look.”</p><p>“Dangerous.”</p><p>“You bought rocks.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>He looked. Did not buy. We kept going. I had three copper. He had none. Balanced.</p><p>“Guild?” I asked.</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“What now?”</p><p>“Tam.”</p><p>There. Name from the green-door building.</p><p>“Who is Tam?”</p><p>“Tam.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“Lives upstairs.”</p><p>“From you?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“What does he do?”</p><p>“Shoes.”</p><p>I looked at Jorren's new boots.</p><p>“Why didn't he make yours?”</p><p>“Doesn't make boots.”</p><p>“Shoes.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Difference?”</p><p>“He'll hit you.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Why Tam?”</p><p>“Needs help moving a table.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“You're going to move furniture in new boots.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“He asked.”</p><p>Simple.</p><p>“Do you need me?”</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Come anyway.”</p><p>Different. I went. The green-door building looked the same. Four floors. Narrow stairs. Someone had left a bucket on the second landing. Jorren kicked the door on the third floor. A voice shouted, “Open.” Jorren opened. Tam was older than I expected. Maybe forty. Thin. Black hair tied back. Round spectacles.</p><p>He sat on the floor beside a low workbench with half a shoe in his lap. Not boot. Shoe. Fine.</p><p>“You brought Greg,” Tam said.</p><p>“You know me?” I asked.</p><p>Tam looked at Jorren.</p><p>“Is that Greg?” Tam asked.</p><p>“Yes,” Jorren said.</p><p>“Then I know Greg.”</p><p>Hostile network again. Tam pointed with a small hammer.</p><p>“Table.”</p><p>The table was against the far wall. Heavy. Square. Covered in leather scraps, lasts, thread, knives, wax, awls, three cups, and a dead plant.</p><p>“Move where?”</p><p>“Window.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Light.”</p><p>“Why now?”</p><p>“Because I asked.”</p><p>Jorren started clearing it. I helped. Tam did not. His shoe remained in his lap.</p><p>“Your table,” I said.</p><p>“Your hands,” Tam said.</p><p>Fair. We cleared. The dead plant went on the floor. Tam said, “Careful.”</p><p>“It is dead.”</p><p>“Still mine.”</p><p>I set it carefully. We lifted. Heavy. Not terrible. My shoulders objected. Quietly. Jorren had one end. I had the other.</p><p>“Window.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>We moved. Chair in way. Tam moved chair with his foot. Doorway narrow. Not relevant. Window side floor sloped. Relevant. We set table down. It rocked. Tam swore.</p><p>“Floor.”</p><p>Jorren said, “Table.” Tam glared. I pressed corners. One leg short? No. Floor uneven. Old building. Tam reached for leather scrap. I said nothing. He folded it. Wedged under leg. Table stable.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg and Tam maneuvering the worktable in the cramped room." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/046/svgPLG_Ch46_Move-the-Cobblers-Table.png"/></figure><p>Solved. No Greg. Excellent.</p><p>“Again,” Tam said.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Bench.”</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>“You said table.”</p><p>Tam said, “I lied.” We moved bench. Then a shelf. Then a chest. This was not helping move a table. This was rearranging a workshop.</p><p>“Why?” I asked.</p><p>Tam pointed at the window.</p><p>“Winter light is bad. Summer light is good. Now summer.”</p><p>Seasonal workshop geometry. Reasonable.</p><p>“Do you do this every year?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why not?”</p><p>“Usually complain.”</p><p>Growth. Maybe. We moved the chest. My back remembered yesterday.</p><p>“Done,” I said.</p><p>Tam looked around.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I sat on the floor.</p><p>“Done for me.”</p><p>Jorren laughed. Tam looked at my hands.</p><p>“You charge?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Jorren owes me breakfast.”</p><p>“I stole bread.”</p><p>“You stole half.”</p><p>Tam said, “There is soup.” Jorren said, “Good.” Apparently payment. We ate soup in Tam's workshop. Three bowls. Tam kept working while eating. He made shoes. Actual shoes. Fine leather. Thin soles. City wear. Not work boots. His hands were fast. Very fast.</p><p>He shaped the upper around a wooden last, pulled tension, fixed with tiny nails. I watched.</p><p>Tam kept working.</p><p>“Questions after this seam.”</p><p>“I can watch.”</p><p>“Then watch.”</p><p>Jorren ate his soup.</p><p>Hostile. I ate soup. Tam had customers. Two while we were there. First woman picked up black shoes. Tam made her walk. She said left pinched. He marked something. Took them back. No argument. Second man wanted repair by tomorrow. Tam said three days. Man said tomorrow. Tam said four days. Man accepted three. Good. I enjoyed him. Jorren knew both customers by sight.</p><p>Not name. The woman asked Jorren if dock job finished. He said yes. She said her brother needed two men at river stairs next week. Jorren said maybe. No Greg. World. After soup, Tam said, “Your friend stares.” Jorren said, “Yes.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>Tam looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You have a question.”</p><p>Several. I chose one.</p><p>“Why thin sole?”</p><p>“Customer walks inside.”</p><p>“That's it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I liked that answer. No universal shoe. Use.</p><p>“What happens when outside?”</p><p>“She owns other shoes.”</p><p>Of course. I stopped. Tam nodded once. Maybe approval. Maybe relief. We left around midday. Jorren's plan had been sleep. He had failed.</p><p>“What now?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“Guild.”</p><p>Finally. We walked there. The contract board had changed again. Three jobs removed. Five added. One red notice. Not emergency. Red meant higher threat. Jorren looked. I looked. No need. Alden was not there. Pessa not there. Dorn not there. Good. Jorren pointed at a posting.</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>I read.</p><p>RIVER STAIRS CLEARING</p><p>TWO BRONZE</p><p>HALF DAY</p><p>DEBRIS / SLIP RISK</p><p>NO KNOWN CREATURE THREAT</p><p>THREE COPPER + MEAL</p><p>“Three.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Low.”</p><p>“Meal.”</p><p>“Bad meal.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>He took the slip.</p><p>“Why that?”</p><p>“River.”</p><p>“That is not an answer.”</p><p>“Close.”</p><p>Ah. Close to home. Short. Maybe Tam's woman had said river stairs next week, but this was tomorrow. Different. Maybe not connected. Do not connect.</p><p>“What about this?”</p><p>I pointed at another.</p><p>WAREHOUSE NIGHT WATCH</p><p>FOUR BRONZE</p><p>SIX COPPER</p><p>NO SLEEPING</p><p>Jorren shook his head.</p><p>“Night.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I like night.”</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“I don't like working night.”</p><p>Preference. Again. I looked at the board. Could take something. No appointment tomorrow except Hessa? Hessa said three days from Chapter 44 morning. This was next day after orchard, so tomorrow would likely be due or near due. Need track.</p><p>Hessa visit yesterday before Bale and orchard invitation. Orchard next day. Today after orchard. Tomorrow is two days since Hessa? She said three days if no symptoms. So not yet. I had time. River stairs with Jorren. Three copper. Meal. Physical labor. No magic expected. My back said no. Not pain. Opinion.</p><p>“I'll pass.”</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>“Really?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Sore.”</p><p>“You're nineteen.”</p><p>“We covered this.”</p><p>He shrugged.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>No persuasion. He signed himself. One Bronze? Posting required two. He looked around. Called to a woman near the practice door.</p><p>“Eli.”</p><p>She turned.</p><p>“River tomorrow?”</p><p>“Pay?”</p><p>“Three and food.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Close.”</p><p>“How close?”</p><p>“East stairs.”</p><p>She considered.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/046/Ch046_Fast-Coverage-003-B08.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 46." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Done. Jorren had another person. Immediate. No need Greg. Good. Something in me noticed. Not hurt. Just noticed. Old Greg had become difficult to replace. Present Greg was extremely replaceable. Correct. Healthy. Annoying. Jorren handed in the slip with Eli. I did not know Eli. No need.</p><p>“What are you doing?” Jorren asked.</p><p>“Maybe Kett.”</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>“Kiln.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Rocks.”</p><p>He stared.</p><p>“Still?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I thought you gave them away.”</p><p>“Physical rocks. Not conceptual rocks.”</p><p>He closed his eyes.</p><p>“Go.”</p><p>I went. Kett's Kiln was farther north than I remembered from Dorrin's directions. Not one kiln. Three. Brick buildings around a yard. Heat even from street. Carts loaded with clay pipe, tile, stone, and sealed ceramic jars. I stopped outside. My shoulders were sore.</p><p>I had spent the morning buying boots without buying boots, moving furniture without being asked, eating soup, and refusing work because my body wanted rest. Kett could wait. But I was here. Dangerous sentence. I went in. A man at the yard entrance said, “Delivery?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pickup?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then office.”</p><p>I went office. A young woman behind a high desk looked up.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Questions about kestrin treatment.”</p><p>“Buying?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Clean.</p><p>“Can I pay for time?”</p><p>She looked at me differently.</p><p>“How much time?”</p><p>“Ten minutes.”</p><p>“One copper.”</p><p>I had three. Reasonable.</p><p>“Who answers?”</p><p>“Depends on question.”</p><p>“Heat treatment for mana behavior.”</p><p>She called through a side door.</p><p>“Kett!”</p><p>A voice shouted, “What?”</p><p>“Ten-minute question!”</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Which Greg?”</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>“Barrier Greg.”</p><p>I hated Carrow. A man came through. Sixty maybe. Huge forearms. White hair. No eyebrows. Possibly kiln.</p><p>“You have ten.”</p><p>I put one copper down.</p><p>“Do you heat-treat kestrin for ward suppliers?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Does heat alone create suppression?”</p><p>“Can.”</p><p>“Retention?”</p><p>“Can.”</p><p>“Consistency?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>“Never?”</p><p>“Not what I said.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Heat control insufficient?”</p><p>“Stone varies.”</p><p>Same.</p><p>“Do you sort before?”</p><p>“If customer pays.”</p><p>“Do customers supply sorted stone?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you treat by batch?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can two batches with same heat behave differently?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How differently?”</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Stone. Moisture. previous treatment. salts. kiln position. size. bad luck.”</p><p>“Can you control kiln position?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Moisture?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Size?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Stone?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Previous treatment?”</p><p>“If they tell me.”</p><p>“Do they?”</p><p>He laughed. Good.</p><p>“Could three sacks from one professional process differ while each sack is internally consistent?”</p><p>I stopped. Too close? Public hypothetical. No seized details beyond three sacks differing, which was evidence. I had just revealed shape. Not owner. Not Guild. Still. Kett looked at me.</p><p>“Could.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Different runs.”</p><p>“Same run, different sorting after?”</p><p>“Could.”</p><p>“Different source lots?”</p><p>“Could.”</p><p>“Different treatment targets?”</p><p>“Could.”</p><p>“Storage?”</p><p>“Could.”</p><p>Everything possible. No narrowing. Good.</p><p>“What would make you call material professionally controlled?”</p><p>He thought.</p><p>“Repeat order.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“If customer comes back and asks for same behavior and I can hit it again.”</p><p>There. Repeatability. Not one impressive batch. Manufacturing version of Greg. Interesting.</p><p>“Can you?”</p><p>“For some.”</p><p>“What limits?”</p><p>“Money.”</p><p>I laughed. He did not.</p><p>“Also kiln.”</p><p>“Also stone.”</p><p>“Also people.”</p><p>“Also weather.”</p><p>“Also idiots.”</p><p>“Which category am I?”</p><p>“Paying.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“Who tests your output?”</p><p>“Usually customer.”</p><p>“You don't?”</p><p>“Heat, weight, appearance. Mana if contract says.”</p><p>“Who supplies mana test?”</p><p>“Customer or we charge.”</p><p>“Do you know Bale?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you supply them?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Direct. Good.</p><p>“Kestrin specifically?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Varo?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What relationship?”</p><p>“Sometimes they treat before me. Sometimes after.”</p><p>“Order changes behavior?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you know Silas Marris?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>No reaction.</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“They move freight.”</p><p>“Do they buy from you?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Have they?”</p><p>“Not that I remember.”</p><p>Good. Not evidence of no relationship beyond his memory.</p><p>“Darrowmere?”</p><p>He frowned.</p><p>“Town?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What about it?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>Stop. No reason. I looked at clock. Probably ten minutes.</p><p>“One more.”</p><p>“You have two.”</p><p>“Why no eyebrows?”</p><p>He stared. Then laughed.</p><p>“Kiln.”</p><p>I nodded. Worth copper. I left. Outside, I wrote.</p><p>KETT</p><p>heat treatment can affect suppression / retention heat alone does not guarantee consistency variables: stone, moisture, prior treatment, salts, kiln position, size, luck professional control = ability to repeat target on repeat order, not one good batch customers often test mana behavior themselves Varo may treat before OR after kiln depending product Bale: Kett says no kestrin supply Silas Marris: known freight company, no remembered purchases from Kett</p><p>Darrowmere: no information asked / no connection</p><p>Then I underlined:</p><p>REPEAT ORDER.</p><p>Edrin's seized sacks differed from one another but were narrow within each. Could be three runs. Could be three targets. Could be storage. Could be source lots. Could be post-sorting. Still broad. But the better question might not be who can make one consistent sack. Who can make the same kind again? No. Edrin had not said sacks matched. They differed. So maybe not.</p><p>Do not improve evidence by wanting it. I crossed out the question. Good. Two copper left. Body tired. No reason to visit Varo. I went home. On the way, I passed Jorren again. He was sitting outside a drink shop in his new boots.</p><p>“Thought you were sleeping.”</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>“You said definitely drink.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He lifted cup. Consistent.</p><p>“Kiln?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good rocks?”</p><p>“Complicated rocks.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>He pointed at empty chair. I looked. Two copper. Drink maybe one. Body tired. No appointment. I sat.</p><p>“What did you learn?” he asked.</p><p>“You don't care.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why ask?”</p><p>“Conversation.”</p><p>Right. I ordered one beer. Bad. Of course. Jorren told me Tam had already moved the table back six inches because the afternoon sun hit his eyes. I laughed. All that work. Six inches.</p><p>“Was it wasted?”</p><p>Jorren asked. I thought.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“He learned six inches.”</p><p>Jorren nodded. That was enough. I drank. No one requested anything. No one needed me. The kiln would fire without me. Tam would make shoes. Jorren would clear river stairs with Eli. Alden was somewhere. Pessa somewhere else. Dorn probably eating an onion incorrectly. Edrin had evidence. Hessa had students. Antonius had businesses. Arlo had my rocks. The city did not pause when I sat down.</p><p>Good. I sat anyway.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="045.html">← Chapter 37</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="047.html">Chapter 39 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/120.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 95: The Repeater — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 95</div><h1>THE REPEATER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Hessa asked about the crutch before she asked about magic.</p><p>“Which one?”</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>“Tip slipped?”</p><p>“Began to.”</p><p>“Fell?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Caught yourself?”</p><p>“I unloaded it before full weight.”</p><p>“With what?”</p><p>“The other crutch and right leg.”</p><p>She looked up.</p><p>“That is not what I meant.”</p><p>I knew.</p><p>“Hands?”</p><p>“Hot after training. Fine by later afternoon.”</p><p>“Calf?”</p><p>“Tired. Fine this morning.”</p><p>“Residual limb?”</p><p>“Baseline.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fingers?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Any urge to move them?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Forearm?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Anything below the left knee that felt different from ordinary phantom sensation?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I sat on the same stool.</p><p>My right sleeve was already rolled above the elbow because experience had finally defeated ceremony.</p><p>Hessa noticed.</p><p>“Efficient.”</p><p>“I am capable of learning.”</p><p>“Occasionally.”</p><p>I looked at the tray.</p><p>Copper.</p><p>Charcoal.</p><p>Cloth.</p><p>Water.</p><p>Nothing else.</p><p>No object waiting to be affected.</p><p>No external-effect apparatus.</p><p>I had known there would not be.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>I was still disappointed.</p><p>That seemed unreasonable.</p><p>She had said closer.</p><p>Closer was a direction, not a destination.</p><p>I hated directions without distances.</p><p>Hessa finished writing.</p><p>“Yesterday was Pessa?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And no magic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The day before?”</p><p>“Theatre. No magic.”</p><p>“After our last test?”</p><p>“No symptoms.”</p><p>“None you forgot to mention because they seemed unrelated?”</p><p>I thought.</p><p>This was a trap only if I deserved it.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She closed the notebook.</p><p>“What do you think we&#x27;re testing today?”</p><p>I did not answer immediately.</p><p>That was growth.</p><p>Or suspicion.</p><p>“Repeatability.”</p><p>“Too broad.”</p><p>“Whether I can reduce an alteration again while maintaining the underlying draw.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Without recruiting my hand.”</p><p>“Also relevant.”</p><p>“And without pushing the alteration somewhere else.”</p><p>“Relevant.”</p><p>“And whether I can tell when it is gone.”</p><p>She tilted her head.</p><p>“That one may be too ambitious.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because last time you could not.”</p><p>“That is why we should test it.”</p><p>“That is why I am not making it the instruction.”</p><p>I disliked this.</p><p>“What is the instruction?”</p><p>“The same useful part as last time.”</p><p>“Same target?”</p><p>“Approximately.”</p><p>“Approximately is a new variable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That defeats repeatability.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It changes location.”</p><p>“Barely.”</p><p>“Barely is not zero.”</p><p>Hessa took the charcoal.</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I am not trying to prove you can reproduce a laboratory result.”</p><p>“We do not have a laboratory.”</p><p>“Then we agree.”</p><p>“That was not agreement.”</p><p>She drew a short line on the intact right forearm, near the wrist-side area she had used last time.</p><p>Not identical.</p><p>I could tell because I had stared at the previous mark for far too long.</p><p>“This is slightly farther inward.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“I did not measure.”</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>Cruel woman.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because your arm is not a board.”</p><p>“It has dimensions.”</p><p>“So does bread. I do not use calipers before breakfast.”</p><p>“That is because bread is not mana.”</p><p>“Good. We have established one difference.”</p><p>I looked at the line.</p><p>“Instruction?”</p><p>“Minimal draw.”</p><p>“Then shape toward the line.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Small.”</p><p>“Same as last time?”</p><p>“As close as you can without turning that into the task.”</p><p>Impossible sentence.</p><p>“And then?”</p><p>“I say RETURN.”</p><p>“One return?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“No refinement?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“If one edge remains?”</p><p>“You leave it.”</p><p>“If it shifts?”</p><p>“You tell me.”</p><p>“If I cannot tell?”</p><p>“You tell me that.”</p><p>“If reduction stops?”</p><p>“You tell me.”</p><p>“If I think I can improve it?”</p><p>“You do not.”</p><p>“That seems targeted.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“At me.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>She moved the copper into place.</p><p>“Before we begin, hands.”</p><p>I opened and closed the right hand.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>She pressed along the forearm.</p><p>“Anything?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good. Minimal draw only.”</p><p>I settled.</p><p>The first part had become familiar enough to be dangerous.</p><p>Not easy.</p><p>Familiar.</p><p>There was a difference.</p><p>I found the draw.</p><p>Small.</p><p>Supervised.</p><p>Nothing like Barrier.</p><p>Nothing completed.</p><p>No external movement.</p><p>Copper responded.</p><p>Hessa watched it.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>The phantom left foot existed because it usually existed.</p><p>Heel.</p><p>Toes.</p><p>A faint sense of the ankle being somewhere it was not.</p><p>Ordinary.</p><p>Not involved.</p><p>“Right forearm only,” Hessa said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Toward the mark. Small.”</p><p>I shaped.</p><p>The alteration gathered near the charcoal line.</p><p>Narrower than the old broad pattern.</p><p>Not perfectly narrow.</p><p>I could feel the temptation to improve it before she said anything.</p><p>Do not.</p><p>That was not an instruction from Pessa.</p><p>Not theatre.</p><p>Not philosophy.</p><p>Hessa had literally told me not to refine.</p><p>Useful distinction.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>Copper response changed.</p><p>Hessa leaned slightly closer.</p><p>My fingers stayed open.</p><p>No urge.</p><p>No cold.</p><p>No thumb.</p><p>“RETURN.”</p><p>I stopped feeding the alteration and tried to reduce it while keeping the underlying draw.</p><p>At first, nothing obvious happened.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not waited.</p><p>Continued the reduction.</p><p>The wrist-side edge softened.</p><p>Then the center.</p><p>The upper edge remained clearer.</p><p>Last time I had tried to fix that.</p><p>This time I did not.</p><p>It was irritating.</p><p>The upper edge persisted.</p><p>I could feel it.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>The rest diminished.</p><p>“Report,” Hessa said.</p><p>“Reduction. Wrist side first. Center dimmer. Upper edge remains.”</p><p>“Any movement?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Urge?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Continue RETURN. Do not correct the edge separately.”</p><p>I continued.</p><p>The upper edge dimmed.</p><p>Not smoothly.</p><p>It seemed to hold, then drop.</p><p>Copper diminished.</p><p>I felt the alteration become harder to distinguish.</p><p>This was where last time I had lost certainty.</p><p>I wanted to search.</p><p>Did not.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Less.”</p><p>“Specific.”</p><p>“Upper edge less distinct. Center maybe still present.”</p><p>“Maybe?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I hated when uncertainty earned approval.</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>The alteration thinned further.</p><p>Or my ability to perceive it did.</p><p>Those were not the same.</p><p>I knew that.</p><p>Could not separate them.</p><p>“I cannot tell whether the center remains.”</p><p>“Do not search.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then stop trying.”</p><p>“I am not.”</p><p>She looked at my face.</p><p>I stopped trying harder.</p><p>That sentence made sense only internally.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>“Maintain underlying draw.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>This was the strange part.</p><p>The draw remained.</p><p>The alteration was uncertain.</p><p>I could still tell those apart.</p><p>I thought.</p><p>KNOW versus THINK.</p><p>“I know the draw remains,” I said.</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“I am more confident of that than whether the alteration remains.”</p><p>“Better answer.”</p><p>Not yes.</p><p>Better answer.</p><p>Hessa watched the copper.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held.</p><p>My right hand stayed still.</p><p>No fingers.</p><p>No wrist.</p><p>No thumb.</p><p>The copper response stayed at the quieter level.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released.</p><p>Everything settled.</p><p>Hessa immediately took my hand.</p><p>“Open.”</p><p>It was open.</p><p>“Close.”</p><p>I closed it.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Open.</p><p>Close.</p><p>Thumb.</p><p>Wrist.</p><p>She checked strength against her fingers.</p><p>“Any tingling?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Numb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Urge?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Left side?”</p><p>“Ordinary phantom foot.”</p><p>“Different?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>Neither of us moved.</p><p>“This is where you tell me what happened.”</p><p>“I am deciding.”</p><p>“That is concerning.”</p><p>“It should be reassuring.”</p><p>“Not historically.”</p><p>She wrote first.</p><p>I tried to read upside down.</p><p>She moved the notebook.</p><p>“That is hostile.”</p><p>“It is medicine.”</p><p>“Those are not mutually exclusive.”</p><p>She finished the line.</p><p>Then looked at me.</p><p>“You reduced it again.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“While maintaining the draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No observed shift toward the elbow.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No motor urge.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No separate correction.”</p><p>“Because you prohibited it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“The remaining edge reduced when you continued the same RETURN instruction.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And you again reached a point where you could not confidently distinguish residual alteration.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She did not continue.</p><p>“That is three.”</p><p>“Three what?”</p><p>“Successful reductions.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Ch111.”</p><p>“Different instruction and different observation.”</p><p>“Ch114.”</p><p>“Messy.”</p><p>“Ch117.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Today.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is at least three.”</p><p>Hessa tapped the charcoal with one finger.</p><p>“You are counting categories I am keeping separate.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because Ch111 was stop-feeding after ENOUGH. Ch114 was the first deliberate RETURN and included an unintended elbowward shift plus finger-curl urge. Ch117 was cleaner overall but you sharpened an edge when you tried to refine. Today I removed the refinement question and asked for one continuous reduction.”</p><p>“All are reduction.”</p><p>“All involve reduction.”</p><p>“That is what I said.”</p><p>“No. You said they are the same count.”</p><p>“I said three.”</p><p>“You are trying to make a score.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>“I did not bring columns.”</p><p>“I am proud of you.”</p><p>“That sounded insulting.”</p><p>“It was mostly sincere.”</p><p>Mostly.</p><p>I looked at the fading charcoal line.</p><p>“So what did today answer?”</p><p>“That you can repeat the broad action under a slightly changed target without the two specific unwanted responses we saw before.”</p><p>“Broad action.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/120/Ch120_Repeated-Shaping-Test.png" alt="Greg repeats a careful shaping test at Hessa&#x27;s table while maintaining an underlying draw." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“Deliberately reduce a small shaped alteration while keeping an underlying draw active.”</p><p>“That sounds less broad.”</p><p>“It is broad compared with precise control.”</p><p>“What would precise control be?”</p><p>“Not today&#x27;s question.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“Does today increase confidence?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Does it change external effect?”</p><p>“It changes my confidence in considering it.”</p><p>My attention sharpened.</p><p>“That is almost clearance.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Scheduling?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then what changed?”</p><p>She looked at me for long enough that I regretted asking in that tone.</p><p>Then she answered anyway.</p><p>“I am less concerned that the moment you deliberately alter a draw, your only options are continue, lose the draw, or recruit some other pattern.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>That was more than I expected.</p><p>She continued.</p><p>“I have now seen you reduce an alteration while the draw remains. More than once. Under instructions that were not identical. Today you did it without the elbowward shift, without the finger urge, and without trying to repair the remaining edge separately.”</p><p>“So the next question is external.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She stared back.</p><p>“You enjoy this.”</p><p>“I enjoy accuracy.”</p><p>“You enjoy accuracy when it hurts me.”</p><p>“That is still accuracy.”</p><p>“What is the next question?”</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>“You know.”</p><p>“I have possibilities.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because then you will spend the next two days practicing a test you are not allowed to practice.”</p><p>“I cannot practice without mana.”</p><p>“You can rehearse decisions.”</p><p>That was offensive because it was true.</p><p>“I would only think about it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is not practicing.”</p><p>She gave me the same look Pessa had given me yesterday when I suggested choosing the route she was less likely to block.</p><p>Apparently my face was becoming a liability across professions.</p><p>I changed direction.</p><p>“How many living days?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“One?”</p><p>“One full day. No magic.”</p><p>“Then return?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Morning?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That sounds almost like momentum.”</p><p>“It sounds like a schedule.”</p><p>“What symptoms change it?”</p><p>“Any thumb tingling. Any finger-curl urge. Any involuntary movement. New weakness. Cold. Numbness. Pain. Anything in the left-side phantom pattern that is distinctly unusual for you. Anything you think is probably nothing but are tempted not to tell me.”</p><p>“That last category is too broad.”</p><p>“It is tailored.”</p><p>I sighed.</p><p>“One day.”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“That is shorter than last time.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/120/Ch120_Fast-Coverage-005-01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 120." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“Because today was cleaner?”</p><p>“In part.”</p><p>“What is the other part?”</p><p>“You tolerated the previous interval without delayed symptom.”</p><p>“That sounds like progress.”</p><p>“It is information.”</p><p>“You have an allergy to the word progress.”</p><p>“I have an allergy to you using it as permission.”</p><p>“I can progress without permission.”</p><p>“Not in here.”</p><p>That was fair enough to be irritating.</p><p>I rubbed my thumb against the crutch grip, then realized I was checking it.</p><p>Normal.</p><p>Hessa noticed.</p><p>“Symptom?”</p><p>“No. Checking.”</p><p>“Stop checking.”</p><p>“That seems medically irresponsible.”</p><p>“Checking once because something feels wrong is useful. Checking every thirty seconds because you want certainty creates noise.”</p><p>I lowered my hand.</p><p>“You cannot possibly know I check every thirty seconds.”</p><p>“I know you.”</p><p>“That is not measurement.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She seemed completely comfortable with this.</p><p>“And then?”</p><p>“Assessment.”</p><p>“Not external effect.”</p><p>“I did not say that.”</p><p>I went still.</p><p>Hessa&#x27;s expression changed immediately.</p><p>Not alarm.</p><p>Annoyance.</p><p>“Do not do that.”</p><p>“Do what?”</p><p>“Turn an omitted answer into permission.”</p><p>“I did not.”</p><p>“You absolutely did.”</p><p>“I observed that you did not exclude it.”</p><p>“That is not clearance.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“This is humiliating.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I hated that word.</p><p>“External-effect testing is not cleared.”</p><p>“Or scheduled.”</p><p>“Or scheduled.”</p><p>“Casting?”</p><p>“Not cleared.”</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“Not cleared.”</p><p>“Left shaping?”</p><p>“Excluded.”</p><p>“Independent draw?”</p><p>“Not allowed.”</p><p>“Independent shaping?”</p><p>“Not allowed.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Now you may be pleased.”</p><p>“I was already pleased.”</p><p>“That was the problem.”</p><p>She wiped the charcoal from my arm.</p><p>I watched the black line smear, then disappear under the damp cloth.</p><p>“Can I ask one question?”</p><p>“You have asked approximately forty.”</p><p>“One more.”</p><p>“You will ask it regardless.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>She put the cloth down.</p><p>“What would make you decide not to test external effect?”</p><p>Her expression changed.</p><p>Small.</p><p>More serious.</p><p>“Several things.”</p><p>“Such as?”</p><p>“A delayed symptom.”</p><p>“Obvious.”</p><p>“A repeat control failure that looks meaningfully different from ordinary inconsistency.”</p><p>“Meaningfully how?”</p><p>“I will decide.”</p><p>I disliked that.</p><p>“Motor recruitment again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Broad familiar pattern?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Loss of ability to release?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That one landed differently.</p><p>I had not lost release.</p><p>Not once.</p><p>Still.</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>“If I decide we do not yet understand enough about what you are doing to make an external question worth the added uncertainty.”</p><p>“External effect is added uncertainty.”</p><p>“Of course.”</p><p>“But isn&#x27;t that the point?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“The point is to ask a question we can interpret.”</p><p>That was annoyingly good.</p><p>“If something happens externally but we don&#x27;t know what internal change caused it, we learn less.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If nothing happens externally, we may also learn less.”</p><p>“Depending on the test.”</p><p>“So you need internal control good enough that external failure or success means something.”</p><p>Hessa&#x27;s mouth tightened.</p><p>I had gone too far.</p><p>Not wrong.</p><p>Too far.</p><p>“Approximately,” she said.</p><p>I wanted the rest.</p><p>I wanted the apparatus.</p><p>I wanted the exact threshold.</p><p>I wanted to know whether tomorrow&#x27;s living day was the last ordinary day before something new.</p><p>No.</p><p>That was not available.</p><p>I put my sleeve down.</p><p>Hessa watched me do it.</p><p>“You can go.”</p><p>“That was abrupt.”</p><p>“The appointment is over.”</p><p>“I am accustomed to more resistance.”</p><p>“To leaving?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That explains much.”</p><p>I stood.</p><p>Crutches.</p><p>Right hand normal on the grip.</p><p>Left.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>No dizziness.</p><p>No symptom.</p><p>At the door I stopped.</p><p>Hessa sighed before I turned.</p><p>“I have not asked yet.”</p><p>“You stopped walking.”</p><p>“That is not a question.”</p><p>“It is with you.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“What should I do today?”</p><p>She stared.</p><p>Then pointed toward the door.</p><p>“Live.”</p><p>“That instruction remains poorly specified.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>Outside, Carrow was offensively normal.</p><p>A cart had lost part of a load of onions near the corner.</p><p>Three people were collecting them while a fourth argued about whose fault it was.</p><p>A dog had acquired one onion and seemed disappointed.</p><p>I stood there longer than necessary.</p><p>One living day.</p><p>Then Hessa.</p><p>Maybe external effect.</p><p>Not scheduled.</p><p>Not cleared.</p><p>Maybe another control test.</p><p>Maybe draw only.</p><p>Maybe nothing.</p><p>I could build a decision tree.</p><p>I did not have the notebook open.</p><p>That was the only thing preventing it.</p><p>I started toward the Guild.</p><p>Not theatre.</p><p>Not because I had decided against theatre.</p><p>It was morning.</p><p>Rehearsal, if they were rehearsing, would be later.</p><p>Pessa might be working.</p><p>Lyssa might be working.</p><p>Jorren was certainly doing something he would refuse to explain properly.</p><p>The Guild would contain work I could accept or decline.</p><p>Food.</p><p>People.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>Options.</p><p>My right forearm felt ordinary beneath the sleeve.</p><p>That was becoming an achievement I did not know how to value.</p><p>At the Guild entrance, I paused.</p><p>A posting board had three new slips.</p><p>Someone I knew only by face was arguing with a clerk about a route.</p><p>Two people came out carrying packs.</p><p>The day was already happening.</p><p>Tomorrow had a rule.</p><p>Today did not.</p><p>I went inside.</p><p>For once, that was enough.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav - `chapters/010.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 7: The Appraiser — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 7</div><h1>THE APPRAISER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Antonius put a dead man's hand on the table. I looked at it. Then at him.</p><p>"That's new."</p><p>"It isn't his hand," Antonius said.</p><p>"That is exactly what someone says before explaining why a hand isn't technically a hand."</p><p>Across the table, Arlo Arwick leaned forward until his nose was perhaps six inches from the object. "It's a gauntlet." The distinction was defensible. Barely. The thing had five articulated fingers, a palm, a wrist, and enough tarnished metal plating to suggest armor, but the proportions were wrong. Too narrow through the palm. Too long in the fingers. Black leather showed beneath strips of dull silver-gray metal, and a cluster of tiny blue stones had been set along the inside of the wrist. One finger was missing. That did not help. Antonius said, "It was offered against a loan."</p><p>"By the dead man?" I asked.</p><p>"He's alive."</p><p>"Then why did you let me think he was dead?"</p><p>"I put a gauntlet on a table."</p><p>"You put a severed-looking hand on a table before breakfast."</p><p>"It's nearly noon." </p><p>I looked toward the window. It was, in fact, nearly noon.</p><p>"That's worse," I said.</p><p>Arlo touched one of the wrist stones with the end of a wooden pick. "Don't."</p><p>"I wasn't going to touch it."</p><p>"Then lean farther back. I don't know whether those wrist stones are live."</p><p>"I lean professionally."</p><p>Arlo did not look up from the stones.</p><p>"Professionally, stay off the table."</p><p>Antonius sat behind his desk with his small leather ledger closed beside one elbow. He had summoned Arlo to the warehouse and then sent Rusk to find me at Hessa's. I had assumed this meant the Tere gauge. It did not.</p><p>The gauge was still mine once the account attached to it reached ten silver, which was simultaneously an absurd bargain and a brutal lesson in short-term financing. We had negotiated five silver for the gauge itself. Vale's interest had done the rest. Antonius claimed this was educational. I claimed he was a bastard. We were both correct. Antonius tapped the metal hand. "What is it worth?" Arlo did not answer.</p><p>I did.</p><p>"To whom?" </p><p>Antonius looked at me.</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>Across the table, Arlo kept the wooden pick poised over the wrist stones and smiled without looking up. Antonius rubbed a thumb along the closed ledger.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="To Whom" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/010/v28_c10_s02_to-whom.png"/></figure><p>"One number first."</p><p>Arlo shook his head.</p><p>"Not until I know what still works."</p><p>"Then tell me what you need to know." </p><p>Antonius pointed at the gauntlet. "A man wants six gold. He says this is worth twelve. I don't know if it's worth twelve copper."</p><p>"Who is he?" I asked.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Occupation?"</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because if he's an adventurer, artificer, thief, grave robber, merchant, collector, soldier, or liar, the answer changes."</p><p>"Everyone is a liar."</p><p>"Useful. What kind?" I asked.</p><p>Antonius rested a hand on the closed ledger. "Salvager."</p><p>"Dungeon?"</p><p>"Mostly."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Antonius."</p><p>"You don't need his route."</p><p>"I might."</p><p>"You don't."</p><p>Constraint. Fine. Arlo rotated the gauntlet without touching the stones. "How old?"</p><p>"Seller says pre-Concord," Antonius said.</p><p>Arlo snorted.</p><p>"So no."</p><p>"Why?" I asked.</p><p>"Because sellers say pre-Concord when they mean old enough that nobody remembers the workshop."</p><p>"Could still be."</p><p>Arlo turned the wrist toward the light.</p><p>"Could. But the seller's date tells me nothing. The build might."</p><p>I looked more closely. Pre-Concord meant before the standardization agreements that had turned half the continent's magical craft from local secrets into merely expensive local secrets. People romanticized the period because old artificing occasionally did something modern artificers found irritatingly difficult to reproduce. Mostly, however, old magical objects were just old.</p><p>Leather rotted. Runes wore. Mana channels cracked. People saw age and imagined lost mastery because nobody wrote ballads about obsolete hinges. The wrist stones bothered me. Not because I recognized them. Because I did not. Blue stones in magical equipment usually meant nothing by themselves. Color was one of the least useful ways to identify mana-active minerals and one of the most popular ways for idiots to do it. I crouched beside the table. Arlo said, "Still don't touch."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"You touched the Tere gauge."</p><p>"That was different."</p><p>"You didn't know what it was."</p><p>"I knew it wasn't going to bite me."</p><p>"How?" Arlo asked.</p><p>"I felt confident." </p><p>Antonius laughed.</p><p>Arlo set the copper rod down.</p><p>"That is exactly why you are not touching it."</p><p>"I survived to, " I stopped.</p><p>Both men looked at me.</p><p>"To nineteen?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"Repeatedly," I said.</p><p>Arlo frowned.</p><p>I pointed at the gauntlet. "Can we make it do something?"</p><p>"Eventually."</p><p>"Why eventually?"</p><p>"Because I like having fingers."</p><p>"You have ten."</p><p>"Nine and a half."</p><p>I looked at his left hand. The tip of his smallest finger was indeed missing. I had never noticed. Arlo caught me looking and tucked the hand under the table.</p><p>"Workshop accident," he said.</p><p>"I didn't ask."</p><p>"You were going to."</p><p>Everyone was becoming Antonius. Terrible. Arlo opened his case. That was when I understood why Antonius had called both of us. Arlo knew objects. I knew consequences. Or, more accurately, I sometimes remembered consequences and then lied to myself about knowing the objects that caused them. Different skill. Useful distinction. Arlo laid out a thin copper rod, two pieces of chalk, a little glass cup, a coil of wire, and a flat stone marked with concentric circles. Antonius looked at the equipment.</p><p>"How much?"</p><p>"Enough that you're not borrowing it," Arlo said.</p><p>"I was asking for the appraisal cost."</p><p>Arlo opened the coil of wire.</p><p>"Then let me finish the appraisal."</p><p>Again. Arlo began testing. Not dramatic testing. He did not chant. Nothing glowed. He touched the copper rod to different plates, marked responses in chalk, connected wire between two points, and muttered increasingly insulting things about whoever had built the gauntlet. I watched. Antonius left the gauntlet to Arlo and watched me wait. I made it nearly a minute before looking back.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><a href="../visual/chapter_art/010/v28_c10_feature_dead-mans-hand.png" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><img alt="Dead Mans Hand" decoding="async" height="1086" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/010/v28_c10_feature_dead-mans-hand.png" width="1448"/></a></figure><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"Nothing," Antonius said.</p><p>"You're watching me instead of Arlo."</p><p>"Yes," Antonius said.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"I know what Arlo is doing."</p><p>"No, you don't."</p><p>"I know enough."</p><p>"What am I doing?"</p><p>"Waiting."</p><p>"Very observant."</p><p>"No. You're waiting to see what I say," I said.</p><p>Antonius smiled slightly.</p><p>That was new. A week ago I would have spent the whole appraisal trying to prove I knew more than Arlo. Today I was interested in why Antonius had chosen six gold as the question. Not whether the gauntlet was valuable. Whether it was useful as security. Different. I looked back at the object.</p><p>"What does the borrower need six gold for?" I asked.</p><p>"No," Antonius said.</p><p>"That's relevant."</p><p>"To whether this is worth six?"</p><p>"To whether you should care if it's worth six." </p><p>Arlo paused.</p><p>Antonius's eyes narrowed. I continued.</p><p>"If he needs six gold to buy a tavern, that's one problem. If he needs six gold to retrieve the other half of whatever this came from, that's another." </p><p>Arlo looked at Antonius. Antonius looked at me.</p><p>"Expedition."</p><p>There.</p><p>"What kind?"</p><p>"Recovery."</p><p>"His own claim?"</p><p>"Shared."</p><p>"How many people?"</p><p>"Four."</p><p>"How much has he already put in?"</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"That's the business."</p><p>"The object."</p><p>"The object is collateral for the business." </p><p>Antonius leaned back.</p><p>"Four gold."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"He has four. Needs six more."</p><p>"Total expedition ten?"</p><p>"His share."</p><p>That was worse. Or better. Depending.</p><p>"Expected return?"</p><p>"He says thirty." </p><p>I laughed. Arlo resumed his testing. </p><p>Antonius said, "Why is that funny?"</p><p>"Because thirty is a number you say when the real answer is 'I hope a lot.'"</p><p>"Agreed."</p><p>"What's the site?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Fine." I looked at Arlo. "Anything?" I asked.</p><p>"Yes," Arlo said.</p><p>"Good?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Bad?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Useful." </p><p>Arlo tapped the palm plate with the copper rod.
