A specialist could reproduce work reliably instead of trusting feel. Forty gold suddenly seemed less stupid.</p><p>Possibly more. Arlo was breathing differently. I noticed.</p><p>"How valuable?" </p><p>He did not answer.</p><p>"Arlo."</p><p>"Shut up."</p><p>"That's not a number." He examined the smallest plate.</p><p>Then another.</p><p>"These aren't all the same alloy."</p><p>"Obviously."</p><p>"No. Greg." </p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>"This is a reference set."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Do you understand what that means?"</p><p>"Enough to have ruined my negotiation."</p><p>"Who else knows you have it?"</p><p>"Antonius."</p><p>"Who else?"</p><p>"Rusk, probably."</p><p>"Who else?"</p><p>"No one." </p><p>Arlo closed the box.</p><p>"Keep it that way." </p><p>I stared.</p><p>"Forty?" </p><p>He laughed.</p><p>Not happily.</p><p>"To most people? Scrap."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"To me?"</p><p>There. I leaned forward.</p><p>"How much?" </p><p>Arlo looked at the box.</p><p>"More than I can pay."</p><p>That was not a number. It was better. For one stupid second, old calibration returned. Gold had once been logistics. Payroll. Equipment. Political favors. Emergency spell components. Numbers large enough that forty gold barely registered in some rooms. Now ten silver was difficult. And sitting between us was a piece of trash that could be worth more than Antonius's visible warehouse to exactly the right handful of people. Not to me.</p><p>That mattered. I could not eat it. Could not cast with it. Could not swing it. Could not pay Hessa with its theoretical value unless I sold it. And selling it to the wrong person would be stupid. The value lived in someone else's hands. Arlo's, perhaps. I looked at him. He was still staring at the box. Not greed. Possibility. I knew that face. Mine probably looked worse.</p><p>"What could you do with it?" Arlo answered immediately.</p><p>Then stopped. Interesting.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Arlo."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"That's Antonius's word."</p><p>"It's useful."</p><p>"What could you do?" He leaned back.</p><p>"Better regulators."</p><p>"How much better?"</p><p>"I don't know."</p><p>"Approximately."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Not enough information yet?" He glared. </p><p>I smiled.</p><p>Then he said, "Consistent." The word was quiet. </p><p>I stopped smiling. There it was. Not stronger. Consistent. Arlo's shale work had already shown me how much of early artificing lived in hands, habits, batches, intuition, tiny corrections nobody wrote down. A reference set changed that. Maybe. If genuine. If complete enough. If Arlo knew how to use it. If we did not destroy it learning.</p><p>Branches. So many. Arwick Works. Future manufacturing. Standards. Scale. My mind opened like a door in a storm. Arlo. Antonius. Capital. Shale ceramics. Regulators. Calibration service. Sell access, not object. License,</p><p>No.</p><p>I stopped. Arlo noticed.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"You had the face."</p><p>"I killed it."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"Mostly." He laughed. </p><p>I put both hands on the table.</p><p>"What do you need from me?" </p><p>Arlo frowned.</p><p>That was not the question he expected.</p><p>Good.</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"Wrong."</p><p>"It's your gauge."</p><p>"Exactly. And it is useless to me."</p><p>"Sell it."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then what?" I looked at the box. Then at Arlo.</p><p>"Use it." He went still.</p><p>Not dramatically. Arlo was not dramatic. His stillness was smaller. More expensive.</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"I didn't say take it."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"I said use it."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>Because Arwick mattered. Because I remembered the name. Because future workshops stamped ARWICK on things important people trusted. Because maybe this was one of the bricks. Because I was better at seeing Arlo's next step than my own. Because the object was worth more in his hands than mine. Too many answers. I chose the present one.</p><p>"Because you're the only artificer I know who understands why it's valuable."</p><p>"That's a terrible reason."</p><p>"It's the reason available."</p><p>"You barely know me."</p><p>"I know your work."</p><p>"You know three weeks of my work."</p><p>"How much do you need?"</p><p>"For what?"</p><p>"To test it without damaging it." </p><p>Arlo looked at me for a long moment. Then at the box.</p><p>"Time."</p><p>"I have debt."</p><p>"Not your time."</p><p>"Oh."</p><p>"Mine."</p><p>That was harder. He had orders. Shale experiments. Actual customers. A roof with ambitions.</p><p>"How much?"</p><p>"Two days."</p><p>"That's not money."</p><p>"It is to me."</p><p>Right.</p><p>I thought of Antonius. What has to be true for repayment to happen? Different problem. What has to be true for Arlo to use the gauge? He needs two days he cannot afford to spend. So the bottleneck was not the gauge. It was Arlo's time. Clean.</p><p>"How much do your next two days earn?"</p><p>Arlo's eyes narrowed.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Approximately."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"One gold?" He laughed.</p><p>"Less."</p><p>"Half?"</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Six silver?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>There.</p><p>"I'll cover six." </p><p>He stared. </p><p>I stared back.</p><p>Then remembered I did not have six silver.</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>Arlo's face changed as he watched me remember.</p><p>"You don't have six silver."</p><p>"Not currently."</p><p>"Get out."</p><p>"I can."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Antonius, "</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Not borrow."</p><p>"That sentence was going to become borrow."</p><p>"I was going to say structure."</p><p>"Out." I laughed.</p><p>"Fine." </p><p>I picked up the box. </p><p>Arlo put one hand on it. </p><p>I looked at his hand. </p><p>He looked at mine.</p><p>"Leave it," he said.</p><p>"Receipt."</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>"Signed."</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>"Value acknowledged."</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>"Ten silver replacement value would be insulting."</p><p>"Forty gold would be insane."</p><p>"Excellent. Somewhere between." He found paper. I smiled.</p><p>There it was again. A problem with edges. Two days of Arlo's time. Six silver, perhaps. A gauge. A workshop. No question about what Greg should become. No new career. No build. Just:</p><p>How do I make Arlo better? The answer came so quickly it was almost embarrassing. I would find the six silver. Not borrow it. Probably. Maybe.</p><p>No.</p><p>Not borrow it. I watched Arlo write the receipt. Outside, evening had settled over Carrow. Somewhere beyond the walls, a salvager was preparing for a dungeon expedition with five of Antonius's gold. I wanted to know where. I wanted to go. I wanted to see what he found. My mana channels had finally held shape for a heartbeat. Arlo had a tool that might change his workshop. Antonius was learning to use me. Everything was moving. For once, I did not add another direction. I had enough.</p><p>Hessa. Barrier. Arlo. Six silver. Tomorrow. I started home. Then stopped. Six silver. I knew exactly where I could make six silver tonight. The Crown and Knives. I stood in the street for a long moment.</p><p>"No."</p><p>A man passing beside me looked over. I ignored him. Six silver. Cards. People. Easy. Probably.</p><p>No.</p><p>I kept walking. Twenty steps. Thirty. At forty, I turned around.</p><p>"Fuck."</p><p>Then turned around again. Home. Constraint. Home. I made it three streets before realizing I was laughing. Being responsible was exhausting.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Home Not Cards" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/010/v28_c10_s03_home-not-cards.png"/></figure></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="009.html">← Chapter 6</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="011.html">Chapter 8 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/179.html:189`: <p>The mana came cleanly.</p>
- `chapters/179.html:246`: <p>The mana was already there.</p>
- `chapters/179.html:283`: <p>The mana held.</p>
- `chapters/179.html:329`: <p>Not mana.</p>

- `chapters/029.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 23: The Witness — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 23</div><h1>THE WITNESS</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The bread remained gone. I checked. That was the first mistake of the morning. Not checking the sill. Caring. The outer ledge held flour dust, two black crumbs, and a streak that might have been butter if butter had survived the night, rain, birds, insects, and my imagination. No footprints. No claw marks. No note. No useful evidence. I closed the window.</p><p>Downstairs, Brina was already angry at dough.</p><p>“Too cold,” she said.</p><p>The dough did not apologize. Alden sat at a table eating yesterday’s coarse bread with jam. He had somehow acquired jam.</p><p>“Where did that come from?”</p><p>“Brina.”</p><p>I looked at Brina. She pointed a floury finger at a crock.</p><p>“Plum.”</p><p>“Why did he get some?”</p><p>“He asked.”</p><p>I looked at Alden. He spread more.</p><p>“That cannot be the lesson.”</p><p>“It is often the lesson.”</p><p>I asked for jam. Brina gave me jam. Terrible. My body had changed overnight. Not improved. Changed. The bruises had become more specific. Yesterday my entire side hurt. Today individual parts had organized themselves into complaints: hip, ribs, shoulder, palm, knee. My channels were quieter. The pressure behind my eyes was gone. The NO CASTING tag remained tied to my wrist. Alden’s NO LIFTING LEFT tag remained too.</p><p>He tested his shoulder when he thought I was not looking. I looked.</p><p>“Don’t.”</p><p>“I’m checking.”</p><p>“You are lifting your arm.”</p><p>“That is how I check.”</p><p>“Your healer can check.”</p><p>“You sound like her.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He lowered it. I ate bread. No bells. That was new.</p><p>“What happened overnight?” I asked Brina.</p><p>“Bread.”</p><p>“In town.”</p><p>“Bread happened in town.”</p><p>“Apart from bread.”</p><p>She thought.</p><p>“East fire out.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Two missing people found.”</p><p>The single bell.</p><p>“Alive?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>Not good.</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“Don’t know.”</p><p>“Creatures?”</p><p>“Ask watch.”</p><p>“Road?”</p><p>“Ask watch.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“Flour wagon came.”</p><p>That mattered to Brina more than creatures. I finished eating. At the door, Brina said, “Rooms tonight are not free.”</p><p>“We worked.”</p><p>“Yesterday.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Four copper each.”</p><p>Alden stopped.</p><p>“Four?”</p><p>“Or work.”</p><p>“What work?”</p><p>“Depends what breaks.”</p><p>I liked that less than a fixed price.</p><p>“Do we need to decide now?”</p><p>“Before midday.”</p><p>Ordinary problem. Again. We left. Darrowmere in morning looked less frightened and more tired. Boards covered two broken windows on Dyer’s Lane. A carpenter repaired a gate while the owner argued that he was using the wrong nails.</p><p>Three children carried a basket of eggs past a watch barricade. Someone had painted EAST ROAD CLOSED on a plank and leaned it against a barrel.</p><p>Below it, smaller:</p><p>NORTH ROAD CONTROLLED.</p><p>WEST OPEN.</p><p>The chalk board in the square had been reorganized. Not cleaned. Reorganized. ROOMS NEEDED had shrunk. WORK CREWS had grown. MISSING PERSONS contained five names. Two were crossed out. One had ALIVE beside it. One had BODY. One remained. Alden stopped. I stopped beside him. Neither of us knew the names. That did not make the board less heavy.</p><p>A new section read:</p><p>RECOVERED PROPERTY.</p><p>CART 14.</p><p>THREE HORSES.</p><p>RED TOOL CHEST.</p><p>SIX SACKS WOOL.</p><p>SWORD, ROAD TEAM.</p><p>Cal’s. Maybe mine.</p><p>“Road team,” Alden said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>We went to command. Captain Doven was asleep at the map table. Standing. Not literally asleep. Close. Nemi Caul was gone. Iris was there. She had a cup in one hand and three written reports in the other. She saw me look at the cup.</p><p>“Coffee.”</p><p>“What is coffee?”</p><p>She looked at me. I knew coffee. Not future memory. Current world. I had simply never seen it here.</p><p>“Bitter bean drink.”</p><p>“That sounds terrible.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>She drank.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Morning.”</p><p>Fair. Alden pointed at the property board outside.</p><p>“Swords?”</p><p>“Yard.”</p><p>“Both?”</p><p>“Recovery brought two.”</p><p>Cal’s sword had been inside the dead creature. Mine had been thrown at a creature and abandoned. Two swords. Good.</p><p>“Bodies?” I asked.</p><p>Iris pointed toward the rear yard.</p><p>“Also there.”</p><p>Of course they were. Alden looked at me.</p><p>“You care more about the bodies.”</p><p>“I care about my sword.”</p><p>“You looked toward the yard before she said sword.”</p><p>“I contain multitudes.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>Doven opened his eyes.</p><p>“I heard that.”</p><p>“You were asleep.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You were dreaming administratively.”</p><p>He rubbed his face.</p><p>“Report if you have one. Otherwise stop being interesting before breakfast.”</p><p>“We slept.”</p><p>“Excellent report.”</p><p>He looked at our tags.</p><p>“Medical review.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Infirmary.”</p><p>“Then bodies?”</p><p>“After.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because if the healer says no, you do not touch anything.”</p><p>“I can look without touching.”</p><p>Doven stared.</p><p>“Medical review.”</p><p>We went. The same healer was there. Unfortunately. She recognized me. More unfortunately.</p><p>“Sit. Wrist first.”</p><p>“I have not asked anything.”</p><p>“Good. Keep it that way until I check you.”</p><p>She cut off the old tag. Good. Then checked my eyes. Palm. Breathing. Ribs. She pressed the bruised spot. I disliked her again.</p><p>“Headache?”</p><p>“Gone.”</p><p>“Channel heat?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Tremor?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cast.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Tiny.”</p><p>“You told me not to.”</p><p>“Yesterday.”</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“Light.”</p><p>“I don’t know light.”</p><p>“Of course you don’t.”</p><p>She pointed at a wooden bead on the table.</p><p>“Move it.”</p><p>I almost laughed. Bean. Bead. The universe lacked imagination.</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Magic.”</p><p>“That is broad.”</p><p>“Then do something small you actually know.”</p><p>I looked at the bead. Barrier. Coin-sized. Brief. No load. I formed it beside the bead and released. Clean. The bead did not move. Good. The healer watched my eyes.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I did. Slight pressure. No pain.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Third. Pressure increased. Not sharp. She held up a hand.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>I stopped. She wrote a new strip.</p><p>LIMITED CASTING.</p><p>I read it.</p><p>“What does limited mean?”</p><p>“Exactly what it sounds like.”</p><p>“That is not measurable.”</p><p>“It means if you start experimenting, I will break your fingers.”</p><p>“Medical terminology has declined.”</p><p>She tied the strip.</p><p>“Small, low-load casting. No repeated pressure work. Stop at headache, heat, tremor, numbness, or visual changes. You do not test where the limit is.”</p><p>“I understand.”</p><p>She narrowed her eyes.</p><p>“I think you understand words.”</p><p>“That is a start.”</p><p>Alden’s review went worse. He could move his shoulder. He could not lift against resistance without pain.</p><p>New tag:</p><p>LIGHT USE LEFT.</p><p>He looked at mine.</p><p>“Yours is better.”</p><p>“It is not a competition.”</p><p>“Yours says casting.”</p><p>“Yours says arm.”</p><p>“I have two arms.”</p><p>“I have one mana system.”</p><p>He considered.</p><p>“I win.”</p><p>“You have misunderstood.”</p><p>We recovered our swords. Mine had a chipped edge. Cal’s had dried black blood in the fuller and a new notch near the tip. Cal himself was not there.</p><p>“Where is he?” Alden asked.</p><p>Property clerk shrugged.</p><p>“Rider.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/029/Ch029_Creature-Under-Canvas.jpg" alt="A butcher lifts canvas from a dead strange creature in the busy watch yard as Greg and Alden observe." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>That was answer enough. He had a job. He had gone back to it. I liked that. The dead creatures were under canvas at the far end of the yard. Four now, not three. That had changed overnight. A watch mage stood beside them. Young man. Maybe twenty-six. Blue cord around one sleeve. He was arguing with a butcher.</p><p>“Muscle attaches here,” the butcher said.</p><p>“I can see that,” the mage said.</p><p>“Then stop calling it abnormal,” the butcher said.</p><p>“It is abnormal,” the mage said.</p><p>“For a dog,” the butcher said.</p><p>“It looks like a dog,” the mage said.</p><p>“It is not a dog,” the butcher said.</p><p>Good. I approached. The mage saw my Bronze pin. Then my tag.</p><p>“Limited casting?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then don’t.”</p><p>“I was not planning to.”</p><p>He looked skeptical. Reasonable. The butcher lifted the canvas. Dead creature. Less frightening. More wrong. Death had taken away the smoothness. Now the joints looked merely excessive. The black ridge along the spine was hair. The chest ridges were visible through pale underside skin. I crouched. Did not touch.</p><p>“Fourth recovered where?”</p><p>The mage said, “East wall.”</p><p>“Last night?”</p><p>“Early morning.”</p><p>“Same?”</p><p>“Mostly.”</p><p>Mostly.</p><p>“What differs?”</p><p>He pointed.</p><p>“This one.”</p><p>Smaller. Narrower skull. Less ridge development. The butcher said, “Female.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>He looked at me. I regretted asking.</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>Alden laughed. The butcher continued.</p><p>“Young too.”</p><p>“How young?”</p><p>“Not a pup. Not old.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/029/Ch029_Fast-Coverage-003-C02.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 29." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>The mage said, “Mana is lower.”</p><p>“Because younger?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“What have you found?”</p><p>The mage shifted between me and the body.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>There it was. Not my investigation.</p><p>“I fought them.”</p><p>“That gets you treatment, not access.”</p><p>Correct. I stood.</p><p>“Fair.”</p><p>I started to leave. His eyes dropped to my wrist tag.</p><p>“Wait.”</p><p>I stopped. He pointed at my wrist.</p><p>“What kind of casting?”</p><p>“Barrier.”</p><p>That changed his face. Not awe. Interest.</p><p>“Guild Barrier?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What school?”</p><p>“Mostly bad decisions.”</p><p>Alden said, “Accurate.” The mage looked at him.</p><p>“Who are you?”</p><p>“Alden.”</p><p>“Helpful.”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>The butcher went back to work. The mage said, “I’m Kellan.”</p><p>“Greg,” I said.</p><p>“I know,” Kellan said.</p><p>Again. I disliked Darrowmere. Kellan crouched by the body.</p><p>“Watch mage yesterday called the mana diffuse.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That was me.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“It changed.”</p><p>I became still.</p><p>“After death?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Dropped.”</p><p>“That is expected.”</p><p>“Not like this.”</p><p>He pointed to three chalk marks on a board. Numbers. Not a scale I knew. Current professional measurement. Good.</p><p>“What are those?”</p><p>“Field saturation readings.”</p><p>I did not pretend.</p><p>“Teach me the units later. What matters now?”</p><p>Kellan tapped the first.</p><p>“Alive estimate from residue at wound site.”</p><p>Second.</p><p>“Immediately after death.”</p><p>Third.</p><p>“This morning.”</p><p>The third was much lower.</p><p>“How much lower than expected?”</p><p>“Enough that I checked the instrument.”</p><p>“Instrument good?”</p><p>“Against reference stone.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Other bodies?”</p><p>“Same direction. Different rates.”</p><p>“Meaning?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>Better. The butcher said, “Meaning dead things stop being magical.” Kellan looked annoyed.</p><p>“That is not precise.”</p><p>“It is useful.”</p><p>Also good. Alden was examining the creature’s feet. Not touching. Learning. He pointed.</p><p>“Claws are worn.”</p><p>The butcher looked.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“From walls?”</p><p>“Could be road.”</p><p>“Could be stone.”</p><p>“Could be both.”</p><p>Alden nodded. No grand conclusion. Good. Kellan lifted one front paw. The pads were cut. Not fresh. Old damage. Scarring.</p><p>“These have been on hard ground,” Alden said.</p><p>“Probably,” the butcher replied.</p><p>Not forest animals wandering in yesterday. Maybe. Do not jump. I looked at the teeth. Ordinary teeth in unusual jaw. One tooth was broken. Another worn flat. The body had history. Whatever it was, it had existed before Darrowmere became afraid of it. That was obvious. Still useful. A shadow crossed the yard. I looked up. Bird. Actual bird. It landed on the roof.</p><p>I watched it. Alden noticed. Said nothing. Good. Kellan covered the body.</p><p>“Watch is sending samples to the city.”</p><p>“Our city?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Who?”</p><p>“Guild warder requested.”</p><p>Edrin. Maybe.</p><p>“Edrin Saye?”</p><p>Kellan looked at me.</p><p>“You know her?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then yes.”</p><p>Interesting. South Canal seal. Darrowmere creature samples. Not necessarily connected. Probably not. One competent warder could receive multiple strange problems because that was her job. Do not make the world smaller. Doven found us in the yard.</p><p>“You two available?”</p><p>Alden said, “Yes.” I said, “For what?” </p><p>Doven looked at Alden.</p><p>“He learns.”</p><p>“Slowly.”</p><p>Doven handed us a paper.</p><p>“West road escort.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“West?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Away from creatures?”</p><p>“That is generally where we send civilians.”</p><p>The paper listed fourteen people. Three children. One injured adult. Two carts. Destination: our city. Escort needed to west checkpoint, then city watch handoff. No monster hunt. No east breach. No mystery. Just people leaving. Alden read it.</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Half hour.”</p><p>“Pay?”</p><p>“Guild relief rate. Eight copper each.”</p><p>Alden looked at me. Eight copper. Enough for rooms, food, and some replacement equipment. Not enough to become interesting. Perfect.</p><p>“Take it,” I said.</p><p>Alden frowned.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You wanted Darrowmere.”</p><p>“We’re in Darrowmere.”</p><p>“You want east.”</p><p>He did. I could see it. So could Doven. Alden looked toward the eastern roofs. Then at his LIGHT USE LEFT tag. Then at the escort sheet.</p><p>“Eight copper?”</p><p>“Each,” Doven said.</p><p>Alden sighed.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>Doven handed him the paper.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“What about after?”</p><p>“If you come back, ask.”</p><p>Not promised. Not denied. Work. We met the civilians outside the west gate. One cart carried bedding, pots, and an old man with a bandaged foot. The other carried sacks and three children who had been told not to touch anything and were touching everything. A woman counted everyone twice. Then a third time.</p><p>“Fourteen,” she said.</p><p>“Fourteen,” Alden agreed.</p><p>She pointed at him.</p><p>“You count too.”</p><p>He counted. Fourteen. I counted. Fourteen. Dema Rusk would have approved. That annoyed me. We started west. The town receded behind us. No bells. No screaming. No monsters. Just wheels, hooves, and children asking how far. The smallest girl stared at my wrist.</p><p>“What does limited casting mean?”</p><p>“It means I am allowed to do very little magic.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I did too much yesterday.”</p><p>“Was it good?”</p><p>“Some of it.”</p><p>“Can you make fire?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Light?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fly?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She looked disappointed.</p><p>“What can you do?”</p><p>“Barrier.”</p><p>“What’s that?”</p><p>I held up my hands.</p><p>“Not demonstrating.”</p><p>She thought.</p><p>“So nothing.”</p><p>Alden laughed. I ignored him. At the first rise outside town, I looked back. Darrowmere sat under clear morning light. Smoke thin now. East wall visible. Bell tower. Roofs. Normal from here. Almost. Something stood on the bell tower. I stopped. Too far. A dark shape. Could be a person. Could be a bird. Could be part of the stone.</p><p>“What?” Alden asked.</p><p>I looked. The shape was gone.</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>He followed my gaze.</p><p>“Still?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He did not joke. That was new. The woman ahead shouted, </p><p>“Are you escorting or sightseeing?” Alden called, “Escort.” He started walking. </p><p>I stayed one second longer. </p><p>Nothing moved on the tower. No proof. No bread. No tap. Just distance. </p><p>I turned west.</p><p>Fourteen people. Two carts. Three children. One injured adult. Eight copper. That was the job. For once, the mystery could wait behind us. It did not feel like it was waiting.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="028.html">← Chapter 22</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="030.html">Chapter 24 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/278.html:134`: <p>The versions I remembered could make crossing the seam harder for air and water. Some later or better work had additional resistance to heat, smell, or mana leakage, but I did not know whether that came from the clasp, the collar, preparation of the vessel, or all three.</p>
- `chapters/049.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 41: The Tester — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 41</div><h1>THE TESTER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The next morning, Sevren went north. I went to Arlo. This was not because Sevren went north. Probably. The regulator was still wrapped in cloth beside my bed. Six washers. Notes. Cold test. Orientation test. Vibration test still owed. Arlo had asked for mechanical vibration specifically. Not mana. Good. I ate before leaving. No dramatic accounting. Also good. The workshop door was open.</p><p>Vessa was carrying a tray of ceramic bodies from the kiln room. She saw me.</p><p>“Wait outside. Glaze firing.”</p><p>“I brought the regulator.”</p><p>“Good. Outside.”</p><p>“Arlo asked.”</p><p>“He can ask from outside too.”</p><p>That meant something. Not my something.</p><p>“How long?”</p><p>She shifted the tray against her hip.</p><p>“Until it is not glaze firing.”</p><p>Reasonable.</p><p>“Can I wait?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Progress. I sat on an overturned crate outside. The lane smelled like wet clay and cabbage. Across the way, a cooper rolled two hoops down the street with a stick. One escaped. A child caught it. No Barrier. Everyone survived.</p><p>Arlo appeared ten minutes later carrying three narrow metal rods and a cup. He saw me.</p><p>“Good,” Arlo said.</p><p>Vessa called from inside, “No.”</p><p>Arlo looked toward her.</p><p>“Why no?” he asked.</p><p>“Glaze,” Vessa said.</p><p>“Right.”</p><p>He handed me the cup. Water. Not coffee. Probably safer.</p><p>“What are you doing?” I asked.</p><p>“Waiting.”</p><p>Good workshop. We waited. This felt inefficient. Then I noticed everyone else was moving. Vessa checked kiln vents. A boy I had not seen before ground pigment at the back bench. Arlo measured one rod against another, rejected one, marked it, and put it aside. A customer came for two lamp housings. Vessa handled it. Arlo did not stop measuring.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Vessa and the workshop crew working around the test frame." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/049/svgPLG_Ch49_Vessas-Vibration-Frame.png"/></figure><p>The workshop was not waiting. I was. Different. I drank water. The boy grinding pigment glanced at me twice.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I asked. He looked down.</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Arlo said, “He knows who you are.” I looked at him.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>The boy said, “Barrier.” Of course.</p><p>“What is your name?”</p><p>“Len.”</p><p>“Do you work here?”</p><p>“Today.”</p><p>Arlo said, “His uncle owes me.” Len said, “You owe him.”</p><p>“Same system.”</p><p>Not my business. Progress again. After maybe twenty minutes, Vessa came out.</p><p>“Now.”</p><p>We went in. The regulator went on the side bench. Arlo had built something. Of course. A wooden frame. Two uprights. Crossbar. Leather straps. Small crank at one side connected to an off-center wheel. When turned, the bench plate shook. Not violently. Fast. Mechanical vibration. Simple. Ugly. Excellent.</p><p>“You made this?”</p><p>“Vessa.”</p><p>I looked at her. She shrugged.</p><p>“Arlo made the bad one.”</p><p>Arlo pointed.</p><p>“First one walked.”</p><p>“Across the floor?”</p><p>“Off the bench.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“So this is second.”</p><p>“Third.”</p><p>Better.</p><p>“What do you want to know?” I asked.</p><p>Arlo looked at my notes.</p><p>“Same flow. Same regulator. Different vibration.”</p><p>“How measured?”</p><p>“By crank speed.”</p><p>“That is not measured.”</p><p>Vessa said, “Here we go.” Arlo ignored her.</p><p>“Marked wheel.”</p><p>He showed me. Four ink marks. Slow. Medium. Fast. Very fast. Not exact frequency. Enough categories.</p><p>“Who turns?” I asked.</p><p>“You,” Arlo said.</p><p>“Why?” I asked.</p><p>“Because your hand was not part of the fixture last time,” Arlo said.</p><p>Fair.</p><p>“What do you want recorded?”</p><p>“Flow stability. Flutter. Any change in output. Any visible shift.”</p><p>“And sound?”</p><p>Arlo looked at me.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>Vessa said, “No mana.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She pointed at me.</p><p>“No Barrier holding anything still.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>That rule existed because of me now. Not proud. We mounted the regulator. Cold water feed. Catch bowl. Same washer as previous baseline. Arlo checked collar. Vessa checked body support. Two supports now. Opposite sides. Ceramic body no longer depended on hand pressure. Good. We ran no vibration first. Flow clean. Low pulse. No leak. Then slow. Small flutter. Then medium. More.</p><p>Fast. Output changed. Not much. Enough. Very fast. The whole fixture hummed. Arlo stopped me.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“Fast.”</p><p>We repeated. Same. Then medium. Same. Then no vibration. Clean again. Good. Reversible. I wrote. Arlo changed washer. Smaller opening. No vibration. Stable. Slow. Stable. Medium. Flutter. Fast. Worse than first washer. Interesting.</p><p>“Pressure sensitivity?” I asked.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Or seat movement.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Or frame resonance.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>Arlo smiled. He liked maybe when it was real. Vessa did not.</p><p>“Can we find out?” I asked.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>Arlo took the regulator apart. Not answer. Method. He swapped one spacer. Reassembled. Run again. Different. Flutter started later.</p><p>“Spacer stiffness,” I said.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Seat compression?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>Vessa said, “I hate both of you.” We kept going. Third configuration. Then fourth. Arlo changed one thing each time. Not always what I would have changed. Good. He knew his object. I knew support behavior. Different. The second spacer was softer. Worse. We returned to first. Better again.</p><p>Then Arlo rotated the whole regulator body ninety degrees without changing the washer. I almost objected because that was two lines of inquiry crossing. Then remembered orientation was already characterized. This was not a clean first experiment. It was a shop.</p><p>“Why rotate now?” I asked.</p><p>“Because customer mounts sideways.”</p><p>There. Actual use.</p><p>“Which customer?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fair.”</p><p>Sideways plus medium vibration produced less flutter than upright plus medium. Unexpected. I checked note twice.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Arlo grinned. Now I was asking. Again. Same. Vessa leaned close.</p><p>“Fixture?”</p><p>“Could be.”</p><p>Arlo touched one support.</p><p>“No hand.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“We should isolate support pressure.”</p><p>I said it too quickly. Arlo nodded toward a pile of work.</p><p>“Tomorrow has already been invented.”</p><p>Right. By midday we had something. Not a solution. A shape. The regulator tolerated low vibration well. At higher vibration, instability arrived sooner with the smaller washer. A stiffer spacer delayed onset but did not eliminate it. Body support helped consistency between runs. Orientation still interacted with vibration rather than disappearing beneath it.</p><p>Sideways mounting might be more stable in one tested configuration, but one fixture was not a law. No mana. No magic. No brilliant breakthrough. Useful. Arlo ate standing. Bread. Cheese. Vessa had an apple. I had brought meat and bread. Len ate outside. We ate around the bench.</p><p>“What does this change?” I asked.</p><p>Arlo chewed.</p><p>“For current piece?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Mounting guidance.”</p><p>“That is all?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“That is useful.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“What guidance?”</p><p>“Do not mount on vibrating frame.”</p><p>I waited. He smiled.</p><p>“More specific later.”</p><p>Vessa said, “Put that on the card.” Arlo said, “Not yet.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Need repeat with hot line.”</p><p>I looked toward the burner bench.</p><p>Vessa pointed at the kiln room.</p><p>“Not during this firing.”</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>Arlo said, “Second bell.”</p><p>Arlo laughed. Hot line meant real operating heat. Different materials. Expansion. Seals. Risk. Not today. Good. I looked at the second body support on the ceramic fixture across the room.</p><p>“Cracks?”</p><p>Arlo followed my eyes.</p><p>“Fewer.”</p><p>“How many?”</p><p>“Two in twelve.”</p><p>“Before?”</p><p>“Three in seven.”</p><p>Not enough data. Promising.</p><p>“Same firing?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Same clay?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Same worker?”</p><p>Vessa looked up.</p><p>“Why?” she asked.</p><p>“Trying to isolate,” I said.</p><p>“No,” Vessa said.</p><p>“What?” I asked.</p><p>“You are trying to turn my week into your experiment,” Vessa said.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/049/Ch049_Fast-Coverage-003-B11.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 49." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>There. I stopped. She pointed the apple at me.</p><p>“We changed support because it was obviously wrong.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“We also changed cooling rack.”</p><p>I had not known.</p><p>“And one glaze batch.”</p><p>Also no.</p><p>“And Arlo stopped stacking them like an idiot.”</p><p>Arlo said, “That was one time.”</p><p>“Four.”</p><p>“So crack reduction is confounded.”</p><p>Vessa blinked.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then we cannot attribute.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Arlo said, “We can still sell the ones that did not crack.” There. Actual objective. Not proving mechanism. Making good pieces. I had almost made their workshop answer my question instead of their customers. Again.</p><p>“I understand.”</p><p>Vessa took another bite.</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“Temporarily.”</p><p>“Good enough.”</p><p>Arlo finished bread.</p><p>“What about regulator?”</p><p>I looked at notes.</p><p>“Current evidence supports mounting guidance. Need hot-line repeat before anything stronger.”</p><p>He nodded. No correction. Good. Then a customer came in carrying a broken lantern frame. Not our problem. Arlo took it. Looked.</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>Customer said, “Today.”</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>“Need tonight.”</p><p>“Then buy new.”</p><p>Customer looked at the price board. Did not.</p><p>“Tomorrow.”</p><p>Done. Arlo put the broken frame in a tray. Work. I started packing the regulator. Vessa said, “Leave it.” I looked up.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Hot line tomorrow.”</p><p>Arlo said, “If you can come.” Requested. Existing thread. Narrow.</p><p>“I can.”</p><p>“Morning.”</p><p>“Which bell?”</p><p>“Second.”</p><p>Good. Specific. I left the regulator. This felt strange. Object stayed in another person's workshop because they had work for it. Not because I had abandoned it. Not because storage cost money. Because it belonged in tomorrow's task. Small thing. Still. I washed my hands. There was clay dust on them anyway. At the door, Arlo called after me.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>I turned. He held up my notes.</p><p>“You wrote sound.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What did you hear?”</p><p>“Fast vibration had a higher rattle before output changed.”</p><p>“Fixture or regulator?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>He handed notes back. That word again. I walked out. I had half a day. No regulator. No Sevren. No urgent note. No reason to go to Varo except curiosity. Dangerous. I went to the Guild instead. Not for a job. Mostly. Alden was in the practice yard. Not sparring. Watching. Two Bronze fighters worked with padded sticks. One was Pessa. The other I did not know.</p><p>Alden stood beside Berren. Berren's right foot was wrapped inside a loose boot. He saw me.</p><p>“Pig.”</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>Pessa heard.</p><p>“Road expert.”</p><p>Excellent. She did not stop sparring. Good. Alden grinned.</p><p>“You working?”</p><p>“Worked.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Regulator.”</p><p>He nodded like that meant something. Probably not. Berren looked at my empty hands.</p><p>“No sword?”</p><p>“I have sword.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Home.”</p><p>He looked offended.</p><p>“I was not planning to fight the Guild.”</p><p>“Coward.”</p><p>Alden's attention returned to the yard. The unknown Bronze overcommitted. Pessa stepped outside line and tapped ribs. Clean. Alden said, “Again.” Not to them. To himself. I watched him. His left arm moved unconsciously once. Practicing timing. No injury. Pattern.</p><p>“What are you working on?” I asked.</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>Lie.</p><p>“Your left hand moved.”</p><p>He looked at it.</p><p>“Fuck.”</p><p>Berren laughed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I asked. Alden shook his head.</p><p>“Later.”</p><p>Good. Not mine. The pair reset. This time the unknown Bronze shortened the first strike. Pessa still touched shoulder. Different opening. Alden's hand moved again. Not copying Pessa. Timing response. He had something. I wanted to ask. I did not. This was becoming irritating. Pessa finished round. Came over sweating.</p><p>“You owe me.”</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Bridge.”</p><p>“What bridge?”</p><p>“West road. Oren finally sent crew. Brace was worse than it looked.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>“I did nothing.”</p><p>“You told farmer.”</p><p>“Alden did.”</p><p>“I reported.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So why owe?”</p><p>She grinned.</p><p>“You don't. Wanted to see your face.”</p><p>I disliked her. Reasonable.</p><p>“Fixed?”</p><p>“Temporary brace. Full repair next week.”</p><p>Good. Infrastructure continued. Without me. Berren shifted foot. Small wince. I noticed. Did not ask. Progress. Then he noticed me noticing.</p><p>“Still attached.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Disappointed?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Liar.”</p><p>Alden said, “He would redesign it.”</p><p>“My foot?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Better ankle.”</p><p>“Fuck both of you.”</p><p>Pessa looked at Berren.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“Bit.”</p><p>“By?”</p><p>“Thing.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>No one elaborated. Good. A runner came from the contract desk and called Alden's name. Alden looked over.</p><p>“Coming.”</p><p>He picked up his coat.</p><p>“What?” Berren asked.</p><p>“North practice.”</p><p>“With who?”</p><p>“Ressa.”</p><p>That name caught. Captain Ressa existed elsewhere in my head. Could be same. Could be not. No. Do not assign.</p><p>“Which Ressa?” I asked.</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Common enough.”</p><p>“Dema's group.”</p><p>Different context. Good. He pulled coat on. Berren said, “You said you were done.”</p><p>“I said I was watching.”</p><p>“That is not done.”</p><p>“Not my problem.”</p><p>He left. Independent. Someone else wanted his time. Or he wanted theirs. Either way. I did not follow. Pessa went to wash. Berren stayed seated. I walked home. On the way, I passed a courier in a brown coat. Not Sevren. For half a second I expected him. Then did not. Good. At lodging, I opened notebook.</p><p>REGULATOR:</p><p>mechanical vibration affects stability smaller washer destabilizes earlier stiffer spacer delays onset support improves repeatability orientation still interacts sideways may be more stable in one configuration hot-line test tomorrow sound change may precede output change cause unknown</p><p>CERAMIC:</p><p>do not steal workshop into experiment I underlined that.</p><p>Then wrote:</p><p>ALDEN LEFT FOR NORTH PRACTICE.</p><p>Crossed it out. Not information I needed. Another improvement. Maybe. I closed notebook. Tomorrow, second bell, Arlo. That was enough.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="048.html">← Chapter 40</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="050.html">Chapter 42 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/011.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 8: The Mage — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 8</div><h1>THE MAGE</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The first Barrier I cast in my second life was approximately the size of a dinner plate. It lasted less than a second. It gave me a headache. Hessa kept two fingers raised where it had vanished, as if the empty air still owed her evidence. I stared too. Then I laughed.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Dinner Plate Barrier" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/011/v28_c11_s01_dinner-plate-barrier.png"/></figure><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>"No," Hessa said.</p><p>"That was a Barrier."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"A real Barrier."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"I cast magic."</p><p>"You did."</p><p>"Again."</p><p>"No." </p><p>I turned toward her. "You cannot possibly expect me to stop there."</p><p>"I expected you to stop before there."</p><p>"That seems pessimistic."</p><p>Hessa stepped between me and the center of the practice room. She was not large, but she had developed a particular way of standing that implied I would have to physically move her if I wanted to continue, and neither of us believed that would end well for me.</p><p>"Sit down," Hessa said.</p><p>"I am not tired."</p><p>"Your left eye is twitching." </p><p>I blinked. </p><p>The left eye twitched.</p><p>"Unrelated."</p><p>"Sit."</p><p>Reasonable. I sat. The room was small enough that my knees nearly touched the chalk circle she had drawn on the floor. Hessa's practice space occupied the back half of a building shared with a laundress, which meant every magical breakthrough in my new life smelled faintly of soap and wet linen. There were worse smells associated with magic. Much worse.</p><p>I had once spent four days maintaining defensive wards around a corpse-eater nest in midsummer. No amount of rank protected a man from discovering that prestige and smell were unrelated systems. I smiled. </p><p>Hessa said, "What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"You are doing it again."</p><p>"Doing what?"</p><p>"Leaving." </p><p>I looked at her. </p><p>She tapped two fingers against her temple. "You go somewhere. Then you come back smiling like someone told a joke."</p><p>"Sometimes they did."</p><p>"Who?"</p><p>"Usually me," I said.</p><p>Hessa let the silence sit until my own joke had nowhere to go.</p><p>I wiped sweat from my forehead. "How bad?"</p><p>"The Barrier?"</p><p>"My channels."</p><p>"Not damaged."</p><p>"Excellent."</p><p>"Because I stopped you."</p><p>"Still excellent."</p><p>"Your definition of success is exhausting."</p><p>"My definition of success is success."</p><p>Hessa crouched and pressed two fingers against the inside of my wrist. Her eyes unfocused slightly as she felt for the weak mana response there. I had once known healers who could diagnose channel damage through a gauntlet in the middle of combat. Hessa needed skin contact, quiet, and time. That did not make her bad. That made her what almost everyone actually was.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Checking The Channel" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/011/v28_c11_s03_checking-the-channel.png"/></figure><p>Useful reminder. I had spent too long surrounded by monsters and then mistaken them for the normal distribution.</p><p>"Again," I said. </p><p>Hessa did not release my wrist. "No."</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Again No" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/011/v28_c11_s02_again-no.png"/></figure><p>"Tomorrow?"</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>"That's Antonius's word."</p><p>"It is a good word."</p><p>"Everyone is conspiring."</p><p>"Against what?"</p><p>"Momentum," I said.</p><p>Hessa laughed. I disliked how often people laughed when I used that word.</p><p>She sat opposite me. "Tell me what you did."</p><p>"Cast Barrier."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"Then we're done."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>Fine.</p><p>I closed my eyes and reconstructed it. Not the spell as old Greg knew it. That would be useless. Old Greg's Barrier was a city viewed from a mountain: obvious streets, familiar districts, entire structures compressed into a shape the mind could hold without noticing every brick. Young Greg had three bricks and enthusiasm.</p><p>"I gathered through the channel," I said. "Held at the wrist, moved toward the palm, shaped a plane, gave it boundary, released." </p><p>Hessa frowned. "You skipped compression."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You did."</p><p>"I didn't need it."</p><p>"Every Barrier needs compression."</p><p>"Every useful Barrier."</p><p>Her face changed. There. This was the problem. Not Hessa being wrong. Hessa teaching the spell correctly. The standard beginner Barrier gathered mana, compressed it enough to stabilize, shaped a broad plane, then anchored the plane to the caster's intent. Sensible. Reliable. Wasteful. Wasteful was acceptable when the student had enough mana to waste. I did not.</p><p>"The plane was barely stable," Hessa said.</p><p>"Correct."</p><p>"It would stop nothing useful. You nearly emptied the channel for less than a second."</p><p>"Probably a moth."</p><p>Hessa looked at my twitching eye.</p><p>"And you are done for today."</p><p>"It existed."</p><p>"For less than a second."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"And you nearly emptied yourself."</p><p>"Also yes."</p><p>"Why are you happy?"</p><p>I opened my eyes. Because I knew what came after. Not tomorrow. Not even soon. But Barrier was no longer theoretical. For weeks my old magic had been a memory stored in a body that could not speak the language. Today the body had produced one syllable. Badly. Quietly. But mine.</p><p>"Because now I can make it cheaper," I said.</p><p>Hessa's expression suggested this was not the answer she wanted.</p><p>"Stronger," she said.</p><p>"Later."</p><p>"Stable."</p><p>"Eventually."</p><p>"Bigger."</p><p>"Why?" </p><p>She blinked.</p><p>"Because it is a Barrier."</p><p>"That's not a reason."</p><p>"It blocks things."</p><p>"Sometimes."</p><p>"That is the purpose."</p><p>"That's one purpose," I said.</p><p>Hessa stood before I finished enjoying the question and pointed at the door. "Go home."</p><p>"You're ending early."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Because I asked what Barrier is for?"</p><p>"Because I know what happens if I let you stay."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You'll spend an hour trying to make a worse spell on purpose."</p><p>I smiled. Hessa pointed at the door. "Exactly." I went home. I did not practice. That statement was technically true if one defined practice as casting magic. I practiced everything immediately adjacent to casting magic. Breathing. Channel awareness. Hand position. Intent shaping without mana. Visualizing boundaries. Reducing the imagined plane. Making it larger.</p><p>Making it smaller. Tilting it. Rotating it. Moving the anchor point from palm to fingertip, then realizing I was importing habits from a body with channels I did not possess and starting again. At some point I found myself standing in the middle of my room with one finger extended toward a cup. The cup had done nothing. I had done nothing. We were locked in a contest of tremendous strategic importance.</p><p>"What am I doing?" I asked aloud.</p><p>The cup declined to answer. Current board. Mana: terrible. Barrier: exists. Debt: still irritating. Arlo: has the Tere gauge. Six silver: still needed if I wanted to buy two days of Arlo's time without borrowing. Sword: neglected yesterday. Antonius: likely to find me if I tried to hide. Dungeon salvager: leaving today, location unknown, absolutely none of my business.</p><p>I looked at the cup. Barrier. One spell. One terrible little spell. What was the strongest version of me available right now? Not mage. Not yet. Student. Annoying. I went to sleep. The next morning Antonius sent Rusk before breakfast. Rusk knocked twice, opened the door without waiting, and looked at me sitting on the floor.</p><p>"What are you doing?"</p><p>"Meditating."</p><p>"You don't meditate."</p><p>"Mana."</p><p>"You look constipated."</p><p>"That's because you interrupted at a delicate moment," I said.</p><p>Rusk held up a folded paper.</p><p>"Work," Rusk said.</p><p>I took it. The paper contained an address and two words.</p><p>PICK UP.</p><p>"Pick up what?" </p><p>Rusk shrugged.</p><p>"From whom?"</p><p>"Address."</p><p>"What's there?"</p><p>"Find out."</p><p>"Antonius has become lazy."</p><p>"Antonius is busy."</p><p>"Difference?"</p><p>Rusk turned toward the stairs.</p><p>"Wait." He stopped. </p><p>I held up one finger.</p><p>"Yesterday I cast Barrier." </p><p>Rusk looked at the finger. Then at me.</p><p>"Congratulations."</p><p>"That response was inadequate."</p><p>"Did it work?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"What did it block?" </p><p>I paused. </p><p>Rusk smiled.</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>He left. The address belonged to a glass merchant named Vennel, who had apparently defaulted on a short-term note and agreed to surrender three crates of imported alchemical glass as partial payment. This sounded interesting. It was not. The crates were heavy. That was the entire problem Antonius had assigned me. A cart waited outside. Vennel's assistant pointed toward the back.</p><p>"Those," the assistant said.</p><p>I inspected them.</p><p>"Any reactive residue?"</p><p>The assistant frowned. "They're empty."</p><p>"That wasn't the question."</p><p>"They're new."</p><p>"Any treated surfaces?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Mana-active packing?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Fragile?"</p><p>He stared at me.</p><p>"Glass."</p><p>"Useful."</p><p>The crates had been packed well. Straw. Dividers. Reinforced corners. No mystery. No hidden future technology. No famous maker. No cursed vial. Just glass. I moved them. This was harder than it should have been because my shoulders were still sore from sword work and because imported alchemical glass was apparently manufactured from condensed resentment. Halfway through the second crate, I thought about using Barrier.</p><p>Not to lift. I could not. Not enough force. But the crate wanted to slide when I tipped it onto the cart. A tiny plane beneath one corner could help.</p><p>No.</p><p>Hessa had said tomorrow maybe. Today was tomorrow. Technically. I put the crate down. The assistant said, "Problem?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>I looked at the cart. Barrier. Small. Momentary. Could brace the lower edge while I changed grip. Useful? Barely. Necessary?</p><p>No.</p><p>Which made it perfect for testing. No danger except breaking expensive glass and having Antonius murder me.</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>I gathered. The mana came slower standing than sitting. Interesting. I had expected that. Probably. My pulse rose anyway. Thread to wrist. Palm. Too much. Reduce. The instinct to shape the whole plane arrived automatically. I cut it down. Not dinner plate. Hand-sized. Smaller. Three fingers across. A translucent distortion appeared against the cart bed. Not light.</p><p>Barrier had never really glowed unless someone made it glow. Beginners imagined magic should announce itself. Mostly it looked like air remembering it could become solid. The crate corner touched it. The Barrier vanished. The crate dropped perhaps half an inch. I caught it. Pain flashed through my wrist. The assistant shouted. I shoved the crate safely onto the cart.</p><p>Then leaned against it, breathing hard. The assistant stared.</p><p>"What was that?"</p><p>"Magic."</p><p>"I know that."</p><p>"Then we're both doing well."</p><p>"You almost dropped the crate."</p><p>"I didn't."</p><p>"You did."</p><p>"Almost is an important word."</p><p>The Barrier had held. For maybe a quarter second. Against perhaps twenty pounds of the crate's shifting weight. Better than the moth. Much better. Also stupid. Hessa was going to know. I did not know how, but competent instructors developed supernatural awareness specifically for student stupidity. I finished the pickup without magic. At Antonius's warehouse, Rusk watched me unload.</p><p>"Why are you favoring your right hand?"</p><p>"I'm not."</p><p>"You are."</p><p>"Observation is a disease."</p><p>"Did you do magic with the boxes?" I stopped.</p><p>"How could you possibly know that?" Rusk smiled.</p><p>"You told me you cast Barrier, then I sent you to move something heavy. You're Greg."</p><p>That was offensive. Also fair.</p><p>"One test."</p><p>"Did it help?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Did it hurt?"</p><p>"Unrelated."</p><p>Rusk laughed and took one end of the crate. We carried it inside. Antonius was arguing with a merchant about lamp oil. I waited. Six days ago, I would have inserted myself because lamp oil prices connected to shipping, storage, winter demand, alchemical solvent use, and probably three future fortunes if I thought hard enough.</p><p>Today I had a more important problem. How small could Barrier become before it stopped being Barrier? I was halfway through imagining a plane the size of a coin when Antonius said, "Greg." </p><p>I looked up. The merchant was gone.</p><p>"Yes?"</p><p>"Did you hear any of that?"</p><p>"Some."</p><p>"How much?"</p><p>"Oil," I said.</p><p>Antonius looked at Rusk.</p><p>Rusk said, "Magic." Antonius looked back at me.</p><p>"You did magic?"</p><p>"Barrier."</p><p>That got a better reaction than Rusk's. Antonius's eyebrows rose. "Actually?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Useful?"</p><p>"Not yet."</p><p>"Then why are you smiling?"</p><p>"Potential." </p><p>Antonius sighed.</p><p>"Keep it out of the ledger until it pays for something."</p><p>"I wasn't going to borrow against it."</p><p>Antonius handed me another paper.</p><p>"Good." He handed me another paper. </p><p>I looked at it.</p><p>"What's this?"</p><p>"Payment."</p><p>Six silver. I looked up.</p><p>"For?"</p><p>"The gauntlet appraisal."</p><p>"No." </p><p>Antonius leaned back.</p><p>"No?"</p><p>"You already own my labor."</p><p>"Not all of it."</p><p>"Apparently enough to send me after glass."</p><p>"That was labor. Yesterday was not." </p><p>I stared at the coins. Six silver. Exactly six. Arlo. Two days. Antonius knew. Of course he knew.</p><p>"Why six?"</p><p>"That's what you said Arlo's time cost."</p><p>"You were listening."</p><p>"I usually am."</p><p>"That's unsettling."</p><p>"Take it." </p><p>I did not. This felt like a trap. Not criminal trap. Antonius trap. Worse.</p><p>"What are the terms?"</p><p>"None."</p><p>"That's impossible."</p><p>"Payment."</p><p>"For an appraisal I was already doing because you told me to?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You are trying to teach me something."</p><p>Antonius's face went blank.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"That's exactly what you'd say."</p><p>"I'm paying you for work I asked you to do outside the labor attached to your debt." I considered. Simple. Suspiciously simple.</p><p>"You want me to give it to Arlo."</p><p>"I don't care."</p><p>Lie. Maybe. Not enough information. I took the six silver.</p><p>"Thank you," I said.</p><p>Antonius blinked. Rusk looked over.</p><p>I frowned. "What?"</p><p>"Nothing," Antonius said.</p><p>"You both reacted."</p><p>"You said thank you."</p><p>"I say thank you." </p><p>Rusk shook his head.</p><p>"Fuck both of you."</p><p>Normal restored. I went to Arlo's workshop with the money. He refused it. I put the coins on his bench. He put them back in my hand.</p><p>"I said two days of time, not that I was selling them to you."</p><p>"That's what time means."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You're an artisan."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Your time has a price."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Six silver."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then how much?" I asked.</p><p>Arlo glared. </p><p>I smiled. He had walked into that.</p><p>"Not the point," Arlo said.</p><p>"What is the point?"</p><p>"The gauge is yours."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"If I spend two days learning from it, I get something."</p><p>"Correct."</p><p>"So why are you paying me?"</p><p>"Because you would otherwise spend those two days earning money."</p><p>"And you get?"</p><p>"A better Arlo."</p><p>Silence. I heard it after I said it. That sounded terrible. Arlo's expression agreed.</p><p>"I mean your work."</p><p>"Worse."</p><p>"Your regulators."</p><p>"Keep going."</p><p>"I am going to stop."</p><p>"Growth." </p><p>I sat on the edge of his worktable. Arlo immediately shoved me off.</p><p>"Chair," Arlo said.</p><p>I took the chair.</p><p>"The gauge has value in your hands," I said. "Not mine. If you can learn from it, we both learn whether the thing I bought is actually worth anything. You lose two days. I cover two days."</p><p>"You don't know what I earn in two days."</p><p>"Approximately six silver."</p><p>"You guessed."</p><p>"You didn't deny it."</p><p>"I was trying to get you out."</p><p>"Still data." </p><p>Arlo looked at the coins. Then at me.</p><p>"Where did you get them?"</p><p>"Antonius."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Payment."</p><p>"Loan?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"I did work."</p><p>"What work?"</p><p>"Appraisal." </p><p>Arlo stared.</p><p>"The gauntlet?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"You were there because Antonius told you to be."</p><p>"Apparently my debt labor has boundaries."</p><p>"Does Antonius know that?"</p><p>"He invented them." </p><p>Arlo picked up one coin. Turned it over.</p><p>"One day."</p><p>"Two."</p><p>"One."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because I have an order due."</p><p>"Delay it."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because somebody paid me."</p><p>There it was. Arlo had his own constraints. Annoying.</p><p>"One day," I said. "Then?"</p><p>"Then I decide whether a second is worth it."</p><p>Reasonable.</p><p>"Fine," I said.</p><p>Arlo took three silver. Pushed three back. I looked at them.</p><p>"Keep it."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Advance."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Materials."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Food."</p><p>"Get out." </p><p>I took the coins.</p><p>"Tomorrow?"</p><p>"Tomorrow."</p><p>Good.</p><p>I left. </p><p>Then went to Hessa. She knew. Of course. I had barely entered before she said, "What did you do?"</p><p>"Good afternoon."</p><p>"What did you do?"</p><p>"Work."</p><p>"With mana."</p><p>"Minimal."</p><p>Her eyes dropped to my right hand. There was no mark. Still she knew.</p><p>"Show me," Hessa said.</p><p>I held it out. Hessa pressed the wrist, waited, and her mouth tightened.</p><p>"Idiot."</p><p>"That's not diagnostic language."</p><p>"You strained the channel."</p><p>"Strained is not damaged."</p><p>"That is how damaged begins."</p><p>"I used less mana than yesterday."</p><p>"Against resistance."</p><p>Ah.</p><p>Right.</p><p>I had reduced the Barrier size but given it a job. Different load. I knew that. Old Greg knew that. Present Greg had apparently decided smaller meant cheaper in all dimensions. It did not.</p><p>"Interesting," I said. Hessa slapped my hand.</p><p>"Ow."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"Violence against students is frowned upon."</p><p>"Leave."</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>Hessa stared. </p><p>I sat on the mat.</p><p>"I'm not casting."</p><p>"Correct."</p><p>"Teach me why the load moved into the channel."</p><p>That changed her expression. Not enough to forgive me. Enough to keep me. She sat. For the next half hour, Hessa made me describe exactly what I had done. The Barrier had been smaller, yes. The shape cost less. But I had anchored it directly through the palm while asking it to resist a moving physical load. The spell collapsed quickly enough that I avoided worse strain, but the force had nowhere elegant to go.</p><p>Old Greg would have distributed it. Through what? Channels I did not have. Reinforcement I could not cast. Anchors I could not form. Again: city from mountain. Three bricks.</p><p>"Then don't anchor through the palm," I said. </p><p>Hessa shook her head. "You need an anchor."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Your palm is the developed path."</p><p>"Currently."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Currently is the only body you have."</p><p>That irritated me. Not because she was wrong. Because she was precisely right. I looked at my hand.</p><p>"What about no resistance?"</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Barrier with no meaningful load."</p><p>"Then why cast it?"</p><p>"Shape practice."</p><p>"You can shape without releasing."</p><p>"Not the same."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"So." </p><p>Hessa sighed.</p><p>"You are going to do this whether I help."</p><p>"Probably."</p><p>"That was not permission."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"Coin-sized." </p><p>I smiled.</p><p>"Coin-sized."</p><p>"No load."</p><p>"Define load."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Nothing touches it."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"Air touches it." </p><p>She stared.</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>I gathered mana. Slower today. Strain. Not damage. Important. Thread. Palm. This time I did not imagine a shield. That word was part of the problem. Shield implied purpose before shape. I imagined a boundary. A circle no wider than a copper coin. Plane. Thin. Do not compress more than necessary. Hessa said, "Slow." I slowed. The mana wanted to spread. Habit from training.</p><p>I kept it small. Release. A tiny distortion appeared above my palm. It was almost invisible. I grinned.</p><p>"Hold," Hessa said.</p><p>One heartbeat. Two. It vanished. I exhaled. No headache. Wrist warm. Not painful. Hessa checked.</p><p>"Again?" I asked. </p><p>She considered.</p><p>"Once."</p><p>Second attempt failed. Nothing formed. I frowned.</p><p>"Again."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"That one didn't count."</p><p>"It used mana."</p><p>"It did not produce a spell."</p><p>"Your body does not care about your scoring system."</p><p>"Poor design."</p><p>"Tomorrow." </p><p>I stood. </p><p>Hessa pointed at me.</p><p>"No crates."</p><p>"Specific."</p><p>"No testing against objects."</p><p>"Very specific."</p><p>"No sword with Barrier," Hessa said.</p><p>I had not thought of that yet. Now I had. Hessa saw it happen.</p><p>"Fuck."</p><p>"Your fault."</p><p>"Go."</p><p>I went to sword practice. Without Barrier. Mostly because Hessa had now made the idea so attractive that I needed to prove I could resist it. Jorren was there. He had become less irritating as I became more capable of hitting him. Correlation, perhaps. We sparred. No magic. He still beat me. Not easily. That mattered. The first time we had fought, my mind had been several exchanges ahead and my body several years behind. Now the gap had narrowed by perhaps an inch.</p><p>An inch was enormous. I read his shoulder. Saw the cut. Moved before it came. My parry arrived correctly. My feet did not cross. I turned his blade. Countered. He blocked.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Again. He pressed. I gave ground. Not too much. His weight shifted. There. Old Greg knew exactly what to do. Drive left, bind, accelerate, reinforce wrist, spoil his footing with a low Barrier, shoulder through, No reinforcement. No Barrier. No old body. I chose the part available. Drive left. Bind. Jorren recovered faster than expected and hit me in the ribs with the flat.</p><p>I swore. He stepped back.</p><p>"You had something."</p><p>"I had several things."</p><p>"Then why didn't you do them?"</p><p>"Budget."</p><p>He laughed. We reset. Second time I simplified sooner. No imaginary magic. No future body. Just sword. He still won. But it took longer. Afterward Jorren tossed me a cloth.</p><p>"You look less old."</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>"Still old."</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>He grinned. I sat against the wall, breathing hard. Mana training in the morning would have made this worse. Crate experiment had made mana worse. Sword training made everything tired. Three systems drawing from one nineteen-year-old body. Old Greg had forgotten what recovery felt like when there was not enough of it.</p><p>No.</p><p>That was false. Old Greg had known. He had simply possessed more ways to cheat. Potions. Reinforcement. Healers. Recovery arrays. Money. Assistants. People. A whole infrastructure around his body. Present Greg had soup. Important distinction. I went home. Ate soup. Responsible. Boring. The next morning Arlo had already dismantled half his workbench when I arrived.</p><p>Not the gauge. His tools. The Tere reference set sat in the center on clean cloth. Arlo had made three new brackets, a measuring frame, and something that looked like a tiny metal gallows. I stared.</p><p>"You were waiting."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You built all this."</p><p>"I work."</p><p>"Before sunrise?"</p><p>"I couldn't sleep."</p><p>There. Possibility. I knew that feeling. I did not say so. Arlo pointed to a chair. "Sit there."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"If you touch anything, I want distance."</p><p>I sat. He spent the morning testing. It was beautiful. Not visually. Visually it was two men staring at pieces of metal while one occasionally swore. But the logic emerged. The Tere plates provided known resistance values. The bridge compared flow. Arlo could pass a tiny controlled mana current through one of his regulators, compare its behavior against a reference plate, adjust, repeat.</p><p>The first regulator was off. The second was off differently. The third was nearly right. That was the problem. Arlo's regulators were good because Arlo was good. But "good" wandered. One day slightly high. One day slightly low. Temperature. Material batch. His hands. His mood. His breakfast, probably. The gauge did not care. By midday Arlo had three regulators behaving within a much narrower range than his normal work.</p><p>He stared at them. I stared too.</p><p>"Consistent," I said. </p><p>Arlo did not answer.</p><p>"That's what you wanted."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"How much better?"</p><p>"Shut up."</p><p>"Arlo."</p><p>"I need more tests."</p><p>"How many?"</p><p>"Enough."</p><p>"That's not a number." He looked at me. </p><p>I smiled. </p><p>He looked back at the regulators.</p><p>"Twenty."</p><p>"Today?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Tomorrow?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"How long?"</p><p>"A week."</p><p>"Excellent," I said.</p><p>Arlo frowned. "Why excellent?"</p><p>"Because now you have a problem."</p><p>"I had problems before you."</p><p>"Not this one." He laughed despite himself. Then his face changed. Not joy. Worry. I knew that too.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"If this works."</p><p>"Yes?"</p><p>"My old jigs are wrong."</p><p>"Some."</p><p>"My regulator molds may be wrong."</p><p>"Some."</p><p>"The shale mix changes response."</p><p>"Probably."</p><p>"The firing temperatures..."</p><p>"Arlo." </p><p>He stopped. Interesting. His board had opened. Branches. I recognized it because I lived there. For once I was standing outside.</p><p>"One regulator," I said. </p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>"Make one exactly repeatable."</p><p>"I need to know..."</p><p>"One."</p><p>"The material..."</p><p>"One."</p><p>"The gauge itself could be incomplete."</p><p>"Then learn that while making one." Arlo stared at me. I enjoyed this far too much.</p><p>"You're annoying," he said.</p><p>"I have excellent teachers." </p><p>He looked at the Tere set. Then at one regulator.</p><p>"One."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>I leaned back. That had been easy. Suspiciously easy. Not the artificing. Arlo. His problem had edges once I gave them back to him. I almost thought about what that implied regarding myself.</p><p>No.</p><p>Later. Hessa. I left Arlo before I could create a manufacturing company. At Hessa's, she checked my wrist first.</p><p>"Better."</p><p>"Barrier?"</p><p>"One."</p><p>"Two."</p><p>"One."</p><p>"One successful?"</p><p>"One attempt."</p><p>"Extortion."</p><p>"Leave."</p><p>"One." She smiled. </p><p>I sat. Gather. Thread. Palm. Coin. Boundary. Release. Nothing. I waited. Hessa said nothing. Failure. Mana spent. Not much. I breathed.</p><p>"Again tomorrow," she said.</p><p>"No."</p><p>Her expression hardened. I held up a hand.</p><p>"Not arguing."</p><p>That surprised both of us. I closed my eyes. What happened? Yesterday I had formed it. Today no. Mana amount? Similar. Shape? Similar. Fatigue?</p><p>Better.</p><p>Intent. Yesterday I wanted a tiny Barrier. Today I wanted success. Different. That was stupid. Also possibly real. Magic was full of stupid things that became real because minds were involved.</p><p>"What are you doing?" Hessa asked.</p><p>"Thinking."</p><p>"Lesson is over."</p><p>"Yes." I stood. Then noticed the cup on her shelf. Small clay cup. I smiled. </p><p>Hessa followed my eyes.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I didn't say anything."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I am leaving."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>I left. I came back the next day. Failed. Next day. Formed it. Half heartbeat. No pain. Next day. Failed. Next. Formed. Two heartbeats. The progress was insulting. I loved it. A week after my first Barrier, Hessa placed a copper coin on a stool. I looked at her.</p><p>"What's that?"</p><p>"Your enemy."</p><p>"I've fought worse."</p><p>"Barrier."</p><p>"Against the coin?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then?" I asked.</p><p>Hessa flicked it. The coin spun through the air.</p><p>"Put the Barrier where it will pass." </p><p>I stared.</p><p>"Moving placement."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"You keep asking for small." </p><p>I smiled. Hessa immediately regretted everything.</p><p>"One attempt."</p><p>"Reasonable."</p><p>She flicked the coin again. I watched the arc. Too fast. Not actually fast. My current casting was slow. Old Greg could have formed Barrier between thought and impact. Young Greg needed gathering, shaping, release. The coin hit the floor.</p><p>"Again," I said. </p><p>Hessa picked it up. Second toss. </p><p>I started before release. Cheating.</p><p>Good.</p><p>Gather. Shape. Place. Barrier appeared six inches too low. Coin passed over it.</p><p>"Again."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"That wasn't load."</p><p>"It was mana."</p><p>"Tomorrow?"</p><p>"Tomorrow."</p><p>The next day I missed. The next I clipped the edge. The Barrier vanished when the coin touched it. The coin changed direction. Barely. It landed perhaps a foot left of where it should have. I stared. Hessa stared. I started laughing.</p><p>"Again," I said. </p><p>Hessa smiled this time.</p><p>"No."</p><p>I looked at the coin on the floor. The Barrier had not stopped it. Had not needed to. That was the thing. A shield thought in absolutes. Stop. Block. Hold. But a tiny plane at the right angle did not need enough strength to stop a force. Only enough to alter it. A sword tip. A foot. A thrown knife. A spell line. A falling vial. A stream of liquid. A fucking coin.</p><p>The possibilities arrived all at once. Too many. Beautiful. Dangerous. Hessa saw my face.</p><p>"Greg," Hessa said.</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>"One thing," she said.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Pick one thing." </p><p>I breathed. </p><p>The room came back. Coin. Tiny Barrier. Angle.</p><p>"Again tomorrow," I said. </p><p>Hessa nodded. That evening Antonius found me at the warehouse with six copper coins lined across a table. He looked at them. Then at me.</p><p>"What are you doing?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"Why are my coins in a line?"</p><p>"Research."</p><p>"They are rent."</p><p>"Temporary research." </p><p>He picked them up.</p><p>"Antonius."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I need targets."</p><p>"Use your own money."</p><p>"That's economically irresponsible."</p><p>"How?"</p><p>"Mine is scarce."</p><p>"So is mine."</p><p>"You have more."</p><p>"Because I don't use it as magical targets," Antonius said.</p><p>I followed him toward the desk.</p><p>"I can redirect a coin."</p><p>"Congratulations."</p><p>"With Barrier."</p><p>"Still congratulations."</p><p>"Do you understand what that means?"</p><p>"That you can protect yourself from very poor assassins."
