Unlike Hessa, he did not care about magical orthodoxy. Unlike Arlo, he did not care how the mechanism worked. He asked, "Useful?"</p><p>"Eventually."</p><p>"How eventually?"</p><p>I paused. Good question. Weeks? Months? Combat application required speed I did not have. Reliable placement. Casting under stress. Mana reserve. Body coordination. A lot.</p><p>"Not tomorrow." </p><p>Antonius smiled.</p><p>"Growth."</p><p>"Fuck you," I said.</p><p>Antonius opened his ledger. I should have left.</p><p>Instead I said, "Do you have anything magical that needs moving?"</p><p>His pen stopped. Slowly.</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Something fragile?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Dangerous?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Something where touching it is bad?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You're not thinking."</p><p>"I'm actively refusing to think."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because if I give you a problem, you'll test a spell you learned last week on property I own."</p><p>"That's unfair."</p><p>"Is it?" I considered the glass crate.</p><p>"Somewhat," I said.</p><p>Antonius returned to his ledger. Then said, "The salvager came back."</p><p>Everything in me changed. I hated that he noticed.</p><p>"The gauntlet?"</p><p>"Still mine."</p><p>"So expedition failed?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Then?"</p><p>"He repaid three gold."</p><p>"Already?"</p><p>"Partial."</p><p>"What did they find?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Antonius."</p><p>He looked at me. I could hear the dungeon in the word. Not literally. Memory did that. Stone corridors. Wet rope. Torch smoke. Mana pressure. Someone breathing too loudly because they were scared. The particular silence parties developed before opening a door nobody trusted. I had missed it. That realization arrived cleanly enough to hurt. Not the danger. Not even the fighting.</p><p>The problem. A dungeon was a machine built out of constraints: bad information, limited supplies, terrain, monsters, time, people. Every room asked a question and punished bad answers. Of course I missed it.</p><p>"What did they find?" I asked again.</p><p>Antonius watched me. Then he reached into a drawer and put something on the desk. A lump of translucent green material, rough as broken glass and veined with black. I did not touch it. Progress.</p><p>"What is that?"</p><p>"You're the expert."</p><p>"I have never claimed that." </p><p>Antonius stared.</p><p>"Recently." </p><p>I leaned closer. Green crystal. Black veins. Mana-active? I could not feel enough to know. Smell? Faint mineral. Sharp. A memory stirred. Cave resin?</p><p>No.</p><p>Monster secretion hardened around...</p><p>No.</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"From the expedition?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Value?"</p><p>"That's what I want to know." </p><p>I laughed. There it was. Next problem. Not Greg. Not Barrier. Not future. A thing on a table. A bounded question. I sat.</p><p>"Get Arlo," I said.</p><p>Antonius said, "He's busy."</p><p>"Then get me a knife."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"You just learned magic."</p><p>"Unrelated."</p><p>"That is never true with you."</p><p>I looked at the green material. </p><p>The black veins looked almost organic. Not stone. Maybe hardened secretion. Maybe alchemical. Maybe useless. Maybe dangerous. My mind reached. Memory. Smell. Texture. A healer's tent. Someone grinding green shards. A woman saying not the black part. Who? Why? </p><p>I leaned closer. </p><p>Antonius said, "Greg."</p><p>"I know."</p><p>"Do you?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>That came out before I could replace it. Antonius smiled. I frowned.</p><p>"Don't."</p><p>"Didn't say anything."</p><p>"Knife."</p><p>"No." </p><p>I looked at the material again. Then at him.</p><p>"What can I use?" </p><p>Antonius considered. He opened a drawer. Took out a spoon. Put it on the desk. </p><p>I stared.</p><p>"A spoon."</p><p>"My spoon."</p><p>"You have a knife."</p><p>"I like my knife."</p><p>"Reasonable."</p><p>I picked up the spoon. The green shard waited. Somewhere inside my wrist, the faint rebuilt channel felt warm from a week's worth of terrible little Barriers. Not enough for anything impressive. Enough to make me curious. That was usually where trouble began. I smiled. Antonius sighed.</p><p>"Excellent," I said.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="010.html">← Chapter 7</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="013.html">Chapter 9 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/133.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 104: The Shaper — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 104</div><h1>THE SHAPER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Hessa had removed the charcoal. Again. I liked that. Which probably meant I had developed opinions about blank forearms. Not ideal.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat. Morning baseline was boring. Excellent. Hands normal. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the vague way it usually was when I thought about it and less present when I did not.</p><p>No thumb. No fingers trying to participate. No unusual cold. No pain. Hessa checked anyway. She always checked anyway. Then she put the folded white towel beneath my right forearm. Copper sat farther up the table.</p><p>Not near enough to be interesting. I looked around. No threads. Still.</p><p>“Disappointed?” Hessa asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You looked.”</p><p>“I have eyes.”</p><p>“Tragic.”</p><p>I rested my arm. The outer forearm was unmarked. No charcoal target. No line. No point. Nothing to accidentally obey. Good. Hessa sat across from me with her notes. She had rewritten something. I could tell because one strip of paper had been pasted over another.</p><p>“What did you change?”</p><p>“My wording.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I wrote that you directed the edge wristward.”</p><p>“That is what happened.”</p><p>“That is what you reported.”</p><p>I looked at her. She looked back.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I hate your notes.”</p><p>“They are not for your emotional comfort.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>She put the pen down.</p><p>“Last time I told you the direction before shaping.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You reported a small asymmetry toward your wrist.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Today I want the same sequence with one change.”</p><p>“Elbowward.”</p><p>She stared at me.</p><p>“That was my guess.”</p><p>“Stop guessing.”</p><p>“You said one change.”</p><p>“I did.”</p><p>“And opposite direction is the cleanest.”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>I smiled. She did not.</p><p>“Your confidence is unattractive.”</p><p>“That seems unrelated.”</p><p>“It isn't.”</p><p>I stopped smiling. Mostly. Hessa touched two fingers lightly to the table near my elbow. Not my arm. Just direction.</p><p>“Elbowward.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not toward my fingers.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“You are indicating with your fingers.”</p><p>“I am indicating a direction. If I move my hand, the direction does not move with it.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“You understand?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“Toward my elbow. Not toward your hand.”</p><p>She moved her hand away. Good. No target. No destination. Only direction. That was cleaner. Probably. Hessa watched me.</p><p>“One draw.”</p><p>“One shape.”</p><p>“One directional instruction.”</p><p>“One RETURN.”</p><p>“One release.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No external question.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do not make the effect larger just to make it easier to report.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Report what happens.”</p><p>I breathed. Not special breathing. Just enough to stop talking.</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I reached. Carefully. The draw came more easily than it had weeks ago. That did not mean easy. It meant familiar. A narrow opening. A small pull. Mana. Contained. No broad flood. No rush into the left.</p><p>No fingers. No thumb. No urge to move my hand. I held. Hessa watched my face more than my arm.</p><p>“Stable?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. The temptation was to prepare for the next instruction. I noticed that. Then I noticed that noticing it was also preparation. Annoying.</p><p>“Shape.”</p><p>Neutral region. Outer right forearm. Small. Localized. Not direction yet. That mattered. I let the familiar alteration form. Not a point. Not a patch exactly. An area with an edge I could feel more clearly than I could describe.</p><p>The center changed first. Then the boundary became legible. Not visible. Mine. Internal.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Localized.”</p><p>“Size?”</p><p>“Small.”</p><p>“That is not size.”</p><p>“About the same as last time.”</p><p>“Comparison is not size.”</p><p>I almost opened my eyes. They were already open. I had been staring at the wall.</p><p>“Two fingers across. Maybe less.”</p><p>“Shape?”</p><p>“Uneven oval.”</p><p>“Already directional?”</p><p>I waited. Checked. Not pushed. Checked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Certain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>She wrote. I hated that too.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. The edge stayed. No broadening. No elbow pull. No wrist pull. Nothing external. Copper remained copper. Wonderful object. Hessa waited long enough that I started wondering whether she had forgotten the next instruction.</p><p>She had not.</p><p>“Smallest directional change toward your elbow.”</p><p>I did not move. That was the first thing. No hand. No wrist. No fingers. No shoulder. Inside. Elbowward. The previous wristward attempt wanted to become relevant. I tried not to use it. Impossible.</p><p>Memory existed. Fine. I did not reverse it. There was nothing to reverse. This was a new shape. Elbowward. For several breaths nothing happened. Or nothing I could distinguish happened. I felt the center.</p><p>The wrist-side edge. The elbow-side edge. The elbow-side edge seemed softer than the wrist side. Wrong. Maybe. I waited. Hessa said nothing. I wanted to fix it. That was dangerous wording. Not fix. Observe.</p><p>Then the elbow-side boundary sharpened. A little. I thought. The wrist side stayed where it was. The center stayed. Elbow side clearer. Not farther. Clearer. Maybe.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Elbow-side edge changed.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Sharper.”</p><p>“Extension?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Other edges?”</p><p>“Wrist side same.”</p><p>“Center?”</p><p>“Same.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Motor?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Force?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Broadening?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Left?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. The sharpened edge remained. Or my expectation of it remained. That was the problem. I knew what I was supposed to find. Hessa knew what I was supposed to find. The arm did not come with a second observer.</p><p>“Still?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Same?”</p><p>“I think.”</p><p>“Think or know?”</p><p>“Think.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She waited.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“RETURN.”</p><p>I reduced. The elbow-side distinction softened first. Then the rest. The localized alteration diminished without sliding. No familiar broad response. No hand urge. No thumb. No fingers. No wrist. No elbow movement. Underlying draw stayed.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“Reduced.”</p><p>“Gone?”</p><p>I checked.</p><p>“Maybe a little center.”</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>I held. It faded.</p><p>“Now?”</p><p>“Gone.”</p><p>“Draw?”</p><p>“Still.”</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released. The draw closed. Nothing chased it. Nothing jumped left. Nothing moved outside me. Hessa waited. Then checked my hand. Forearm. Wrist. Thumb. Asked about fingers. Asked about phantom foot. Asked about the left.</p><p>All boring. Excellent. She sat back. I looked at the copper. It had contributed nothing. Also excellent.</p><p>“Well?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“That is not an answer.”</p><p>“It is my answer to the answer you want.”</p><p>“What answer do I want?”</p><p>“That you can direct it.”</p><p>“I would accept that.”</p><p>“You would enjoy it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is why I am saying no.”</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>“So what happened?”</p><p>“You reported a small asymmetry toward the instructed elbow side under a direction-first condition with no prepared destination.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is the second time your report has favored the instructed side.”</p><p>“Opposite sides.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So.”</p><p>“So my confidence increases.”</p><p>I waited. She did not continue.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“More than last time.”</p><p>“That is not a number.”</p><p>“I did that intentionally.”</p><p>“Can I direct it?”</p><p>“I am not writing that.”</p><p>“Can I probably direct it?”</p><p>“I am not writing that either.”</p><p>“What are you writing?”</p><p>She turned the page enough that I could read the line. REPORTED ASYMMETRY FOLLOWED OPPOSITE INSTRUCTED DIRECTION UNDER OTHERWISE SIMILAR DIRECTION-FIRST CONDITION.</p><p>Below it:</p><p>NO INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION. I read it twice.</p><p>“That is obnoxious.”</p><p>“It is accurate.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is usually why you dislike things.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at my arm. Nothing visible. Nothing externally measurable. Two reports. Two directions. Same problem. But not the same problem as before. That mattered. I wanted to do it again. Of course.</p><p>“Next time wrist again?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I have not decided.”</p><p>“We could alternate.”</p><p>“We could do many stupid things in orderly patterns.”</p><p>“That is unfair.”</p><p>“It is extremely fair.”</p><p>She closed the notes.</p><p>“One full no-magic day.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I am fine.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That argument should eventually help me.”</p><p>“It does.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“You get one day instead of several.”</p><p>Annoying. Fair.</p><p>“Then next assessment?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Direction?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I narrowed my eyes. She noticed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Everyone says maybe now.”</p><p>“Perhaps you are contagious.”</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>Hessa stood. Assessment over. I rolled my sleeve down. My forearm felt normal. My whole body felt normal. That should have been satisfying. It was. Also I wanted a third direction. There were not many useful directions on a forearm.</p><p>Wrist. Elbow. Up. Down. Inward. Outward. That was already too much thinking. Hessa waited until I finished my sleeve.</p><p>“Tomorrow is not an unrecorded assessment.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Say it.”</p><p>“Tomorrow is not an unrecorded assessment.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I got my crutches.</p><p>At the door she said:</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>I turned.</p><p>“If you go to the theatre, do not decide that acting counts as neurological training.”</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“The herb seller.”</p><p>“Oh, fuck all of you.”</p><p>Hessa smiled. Barely. I left. The bread seller was outside. I crossed the street before he could speak. He shouted anyway.</p><p>“LANDLORD.”</p><p>I kept going.</p><p>“MESSENGER.”</p><p>Better. I raised one crutch without turning. Probably rude. He laughed. I had no magic tomorrow. I had Hessa again after that. And I had two opposite directional reports that were not proof. Good.</p><p>I could live with that. For one day. Probably. I turned toward the theatre without deciding to. That was becoming a lie I told myself. Fine. I decided. The theatre doors were open. I heard voices before I reached them.</p><p>Not rehearsal voices. Argument voices. Better. Inside, the soot-shirt worker was standing onstage with a sword. Not a real sword. A prop. Long. Silver-painted. Ridiculous crossguard.</p><p>A red stone in the pommel large enough to purchase a small house if it had been real. The servant actor stood three paces away with both hands spread.</p><p>“It sounds stupid.”</p><p>“It is a sword,” the soot-shirt worker said.</p><figure class="chapter-art feature-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/133/Ch133_Legendary-Sword-Argument.jpg" alt="A soot-shirted theatre worker raises the ridiculous legendary sword as the company argues and Greg arrives." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“It is a legendary sword.”</p><p>“It is wood.”</p><p>“Onstage it is legendary.”</p><p>The recurring woman sat on the edge of the stage. Teren stood below with pages. Nobody noticed me for several seconds. I liked that. The servant actor pointed at the sword.</p><p>“It cannot sound like Teren.”</p><p>Teren looked offended.</p><p>“I do not sound like that.”</p><p>“You do.”</p><p>“I absolutely do not.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker saw me. Her face changed. Danger.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I said it immediately. She held the sword out.</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The recurring woman turned.</p><p>“Landlord.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Teren looked at his pages. Then at me. Then at the sword. I should have left. I did not.</p><p>“What?” I asked.</p><p>The servant actor grinned.</p><p>“The sword talks.”</p><p>I looked at the prop. Of course it did.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>Everyone answered at once.</p><p>I caught:</p><p>“curse”</p><p>“king”</p><p>“third act”</p><p>“because it's funny”</p><p>and from Teren:</p><p>“Page forty-two.”</p><p>He held out the pages. I did not take them.</p><p>“What happened to whoever talks for it?”</p><p>“Nothing,” Teren said.</p><p>“He is standing right there,” the recurring woman said.</p><p>The servant actor pointed at himself.</p><p>“I hate doing both.”</p><p>“You have three lines,” Teren said.</p><p>“I hate all three.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker extended the sword another inch toward me.</p><p>“Voice it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I am not a sword.”</p><p>The recurring woman smiled.</p><p>“You were a person.”</p><p>“That was broader.”</p><p>The servant actor laughed.</p><p>Teren said:</p><p>“Gregory.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“Read the lines.”</p><p>“From here?”</p><p>“From wherever.”</p><p>That was suspiciously permissive. I took the pages. Page forty-two. Three sword lines. Not many.</p><p>The first was:</p><p>YOU HAVE DRAWN ME, LITTLE KING. TRY NOT TO EMBARRASS US BOTH. I read it silently. Then again. The line was stupid. I liked it. No. The servant actor climbed onto the stage. He took the sword from the worker.</p><p>Held it in front of him.</p><p>“Start before.”</p><p>Teren pointed. The recurring woman stood. Another actor moved into place. Apparently we were doing this. I stayed below the stage. Seated would have been smarter. There was a chair. I took it. Good.</p><p>Teren started them. The servant actor crossed. The recurring woman said something about the sealed tomb. The servant actor drew the sword. Held it up. Everyone looked at me. I looked at the line.</p><p>“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”</p><p>Silence. The servant actor lowered the sword.</p><p>“That is Greg.”</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>“The sword cannot be Greg.”</p><p>“Then use someone else.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker said:</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I looked at her. She shrugged. Apparently everyone had learned Teren's word. The servant actor reset. They started again. Sword came out. I tried lower.</p><p>“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”</p><p>The recurring woman made a face.</p><p>“Now it is Greg pretending to be old.”</p><p>“I am old.”</p><p>Everyone looked at me. Fuck.</p><p>“Older.”</p><p>The servant actor laughed. Teren did not. He was listening.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Third time. I stared at the sword. Wood. Silver paint. Ridiculous red stone. Legendary. Supposedly. What did legendary sound like? Wrong question. What did this sword want? Also probably wrong. I had three lines.</p><p>The first insulted a king. Not loudly. Not angrily. It expected to be obeyed. I hated that I knew the difference.</p><p>“Again,” I said.</p><p>Teren looked at me.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>The actors reset. The servant actor drew the sword. I waited half a beat longer than before. Not much. Enough that everyone was looking at the blade.</p><p>Then I said:</p><p>“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”</p><p>Different. The servant actor smiled. Not as himself. As the idiot king. The recurring woman looked at the sword. Not me. That was interesting. Teren tapped the page.</p><p>“Continue.”</p><p>I had forgotten there were more lines. Of course.</p><p>The king said:</p><p>“You know me?”</p><p>Sword:</p><p>“I knew better kings.”</p><p>I said it. Too fast.</p><p>Teren:</p><p>“Again from sword.”</p><p>“I knew better kings.”</p><p>The servant actor flinched. Small. Funny. The recurring woman laughed. Not audience laugh. Actor laugh. She covered it badly. The servant actor pointed the sword toward me.</p><p>“Fuck you.”</p><p>“That is not in the play.”</p><p>“It should be.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker said:</p><p>“Keep it.”</p><p>Teren said:</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Everyone argued. I looked down at the third line. The sword apparently had opinions about doors. Of course. I wanted to read it. That was the problem. Not a large problem. A very small one.</p><p>Three lines. Wooden sword. No magic. No role. No casting. Nothing. I looked at Teren.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>He smiled.</p><p>“Page forty-one.”</p><p>That was more than three lines. I opened to forty-one. The sword had been talking before it was drawn. From inside the scabbard. Ridiculous. Excellent. There were seven more lines before page forty-two. One complained about darkness.</p><p>One told the king his grip was embarrassing. One refused to answer a question because the king had asked it badly. I looked at Teren.</p><p>“Who wrote this?”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“It is rude.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Constantly.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The servant actor said:</p><p>“You like it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You moved your chair.”</p><p>I looked down. I had. The recurring woman leaned toward the sword.</p><p>“Ask it something.”</p><p>“That is not how scripts work,” Teren said.</p><p>She ignored him.</p><p>“Oh, great blade, should Gregory be allowed near a stage?”</p><p>I looked at the sword. Then at her. Then back at the line in front of me. There was no answer for that. Good. I lowered my voice slightly.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The servant actor folded over laughing. The recurring woman pointed at me.</p><p>“That one stays.”</p><p>Teren said:</p><p>“It absolutely does not.”</p><p>The soot-shirt worker said:</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I was starting to understand how nothing ever got finished here. I moved the chair closer. Not onto the stage. Just closer. Tomorrow was no magic. Fine. Apparently I was a sword.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="129.html">← Chapter 103</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="135.html">Chapter 105 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/031.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 25: The Reporter — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 25</div><h1>THE REPORTER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Alden bought the scarf. This was objectionable for several reasons. First, I did not owe him one. Second, he paid three copper for it. Third, it was red. Not the same red. Darker. That should not have mattered. It did.</p><p>The cloth seller measured a length against Alden’s outstretched right arm. His left remained tucked close, obedient to the LIGHT USE LEFT tag.</p><p>“Two feet?” she asked.</p><p>“Three.”</p><p>“You only need two.”</p><p>“I like three.”</p><p>The seller shrugged. People were allowed preferences. Alden paid. Then looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You owe me three copper.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“One scarf.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Three copper.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>The seller looked between us.</p><p>“Married?”</p><p>We both said no. She did not look convinced. I left. Alden followed me into the market. The city had absorbed Darrowmere without becoming Darrowmere. That was the first thing I noticed. More wagons. More people asking directions. Three inns had boards outside advertising FLOOR SPACE.</p><p>A cooper was charging one copper more for small water casks than he had last week. A woman sold printed sheets titled DARROWMERE ROAD CONDITIONS for half a copper each. I bought one. Alden stared.</p><p>“You said rumors were useless.”</p><p>“This is printed.”</p><p>“That makes it better?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I read it. Half was already wrong. North road listed as open under escort. It had been controlled when we left. Maybe open now. Maybe old information. East road still closed. Two creatures killed. Wrong. At least four recovered. Possible evacuation of whole town. Wrong. Watch requesting archers. Maybe. The bottom said UPDATED MORNING. It was afternoon. I folded it. </p><p>Alden said, “Worth half a copper?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Now I know what people think they know.”</p><p>He considered that.</p><p>“Still sounds like a bad purchase.”</p><p>“You bought three feet of scarf.”</p><p>“That’s useful.”</p><p>He tied it around his wrist. The old torn strip disappeared beneath the new cloth. I looked away before the memory could decide it had permission. Alden noticed. He did not ask. That was new too. At the Guild, the Darrowmere board had grown. Not bigger. More organized. Three columns.</p><p>RELIEF.</p><p>ROAD.</p><p>RECOVERY.</p><p>No creature contract. Good. Berren’s name had been moved from relief to recovery with a note beside it.</p><p>RETURNED. MINOR INJURY.</p><p>He had made it back. Lio’s name was nowhere. Cass’s name was nowhere. Dema Rusk’s continuing-practice notice had been pushed down by road assignments. Life continued. The ink-thumb clerk saw me.</p><p>“You’re alive.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You owe two days on Antonius Vale’s notice.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What notice?”</p><p>She slid a folded paper across the desk. Of course. Antonius had not forgotten I existed because monsters happened twelve miles away. The paper was brief.</p><p>GREG.</p><p>RETURN WHEN AVAILABLE.</p><p>WEST STOREHOUSE.</p><p>RUSK HAS WORK.</p><p>NO URGENCY.</p><p>That last line was threatening. Alden read over my shoulder.</p><p>“No urgency.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You look worried.”</p><p>“Antonius understands urgency.”</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“If he says there is none, then he has time.”</p><p>“That is worse?”</p><p>“Potentially.”</p><p>The clerk slid another note.</p><p>“Hessa Marr.”</p><p>I looked at it. Three words.</p><p>COME WHEN FUNCTIONAL.</p><p>I held up my LIMITED CASTING tag.</p><p>The clerk said, “Functional enough.”</p><p>“You are not a healer.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why say that?”</p><p>“Because you’re standing.”</p><p>Alden leaned on the counter.</p><p>“Anything for me?”</p><p>She checked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He looked offended.</p><p>“You could make something up.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Excellent service.”</p><p>She looked at his shoulder tag.</p><p>“You should get that checked tomorrow.”</p><p>“I did today.”</p><p>“Then tomorrow.”</p><p>He frowned. She had won. Outside, Alden stopped.</p><p>“I’m getting my sword done.”</p><p>“Done?”</p><p>“Edge.”</p><p>His blade had taken two ugly contacts on the road and another against the wagon creature.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Then I’m finding Berren.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“He was there.”</p><p>“So were we.”</p><p>“He was somewhere else.”</p><p>Right. Different piece of Darrowmere. He wanted comparison. Information. Maybe just someone who had also gone.</p><p>“I’ll see you later,” he said.</p><p>Not, Are you coming? Not, What are we doing? Good.</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>He pointed at me.</p><p>“Three copper.”</p><p>I walked away. Hessa’s door was open. That was unusual. Not impossible. Just unusual enough that I slowed. A young man stood outside holding a chipped cup and looking miserable. He saw me looking.</p><p>“She made me stop.”</p><p>“What did you do?”</p><p>“Seven.”</p><p>“Seven what?”</p><p>“Attempts.”</p><p>“At?”</p><p>He held up the cup. A hairline crack ran from rim to base.</p><p>“Repair.”</p><p>“Did six work?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why seven?”</p><p>He looked offended.</p><p>“That’s what she said.”</p><p>Good. He left. Normal magical failure. No explosion. No revelation. Just a ruined cup and someone annoyed that effort did not imply improvement. Inside, Hessa was not waiting for me. She was working. A woman stood at the central table with a block of pale stone between both hands. Late twenties, maybe. Work clothes. Gray dust in the seams. Thick fingers. One thumbnail black from an old impact.</p><p>Stoneworker before magic. That was obvious. Hessa stood beside her.</p><p>“Again,” Hessa said.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/031/Ch031_Stoneworker-Demonstration.jpg" alt="A stoneworker splits a block cleanly at Hessa&#x27;s worktable while Greg watches." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>The woman placed two fingers against the stone. Mana moved. Cleanly. I felt it before I understood the shape. Not much power. No. That was wrong. Plenty of power. Restrained. A thin pressure entered the block along a line I could not see. The stone clicked. A flake separated from the corner. Small. Precise. The woman swore. </p><p>Hessa said, “Why?”</p><p>“Too deep.”</p><p>“How deep?”</p><p>“Finger width.”</p><p>“It’s half.”</p><p>“It feels like a finger.”</p><p>“Measure.”</p><p>The woman measured. Half. She swore again. Hessa wrote something in a ledger. I stayed by the door. The woman noticed me.</p><p>“Waiting?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You can sit.”</p><p>There were three chairs. One held tools. One held a coat. One was technically available. I sat. She reset the stone. This time Hessa did not speak. The woman touched. Mana entered. The block split along a shallow groove. Perfectly. Not spectacular. Very good. Actually, better than very good.</p><p>The force control was clean enough that my mind immediately became irritating. Fine splitting. Directional vibration. Load mapping. Barrier interaction. Support architecture. If she could feel stress through stone at that resolution, then with proper training she could probably learn to read structural load through walls. Maybe foundations. Maybe fortifications. Maybe collapse points. Combat applications multiplied. Counter-architecture multiplied faster. Hessa said, “Better.”</p><p>The woman smiled. That was all.</p><p>“What changed?” Hessa asked.</p><p>“Stopped trying to push it.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“Followed the weak line.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“Didn’t get greedy.”</p><p>Hessa nodded. The woman rubbed stone dust from her hands.</p><p>“That enough for today?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She packed her tools. I failed to stop myself.</p><p>“What do you use it for?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Stone.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Silence. Hessa did not help.</p><p>“What kind of work?” I asked.</p><p>“Facing. Steps. Corners. Sometimes lettering if the carver is behind,” the woman said.</p><p>“You can feel stress through the block,” I said.</p><p>“Sometimes,” she said.</p><p>“How far?”</p><p>She shrugged.</p><p>“Depends on stone.”</p><p>“Granite?”</p><p>“Worse.”</p><p>“Limestone?”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“Mortared wall?”</p><p>She looked at Hessa.</p><p>Hessa kept her pencil on the ledger.</p><p>The woman said, “Why would I do a wall?”</p><p>There it was.</p><p>“Because if you can trace the load through joined stone, you could probably map where the wall is carrying weight.”</p><p>She blinked.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And then identify failure points.”</p><p>Another blink.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And with enough practice you could potentially redirect stress instead of only reading it.”</p><p>She stared. </p><p>Hessa turned a page in her ledger.</p><p>“I make stairs,” the woman said.</p><p>“I understand,” I said.</p><p>“No, I make good stairs,” she said.</p><p>I stopped. She continued.</p><p>“Bad split ruins the corner. Then we cut the whole piece down or throw it into fill. If I can catch the weak line before I strike, I lose less stone.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That pays.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“My father’s knees are bad. My brother is fast but careless. I do the finish work.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I don’t want to break walls.”</p><p>“I did not say you should.”</p><p>She looked at me. I had absolutely implied she should. Not should. Could. Those were different. Mostly. Hessa still said nothing. The woman tied her tool roll.</p><p>“I come here twice a month because she keeps me from getting stupid with it.”</p><p>Hessa said, “Once last month.”</p><p>“Wedding.”</p><p>“You said twice.”</p><p>“Usually.”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“You new?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Hessa said, “Yes.”</p><p>Traitor.</p><p>The woman smiled.</p><p>“Good luck.”</p><p>“What’s your name?”</p><p>“Rinna.”</p><p>No. We already had Captain Ressa. I stopped her.</p><p>“Sorry. Again?”</p><p>“Rinna.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/031/Ch031_Fast-Coverage-003-C03.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 31." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Of course. The world reused names too. She left. I watched the door close. Hessa wrote in the ledger. I looked at the stone. Clean split. Half-width corner. Very little waste. Waste. That word arrived before I invited it. She could do more. Obviously. Her control was better than mine had been at twenty-five.</p><p>Better than most beginning Barrier workers I had known at thirty. She had the sense. The patience. The feedback loop. She could build. She could become dangerous. Important. Rare. Instead she made stairs. Hessa closed the ledger.</p><p>“How long are you going to keep redesigning her work?”</p><p>“I am not redesigning it.”</p><p>“You turned stairs into wall failure before she packed her tools.”</p><p>I disliked everyone knowing my faces.</p><p>“She is talented.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Very.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You agree.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And she makes stairs.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I waited. Hessa waited. Annoying.</p><p>“How long has she trained?”</p><p>“With me? Nine months.”</p><p>“Nine?”</p><p>“Twice a month, usually.”</p><p>That was absurd.</p><p>“No formal foundation?”</p><p>“Some apprenticeship casting. Her guild has a stone sense drill.”</p><p>“Her control is excellent.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“She could be much better.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Again. No correction. That was worse.</p><p>“Does she know?”</p><p>“She knows she is good.”</p><p>“No. Does she know what she could do?”</p><p>Hessa set the ledger down.</p><p>“What could she do?”</p><p>I started. Barrier load tracing. Structural diagnostics. Siege support. Counter-collapse. Maybe reinforcement. Maybe shaped fracture. Maybe a dozen things no one here had combined because stoneworkers did not need to. Then I stopped. Because Hessa had not asked what I could imagine. She had asked what Rinna could do. Different question.</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She pointed at my wrist.</p><p>“Now you.”</p><p>That was all. No lesson. No speech about fulfillment. No argument that stairs mattered. Just me. I hated her.</p><p>“Limited casting.”</p><p>“I can read.”</p><p>“Everyone says that.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat. She checked my eyes. Then wrists. Then had me hold a low Barrier the size of two fingers over the table. Three breaths. Release.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>I did. Five breaths. Pressure behind the eyes. Not pain.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>I stopped. She did not ask for another.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>“Pressure.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Two.”</p><p>“Out of?”</p><p>“Ten.”</p><p>“Yesterday?”</p><p>“Seven after the road.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I passed the infirmary check.”</p><p>“I am not the infirmary.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>She tapped the tag.</p><p>“Keep it.”</p><p>“For how long?”</p><p>“Until tomorrow.”</p><p>“That is arbitrary.”</p><p>“So is your body.”</p><p>“That is not how bodies work.”</p><p>She stared. I reconsidered.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She moved the stone block Rinna had used. I watched the fracture.</p><p>“You want to try it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You do.”</p><p>“I am restricted.”</p><p>“That is the first useful thing the tag has done.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“You knew I would.”</p><p>“I know you.”</p><p>That carried more weight than I wanted. I changed subjects.</p><p>“Darrowmere samples are coming to Edrin.”</p><p>“Already came.”</p><p>I looked up.</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“This morning.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You were walking.”</p><p>Right. World continued.</p><p>“What did she find?”</p><p>Hessa shrugged.</p><p>“I teach mana.”</p><p>“You know her.”</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“You could ask.”</p><p>“So could you.”</p><p>“I just got back.”</p><p>“That sounds temporary.”</p><p>I stood. She pointed.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you are not done.”</p><p>“I thought we were.”</p><p>“You thought wrong.”</p><p>She handed me a cup. Not chipped. Water. I drank. </p><p>Then waited. A boy arrived. Fourteen, maybe. Too thin. Nervous. He stood in the doorway. </p><p>Hessa said, “You’re early.”</p><p>“My mother said early is better.”</p><p>“She’s wrong.”</p><p>He looked terrified. Hessa sighed.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>He sat in the chair I had just left. </p><p>I moved aside. His lesson began with breathing. Nothing magical happened for five minutes. Then he tried to gather mana into his palm. Failed. Tried again. A faint warmth. </p><p>He smiled. </p><p>Hessa said, “Again.” Not special. Not bad. Normal.</p><p>He would probably take months to do what I had done badly in days at twenty-five. Maybe years. Maybe he would stop. Maybe he would become competent enough to warm metal rivets in his father’s shop. Maybe he would become something else. The distribution. There it was. Not spoken. One cracked cup.</p><p>One stoneworker with excellent control and no interest in siege architecture. One boy pleased by warmth in his palm. And me. I suddenly felt more conspicuous than I had in Darrowmere. Hessa looked at me. Noticed. Of course. She did not say anything. Good. I left. At the Guild, an envelope waited. Not Antonius. Edrin Saye. The ink-thumb clerk handed it over.</p><p>“She said today if possible.”</p><p>I opened it.</p><p>GREG.</p><p>SOUTH CANAL SEAL OPENED.</p><p>CONTENTS IDENTIFIED ENOUGH TO BECOME MORE ANNOYING.</p><p>YOUR QUESTIONS MAY NOW BE USEFUL.</p><p>DO NOT TOUCH ANYTHING.</p><p>EDRIN.</p><p>I read it twice. Alden was somewhere getting his sword repaired and finding Berren. Antonius had work waiting without urgency. Hessa had told me not to experiment. Darrowmere samples had reached Edrin. And the South Canal sacks, which had nearly gotten people killed before any monsters existed, were finally open. There. The world had chosen. I folded the note.</p><p>The clerk said, “Going?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>I looked at the light through the Guild windows. Still afternoon. My body hurt less. My channels were limited. I had eight copper minus food, paper, and dignity. Edrin had specifically written do not touch. That was encouraging.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>The clerk nodded.</p><p>“South Canal.”</p><p>“I remember.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I started toward the door. Then stopped.</p><p>“What happened to the Darrowmere samples?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Edrin has them.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“That is what happened.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. Separate problems until evidence connected them. I left for South Canal. Behind me, the Darrowmere board kept changing without permission.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="030.html">← Chapter 24</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="032.html">Chapter 26 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/016.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 12: The Teacher — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 12</div><h1>THE TEACHER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Jorren answered the question the next morning.</p><p>Not immediately. He made me earn it by walking to the guild yard with him in silence while he carried two practice swords over one shoulder and behaved as though I had personally invented irritating young men.</p><p>I let him have almost half a street.</p><p>"Well?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You said fuck. That implied analysis."</p><p>"It implied regret."</p><p>"Useful regret?"</p><p>Jorren kept walking.</p><p>Third bell had not sounded yet. Carrow was already awake in the practical way cities became awake before respectable people admitted morning had begun. Bakers had fires. Porters had curses. A wagon wheel somewhere ahead had developed a scream exactly like a dying animal and was being ignored by everyone involved.</p><p>I waited another ten steps.</p><p>"What does he do badly?"</p><p>Jorren stopped so abruptly I nearly walked into him.</p><p>"He thinks winning the first part means he owns the second."</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>Jorren pointed one practice sword at my chest.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Two Swords" decoding="async" height="308" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/016/v28_c16_s08_two-swords.png" width="273"/></figure><p>"Stop."</p><p>"What?" I asked.</p><p>"You stopped watching his feet," Jorren said.</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>"You do that when you start building the whole person in your head," Jorren said.</p><p>"People are much less predictable than furniture."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Fine. Explain."</p><p>He lowered the sword.</p><p>"Yesterday. Knife man. He got the wrist, broke the line, had the man done. Then he chased the next movement too hard. Same with the one behind the wagon. Once he thinks he's ahead, he starts spending the lead before he knows what it bought him."</p><p>That was better than the answer I had built overnight.</p><p>Mine had involved ambition, command instinct, probable relationship to authority, the song, and a theory about why certain men become dangerous when the world starts rewarding confidence.</p><p>Jorren had watched his feet.</p><p>I hated when other people were useful before I finished being clever.</p><p>"So he overcommits."</p><p>"Sometimes."</p><p>"When he's winning."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Not when he's losing."</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>There.</p><p>"You saw that too," I said.</p><p>"I hit people for a living. Occasionally I watch them."</p><p>"That's exactly the sort of hidden depth I keep discovering in you."</p><p>He resumed walking.</p><p>"I'm going to hit you first."</p><p>"That seems unrelated."</p><p>"It isn't."</p><p>The guild yard sat behind the training annex, enclosed on three sides by stone and on the fourth by a fence high enough to discourage spectators who had not paid. The guild understood human nature. If two people were going to hit each other, someone would eventually monetize the view.</p><p>The yard was already half full. A pair of Copper adventurers practiced shield transitions near the wall. Three Bronzes ran footwork around chalk marks while an instructor insulted their knees. Someone farther back was learning to fall correctly and failing with commitment.</p><p>Alden was there before us.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="The Bill" decoding="async" height="308" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/016/v28_c16_s09_the-bill.png" width="296"/></figure><p>Of course he was.</p><p>He stood beside the weapon rack with his red scarf tied around one wrist instead of his neck. No goat.</p><p>That was disappointing.</p><p>He saw us and smiled.</p><p>"You came," Alden said.</p><p>I looked at Jorren.</p><p>"Apparently he thought this was optional," I said.</p><p>"It was," Alden said.</p><p>"For you," I said.</p><p>Alden shrugged. "Nobody stopped me."</p><p>Jorren handed him a practice sword.</p><p>"Good philosophy for losing teeth."</p><p>Alden tested the balance once, then twice. He did not flourish it. Good. He checked the grip, flexed his fingers, glanced at Jorren's stance, and adjusted his own by half an inch.</p><p>Also good.</p><p>I felt the reach again. Not hunger exactly. Recognition of leverage. That was worse because it sounded respectable.</p><p>"Rules?" Alden asked.</p><p>"First clean touch," Jorren said. "Head counts. Hands count. Don't break anything we need later."</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>"And him?" Alden asked.</p><p>Jorren pointed toward the edge of the yard.</p><p>"He stays out of the ring."</p><p>"Consultant," I said.</p><p>Alden smiled. "From over there?"</p><p>"Safest kind," I said.</p><p>I moved to the edge of the yard.</p><p>This should have been simple.</p><p>Observe.</p><p>Identify the flaw.</p><p>Offer one correction.</p><p>See whether it transferred.</p><p>No future. No song. No history. No imagined armies. Just two men with wooden swords in a guild yard.</p><p>I could do that.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>Jorren raised his blade.</p><p>Alden matched him.</p><p>The first exchange told me almost nothing because Alden attacked immediately.</p><p>Not wildly. Fast.</p><p>He stepped inside Jorren's preferred distance before Jorren had fully settled, cut high, changed low, then drove his shoulder forward when Jorren turned the second strike. Jorren gave ground once, redirected, and tapped Alden's ribs with the flat.</p><p>Alden stopped.</p><p>Looked down.</p><p>"That was fast."</p><p>"You were faster," Jorren said.</p><p>Alden frowned.</p><p>Good.</p><p>They reset.</p><p>Second exchange, Alden waited.</p><p>Better already.</p><p>Jorren tested the outside line. Alden did not take it. Jorren stepped closer. Alden gave him nothing. Then Jorren's weight shifted forward and Alden moved.</p><p>Three beats.</p><p>First, Alden caught the blade.</p><p>Second, he drove Jorren's point aside and stepped in.</p><p>Third, he chased the advantage.</p><p>There.</p><p>Jorren had already recovered. He let Alden believe the center remained open, turned his hips, and hooked Alden's lead leg with his foot.</p><p>Alden hit the sand hard. He rolled, came up on one knee, and laughed. Not embarrassed. Not angry. Interested. That changed my model. Small change. Important.</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="Ribs" decoding="async" height="308" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/016/v28_c16_s10_ribs.png" width="331"/></figure><p>Men with that much confidence often hated public correction. Alden appeared to hate only wasted correction.</p><p>"Again," Alden said.</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>I shrugged.</p><p>Jorren tossed Alden his practice sword.</p><p>"Then get up."</p><p>Alden grinned and rose.</p><p>They went again.</p><p>Alden lost the third exchange too, but differently. Jorren forced him backward, and Alden became much harder to touch. No chasing. No pride in holding ground. He gave distance, reset, cut at Jorren's hand, nearly escaped, then got caught at the shoulder when Jorren changed rhythm.</p><p>Interesting. Jorren had been exactly right. Alden was less dangerous when he believed he had won. No. Wrong wording. He became less careful when he believed he had won. Danger remained. That distinction mattered.</p><p>"Stop," I said.</p><p>Both men looked at me.</p><p>Jorren lowered his sword.</p><p>Alden did not.</p><p>"Why?" Alden asked.</p><p>"Because you're doing the same thing three different ways," I said.</p><p>Alden lowered the sword but stayed in stance.</p><p>"Which thing?"</p><p>I walked closer.</p><p>Jorren's expression said he had already decided this was a mistake and wanted credit later.</p><p>"You think the exchange ends when you get what you wanted."</p><p>Alden's smile faded.</p><p>Good.</p><p>"Explain."</p><p>"First bout, you wanted distance before he settled. You got it. Then you kept pressing because the first success felt like proof the rest belonged to you. Second, you broke his center. Good. Then you chased the opening he gave you after you had already won the useful part."</p><p>"I lost."</p><p>"Eventually."</p><p>"That's usually the part people count."</p><p>"Only because dead people are difficult to survey."</p><p>Jorren groaned.</p><p>Alden ignored him.</p><p>"And the third?"</p><p>"You were losing, so you stopped assuming anything belonged to you. You became patient. You gave him distance. You made him earn every step. You almost touched his hand."</p><p>Alden looked at Jorren.</p><p>Jorren nodded once.</p><p>I continued.</p><p>"You're better when the fight tells you you're in danger than when the fight tells you you're right."</p><p>Silence. The sentence had come out larger than the sword work. Jorren looked at me sharply. I adjusted.</p><p>"So stop trying to win twice."</p><p>Alden looked back at me.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"If you take the first advantage, keep it. Don't immediately spend it proving the advantage was real. Make him solve the new problem."</p><p>Alden's eyes narrowed. Thinking, not accepting. Good.</p><p>"That's it?"</p><p>"For now."</p><p>"You dragged me here for that?"</p><p>"You came voluntarily."</p><p>"You wanted me here."</p><p>"Those aren't contradictory."</p><p>Alden rolled the practice sword once in his hand.</p><p>"Show me."</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>Jorren said, "No."</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>"Again, you are answering questions directed at me."</p><p>"I'm saving time."</p><p>Alden looked at the sword on my hip, then at my stance.</p><p>"Can you?"</p><p>There were several possible lies.</p><p>Old Greg would have demonstrated the principle beautifully.</p><p>Current Greg could demonstrate the first half and then discover which part of the yard tasted best.</p><p>"Not reliably," I said.</p><p>Alden blinked.</p><p>Jorren smiled.</p><p>I disliked both of them.</p><p>"Then how do you know?" Alden asked.</p><p>"Because doing and seeing are different skills."</p><p>"Convenient."</p><p>"Very."</p><p>Alden rolled the practice sword once in his palm, then looked at Jorren.</p><p>"Again."</p><p>Jorren raised his sword.</p><p>"You heard him."</p><p>"Unfortunately."</p><p>This time Alden did not attack.</p><p>That alone changed the exchange.</p><p>Jorren moved first. Alden gave him a narrow outside line, enough to invite pressure. Jorren took it cautiously. Alden caught the blade, stepped inside, and for one heartbeat reached exactly the same position as the second bout.</p><p>His body wanted the next strike. I saw it in the shoulder tightening and the weight beginning to move. Then he stopped. Not froze. Stopped. He took one small step back instead.</p><p>Jorren had already begun the recovery that would have punished the chase.</p><p>Now the recovery cut empty air.</p><p>Alden smiled.</p><p>Jorren did not.</p><p>Alden had kept the advantage.</p><p>Jorren had to rebuild distance from a bad angle.</p><p>Alden waited.</p><p>Waited.</p><p>Then Jorren moved.</p><p>Alden touched his shoulder.</p><p>Clean.</p><p>The sound was barely anything. Wood against leather. My entire body reacted as though someone had struck a bell inside my chest. Not the song. Pleasure. Pure and immediate. I had forgotten that part.</p><p>No mana.</p><p>No reinforcement.</p><p>No spellwork layered through three other people.</p><p>Just one observation placed in the correct mind at the correct time, and suddenly the person in front of me became harder to beat.</p><p>That had always felt good.</p><p>Too good.</p><p>Alden stared at the place his practice sword had touched Jorren.</p><p>Then he looked at me.</p><p>There was no gratitude in his face. Excellent. There was appetite. Worse.</p><p>"Again," Alden said.</p><p>Jorren hit him in the mouth.</p><p>Not maliciously.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>Alden stepped into the next exchange too eagerly, tried to recreate the correction as a trick rather than understand it, and Jorren punished him before he finished setting it up.</p><p>Alden sat in the sand with one hand over his lip.</p><p>Jorren rested the practice sword across one shoulder and looked at me.</p><p>"Your student."</p><p>"I have taught him one sentence," I said.</p><p>Alden checked his fingers for blood.</p><p>"Good sentence," Alden said.</p><p>"Bad religion," I said.</p><p>He laughed, which made his lip hurt, which made him swear.</p><p>Better.</p><p>Jorren offered him a hand. Alden took it.</p><p>They reset.</p><p>The next four exchanges were less dramatic and much more useful.</p><p>Alden did not suddenly become excellent.</p><p>He overcorrected. Once he refused to spend an advantage at all and let Jorren escape. Another time he waited so deliberately that Jorren simply hit him. Then he found the middle. Not every time. Enough.</p><p>Jorren adapted too. Of course he did. Improvement did not freeze everyone else in place.</p><p>I watched the loop form: action, correction, response, new problem. There. Home.</p><p>I had spent years inside that shape, later with spells and battle lines and mistakes that killed people. Here it fit inside one yard.</p><p>Jorren stepped out of range and lowered his sword.</p><p>"Enough."</p><p>Alden was breathing hard now. Sweat darkened the collar of his shirt. His hair had escaped whatever inadequate tie had been holding it.</p><p>"I'm not tired."</p><p>"You're lying."</p><p>"I'm less tired than you."</p><p>"Also lying."</p><p>Alden smiled.</p><p>Jorren pointed the practice sword at him.</p><p>"And now you're about to learn something else badly."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Stopping."</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>"You agree with him?"</p><p>I considered the answer.</p><p>Old Greg had trained through exhaustion because old Greg could reinforce tissue, manage recovery, recognize the exact line between adaptation and damage, and still crossed it sometimes because being able to see a cliff did not prevent a man from walking off one.</p><p>Current Greg had recently done almost the same thing without most of those advantages.</p><p>"Unfortunately."</p><p>Alden tossed the practice sword toward the rack.</p><p>It landed correctly.</p><p>Show-off.</p><p>He drank from a waterskin, then pointed it at me.</p><p>"My turn," Alden said.</p><p>"To drink?" I asked.</p><p>"To ask," Alden said.</p><p>That was not what I wanted.</p><p>Good.</p><p>"Ask."</p><p>Alden nodded toward Jorren.</p><p>"What does he do badly?" Alden asked.</p><p>Jorren went very still.</p><p>I smiled before I could stop myself.</p><p>"Interesting."</p><p>"You asked him about me."</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>Traitor was too strong a word for his expression.</p><p>Not by much.</p><p>"I did."</p><p>"So?"</p><p>This was different.</p><p>I had expected Alden to want more correction about himself. That fit the model. Ambitious young man recognizes useful advisor, requests additional optimization, increasingly values Greg, eventually,</p><p>No.</p><p>That was me writing both sides again.</p><p>Alden had found the structure and turned it around.</p><p>Of course he had.</p><p>I looked at Jorren.</p><p>Jorren spread his arms slightly.</p><p>"Go on."</p><p>That surprised me.</p><p>"You're allowing this?"</p><p>"I want to hear what you think."</p><p>Dangerous phrase.</p><p>I looked at him more carefully.</p><p>Jorren's strongest habit was not the heavy right. He had corrected that weeks ago because I had pointed it out often enough to become annoying. He remained physically more conditioned than either of us, technically cleaner than Alden, and patient enough to let another man make mistakes. What did he do badly? Several things. Everyone did. Which one mattered here?</p><p>Jorren disliked yielding initiative once he had chosen a rhythm. Not because of pride exactly. His technique was built around reading the opponent, setting a pace, then punishing deviation. When somebody broke that pace without becoming reckless, he took half a beat too long to abandon his first read.</p><p>I could tell Alden that and watch him use it against Jorren, who had just answered my question honestly. The resistance I felt was small and ugly enough to be interesting.</p><p>Giving someone a weakness felt different from giving them a correction.</p><p>"He trusts his first read too long," I said.</p><p>Jorren's face changed.</p><p>Alden immediately looked at him.</p><p>"Meaning?"</p><p>"Meaning if he decides what kind of exchange you're building, he'll commit to solving that version longer than he should. Don't fake high and go low. That's obvious. Give him a real pattern. Let him understand it. Then stop being that fighter."</p><p>Jorren stared at me.</p><p>"Fuck you."</p><p>"You asked."</p><p>"I wanted to know."</p><p>"Now you do."</p><p>Alden was smiling again.</p><p>Jorren pointed at him.</p><p>"If you get clever, I hit harder."</p><p>"That's not very instructional."</p><p>"It teaches consequences."</p><p>They went again.</p><p>Alden lost the first two exchanges because he tried too hard to become a different fighter.</p><p>Good.</p><p>You could not simply wear a new pattern like a coat because someone described it. Bodies had habits. Decisions had timing. False behavior looked false when it was selected from outside.</p><p>Third exchange, Alden stopped trying to trick Jorren. He simply fought. Pressure forward. Fast entry. Aggressive second beat. Jorren recognized it. Of course. Alden repeated it in the fourth. Jorren punished him. Fifth exchange, same opening, same pressure. Jorren settled into the answer. Then Alden left. Not physically. Pattern.</p><p>The first beat came fast.</p><p>The second never arrived.</p><p>Jorren's counter cut entered empty space because he had already begun answering the continuation.</p><p>Alden stepped outside and touched his ribs.</p><p>Jorren looked down.</p><p>Then at me.</p><p>Then at Alden.</p><p>"I hate both of you."</p><p>Alden laughed.</p><p>I did too.</p><p>There it was again: the old pleasure. Not dominating either man. Making the room harder. I had missed this.</p><p>Jorren reclaimed the next three exchanges with increasing violence.</p><p>Alden learned that strategic insight did not make his ribs less reachable.</p><p>Also useful.</p><p>Eventually the yard instructor shouted at us because we had occupied the lane past our paid time.</p><p>Material constraints remained undefeated.</p><p>We moved to the wall.</p><p>Alden sat on the low stone ledge and drank more water. Jorren stayed standing because sitting after hard work made his legs stiff, or because he wanted to look superior. Both could be true.</p><p>I leaned against the fence.</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>"How much?"</p><p>"For what?"</p><p>"That."</p><p>I knew what he meant.</p><p>I made him say it anyway.</p><p>"Words? Usually free. That's why people waste so many."</p><p>"Training. Watching. Whatever you call it."</p><p>The answer arrived as terms: weekly fee, contract percentage, access, training exchange. Alden had handed me the arrangement I wanted yesterday.</p><p>Old Greg would have defined it immediately. Ambiguity wasted leverage.</p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>Jorren looked at me.</p><p>Not warning.</p><p>Watching.</p><p>Annoying man.</p><p>I looked at Alden. Twenty-one. Sweating. Split lip. Good enough to make a Bronze robbery look easy, not good enough to avoid getting hit repeatedly by Jorren after one useful correction. A song waited forty years away and knew something I did not. None of that answered the present question.</p><p>"I don't know," I said.</p><p>Alden frowned.</p><p>"You don't know what you charge?"</p><p>"I don't know what this is yet."</p><p>Jorren made a small sound.</p><p>I ignored him.</p><p>Alden studied me.</p><p>"You wanted something yesterday."</p><p>"I still do."</p><p>"Which is?"</p><p>"To see whether I can make you better."</p><p>That was more truth than I intended.</p><p>Alden's eyes sharpened.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>There were too many answers: I needed capability now. I remembered his name. There was a song about him that made my skin cold.</p><p>Old Greg could stand behind a better fighter and change the result of the room. When Alden touched Jorren's shoulder after one sentence, something in me had come home.</p><p>"Because I'm good at it."</p><p>Alden smiled slowly.</p><p>"There he is."</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>"What does that mean?"</p><p>"Yesterday you kept talking around it."</p><p>"I did not."</p><p>"You did. You're strange when you're pretending not to want something."</p><p>Jorren laughed.</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>"You are enjoying this too much."</p><p>"Immensely."</p><p>Alden stood.</p><p>"Fine. Don't charge me yet."</p><p>"Generous."</p><p>"You can come on a contract tomorrow."</p><p>That was not the direction I expected.</p><p>Good.</p><p>"What contract?"</p><p>"South canal. Warehouse owner says something is getting into grain stores at night. Missing sacks, broken boards, tracks near the water. Guild posted it this morning. Bronze. Two to four people."</p><p>"People?"</p><p>"Adventurers."</p><p>"I meant what is getting into the grain."</p><p>"If I knew, the contract would be cheaper."</p><p>Jorren asked, "You already took it?"</p><p>Alden nodded.</p><p>"With who?" Jorren asked.</p><p>"Nobody yet," Alden said.</p><p>"Then you didn't take it," Jorren said.</p><p>"I reserved it," Alden said.</p><p>"That's not a thing," Jorren said.</p><p>"Clerk let me put my name on it while I found bodies," Alden said.</p><p>"Which clerk?" I asked.</p><p>Alden looked at me.</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Professional curiosity."</p><p>"Ink on her hands. Looks like she hates everyone."</p><p>That described at least one useful person in every guild hall I had ever known.</p><p>"And you want me?" I asked.</p><p>Alden looked at Jorren first.</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>"Both of you," Alden said.</p><p>Jorren shook his head.</p><p>"I have work," Jorren said.</p><p>Alden did not argue.</p><p>Also interesting.</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>"You?" Alden asked.</p><p>My first instinct was yes, so I made myself wait.</p><p>South canal. Grain stores. Night intrusion. Unknown threat. Bronze. Bounded problem. Actual adventuring. Alden.</p><p>A chance to see whether the correction survived outside a clean training lane, and whether Alden did.</p><p>I could build seventeen reasons. I did not need them.</p><p>"What does it pay?"</p><p>Alden smiled.</p><p>"Twelve copper each if it's vermin. Eighteen if it's people. More if there is recoverable loss."</p><p>"And if it's neither?"</p><p>"Then we get surprised."</p><p>I looked at Jorren.</p><p>He raised both hands.</p><p>"Don't ask me."</p><p>That was fair.</p><p>I looked back at Alden.</p><p>"When?"</p><p>"Dusk."</p><p>"Tomorrow?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"I'll look at the posting first."</p><p>Alden laughed.</p><p>"Of course you will."</p><p>"That's called reading the contract."</p><p>"I read it."</p><p>"You summarized it in four sentences."</p><p>"Efficiently."</p><p>I almost liked him.</p><p>That was probably premature.</p><p>He untied the red scarf from his wrist and put it around his neck again.</p><p>For half a heartbeat, the color caught the morning light and something moved behind my eyes.</p><p>Music, not words. A room full of voices with one note held too long. Then gone. I did not chase it. That was new.</p><p>Alden started toward the yard gate.</p><p>"Tomorrow," he said.</p><p>"Maybe."</p><p>He walked backward three steps.</p><p>"You're coming."</p><p>"That confidence is one of the things you do badly."</p><p>He grinned.</p><p>"Worked today."</p><p>Then he turned and left.</p><p>Jorren waited until Alden was out of sight.</p><p>"You look happy."</p><p>"I am evaluating."</p><p>"You look happy while evaluating."</p><p>"Sometimes evaluation is pleasant."</p><p>"You made him better."</p><p>There was no accusation in it.</p><p>That made the question worse.</p><p>"A little."</p><p>"And you liked it."</p><p>I looked toward the gate.</p><p>I could have denied that.</p><p>There was no point.</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>Jorren nodded once.</p><p>Then he handed me a practice sword.</p><p>I stared at it.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Your turn."</p><p>"We finished."</p><p>"He finished."</p><p>"The lane time expired."</p><p>Jorren pointed toward the far corner where an unused strip of sand ran beside the wall.</p><p>"Free space."</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>He smiled.</p><p>"You spent the whole morning making other people better."</p><p>Ah. There it was. The bill.</p><p>I took the sword.</p><p>Jorren raised his.</p><p>"What do I do badly?" I asked.</p><p>He hit me in the ribs.</p><p>I went down.</p><p>From the sand I said, "That was not an answer."</p><p>Jorren stood over me.</p><p>"You keep forgetting you're one of the people."</p><p>I stared up at him.</p><p>That was annoyingly good.</p><p>Then he hit me again.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="015.html">← Chapter 11</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="017.html">Chapter 13 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
