- `chapters/002.html:2`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 2: The Borrower — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 2</div><h1>THE BORROWER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Carrow looked wrong at street level. From the window, the differences had been architectural. Down here, they had faces. I made it twelve steps before staring at a woman long enough that she checked whether something was wrong with her clothes. Nothing was. I knew the name above the shop behind her, Vella, and for several uncomfortable seconds I tried to decide whether I knew her too. Nothing.</p><p>"Sorry," I said.</p><p>"For what?" the woman asked.</p><p>"For thinking you were someone else."</p><p>"Do I look like her?" she asked.</p><p>"Not remotely."</p><p>She walked away faster. Every face wanted to become a question. Who are you? Did I know you? Did you become somebody? Did you die? Did I help? Did I make it worse? Most gave me nothing. Forty years of life did not turn memory into a census. A guild runner named Daven caught my attention because I knew a Daven decades later. I asked for his family name. He asked why. His friend began laughing when I told him I might owe a Daven money. Three streets later I remembered the man I meant. Wrong Daven.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg moving through younger Carrow as familiar faces catch his attention." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/002/v28_c02_s01_carrow-street-memory.png"/></figure><p>"Excellent," I muttered.</p><p>Forty years of memory was a warehouse after an earthquake. Useful things were in there. Finding them was the problem. So I did not go directly to the lender. First I walked. I checked the city against memory. The northern freight road was still half dirt. The Exchange did not exist. Businesses I remembered as institutions were one-room shops or empty lots. I bought paper with one of my three copper and sat across from the east market.</p><p>Walking was not wasted time anymore. It was indexing. A street corner reminded me of a riot. The riot reminded me of the guild captain who mishandled it. His name reminded me of a shipping family, and the shipping family reminded me that their fortune had started somewhere boring. Most tangents died after two steps. A few did not.</p><p>That became the method. Let the present tug on the future until something connected strongly enough to investigate. I did not need an exact winning bet. I needed one chain of cause and effect that still existed at this end of history. The lender was only a tool for the first step. Before I borrowed anything, I needed one present-day fact I could turn into a believable use for his money. Future knowledge was worthless if I could not show where it touched the world now.</p><p>WHAT BECOMES VALUABLE?</p><p>That was better than asking what happened tomorrow. Tomorrow was mush. Causes were clearer. Mana-glass. Blue salt. Certain dungeon waste. Alchemical filtration. A porter dumped gray stone chips beside a masonry stall. I knew the stone. Kestrin shale. Cheap. Brittle. Mildly mana-reactive. Mostly rubbish. Years later it would be used in filtration ceramics because the property everybody hated about it was exactly what made it useful. I did not remember the date or the inventor. I remembered the reason. That was enough to investigate.</p><p>Not enough to invest. Present Greg still needed to prove the property was already there, that someone could reproduce it, and that the economics were not completely different forty years earlier. Memory gave me a lead. The city had to give me confirmation.</p><p>"How much for a cart?" I asked the stall owner. </p><p>She looked at my Bronze plate. "Why?"</p><p>"Research," I said.</p><p>"You a mage?" she asked.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Artificer?" she asked.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Builder?" she asked.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"What do you research?" she asked.</p><p>"Bad decisions," I said.</p><p>She laughed. "Two silver." I had two copper. Progress. The name ARWICK came back while I was walking away. Not a person at first. A maker's stamp on filter housings decades from now. Arwick Works existed already, if one rented room behind a cooper counted as works. Arlo Arwick repaired lamp regulators. He was not famous yet. I stared at him too long.</p><p>The future gave me his surname. The present gave me an artificer with a workshop, tools, and enough technical knowledge to tell me whether my memory was nonsense. I did not know if Arlo himself became the Arwick I remembered, if a child inherited the work, or if somebody bought the name later. For now, he was the man who could test the first idea on my list.</p><p>That should have been simple. It was not. The future version of a name carried weight, and weight distorted judgment. I could feel myself wanting Arlo to be important because that would make my memory cleaner. Cleaner memories were easier to monetize. Easier to control. That was exactly the kind of reasoning I needed to notice before it became a decision.</p><p>"Can I help you?" Arlo asked.</p><p>Maybe you make a fortune. Maybe your son does. Maybe I am remembering the wrong Arwick entirely.</p><p>"Do you work with mana-reactive ceramics?" I asked.</p><p>His annoyance became interest when I explained the shale. Not the future. The present properties. Powder. Heat. Trace mana. Binding residue.</p><p>"That would contaminate the batch," Arlo said.</p><p>"Unless the contamination binds preferentially," I said.</p><p>He put down his tool. There. Not proof. Evidence. A test would cost six silver. I had two copper.</p><p>Now I went to Antonius Vale. I remembered the man he became much better than the man he was now, and I even went to the wrong building first. Eventually a narrow man with a scar led me into a gambling room, and Antonius came out to meet me. I knew him immediately. Younger. Leaner. Black hair instead of silver at the temples. Cheap coat by his later standards. The eyes were the same.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Pell Arwick putting down his tool as Greg catches his technical interest." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/002/v28_c02_s02_pell-takes-interest.png"/></figure><p>I had found something plausible and someone capable of testing it, but I could not afford the test. Antonius was not yet the financial predator I remembered from later life. Right now he was simply a lender with criminal edges and enough appetite for risk that a strange young adventurer might get through the door. I needed his silver, not his friendship. Ideally I would repay him before he had time to decide I was more valuable than the debt.</p><p>The sequence was clean enough: prove one remembered advantage, use the proof to borrow, turn the borrowed money into real capital, then use the capital to accelerate magic. Every step depended on the one before it. One false memory could poison the whole chain.</p><p>I considered abandoning the shale and finding a safer idea. Then I considered how long "safer" would take. The thought lasted perhaps three seconds. Old habits again. I was already trading certainty for speed.</p><p>"Have we met?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"You are staring."</p><p>"I'm adjusting."</p><p>"To what?"</p><p>"Your age," I said.</p><p>Antonius smiled. "How old did you expect me to be?"</p><p>"Richer."</p><p>That got me inside. His office was a storage room with a ham hanging from the ceiling. Future Antonius had owned rooms designed to make nobles feel poor. I had to work very hard not to enjoy this.</p><p>"What do you want?" he asked.</p><p>"A loan," I said.</p><p>"How much?" Antonius asked. </p><p>I named the offensive number. </p><p>The man with the scar laughed.</p><p>Antonius looked at my Bronze plate. "Collateral?"</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Property?" he asked.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Guarantor?" Antonius continued.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Family?" he asked.</p><p>"Dead," I said.</p><p>"Useful friends?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"Not yet," I said.</p><p>"What do you have?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"Information," I said. I gave him the Kestrin argument. Present facts only. Guild salvage price. Material properties. Arwick's willingness to test it. What the test would cost.</p><p>"You're asking for twenty times that," Antonius said.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"Why?" Antonius asked.</p><p>"Because if it works, I don't want to come back tomorrow."</p><p>His man laughed again.</p><p>Antonius did not. "How does a nineteen-year-old Bronze know this?"</p><p>"If I had an answer you'd believe, I wouldn't need your money."</p><p>He denied the large loan. Of course he did. Old Greg's reputation did not exist. Charisma was not collateral. So I changed roles.</p><p>"Smaller loan," I said. "Enough for the shale, the test, food, and guild fees. I repay principal plus twenty percent in ten days."</p><p>"Forty."</p><p>"Twenty-five."</p><p>"Forty."</p><p>"Thirty, and if I fail, I work contracts through you until the balance is cleared."</p><p>His expression changed. There it was. Me. A Bronze adventurer was cheap. A Bronze adventurer volunteering his future labor while talking like a merchant was interesting.</p><p>"Thirty-five," Antonius said. "Eight days."</p><p>"Nine."</p><p>"Eight."</p><p>"Fine," I said.</p><p>Antonius counted silver onto the desk.</p><p>I should have felt relief. Instead I felt acceleration. I knew that feeling. Hubris putting on its boots.</p><p>"If you run," Antonius said, "I find you."</p><p>"I know," I said.</p><p>His hand stopped. Too fast.</p><p>"How?"</p><p>Shit. I let some uncertainty into my face. Nineteen-year-old uncertainty. A boy pretending he had more control than he did.</p><p>"I asked around."</p><p>I had shifted before deciding to. Confident expert to nervous boy because nervous boy was safer. Voice slightly smaller. Shoulders less certain. Let Antonius feel older, sharper, more in control. Give him the version of Greg that made his next decision easiest. Useful. Also something I should probably examine later.</p><p>Antonius pushed the coins toward me. "Eight days, Greg."</p><p>I picked them up.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Antonius pushing the eight-day loan across the table to Greg." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/002/v28_c02_s03_eight-days-antonius.png"/></figure><p>"You're going to remember me."</p><p>"I remember everyone who owes me money."</p><p>"No. I mean later."</p><p>His eyes narrowed. I should have stopped. Apparently being nineteen again had restored my need for an audience too. I grinned. "Eight days." Outside, I nearly walked into a young guild clerk carrying forms.</p><p>"Watch it."</p><p>"Sorry."</p><p>Ink on two fingers. Gray uniform. Irritated voice. Something caught.</p><p>"Sella?"</p><p>She stopped. "Do I know you?"</p><p>I knew her future immediately. Not every detail, but the shape. Years from now she would run half the guild hall through force of personality and a filing system nobody else understood. Today she was twenty-two and looking at me like I collected teeth.</p><p>"No," I said.</p><p>"Then how do you know my name?"</p><p>Her name was written on the top form. I pointed. She looked down. Then back at me.</p><p>"You were staring before that."</p><p>"You remind me of someone."</p><p>"Who?"</p><p>"You," I said. </p><p>She stared. </p><p>I smiled.</p><p>"Freak," Sella said, and walked around me.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Sella moving around Greg after their near collision in the street." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/002/v28_c02_s04_sella-collision.png"/></figure><p>I watched her go. Who are you now? That was harder than who do you become. I had the uncomfortable suspicion it was also more important. Then I remembered I had eight days to turn borrowed silver into enough money that Antonius Vale did not own my schedule. Reflection could wait. I went to buy garbage.</p><p>So that was the board after one day. Money: borrowed. Deadline: eight days. First investment: a cart of material most people considered rubbish. Arlo: interested enough to test it, not yet mine to command, which was probably healthy. Antonius: watching. Magic: still theoretical. Reputation: nonexistent. The immediate job was simple enough. Make the shale prove something, turn that proof into enough money to clear Vale, then buy myself the time to start becoming a mage six years early.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="001.html">← Chapter 1</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="004.html">Chapter 3 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/026.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 20: The Patient — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 20</div><h1>THE PATIENT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The healer took my shirt. Not metaphorically. She cut it off.</p><p>“That was unnecessary,” I said.</p><p>“It was stuck.”</p><p>“It had buttons.”</p><p>“It had blood.”</p><p>“Mostly not mine.”</p><p>“That is not reassuring.”</p><p>The Darrowmere infirmary occupied what had probably been a meeting hall yesterday. Long tables had been pushed against the walls. Bedrolls covered the floor. Somebody had hung blankets between benches to create the illusion of privacy and failed.</p><p>Alden sat three places down with his coat off and his shoulder being cleaned by a healer who looked younger than him and much less impressed by him than he preferred. Cal was on my other side. His arm needed stitches. Mine needed soap. This offended him.</p><p>“You bled more than me,” he said.</p><p>“Most of this is monster.”</p><p>“That is worse.”</p><p>The healer washing my side stopped.</p><p>“Monster?”</p><p>“Creature.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>“We do not know what it is.”</p><p>“Then stop naming it while I am checking whether it put anything inside you.”</p><p>That was a good point. I stopped. For approximately eight seconds.</p><p>“Have the bites been poisonous?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>“Eight seconds.”</p><p>“Longer than usual.”</p><p>“Quiet.”</p><p>I obeyed. Mostly because my head hurt. The headache had stopped being sharp and become dense. A pressure behind both eyes. My channels felt scraped rather than burned. Three Barriers in a short fight, maybe four depending on whether the buckle attempt counted as a cast or merely a failed insult to magic. My palm was split. My hip was bruised. My left shoulder had begun complaining about hitting the wagon.</p><p>No bite. No claw wound. No broken bones. Good. The healer pressed two fingers below my ribs. I flinched.</p><p>“Bruise.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Deep?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“How do you know?”</p><p>“I have had deeper.”</p><p>“That is not an answer.”</p><p>Everyone was using my own techniques against me now. The world had become intolerable. Alden said, “He does that.” The healer working on him laughed. </p><p>I turned my head.</p><p>“Do what?” I asked.</p><p>“Answers a different question,” Alden said.</p><p>“I answer useful questions,” I said.</p><p>“You answer the one you wanted.”</p><p>“That is usually the useful one.”</p><p>The first healer tightened a bandage around my palm.</p><p>“Not in here.”</p><p>I liked her. That was happening too often.</p><p>“What’s your name?”</p><p>“Doesn’t matter. Hold still.”</p><p>Alden laughed hard enough to wince.</p><p>“Shoulder?” I asked.</p><p>“Shut up,” he said.</p><p>Good. He was fine. Not fine. Fine enough. The torn scarf remained tied around his wrist. I avoided looking at it. That took effort. The healer noticed. Of course she did.</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Dizzy?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Nausea?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Light sensitivity?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Magic?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Three small Barriers.”</p><p>She looked at me for the first time as something other than an inconvenient body.</p><p>“Three?”</p><p>“Possibly four.”</p><p>“What does possibly mean?”</p><p>“One failed before it formed properly.”</p><p>“What size?”</p><p>“Coin to palm.”</p><p>“Load?”</p><p>“One deflection against a charging creature. One foot disruption. One attempted brace on a harness buckle.”</p><p>“Attempted brace?”</p><p>“Failed.”</p><p>“Pressure casting?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She sat back.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“I have stopped.”</p><p>“No more today.”</p><p>“That may not be practical.”</p><p>“Then become practical.”</p><p>I opened my mouth. She pointed toward Alden.</p><p>“If he gets bitten because you gave yourself a channel seizure trying to save him, I will charge him for the bed.”</p><p>Alden said, “Why me?”</p><p>“You look richer.”</p><p>“I’m not.”</p><p>“Then both of you lose.”</p><p>Excellent medical reasoning. I nodded.</p><p>“No more magic today.”</p><p>She stared.</p><p>“That was too easy.”</p><p>“I am capable of learning.”</p><p>Alden said, “Sometimes.” The healer wrote something on a strip of paper and tied it to my wrist.</p><p>“What is this?”</p><p>“Restriction.”</p><p>“You tagged me?”</p><p>“Yes. No casting until someone rechecks you.”</p><p>“Today?”</p><p>“At least today.”</p><p>I looked at Alden. He was enjoying this too much. His healer gave him a smaller strip. Alden read it.</p><p>“NO LIFTING LEFT.”</p><p>He looked offended.</p><p>“Left what?”</p><p>“Arm,” she said.</p><p>“That is badly written.”</p><p>“Go away.”</p><p>We went away. Outside, Darrowmere smelled like wet straw, smoke, manure, and boiled grain. Not destroyed. The first thing rumors had gotten wrong was scale. People were still living here. A woman stood in a doorway beating mud from a rug. Two boys carried buckets.</p><p>A cooper had reopened his shop despite a watch barricade twenty yards away. Someone sold bread from a cart. The eastern bell tower rose above the roofs, dark stone, square top, one bronze bell visible through the opening. Three quick strokes. Pause. Three. Road warning. The bell sounded again. Alden looked east.</p><p>“Still going.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What now?”</p><p>We had been told to report. That was the obvious answer. I did not want the obvious answer. My body did. My channels definitely did.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>Alden nodded. No argument. That was almost suspicious. The watch command post occupied a grain office beside the central square. Green-coated watch moved in and out carrying messages, maps, water, and once a dead chicken. Nobody explained the chicken. Inside, Captain Harl Doven stood over a table. He was not old. I had expected old.</p><p>Command often looked older in memory because responsibility flattened everyone into categories. Doven was maybe thirty-five, narrow-faced, with one side of his hair burned short. Nemi Caul sat in a chair beside him with her injured leg elevated on a crate. She saw us.</p><p>“Oh.”</p><p>I did not know whether that was good. Doven looked up.</p><p>“Road wagon?”</p><p>Cal raised a hand.</p><p>“Cal Serren. Contract rider.”</p><p>“Alden Marr.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>Doven looked at me.</p><p>“You’re the questions.”</p><p>“I have been called worse.”</p><p>Nemi said, “Not by me.”</p><p>“Yet.”</p><p>Doven pointed at three empty chairs.</p><p>“Sit. Report in order. Do not improve it.”</p><p>I sat. I liked him immediately. Cal went first. He had seen the first creature at the orchard wall. He described it. Doven interrupted only for position, distance, direction, and time. Alden went next. His account was shorter. I noticed that. He did not dramatize getting dragged. Did not mention the scarf. Did not mention my Barrier unless directly asked. Then me.</p><p>I reported one creature at the wall. Gray. Long-bodied. Four legs. Dark hair or bristles along spine. Abnormal turning behavior. Black blood. Steel penetrated hide. Creature demonstrated rapid lateral redirection without visible ordinary footwork. Doven stopped me.</p><p>“Visible to you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Could you have missed it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I continued. Second creature from west targeted horses rather than us. Possibly relevant. One creature killed on road. Sword remained in body. Three creatures approached from east later. Unknown whether wounded first creature among them. One followed wagon until watch crossbow hit it. I mentioned the ridges under the chest. Doven frowned.</p><p>“What ridges?”</p><p>“Small hard structures along the underside of the sternum. I saw them when one reared vertically.”</p><p>“Bone?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Armor?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“Natural?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>He looked at Nemi. She smiled faintly.</p><p>“He does know the phrase.”</p><p>“I learned it recently.”</p><p>Doven marked the map. There were already six black circles east and north of town. Three red crosses. One blue line along the north road.</p><p>“What are the crosses?” I asked.</p><p>“Dead creatures recovered.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Dead Creature" decoding="async" height="335" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/026/v28_c26_s01_the-dead-creature.png" width="303"/></figure><p>My attention sharpened.</p><p>“Three?”</p><p>“Three bodies.”</p><p>“Examined?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“By?”</p><p>“Apothecary. Tanner. Watch mage.”</p><p>I leaned forward. My wrist tag swung.</p><p>NO CASTING.</p><p>Doven noticed.</p><p>“Keep that on until the infirmary clears you.”</p><p>“I dislike it.”</p><p>“Most patients do.”</p><p>“What did they find?”</p><p>Doven looked at me.</p><p>“Why do you need to know?”</p><p>Unknown architecture. Black blood. Movement without preparation. Hard ridges. If this was magical alteration, I might recognize the shape before I recognized the species. Also, I wanted to know.</p><p>“Because if I see another one, I want fewer surprises.”</p><p>That was the clean answer. Doven considered.</p><p>“Black blood is blood.”</p><p>“Meaning?”</p><p>“Not tar. Not magical residue. Actual blood. Thick. Warmer than human.”</p><p>“Organs?”</p><p>“Normal enough to disappoint everyone.”</p><p>Alden asked, “Everyone?”</p><p>“People prefer monsters to be interesting after they’re dead,” Nemi said.</p><p>Correct. Doven continued.</p><p>“Four-limbed. Mammal structure, mostly. Stomach had sheep. Teeth are ordinary teeth in an unusual jaw. No embedded metal. No obvious rune work. No collar marks. No brand.”</p><p>“Mana?”</p><p>“Present.”</p><p>That mattered.</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>Doven looked at Nemi. She answered.</p><p>“More than a normal animal. Less than a trained war-beast.”</p><p>“Pattern?”</p><p>“Watch mage says diffuse.”</p><p>I paused. Diffuse. Not structured around a single organ. Not necessarily spellwork.</p><p>“Did the mage know the species?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Did anyone?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. Bad. I asked, “Do the chest ridges appear on the bodies?” </p><p>Doven looked at a note.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What are they?”</p><p>“Bone growth.”</p><p>“Natural?”</p><p>Nemi said, “You are going to make that word do too much.” She was right.</p><p>“Present in all three?”</p><p>“Two. Third was damaged.”</p><p>“Same placement?”</p><p>“Approximately.”</p><p>Alden shifted beside me. I could feel him getting bored. Not bored exactly. Restless. We had nearly died an hour ago and I was discussing sternums. That was a me problem. Doven tapped the map.</p><p>“Now the useful part.”</p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>“That was useful.”</p><p>“For tomorrow.”</p><p>He tapped again.</p><p>“This is today.”</p><p>Six black circles. Sightings. The pattern was not random. I saw it. Then I did not. Because I wanted one too quickly. North road. East pens. Orchard route. Canal ditch. No. Not canal. Drainage ditch. Farm lanes. Livestock. Edges.</p><p>“They’re avoiding the center,” Alden said.</p><p>I looked at him. Doven did too. Alden pointed.</p><p>“All these are outside the dense streets.”</p><p>“Yes,” Doven said.</p><p>“Because people?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/026/Ch026_Fast-Coverage-003-A15.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 26." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“Because walls?” I asked.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Because food,” Nemi said.</p><p>She tapped the sheep pens. Then the mule yard. Then a poultry enclosure.</p><p>“Most confirmed contact is livestock.”</p><p>That changed it. Not an invasion. Not yet. Predation. But predators did not usually ring alarm bells. People did.</p><p>“What is the problem right now?” Doven asked.</p><p>Alden said, “Keep them out.” </p><p>Doven shook his head.</p><p>“Too large,” Doven said.</p><p>I disliked how familiar this was becoming. I looked at the map.</p><p>“Know where they are?” I asked.</p><p>“Closer,” Doven said.</p><p>Nemi said, “Keep people from feeding them.” There. </p><p>Doven nodded.</p><p>“Livestock inside the east quarter is scattered. Pens are damaged. Families evacuated faster than animals could be moved. Creatures keep returning to the same food.”</p><p>“So move the animals,” Alden said.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Simple. Terrible. Doven pointed to three locations.</p><p>“Two crews are already working. Third pen is here.”</p><p>Alden stood. His healer tag fluttered.</p><p>NO LIFTING LEFT.</p><p>Doven looked at it.</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>Alden sat. I almost laughed.</p><p>“Not you,” Doven said.</p><p>“Why not?”</p><p>“Your shoulder.”</p><p>“It works.”</p><p>“Your healer says otherwise.”</p><p>“She says no lifting.”</p><p>“Moving goats involves lifting goats.”</p><p>“Why would I lift a goat?”</p><p>Nemi said, “You have never moved goats.” </p><p>Alden stopped.</p><p>“I have not.”</p><p>“Then trust the tag.”</p><p>Doven pointed at me.</p><p>“You can walk?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Carry?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Cast?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fight?”</p><p>“Three.”</p><p>He stared. </p><p>Alden put his face in his hand. </p><p>Cal laughed. I regretted honesty. </p><p>Doven said, “What does three mean?”</p><p>“It means I can be useful if someone competent is between me and the dangerous thing.”</p><p>Doven nodded.</p><p>“Finally, a Bronze who understands numbers.”</p><p>Alden said, “He does not.”</p><p>“Quiet.”</p><p>Doven looked at Cal.</p><p>“Arm?”</p><p>“Works.”</p><p>“Good. You two go with Pen Crew Three.”</p><p>He meant Cal and me. Alden leaned forward.</p><p>“What about me?”</p><p>“You stay.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Doven did not react. Alden said it again.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>There was something different in it. Not defiance for sport. He had come here. He had fought. He had bled. Now someone was telling him to remain in a command post while the job continued. I understood exactly why he hated it. That did not make him right.</p><p>Doven said, “Your left shoulder is restricted. Crew Three needs animal handling, hauling, fence work, and possibly fighting. You are poor for three of four.”</p><p>“I can fight.”</p><p>“Can you?”</p><p>Alden’s jaw tightened. Doven pointed at the wrist tag.</p><p>“I am not debating your self-image.”</p><p>That landed. Hard. Alden stood anyway. </p><p>Nemi said, “Marr.” He looked at her.</p><p>“Sit down.”</p><p>He did. Interesting. Authority from Doven made him push. Authority from Nemi made him stop. She had arrived injured from the same roads. Earned information. I filed that away. Bad habit. Cal and I were almost at the door when </p><p>Alden said, “Greg.” </p><p>I turned.</p><p>“Don’t.”</p><p>One word. I knew what he meant. Do not turn this into proving something. Do not cast. Do not chase. Do not get clever. Possibly all three.</p><p>“I have a tag.”</p><p>“That has never stopped anyone.”</p><p>“Good point.”</p><p>I left. Pen Three was not a pen. It was a disaster involving goats. There were thirty-one. Someone had counted. That was the only part working. The fence had collapsed along one side. Three goats were on a roof. Two had entered a dye shed. One stood on a cart with the moral certainty of a king.</p><p>Five townspeople were trying to move them into a stone-walled courtyard. The goats disagreed. Cal stopped beside me.</p><p>“Monsters?”</p><p>“Worse.”</p><p>A woman holding a broom pointed at us.</p><p>“You guild?”</p><p>“Unfortunately.”</p><p>“Good. Grab that gate.”</p><p>I grabbed the gate. No introduction. No briefing. Just gate. Excellent. We moved goats. This was harder than combat in several important ways. A creature wanted something predictable. Goats wanted the collapse of civilization. One refused to move until everyone stopped trying. Another moved only when nobody wanted it to. The cart king jumped onto my back. I made a sound I would deny later.</p><p>Cal laughed so hard he lost two goats.</p><p>“Useful?” I asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then suffer quietly.”</p><p>The broom woman was named Senn. She knew every goat by either name or insult.</p><p>“Blue ear goes first.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“She follows Brownie.”</p><p>“Which one is Brownie?”</p><p>“The brown one.”</p><p>There were eleven brown goats. I stared. </p><p>Senn said, “City boy?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why are you useless?”</p><p>Fair. We got fourteen into the courtyard. Then twenty. Then twenty-six. The roof goats remained. I looked at my restriction tag.</p><p>NO CASTING.</p><p>I looked at the roof. A tiny Barrier could have nudged one. No. No magic. Fine. I climbed. </p><p>Senn shouted, “Don’t.” </p><p>I stopped halfway.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You’ll push them off.”</p><p>“I was going to guide them.”</p><p>“They’ll jump.”</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“On you.”</p><p>I climbed down. Professional competence. Again. Senn shook grain into a bucket. The roof goats came down on their own. I hated goats. Twenty-nine. Thirty. Thirty-one. Gate shut. Done. Nobody died. No monster appeared. That was when the screaming started. Not from our courtyard. Two streets east. Cal drew his sword. I did not have one. Right. My sword remained somewhere on the road.</p><p>Senn grabbed the broom with both hands.</p><p>“What was that?”</p><p>I knew the sound. Not creature. Human. Again. Then bells. Not road warning. Different. One long. Two short. Senn went pale.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“East breach.”</p><p>Cal looked at her.</p><p>“Breach?”</p><p>“Inside wall.”</p><p>The goats exploded into noise behind us. Every one of them faced east. Not random. All at once. Ears forward. Bodies still. I felt the change before I understood it. The air did not move. No smell I noticed. No sound beyond bells. But the goats knew something. </p><p>Cal said, “Back to command?” Yes. Correct. Report. Wait. No independent pursuit. </p><p>I looked east.</p><p>A black shape crossed the roofline two streets away. Fast. Another followed. Not one creature. Two. Inside. </p><p>Cal said, “Greg.”</p><p>“I see.”</p><p>Senn said, “My house.” She was already moving. Wrong direction. East.</p><p>“Stop.”</p><p>“My daughter.”</p><p>There it was. Not goat problem anymore.</p><p>“Where?”</p><p>“Dyer’s lane.”</p><p>Two streets east. Breach. Creatures. Her daughter. Cal grabbed her arm. She hit him with the broom. He released her. She ran. Cal looked at me. Command post was west. Senn was east. Alden was west. No casting. No sword. Three out of ten on a good day. This was not a good day.</p><p>“What do we do?” Cal asked.</p><p>I hated that he asked me. I hated that I already had an answer.</p><p>“We do not chase monsters.”</p><p>Senn disappeared around the corner.</p><p>“We chase the woman.”</p><p>Cal nodded. That was enough. We ran east.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="025.html">← Chapter 19</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="027.html">Chapter 21 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/129.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 103: The Student — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 103</div><h1>THE STUDENT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>The threads were gone. I noticed before I sat down. The frame was gone too. No tile. No copper beside it. No white sleeve. No gray sleeve. Hessa had a cup of tea. This was worse.</p><p>“You stopped.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>“You stopped the thread test.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>I sat. She checked my hands first. Palms normal. No tenderness from yesterday. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the usual impossible way, mostly heel this morning. Thumb fine. Fingers fine.</p><p>Wrist fine. Grip. Again. Fine. Hessa wrote. I waited. She drank tea.</p><p>“You stopped.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There. I did not like how quickly she said it.</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I reviewed the three attempts.”</p><p>“And?”</p><p>“The apparatus is not giving me enough interpretable signal to justify spending more of your safe attempts on it right now.”</p><p>I stared at the empty table.</p><p>“One failed replication.”</p><p>“One failed replication after two ambiguous attempts.”</p><p>“The second was better than ambiguous.”</p><p>“It was more interesting.”</p><p>“That is not the same word.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“The near thread moved toward me during REACH while the far thread didn&#x27;t.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is a differential observation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then the next test should repeat it.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because we did.”</p><p>“Once.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is not enough.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then repeat again.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I hated this. Hessa put down her cup.</p><p>“What answer are you trying to get?”</p><p>“Whether I moved it.”</p><p>“Can this apparatus tell us?”</p><p>“Eventually.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Then why stop?”</p><p>“Because your attempts are not free.”</p><p>“I am fine.”</p><p>“You are fine after the attempts we have done.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That does not make the next ten free.”</p><p>“I said one.”</p><p>“You will say one after that.”</p><p>“Only if it is useful.”</p><p>“You currently think another thread attempt is useful.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“I don&#x27;t.”</p><p>There it was. Jurisdiction. Annoying. Clean. I looked at the empty table again.</p><p>“So what did the three tests establish?”</p><p>“That thread moves.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“You asked.”</p><p>She ignored me.</p><p>“First, they established that suspended thread in this room is sensitive to more things than we can cheaply isolate.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Air movement. Heat. vibration. twist. static. position. breathing. room traffic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Second, they established that two threads exposed to much of the same room can still behave differently without your magic.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Third, we observed one movement during REACH that was interesting enough to repeat.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“We repeated it.”</p><p>“It didn&#x27;t happen.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>“That does not disprove it.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>I stopped. She waited. That was the problem. She was not saying impossible. She was saying not enough. Harder to argue with.</p><p>“Fourth,” she said, “the reliable part of all three external attempts was not external.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Your control.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You established the small alteration where instructed. You maintained the underlying draw. You attempted a directional change without broadening into the older response. You did not recruit your hand. You did not chase sensation when the apparatus did something interesting. You RETURNed when told.”</p><p>“Mostly.”</p><p>“What does mostly mean?”</p><p>“I argued afterward.”</p><p>“Afterward is allowed.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Your internal sequence is becoming more repeatable than the external observation.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So that is what we test today.”</p><p>I looked at the empty space where the frame had been.</p><p>“Did you throw it away?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Where is it?”</p><p>“Cabinet.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because if I leave it out, you will spend the entire assessment looking at it.”</p><p>“I am looking at where it was.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That proves nothing.”</p><p>“It proves I know you.”</p><p>I did not answer. She pulled the three old pages from beneath a newer sheet. I recognized the white and gray labels in the margins.</p><p>“You kept the notes.”</p><p>“Obviously.”</p><p>“Show me.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you will argue with my abbreviations.”</p><p>“I can read.”</p><p>“That has not protected me before.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She turned the first page toward herself, not me.</p><p>“Attempt one. Single thread. Baseline movement. One movement toward arm during bounded external question, another later movement with multiple room confounds. No attribution.”</p><p>“Two movements.”</p><p>“I said one during the bounded question.”</p><p>“The other was still during maintained draw.”</p><p>“Which is why it is written down.”</p><p>Second page.</p><p>“Attempt two. Paired threads. Baseline differential behavior demonstrated before draw. During REACH, closer thread moved toward arm while farther did not at that same moment. Later farther moved independently.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Attempt three. Same general setup. During shape, closer moved away, farther moved shortly after. During REACH, no recorded movement from either.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She stacked the pages.</p><p>“If I only owned the second page, I would repeat.”</p><p>“You did.”</p><p>“If I owned the first two, I would repeat.”</p><p>“You did.”</p><p>“If I own all three, I have to ask whether a fourth attempt is the best use of your current tolerance.”</p><p>“And you decided no.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What would make you return to it?”</p><p>“Better reason.”</p><p>“That is vague.”</p><p>“A stronger external signal from some other bounded question. Better control. More mature shaping. A reason to think the thread&#x27;s sensitivity is useful instead of merely noisy.”</p><p>“Or time.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“So not abandoned.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>That helped more than it should have. I did not want the thread. I wanted the possibility to remain alive. It did. Annoyingly. I looked around.</p><p>“No apparatus.”</p><p>“Your arm is the apparatus.”</p><p>“That sounds medically threatening.”</p><p>“It should.”</p><p>She brought out the copper. Relief was embarrassing. Not because copper did anything important. Because it belonged to the sequence I knew. Hessa noticed.</p><p>“You expected it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“You always use copper.”</p><p>“Not always.”</p><p>“Recently.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What does that tell you?”</p><p>“That you are predictable.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“No, that was an insult.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>She set it down well away from the old thread position. I watched her choose the place.</p><p>“Is that placement part of the test?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then why there?”</p><p>“Because my tea is here.”</p><p>I looked at the tea. Reasonable constraints continued ruining elegant interpretation.</p><p>“What question?”</p><p>“Whether you can produce the same bounded directional change and RETURN at a different right-forearm target without an external object to pull your attention.”</p><p>“That is less interesting.”</p><p>“To you.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Why remove the target?”</p><p>“Because I want to know whether REACH is currently an instruction you can execute internally, or whether the thread is part of what makes the response happen.”</p><p>I sat straighter. That was better. Not thread. Still a question.</p><p>“What direction?”</p><p>“Not toward the old thread position.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because you have practiced that direction three times.”</p><p>“Two.”</p><p>“Three external attempts.”</p><p>“The first geometry differed.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She marked my forearm. Charcoal. Small target closer to the upper outer side than the recent wrist-near work. Not elbowward. Not the familiar broad direction. Different. I looked.</p><p>“Outward?”</p><p>“Toward that mark.”</p><p>“There is no object.”</p><p>“The mark is an object.”</p><p>“External object.”</p><p>“No suspended target.”</p><p>“You know what I mean.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can I look at it?”</p><p>“Before draw. Not during.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I want your report, not you steering with your eyes.”</p><p>“That is not how mana works.”</p><p>“Good. Then it should not matter.”</p><p>I disliked that answer. She checked position. Right forearm supported. Hand relaxed. Fingers visible. Copper was present after all. On the other side of the table. Not part of a thread apparatus. Just copper.</p><p>Familiar. Hessa placed two fingers above the new charcoal mark.</p><p>“Question is small.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One shape.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One directional instruction.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One RETURN.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“If the response broadens, changes direction, recruits hand or wrist, produces thumb or finger symptoms, produces unusual left response, pain, cold, numbness, weakness, or anything you cannot describe, you stop.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No external effect question.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No spell.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No Barrier.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No proving anything.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“That one was unnecessary.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I did. Minimal. Copper answered. Right forearm. Stable. No hand. No thumb. No left.</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>I did.</p><p>“Shape.”</p><p>Localized. The altered region came slower than last time. Not much slower. Enough to notice. I said so.</p><p>“Continue only if stable.”</p><p>I waited. It settled. Small. Near the charcoal mark but not on it.</p><p>“Location?”</p><p>I described it. Hessa touched the skin outside the region. No change.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>Held. Then she moved her fingers. Not toward the mark. Away. Two inches farther up and outward. I looked at her.</p><p>“That is not the mark.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You said toward the mark.”</p><p>“I changed the instruction.”</p><p>“That seems bad.”</p><p>“Can you follow it?”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/129/Ch129_Direction-Without-Thread.jpg" alt="Hessa points through the empty air over Greg&#x27;s supported forearm for a direction-only assessment." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Maybe. That was different. Not REACH toward something. REACH from the altered region toward a direction Hessa indicated in space over my arm. No thread. No fixed destination. Just direction.</p><p>“Smallest extension,” she said. “Toward my fingers. No force. Maintain draw.”</p><p>I did. Or tried. The near edge sharpened. Wrong edge. Toward the charcoal mark. I stopped.</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Report.”</p><p>“It went toward the mark.”</p><p>“Did you intend that?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Stop directional instruction. Hold.”</p><p>Held. Interesting. Bad. Interesting. She moved her fingers away.</p><p>“RETURN.”</p><p>I returned. The alteration reduced. Underlying draw remained. No hand. No thumb. No broadening.</p><p>“Hold.”</p><p>Held.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>Released. Hessa checked everything. Again. Fine. I looked at the charcoal mark.</p><p>“You tricked me.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You established a target and then changed it.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That was intentional.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So you were testing whether I was following the instruction or the prepared target.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“That is a trick.”</p><p>“It is a test.”</p><p>“You could have told me.”</p><p>“That would change the test.”</p><p>I hated that she was right. Mostly.</p><p>“What did I do?”</p><p>“You shaped near the prepared target.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“When I redirected the directional instruction, your first altered edge sharpened toward the prepared target instead of toward my indicated direction.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So I failed.”</p><p>“You did not execute the changed direction as instructed.”</p><p>“That is failure.”</p><p>“For that question, yes.”</p><p>Clean. Again. I appreciated it. Also hated it.</p><p>“Did the altered region move at all?”</p><p>“The edge changed.”</p><p>“Toward the prepared mark.”</p><p>“By your report.”</p><p>“You did not feel it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Copper?”</p><p>“Changed with draw and shape. Nothing I would distinguish during the directional instruction.”</p><p>“So no independent confirmation.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Could I have simply reported what I expected?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“That is a problem.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You believe me?”</p><p>“I believe you are trying to report accurately.”</p><p>“That is not the same.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Good. More problems. I had missed having enough problems.</p><p>“Can you touch the edge while I do it?”</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Contact changes sensation.”</p><p>“Could still be useful.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then next time.”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You hate commitments.”</p><p>“I make them when I have enough information.”</p><p>“That is a lie. You committed to no magic tomorrow very quickly.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/129/Ch129_Fast-Coverage-005-01.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 129." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>“That decision has excellent evidence.”</p><p>I laughed despite myself. She wrote something.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You wrote because I laughed.”</p><p>“I wrote because your hand stayed relaxed while you laughed.”</p><p>I looked at my right hand. Still open on the support.</p><p>“That matters?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“You just did it.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Made everything information.”</p><p>“Everything is information.”</p><p>“That is convenient.”</p><p>“Only if I don&#x27;t care what it says.”</p><p>I recognized that. She knew I recognized it. Neither of us mentioned the last time.</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“I don&#x27;t know yet.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“It may mean the prepared target strongly organizes what you are doing.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It may mean changing directional instruction after shaping is harder than beginning with the intended direction.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It may mean you anticipated the old sequence.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“It may mean my instruction was poor.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“One attempt.”</p><p>“I am fine.”</p><p>“One attempt.”</p><p>“But this is internal.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And it failed.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So repeat.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because failure is data before it is an invitation.”</p><p>That sentence was offensive. I leaned back.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“No magic.”</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How many days?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“Then assessment?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What are you going to test?”</p><p>“I don&#x27;t know.”</p><p>“You absolutely know.”</p><p>“I have questions.”</p><p>“Which?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>She picked up her tea. Cold now, probably.</p><p>“Today I learned something I did not know.”</p><p>“That I follow charcoal instead of fingers.”</p><p>“Possibly.”</p><p>“That sounds stupid.”</p><p>“It sounds like learning.”</p><p>“I knew the charcoal was the target.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>I stopped. She drank. I thought about it. I had built the shape around the mark before she changed the instruction. Of course the response favored it. Maybe. Or I had simply failed to redirect.</p><p>Or REACH was not direction at all and I had been interpreting noise. Or the thread had mattered. Or Hessa&#x27;s fingers were a terrible target. Many possibilities. I started listing them. Hessa held up a hand.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I have four.”</p><p>“Keep them.”</p><p>“I can tell you.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“You do not know mine.”</p><p>“I know enough.”</p><p>“That is arrogant.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Fair. I looked at my forearm. Charcoal still there. Nothing else.</p><p>“Are we farther from external effect than we were?”</p><p>“That is not how I would describe it.”</p><p>“How would you?”</p><p>“We stopped spending attempts on a poor measurement.”</p><p>“That is farther.”</p><p>“It is different.”</p><p>“It feels farther.”</p><p>She considered that.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>Good. At least she allowed that. I expected the feeling to disappear once named. It did not. Three days ago I had been staring at a thread that might have moved because of me.</p><p>Today Hessa had put the thread in a cabinet and made me fail to follow two fingers. Objectively, that felt like retreat. Also objectively, my arm had done something small on command and then stopped when told.</p><p>Again. The second fact was less exciting. It was also the one Hessa trusted. I knew which one I preferred. That did not change which one she trusted. I rubbed neither arm. Kept hands still.</p><p>Not because instructed. Habit.</p><p>“Am I getting better?”</p><p>“At the parts we can currently observe reliably.”</p><p>“That is a Hessa answer.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Which parts?”</p><p>“Minimal draw. Localized shaping. maintaining draw while altering. RETURN. avoiding the older broad response. avoiding motor recruitment.”</p><p>“Directional control?”</p><p>“Unclear.”</p><p>“External?”</p><p>“Unestablished.”</p><p>“Casting?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“Barrier?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I sighed. She smiled. Actually smiled. Small. Cruel woman.</p><p>“Go live tomorrow.”</p><p>“I lived yesterday.”</p><p>“You were a messenger.”</p><p>I froze. Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“How do you know that?”</p><p>“Teren&#x27;s sister buys herbs from the woman downstairs.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“She mentioned the theatre had acquired a tall messenger on crutches who forgot his letter.”</p><p>I closed my eyes. No. Absolutely not.</p><p>“That was rehearsal.”</p><p>“I assumed.”</p><p>“I was not acquired.”</p><p>“I assumed.”</p><p>“I am not a messenger.”</p><p>“You were yesterday.”</p><p>“For thirty minutes.”</p><p>“That seems sufficient.”</p><p>“This city is too small.”</p><p>“Carrow is not small.”</p><p>“Then people need to stop talking.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stood. She pointed at my forearm.</p><p>“Wash the charcoal off later.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No magic tomorrow.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“No practicing directional attention.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What does that mean?”</p><p>“You know exactly what it means.”</p><p>“I cannot stop looking at things.”</p><p>“You can stop sitting at a table trying to recreate today&#x27;s task without mana.”</p><p>“That would not be magic.”</p><p>“It would be rehearsal.”</p><p>I stared. She raised an eyebrow. I refused to give her that.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I left. Outside, the morning had become bright. Not warm. Bright. I walked three streets before realizing I was heading toward the theatre. I stopped. Hessa tomorrow was no magic. Theatre was allowed. That was not why I had turned.</p><p>Probably. I looked west. Then east. Then at the street ahead. No test. No conclusion. No thread. My right forearm felt completely ordinary. I went to buy lunch.</p><p>At the bread stall, the seller said:</p><p>“Messenger.”</p><p>I nearly left Carrow.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="128.html">← Chapter 102</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="133.html">Chapter 104 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/044.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 35: The Patient — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 35</div><h1>THE PATIENT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>I woke because my right hand was numb. This was alarming for approximately one second. Then I discovered I had slept on it. Less alarming. I rolled onto my back and waited for sensation to return. Pins. Needles. Pain. Good. My shoulders remembered yesterday. My back remembered yesterday more. Carrying sacks used muscles fighting did not. Or used them differently. Old Greg had known this.</p><p>Old Greg had also employed porters. Knowledge became less impressive when somebody else had done the lifting. I flexed my hand. Blisters nearly gone. Ribs quiet. Channels quiet. No reason not to go to Bale. Several reasons not to go immediately. Breakfast first. Then Hessa. I had not been summoned. That mattered.</p><p>Hessa had said small utility casting, no repeated load testing. I had used two small Barriers during the spar, one producing mild pressure, then one coin-sized Barrier at the storehouse with no symptoms. I could decide I was fine. That would be efficient. I went to Hessa. Her door was open.</p><p>A woman I did not know stood inside holding a strip of cloth between both hands. Mid-thirties. Strong wrists. Work clothes. The cloth hung straight. Nothing happened. Hessa sat opposite her.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>The woman breathed. The cloth moved. Barely. Not wind. One edge lifted and stayed. Three breaths. Dropped. The woman smiled. Hessa said, “Again.” I waited outside. No reason to interrupt. A cart passed. Someone across the street was repairing a shutter.</p><p>A boy carried six loaves stacked against his chest and lost the top one. He caught it against his chin. Good. Inside, the woman lifted the cloth again. Longer. Hessa stopped her. They talked quietly. I could not hear. I did not try. Eventually the woman came out. She saw me.</p><p>“Waiting?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Long?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>She left. Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“You weren’t scheduled.”</p><p>“I know.”</p><p>“Then?”</p><p>“Check.”</p><p>“For?”</p><p>“Progress.”</p><p>“That is vague.”</p><p>“Barrier symptoms.”</p><p>“Better.”</p><p>I sat. She checked eyes. Pulse. Hands.</p><p>“Work?”</p><p>“Five hours yesterday.”</p><p>“What kind?”</p><p>“Carrying.”</p><p>She looked at my shoulders.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“One cast.”</p><p>“Size?”</p><p>“Coin.”</p><p>“Load?”</p><p>“Barrel.”</p><p>Her hand stopped.</p><p>“Explain.”</p><p>“Not stopping the barrel.”</p><p>“Explain better.”</p><p>“Half barrel rolling on a ramp. I placed the Barrier beside the hoop. Contact shifted it enough for a worker to clear his ankle. Barrier broke immediately.”</p><p>“Symptoms?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“After?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Later?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She nodded.</p><p>“Show me.”</p><p>I looked around.</p><p>“No barrel.”</p><p>“Barrier.”</p><p>Right. Coin-sized. Three breaths. Clean. Release.</p><p>“Again.”</p><p>Same. Four breaths. Clean.</p><p>“Palm.”</p><p>I formed it. Low density. Three breaths. Pressure. One. Not pain. Release. Hessa waited.</p><p>“Pressure?”</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“Gone?”</p><p>“Almost.”</p><p>We waited. Gone.</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>I asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Of course.</p><p>“What changed?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“That is not true.”</p><p>“Nothing important.”</p><p>I frowned. She continued.</p><p>“Small cast remains clean. Larger sustained load still produces symptoms. Recovery is improving. Limit is still there.”</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“Small utility is fine. Palm-sized Barrier only when necessary, brief. No repeated palm work.”</p><p>“Necessary according to?”</p><p>“You.”</p><p>That was worse. I looked at her.</p><p>“You are giving me discretion.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“If you have time to ask whether it is necessary, probably don’t cast it.”</p><p>“That is not a measurement.”</p><p>“It is a rule.”</p><p>“Bad rule.”</p><p>“Useful rule.”</p><p>I considered arguing. Did not. She noticed.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“You’re learning.”</p><p>“Do not ruin it.”</p><p>“Any fighting?”</p><p>“Not planned.”</p><p>“Any work?”</p><p>“Probably.”</p><p>“Any drinking?”</p><p>“Not planned.”</p><p>“That has never stopped you.”</p><p>“One time.”</p><p>“Enough.”</p><p>I stood.</p><p>“Come back when?”</p><p>“Three days if no symptoms. Earlier if symptoms.”</p><p>“Can I test coin-sized directional work?”</p><p>“No deliberate load testing.”</p><p>“That was not what I asked.”</p><p>“Yes, if the task itself is ordinary and the cast stays small.”</p><p>There. Not laboratory. Use. Observe. Do not manufacture danger to justify experiment. Good. I left.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Patient Magic Check" decoding="async" height="169" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/044/v45_c44_patient-magic-check.png" width="497"/></figure><p>Bale was still available. So was lunch. Too early. Bale won. The master was there. I knew because the clerk from yesterday saw me enter and immediately pointed toward the back.</p><p>“He’s here.”</p><p>That sounded accusatory.</p><p>“Good morning.”</p><p>“You ask too many questions.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>A man emerged from behind a curtain carrying a wooden tray of gray pellets. Late forties. Round face. Clean apron. Three fingers on his left hand stained blue.</p><p>“Greg?” he asked.</p><p>“Yes,” I said.</p><p>“I’m Holl,” he said.</p><p>“Master?” I asked.</p><p>“Owner,” Holl said.</p><p>Better.</p><p>“Your clerk said you might know about house testing.”</p><p>“My clerk said you bought one scoop and asked twelve questions.”</p><p>“Approximately.”</p><p>“Fourteen.”</p><p>Good clerk. Holl set the tray down.</p><p>“What are you making?”</p><p>“I still don’t know.”</p><p>“Then why are you here?”</p><p>“I want to understand how consistent treated kestrin gets made.”</p><p>“Made by whom?”</p><p>“Anyone.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Curiosity.”</p><p>He stared. Nessa would approve.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>That surprised me.</p><p>“Fine?”</p><p>“I like rocks.”</p><p>Good. We were doomed. Holl lifted one pellet.</p><p>“People talk about treatment too much.”</p><p>“Dorrin said sorting first.”</p><p>“Dorrin is right.”</p><p>“Arlo too.”</p><p>“Arlo owes Dorrin money.”</p><p>Everyone knew.</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Stone people talk.”</p><p>Right. Holl pointed at the tray.</p><p>“This is basic bed grade. We buy treated stock, then reject.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Varies.”</p><p>“Typical.”</p><p>“Ten to twenty percent.”</p><p>That was large.</p><p>“For visible defects?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Reaction?”</p><p>“Some.”</p><p>“Then you rebatch.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There. Confirmed at least here.</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Not complicated.”</p><p>He brought out three shallow trays. Different marks.</p><p>“Supplier lot comes in. We sample. If it sits inside our sale band, keep. If parts run high or low, we separate obvious outliers when worth doing.”</p><p>“Every piece?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then low variance on your card is not every pellet.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What is it?”</p><p>“A promise that a scoop behaves close enough for the uses we sell it for.”</p><p>Important. Not perfect consistency. Commercial tolerance.</p><p>“What uses?”</p><p>“Ward beds. Fixture packing. Low-grade isolation. Training benches. Things where failure means annoyance before death.”</p><p>Excellent specification.</p><p>“Do you test suppression?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Retention?”</p><p>“For some grades.”</p><p>“Basic?”</p><p>“Spot only.”</p><p>“What is house test?”</p><p>He pointed toward the back.</p><p>“Come.”</p><p>Different scene. He invited. Good. The testing bench was simple. A brass line. Two ceramic posts. A hand-sized mana bead. A sliding tray under the line. Not Edrin’s equipment. Cheaper. Faster. Holl put untreated shale under the line. The bead glowed pale blue. Treated pellets. Slightly dimmer. He swapped trays. Another treated sample. Similar. Not identical.</p><p>“Operator reads bead?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“By eye?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“And rejects?”</p><p>“By eye.”</p><p>“For low variance?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Low enough variance.”</p><p>Right.</p><p>“Do you calibrate the bead?”</p><p>“Morning and midday.”</p><p>“With?”</p><p>He showed me two reference tiles. One white. One black.</p><p>“Known response?”</p><p>“Known enough.”</p><p>I wanted to ask source. No.</p><p>“Who treats your stock?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Boundary.</p><p>“Do you use Kett?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>Public enough.</p><p>“Varo?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Same product?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Heat versus salt?”</p><p>“Sometimes both.”</p><p>“Order?”</p><p>“Depends.”</p><p>I laughed. Holl smiled.</p><p>“You’ve met tradespeople.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Who taught you magic?”</p><p>“Hessa Marr.”</p><p>His expression changed. Recognition.</p><p>“You survive?”</p><p>“So far.”</p><p>“She tested our training fill once.”</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Last year.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Student bench was running hot.”</p><p>“Cause?”</p><p>“Not stone.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Bad ground plate.”</p><p>Another interface. Not relevant. Maybe. No. I looked at the trays.</p><p>“If you wanted unusually narrow behavior, narrower than your basic grade, what would you do?”</p><p>“Pay.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>He waited. I waited. Then he laughed.</p><p>“Sort harder. Test more pieces. Buy from fewer source lots. Specify treatment. Reject more. Maybe blend.”</p><p>“Blend high and low?”</p><p>“Sometimes.”</p><p>“Does that work?”</p><p>“For bulk beds.”</p><p>“Individual pellets still vary.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So a sack where individual pellets are unusually consistent would require more.”</p><p>Holl looked at me carefully. There. I had approached evidence edge.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“What more?”</p><p>“Better raw sorting. Better process control. Piece testing. Narrow source. Or luck.”</p><p>“Piece testing expensive.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How expensive?”</p><p>“Enough that cheap shale stops being cheap.”</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/044/Ch044_Fast-Coverage-003-B06.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 44." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>That mattered. Unless scale reduced cost. Unless testing automated. Future memory stirred. No. Present.</p><p>“Who does piece testing?”</p><p>“Specialty ward suppliers. Some artificers. Military contracts maybe. I don’t.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“No customer pays me enough.”</p><p>Clean.</p><p>“Could someone test after treatment and rebatch by individual response?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Would that create consistent sacks without better treatment?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>There. Possible. Not proof.</p><p>“How fast?”</p><p>“Slow.”</p><p>“Unless?”</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“Unless you have a better test.”</p><p>There. My attention sharpened.</p><p>Holl slid the tray back toward himself.</p><p>“If you want to redesign the bench, come back when I am not filling orders.”</p><p>“I was only asking.”</p><p>“Then ask about the test I have.”</p><p>“I don’t know. Faster line. Multiple pieces. Mechanical feed. Something.”</p><p>Arlo. No. Do not connect because Arlo makes fixtures. Could be anyone.</p><p>“What limits yours?”</p><p>“Hands.”</p><p>He slid a tray through the sequence again. Place sample. Wait. Read. Record. Remove.</p><p>“One operator, one sample path,” Holl said. “That is the limit.”</p><p>“What if the tray held multiple channels?”</p><p>Holl shook his head.</p><p>“Not today.”</p><p>“What if the bead response could be compared against reference simultaneously?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“What if,” I began.</p><p>“Greg,” Holl said.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“This is my morning,” Holl said.</p><p>Right. He had given me time. Not hired me. Not requested optimization.</p><p>“Sorry.”</p><p>“Good questions.”</p><p>“Still no?”</p><p>“Still no.”</p><p>I nodded. He relaxed. That mattered.</p><p>“What can I buy that shows narrower tolerance?”</p><p>He considered. Then brought a smaller packet from a locked cabinet.</p><p>“Fine bed.”</p><p>“How much?”</p><p>“Eight copper.”</p><p>I had one. Maybe more total, but not eight casually.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You don’t know what you need.”</p><p>Again. Hostile competence.</p><p>“Can I see the specification?”</p><p>He handed me a card.</p><p>FINE BED KESTRIN</p><p>CONTROLLED LOW RESPONSE</p><p>DRY OR SEALED USE</p><p>LOT TESTED</p><p>REFERENCE RANGE AVAILABLE ON PURCHASE</p><p>“Lot tested.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Not piece.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Supplier?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Can I ask whether Silas Marris sells you anything?”</p><p>His face did not change. Good.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Customer or supplier privacy.</p><p>“Can I ask whether you know the company?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“How?”</p><p>“Trading.”</p><p>“That is not information.”</p><p>“It is all you get.”</p><p>Fair. No suspicious reaction. No connection. I had reached the useful edge.</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>Holl nodded. Then said, “If you ever build a faster cheap test, come back.” I stopped. Requested? No. Invitation. Possibility. Different.</p><p>“What would cheap mean?”</p><p>He pointed at the door. Right. I left. Outside, I wrote immediately.</p><p>BALE / HOLL</p><p>basic bed: treated stock purchased, then retail rejection / sorting 10-20% rejection typical depending lot house test = simple brass line + bead + reference tiles basic promise = commercial tolerance for low-consequence uses, not identical pieces</p><p>narrower consistency costs through:</p><p>raw sorting treatment specification more testing narrow source lots rejection possible blending individual piece testing possible but expensive / slow faster cheap testing could change economics</p><p>Then:</p><p>PEL MARRIS: Holl knows as trading company. No further info. No reaction. Good. No connection. I closed the notebook. My stomach voted. Lunch. I bought a meat bun from a street stall. One copper. Zero from yesterday’s special pay. Debt work had not paid cash. Rocks had eaten the rest. Financial genius. I ate walking.</p><p>At the Guild, a crowd had formed around the contract board. Not crisis. New postings. People always became excited when paper appeared. I could keep walking. I did. Then heard Alden.</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>I turned. He stood with two other Bronze adventurers. Not Berren. One woman with cropped hair and a short spear. One man with a padded coat and a nose that had healed sideways. Alden wore the red scarf. Normal.</p><p>“Where have you been?”</p><p>“Rocks.”</p><p>He nodded as if that explained me.</p><p>“Tomorrow?”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Road job.”</p><p>I looked at the board.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He frowned.</p><p>“You don’t know the job.”</p><p>“I have Hessa limits.”</p><p>“No magic needed.”</p><p>“That is what jobs say before magic.”</p><p>The spearwoman laughed. Alden pointed.</p><p>“West orchard delivery. Two carts. One day. Four Bronze preferred. Six copper.”</p><p>“Why me?”</p><p>There. Important. Alden shrugged.</p><p>“You’re good on roads.”</p><p>Simple. Not because Greg was special. Because he had worked roads with Alden.</p><p>“What’s cargo?”</p><p>“Tools and lamp oil.”</p><p>“Threat?”</p><p>“Low.”</p><p>“Return?”</p><p>“Same day if wheels behave.”</p><p>“Who are they?”</p><p>Alden named them.</p><p>“Pessa. Dorn.”</p><p>They nodded. Independent people.</p><p>“Berren?”</p><p>“Resting.”</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Jorren?”</p><p>“Working.”</p><p>Also good.</p><p>“When leave?”</p><p>“First light.”</p><p>Hessa had said small utility fine. No fighting planned. Road job. Six copper. Money. Actual Bronze work. I looked at Alden. He was not asking permission. Not recruiting a student. He wanted a fourth person. Me.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>Alden smiled.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Pessa said, “Can he stop talking?”</p><p>“No,” Alden said.</p><p>Dorn said, “Can he carry?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I said, “Apparently.” Done. They went back to the board. I was not included in whatever they had been discussing before. Good. I finished the bun. Tomorrow, road. Today, nothing urgent. I could go to Kett. Varo. Arlo. Edrin. Antonius. No. I had enough. Hessa in the morning. Holl and Bale. Alden road job tomorrow. The city could keep the rest. I went home.</p><p>On the way, I passed a narrow alley where three children were trying to float a wooden box through a gutter stream left by the rain. The box kept catching on a stone. One child moved the stone. The box passed. No Barrier. Excellent. At my lodging, the space behind the desk was empty. No rocks. Wealth. Upstairs, I checked my gear.</p><p>Sword. Knife. Coat. Water. Bandage. Food tomorrow. Boots. My right boot needed oil. I did that. Leather first. Then sword edge. Then straps. Young Greg used to pack at dawn while swearing. Old Greg had people. Present Greg had tonight. I laid everything out. No grand plan. Just a road job. Six copper. Alden had asked because I was good on roads.</p><p>Holl had said come back if I ever built a better test. Hessa had trusted me to decide when a palm-sized Barrier was actually necessary. Three different kinds of permission. No. Not permission. Trust? Too early. Expectation? Maybe. I stopped naming it. That was becoming another way to interfere. I finished oiling the boot. Tomorrow I would be a Bronze adventurer. That was enough.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="042.html">← Chapter 34</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="045.html">Chapter 36 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
