not.</p><p>I ate the bread.</p><p>Then went home.</p><p>Not theatre.</p><p>Home.</p><p>Upstairs, the green shirt still smelled faintly of smoke.</p><p>I hung it near the window.</p><p>I opened the notebook.</p><p>Wrote:</p><p>NINTH MINIMAL DRAW.<br/>RIGHT FOREARM.<br/>DELIBERATE ALTERATION.<br/>RETURN INSTRUCTION.<br/>PARTIAL REDUCTION WHILE DRAW MAINTAINED.<br/>INITIAL SHIFT TOWARD ELBOW.<br/>LATER NARROWING / DIMMING.<br/>UNREQUESTED URGE TO CURL FINGERS. NO MOVEMENT.<br/>RELEASED ON HESSA INSTRUCTION.<br/>NO PAIN / TINGLING / NUMBNESS / COLD / WEAKNESS AFTER.<br/>NO CONCLUSION YET.</p><p>That belonged in the notebook.</p><p>I looked at the empty part of the table where Teren's page had been.</p><p>Nothing to write.</p><p>Tomorrow I could ask Pessa to train.</p><p>I could find Lyssa after work.</p><p>I could do nothing.</p><p>I could go west.</p><p>Four options.</p><p>Probably more.</p><p>Theatre was only one.</p><p>That should have made it smaller.</p><p>It did not.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="112.html">← Chapter 89</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="115.html">Chapter 91 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/018.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 14: The Experimenter — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 14</div><h1>THE EXPERIMENTER</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Hessa had beans.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Hessa Has Beans" decoding="async" height="357" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/018/v28_c18_s14_hessa-has-beans.png" width="296"/></figure><p>This was worse than anger.</p><p>I had spent most of the walk to her rooms constructing possible versions of the conversation. She believed me. She did not believe me. She believed enough to stop teaching me. She believed enough to ask questions I could not answer. She had told somebody. She had found a scholar. She had found a priest. She had found a very large man with a sack.</p><p>Instead, she opened the door, looked at my bruised face, and said, "You're late."</p><p>"I was robbed yesterday."</p><p>"Were you?"</p><p>"Technically somebody else was being robbed. Then I became involved."</p><p>"That sounds more like you."</p><p>She stepped aside.</p><p>The three wooden cups were gone from the table. In their place sat a shallow bowl filled with dried white beans, another empty bowl, a clay lamp, and a folded cloth.</p><p>I stared at the beans.</p><p>Hessa waited beside the table until I looked up.</p><p>"Problem?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"You look offended."</p><p>"I have complicated feelings about legumes."</p><p>"You told me you were fifty-eight years old."</p><p>"Mentally."</p><p>"And beans frighten you."</p><p>"They don't frighten me."</p><p>Hessa shut the door. "Sit."</p><p>I sat.</p><p>That was progress. Three days ago, I would have made a joke about obedience and then sat. The difference was microscopic and probably meaningless, which meant I immediately wanted credit for it.</p><p>Hessa took the chair opposite me.</p><p>For several breaths she did nothing.</p><p>She did not ask about the Chronoclast.</p><p>She did not ask about the future.</p><p>She did not ask whether I had spent the last few days remembering additional impossible things.</p><p>She looked at the bruise along my jaw.</p><p>"What happened?"</p><p>"A man hit me."</p><p>"I had gathered that."</p><p>"He was very committed to the traditional method."</p><p>"Did you cast?"</p><p>"Once."</p><p>Her eyes moved from my jaw to my hands.</p><p>"Barrier?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"What did you block?"</p><p>"An iron hook."</p><p>"With your current Barrier?"</p><p>"Not exactly."</p><p>That got her attention.</p><p>I explained the warehouse. Not all of it. Alden's name stayed out. So did the bells. Hessa had enough impossible information without me adding a young adventurer who made my memory sound like a drunk soldier trying to remember the fourth verse of a tavern song.</p><p>I described the hook coming through the broken partition. I described its angle, the man pulling from the other side, and the amount of time I had.</p><p>"I couldn't stop it," I said.</p><p>"You tried anyway."</p><p>"No."</p><p>Hessa's expression changed slightly.</p><p>I held up one finger.</p><p>"I touched the side of it."</p><p>"You touched an iron hook with Barrier."</p><p>"Briefly."</p><p>"How briefly?"</p><p>"I don't know."</p><p>"Then you don't know what you did."</p><p>"I know what happened."</p><p>"That is not the same sentence."</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>Hessa slid the bowl of beans between us.</p><p>I stopped smiling.</p><p>"The hook moved," I said. "Not much. Enough to miss my head and catch my sleeve instead."</p><p>Hessa leaned back.</p><p>"What shape?"</p><p>"Small plane."</p><p>"How small?"</p><p>I showed her with thumb and forefinger.</p><p>Her eyebrows rose.</p><p>"That is smaller than the one you put in the cup."</p><figure class="chapter-art sketch-beat"><img alt="The Cup" decoding="async" height="357" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/018/v28_c18_s15_the-cup.png" width="331"/></figure><p>"Yes."</p><p>"And you formed it while somebody was trying to put iron through your skull."</p><p>"Wall."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"He was trying to put iron through the wall. My skull was an incidental complication."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"About that size."</p><p>She looked at my fingers again.</p><p>Then she reached for the bowl of beans.</p><p>Of course she did.</p><p>"What are these for?" I asked.</p><p>"Teaching."</p><p>"That is a category, not an answer."</p><p>"It is the answer you are getting."</p><p>Hessa took one bean and placed it on the table between us.</p><p>"Move it," Hessa said.</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>"With Barrier?" I asked.</p><p>Hessa looked at me until I answered the unnecessary question myself.</p><p>I hated teachers.</p><p>I gathered mana.</p><p>The sensation was still wrong. That had become less surprising, which was its own kind of danger. The first days, every attempt had screamed at me that I was wearing somebody else's channels. Now the pathways were beginning to become familiar. Not good. Not strong. Familiar. That made it easier to forget how little they could actually carry.</p><p>I formed the smallest plane I could manage beside the bean.</p><p>The structure wanted to become something I recognized.</p><p>Flat. Anchored. Resistant.</p><p>Barrier.</p><p>I pressed.</p><p>The bean skittered three inches and rolled off the table.</p><p>Hessa watched it fall, reached into the bowl, and put a fresh bean on the same spot before I could bend to retrieve the first.</p><p>"Again," Hessa said.</p><p>I looked at the bowl.</p><p>"That is an irresponsible attitude toward beans," I said.</p><p>"Again," Hessa said.</p><p>Second bean.</p><p>This time I put the plane closer.</p><p>Too close.</p><p>The Barrier formed partly through the bean's edge, failed to stabilize, and collapsed before it fully existed.</p><p>A needle of pain ran behind my right eye.</p><p>Hessa did not reach for the next bean.</p><p>"What changed?"</p><p>"Placement. I intersected the target," I said.</p><p>The cup had been larger. That mattered more than I wanted it to.</p><p>Hessa slid another bean onto the table.</p><p>I tried again.</p><p>The third moved.</p><p>The fourth did not.</p><p>The fifth jumped hard enough to strike the bowl.</p><p>The sixth rolled in a beautiful straight line, which pleased me more than it should have.</p><p>The seventh taught me nothing.</p><p>The eighth taught me that the seventh had probably taught me something and I had been too pleased with the sixth to notice.</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Hessa stopped reaching for beans.</p><p>"The anchor," I said.</p><p>I looked at the table.</p><p>Barrier had always been easiest to teach as a wall because walls were intuitive. Put a thing here. Tell the world no.</p><p>That was not how I thought about it anymore. It had not been for decades.</p><p>But I was not decades old in the part of me that mattered to the spell.</p><p>I touched the tabletop.</p><p>"When I pushed the bean, I anchored against the room," I said.</p><p>Hessa waited.</p><p>I could feel the old answer behind my teeth. There were names for this. Later names. Better diagrams. At least I thought there were. A lecture hall with blue chalk flashed through my memory, followed by a woman with silver rings on every finger arguing that half the terminology was fraudulent.</p><p>I could not remember her name.</p><p>I could remember that she had been right about something.</p><p>Useful.</p><p>"I think I'm doing too much," I said.</p><p>"The spell is holding a position it doesn't need to hold. I'm making a wall for a job that needs a tap," I said.</p><p>Hessa's eyes narrowed.</p><p>"What would you change?" Hessa asked.</p><p>"I don't know," I said.</p><p>"Good," Hessa said.</p><p>I looked up.</p><p>She meant it.</p><p>Not as mockery.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I had said I did not know.</p><p>Something in my chest disliked that. Something else, quieter and newer, was beginning to enjoy it.</p><p>Hessa pushed the bowl toward me.</p><p>"Find out," Hessa said.</p><p>I took a bean.</p><p>This time I did not cast.</p><p>I turned it between my fingers.</p><p>"What does Barrier need to be Barrier?" I asked.</p><p>Hessa tapped the bean once with a fingertip.</p><p>"What does this exercise need?" Hessa asked.</p><p>I almost answered immediately.</p><p>Then I understood why she had asked.</p><p>I had done it again.</p><p>Given a bean and a table, I had tried to solve Barrier.</p><p>Not move the bean.</p><p>Barrier.</p><p>The whole spell. Its architecture. Its history. Its assumptions. Every possible future use waiting behind the stupid white thing between my fingers.</p><p>I put the bean down.</p><p>"It needs the bean to move," I said.</p><p>I looked at Hessa.</p><p>"How far?" I asked.</p><p>"One finger," Hessa said.</p><p>I stared at her.</p><p>"That's all?" I asked.</p><p>"One finger," Hessa said.</p><p>"You have been letting me throw them across the table," I said.</p><p>"I have been watching you decide what the problem was," Hessa said.</p><p>That was unfair.</p><p>It was also excellent.</p><p>I hated that more.</p><p>I gathered mana again.</p><p>One finger.</p><p>Not a wall.</p><p>Not a defense.</p><p>Not a theory.</p><p>A movement.</p><p>I formed the plane close to the bean and let it exist for as little time as I could manage.</p><p>The Barrier flickered.</p><p>The bean clicked sideways.</p><p>About two fingers.</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>The mana cost had been tiny.</p><p>Not nothing. Nothing was free. But tiny compared with holding the structure long enough to feel stable.</p><p>Hessa's gaze sharpened.</p><p>"Again," Hessa said.</p><p>I did.</p><p>Too weak.</p><p>The Barrier vanished without moving the bean.</p><p>Again.</p><p>Too close. Collapse.</p><p>Again.</p><p>The bean moved half a finger.</p><p>Again.</p><p>One and a half.</p><p>My headache remained a pressure instead of becoming a spike.</p><p>That was interesting.</p><p>Very interesting.</p><p>I forgot Hessa for perhaps thirty seconds.</p><p>Duration.</p><p>I had been shortening duration because I wanted lower cost. Obvious. Basic. Except there was a difference between a short Barrier and a Barrier that never intended to remain.</p><p>I knew that difference.</p><p>I thought I knew that difference.</p><p>Did I?</p><p>Old Greg could hold layered defenses across moving people while changing them under impact. Old Greg had done things with persistence and termination that current me could not reproduce if somebody gave me a month and a second brain.</p><p>But this was not that.</p><p>This was pathetic.</p><p>Tiny.</p><p>A bean.</p><p>My pulse quickened.</p><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>Hessa reached across the table and covered the bowl with the cloth.</p><p>"I've barely started," I said.</p><p>"Nineteen casts," Hessa said.</p><p>I counted backward. I lost track at twelve. That was concerning.</p><p>"I feel fine," I said.</p><p>"You feel interested," Hessa said.</p><p>Hessa left the bowl covered.</p><p>I leaned back.</p><p>The pressure behind my eye had spread toward my temple.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>She had a point.</p><p>I disliked points when other people had them.</p><p>Hessa folded her arms.</p><p>"Tell me what you learned," Hessa said.</p><p>"Brief structures cost less," I said.</p><p>"Do they?" Hessa asked.</p><p>I paused.</p><p>"Mine did," I said.</p><p>"Today," Hessa said.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"With this shape," Hessa said.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"At this size," Hessa said.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"Against a bean," Hessa said.</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>"Good," Hessa said.</p><p>There it was again. Know. Think. Check.</p><p>I knew what had happened. I thought I knew why. I needed to test whether the explanation survived anything more demanding than legumes.</p><p>I said it aloud.</p><p>Hessa nodded once.</p><p>Then she asked, "What did you expect?"</p><p>That was harder.</p><p>"I expected the cost to fall."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because it should."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Because I remember it."</p><p>Her expression went still.</p><p>There was the Chronoclast between us again.</p><p>Not named.</p><p>Not needed.</p><p>"I remember very short structures being cheap," I said. "Cheap enough that I used them constantly."</p><p>"At fifty-eight."</p><p>"Before that."</p><p>"How long before?"</p><p>I opened my mouth.</p><p>Nothing useful arrived.</p><p>A battlefield.</p><p>Rain.</p><p>A Barrier no larger than a thumbnail appearing against the flat of a spearhead.</p><p>A boot sliding where it should have planted.</p><p>Someone laughing.</p><p>Blood on yellow grass.</p><p>I knew the technique.</p><p>I did not know when I had learned it.</p><p>"Years," I said.</p><p>"That is not an answer."</p><p>"It's the one I have."</p><p>Hessa studied me.</p><p>Then she uncovered the bowl.</p><p>I reached for a bean.</p><p>She slapped my hand.</p><p>"Ow."</p><p>"Not today."</p><p>"You just uncovered them."</p><p>"To count."</p><p>She began moving beans from one bowl to the other.</p><p>I watched.</p><p>"You're really counting them."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because I want to know how many times you cast."</p><p>"You could have counted while I was doing it."</p><p>"I did."</p><p>"Then why count again?"</p><p>"Because unlike you, I check."</p><p>I considered stealing a bean.</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>I left the beans alone.</p><p>"Are you going to keep teaching me?" I asked.</p><p>Her hands stopped.</p><p>There it was.</p><p>The actual reason I had come.</p><p>Everything else had been easier.</p><p>Hessa set the last bean into the second bowl.</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>I had prepared for several answers.</p><p>That one hit harder than expected.</p><p>I nodded.</p><p>"Under conditions," she said.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>"What conditions?"</p><p>"You tell me when something you remember conflicts with what your body does."</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>"You tell me before you test anything dangerous."</p><p>"Define dangerous."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"That seems structurally weak."</p><p>"It is intentionally broad."</p><p>I sighed.</p><p>She continued.</p><p>"You do not use me to prove your future right."</p><p>"I don't do that."</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>"Frequently."</p><p>"I do it less now."</p><p>"That is not the same sentence."</p><p>I rubbed my temple.</p><p>"What else?"</p><p>"You stop when I tell you to stop."</p><p>"Within reason."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Hessa."</p><p>"No."</p><p>I considered the problem.</p><p>She waited.</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>"Say it properly."</p><p>"I will stop when you tell me to stop."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>"I reserve the right to complain."</p><p>"I assumed."</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>This time she almost did.</p><p>Almost.</p><p>Then she pointed at my bruised jaw.</p><p>"And if you are going to keep doing guild work, I want to know when you cast under pressure."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because you formed something yesterday that you could not reliably form here three days ago."</p><p>I sat a little straighter.</p><p>"I noticed."</p><p>"Of course you noticed."</p><p>"Pressure can improve access."</p><p>"Or destroy control."</p><p>"Both."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>That answer pleased me. Two things were true at once. Those were usually the interesting problems.</p><p>I looked at the covered beans.</p><p>"Can I ask you something?"</p><p>"You usually do."</p><p>"What do they teach about Barrier now?"</p><p>Hessa's face changed.</p><p>Not much.</p><p>Enough.</p><p>"Now?"</p><p>I had made the mistake before I finished the sentence.</p><p>Current Greg would have said here.</p><p>Old Greg said now.</p><p>I corrected.</p><p>"At the guild schools. Basic structure."</p><p>"You were taught Barrier."</p><p>"Badly."</p><p>"According to you."</p><p>"According to the number of times I got hit."</p><p>"That may have been the student."</p><p>"Unlikely."</p><p>Hessa ignored that.</p><p>"The common beginner form is fixed-plane anchoring. Broad enough to visualize, simple boundary, external reference. You know this."</p><p>"I know the form."</p><p>"Then what are you asking?"</p><p>"Why they teach it that way."</p><p>"Because it is stable."</p><p>I waited.</p><p>She waited back.</p><p>"That's it?"</p><p>"Do you need a mystical answer?"</p><p>"No. I was hoping for a more interesting one."</p><p>"Stable is interesting when the alternative is a student collapsing a spell inside their own hand."</p><p>"Fair."</p><p>"It is easy to see when it fails. Easy to correct. Easy to compare between students. It teaches feed, shape, boundary, anchor, release."</p><p>That was a better answer than the one I remembered.</p><p>Or perhaps I had simply been a worse student than I remembered.</p><p>"Do they teach transient forms?"</p><p>"Not to beginners."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because beginners are bad at them."</p><p>"That is circular."</p><p>"No. A fixed form gives them time to observe what they made. A transient form disappears before an inexperienced caster can tell which part failed."</p><p>I looked at the bean.</p><p>That was annoyingly sensible.</p><p>Later schools had taught quick structures earlier. I remembered that. Probably. But later schools also had better measurement tools, better instructors, standardized exercises, and at least three pieces of equipment that did not exist yet. Maybe. I knew two of them did not. The third might have existed under another name. I had been about to judge an older teaching method by infrastructure it did not possess. Again.</p><p>"That makes sense," I said.</p><p>Hessa stared at me.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You agreed."</p><p>"I agree with people constantly."</p><p>"No."</p><p>"I agree internally."</p><p>"That does not count."</p><p>"It should."</p><p>She stood.</p><p>Lesson over.</p><p>I stood too.</p><p>My head felt better than it had any right to after nineteen casts.</p><p>That bothered me.</p><p>Which meant I wanted to do twenty more.</p><p>I did not.</p><p>Hessa noticed that too.</p><p>"Tomorrow," she said.</p><p>"I have training."</p><p>"With Jorren?"</p><p>"And someone else."</p><p>Her eyes flicked to me.</p><p>"Someone else."</p><p>"Alden."</p><p>I had not intended to say the name.</p><p>The room did not change.</p><p>No bells.</p><p>No half-remembered verse.</p><p>Just Hessa waiting.</p><p>"Marr," I added.</p><p>That changed something.</p><p>Very small.</p><p>Her mouth tightened.</p><p>I noticed because I was looking for reactions now.</p><p>"Hessa?"</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"You know him?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>Too quick.</p><p>Not necessarily a lie.</p><p>I had learned that lesson recently.</p><p>Pattern was not proof.</p><p>Still.</p><p>"You share a name."</p><p>"Many people share names."</p><p>"Do they?"</p><p>"Yes, Greg."</p><p>"How many Marrs do you know?"</p><p>"Enough to know this conversation is over."</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>I almost pushed.</p><p>Old Greg had several ways.</p><p>A joke. A false assumption. A deliberately wrong relationship she would correct. Silence held long enough to make the other person fill it.</p><p>I knew where the pressure points were.</p><p>Or thought I did.</p><p>Hessa had just agreed to keep teaching me after I told her the most impossible thing I knew.</p><p>I let the question go.</p><p>That surprised both of us.</p><p>"Third bell tomorrow?" she asked.</p><p>"Earlier."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>I reached the door.</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>I looked back.</p><p>"Do not experiment with the short Barrier while fighting."</p><p>"I wasn't planning to."</p><p>"You are lying."</p><p>"I am predicting poorly."</p><p>"Do not."</p><p>I opened the door.</p><p>Outside, the morning street was bright and already busy. A cart rolled past with three barrels lashed badly enough that I spent six seconds redesigning the knots in my head.</p><p>Then I thought about the hook.</p><p>A full Barrier would have failed.</p><p>A tiny one had not stopped anything.</p><p>It had changed something already moving.</p><p>Less work.</p><p>Different problem.</p><p>My mind began building tests.</p><p>Bean.</p><p>Pebble.</p><p>Dropped coin.</p><p>Thrown coin.</p><p>Wooden bead.</p><p>Moving stick.</p><p>Too fast.</p><p>Slow first.</p><p>Different angles.</p><p>No.</p><p>One variable.</p><p>I stopped walking.</p><p>Hessa's door opened behind me.</p><p>"No."</p><p>I turned.</p><p>She stood in the doorway.</p><p>"I didn't say anything."</p><p>"You stopped walking."</p><p>"I was thinking."</p><p>"Go home."</p><p>"I am not going home."</p><p>"Where are you going?"</p><p>"The guild."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>I remembered Alden asking for training.</p><p>Jorren's expression when I had spent half a morning improving everybody except myself.</p><p>The South Canal sacks sitting somewhere under guild authority, unidentified and irritating.</p><p>Antonius, who would eventually hear about anything valuable if the city contained enough merchants.</p><p>Alden, who had learned to wait once and immediately wanted another lesson.</p><p>My own body, which still moved half a beat behind decisions it remembered making faster.</p><p>And nineteen beans.</p><p>"I have things to do."</p><p>Hessa looked at me for a long moment.</p><p>"One thing at a time."</p><p>"That is an unreasonable number of things."</p><p>"Greg."</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>I stepped into the street.</p><p>One thing.</p><p>I made it almost half a block before I began wondering whether a Barrier had to be anchored to the room at all.</p><p>That was not an experiment.</p><p>It was only a question.</p><p>Questions were free.</p><p>Mostly.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="017.html">← Chapter 13</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="019.html">Chapter 15 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/013.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 9: The Student — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 9</div><h1>THE STUDENT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>Arlo had improved the regulator without me. I disliked this for almost three seconds. Then I remembered that was the point. He stood at the far end of his workbench with six ceramic housings arranged in a row. Same clay. Same copper contacts. Same little etched channel running around the waist. If I had seen them a month ago, I would have called them identical.</p><p>They were not. That was why the brass-and-glass Tere reference set sat open beside them. Arlo pointed at the first regulator.</p><p>"Tell me." </p><p>I looked at him.</p><p>"Tell you what?"</p><p>"Which is best."</p><p>"Without testing?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Impossible."</p><p>"Good," Arlo said.</p><p>He seated the first regulator into the wooden testing frame.</p><p>"Then watch the test," Arlo said.</p><p>Antonius was spreading. This was becoming a public-health problem. I picked up the first regulator. Arlo slapped my hand. I stared at him. </p><p>He stared back.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Dont Touch Them" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/013/v28_c13_s01_dont-touch-them.png"/></figure><p>"What?"</p><p>"Don't touch them."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because I spent two days making them and I want the six tested in the same condition."</p><p>"I paid for one."</p><p>"You paid for one day. You did not buy the batch," Arlo said.</p><p>I put my hands behind my back.</p><p>"Fine. Explain."</p><p>Arlo did not explain. He picked up the first regulator with wooden tongs and seated it into a crude testing frame. That was new. Not the regulator. The frame. Two uprights. A crosspiece. Copper contacts. A little ceramic cradle. A weighted arm hanging from a pin. Ugly. Functional. I leaned closer.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="The Ugly Fixture" decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/013/v28_c13_s02_the-ugly-fixture.png"/></figure><p>"You made a fixture."</p><p>Arlo tightened the clamp on the frame without looking at me.</p><p>"I made something to stop holding the fucking things in my hand."</p><p>"That's a fixture."</p><p>"It's wood."</p><p>"Wood can be a fixture."</p><p>"It's scrap."</p><p>"Scrap can be a fixture."</p><p>"It took twenty minutes."</p><p>"Many excellent things do."</p><p>Arlo pointed at the wall. I did not leave. He knew I would not. He turned the regulator's input screw a quarter turn. The weighted arm lifted. Not much. He marked the height on a strip of paper fixed behind it. Then he removed the regulator. Second. Same input. The arm lifted. Nearly the same height. Third. Same. Fourth. Slightly lower. Fifth. Almost exactly first.</p><p>Sixth. Higher. Arlo left the regulator in the frame and stepped aside. I leaned over the marks. The spread was narrow. Not perfect. Not even close to what late Arwick Works would eventually produce. But compared with the regulators we had tested before?</p><p>"Fuck," I said.</p><p>"Yes," Arlo said.</p><p>"Again," I said.</p><p>"Six runs answered this test," Arlo said.</p><p>"Then change the order. Warm them first. Cold after. Change the input," I said.</p><p>Every answer had opened three more doors and apparently I intended to kick all of them at once.</p><p>Arlo lifted the testing frame off the bench and put it on the shelf. I experienced actual pain.</p><p>"Those are other tests. I spent two days answering this one," Arlo said.</p><p>I stared at the six regulators.</p><p>"What changed?" I asked.</p><p>Arlo slid the notebook closer to himself.</p><p>I looked from the notebook to the six regulators, trying to inventory clay, firing time, copper thickness, etch depth, cooling, assembly sequence, every reference piece he might have used. The whole workshop wanted to become one answer.</p><p>"You can ask about the result. The process changes are mine until I decide otherwise," Arlo said.</p><p>I closed my mouth. Fair. Annoying. Fair. I had brought him the Tere set. I did not own what he learned from it.</p><p>Arlo took a cracked regulator from beneath the bench. The copper winding had darkened.</p><p>"First I changed the clay. Then the winding. Then the firing. Twenty measurements," Arlo said.</p><p>He opened the notebook to a page of readings and turned that page toward me without surrendering the rest of the notes.</p><p>I read the numbers. Then reread them. The spread had dropped by more than half. Not because the regulator improved. Because the measurement did.</p><p>"That dropped by more than half," I said.</p><p>"I stopped holding the input lead by hand," Arlo said.</p><p>"You separated measurement error from object variation," I said.</p><p>Arlo tapped one finger against the wooden fixture.</p><p>"I stopped holding the wire," Arlo said.</p><p>His version was cheaper and, annoyingly, harder to turn into a lecture.</p><p>"Then the regulators still spread?" I asked.</p><p>"Yes. So I changed one thing. Winding tension," Arlo said.</p><p>Arlo pointed at another object beside the mandrel. A stick. A spool. A hanging weight.</p><p>The copper wire ran from the spool, over a small peg, beneath the weight, then toward the winding mandrel. Constant tension. Crude. Good. Very good.</p><p>"You built a tensioner," I said.</p><p>"I hung a weight on a string," Arlo said.</p><p>"That is what a tensioner is if you are poor," I said.</p><p>Arlo laughed once despite himself, then reached for the next regulator.</p><p>I looked around the workshop. The roof still sagged. The shelves still held too many half-finished jobs. A cracked crucible sat beside a bucket. There was clay under Arlo's fingernails and a burn on one thumb. Nothing had transformed. That mattered. I had been expecting breakthroughs to arrive with visible grandeur because I remembered the future result.</p><p>ARWICK.</p><p>Factories. Precision. A name stamped on devices used in half the civilized world. But perhaps this was what the beginning actually looked like. A man stopped holding a wire. Then hung a weight from a string. History was insulting.</p><p>"What did the tensioner do?" I asked.</p><p>"Reduced spread again," Arlo said.</p><p>"How much?" I asked.</p><p>Arlo showed me. I read. She sighed.</p><p>"What was the relic called?"</p><p>"Chronoclast."</p><p>Her eyes narrowed.</p><p>"You know the name."</p><p>"It was written on it."</p><p>"Language?"</p><p>"I could read it."</p><p>"That's not what I asked," Hessa said.</p><p>I thought back. The lettering. Had I known the script? I remembered the word. Not the letters. That was bad.</p><p>"I don't remember."</p><p>"Convenient."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Where did you find it?" Hessa asked.</p><p>I hesitated.</p><p>"Late-life expedition."</p><p>"Where?"</p><p>"I can tell you what I remember. Not what I can prove."</p><p>"Good."</p><p>So I did. Not everything. Not names that could become weapons. Not wars. Not people. Not Antonius's future. Not Arlo's. I told her the shape of the event: old ruin, unknown relic, touch, activation, wake, nineteen. She interrupted constantly. Did I feel mana? Maybe. Pain? Not exactly. Light?</p><p>Yes.</p><p>Color? I thought blue. Then doubted it. Sound? Maybe metal. Did the relic come with me?</p><p>No.</p><p>Did anything else?</p><p>No.</p><p>Clothes?</p><p>No.</p><p>Injuries?</p><p>No.</p><p>Scars? Gone. Mana development? Gone. Memory? Present but imperfect. She made me separate observation from interpretation. I recognized the method.</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Nothing."</p><p>"You smiled."</p><p>"I made lists."</p><p>"When?"</p><p>"First morning."</p><p>"What lists?"</p><p>"What I know. What I think I know. What I can verify," I said.</p><p>Hessa stared at me. Then laughed. This one was real. Small.</p><p>"You woke up forty years younger and made categories."</p><p>"It was a stressful morning."</p><p>"You're an idiot."</p><p>"I've heard," I said.</p><p>Hessa looked at the cup again.</p><p>"Good categories."</p><p>"Thank you."</p><p>"Use them."</p><p>"I do."</p><p>"No. You use them when you're frightened enough to remember you're not omniscient."</p><p>That was rude. Accurate. Rude. I pulled the wrapped regulator from my pocket. Hessa's eyes narrowed.</p><p>"What is that?"</p><p>"One thing."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"A regulator Arlo made."</p><p>"Who is Arlo?"</p><p>"Artificer."</p><p>"Why do you have it?"</p><p>"He gave it to me."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"Because I brought him a calibration set from a failed artificer whose work becomes historically important," I said.</p><p>Hessa stared.</p><p>"That sentence is why I regret asking."</p><p>"Yes," I said.</p><p>Hessa held out her hand. I gave her the regulator. She turned it over.</p><p>"Does it work?"</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"What are you doing with it?"</p><p>"I don't know."</p><p>"Good," Hessa said.</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>"Everyone keeps saying that."</p><p>"Maybe because you keep trying to know what everything becomes before you know what it is."</p><p>I took the regulator back. Arlo's fifth regulator. Not Arwick Works. Not a revolution. A low-flow regulator that could run a lamp. Maybe a heater. Maybe a measuring instrument. One thing. Hessa pointed at my pocket.</p><p>"Put it away." </p><p>I did. Then she picked up the cup.</p><p>"Tomorrow."</p><p>"More cups?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"What?"</p><p>"Beans." I stared.</p><p>"Beans."</p><p>"Yes."</p><p>"Why?"</p><p>"You'll see."</p><p>"Are they magical beans?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Can they be?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"Do I get to throw them?"</p><p>"No."</p><p>"This training has declined sharply."</p><p>"Tomorrow." </p><p>I stood. At the door, </p><p>she said, "Greg." </p><p>I turned. </p><p>She looked less certain than she had during the lesson. That frightened me more.</p><p>"If this is a lie..."</p><p>"It isn't."</p><p>"I didn't finish."</p><p>"Sorry."</p><p>"If this is a lie, I stop teaching you."</p><p>"Fair."</p><p>"If it's true, I may still stop teaching you."</p><p>That hurt. I nodded.</p><p>"Fair."</p><p>"I need to think."</p><p>"Okay."</p><p>"And you don't tell anyone I know."</p><p>"Obviously."</p><p>"Nothing is obvious with you."</p><p>"Fair." I reached for the door.</p><p>"Greg." </p><p>I looked back again.</p><p>"Do not touch any relics," Hessa said.</p><p>I considered the wording.</p><p>"Unknown relics?"</p><p>"Any."</p><p>"That seems broad."</p><p>"Any."</p><p>"What if..."</p><p>"Any."</p><p>"Fine."</p><p>I left. Outside, Carrow continued existing with insulting normality. Carts. Mud. A dog barking at a wheel. Two women arguing over onions. A boy running with a loaf under one arm. No thunder. No temporal investigators. No gods descending to tell me I had violated the terms of my impossible second life. I walked. My chest felt strange. Hessa knew. Not suspected.</p><p>Knew what I had told her. Whether she believed it was another question. For the first time since waking, the secret existed outside my skull. I regretted it. Then didn't. Then did again. Very efficient. I passed a lamp-maker's shop. Stopped. Looked at the wrapped regulator in my hand. Low flow. Lamp. One thing. I could buy a lamp assembly.</p><p>Test the regulator. Learn what Arlo had actually made. Then I could...</p><p>No.</p><p>I laughed. The shopkeeper looked at me through the window. I kept walking. One thing did not mean I had to choose the thing today. That was apparently allowed. At the next corner, someone shouted my name. I turned. Jorren stood across the street carrying two practice swords.</p><p>"You're late."</p><p>"For what?"</p><p>"Me."</p><p>"I wasn't coming to you today."</p><p>"You said third bell," Jorren said.</p><p>I searched memory. Today. Third bell. Sword. Fuck.</p><p>"Correct," I said.</p><p>Jorren tossed me a wooden sword. I caught it. Barely. </p><p>He smiled.</p><p>"You look distracted."</p><p>"I've had an educational morning."</p><p>"Good." He stepped into the alley beside the training yard. </p><p>I followed.</p><p>"What did you learn?" Jorren asked.</p><p>I looked at the sword. At my hand. At the young wrist beneath it. Then I smiled.</p><p>"Apparently I don't know how to use this," I said.</p><p>Jorren stopped.</p><p>"Finally," Jorren said.</p><p>I hit him with the practice sword. He blocked it. Then hit me in the ribs. Hard. I folded.</p><p>"Still an asshole," I wheezed.</p><p>"That you know," Jorren said.</p><p>He was right. Useful. </p><p>We started again.</p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="011.html">← Chapter 8</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="014.html">Chapter 10 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

Gone by evening.</p><p>Residual limb baseline.</p><p>Right calf ordinary.</p><p>Everything boring.</p><p>Excellent.</p><p>Hessa had examined all of it anyway.</p><p>Then she had drawn the dot.</p><p>I said, “Why there?”</p><p>“Because it is not your thumb.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>“And because I want a small target that does not require you to rotate the wrist to look at it once your hand is down.”</p><p>“You think I moved because I was aiming visually.”</p><p>“I think movement was one thing that happened.”</p><p>“Not necessarily cause.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“You're training me.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You just praised the distinction.”</p><p>“That is not training.”</p><p>“It feels like training.”</p><p>“Greg.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>The straight copper strip lay on the table.</p><p>No curved one.</p><p>A shallow ceramic dish sat beside it.</p><p>Empty.</p><p>I looked at the dish.</p><p>“What is that?”</p><p>“A dish.”</p><p>“Useful.”</p><p>“Thank you.”</p><p>“What is it for?”</p><p>“Nothing yet.”</p><p>I hated nothing yet.</p><p>It had become a whole category of threat.</p><p>Hessa sat across from me.</p><p>“Today's test is one attempt.”</p><p>I stopped joking.</p><p>“One.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Even if nothing happens?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Even if I fail immediately?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Even if I succeed?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That last one mattered.</p><p>I nodded.</p><p>“Instruction?”</p><p>“Minimal draw.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Hold stable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Then make one deliberate alteration toward the marked point.”</p><p>“Into the hand?”</p><p>“Toward the marked point.”</p><p>“How localized?”</p><p>“Smaller than the whole hand.”</p><p>“That is generous.”</p><p>“It is deliberately less precise than the thumb instruction.”</p><p>I thought about that.</p><p>“You changed difficulty.”</p><p>“I changed the question.”</p><p>“Which is?”</p><p>“Whether you can make a deliberate unfamiliar alteration toward a new intact-side target without immediately falling into the same broader pattern we saw before.”</p><p>There.</p><p>Clean.</p><p>Not whether I could make perfect finger magic.</p><p>Not whether Barrier If hand symptoms return, tell me and use judgment before loading it heavily.”</p><p>“Use judgment again.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You are degrading.”</p><p>“I am adapting to circumstance.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>My own sentence.</p><p>Theft.</p><p>“I hate you.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Professionally.”</p><p>“Still no.”</p><p>I stood.</p><p>At the door I stopped.</p><p>“Right hand only still?”</p><p>“For shaping tests?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“For now.”</p><p>“Left remains not yet.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Because you don't want the missing-side question.”</p><p>“Correct.”</p><p>Not fear.</p><p>Not hidden knowledge.</p><p>Just scope.</p><p>Good.</p><p>“Can you wash the dot off?”</p><p>“There's a basin.”</p><p>I went to it.</p><p>Water.</p><p>Soap.</p><p>Charcoal faded.</p><p>I noticed the hand moving.</p><p>Did not turn it into a test.</p><p>Mostly.</p><p>When I came back, Hessa was writing.</p><p>“Gone.”</p><p>“I can see.”</p><p>“Any significance?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>I left.</p><p>Outside, I wanted to tell someone.</p><p>Immediately.</p><p>This was not a subtle desire.</p><p>Jorren first.</p><p>No.</p><p>He would say I succeeded at hand failure.</p><p>Alden would ask twenty questions and then try to invent an audience.</p><p>Lyssa.</p><p>That thought arrived differently.</p><p>Not because she would understand the magical mechanics better.</p><p>She would not.</p><p>Because I wanted her to know.</p><p>Simple.</p><p>I started toward where she worked.</p><p>Then stopped.</p><p>Independent schedules.</p><p>She might be busy.</p><p>That did not mean I could not go.</p><p>It meant I could not expect availability.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>I went.</p><p>She was busy.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>I saw her through the open front of the shop speaking to a customer and holding up two lengths of ribbon.</p><p>One dark.</p><p>One pale.</p><p>Her natural hair made a soft dark shape around her head, and she stood taller than the customer beside her.</p><p>She saw me.</p><p>One glance.</p><p>Then back to the customer.</p><p>No rescue.</p><p>Good.</p><p>I waited outside.</p><p>Not directly in the doorway.</p><p>Learned civilization.</p><p>Five minutes.</p><p>Maybe ten.</p><p>I did not time it.</p><p>Eventually the customer left with the pale ribbon.</p><p>Lyssa came out.</p><p>“You're lurking.”</p><p>“I am waiting.”</p><p>“Suspiciously.”</p><p>“I shaped mana.”</p><p>Her face changed.</p><p>Not huge.</p><p>Real.</p><p>“You what?”</p><p>“Small.”</p><p>“What does small mean?”</p><p>“Hand.”</p><p>She looked at my right hand.</p><p>Everyone did this.</p><p>I held it up.</p><p>“Nothing visible.”</p><p>“Did it hurt?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Are you allowed?”</p><p>“Yes. One attempt. Supervised.”</p><p>“Hessa?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Did she look angry?”</p><p>“Her normal face.”</p><p>“That bad.”</p><p>“Exactly.”</p><p>Lyssa smiled.</p><p>Then looked at me more carefully.</p><p>“You're happy.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>That was all.</p><p>No explanation.</p><p>No recovery speech.</p><p>No question about whether this meant I was fixed.</p><p>She stepped closer and kissed my cheek.</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Jorren had said the same word.</p><p>Completely different.</p><p>I smiled like an idiot.</p><p>“What happened?”</p><p>I told her the short version.</p><p>Not Hessa's version.</p><p>“I had to move a tiny amount toward a charcoal mark on my hand. First time I tried shaping, it went wrong and started doing something that felt like Barrier. Today it went where I wanted. Mostly.”</p><p>“Mostly?”</p><p>“Close enough for Hessa to use the word shaped.”</p><p>“That sounds serious.”</p><p>“It is extremely serious.”</p><p>“Can you do magic now?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>She laughed.</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>“I can do one useless tiny thing once under supervision.”</p><p>“Very impressive.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“I believe you.”</p><p>She did.</p><p>That was dangerous.</p><p>“What are you doing?”</p><p>“Working.”</p><p>“I noticed.”</p><p>“I have another customer coming.”</p><p>“When?”</p><p>“Soon.”</p><p>“Specific.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>Everyone hated precision now.</p><p>“Food later?”</p><p>She considered.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>I groaned.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“That word.”</p><p>“What word?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>She smiled.</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>Cruel.</p><p>“I'll be at the Guild.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“I don't know.”</p><p>“Good reason.”</p><p>“Maybe Jorren.”</p><p>“Tell him I said your hand is heroic.”</p><p>“I will not.”</p><p>“Coward.”</p><p>She went back inside.</p><p>I stayed there another second.</p><p>Not because there was more.</p><p>Because I was happy.</p><p>Then I went.</p><p>At the Guild, Jorren was there.</p><p>Of course.</p><p>He had the dark-handled food knife out.</p><p>Not threatening anyone.</p><p>Cutting an apple with ceremonial seriousness.</p><p>I sat.</p><p>He looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“I shaped.”</p><p>“Thumb?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He stopped cutting.</p><p>“That sounds like cheating.”</p><p>“Hessa changed target.”</p><p>“What target?”</p><p>“Back of hand.”</p><p>“Did you fail it?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>He looked disappointed.</p><p>“Sorry.”</p><p>“You succeeded?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>There it was again.</p><p>He cut another apple slice.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>Nothing.</p><p>“That is all?”</p><p>“What do you want?”</p><p>“I don't know. Awe.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Questions?”</p><p>“Did it hurt?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Can you cast?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Then good.”</p><p>He handed me apple.</p><p>I took it.</p><p>That was enough.</p><p>Later, my thumb did not tingle.</p><p>Neither did the marked patch.</p><p>Nothing strange happened.</p><p>This was almost disappointing.</p><p>I wrote the report upstairs:</p><p>One supervised shaping attempt. New intact-side target on outer back of right hand. Small localized alteration toward target. No broad palm/wrist pattern. No obvious Barrier-like setup. No pain, tingling, weakness, cold, numbness, or external release. No unusual below-knee sensation.</p><p>Then I added:</p><p>Hessa used the word shaped.</p><p>I looked at it.</p><p>That was not a symptom.</p><p>It stayed.</p><p>For once, the conclusion was allowed to be small and still be a conclusion.</p><p>I had shaped mana.</p><p>Once.</p><p>Nothing more.</p><p>Nothing less.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="106.html">← Chapter 84</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="109.html">Chapter 86 →</a></nav></main></body></html>
- `chapters/099.html:3`: <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" name="viewport"/><title>Chapter 79: The Instrument — Peg-Leg Greg</title><link href="../assets/reader.css" rel="stylesheet"/></head><body><header class="site-head"><a href="../index.html">PEG-LEG GREG</a><nav aria-label="Reader navigation" class="site-nav"><a href="../art.html">ART</a><a href="../r2/">R2</a></nav></header><main class="chapter-shell"><header class="chapter-title"><div class="number">CHAPTER 79</div><h1>THE INSTRUMENT</h1></header><article class="prose"><p>My leg was normal in the morning.</p><p>Normal for now.</p><p>That qualification had become permanent.</p><p>The residual limb was its usual size. No extra heat. No tenderness beyond the places that were normally tender when pressed by someone professionally committed to pressing them.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img alt="Greg bent over papers at a worktable with an older craftsman or mentor beside him." decoding="async" loading="lazy" onerror="this.closest('figure').remove()" src="../visual/chapter_art/099/Ch99_Scholar-at-the-Worktable.png"/></figure><p>I went to Hessa.</p><p>I wore the green shirt.</p><p>This was unrelated.</p><p>Probably.</p><p>Hessa opened the door and looked at me.</p><p>“New shirt.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I waited.</p><p>“That’s all?”</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>“I don’t know.”</p><p>“You look disappointed.”</p><p>“I am learning that everyone has insufficient vocabulary.”</p><p>“Sit.”</p><p>The chair remained bad.</p><p>Good.</p><p>The copper strip was on the table.</p><p>No stones.</p><p>No tea yet.</p><p>A folded blanket sat on the examination cot.</p><p>That was new.</p><p>I looked at it.</p><p>Hessa noticed.</p><p>“It’s a blanket.”</p><p>“What is it for?”</p><p>“Being a blanket.”</p><p>I narrowed my eyes.</p><p>She almost smiled.</p><p>“Leg first.”</p><p>Wrapping off.</p><p>Check.</p><p>Temperature.</p><p>Skin.</p><p>Pressure.</p><p>Questions.</p><p>No new swelling.</p><p>No drainage.</p><p>No heat.</p><p>No pain.</p><p>Hands fine.</p><p>Right calf fine.</p><p>Hip fine.</p><p>Shoulder fine.</p><p>She rewrapped the limb.</p><p>“Pessa?”</p><p>“Not since the shield session.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“That sounds like approval.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“She might train me later.”</p><p>“That is between you and Pessa.”</p><p>“After this?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“You just said it was between me and Pessa.”</p><p>“It is. I am telling you I think doing both today would be stupid.”</p><p>“That is structurally inconsistent.”</p><p>“No. You may ask Pessa whether she wants to participate in your stupidity.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“No training today.”</p><p>“Medical advice?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>She picked up the copper strip.</p><p>I sat straighter.</p><p>“Not yet.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Lie down.”</p><p>I looked at the cot.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because we have done two seated draws.”</p><p>“So?”</p><p>“So today I want one variable changed.”</p><p>I looked at her.</p><p>“You said not to turn this into a research project.”</p><p>“I am allowed.”</p><p>“That is becoming your answer to everything.”</p><p>“It works.”</p><p>I moved to the cot.</p><p>Getting onto it was less elegant than chairs.</p><p>One crutch leaned against the wall.</p><p>Right hand on cot.</p><p>Turn.</p><p>Sit.</p><p>Lift what remained of the left leg.</p><p>Swing right leg up.</p><p>Then lie back.</p><p>The blanket went under my head, not over me.</p><p>I felt cheated.</p><p>Hessa moved the second crutch farther from the edge.</p><p>“Why lying?”</p><p>“Less load through the right leg. Less active balance. Different body position.”</p><p>“You think that changes the phantom sensation.”</p><p>“I think it might.”</p><p>“Because?”</p><p>“Because body position changes body sensation.”</p><p>“That is offensively broad.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Do you expect the below-knee feeling to return?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“You expect it not to?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Excellent.”</p><p>She sat beside the cot.</p><p>The ceiling had a crack running from one corner toward the center.</p><p>I had not seen it before.</p><p>There were two small brown water marks near the wall.</p><p>Carrow construction remained committed to uncertainty.</p><p>“Eyes closed,” Hessa said.</p><p>I closed them.</p><p>“Same amount.”</p><p>“As best I can.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>She looped the copper around her fingers.</p><p>I could hear it scrape lightly against skin.</p><p>“Draw.”</p><p>I reached.</p><p>Mana came.</p><p>Third time was easier.</p><p>That worried me.</p><p>Not because anything was wrong.</p><p>Because ease felt like permission and permission was not what ease meant.</p><p>Chest.</p><p>Shoulders.</p><p>Arms.</p><p>Right side.</p><p>Hip.</p><p>Thigh.</p><p>Lower leg.</p><p>Foot.</p><p>Left hip.</p><p>Thigh.</p><p>Knee.</p><p>Then calf.</p><p>I almost lost the draw.</p><p>Not a real calf.</p><p>Sensation.</p><p>Shape.</p><p>Something.</p><p>It continued lower.</p><p>Not like the first time.</p><p>The first had been organized fullness. Occupied.</p><p>This was narrower.</p><p>A line?</p><p>No.</p><p>That was too visual.</p><p>A sense of extension from knee to ankle.</p><p>The foot was not full.</p><p>The ankle felt bent.</p><p>My absent ankle.</p><p>Bent slightly outward.</p><p>I had no evidence it was magical.</p><p>I had no ankle.</p><p>This remained rude.</p><p>“Hold,” Hessa said.</p><p>I held.</p><p>The sensation stayed.</p><p>My ordinary phantom toes appeared on top of it.</p><p>Or within it.</p><p>I could not separate them.</p><p>I tried.</p><p>That changed it.</p><p>The ankle sensation became stronger.</p><p>Fuck.</p><p>Attention mattered.</p><p>Or seemed to.</p><p>Or I had just changed my own report by examining it.</p><p>“Release.”</p><p>I released immediately.</p><p>Mana left.</p><p>The narrow extension vanished.</p><p>The phantom ankle remained bent for perhaps two breaths.</p><p>Then returned to its usual vague position.</p><p>I opened my eyes.</p><p>Hessa was looking at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>I told her.</p><p>She did not write yet.</p><p>“Again, without interpretation.”</p><p>I stared at the ceiling.</p><p>“Draw felt normal enough. Left awareness continued below the knee. Narrower than first time. Sense from knee toward ankle. Absent ankle felt angled outward. Foot did not feel occupied. While holding, I tried to separate that from ordinary phantom sensation. The ankle sensation increased when I attended to it. After release the extension disappeared first. Phantom ankle position remained briefly.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cold?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Heat?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Pressure?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Cramping?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Residual limb?”</p><p>“Nothing unusual.”</p><p>“Right side?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>“Breathing?”</p><p>“Normal.”</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>I waited.</p><p>“Copper?”</p><p>“Confirmed draw.”</p><p>“Your sensing?”</p><p>“Broadly consistent with the other two.”</p><p>“Above knee?”</p><p>“Present.”</p><p>“Below?”</p><p>“I did not establish below-knee channel response.”</p><p>I exhaled.</p><p>“You enjoy that sentence.”</p><p>“It remains true.”</p><p>I sat up.</p><p>“Stay there.”</p><p>“I am sitting.”</p><p>“On the cot.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because I want to check aftereffects before you stand.”</p><p>Fine.</p><p>I sat.</p><p>The phantom ankle felt normal.</p><p>Normal was now doing dangerous amounts of labor.</p><p>“What did changing position tell us?” I asked.</p><p>Hessa kept writing.</p><p>“That you can draw lying down.”</p><p>“That was not in doubt.”</p><p>“It was untested.”</p><p>I hated that.</p><p>“What else?”</p><p>“Your subjective below-knee experience changed again.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“So now we have occupied, nothing, and narrow extension.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Which means?”</p><p>“That your reports are inconsistent.”</p><p>“Or variable.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Dependent on position?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Attention?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Expectation?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Channel behavior?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Body map?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Interaction?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“This is terrible.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“It is three incompatible results.”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Occupied, absent, line.”</p><p>“Those are your descriptions. They are not necessarily three different mechanisms.”</p><p>I stopped.</p><p>Fine.</p><p>“Also,” she said, “you are trying to make the subjective sensation the main result again.”</p><p>“It is interesting.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“You don’t find it interesting?”</p><p>“Very.”</p><p>“Then.”</p><p>“The main result is still that you completed another minimal draw without pain, instability, obvious shaping, or immediate physical consequence.”</p><p>Third draw.</p><figure class="chapter-art scene-illustration"><img src="../visual/chapter_art/099/Ch099_Fast-Coverage-003-C14.jpg" alt="A sketch-style story scene from Chapter 99." loading="lazy"/></figure><p>Three successful draws.</p><p>That mattered.</p><p>I looked at my hands.</p><p>Nothing visible.</p><p>Still.</p><p>“Three.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Hessa.”</p><p>“Three clean draws do not clear shaping.”</p><p>I had been about to ask.</p><p>“Fine.”</p><p>“What would?”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>She finally poured tea.</p><p>From where had the tea been hiding?</p><p>There was apparently an infinite supply.</p><p>I stayed on the cot because getting down for tea seemed inefficient.</p><p>Hessa handed me the cup.</p><p>“Are you going to repeat lying down next time?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Or seated?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Standing?”</p><p>“Maybe.”</p><p>“Your profession is built on this word.”</p><p>“Your profession is built on asking questions that deserve it.”</p><p>Fair.</p><p>I drank.</p><p>“What would make you move to shaping?”</p><p>She looked at me.</p><p>Not annoyed.</p><p>Considering.</p><p>That was worse for my pulse.</p><p>“Enough confidence that minimal draw is repeatable without concerning immediate or delayed effects.”</p><p>“How much is enough?”</p><p>“I don’t know yet.”</p><p>“Then what are you looking for?”</p><p>“Patterns.”</p><p>“That is vague.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Pain?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Delayed swelling?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Fatigue?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Instability?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Unintended shaping?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Changes in baseline phantom symptoms?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Anything else?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Things I have not thought of.”</p><p>I frowned.</p><p>“That is not measurable.”</p><p>“It is reality.”</p><p>Holl’s testing room appeared in my head.</p><p>Sticky tray.</p><p>Fields that did not include sticky tray.</p><p>I almost said it.</p><p>I did not.</p><p>Hessa looked at me.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“Nothing.”</p><p>“That was real nothing?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>Personal record.</p><p>“Can I see your notebook now?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>“Still because I’ll reproduce it?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“But I already know my reports.”</p><p>“You know what you remember saying.”</p><p>“That is hostile.”</p><p>“It is accurate.”</p><p>“Can I keep my own notes?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I blinked.</p><p>“What?”</p><p>“You can write what you experienced after you leave.”</p><p>“You told me not to research myself.”</p><p>“I told you not to chase records or self-test. Writing symptoms is not self-testing.”</p><p>“What if I compare them?”</p><p>“You will.”</p><p>“That sounded resigned.”</p><p>“It is.”</p><p>“So allowed?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Can I make a table?”</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I laughed.</p><p>She did too.</p><p>Briefly.</p><p>There.</p><p>Human.</p><p>Then gone.</p><p>“Paragraphs,” she said.</p><p>“You are prescribing prose?”</p><p>“I am preventing columns.”</p><p>“This is discrimination against structure.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>I finished the tea.</p><p>Hessa checked the residual limb again.</p><p>No change.</p><p>Hands.</p><p>No tremor.</p><p>Pulse had settled.</p><p>She had me sit another few minutes.</p><p>Then:</p><p>“Stand.”</p><p>Both crutches.</p><p>Right foot.</p><p>Push.</p><p>No problem.</p><p>The phantom foot felt present but not planted.</p><p>No cold.</p><p>No extension.</p><p>No magical anything.</p><p>I reported it.</p><p>She wrote.</p><p>“Tomorrow?” I asked.</p><p>“No.”</p><p>I stared.</p><p>“Another boring day?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“This is becoming excessive.”</p><p>“Day after.”</p><p>“Again?”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>“Why?”</p><p>“Because three successful draws in four days is enough information for now.”</p><p>“That sounds almost optimistic.”</p><p>“It is cautious.”</p><p>“Those can coexist.”</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I smiled.</p><p>She pointed at the door.</p><p>“Go.”</p><p>“Pessa?”</p><p>“Tell her no training today.”</p><p>“She owns movement.”</p><p>“Tell her I said no training today.”</p><p>“And if she disagrees?”</p><p>“She won’t.”</p><p>“That is confidence.”</p><p>“That is knowing Pessa.”</p><p>Interesting.</p><p>I collected the crutches.</p><p>At the door Hessa said, “Greg.”</p><p>I turned.</p><p>“No draw.”</p><p>“I will not draw mana without you or someone you explicitly clear.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“No shaping.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“No casting.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“No private experiments.”</p><p>“Good.”</p><p>“I may write paragraphs.”</p><p>She sighed.</p><p>“Yes.”</p><p>I opened the door.</p><p>“Not tables.”</p><p>“I heard you.”</p><p>Outside, Carrow was bright and loud and entirely uninterested in my third successful mana draw.</p><p>A wagon nearly splashed me with gutter water.</p><p>Someone was arguing about onions.</p><p>A bell rang twice from somewhere west.</p><p>I stood there in my green shirt with two crutches and a body that remained an instrument no one had calibrated.</p><p>Three draws.</p><p>Three different below-knee reports.</p><p>No pain.</p><p>No answer.</p><p>I was pleased anyway.</p><p>Then the onion argument became more interesting.</p><p>I went that way.<br/></p></article><nav class="chapter-nav chapter-nav-top" aria-label="Chapter navigation"><a rel="prev" href="098.html">← Chapter 78</a><a href="../index.html#books">Chapters</a><a rel="next" href="100.html">Chapter 80 →</a></nav></main></body></html>

- `exports/notebooklm/PLG_BOOK_II_CH083-180.md:8483`: I felt the familiar internal readiness that came before drawing mana, except smaller and incomplete, like hearing the first note of a song and knowing the next one without singing it.
